Even a tenant at will (one with no formal lease) who pays the full value of the land is not completely dependent upon the landlord. The financial advantages they receive from one another are mutual and equal. Such a tenant will not risk his life or his fortune in the service of the landowner. But if a tenant has a lease for a long term of years, he is **altogether independent**. His landlord must not expect from him even the most trivial service beyond what is either expressly stated in the lease or required of him by the common and known law of the country.

#### The Fall of the Lords and Rise of Order

With the tenants having become independent in this manner, and the retainers being dismissed, the great landowners were no longer capable of interrupting the regular execution of justice or of disturbing the peace of the country.
* They had sold their birthright (their power and authority), not like Esau in the Bible for a bowl of stew in a time of hunger and necessity, but in the indulgence of plenty, for trinkets and baubles that were more fit to be the playthings of children than the serious pursuits of men.
* As a result, they became as insignificant as any substantial townsman or tradesman in a city.
* A regular government was established in the country as well as in the city. Nobody had sufficient power to disturb its operations in one place any more than in the other.

#### An Aside: Old Families in Commercial vs. Non-Commercial Countries

It does not, perhaps, directly relate to the present subject, but I cannot help remarking that very old families—those that have possessed some considerable estate from father to son for many successive generations—are very rare in commercial countries. In countries that have little commerce, on the contrary, such as Wales or the highlands of Scotland, they are very common. Arabian histories seem to be full of genealogies. There is a history written by a Tartar Khan, which has been translated into several European languages, and which contains scarcely anything else. This is proof that ancient families are very common among those nations.

In countries where a rich man can spend his income in no other way than by supporting as many people as that income can maintain, he is not likely to run through his fortune quickly. His generosity, it seems, is seldom so excessive as to attempt to support more people than he can afford. But where he can spend the greatest income on his own person, he frequently has no limits to his expense. This is because he frequently has no limits to his vanity or to his affection for his own person. In commercial countries, therefore, riches, despite the most forceful laws designed to prevent their being wasted, very seldom remain long in the same family. Among simple nations, on the contrary, riches frequently do remain in the same family without any such laws. For among nations of shepherds, such as the Tartars and Arabs, the consumable nature of their property (mostly livestock) necessarily makes all such laws to preserve wealth in families impossible.

#### An Unintended Revolution

A revolution of the greatest importance to public happiness was brought about in this way by two different groups of people who had not the least intention to serve the public:
1.  **The great landowners:** Their sole motive was to satisfy the most childish vanity.
2.  **The merchants and craftsmen:** They were much less ridiculous. They acted merely from a view to their own interest, and in pursuit of their own "peddler principle" of turning a penny wherever a penny was to be made.

Neither of these groups had any knowledge or foresight of the great revolution that the foolishness of the one and the industry of the other was gradually bringing about.

### Conclusion: How City Commerce Transformed the Countryside

It is in this way that, through the greater part of Europe, the commerce and manufactures of cities, instead of being the *effect* of the improvement and cultivation of the country, have actually been the *cause and occasion* of it.

This order of development, however, being contrary to the natural course of things (where agriculture improves first and then supports cities), is necessarily both **slow and uncertain**.
* Compare the slow progress of those European countries whose wealth depends very much on their commerce and manufactures with the rapid advances of our North American colonies, whose wealth is founded entirely on agriculture.
* Through the greater part of Europe, the number of inhabitants is not thought to double in less than five hundred years. In several of our North American colonies, it is found to double in twenty or twenty-five years.

In Europe, the law of primogeniture and various types of perpetuities (like entails) prevent the division of great estates. This, in turn, hinders the multiplication of small landowners.
* A **small landowner**, however, who knows every part of his little territory, who views it with all the affection that property (especially small property) naturally inspires, and who for that reason takes pleasure not only in cultivating it but in adorning it, is generally, of all improvers, the most industrious, the most intelligent, and the most successful.
* These same regulations also keep so much land out of the market that there are always more people with capital wanting to buy land than there is land available to sell. As a result, what land is sold always sells at a monopoly price. The rent from the land never pays the interest that could have been earned on the purchase money. Besides, owning land comes with the burden of repairs and other occasional charges, to which money lent out at interest is not liable.
* To purchase land is everywhere in Europe a **most unprofitable use of a small amount of capital.**
* For the sake of the superior security it offers, a man of moderate circumstances, when he retires from business, will sometimes choose to invest his small capital in land. A professional person too, whose income is derived from another source, often loves to secure his savings in the same way.
* But a young man who, instead of going into trade or some profession, were to use a capital of two or three thousand pounds to purchase and cultivate a small piece of land, might indeed expect to live very happily and very independently. However, he must say goodbye forever to all hope of either great fortune or great public recognition, which he might have had the same chance of acquiring as other people if he had used his capital differently.
* Such a person too, though he cannot aspire to be a landowner, will often disdain to be merely a farmer.
* Therefore, the small quantity of land that is brought to market, and the high price of what is brought there, prevents a great number of capitals from being used in its cultivation and improvement, capitals which would otherwise have taken that direction.

In North America, on the contrary, fifty or sixty pounds is often found to be a sufficient amount of capital to begin a plantation with. The purchase and improvement of uncultivated land is there the most profitable employment for the smallest as well as the largest amounts of capital. It is also the most direct road to all the fortune and public recognition that can be acquired in that country. Such land, indeed, is available in North America for almost nothing, or at a price much below the value of what it can naturally produce – a situation impossible in Europe, or indeed, in any country where all lands have long been private property.

If landed estates, however, were divided equally among all the children upon the death of any landowner who left a numerous family, the estate would generally be sold. So much land would come to market that it could no longer sell at a monopoly price. The free rent of the land (rent after all expenses) would come closer to paying the interest on the purchase-money, and a small capital might be used in purchasing land as profitably as in any other way.

### England's Situation

England, on account of:
* The natural fertility of its soil,
* The great extent of its sea-coast in proportion to the size of the whole country,
* And the many navigable rivers that run through it and provide the convenience of water transport to some of the most inland parts of it,
is perhaps as well-suited by nature as any large country in Europe to be the center of foreign commerce, of manufactures for distant sale, and of all the improvements that these can bring.

From the beginning of the reign of Queen Elizabeth I, the English legislature has also been particularly attentive to the interests of commerce and manufactures. In reality, there is no country in Europe, not even Holland itself, whose laws are, on the whole, more favorable to this sort of industry. Commerce and manufactures have accordingly been continually advancing during all this period.

The cultivation and improvement of the country has, no doubt, been gradually advancing too. But it seems to have followed slowly, and at a distance, the more rapid progress of commerce and manufactures. The greater part of the country must probably have been cultivated before the reign of Elizabeth I. Yet, a very great part of it still remains uncultivated today, and the cultivation of the far greater part is much inferior to what it could be.



The law of England, however, helps farming not only indirectly by protecting trade but also with several direct encouragements.
* **Exporting Grain:** Except in times of food shortages, exporting grain (corn) is not only allowed but also encouraged with a government payment (a bounty) to exporters.
* **Importing Grain:** In times when there is a moderate amount of grain, taxes on importing foreign grain are so high that they pretty much stop such imports.
* **Importing Livestock:** Importing live cattle, except from Ireland, is banned at all times. Permission to import them from Ireland was only granted recently.

Because of these rules, those who farm the land in England have a kind of monopoly against their own countrymen for the two biggest and most important products of the land: bread and meat.

These encouragements, though perhaps ultimately not as effective as they seem (as I will try to show later), at least demonstrate the good intention of the lawmakers to support agriculture. But what is much more important than all of them is that the **independent farmers (the yeomanry) of England are made as secure, as independent, and as respected as the law can make them.**

Therefore, no country that has the law of primogeniture (where the eldest son inherits all the land), that pays tithes (a tax to the church), and where land can be tied up indefinitely in families (perpetuities, like entails), even if this goes against the general spirit of the law, can give more encouragement to agriculture than England does.

Even so, this is the current state of farming in England (meaning it's not as good as it could be). What would it have been like if the law had given no direct encouragement to agriculture beyond what comes indirectly from the progress of trade, and if the independent farmers had been left in the same poor condition as in most other countries of Europe? It is now more than two hundred years since the beginning of the reign of Queen Elizabeth I, a period as long as the course of human prosperity usually lasts.

### Comparing England with Other Nations

* **France:** France seems to have had a considerable amount of foreign trade nearly a century before England became well-known as a commercial country. The French navy was quite large for its time, even before King Charles VIII’s expedition to Naples in the late 15th century. However, the farming and agricultural improvement of France are, on the whole, not as advanced as England's. The laws of France have never given the same direct encouragement to agriculture.

* **Spain and Portugal:** The foreign trade of Spain and Portugal with other parts of Europe is very significant, though it is mostly carried on in foreign ships. Their trade with their own colonies is carried on in their own ships and is much greater, because of the great riches and size of those colonies. But this trade has never led to any significant manufacturing industries for distant sale in either Spain or Portugal. The greater part of both countries still remains uncultivated. Portugal's foreign trade is older than that of any other large country in Europe, except for Italy.

* **Italy:** Italy is the only large country in Europe that seems to have been cultivated and improved in every part by means of foreign trade and manufacturing for distant sale. According to the historian Guicciardini, before the invasion of Charles VIII of France (late 15th century), Italy was cultivated just as much in its most mountainous and barren parts as in its flattest and most fertile plains. The advantageous location of the country and the great number of independent states that existed in it at that time probably contributed significantly to this general cultivation. It is also possible, despite this general statement from one of the most sensible and careful modern historians, that Italy at that time was not better cultivated than England is at present.

### The Fragility of Wealth from Trade Alone

However, the capital (wealth) that is acquired by any country through commerce and manufactures is a very **precarious and uncertain possession**. This is true until some part of that capital has been secured and made real by being invested in the cultivation and improvement of its lands.

It has been said very correctly that a merchant is not necessarily the citizen of any particular country. It makes little difference to him from what place he carries on his trade. A very small problem or annoyance will make him move his capital, and along with it all the industry and jobs it supports, from one country to another. No part of his capital can truly be said to belong to any particular country until it has been spread, so to speak, over the face of that country, either in the form of buildings or in the lasting improvement of lands.

For example, no trace now remains of the great wealth said to have been possessed by most of the Hanseatic towns (a medieval trading league in Northern Europe), except in obscure history books from the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. It is even uncertain where some of them were located, or to what modern towns in Europe the Latin names given to some of them belong.

But consider this contrast:
* Although the misfortunes of Italy at the end of the fifteenth and beginning of the sixteenth centuries greatly reduced the trade and manufacturing of the cities in Lombardy and Tuscany, those regions **still continue to be among the most populous and best-cultivated in Europe.**
* The civil wars in Flanders, and the Spanish government that followed them, chased away the great commerce of cities like Antwerp, Ghent, and Bruges. But Flanders **still continues to be one of the richest, best-cultivated, and most populous provinces of Europe.**

The ordinary upheavals of war and changes in government can easily dry up the sources of wealth that arise from commerce only. Wealth that arises from the more solid improvements of agriculture is much more durable. It cannot be destroyed except by those more violent and prolonged disasters caused by the destructive raids of hostile and barbarous nations, continued for a century or two together – such as those that happened for some time before and after the fall of the Roman Empire in the western provinces of Europe.

## BOOK FOUR

**Of Systems of Political Economy**

Political economy, considered as a branch of the knowledge required of a statesman or legislator, has two distinct objects. The first is to provide a plentiful revenue or livelihood for the people, or, more precisely, to enable them to provide such a revenue or livelihood for themselves. The second is to supply the state or commonwealth with a revenue sufficient for the public services. Its aim, in short, is to enrich both the people and the sovereign.

Because wealth has advanced differently in different ages and nations, two distinct systems of political economy have arisen concerning how to enrich the people. One may be called the system of commerce, the other the system of agriculture. I shall try to explain both as fully and clearly as I can, beginning with the system of commerce. It is the modern system, and it is best understood in our own country and in our own times.

### CHAPTER I: OF THE PRINCIPLE OF THE COMMERCIAL OR MERCANTILE SYSTEM

The popular belief that wealth consists in money, or in gold and silver, arises naturally from the two functions that money performs: it is the instrument of commerce, and it is the measure of value. Because it is the instrument of commerce, money lets us obtain whatever else we need more readily than any other commodity could. The great task, we always find, is to get the money; once we have it, every later purchase is easy. Because it is the measure of value, we judge the worth of every other commodity by the quantity of money it will fetch in exchange. We say that a rich man is worth a great deal of money and that a poor man is worth very little. A thrifty man, or a man eager to be rich, is said to love money, while a careless, generous, or extravagant man is said to be indifferent to it. To grow rich is to get money, and in everyday speech wealth and money are treated as identical in every respect.

A rich country, like a rich man, is assumed to be one that abounds in money, and piling up gold and silver within a country is assumed to be the quickest way to make it rich. For some time after the discovery of America, the first question the Spaniards asked on reaching any unknown coast was whether gold or silver could be found nearby. On the strength of the answer, they decided whether the place was worth settling, or whether the country was worth conquering. Plano Carpino, a monk sent as ambassador from the king of France to one of the sons of the famous Genghis Khan, reports that the Tartars often asked him whether the kingdom of France had plenty of sheep and oxen. Their question had the same purpose as the Spaniards'. They wanted to know whether the country was rich enough to be worth conquering. Among the Tartars, as among all pastoral peoples, who generally do not know the use of money, cattle are the instruments of commerce and the measures of value. To them, therefore, wealth consisted in cattle, just as to the Spaniards it consisted in gold and silver. Of the two notions, the Tartar one was perhaps the closer to the truth.

Mr. Locke draws a distinction between money and all other movable goods. Every other kind of movable property, he says, is so easily consumed that wealth made up of it cannot be relied upon. A nation that has an abundance of such goods one year may, without exporting any of them, and simply through its own waste and extravagance, find itself badly short of them the next. Money, by contrast, is a steady friend. It may pass from hand to hand, but so long as it can be kept from leaving the country, it is not very likely to be wasted and used up. Gold and silver, in his view, are therefore the most solid and substantial part of a nation's movable wealth, and for that reason increasing the quantity of those metals ought, he thinks, to be the chief aim of its political economy.

Others concede that if a nation could be cut off from the rest of the world, it would make no difference how much or how little money circulated within it. The consumable goods that this money circulated would simply be exchanged for a larger or smaller number of coins, and the country's real wealth or poverty, they acknowledge, would depend entirely on how plentiful or scarce those goods were. But the case is different, they argue, for countries that have dealings with foreign nations, that must fight foreign wars, and that must maintain fleets and armies in distant lands. None of this can be done without sending money abroad to pay for it, and a nation cannot send much money abroad unless it has a great deal at home. Every such nation, they conclude, must try in peacetime to accumulate gold and silver, so that when the need arises it will have the means to wage war abroad.

As a result of these popular notions, every nation in Europe has studied, with little success, every conceivable way of accumulating gold and silver within its borders. Spain and Portugal, which own the principal mines supplying Europe with those metals, have either prohibited their export under the harshest penalties or subjected it to a heavy duty. A similar prohibition seems to have been part of the policy of most other European nations in earlier times. It appears even where one would least expect it, in some old Scottish acts of Parliament, which forbid, under heavy penalties, the carrying of gold or silver out of the kingdom. The same policy was once in force in both France and England.

When these countries took up commerce, their merchants found the prohibition extremely inconvenient on many occasions. They could often buy the foreign goods they wanted, whether to bring home or to carry on to some other foreign country, on better terms with gold and silver than with any other commodity. They therefore protested against the prohibition as harmful to trade.

Their first argument was that exporting gold and silver to buy foreign goods did not always reduce the quantity of those metals in the kingdom, and might often increase it. If the country's own consumption of foreign goods did not rise as a result, those goods could be re-exported to other countries and sold there at a large profit, bringing back far more treasure than had originally been sent out to buy them. Mr. Mun compares this operation of foreign trade to the sowing and harvesting of a farm. "If we look only at the actions of the farmer at seed-time," he writes, "when he throws a great deal of good grain into the ground, we will take him for a madman rather than a farmer. But when we consider his labors at harvest, which is the purpose of all his efforts, we will see the value and the abundant increase of what he did."

Their second argument was that the prohibition could not in any case stop gold and silver from leaving the country, since those metals, being so small in bulk relative to their value, could easily be smuggled abroad. The only way to prevent their export, the merchants said, was to pay proper attention to what they called the balance of trade. When a country exported goods of greater value than it imported, foreign nations owed it a balance, which was necessarily paid in gold and silver and so increased the quantity of those metals in the kingdom. When it imported goods of greater value than it exported, the country owed a balance to foreign nations, which was necessarily paid in the same way and so reduced that quantity. In this second case, they continued, a prohibition on exporting the metals could not prevent their export; it could only make it more dangerous and therefore more expensive. The rate of exchange was thereby turned further against the debtor country than it would otherwise have been. A merchant who needed to make a payment abroad bought a bill of exchange, a written order directing a correspondent in the foreign country to pay the sum there, and the banker who sold him that bill had to be compensated not only for the ordinary risk, trouble, and expense of sending money abroad, but also for the additional risk created by the prohibition. And the more the exchange ran against a country, they argued, the more the balance of trade necessarily ran against it as well, because that country's money necessarily lost value in comparison with the money of the country to which the balance was owed. Suppose, for example, that the exchange between England and Holland stood five percent against England. It would then take 105 ounces of silver in England to buy a bill for 100 ounces of silver in Holland. In that case 105 ounces of silver in England would be worth only 100 ounces in Holland and would buy only a correspondingly smaller quantity of Dutch goods, while 100 ounces of silver in Holland would be worth 105 ounces in England and would buy a correspondingly larger quantity of English goods. English goods sold to Holland would therefore sell that much more cheaply, and Dutch goods sold to England that much more dearly, by the amount of the difference in the exchange. The first trade would draw that much less Dutch money into England, and the second would draw that much more English money into Holland. The balance of trade, they concluded, would necessarily turn that much further against England, and a still larger balance of gold and silver would have to be exported to Holland.

These arguments were partly sound and partly specious. They were sound insofar as they held that exporting gold and silver in the course of trade might often benefit the country. They were sound, too, in holding that no prohibition could prevent the export of those metals whenever private individuals found it profitable to export them. But they were specious in assuming that preserving or increasing the quantity of those metals demanded more attention from government than preserving or increasing the quantity of any other useful commodity, which free trade, without any such attention, never fails to supply in the proper amount. They were perhaps specious as well in claiming that a high rate of exchange necessarily enlarged what they called the unfavorable balance of trade, or caused a greater quantity of gold and silver to be exported. That high rate was certainly very damaging to merchants who had payments to make abroad, since they paid that much more for the bills their bankers drew for them on foreign countries. But although the risk created by the prohibition might impose some extra expense on the bankers, it would not necessarily send any more money out of the country. That expense would generally be spent entirely at home, on smuggling the money out, and could rarely cause the export of a single sixpence beyond the exact sum for which the bill was drawn. A high rate of exchange would also naturally lead merchants to try to make their exports roughly equal their imports, so that they would have to pay the high rate on as small a sum as possible. Beyond this, a high rate of exchange must necessarily have acted as a tax, raising the price of foreign goods and so reducing their consumption. It would tend, therefore, not to enlarge but to shrink what they called the unfavorable balance of trade, and with it the export of gold and silver.

Whatever their merits, these arguments convinced the people to whom they were addressed. They were put by merchants to parliaments and royal councils, to nobles and country gentlemen; by those who were supposed to understand trade, to those who knew perfectly well that they understood nothing about it. Experience had shown the nobles and country gentlemen, as well as the merchants, that foreign trade enriched the country, but none of them really knew how. The merchants knew exactly how it enriched themselves; that was their business. But knowing how it enriched the country was no part of their business. The question never occurred to them except when they had reason to petition their country for some change in the laws governing foreign trade. At such moments it became necessary to say something about the benefits of foreign trade and about how the existing laws obstructed them. To the judges who had to decide the matter, it seemed an entirely satisfactory account to be told that foreign trade brought money into the country, and that the laws in question prevented it from bringing in as much as it otherwise would. The arguments therefore had the desired effect. In France and England, the ban on exporting gold and silver was restricted to each country's own coin, and the export of foreign coin and of bullion was made free. In Holland, and in some other places, this freedom was extended even to the country's own coin. Government attention shifted from guarding against the export of gold and silver to watching over the balance of trade, now regarded as the only thing that could increase or decrease the quantity of those metals. It turned from one fruitless concern to another, far more complicated, far more troublesome, and just as fruitless. The title of Mun's book, *England's Treasure by Foreign Trade*, became a fundamental maxim of political economy, not in England alone but in every other commercial country. The inland or home trade, the most important of all, the trade in which a given amount of capital yields the greatest revenue and provides the most employment to the country's own people, came to be regarded as merely subordinate to foreign trade. It neither brought money into the country, people said, nor sent any out. The country could therefore never grow richer or poorer through it, except insofar as its prosperity or decline might indirectly affect the state of foreign trade.

A country with no mines of its own must, of course, obtain its gold and silver from abroad, just as a country with no vineyards of its own must obtain its wine from abroad. There seems no reason, however, why the government should pay more attention to the one than to the other. A country that has the means to buy wine will always get the wine it needs, and a country that has the means to buy gold and silver will never lack those metals. They can be bought at a certain price, like every other commodity; and just as they are the price of all other commodities, so all other commodities are the price of them. We trust, with complete confidence, that free trade, without any government attention, will always supply us with the wine we need. We may trust, with equal confidence, that it will always supply us with all the gold and silver we can afford to buy or to use, whether in circulating our goods or for any other purpose.

In every country, the quantity of each commodity that human industry can buy or produce naturally adjusts itself to the effectual demand, that is, to the demand of those who are willing to pay the full rent, wages, and profits that must be paid to prepare the commodity and bring it to market. But no commodities adjust themselves to this effectual demand more easily or more precisely than gold and silver. Because of their small bulk and great value, nothing can be moved more easily from one place to another: from where they are cheap to where they are dear, from where they exceed the effectual demand to where they fall short of it. If there were an effectual demand in England, for example, for an additional quantity of gold, a single packet-boat, one of the small vessels that carried mail and passengers on regular routes, could bring from Lisbon, or from wherever else it could be had, fifty tons of gold, enough to be coined into more than five million guineas. But if there were an effectual demand for grain of the same value, importing it, at five guineas a ton, would require a million tons of shipping, or a thousand ships of a thousand tons each. The entire English navy would not be enough.

When the quantity of gold and silver imported into a country exceeds the effectual demand, no vigilance on the part of government can prevent their export. All the bloody laws of Spain and Portugal cannot keep their gold and silver at home. The constant imports from Peru and Brazil exceed the effectual demand of those two countries and drive the price of the metals there below their price in neighboring countries. If, on the other hand, the quantity in some particular country fell short of the effectual demand, so that their price rose above that in neighboring countries, the government would not need to take any trouble to import them. Even if it took trouble to keep them out, it could not succeed. Once the Spartans had the means to buy those metals, the metals broke through every barrier that the laws of Lycurgus had raised against their entry into Lacedaemon. All the bloody customs laws cannot prevent the import of tea from the Dutch and Gothenburg East India companies, because it is somewhat cheaper than the tea of the British company. Yet a pound of tea is about a hundred times the bulk of sixteen shillings in silver, one of the highest prices commonly paid for it, and more than two thousand times the bulk of the same price in gold, and is therefore that many times harder to smuggle.

It is partly because gold and silver are so easily carried from where they are plentiful to where they are needed that their price does not fluctuate constantly, as does the price of most other commodities, whose bulk prevents them from shifting location when a market happens to be overstocked or understocked. The price of these metals is not entirely free from variation, but the changes it undergoes are generally slow, gradual, and steady. In Europe, for example, it is supposed, perhaps without much foundation, that over the course of the present century and the one before, the metals have been steadily but gradually losing value because of the continual imports from the Spanish West Indies. But to produce any sudden change in the price of gold and silver, one large enough to raise or lower the money price of every other commodity noticeably and all at once, requires a revolution in commerce on the scale of the one brought about by the discovery of America.

If, despite all this, a country that has the means to buy gold and silver should at some point find itself short of them, there are more ways of making up for their absence than for the absence of almost any other commodity. If raw materials for manufacturing are lacking, industry must stop. If food is lacking, the people must starve. But if money is lacking, barter will take its place, though with considerable inconvenience. Buying and selling on credit, with dealers settling their accounts against one another once a month or once a year, will take its place with less inconvenience. A well-regulated paper money will take its place not only without any inconvenience but, in some cases, with certain advantages. On every count, therefore, government attention was never so needlessly employed as when it was directed toward preserving or increasing the quantity of money in a country.

Yet no complaint is more common than that money is scarce. Money, like wine, must always be scarce for those who have neither the means to buy it nor the credit to borrow it. Those who have either will seldom lack the money, or the wine, that they need. This complaint of a scarcity of money, however, is not always confined to reckless spendthrifts. Sometimes it spreads through an entire trading town and the surrounding countryside. The usual cause is over-trading. Sober men whose projects have outgrown their capital are just as likely to have neither the means to buy money nor the credit to borrow it as are prodigals whose spending has outgrown their income. Before their projects can bear fruit, their capital is gone, and their credit with it. They run everywhere trying to borrow money, and everyone tells them there is none to lend. Even such widespread complaints of a scarcity of money do not always prove that the usual number of gold and silver coins has stopped circulating in the country; they show only that many people want those coins who have nothing to give in exchange for them. When the profits of trade happen to be higher than usual, over-trading becomes a general error among large and small dealers alike. They do not always send more money abroad than usual, but they buy on credit, at home and abroad, an unusually large quantity of goods, which they ship to some distant market in the hope that the proceeds will come back before payment falls due. Instead, the demand for payment arrives before the proceeds, and they have nothing on hand with which either to buy money or to offer solid security for a loan. The general complaint about a scarcity of money arises not from any real shortage of gold and silver, but from the difficulty such people have in borrowing, and the corresponding difficulty their creditors have in getting paid.

It would be ridiculous to set out seriously to prove that wealth does not consist in money, or in gold and silver, but in what money buys, and that money is valuable only for what it can buy. Money certainly always forms part of a nation's capital. But it has already been shown that it generally forms only a small part, and always the least profitable part.

A merchant generally finds it easier to buy goods with money than to buy money with goods. This is not because wealth consists more essentially in money than in goods. It is because money is the known and established instrument of commerce: everything is readily given in exchange for it, but it cannot always be obtained as readily in exchange for everything else. Most goods, moreover, are more perishable than money, and the merchant may often suffer a far greater loss by holding them. While his goods remain unsold, he is also more exposed to demands for payment that he may be unable to meet than when he has their price safely in his strongbox. Above all, his profit comes more directly from selling than from buying. For all these reasons, he is generally much more anxious to exchange his goods for money than his money for goods. Yet although a particular merchant with a warehouse full of goods may sometimes be ruined because he cannot sell them in time, a nation is not exposed to the same accident. A merchant's entire capital often consists of perishable goods intended to be sold for money. But only a very small part of the annual produce of a country's land and labor can ever be intended for buying gold and silver from its neighbors. By far the greater part is circulated and consumed at home, and even of the surplus sent abroad, most is generally meant to buy other foreign goods. Even if gold and silver could not be obtained in exchange for the goods intended to buy them, then, the nation would not be ruined. It might suffer some loss and inconvenience, and be driven to some of the expedients people adopt to make up for a lack of money. But the annual produce of its land and labor would remain the same as usual, or very nearly so, because the same, or very nearly the same, consumable capital would be employed in maintaining it. And although goods do not always attract money as readily as money attracts goods, in the long run they attract it more inevitably than it attracts them. Goods can serve many purposes besides buying money, but money can serve no purpose except buying goods. Money therefore necessarily pursues goods, while goods do not always or necessarily pursue money. The person who buys does not always intend to sell again; often he means to use or consume what he has bought. The person who sells, by contrast, always intends to buy again. The buyer may often have completed his entire business, but the seller can never have done more than half of his. People do not desire money for its own sake, but for the sake of what they can buy with it.

It is argued that consumable goods are quickly destroyed, whereas gold and silver are durable and, were it not for their continual export, might be accumulated over many ages, to the incredible increase of the country's real wealth. Nothing, the argument goes, can be more harmful to a country than a trade that exchanges such lasting commodities for such perishable ones. Yet we do not consider it a harmful trade to exchange English hardware for French wine, even though hardware is a very durable commodity and, were it not for its continual export, might likewise be accumulated over many ages, to the incredible increase of the country's pots and pans. Everyone readily sees that the number of such utensils in any country is necessarily limited by the use there is for them. It would be absurd to own more pots and pans than are needed to cook the food usually eaten there, and if the quantity of food were to increase, the number of pots and pans would readily increase along with it, since part of the additional food would be used to buy them, or to support additional workers whose trade it was to make them. It should be just as readily seen that the quantity of gold and silver in any country is limited by the use there is for those metals. Their use consists in circulating goods, in the form of coin, and in providing a kind of household furnishing, in the form of plate, the gold and silver tableware and ornaments of wealthy homes. The quantity of coin in a country is governed by the value of the goods it has to circulate: increase that value, and part of it will immediately be sent abroad to buy, wherever it can be had, the additional coin needed to circulate them. The quantity of plate is governed by the number and wealth of the private families who choose to indulge in that sort of splendor: increase the number and wealth of such families, and part of their increased wealth will very probably be spent on buying, wherever it can be found, additional plate. To try to increase a country's wealth by bringing in, or keeping in, an unnecessary quantity of gold and silver is as absurd as trying to improve the meals of private families by forcing them to keep an unnecessary number of kitchen utensils. Just as the cost of buying those unnecessary utensils would reduce, rather than increase, either the quantity or the quality of the family's food, so the cost of buying an unnecessary quantity of gold and silver must, in any country, just as surely reduce the wealth that feeds, clothes, and houses the people, and that maintains and employs them. It must be remembered that gold and silver, whether as coin or as plate, are utensils just as much as the furnishings of the kitchen. Increase their use, increase the consumable goods that are to be circulated, managed, and prepared by means of them, and you will infallibly increase their quantity. But if you try by extraordinary measures to increase their quantity, you will just as infallibly reduce their use, and in the end even their quantity, which can never exceed what their use requires. If they were ever accumulated beyond that amount, they are so easy to transport, and the loss from leaving them idle and unemployed is so great, that no law could prevent their being sent out of the country at once.

It is not always necessary to accumulate gold and silver in order to enable a country to wage foreign wars and to maintain fleets and armies in distant lands. Fleets and armies are maintained not with gold and silver but with consumable goods. A nation that has the means to buy those goods in distant countries, drawn from the annual produce of its domestic industry and from the annual revenue arising out of its land, labor, and consumable stock, can carry on wars there.

A nation may pay and provision an army in a distant country in three different ways: by sending abroad, first, some part of its accumulated gold and silver; second, some part of the annual produce of its manufactures; or, finally, some part of its annual raw produce.

The gold and silver that can properly be considered as accumulated, or stored up, in any country may be divided into three parts: first, the money in circulation; second, the plate of private families; and finally, the money that may have been gathered through many years of frugality and laid up in the prince's treasury.

Little can usually be spared from a country's circulating money, because there is seldom much surplus in it. The value of the goods bought and sold in a country each year requires a certain quantity of money to circulate them and distribute them to their consumers, and it can give employment to no more. The channel of circulation necessarily draws in a sum sufficient to fill it, and never admits any more. Something, however, is generally withdrawn from this channel during a foreign war. Because a great many people are maintained abroad, fewer are maintained at home; fewer goods circulate there, and less money is needed to circulate them. In England, moreover, an extraordinary quantity of paper money of one kind or another, such as exchequer notes, navy bills, and bank notes, is generally issued on such occasions, and by taking the place of circulating gold and silver, it allows a larger quantity of those metals to be sent abroad. All this, however, could provide only a meager resource for sustaining a foreign war of great expense and several years' duration.

Melting down the plate of private families has, on every occasion, proved an even more insignificant resource. At the beginning of the last war, the French did not gain enough by this expedient to make up for the loss of the craftsmanship, the value of the workmanship that was destroyed when the pieces were melted.

In earlier times, the accumulated treasures of princes provided a much greater and more lasting resource. In the present age, with the exception of the King of Prussia, accumulating treasure seems to form no part of the policy of European princes.

The funds that sustained the foreign wars of the present century, which are perhaps the most expensive in recorded history, seem to have depended very little on the export of circulating money, of private plate, or of royal treasure. The last war with France cost Great Britain more than £90 million. This includes not only the £75 million of new debt that was incurred, but also the additional land tax of two shillings in the pound and the sums borrowed each year from the sinking fund, the fund set aside to pay down the national debt. More than two-thirds of this expense was spent in distant countries: in Germany, Portugal, and America, in the ports of the Mediterranean, and in the East and West Indies. The kings of England had no accumulated treasure. We never heard of any extraordinary quantity of plate being melted down. The circulating gold and silver of the country had not been thought to exceed £18 million, although since the recent recoinage of the gold it is believed to have been considerably underestimated. Let us suppose, then, following the most exaggerated estimate I recall ever having seen or heard, that the gold and silver together amounted to £30 million. Had the war been financed with our money, the whole of it, even by this estimate, must have been sent out and returned again at least twice within a period of six to seven years. If this were supposed, it would furnish the most decisive argument that government need not watch over the preservation of money, since on this supposition the country's entire stock of money must have left it and come back twice in so short a time without anyone knowing anything about it. Yet at no point during this period did the channel of circulation appear emptier than usual. Few people who had the means to pay for money went without it. The profits of foreign trade were indeed higher than usual throughout the war, and especially toward its end. This produced what it always produces, a general overtrading in all the ports of Great Britain, and that in turn produced the usual complaint of a scarcity of money that always follows overtrading. Many people wanted money who had neither the means to buy it nor the credit to borrow it, and because debtors found it hard to borrow, creditors found it hard to get paid. Gold and silver, however, were generally available at their value to anyone who had that value to give for them.

The enormous expense of the late war must therefore have been paid chiefly not by exporting gold and silver, but by exporting British goods of one kind or another. When the government, or those acting under it, contracted with a merchant to remit funds to some foreign country, the merchant would naturally try to pay his foreign correspondent, on whom he had drawn a bill, by sending goods rather than gold and silver. If British goods were not in demand in that country, he would try to send them to some other country where he could buy a bill payable in the first. The shipment of goods suited to the market always yields a considerable profit, whereas the shipment of gold and silver scarcely ever yields any. When those metals are sent abroad to buy foreign goods, the merchant's profit comes not from the purchase but from the sale of the goods he brings back. But when they are sent abroad merely to pay a debt, he brings nothing back and therefore makes no profit. He naturally exerts his ingenuity, then, to find a way of paying his foreign debts by exporting goods rather than gold and silver. The author of *The Present State of the Nation* accordingly remarks on the great quantity of British goods exported during the late war without bringing back any return.

Besides the three kinds of gold and silver mentioned above, every great commercial country has a good deal of bullion that is alternately imported and exported for the purposes of foreign trade. Because this bullion circulates among commercial countries in the same way that a national coinage circulates within each country, it may be regarded as the money of the great mercantile republic, the community of trading nations taken as a whole. The national coinage receives its movement and direction from the goods circulated within the borders of each particular country; the money of the mercantile republic receives its movement and direction from the goods circulated between countries. Both are used to facilitate exchange, the one between individuals of the same nation, the other between those of different nations. Part of this money of the great mercantile republic may have been, and probably was, used in carrying on the late war. During a general war it is natural to suppose that it would be given a movement and direction different from its usual course in times of settled peace: that it would circulate more around the theater of war and be used more heavily there, and in neighboring countries, to buy the pay and provisions of the various armies. But whatever part of this money of the mercantile republic Great Britain may have used in this way each year, it must have been bought each year either with British goods or with something else that had been bought with them. This brings us back once more to goods, to the annual produce of the country's land and labor, as the ultimate resources that enabled us to carry on the war. It is natural to suppose, indeed, that so great an annual expense must have been paid out of a great annual produce. The expense for 1761, for example, came to more than £19 million. No accumulated store could have supported so great an annual outlay. No annual produce, even of gold and silver, could have supported it. According to the best accounts, the total gold and silver imported each year into Spain and Portugal together does not usually much exceed £6 million sterling, which in some years would scarcely have paid four months' expenses of the late war.

The goods best suited for shipment to distant countries, whether to buy the pay and provisions of an army directly or to buy some part of the money of the mercantile republic to be spent on them, seem to be the finer and more highly worked manufactures, those that contain great value in small bulk and can therefore be exported over great distances at little cost. A country whose industry produces a large annual surplus of such manufactures, which are ordinarily exported, may carry on a very expensive foreign war for many years without exporting any considerable quantity of gold and silver, or even possessing any such quantity to export. In that case, a considerable part of the annual surplus of its manufactures must indeed be exported without bringing any return to the country, though it does bring one to the merchant, since the government buys from the merchant his bills on foreign countries in order to purchase the pay and provisions of an army there. Some part of this surplus, however, may still continue to bring back a return. During the war, manufacturers will face a double demand. They will be called upon, first, to produce goods to be sent abroad to pay the bills drawn on foreign countries for the army's pay and provisions, and second, to produce the goods needed to buy the ordinary imports that the country had usually consumed. In the midst of the most destructive foreign war, therefore, most manufactures may often flourish greatly, and, conversely, they may decline when peace returns. They may thrive amid their country's ruin and begin to decay when its prosperity returns. The varying condition of many different branches of British manufacturing during the late war, and for some time after the peace, illustrates what has just been said.

No foreign war of great expense or long duration could conveniently be financed by exporting the raw produce of the land. The cost of sending abroad enough of it to buy the pay and provisions of an army would be too great. Few countries, moreover, produce much more raw produce than is needed to feed their own inhabitants. To send any large quantity of it abroad would therefore be to send away part of the people's necessary subsistence. The export of manufactures is a different matter. The food and upkeep of the people who make them stays at home, and only the surplus of their work is sent abroad. Mr. Hume frequently notes how unable the ancient kings of England were to carry on any long foreign war without interruption. In those days the English had nothing with which to buy the pay and provisions of their armies abroad except the raw produce of the land, of which no considerable part could be spared from home consumption, or a few manufactures of the coarsest kind, which, like the raw produce, were too expensive to transport. This inability arose not from a lack of money but from a lack of finer and more highly worked manufactures. Buying and selling in England was carried on with money then as it is now. The quantity of money in circulation must have borne the same proportion to the number and value of the purchases and sales ordinarily made at that time as it bears to those made at present, or rather a greater proportion, because there was then no paper money, which now does much of the work of gold and silver. Among nations that know little of commerce and manufacturing, the sovereign can seldom draw any considerable aid from his subjects in times of emergency, for reasons that will be explained later. It is in such countries, therefore, that he generally tries to accumulate a treasure, as his only resource against such emergencies. Quite apart from this necessity, his situation naturally inclines him to the frugality that accumulation requires. In that simple state of society, even a sovereign's spending is not directed by the vanity that delights in the gaudy finery of a court, but goes to generosity toward his tenants and hospitality toward his retainers. But generosity and hospitality very rarely lead to extravagance, whereas vanity almost always does. Every Tartar chief, accordingly, keeps a treasure. The treasures of Mazepa, chief of the Cossacks in the Ukraine and the famous ally of Charles XII of Sweden, are said to have been very great. The French kings of the Merovingian line all had treasures, and when they divided their kingdom among their children, they divided their treasures as well. The Saxon princes, and the first kings after the Norman Conquest, seem likewise to have accumulated treasures. The first act of every new reign was usually to seize the treasure of the previous king, since this was the most essential step in securing the succession. The sovereigns of advanced commercial countries are under no such necessity of hoarding, because they can generally draw extraordinary contributions from their subjects on extraordinary occasions. They are also less inclined to hoard. They naturally, perhaps necessarily, follow the fashion of the times, and their spending comes to be governed by the same extravagant vanity that governs the spending of every other great landowner in their dominions. The empty pageantry of their courts grows more dazzling every day, and its cost not only prevents any accumulation but often eats into the funds set aside for more necessary purposes. What the Spartan commander Dercyllidas said of the Persian court might be said of several European courts: that he saw there much splendor but little strength, and many servants but few soldiers.

The import of gold and silver is not the principal benefit a nation draws from its foreign trade, still less the only one. Whatever places carry on foreign trade with one another, each derives two distinct benefits from it. Trade carries away the surplus portion of the produce of their land and labor for which there is no demand at home, and brings back in exchange something for which there is a demand. It gives value to what would otherwise be superfluous, by exchanging it for goods that satisfy some of their wants and add to their comforts and pleasures. Through foreign trade, the narrowness of the home market no longer prevents the division of labor in any particular craft or manufacture from being carried to its highest perfection. By opening a wider market for whatever part of the produce of their labor exceeds what they consume at home, it encourages them to improve the productive power of that labor, to raise its annual output to the utmost, and so to increase the real revenue and wealth of the society. These are the great and important services that foreign trade continually performs for all the countries between which it is carried on. All of them benefit substantially, although the country in which the merchant lives generally benefits most, since he is usually more occupied in supplying the wants and carrying off the surplus of his own country than of any other single country. Importing the gold and silver that may be needed into countries without mines is, no doubt, part of the business of foreign commerce. It is, however, a trivial part. A country that carried on foreign trade for this purpose alone would hardly need to load a single ship in a century.

It is not by importing gold and silver that the discovery of America has enriched Europe. Because of the abundance of the American mines, those metals have become cheaper. A set of silver tableware can now be bought for about a third of the grain, or a third of the labor, it would have cost in the fifteenth century. With the same yearly outlay of labor and goods, Europe can now buy roughly three times as much silverware each year as it could then. But when a commodity comes to sell for a third of its former price, not only can those who bought it before now buy three times their previous quantity, but it also comes within reach of a much larger number of buyers, perhaps more than ten, perhaps more than twenty times as many. Europe may therefore contain at present not merely three times, but twenty or thirty times, the quantity of silverware it would have contained, even at its present stage of development, had the American mines never been discovered. To that extent Europe has undoubtedly gained a real convenience, though certainly a very trifling one. At the same time, the cheapness of gold and silver makes them somewhat less suitable for use as money than they were before. To make the same purchases, we must burden ourselves with a greater quantity of them, carrying a shilling in our pocket where a groat, the old fourpenny coin, would once have done. It is hard to say which is more trivial, this inconvenience or the corresponding convenience. Neither could have made any very significant change in the condition of Europe. The discovery of America, however, certainly did make a significant change. By opening a new and inexhaustible market for all the goods of Europe, it gave rise to new divisions of labor and improvements in technique that could never have occurred within the narrow circle of the old commerce, for lack of a market to absorb the greater part of their output. The productive powers of labor improved, and its output increased, in every country of Europe, and with it the real revenue and wealth of their inhabitants. Nearly all the goods of Europe were new to America, and many of America's goods were new to Europe. A new set of exchanges therefore began, which had never been imagined before, and which ought naturally to have proved as advantageous to the new continent as it certainly did to the old. The savage injustice of the Europeans turned an event that should have benefited everyone into a source of ruin and destruction for several of those unfortunate countries.

The discovery of a route to the East Indies around the Cape of Good Hope, which occurred at roughly the same time, opened perhaps an even wider field to foreign commerce than America did, despite the greater distance. There were only two nations in America that were in any respect superior to savages, and these were destroyed almost as soon as they were discovered. The rest were simply savages. But the empires of China, Hindustan, and Japan, along with several others in the East Indies, though they had no richer mines of gold or silver, were in every other respect far richer, better cultivated, and more advanced in all the arts and manufactures than either Mexico or Peru, even if we were to believe what plainly deserves no belief: the exaggerated accounts the Spanish writers have given of the former state of those empires. And rich, civilized nations can always exchange goods to a much greater value with one another than with savages and barbarians. Yet Europe has so far drawn much less advantage from its commerce with the East Indies than from its commerce with America. The Portuguese kept the East India trade to themselves for about a century, and the other nations of Europe could send goods there or receive goods from there only indirectly, through them. When the Dutch began to encroach on the Portuguese at the start of the seventeenth century, they placed their entire East India commerce in the hands of an exclusive company. The English, French, Swedes, and Danes have all followed their example, so that no great European nation has ever yet enjoyed the benefit of free trade with the East Indies. No other reason is needed to explain why that trade has never been as advantageous as the trade to America, which, between almost every European nation and its own colonies, is open to all its subjects. The exclusive privileges of the East India companies, their great wealth, and the great favor and protection this wealth has won them from their governments have aroused much envy against them. That envy has often portrayed their trade as entirely harmful, because of the great quantities of silver it exports every year from the countries that carry it on. The companies have replied that this continual export of silver might indeed tend to impoverish Europe as a whole, but not the particular country conducting the trade, because, by re-exporting part of its returns to other European countries, the trade brought home each year far more of that metal than it sent out. Both the objection and the reply rest on the popular notion I have just been examining, so there is no need to say anything more about either. Because of the yearly export of silver to the East Indies, silverware is probably somewhat dearer in Europe than it would otherwise be, and coined silver probably buys a larger quantity of both labor and goods. The first effect is a very small loss, the second a very small gain, and both are too insignificant to deserve any share of public attention. By opening a market for the goods of Europe, or, what amounts to nearly the same thing, for the gold and silver bought with those goods, the East India trade must necessarily tend to increase the annual production of European goods, and consequently the real wealth and revenue of Europe. That it has so far increased them so little is probably owing to the restrictions under which it labors everywhere.

I thought it necessary, even at the risk of being tedious, to examine at full length the popular notion that wealth consists in money, or in gold and silver. As I have already observed, the word "money" in ordinary speech frequently means wealth, and this ambiguity has made the popular notion so familiar to us that even those convinced of its absurdity are very apt to forget their own principles and, in the course of their reasoning, to take it for granted as a certain and undeniable truth. Some of the best English writers on commerce begin by observing that a country's wealth consists not only in its gold and silver but in its land, its houses, and its consumable goods of every kind. As their reasoning proceeds, however, the land, the houses, and the consumable goods seem to slip from their memory, and the drift of their argument often assumes that all wealth consists in gold and silver and that multiplying those metals is the great object of national industry and commerce.

Once two principles were established, however—that wealth consisted in gold and silver, and that a country without mines could acquire those metals only through the balance of trade, by exporting goods of greater value than it imported—it necessarily became the great object of political economy to reduce as far as possible the import of foreign goods for home consumption and to increase as far as possible the export of the produce of domestic industry. Its two great instruments for enriching the country were therefore restrictions on imports and encouragements to exports.

The restrictions on imports were of two kinds.

First, restrictions on importing, from whatever country, foreign goods for home consumption that could be produced at home.

Second, restrictions on importing goods of almost every kind from those particular countries with which the balance of trade was supposed to be unfavorable.

These restrictions took the form sometimes of high duties and sometimes of outright prohibitions.

Exports were encouraged sometimes by drawbacks, sometimes by bounties, sometimes by favorable commercial treaties with foreign states, and sometimes by founding colonies in distant countries.

Drawbacks, which were refunds of duties already paid, were granted on two kinds of occasion. When domestic manufactures were subject to a duty or excise tax, all or part of it was often refunded when the goods were exported. And when dutiable foreign goods were imported for the purpose of being exported again, all or part of the duty was sometimes refunded on their re-export.

Bounties, which were direct payments from the government, were granted to encourage either new manufactures in their infancy or other kinds of industry thought to deserve special favor.

Through favorable commercial treaties, the goods and merchants of a country obtained particular privileges in some foreign state beyond those granted to the goods and merchants of other countries.

Through the founding of colonies in distant countries, the goods and merchants of the founding country frequently obtained not merely particular privileges but a monopoly.

The two kinds of import restrictions described above, together with these four encouragements to export, make up the six principal means by which the commercial system proposes to increase the quantity of gold and silver in a country by turning the balance of trade in its favor. I shall consider each of them in a separate chapter. Without paying much further attention to their supposed tendency to bring money into the country, I shall chiefly examine what their likely effects are on the annual produce of its industry. Insofar as they tend to increase or diminish the value of this annual produce, they must evidently tend to increase or diminish the real wealth and revenue of the country.

### CHAPTER II: OF RESTRAINTS UPON IMPORTATION FROM FOREIGN COUNTRIES OF SUCH GOODS AS CAN BE PRODUCED AT HOME

When a country restrains the importation of foreign goods that could also be produced at home, whether through high duties or outright prohibition, it more or less secures a monopoly of the home market for the domestic industry that produces them. The ban on importing live cattle or salted provisions, for instance, gives the graziers of Great Britain a monopoly of the home market for butcher's meat. The high duties on imported grain, which in years of moderate plenty amount to a prohibition, give the same advantage to those who grow it. The ban on imported woollen goods favors the woollen manufacturers in the same way. The silk industry, although it works entirely with foreign raw materials, has recently won the same privilege. The linen industry has not yet obtained it, but is moving quickly in that direction. Many other branches of manufacture in Great Britain have likewise secured a monopoly against their own countrymen, either complete or very nearly so. The range of goods whose importation into Great Britain is forbidden, either absolutely or under certain conditions, is far greater than anyone unfamiliar with the customs laws would readily suspect.

There can be no doubt that a monopoly of the home market often gives great encouragement to the particular industry that enjoys it, and often draws into that line of work a larger share of the nation's labor and capital than would otherwise have gone there. But whether such a monopoly increases the total industry of the society, or directs it toward its most advantageous use, is perhaps not quite so obvious.

The total industry of a society can never exceed what its capital is able to employ. Just as the number of workers any one person can keep employed must bear a certain proportion to his capital, so the number of people who can be continuously employed by all the members of a great society must bear a certain proportion to the whole capital of that society, and can never exceed it. No regulation of commerce can raise the quantity of industry in a society beyond what its capital can support. It can only divert part of that industry into a channel it might not otherwise have entered, and it is by no means certain that this artificial direction will benefit the society more than the one industry would have found on its own.

Every individual is constantly working to discover the most advantageous use for whatever capital he controls. It is his own advantage, of course, and not the society's, that he has in view. But the pursuit of his own advantage naturally, or rather necessarily, leads him to prefer the employment that is most advantageous to the society.

First, every individual tries to employ his capital as close to home as he can, and therefore as much as possible in support of domestic industry, provided he can earn the ordinary rate of profit on it, or not much less.

So, where profits are equal or nearly equal, every wholesale merchant naturally prefers the home trade to the foreign trade of consumption, meaning the trade that buys foreign goods for use at home, and he prefers the foreign trade of consumption to the carrying trade, which ships goods between two foreign countries without bringing them home. In the home trade his capital is never out of his sight for as long as it often is in the foreign trade of consumption. He can better judge the character and circumstances of the people he trusts, and if he is cheated, he knows the laws of the country in which he must seek redress. In the carrying trade, the merchant's capital is, in effect, split between two foreign countries; no part of it ever needs to come home or to be placed under his direct observation and control. An Amsterdam merchant who carries grain from Königsberg to Lisbon, and fruit and wine from Lisbon to Königsberg, must generally keep half of his capital in Königsberg and the other half in Lisbon. None of it ever needs to pass through Amsterdam. Such a merchant's natural place of residence would be either Königsberg or Lisbon, and only some very unusual circumstances could make him prefer to live in Amsterdam. Yet the unease he feels at being so far separated from his capital generally leads him to bring part of the Königsberg goods meant for Lisbon, and part of the Lisbon goods meant for Königsberg, to Amsterdam. Although this necessarily subjects him to the double cost of loading and unloading, as well as to certain duties and customs charges, he willingly accepts this extra expense for the sake of keeping some portion of his capital always under his own eye and control. This is how every country that holds a considerable share of the carrying trade comes to be the emporium, or general market, for the goods of all the countries whose trade it handles. To save himself a second round of loading and unloading, the merchant always tries to sell as much of those countries' goods as he can in the home market, and in this way, as far as possible, he converts his carrying trade into a foreign trade of consumption. In the same manner, a merchant engaged in the foreign trade of consumption, when he gathers goods for foreign markets, will always be glad, where profits are equal or nearly so, to sell as large a share of them at home as he can. By converting his foreign trade of consumption into a home trade wherever possible, he spares himself the risk and trouble of exporting. Home is thus the center, so to speak, around which the capital of every country's inhabitants continually circulates and toward which it always tends, even though particular causes may sometimes drive it away toward more distant employments. But it has already been shown that capital employed in the home trade necessarily sets in motion a greater quantity of domestic industry, and provides income and employment to a greater number of the country's inhabitants, than an equal capital employed in the foreign trade of consumption; and capital employed in the foreign trade of consumption has the same advantage over an equal capital employed in the carrying trade. Where profits are equal or only nearly equal, then, every individual naturally inclines to use his capital in whatever way is likely to give the greatest support to domestic industry and to provide income and employment for the greatest number of his own countrymen.

Second, every individual who employs his capital in support of domestic industry necessarily tries to direct that industry so that its produce will be of the greatest possible value.

The produce of industry is what it adds to the materials on which it works. The profits of the employer will be large or small in proportion as the value of this produce is large or small. Since profit is the only reason anyone employs capital in support of industry, he will always try to employ it in the industry whose produce is likely to be of the greatest value, or to exchange for the greatest quantity of money or other goods.

But the annual revenue of every society is always exactly equal to the exchangeable value of the whole annual produce of its industry; indeed, it is precisely the same thing as that exchangeable value. Since every individual tries, as far as he can, both to employ his capital in support of domestic industry and to direct that industry so that its produce has the greatest value, every individual necessarily works to make the society's annual revenue as large as he can. He generally neither intends to promote the public interest nor knows how much he is promoting it. By preferring to support domestic rather than foreign industry, he intends only his own security; and by directing that industry so that its produce will be of the greatest value, he intends only his own gain. In this, as in many other cases, he is led by an invisible hand to promote an end that was no part of his intention. Nor is it always worse for society that it was no part of his intention. By pursuing his own interest, he frequently promotes that of society more effectively than when he actually sets out to promote it. I have never known much good to be done by those who made a show of trading for the public good. It is an affectation not very common among merchants, and very few words are needed to talk them out of it.

As for which kind of domestic industry his capital can employ, and whose produce is likely to be of the greatest value, it is evident that every individual, in his own local situation, can judge far better than any statesman or lawgiver could judge for him. A statesman who tried to direct private people in how they should employ their capital would not only burden himself with a wholly unnecessary task, but would assume an authority that could safely be entrusted to no single person, nor indeed to any council or senate whatever, and that would nowhere be so dangerous as in the hands of a man foolish and presumptuous enough to imagine himself fit to exercise it.

To grant domestic industry a monopoly of the home market in any particular craft or manufacture is, to some degree, to direct private people in how they should employ their capital, and in almost every case it must be either a useless regulation or a harmful one. If domestic produce can be brought to market as cheaply as foreign produce, the regulation is plainly useless. If it cannot, the regulation must generally be harmful. Every prudent head of a household follows the rule never to try making at home what would cost him more to make than to buy. The tailor does not try to make his own shoes, but buys them from the shoemaker. The shoemaker does not try to make his own clothes, but hires a tailor. The farmer tries to make neither, but employs both of these tradesmen. Each of them finds it in his interest to devote his whole industry to work in which he has some advantage over his neighbors, and to buy whatever else he needs with part of what he produces, or, what amounts to the same thing, with the price of part of it.

What is prudent in the conduct of every private family can hardly be folly in that of a great kingdom. If a foreign country can supply us with a commodity more cheaply than we can make it ourselves, we had better buy it from them with part of the produce of our own industry, employed in some way in which we have an advantage. Since the country's total industry is always proportioned to the capital that employs it, it will no more be diminished by this than the industry of the tradesmen just mentioned; it will simply be left free to find the use in which it can be employed to the greatest advantage. It is certainly not employed to the greatest advantage when it is directed toward making something it could buy more cheaply than it can make. The value of its annual produce is certainly reduced, to a greater or lesser degree, when it is diverted from producing commodities clearly worth more than the commodity it is now directed to produce. By the terms of the case, that commodity could be bought from abroad more cheaply than it can be made at home. It could therefore have been purchased with only part of the commodities, or, what is the same thing, with only part of the price of the commodities, that the industry employed by an equal capital would have produced at home had it been left to follow its natural course.
