The country's industry is thus turned from a more advantageous employment to a less advantageous one, and the exchangeable value of its annual produce, instead of rising as the lawgiver intended, must necessarily fall with every such regulation.

It is true that such regulations may sometimes allow a country to acquire a particular manufacture sooner than it otherwise would have, and that after a time the article may be made at home as cheaply as abroad, or more cheaply. But although the society's industry may thus be guided profitably into a particular channel sooner than it otherwise would have been, it by no means follows that the sum total of either its industry or its revenue can ever be increased by any such regulation. A society's industry can grow only as fast as its capital grows, and its capital can grow only in proportion to what can gradually be saved out of its revenue. The immediate effect of every such regulation, however, is to reduce that revenue, and whatever reduces revenue is hardly likely to make capital grow faster than it would have grown on its own, had both capital and industry been left to find their natural employments.

Even if, for lack of such regulations, the society never acquired the manufacture in question, it would not necessarily be any poorer at any point in its history on that account. At every stage, its whole capital and industry might still have been employed, though on different objects, in the way most advantageous at the time. At every stage its revenue might have been the greatest its capital could yield, and both capital and revenue might have increased as rapidly as possible.

The natural advantages one country has over another in producing particular commodities are sometimes so great that the whole world acknowledges it would be futile to compete with them. With glass frames, hotbeds warmed by fermenting manure, and walls heated from within to ripen fruit trained against them, very good grapes can be grown in Scotland, and very good wine can be made from them, at roughly thirty times the cost at which wine at least as good can be brought in from abroad. Would it be a reasonable law that prohibited the importation of all foreign wines merely to encourage the making of claret and Burgundy in Scotland? And if it would be a manifest absurdity to devote to any employment thirty times more of the country's capital and industry than would be needed to buy an equal quantity of the desired goods from abroad, then there must be an absurdity of exactly the same kind, though not quite so glaring, in devoting to any such employment even a thirtieth or a three-hundredth part more of either. Whether one country's advantages over another are natural or acquired makes no difference in this respect. As long as one country possesses those advantages and the other lacks them, it will always be better for the second to buy from the first than to make for itself. The advantage one tradesman has over a neighbor who practices a different trade is merely an acquired one, and yet each finds it more profitable to buy from the other than to make what lies outside his own particular trade.

Merchants and manufacturers are the people who gain most from this monopoly of the home market. The ban on importing foreign cattle and salted provisions, together with the high duties on foreign grain, which in years of moderate plenty amount to a prohibition, are nowhere near as beneficial to the graziers and farmers of Great Britain as similar regulations are to its merchants and manufacturers. Manufactured goods, especially the finer kinds, are more easily carried from one country to another than grain or cattle, and it is accordingly in fetching and carrying manufactured goods that foreign trade is chiefly occupied. In manufactures, a very small advantage will let foreigners undersell our own workmen, even in the home market; in the raw produce of the land, it would take a very large one. If foreign manufactures were allowed in freely, several domestic manufactures would probably suffer, some might be ruined altogether, and a considerable part of the capital and labor now employed in them would be forced to find some other use. But even the freest importation of raw agricultural produce could have no such effect on the country's farming.

However free the importation of foreign cattle were made, for example, so few could actually be imported that the grazing trade of Great Britain would scarcely be affected. Live cattle are perhaps the only commodity that costs more to transport by sea than by land. Over land, they carry themselves to market. By sea, not only the cattle but also their feed and water must be shipped, at considerable expense and inconvenience. The short stretch of sea between Ireland and Great Britain does make the importation of Irish cattle easier. Yet even if their free importation, which was recently permitted only for a limited period, were made permanent, it could have no significant effect on the interests of British graziers. The parts of Great Britain bordering the Irish Sea are all grazing country. Irish cattle could never be imported for use in those districts; they would have to be driven across those very extensive regions, at considerable expense and inconvenience, before reaching their proper market. Fattened cattle could not be driven so far, so only lean cattle could be imported. Such imports could not harm the interests of the feeding or fattening districts, to which they would actually be an advantage by lowering the price of lean cattle; they could affect only the breeding districts. The small number of Irish cattle imported since the trade was permitted, together with the good prices lean cattle still fetch, seem to show that even the breeding districts of Great Britain are never likely to be much affected by the free importation of Irish cattle. The common people of Ireland, it is true, are said to have sometimes violently opposed the exportation of their cattle. Yet had the exporters found any real advantage in keeping the trade going, they could easily have overcome this mob resistance, since the law was on their side.

There is a further consideration. The regions that feed and fatten cattle must always be highly improved, while the regions that breed them are generally uncultivated. A high price for lean cattle, the young unfattened stock sold off for fattening elsewhere, raises the value of uncultivated land and so acts as a kind of reward paid against improvement. A country improved throughout would find it more profitable to import its lean cattle than to breed them, and the province of Holland is said to follow exactly this principle at present. The mountains of Scotland, Wales, and Northumberland are admittedly not capable of much improvement and seem destined by nature to be the breeding grounds of Great Britain. Yet even the freest importation of foreign cattle could do no more than stop these breeding regions from exploiting the growing population and improvement of the rest of the kingdom. It would prevent them from driving their prices to an exorbitant height and from levying, in effect, a real tax on all the more improved and cultivated parts of the country.

In the same way, the freest importation of salted provisions could affect the interests of British graziers as little as the importation of live cattle. Salted meat is not only a very bulky commodity. Compared with fresh meat, it is also of worse quality and, because it costs more labor and expense to prepare, of higher price. It could never compete with fresh meat, though it might compete with the salted meat produced at home. It might be used to provision ships for long voyages and for similar purposes, but it could never form any considerable part of the people's diet. The small quantity of salted provisions imported from Ireland since that trade was made free is practical proof that our graziers have nothing to fear from it. There is no sign that the price of butcher's meat has ever been noticeably affected.

Even the free importation of foreign grain could affect the interests of British farmers very little. Grain is a far bulkier commodity than butcher's meat: a pound of wheat at a penny costs as much as a pound of meat at fourpence. The small quantity of foreign grain brought in even in times of the worst scarcity should convince our farmers that they have nothing to fear from the freest importation. According to the very well-informed author of the *Tracts upon the Corn Trade*, the average amount imported, taking one year with another, comes to only 23,728 quarters of all kinds of grain (a quarter being a measure of eight bushels), which is no more than one five-hundred-and-seventy-first part of the annual consumption. But the bounty on grain, the government payment made on every quarter exported, produces greater exports in years of plenty, and it must therefore produce greater imports in years of scarcity than would otherwise occur, given the existing level of cultivation. Because of the bounty, the surplus of one year cannot make up for the shortage of another. And since the bounty necessarily increases the average quantity exported, it must also, given the existing level of cultivation, increase the average quantity imported. If there were no bounty, less grain would be exported, and it is probable that, one year with another, less would also be imported than at present. The grain merchants, who fetch and carry grain between Great Britain and foreign countries, would then have much less business and might suffer considerably, but the country gentlemen and farmers could suffer very little. It is among the grain merchants, accordingly, rather than among the country gentlemen and farmers, that I have observed the greatest anxiety for the renewal and continuation of the bounty.

Country gentlemen and farmers are, to their great credit, of all people the least prone to the wretched spirit of monopoly. The proprietor of a large manufacturing works is sometimes alarmed if another works of the same kind is set up within twenty miles of him. The Dutch proprietor of the woolen manufacture at Abbeville went so far as to stipulate that no works of the same kind should be established within thirty leagues, roughly ninety miles, of that city. Farmers and country gentlemen, by contrast, are generally inclined to encourage rather than obstruct the cultivation and improvement of their neighbors' farms and estates. They keep no trade secrets, as most manufacturers do. On the contrary, they generally like to share with their neighbors, and to spread as widely as possible, any new practice they have found profitable. "The farmer's gain," says old Cato, "is the most honorable, the most secure, and the least envied, and those who are engaged in that pursuit are the least given to evil designs." Country gentlemen and farmers, scattered across different parts of the country, cannot combine as easily as merchants and manufacturers. These are gathered together in towns and accustomed to the exclusive corporate spirit that prevails there, so they naturally try to obtain against all their fellow countrymen the same exclusive privilege they generally hold against the other inhabitants of their own towns. They seem, accordingly, to have been the original inventors of those restrictions on foreign imports that secure for them a monopoly of the home market. It was probably in imitation of them, and to put themselves on an equal footing with people they found disposed to oppress them, that the country gentlemen and farmers of Great Britain so far forgot the generosity natural to their position as to demand the exclusive privilege of supplying their countrymen with grain and butcher's meat. They did not, perhaps, stop to consider how much less their interests could be affected by free trade than the interests of the people whose example they were following.

To prohibit the importation of foreign grain and cattle by a permanent law is, in reality, to decree that the population and industry of the country shall never exceed what the raw produce of its own soil can support.

There appear, however, to be two cases in which it will generally be advantageous to place some burden on foreign industry in order to encourage domestic industry.

The first is when a particular kind of industry is necessary for the defense of the country. The defense of Great Britain, for example, depends heavily on the number of its sailors and ships. The Navigation Act therefore quite properly tries to give British sailors and shipping a monopoly of their own country's trade, in some cases through outright prohibitions and in others through heavy burdens on the shipping of foreign countries. The principal provisions of the act are as follows.

First, all ships whose owners, masters, and three-quarters of whose crews are not British subjects are forbidden, on pain of forfeiting both ship and cargo, to trade with the British settlements and plantations or to be employed in the coastal trade of Great Britain.

Second, a wide range of the bulkiest imported goods may be brought into Great Britain only in ships of the kind just described, or in ships of the country where the goods are produced whose owners, masters, and three-quarters of whose crews belong to that same country. Even when imported in ships of this second kind, the goods are subject to double aliens' duty, the additional tax levied on goods brought in by foreigners. If they are imported in the ships of any other country, the penalty is forfeiture of ship and goods. When this act was passed, the Dutch were, as they still are, the great carriers of Europe, and this provision shut them out entirely from carrying goods to Great Britain or from bringing us the goods of any other European country.

Third, a wide range of the bulkiest imported goods are forbidden, even in British ships, from being brought in from any country other than the one in which they are produced, on pain of forfeiting ship and cargo. This provision, too, was probably aimed at the Dutch. Holland was then, as it is now, the great warehouse for all European goods, and this rule prevented British ships from loading the goods of any other European country in Holland.

Fourth, salt fish of all kinds, whale fins, whalebone, whale oil, and blubber not caught by and cured aboard British vessels are subject, when imported into Great Britain, to double aliens' duty. The Dutch, who are still the principal fishers in Europe supplying foreign nations with fish, were then the only ones attempting it. This provision placed a very heavy burden on their trade with Great Britain.

When the Navigation Act was passed, England and Holland were not actually at war, but the most violent hostility existed between the two nations. It had begun under the Long Parliament, which first drew up the act, and it broke out soon afterward in the Dutch wars under the Protector, Oliver Cromwell, and under Charles II. It is therefore not impossible that some provisions of this famous act sprang from national hostility. They are nonetheless as wise as if every one had been dictated by the most deliberate wisdom. National hostility, at that particular moment, aimed at exactly the object that the most deliberate wisdom would have recommended: the reduction of the naval power of Holland, the only naval power that could endanger the security of England.

The Navigation Act is not favorable to foreign commerce or to the growth of the wealth that can arise from it. In its commercial dealings with foreign nations, a nation's interest is the same as a merchant's in dealing with his various customers and suppliers: to buy as cheaply and sell as dearly as possible. It will be most likely to buy cheaply when, through the most perfect freedom of trade, it encourages all nations to bring it the goods it needs to purchase. For the same reason, it will be most likely to sell dearly when its markets are filled with the greatest number of buyers. The Navigation Act, it is true, imposes no burden on foreign ships that come to carry away the products of British industry. Even the old aliens' duty, which used to be paid on all goods, exports as well as imports, has been lifted by several later acts from most articles of export. But if foreigners are prevented, by prohibitions or high duties, from coming to sell, they cannot always afford to come to buy, because a ship arriving without a cargo loses the freight it would have earned on the voyage from its own country to Great Britain. By reducing the number of sellers, therefore, we necessarily reduce the number of buyers, and so we are likely not only to buy foreign goods more dearly but also to sell our own more cheaply than we would under a more perfect freedom of trade. Since defense, however, matters far more than wealth, the Navigation Act is perhaps the wisest of all the commercial regulations of England.

The second case in which it will generally be advantageous to place some burden on foreign industry for the encouragement of domestic industry is when a tax has been imposed at home on the products of domestic industry. In that case it seems reasonable to impose an equal tax on the same products from abroad. This would not give domestic industry a monopoly of the home market, nor would it direct toward any particular occupation a larger share of the country's capital and labor than would naturally flow there. It would merely prevent the tax from diverting part of what would naturally flow there into some less natural channel, and it would leave competition between foreign and domestic industry, after the tax, on as nearly the same footing as before. In Great Britain, whenever such a tax is laid on the products of domestic industry, it is customary at the same time, in order to silence the loud complaints of our merchants and manufacturers that they will be undersold at home, to impose a much heavier duty on all foreign imports of the same kind.

According to some people, this second exception to free trade ought, on most occasions, to be carried much further than the specific foreign goods that compete with those taxed at home. When the necessities of life have been taxed in any country, they argue, it becomes proper to tax not only the same necessities imported from abroad but every kind of foreign good that competes with anything produced by domestic industry. Such taxes, they say, inevitably make subsistence dearer, and the price of labor must always rise with the price of the laborer's subsistence. Every product of domestic industry, therefore, even if not taxed directly, becomes dearer as a result of these taxes, because the labor that produces it becomes dearer. Such taxes, they conclude, are really equivalent to a tax on every individual commodity produced at home. To put domestic industry on the same footing as foreign industry, it therefore becomes necessary, in their view, to impose on every foreign commodity a duty equal to the rise in price of the home commodity with which it competes.

Whether taxes on the necessities of life, such as those levied in Great Britain on soap, salt, leather, candles, and the like, necessarily raise the price of labor and consequently the price of all other commodities, I shall consider later, when I come to discuss taxation. Supposing for the moment that they do have this effect, and they undoubtedly do, this general rise in the price of all commodities as a consequence of dearer labor differs in two respects from the case of a particular commodity whose price has been raised by a tax imposed directly on it.

First, it could always be known with great precision how far the price of a particular commodity would be raised by such a tax. But how far a general rise in the price of labor would affect the price of each different commodity on which labor was employed could never be known with any tolerable precision. It would therefore be impossible to match, with any tolerable precision, the tax on each foreign commodity to the rise in price of each domestic one.

Second, taxes on the necessities of life have nearly the same effect on the circumstances of a people as poor soil and a bad climate. Food is made dearer by them, exactly as if it required extraordinary labor and expense to produce. Under the natural scarcity that comes from soil and climate, it would be absurd to direct people in how they should employ their capital and industry, and it is equally absurd under the artificial scarcity created by such taxes. In both cases, what would plainly serve them best is to be left to adapt their industry to their situation as well as they can, and to discover those occupations in which, despite their unfavorable circumstances, they might hold some advantage in either the home or the foreign market. To lay a new tax on them because they are already overburdened with taxes, and because they already pay too much for the necessities of life, so that they must also pay too much for most other commodities, is certainly a most absurd way of making amends.

Such taxes, once they have grown to a certain height, are a curse equal to the barrenness of the earth and the harshness of the skies. Yet it is in the richest and most industrious countries that they have been most widely imposed, since no other countries could withstand so great a disorder. Just as only the strongest constitutions can survive and stay healthy under an unwholesome diet, so only those nations with the greatest natural and acquired advantages in every kind of industry can survive and prosper under such taxes. Holland is the country in Europe where they are most abundant, and owing to peculiar circumstances it continues to prosper, not because of them, as has been most absurdly supposed, but in spite of them.

Just as there are two cases in which it will generally be advantageous to place some burden on foreign industry for the encouragement of domestic industry, there are two others in which the matter may sometimes call for deliberation. In the first, the question is how far it is proper to continue the free importation of certain foreign goods. In the second, the question is how far, and in what manner, it may be proper to restore free importation after it has been interrupted for some time.

The case in which it may sometimes be worth deliberating how far to continue the free importation of certain foreign goods arises when some foreign nation restricts, by high duties or prohibitions, the importation of some of our manufactures into its territory. Revenge in this case naturally calls for retaliation, demanding that we impose similar duties and prohibitions on the importation of some or all of their manufactures into ours. Nations, accordingly, seldom fail to retaliate in this way. The French have been particularly eager to favor their own manufactures by restricting imports of any foreign goods that might compete with them. This made up a large part of the policy of Jean-Baptiste Colbert, who, for all his great abilities, seems in this instance to have been taken in by the sophistry of merchants and manufacturers, who are forever demanding a monopoly against their own countrymen. It is now the opinion of the most intelligent men in France that his measures of this kind did their country no good. Through the tariff of 1667, that minister imposed very high duties on a great number of foreign manufactures. When he refused to moderate them in favor of the Dutch, they retaliated in 1671 by prohibiting the importation of French wines, brandies, and manufactures. The war of 1672 seems to have been caused in part by this commercial dispute. The Peace of Nijmegen ended it in 1678 by moderating some of those duties in favor of the Dutch, who in turn lifted their prohibition. It was at about this same time that the French and English began to oppress each other's industry with similar duties and prohibitions, of which the French, however, seem to have set the first example. The hostility that has persisted between the two nations ever since has so far prevented either side from moderating them. In 1697 the English prohibited the import of bone lace, a product of Flanders. The government of that country, then under Spanish rule, retaliated by prohibiting the import of English woollens. In 1700 England lifted its ban on bone lace, on condition that English woollens be admitted into Flanders on the same terms as before.

Retaliation of this kind may be sound policy when there is a reasonable prospect that it will secure the repeal of the high duties or prohibitions being complained of. Regaining a large foreign market will generally more than make up for the passing inconvenience of paying higher prices for certain goods for a short time. Whether such retaliation is likely to have that effect, however, is perhaps a question less for the science of the legislator, whose deliberations ought to be governed by general principles that never change, than for the skill of that insidious and crafty creature commonly called a statesman or politician, whose counsels are guided by the shifting circumstances of the moment. When there is no real prospect of securing a repeal, it seems a poor way of compensating certain classes of our people for an injury done to them to inflict a further injury ourselves, not only on those classes but on nearly every other class as well. When our neighbors prohibit one of our manufactures, we generally respond by prohibiting not only the same product of theirs, since that alone would seldom hurt them much, but some other of their manufactures as well. This may well encourage a particular class of workers at home, and by shutting out some of their competitors, it may allow them to raise their prices in the domestic market. But the workers who were harmed by our neighbors' prohibition gain nothing from ours. On the contrary, they and almost every other class of citizen are now forced to pay more than before for certain goods. Every such law, therefore, imposes a real tax on the whole country, and it does so for the benefit not of the workers who were injured by our neighbors' prohibition, but of some other class entirely.

There is one case in which it may sometimes be a matter for genuine deliberation how far, and in what manner, the free importation of foreign goods should be restored after it has been interrupted for some time. This is when particular manufactures, sheltered by high duties or prohibitions on every foreign good that could compete with them, have grown so large that they employ a great multitude of workers. Humanity may then require that free trade be restored only by slow degrees, and with considerable caution and restraint. If those high duties and prohibitions were removed all at once, cheaper foreign goods of the same kind might pour into the home market so quickly as to strip many thousands of our people, at a single stroke, of their usual work and livelihood. The disruption this would cause might certainly be very considerable. In all likelihood, however, it would be much smaller than is commonly supposed, for the following two reasons.

First, any manufacture of which some portion is regularly exported to other European countries without a bounty, that is, without a government subsidy on exports, could be very little affected by even the freest importation of foreign goods. Such goods must be sold abroad as cheaply as any foreign goods of the same quality and kind, and must therefore be sold more cheaply at home. They would consequently keep their hold on the home market. A capricious man of fashion might occasionally prefer foreign wares simply because they were foreign, over cheaper and better goods of the same kind made at home, but this folly could, by the very nature of things, extend to so few people that it would make no perceptible difference to the general employment of the population. Now a large part of every branch of our woollen manufacture, of our tanned leather, and of our hardware is exported each year to other European countries without any bounty, and these are precisely the manufactures that employ the largest number of workers. Silk is perhaps the manufacture that would suffer most from such freedom of trade, and after it linen, though linen much less than silk.

Second, even if restoring free trade did throw a great number of people out of their usual work and customary means of living all at once, it would by no means follow that they would be left without employment or subsistence altogether. When the army and navy were reduced at the end of the recent war, more than 100,000 soldiers and seamen, a number equal to the workforce of the largest manufactures, were suddenly thrown out of their usual employment. They no doubt suffered some hardship, but they were not left without all work and means of support. Most of the seamen, it is likely, gradually moved into the merchant service as opportunities arose, and in the meantime both they and the soldiers were absorbed into the great mass of the population and found work in a wide variety of occupations. So great a change in the situation of more than 100,000 men, all accustomed to the use of arms and many of them to pillage and plunder, produced not only no great upheaval but no perceptible disorder at all. The number of vagrants scarcely rose noticeably anywhere, and so far as I have been able to learn, wages fell in no occupation except that of seamen in the merchant service.

And if we compare the habits of a soldier with those of any kind of manufacturing worker, we find that the worker's habits do not unfit him for a new trade nearly so much as the soldier's habits unfit him for any trade at all. The manufacturing worker has always been used to looking to his own labor alone for his living; the soldier, to expecting it from his pay. Diligence and industry are familiar to the one; idleness and dissipation to the other. Yet it is surely far easier to redirect industry from one kind of labor to another than to turn idleness and dissipation toward any labor whatsoever. Moreover, as has already been observed, most manufactures have related branches so similar in nature that a worker can easily shift his industry from one to another. Most such workers are also employed from time to time in farm labor. The capital that previously employed them in a particular manufacture will still remain in the country, ready to employ an equal number of people in some other way. With the country's capital unchanged, the demand for labor will likewise stay the same, or very nearly so, even if it is exercised in different places and for different occupations. Soldiers and seamen, it is true, once discharged from the king's service, are free to practice any trade in any town or place in Great Britain or Ireland. Let that same natural liberty to pursue whatever kind of work they please be restored to all of His Majesty's subjects, just as it is to soldiers and seamen. That is, break down the exclusive privileges of the corporations, the chartered trade bodies that control who may work in the towns; repeal the Statute of Apprenticeship, which bars a man from practicing a trade until he has served a long apprenticeship in it, since both are real encroachments on natural liberty; and repeal in addition the law of settlements, which allows a parish to send a poor newcomer back to the parish he came from. Then a poor worker, when thrown out of work in one trade or one place, could seek it in another trade or another place without fear of either prosecution or removal, and neither the public nor individuals would suffer much more from the occasional disbanding of particular groups of manufacturing workers than from the disbanding of soldiers. Our manufacturers no doubt have great merit in the eyes of their country, but they cannot have more than those who defend it with their blood, nor do they deserve to be treated with greater delicacy.

To expect that freedom of trade will ever be entirely restored in Great Britain is, in truth, as absurd as to expect that an Oceana or a Utopia, the ideal commonwealths imagined by James Harrington and Thomas More, will ever be established there. Not only the prejudices of the public but, far harder to overcome, the private interests of many individuals stand irresistibly against it. Suppose the officers of the army opposed any reduction in the number of troops with the same zeal and unanimity with which master manufacturers set themselves against every law likely to increase the number of their rivals in the home market. Suppose, further, that the officers incited their soldiers, as the manufacturers inflame their workers, to attack the proposers of any such measure with violence and outrage. Then attempting to reduce the army would be as dangerous as it has now become to attempt to reduce, in any respect, the monopoly our manufacturers have secured against us. This monopoly has so swelled the numbers of certain groups among them that, like an overgrown standing army, they have become formidable to the government and on many occasions intimidate the legislature. A member of Parliament who supports every proposal for strengthening this monopoly is sure to gain not only a reputation for understanding trade but also great popularity and influence with a class of men whose numbers and wealth make them highly important. If, on the other hand, he opposes them, and still more if he has enough authority to thwart them, then neither the most widely acknowledged integrity, nor the highest rank, nor the greatest public service can protect him from the most scurrilous abuse and slander, from personal insults, and sometimes even from real danger, arising from the insolent fury of enraged and disappointed monopolists.

The owner of a large manufacturing enterprise who was forced to abandon his business because the home market had suddenly been thrown open to foreign competition would certainly suffer a great deal. The part of his capital normally used to buy materials and pay his workers might perhaps find another use without much difficulty. But the part fixed in workshops and in the tools and equipment of the trade could hardly be disposed of without considerable loss. Fair regard for his interests therefore requires that changes of this kind never be introduced suddenly, but slowly, gradually, and after very long warning. If the legislature's deliberations could always be guided not by the clamorous pressure of particular interests but by a broad view of the general good, it ought, perhaps for this very reason, to take special care neither to establish any new monopolies of this kind nor to extend further those already established. Every such regulation introduces some degree of real disorder into the constitution of the state, a disorder that will afterward be difficult to cure without causing another.

How far it may be proper to tax foreign imports, not in order to prevent their importation but to raise revenue for the government, I shall consider later, when I come to treat the subject of taxes. Taxes imposed with the aim of preventing, or even reducing, importation are plainly as destructive to the revenue of the customs as they are to the freedom of trade.

### CHAPTER III: OF THE EXTRAORDINARY RESTRAINTS UPON THE IMPORTATION OF GOODS OF ALMOST ALL KINDS, FROM THOSE COUNTRIES WITH WHICH THE BALANCE IS SUPPOSED TO BE DISADVANTAGEOUS

#### Part I: The Unreasonableness of Those Restraints, Even by the Principles of the Commercial System

The second expedient by which the commercial system proposes to increase a nation's stock of gold and silver is to place extraordinary restraints on the importation of nearly every kind of goods from those particular countries with which the balance of trade is supposed to be unfavorable. In Great Britain, for example, Silesian lawns, a fine linen, may be imported for home consumption on payment of certain duties, but French cambrics and lawns are banned from import except into the port of London, where they must be held in warehouses for re-export. The wines of France carry higher duties than those of Portugal, or indeed of any other country. Under what is called the Impost of 1692, a duty of twenty-five percent of the official rate or value was laid on all French goods, while most goods from other nations were subject to much lighter duties, seldom exceeding five percent. French wine, brandy, salt, and vinegar were exempted from this particular duty, but only because they were already burdened with other heavy duties, imposed either by separate laws or by special clauses of the same law. In 1696, since the first duty had not been judged a sufficient discouragement, a second duty of twenty-five percent was imposed on all French goods except brandy, together with a new duty of twenty-five pounds per ton on French wine and another of fifteen pounds per ton on French vinegar. French goods have never been left out of any of the general subsidies, those duties of five percent levied on all or most of the goods listed in the book of rates, the official schedule by which customs officers valued imports. If the subsidy of one-third and the subsidy of two-thirds are counted together as one complete subsidy, there have been five of these general subsidies; so that before the present war began, seventy-five percent may be considered the lowest duty to which most goods grown, produced, or manufactured in France were liable. On most goods, duties of that height amount to an outright prohibition. The French, I believe, have treated our goods and manufactures just as harshly in return, though I am less familiar with the particular burdens they have imposed. These mutual restraints have put an end to almost all lawful commerce between the two nations, and smugglers are now the principal importers of British goods into France and of French goods into Great Britain. The principles I examined in the previous chapter arose from private interest and the spirit of monopoly; those I am about to examine in this one arise from national prejudice and animosity. As might be expected, they are even more unreasonable. They are unreasonable even by the principles of the commercial system itself.

First, even if it were certain that under free trade between France and England the balance would favor France, it would by no means follow that such trade would harm England, or that the general balance of England's entire trade would be turned further against it. If the wines of France are better and cheaper than those of Portugal, or its linens better and cheaper than those of Germany, it would be more advantageous for Great Britain to buy from France all the wine and foreign linen it needed, rather than buy them from Portugal and Germany. The value of annual imports from France would rise considerably, but the value of Britain's total annual imports would fall, in proportion as French goods of the same quality were cheaper than those of the other two countries. This would hold true even on the assumption that every French good imported was consumed within Great Britain.

Second, a large share of those goods might be re-exported to other countries, where they could be sold at a profit and bring back a return equal in value, perhaps, to the original cost of all the French goods imported. What has often been said of the East India trade might well prove true of the French trade: that although most East India goods were bought with gold and silver, the re-export of part of them to other countries brought back more gold and silver to the nation conducting the trade than the original cost of the whole amounted to. One of the most important branches of Dutch commerce today consists of carrying French goods to other European countries. Some of the French wine drunk in Great Britain is itself smuggled in from Holland and Zeeland. If there were free trade between France and England, or if French goods could be imported on paying only the same duties as those of other European nations, with those duties refunded on re-export, England might win some share of a trade that Holland finds so profitable.

Third and last, there is no reliable criterion by which to determine on which side the so-called balance between two countries lies, or which of them exports the greater value. Our judgment on every question concerning it is generally directed by national prejudice and animosity, always prompted by the private interest of particular traders. Two criteria, however, have often been appealed to on such occasions: the customhouse books and the course of exchange. It is now, I think, generally acknowledged that the customhouse books are a very uncertain criterion, because of the inaccurate valuations at which most goods are recorded in them. The course of exchange is perhaps almost equally unreliable.

When the exchange between two places, such as London and Paris, stands at par, this is said to show that the debts owed by London to Paris are offset by the debts owed by Paris to London. When, on the contrary, a premium must be paid in London for a bill of exchange drawn on Paris, this is said to show that London's debts to Paris are not offset by Paris's debts to London, and that a balance in money must be sent out of London; the premium is demanded and paid to cover the risk, trouble, and expense of shipping that money. The ordinary state of debt and credit between the two cities, the argument continues, must necessarily be governed by the ordinary course of their dealings with one another. When neither imports from the other more than it exports to that other, the debts and credits of each may cancel out. But when one imports from the other a greater value than it exports to it, the first necessarily falls into debt to the second for a larger sum than the second owes in return. Their debts and credits no longer cancel out, and money must be sent from the place whose debts exceed its credits. Since the ordinary course of exchange indicates the ordinary state of debt and credit between two places, it must therefore also indicate the ordinary course of their exports and imports, which necessarily govern that state.

Yet even granting that the ordinary course of exchange sufficiently indicates the ordinary state of debt and credit between two places, it would not follow that the balance of trade favored whichever place had that state of debt and credit in its favor. The ordinary state of debt and credit between two places is not always governed entirely by their dealings with one another; it is often influenced by the dealings of either one with many other places. If, for example, English merchants customarily pay for goods bought from Hamburg, Danzig, Riga, and elsewhere with bills drawn on Holland, then the state of debt and credit between England and Holland will not be governed entirely by the dealings of those two countries with each other, but will be influenced by England's dealings with those other places. England might be obliged to send money to Holland every year even though its annual exports to Holland far exceeded the value of its annual imports from there, and even though the so-called balance of trade lay heavily in England's favor.

Moreover, given the way the par of exchange has been calculated up to now, the ordinary course of exchange cannot sufficiently show that the ordinary state of debt and credit favors the country that appears to have, or is supposed to have, the exchange in its favor. The real exchange may differ, and in fact often does differ, so widely from the computed exchange that on many occasions no firm conclusion about the one can be drawn from the course of the other.

Exchange is said to be at par between England and France when, for a sum of money paid in England that contains, by the standard of the English mint, a certain number of ounces of pure silver, you receive a bill for a sum payable in France that contains, by the standard of the French mint, the same number of ounces of pure silver. When you pay more than this, you are supposed to be paying a premium, and the exchange is said to be against England and in favor of France. When you pay less, you are supposed to be receiving a premium, and the exchange is said to be against France and in favor of England.

But first, we cannot always judge the value of different countries' circulating money by the standards of their respective mints. In some countries the coinage is more worn, clipped, and otherwise debased below its standard; in others, less so. The value of each country's circulating coin, compared with that of any other country, is proportional not to the quantity of pure silver it ought to contain, but to the quantity it actually does contain. Before the recoinage of the silver currency in King William's reign, the exchange between England and Holland, calculated in the usual way according to the standards of their respective mints, ran twenty-five percent against England. But the circulating coin of England at that time, as we learn from Mr. Lowndes, was worth rather more than twenty-five percent below its standard value. The real exchange, therefore, may well have favored England even then, however strongly the computed exchange ran against it. A smaller number of ounces of pure silver actually paid in England may have bought a bill for a larger number of ounces of pure silver payable in Holland, and the man supposed to be paying the premium may in reality have been receiving it. Before the recent recoinage of English gold, French coin was much less worn than English coin, and stood perhaps two or three percent nearer its standard. If the computed exchange with France ran no more than two or three percent against England, then, the real exchange might have been in England's favor. Since the recoinage of the gold, the exchange has consistently favored England and gone against France.

Second, in some countries the cost of minting is paid by the government; in others it is paid by the private individuals who bring their bullion to the mint, and the government even draws some revenue from the coinage. In England the government bears the cost: if you bring a pound weight of standard silver to the mint, you receive sixty-two shillings containing a pound weight of silver of the same standard. In France a duty of eight percent is deducted for minting, which not only covers the expense but yields a small revenue to the government. In England, since minting costs nothing, the circulating coin can never be worth much more than the bullion it actually contains. In France, the workmanship, because it is paid for, adds to the value of the coin, just as craftsmanship adds to the value of wrought silver plate. A sum of French money containing a given weight of pure silver is therefore worth more than a sum of English money containing the same weight, and it takes more bullion, or more of other goods, to buy it. Even if the circulating coin of the two countries were equally close to the standards of their respective mints, a sum of English money could not readily buy a sum of French money containing an equal number of ounces of pure silver, nor, consequently, a bill on France for such a sum. If the additional money paid for such a bill were no more than enough to cover the cost of French minting, the real exchange between the two countries might stand at par, and their debts and credits might offset one another, while the computed exchange ran considerably in favor of France. If less than this were paid, the real exchange might favor England while the computed exchange favored France.

Third and last, in some places, such as Amsterdam, Hamburg, and Venice, foreign bills of exchange are paid in what is called bank money, while in others, such as London, Lisbon, Antwerp, and Leghorn, they are paid in the ordinary currency of the country. Bank money is always worth more than the same nominal sum in ordinary currency. A thousand guilders held in the Bank of Amsterdam, for example, are worth more than a thousand guilders of Amsterdam currency. The difference between them is called the agio of the bank, and at Amsterdam it is generally about five percent. Suppose the circulating money of two countries stands equally close to the standards of their respective mints, and one pays foreign bills in ordinary currency while the other pays them in bank money. Plainly, the computed exchange may favor the country that pays in bank money even when the real exchange favors the one paying in currency, for the same reason that the computed exchange may favor a country paying in better money, closer to its own standard, even when the real exchange favors the one paying in worse. Before the recent recoinage of the gold, the computed exchange generally ran against London in its dealings with Amsterdam, Hamburg, Venice, and, I believe, every other place that pays in bank money. It by no means follows that the real exchange ran against it. Since the recoinage, the exchange has favored London even with those places. The computed exchange has generally favored London in its dealings with Lisbon, Antwerp, Leghorn, and, France excepted, I believe with most other parts of Europe that pay in ordinary currency; and it is not unlikely that the real exchange did as well.

#### A Digression on Banks of Deposit, Particularly the Bank of Amsterdam

The currency of a large state, such as France or England, generally consists almost entirely of its own coin. If that currency should at any time become worn, clipped, or otherwise debased below its standard value, the state can effectively restore it by recoining. But the currency of a small state, such as Genoa or Hamburg, can rarely consist wholly of its own coin; it must be made up largely of the coins of all the neighboring states with which its inhabitants are in constant dealings. Such a state, by reforming its coin, cannot always reform its currency. If foreign bills of exchange are paid in this currency, the uncertain value of any given sum of something so inherently uncertain must keep the exchange heavily against that state, since every foreign state will necessarily value its currency even below what it is actually worth.

To relieve their merchants of the burden of this unfavorable exchange, such small states, once they began to attend to the interests of trade, often decreed that foreign bills of exchange above a certain value should be paid not in ordinary currency but by an order on, or a transfer in the books of, a particular bank established on the credit and under the protection of the state. This bank was always obliged to pay in good, sound money that conformed exactly to the state's standard. The banks of Venice, Genoa, Amsterdam, Hamburg, and Nuremberg all seem to have been founded originally for this purpose, though some of them may later have been turned to other uses. Because the money of such banks was better than the ordinary currency of the country, it necessarily carried an agio, larger or smaller according to how far the currency was thought to have fallen below the state's standard. The agio of the Bank of Hamburg, for example, said to run commonly at about fourteen percent, represents the supposed difference between the state's good standard money and the clipped, worn, and diminished currency that poured in from all the neighboring states.

Before 1609, the great quantity of clipped and worn foreign coin that Amsterdam's extensive trade drew in from every part of Europe had reduced the value of its currency to about nine percent below that of good money fresh from the mint. Such good money was melted down or carried away as soon as it appeared, as always happens in such circumstances. Merchants with plenty of currency could not always find enough good money to pay their bills of exchange, and the value of those bills, despite several regulations made to prevent it, became largely uncertain.

To remedy these difficulties, a bank was established in 1609 under the guarantee of the city. The bank accepted both foreign coin and the light and worn coin of the country at its real intrinsic value in good standard money, deducting only what was needed to cover the cost of minting and the other necessary costs of management. For the value remaining after this small deduction, it gave a credit in its books. This credit was called bank money. Because it represented money exactly at the mint standard, it always held the same real value and was intrinsically worth more than circulating currency. At the same time it was decreed that all bills drawn on or negotiated at Amsterdam for 600 guilders or more must be paid in bank money, which at a stroke removed all uncertainty about the value of those bills. As a result of this regulation, every merchant had to keep an account with the bank in order to pay his foreign bills of exchange, and this necessarily created a steady demand for bank money.

Beyond its intrinsic superiority to currency and the additional value that this demand necessarily gives it, bank money has several other advantages. It is safe from fire, robbery, and other accidents; the city of Amsterdam stands surety for it; and it can be paid out by a simple transfer, without the trouble of counting it or the risk of carrying it from one place to another. Because of these various advantages, it seems to have carried an agio from the very beginning, and it is generally believed that all the money originally deposited in the bank was left there, since nobody cared to demand payment of a debt that he could sell for a premium in the market. By demanding payment from the bank, the owner of a bank credit would forfeit that premium. Just as a shilling fresh from the mint will buy no more goods in the market than one of our ordinary worn shillings, so the good, sound money that might be moved from the bank's coffers into a private person's would, once mixed and confused with the ordinary currency of the country, be worth no more than that currency, from which it could no longer be easily told apart. While it stayed in the bank's coffers, its superiority was known and certain. Once in private hands, that superiority could not readily be established without more trouble than the difference was perhaps worth. Taken out of the bank's coffers, moreover, it lost all the other advantages of bank money: its security, its easy and safe transferability, and its use in paying foreign bills of exchange. On top of all this, as will appear shortly, it could not be taken out of those coffers without first paying a fee for its safekeeping.

These deposits of coin, or deposits that the bank was obliged to repay in coin, made up the bank's original capital, the entire value represented by what is called bank money. Today they are thought to make up only a very small part of it. To facilitate the trade in bullion, the bank has for many years been in the practice of giving credit in its books for deposits of gold and silver bullion. This credit is generally about five percent below the mint price of the bullion. At the same time the bank issues what is called a *recipice*, or receipt, which entitles the depositor, or whoever holds the receipt, to withdraw the bullion at any time within six months. To do so, he must transfer to the bank a quantity of bank money equal to the credit given in its books when the deposit was made, and pay a fee for the safekeeping of one-quarter percent if the deposit was silver, or one-half percent if it was gold. The bank declares at the same time that if this payment is not made before the term expires, the deposit becomes the property of the bank at the price at which it was received, that is, the price credited in the transfer books. What is paid for the safekeeping of the deposit may be regarded as a kind of warehouse rent, and several reasons have been offered for why this rent should be so much higher for gold than for silver. The fineness of gold, it has been said, is harder to determine than that of silver. Frauds are easier to commit with the more precious metal, and they cause greater loss. Silver, besides, being the standard metal, the state is said to wish to encourage deposits of silver more than deposits of gold.

Deposits of bullion are most often made when its price is somewhat lower than usual, and withdrawn when the price happens to rise. In Holland the market price of bullion generally stands above the mint price, for the same reason that it did in England before the recent recoinage of the gold. The difference is said to run commonly from about six to sixteen stivers (the Dutch coin worth one-twentieth of a guilder) on the mark, a weight of eight ounces of silver composed of eleven parts fine metal and one part alloy. The bank price, meaning the credit the bank gives for deposits of such silver when made in foreign coin of well-known and established fineness, such as Mexican dollars, is twenty-two guilders the mark. The mint price is about twenty-three guilders, and the market price runs from twenty-three guilders six stivers to twenty-three guilders sixteen stivers, or from two to three percent above the mint price.

The following are the prices at which the Bank of Amsterdam currently (as of September 1775) accepts bullion and coin of various kinds:

**Silver**

| Coin or bullion | Price |
|---|---|
| Mexico dollars | 22 guilders per mark |
| French crowns | 22 guilders per mark |
| English silver coin | 22 guilders per mark |
| Mexico dollars, new coin | 21 guilders, 10 stivers per mark |
| Ducatoons | 3 guilders each |
| Rix-dollars | 2 guilders, 8 stivers each |

Bar silver that is eleven-twelfths fine silver is received at 21 guilders per mark, and at proportionally lower rates down to bars only one-quarter fine, for which 5 guilders are given. Bars of fine silver are received at 28 guilders per mark.

**Gold**

| Coin or bullion | Price |
|---|---|
| Portuguese coin | 310 guilders per mark |
| Guineas | 310 guilders per mark |
| Louis d'or, new | 310 guilders per mark |
| Louis d'or, old | 300 guilders per mark |
| New ducats | 4 guilders, 19 stivers, 8 pennings per ducat |

Bar or ingot gold is received in proportion to its fineness, measured against the foreign gold coins listed above. For bars of fine gold the bank gives 340 guilders per mark. In general, however, the bank gives somewhat more for coin of known fineness than for bars of gold and silver, whose fineness can be established only by melting them down and assaying them.

The bank price, the mint price, and the market price of gold bullion stand in nearly the same proportions to one another as they do for silver. A depositor can generally sell his receipt for the difference between the mint price of bullion and its market price. Because a receipt for bullion is almost always worth something, people very seldom let their receipts expire. They rarely allow their bullion to pass to the bank at the price at which it was received, whether by failing to withdraw it before the six months are up or by neglecting to pay the quarter or half percent required to obtain a new receipt for another six months. Although this happens seldom, it is said to happen occasionally, and more often with gold than with silver, because the warehouse rent charged for storing the more precious metal is higher.

A person who deposits bullion obtains both a bank credit and a receipt. He pays his bills of exchange with the bank credit as they fall due, and he either sells or keeps the receipt depending on whether he expects the price of bullion to rise or fall. The receipt and the bank credit seldom stay together for long, and there is no reason why they should. Anyone who holds a receipt and wants to withdraw bullion can always find plenty of bank credits, or bank money, to buy at the ordinary price; and anyone who holds bank money and wants to withdraw bullion can always find receipts in equal abundance.

The owners of bank credits and the holders of receipts are thus two distinct kinds of creditors of the bank. The holder of a receipt cannot withdraw the bullion it was issued for without signing back to the bank a sum of bank money equal to the price at which that bullion was originally received. If he has no bank money of his own, he must buy it from those who do. The owner of bank money, for his part, cannot withdraw bullion without presenting receipts for the quantity he wants, and if he has none, he must buy them from those who have them. When the holder of a receipt buys bank money, he is buying the power to withdraw a quantity of bullion whose mint price is five percent above the bank price. The agio, or premium, of five percent that he commonly pays for bank money is therefore paid not for an imaginary value but for a real one. When the owner of bank money buys a receipt, he is buying the power to withdraw a quantity of bullion whose market price is commonly two to three percent above the mint price, so the price he pays is likewise paid for a real value. Between them, the price of the receipt and the price of the bank money make up the full value, or price, of the bullion.

The bank also grants receipts, along with bank credits, for deposits of the coin that circulates within the country. These receipts, however, are frequently worthless and fetch no price on the market. Ducatoons, for example, circulate in the ordinary currency at three guilders three stivers apiece, but the bank credits only three guilders for each, five percent below their current value. It also issues a receipt entitling the bearer to withdraw the same number of ducatoons at any time within six months, on payment of a quarter percent for their keeping. Such a receipt will frequently bring no price at all. Three guilders in bank money generally sell on the market for three guilders three stivers, which is the full value the ducatoons would have if they were taken out of the bank; and since a quarter percent must be paid for their keeping before they can be withdrawn, the holder of the receipt would simply lose that amount. If the bank's agio ever fell to three percent, such receipts might command some price, selling perhaps for one and three-quarters percent. But because the agio now generally stands at about five percent, these receipts are frequently allowed to expire, or, in the local phrase, to "fall to the bank." Receipts issued for deposits of gold ducats fall to the bank even more often, because a higher warehouse rent of half a percent must be paid for their keeping before they can be withdrawn. The five percent the bank gains when deposits of either coin or bullion fall to it may be regarded as a warehouse rent for keeping those deposits permanently.

The sum of bank money whose receipts have expired must be very large. It must include the entire original capital of the bank, which is generally believed to have remained there since it was first deposited, because, for the reasons already given, no one could either renew his receipt or withdraw his deposit without losing by it. Yet whatever the size of this sum, it is thought to form only a very small proportion of the total mass of bank money. For many years now, the Bank of Amsterdam has been the great warehouse of bullion for all of Europe, and receipts for bullion are very seldom allowed to expire. The far greater part of the bank money, that is, of the credits on the bank's books, is believed to have been created over these many years by such deposits, which the dealers in bullion are continually making and withdrawing.

No claim can be made on the bank except by means of a receipt. The smaller mass of bank money whose receipts have expired is mixed together indistinguishably with the much larger mass whose receipts are still in force. Consequently, although there may be a considerable sum of bank money for which no receipts exist, there is no particular portion of it that might not be claimed at any moment by someone holding a receipt. The bank cannot be in debt to two people for the same thing, and so the owner of bank money who has no receipt cannot demand payment until he buys one. In ordinary, peaceful times he will have no difficulty finding one at the market price, which generally matches the price at which he can sell the coin or bullion the receipt entitles him to withdraw.

During a public calamity, things might be different: an invasion, for example, such as the French invasion of 1672. The owners of bank money would then all be eager to withdraw it and hold it themselves, and their demand for receipts might drive the price to an exorbitant height. The holders of receipts might form extravagant expectations and, instead of two or three percent, demand half the bank money that had been credited against the deposits for which their receipts were issued. An enemy who understood how the bank was organized might even buy up the receipts in order to prevent the treasure from being carried away. In such emergencies, it is supposed, the bank would abandon its ordinary rule of paying only those who hold receipts. Holders of receipts who owned no bank money would already have received all but two or three percent of the value of the deposits for which their receipts were granted. The bank, it is said, would therefore have no hesitation in paying, in coin or bullion, the full value of what the owners of bank money who could obtain no receipts were credited with on its books, while paying two or three percent to those holders of receipts who had no bank money, since that was all that could fairly be considered owed to them under the circumstances.

Even in ordinary, peaceful times, it is in the interest of the holders of receipts to push the agio down. A lower agio lets them buy bank money more cheaply, and with it the bullion their receipts would then allow them to withdraw; or it lets them sell their receipts at a higher price to owners of bank money who wish to withdraw bullion, since the price of a receipt is generally equal to the difference between the market price of bank money and that of the coin or bullion for which the receipt was granted. The owners of bank money, on the contrary, have an interest in raising the agio, so that they can either sell their bank money at a higher price or buy a receipt more cheaply. To prevent the speculative manipulation that these opposing interests might sometimes provoke, the bank has in recent years resolved to sell bank money for ordinary currency at all times at an agio of five percent, and to buy it back at an agio of four percent. As a result of this policy, the agio can never rise above five percent or fall below four, and the ratio between the market price of bank money and that of current money is kept at all times very close to the ratio between their intrinsic values. Before this policy was adopted, the market price of bank money sometimes rose as high as a nine percent agio and sometimes sank as low as par, depending on which of the opposing interests happened to sway the market.

The Bank of Amsterdam professes to lend out no part of what is deposited with it, and to keep in its vaults the value of one guilder in coin or bullion for every guilder it credits on its books. There can be little doubt that it keeps in its vaults all the coin and bullion covered by receipts still in force, since it may be called upon for this at any time, and in practice it is continually flowing out and returning. Whether it does the same with the part of its capital whose receipts expired long ago may seem more uncertain. That portion cannot be claimed in ordinary, peaceful times, and in all likelihood it will remain with the bank forever, or at least as long as the States of the United Provinces endure. At Amsterdam, however, no article of faith is more firmly established than the belief that for every guilder circulating as bank money, a corresponding guilder in gold or silver lies in the bank's treasury. The city itself guarantees that this is so. The bank is under the direction of the four reigning burgomasters, the city's chief magistrates, who are replaced every year. Each new set of burgomasters inspects the treasure, compares it with the books, takes charge of it under oath, and hands it over with the same solemn ceremony to the set that follows; and in that sober and religious country, oaths are not yet treated lightly. A rotation of this kind seems in itself a sufficient safeguard against any practice that could not be openly acknowledged. Through all the upheavals that faction has ever caused in the government of Amsterdam, the victorious party has never once accused its predecessors of dishonesty in managing the bank. No accusation could have damaged the reputation and fortunes of the defeated party more severely, and if such a charge could have been sustained, we may be sure it would have been made. In 1672, when the French king was at Utrecht, the Bank of Amsterdam paid out so promptly that it left no doubt about the fidelity with which it had kept its commitments. Some of the coins brought out of its vaults at that time appeared to have been scorched by the fire that broke out in the town hall shortly after the bank was founded. Those coins, therefore, must have been lying there ever since.

How much treasure the bank holds is a question that has long occupied the speculations of the curious, and nothing but conjecture can be offered in reply. It is generally estimated that about 2,000 people keep accounts with the bank. If we allow each of them, on average, the value of £1,500 sterling in his account, which is a very generous allowance, the total quantity of bank money, and therefore of treasure in the bank, will come to about £3,000,000 sterling, or, at eleven guilders to the pound sterling, 33,000,000 guilders. This is a great sum, large enough to sustain a very extensive circulation, but vastly below the extravagant notions some people have formed of this treasure.

The city of Amsterdam draws a considerable revenue from the bank. Besides what may be called the warehouse rent described above, each person pays a fee of ten guilders on first opening an account with the bank, and three guilders three stivers for every new account thereafter. Every transfer costs two stivers, and a transfer of less than 300 guilders costs six stivers, so as to discourage a multitude of small transactions. Anyone who fails to balance his account twice a year forfeits twenty-five guilders. Anyone who orders a transfer for more than his account holds must pay three percent on the amount overdrawn, and his order is cancelled into the bargain. The bank is also thought to make a considerable profit from selling the foreign coin or bullion that sometimes falls to it when receipts expire, which it always holds until it can be sold to advantage. It profits as well by selling bank money at a five percent agio and buying it back at four. Together these sources of income come to a good deal more than is needed to pay the officers' salaries and cover the costs of management. The fees charged for keeping bullion on receipts are alone believed to yield a net annual revenue of between 150,000 and 200,000 guilders. Yet public utility, not revenue, was the original purpose of this institution. Its aim was to relieve merchants of the burden of an unfavorable exchange rate, and the revenue that has arisen from it was unforeseen and may be regarded as incidental.

It is now time to return from this long digression, into which I was gradually drawn while trying to explain why the exchange between countries that pay in what is called bank money and countries that pay in ordinary currency should generally appear to favor the former and to tell against the latter. The former pay in a kind of money whose intrinsic value is always the same and corresponds exactly to the standard of their respective mints. The latter pay in a kind of money whose intrinsic value is constantly changing and is almost always somewhat below that standard.

#### Part II: The Unreasonableness of Those Extraordinary Restraints on Other Principles

In the first part of this chapter, I tried to show, even on the principles of the commercial system itself, how unnecessary it is to impose extraordinary restraints on imports from countries with which the balance of trade is supposed to be unfavorable.

Nothing, however, could be more absurd than the whole doctrine of the balance of trade, on which not only these restraints but nearly all the other regulations of commerce are founded. When two places trade with each other, this doctrine assumes that if the balance is even, neither of them gains or loses; but that if it tilts at all to one side, one of them loses and the other gains, in proportion to how far the balance departs from exact equilibrium. Both assumptions are false. A trade that is forced into being by bounties and monopolies may be, and commonly is, harmful to the very country it was meant to benefit, as I shall try to show later on. But a trade carried on naturally and regularly between any two places, without force or constraint, is always advantageous to both, though not always equally so.

By advantage or gain I mean not an increase in the quantity of gold and silver, but an increase in the exchangeable value of the annual produce of the country's land and labor, or, put another way, an increase in the annual revenue of its inhabitants.

If the balance is even, and the trade between the two places consists entirely of exchanging their native commodities, then in most cases both will not only gain but gain equally, or very nearly so. Each will provide a market for part of the other's surplus produce. Each will replace a capital that the other had spent in growing or making that part of its surplus produce and preparing it for market, a capital that had been distributed among a certain number of the other's inhabitants and had given them revenue and maintenance. Some of the inhabitants of each country will therefore draw their revenue and maintenance directly from the other. And since the commodities exchanged are assumed to be of equal value, the two capitals employed in the trade will in most cases be equal, or very nearly so; and because both are employed in producing the native commodities of their two countries, the revenue and maintenance they provide to the inhabitants of each, as they are paid out, will also be equal or very nearly equal. The revenue and maintenance that each thus provides to the other will be greater or smaller according to the volume of their dealings. If these amounted to £100,000 a year on each side, for example, or to £1,000,000, each country would provide the inhabitants of the other with an annual revenue of £100,000 in the first case and £1,000,000 in the second.

Suppose instead that one country exported nothing to the other but native commodities, while the other paid entirely in foreign goods. The balance would still be considered even in this case, since commodities would be paid for with commodities. Here, too, both would gain, but not equally, and the inhabitants of the country that exported only native commodities would draw the greater revenue from the trade. Suppose, for example, that England imported from France nothing but French native commodities, and, having no commodities of its own that were in demand there, paid for them each year by sending a large quantity of foreign goods, say tobacco and East India goods. This trade would give some revenue to the inhabitants of both countries, but more to the French than to the English. The whole French capital employed in it each year would be distributed annually among the people of France. Of the English capital, however, only the part employed in producing the English commodities with which those foreign goods were bought would be distributed annually among the people of England. The greater part of it would go to replace the capitals that had been employed in Virginia, Hindustan, and China, which had given revenue and maintenance to the inhabitants of those distant countries. If the two capitals were equal or nearly equal, then, the French capital employed in this way would add much more to the revenue of the people of France than the English capital would add to the revenue of the people of England. France would in this case be carrying on a direct foreign trade of consumption with England, while England would be carrying on a roundabout trade of the same kind with France. The different effects of capital employed in the direct and in the roundabout foreign trade of consumption have already been fully explained.

There is probably no trade between any two countries that consists entirely of native commodities exchanged on both sides, or entirely of native commodities on one side and foreign goods on the other. Nearly all countries exchange a mixture of native and foreign goods with one another. Still, the country whose cargoes contain the greatest proportion of native goods and the smallest proportion of foreign ones will always be the chief gainer.

If England paid for its annual imports from France not with tobacco and East India goods but with gold and silver, the balance would in this case be considered uneven, since commodities would be paid for not with commodities but with gold and silver. Yet in this case, as in the previous one, the trade would give some revenue to the inhabitants of both countries, though more to the French than to the English. It would still give some revenue to the English. The capital that had been employed in producing the English goods with which this gold and silver was bought, a capital that had been distributed among certain inhabitants of England and had given them revenue, would be replaced by it and enabled to continue in that employment. The total capital of England would no more be diminished by this export of gold and silver than by the export of an equal value of any other goods. On the contrary, it would in most cases be increased. No goods are sent abroad except those for which demand is thought to be greater abroad than at home, and whose returns are therefore expected to be worth more at home than the commodities exported. If tobacco worth only £100,000 in England will buy, when sent to France, wine worth £110,000 in England, the exchange will increase England's capital by £10,000. In the same way, if £100,000 of English gold buys French wine worth £110,000 in England, that exchange will equally increase England's capital by £10,000. A merchant with £110,000 worth of wine in his cellar is a richer man than one with only £100,000 worth of tobacco in his warehouse, and likewise richer than one with only £100,000 worth of gold in his coffers. He can set a greater quantity of industry in motion and provide revenue, maintenance, and employment to more people than either of the other two. But the capital of a country is equal to the combined capital of all its inhabitants, and the quantity of industry it can maintain each year is equal to what all those individual capitals can maintain. Both the country's capital and the quantity of industry it can maintain each year must therefore generally be increased by this exchange.
