It would, admittedly, be more advantageous for England to buy French wines with its own hardware and broadcloth than with either Virginia tobacco or the gold and silver of Brazil and Peru, since a direct foreign trade of consumption is always more advantageous than a roundabout one. But a roundabout foreign trade of consumption carried on with gold and silver does not appear to be any less advantageous than any other equally roundabout trade. Nor is a country that has no mines any more likely to be drained of gold and silver by sending those metals abroad every year than a country that grows no tobacco is likely to be drained of tobacco by sending that plant abroad every year. A country that has the means to buy tobacco will never go without it for long, and a country that has the means to buy gold and silver will never go without those metals for long either.

It is said that a workman's trade with the alehouse is a losing trade, and that the trade a manufacturing nation would naturally carry on with a wine-producing country may be regarded as a trade of the same kind. My answer is that trade with the alehouse is not necessarily a losing one. In its own nature it is just as advantageous as any other, though it is perhaps somewhat more open to abuse. The brewer's occupation, and even that of the retailer of fermented liquors, are as necessary a part of the division of labour as any other. It will generally pay a workman better to buy from the brewer whatever quantity he needs than to brew it himself, and if he is poor, it will generally pay him better to buy it a little at a time from the retailer than in bulk from the brewer. He may certainly buy too much from either, just as he may from any other dealer in his neighbourhood: from the butcher, if he is a glutton, or from the draper, if he wants to cut a fashionable figure among his companions. It is still to the advantage of the great body of working people that all these trades should be free, even though that freedom may be abused in every one of them, and perhaps more readily in some than in others. Moreover, although individuals may sometimes ruin themselves by drinking to excess, there seems to be no danger that a whole nation will do so. In every country there are many people who spend more on such liquors than they can afford, but there are always many more who spend less.

It is also worth remarking that, if we consult experience, cheap wine appears to cause not drunkenness but sobriety. The inhabitants of the wine countries are, on the whole, the most sober people in Europe, as the Spaniards, the Italians, and the people of the southern provinces of France all show. People seldom overindulge in what is their everyday fare. No one tries to display generosity and good fellowship by pouring out freely a drink that costs no more than small beer, the weak and inexpensive beer of ordinary households. By contrast, in countries that grow no grapes because of extreme heat or cold, and where wine is therefore scarce and expensive, drunkenness is a common vice, as it is among the northern nations and among all the peoples who live between the tropics, such as the inhabitants of the coast of Guinea. I have often heard it observed that when a French regiment arrives from one of the northern provinces of France, where wine is somewhat expensive, to be stationed in the south, where it is very cheap, the soldiers are at first led into excess by the cheapness and novelty of good wine, but after a few months there most of them become as sober as the local inhabitants. In the same way, if the duties on foreign wines and the excise taxes on malt, beer, and ale were abolished all at once, Great Britain might see a fairly general but temporary drunkenness among the middle and lower ranks of people, which would probably soon give way to a permanent and almost universal sobriety. As things stand, drunkenness is by no means the vice of fashionable people, or of those who can easily afford the most expensive drinks. A gentleman drunk on ale is almost never seen among us.

Besides, the restrictions on the wine trade in Great Britain do not seem designed so much to keep people from going to the alehouse, so to speak, as to keep them from going where they can buy the best and cheapest drink. They favour the wine trade of Portugal and discourage that of France. The Portuguese, it is claimed, are better customers for our manufactured goods than the French are, and should therefore be favoured over them; since they give us their business, we ought to give them ours. In this way the petty tactics of small shopkeepers have been elevated into political principles for governing a great empire, for it is only the pettiest shopkeepers who make it a rule to buy chiefly from their own customers. A great merchant always buys his goods wherever they are cheapest and best, without regard to any small consideration of that kind.

Yet it is by principles like these that nations have been taught that their interest lies in impoverishing all their neighbours. Each nation has been led to look with envy on the prosperity of every nation it trades with, and to regard their gain as its own loss. Commerce, which ought naturally to be a bond of union and friendship among nations, as it is among individuals, has become the most abundant source of discord and hostility. During this century and the last, the capricious ambition of kings and ministers has not been more destructive to the peace of Europe than the meddlesome jealousy of merchants and manufacturers. The violence and injustice of those who rule mankind is an ancient evil for which, I fear, the nature of human affairs scarcely allows a remedy. But the mean greed and monopolizing spirit of merchants and manufacturers, who neither are nor ought to be the rulers of mankind, though perhaps incurable, can very easily be prevented from disturbing the peace of anyone but themselves.

There can be no doubt that it was the spirit of monopoly that first invented this doctrine and then spread it, and those who first taught it were far from being such fools as those who believed it. In every country it always is, and must be, in the interest of the great body of the people to buy whatever they need from whoever sells it cheapest. The proposition is so obvious that it seems absurd to take any trouble to prove it, and it could never have been questioned at all had the self-interested sophistry of merchants and manufacturers not confused the common sense of mankind. On this point their interest runs directly against that of the great body of the people. Just as the freemen of a corporation, the members of a chartered town guild, have an interest in preventing the town's other inhabitants from hiring any workmen but themselves, so the merchants and manufacturers of every country have an interest in securing for themselves a monopoly of the home market. Hence, in Great Britain and most other European countries, the extraordinary duties on nearly all goods imported by foreign merchants. Hence the high duties and outright bans on all foreign manufactures that might compete with our own. And hence, too, the extraordinary restrictions on importing almost every kind of goods from those countries with which the balance of trade is supposed to be unfavourable, which is to say, from those against whom national hostility happens to burn most fiercely.

The wealth of neighbouring nations, however dangerous in war and politics, is certainly an advantage in trade. In wartime it may allow our enemies to maintain fleets and armies larger than our own, but in times of peace and commerce it must equally allow them to trade with us on a larger scale and to offer a better market, either for the direct products of our own industry or for whatever we buy with those products. Just as a rich man is likely to be a better customer than a poor one to the hardworking people around him, so is a rich nation. A rich man who is himself a manufacturer is, admittedly, a very dangerous neighbour to everyone in the same line of business. But all the rest of the neighbourhood, by far the larger number, profit from the good market his spending provides. They even profit from his underselling the poorer workmen in his own trade. In the same way, the manufacturers of a rich nation may certainly be formidable rivals to those of its neighbours. Yet that very competition benefits the great body of the people, who also gain a great deal from the good market that such a nation's heavy spending opens to them in every other respect. Private individuals who want to make their fortune never think of moving to the remote and poor provinces of their country; they go instead to the capital or to one of the great commercial towns. They know that where little wealth circulates there is little to be earned, but that where a great deal of it is in motion, some share may come their way. The same principle that guides the common sense of one, ten, or twenty individuals should govern the judgment of one, ten, or twenty million, and should lead a whole nation to regard the wealth of its neighbours as a likely cause of, and opportunity for, its own enrichment. A nation that hopes to grow rich through foreign trade is certainly most likely to succeed when its neighbours are all rich, industrious, and commercial. A great nation surrounded on every side by wandering savages and poor barbarians might no doubt grow rich by cultivating its own land and through its own internal commerce, but not through foreign trade. This appears to be how the ancient Egyptians and the modern Chinese acquired their great wealth. The ancient Egyptians are said to have neglected foreign commerce, and the modern Chinese are known to hold it in the deepest contempt, scarcely deigning to grant it the ordinary protection of the law. The modern principles of foreign commerce aim at impoverishing all our neighbours, and insofar as they achieve what they intend, they tend to make that very commerce trivial and contemptible.

It is because of these principles that trade between France and England has been subjected, in both countries, to so many obstacles and restrictions. Yet if those two countries were to consider their real interest, free of mercantile jealousy and national hostility, trade with France might be more advantageous to Great Britain than trade with any other country, and for the same reason, trade with Great Britain might be more advantageous to France than any other. France is Great Britain's nearest neighbour. In trade between the southern coast of England and the northern and northwestern coasts of France, capital might be expected to return to the merchant four, five, or six times a year, just as in domestic trade. The capital employed in this trade could therefore, in each of the two countries, set in motion four, five, or six times as much industry, and provide employment and a living for four, five, or six times as many people, as an equal capital could in most other branches of foreign trade. Between the parts of France and Great Britain farthest from each other, returns might be expected at least once a year, and even this trade would be at least as advantageous as most other branches of our foreign trade within Europe. It would be at least three times more advantageous than our much-praised trade with the North American colonies, in which returns seldom came in less than three years and often not in less than four or five. France, moreover, is thought to have 24 million inhabitants, whereas our North American colonies were never thought to have more than 3 million; and France is a much richer country than North America, although, because wealth there is more unequally distributed, it has far more poverty and begging. France could therefore offer a market at least eight times larger than any our North American colonies ever provided, and, because capital would return so much more often, twenty-four times more advantageous. Trade with Great Britain would be just as advantageous to France, and, in proportion to the wealth, population, and proximity of the two countries, would enjoy the same superiority over the trade France carries on with her own colonies. Such is the enormous difference between the trade that the wisdom of both nations has seen fit to discourage and the trade it has favoured most.

But the very circumstances that would have made open and free commerce between the two countries so advantageous to both have produced the chief obstacles to it. Being neighbours, they are necessarily enemies, and for that reason the wealth and power of each becomes all the more alarming to the other; what would increase the benefits of national friendship serves only to inflame national hostility. Both are rich and industrious nations, and the merchants and manufacturers of each dread competition from the skill and energy of those of the other. Mercantile jealousy is aroused, and it both inflames and is itself inflamed by violent national hostility. The traders of both countries have proclaimed, with all the passionate confidence of self-interested falsehood, that each country faces certain ruin from the unfavourable balance of trade which, they claim, unrestricted commerce with the other would inevitably produce.

There is no commercial country in Europe whose impending ruin has not often been predicted, on account of an unfavourable balance of trade, by the self-styled experts of this system. Yet after all the anxiety they have stirred up on this subject, and after all the futile efforts of nearly every trading nation to tip that balance in its own favour and against its neighbours, there is no sign that any nation in Europe has been impoverished in any way by this cause. On the contrary, every town and country has been enriched in proportion as it has opened its ports to all nations, rather than ruined by this free trade, as the principles of the commercial system would lead us to expect. Although there are, it is true, a few towns in Europe that in some respects deserve the name of free ports, there is no country that does. Holland perhaps comes closest to that character, though it is still very far from it; and Holland, it is generally acknowledged, draws not only its entire wealth but a large part of its basic subsistence from foreign trade.

There is, indeed, another balance, already explained, which is very different from the balance of trade and which, depending on whether it is favourable or unfavourable, necessarily brings about the prosperity or decline of every nation. This is the balance between annual production and annual consumption. If the exchangeable value of the annual produce exceeds that of the annual consumption, then, as has already been observed, the society's capital must grow every year in proportion to that surplus. In that case the society is living within its income, and whatever it saves each year from that income is naturally added to its capital and used to increase the annual produce still further. If, on the other hand, the exchangeable value of the annual produce falls short of the annual consumption, the society's capital must shrink every year in proportion to the shortfall. In that case the society's spending exceeds its income and necessarily eats into its capital. Its capital must therefore decline, and with it the exchangeable value of the annual produce of its industry.

This balance of production and consumption is entirely different from what is called the balance of trade. It could exist in a nation that had no foreign trade at all and was wholly cut off from the rest of the world. It can exist for the entire globe, whose wealth, population, and level of improvement may be either gradually increasing or gradually declining.

The balance of production and consumption may consistently favour a nation even when what is called the balance of trade generally runs against it. A nation may import more than it exports for perhaps half a century at a stretch; all the gold and silver that comes into it during that time may be sent straight back out; its circulating coin may steadily dwindle, with various kinds of paper money taking its place; and even the debts it owes in the principal nations it trades with may steadily mount. Yet throughout that same period its real wealth, the exchangeable value of the annual produce of its land and labour, may have been growing in a far greater proportion. The condition of our North American colonies, and of the trade they carried on with Great Britain before the present disturbances began (I write this in the year 1775), may prove that this is by no means an impossible supposition.

### CHAPTER IV: OF DRAWBACKS

Merchants and manufacturers are not satisfied with a monopoly of the home market; they also want the widest possible sale for their goods abroad. Their own country has no jurisdiction over foreign nations and so can rarely secure them any monopoly there. As a result, they generally have to settle for petitioning the government for various encouragements to exportation.

Of these encouragements, what are called drawbacks seem the most reasonable. A drawback allows a merchant, when he exports goods, to recover all or part of whatever excise or other internal duty has been imposed on their domestic production. Such a refund can never cause more goods to be exported than would have been exported had no duty been imposed in the first place. It does not tend to steer a larger share of the nation's capital toward any particular employment than would have flowed there on its own; it only prevents the duty from driving part of that share away into other employments. It does not upset the balance that naturally establishes itself among all the various employments of a society, but keeps the duty from upsetting it. It does not destroy but preserves what in most cases is advantageous to preserve: the natural division and distribution of labour within the society.

The same can be said of drawbacks on the re-exportation of imported foreign goods, which in Great Britain generally amount to by far the largest part of the import duty. Under the second of the rules attached to the act of Parliament that imposed what is now called the old subsidy, every merchant, whether English or foreign, was allowed to recover half of that duty upon exportation. The English merchant could do so provided the goods were exported within twelve months; the foreign merchant, provided they were exported within nine. Wines, currants, and finished silks were the only goods excluded from this rule, since they enjoyed other and more generous allowances. At that time, the duties imposed by this act were the only duties levied on imported foreign goods. The period within which this drawback, and all others, could be claimed was later extended to three years by a statute passed in the seventh year of the reign of George I.

Most of the duties imposed since the old subsidy are refunded in full upon exportation. This general rule, however, is subject to a great many exceptions, and the law of drawbacks has become far less simple than it was when they were first introduced.

On the export of certain foreign goods whose importation was expected to far exceed what the home market required, the entire duties are refunded, without retaining even the half of the old subsidy. Before the revolt of our North American colonies, we held a monopoly of the tobacco of Maryland and Virginia. We imported about ninety-six thousand hogsheads, the large casks in which tobacco was shipped, while home consumption was not thought to exceed fourteen thousand. To ease the enormous exportation needed to rid us of the remainder, all duties were refunded, provided the tobacco was exported within three years.

We still hold, if not entirely then very nearly, a monopoly of the sugar of our West Indian islands. If sugar is exported within a year, therefore, all import duties on it are refunded; if it is exported within three years, all duties are refunded except half the old subsidy, which is still retained on the export of most goods. Although sugar imports exceed home consumption by a good margin, that surplus is small compared with what the surplus of tobacco used to be.

Certain goods, which are the particular objects of our own manufacturers' jealousy, are prohibited from being imported for domestic consumption. They may nonetheless be imported and held in warehouses for re-export, on payment of certain duties. But when they are exported, no part of those duties is refunded. Our manufacturers, it seems, do not want even this restricted importation to be encouraged, and they fear that some portion of these goods might be stolen from the warehouses and so come into competition with their own. Only under these regulations may we import finished silks, French cambrics and lawns (both fine linen fabrics), and calicoes that have been painted, printed, stained, or dyed, among other goods.

We are unwilling even to act as carriers of French goods, and we prefer to give up a profit ourselves rather than allow those we regard as our enemies to profit by our means. On the export of all French goods, not only half the old subsidy but also the additional twenty-five per cent duty levied on them is retained.

Under the fourth of the rules attached to the old subsidy, the drawback allowed on the export of all wines came to a great deal more than half the duties then paid on their importation, and the legislature at that time appears to have intended to give the carrying trade in wine somewhat more than ordinary encouragement. Several other duties, imposed either at the same time as the old subsidy or afterward, were also allowed to be refunded in full on export: what was called the additional duty, the new subsidy, the one-third and two-thirds subsidies, the impost of 1692, and the tonnage on wine. All of these duties except the additional duty and the impost of 1692, however, had to be paid in cash at the moment of importation, and the interest on so large a sum created an expense that made it unreasonable to expect any profitable carrying trade in wine. Consequently, only part of the duty called the impost on wine was refunded on export, and no part at all of the duty of twenty-five pounds a ton on French wines, or of the duties imposed in 1745, 1763, and 1778. The two duties of five per cent imposed in 1779 and 1781 on top of all the earlier customs duties were refunded in full on the export of all other goods, and so were refunded on wine as well. The most recent duty imposed specifically on wine, that of 1780, is refunded in full, an indulgence which, while so many heavy duties remain unrefunded, probably could never cause the export of a single ton of wine. These rules applied to all places to which goods could lawfully be exported, with the exception of the British colonies in America.

The statute passed in the fifteenth year of Charles II's reign, known as the Act for the Encouragement of Trade, had given Great Britain the monopoly of supplying the colonies with all goods grown or manufactured in Europe, and therefore with wines. Our North American and West Indian colonies had an extensive coastline, and our authority there was always very slight. Their inhabitants were permitted to ship their non-enumerated commodities, those not on the official list of goods that could be sent only to Britain, in their own vessels, at first to every part of Europe and later to every part of Europe south of Cape Finisterre, at the northwestern tip of Spain. Under these conditions it is unlikely that the monopoly was ever much respected, and the colonists probably always found ways of bringing back some return cargo from the countries to which they were allowed to send one out. They seem, however, to have had some difficulty importing European wines directly from the places where they were made, and they could not readily import them from Great Britain, where the wines were burdened with many heavy duties, a considerable portion of which was not refunded on export. Madeira wine, not being a European product, could be imported directly into America and the West Indies, since those colonies enjoyed free trade with the island of Madeira in all their non-enumerated commodities. These circumstances probably account for the general taste for Madeira that our officers found established throughout the colonies at the outbreak of the war that began in 1755, a taste they brought home with them to the mother country, where the wine had not previously been much in fashion. When that war ended in 1763, a statute passed in the fourth year of George III's reign allowed all duties except three pounds ten shillings to be refunded on the export to the colonies of all wines except French wines, whose trade and consumption national prejudice would not permit to receive any encouragement whatsoever. The interval between the granting of this indulgence and the revolt of our North American colonies was probably too short to allow any significant change in the habits of those countries.

The same act that, in its drawbacks on all wines other than French, favoured the colonies so much more than other countries, favoured them much less in the drawbacks on most other commodities. On the export of most commodities to other countries, half the old subsidy was refunded. But this law provided that no part of that duty should be refunded on the export to the colonies of any goods grown or manufactured in Europe or the East Indies, with the exception of wines, white calicoes, and muslins.

Drawbacks were perhaps originally granted to encourage the carrying trade, the business of transporting goods between foreign countries. Because the freight charges in that trade are often paid by foreigners in money, it was thought to be especially well suited to bringing gold and silver into the country. But although the carrying trade certainly deserves no special encouragement, and although the motive behind the institution was perhaps thoroughly foolish, the institution itself seems reasonable enough. Such drawbacks cannot force into this trade a larger share of the nation's capital than would have gone to it of its own accord had there been no import duties; they only prevent the trade from being shut out entirely by those duties. The carrying trade, though it deserves no preference, ought not to be excluded but left free, like every other trade. It is a necessary outlet for capital that cannot find employment in the country's agriculture or manufactures, in its home trade, or in its foreign trade of consumption, the trade that brings in foreign goods for use at home.

Far from suffering, the customs revenue gains from such drawbacks through the portion of the duty that is retained. Had the entire duties been retained, the foreign goods on which they were paid could rarely have been exported, and consequently, for want of a market, would rarely have been imported. The duties, a part of which is now retained, would therefore never have been paid at all.

These reasons seem sufficient to justify drawbacks, and would justify them even if the entire duties, whether on domestic produce or on foreign goods, were always refunded on export. In that case the excise revenue would admittedly suffer a little, and the customs revenue a good deal more. But the natural balance of industry, the natural division and distribution of labour, which such duties always disturb to some degree, would be more nearly restored by such a regulation.

These reasons, however, justify drawbacks only on goods exported to countries that are wholly foreign and independent, not to those in which our merchants and manufacturers enjoy a monopoly. A drawback on the export of European goods to our American colonies, for example, will not always produce a larger export than would have occurred without it. Because of the monopoly our merchants and manufacturers enjoy there, the same quantity might often be sent even if the entire duties were retained. In such cases the drawback may often be a pure loss to the excise and customs revenue, without altering the state of the trade or extending it in any way. How far such drawbacks can be justified as a proper encouragement to the industry of our colonies, and how far it benefits the mother country that the colonists should be exempted from taxes paid by all their fellow subjects, will become clear later, when I come to treat of colonies.

It must always be understood, however, that drawbacks are useful only where the goods on which they are granted are actually exported to some foreign country and not secretly brought back into our own. It is well known that some drawbacks, particularly those on tobacco, have frequently been abused in this way and have given rise to many frauds, equally harmful to the revenue and to the honest trader.

### CHAPTER V: OF BOUNTIES

In Great Britain, people frequently petition for export bounties, and Parliament sometimes grants them, for the products of particular branches of domestic industry. These payments, it is claimed, will enable our merchants and manufacturers to sell their goods as cheaply as their rivals in foreign markets, or more cheaply still. A greater quantity will then be exported, the argument runs, and the balance of trade will consequently turn further in our country's favor. We cannot give our workers a monopoly in foreign markets as we have done in the home market; we cannot force foreigners to buy their goods as we have forced our own countrymen. The next best expedient, it has therefore been thought, is to pay foreigners for buying them. This is how the mercantile system proposes to enrich the whole country, and to put money into all our pockets, by means of the balance of trade.

It is granted that bounties ought to be given only to those branches of trade that cannot be carried on without them. But any branch of trade in which the merchant can sell his goods at a price that replaces the whole capital spent in preparing them and sending them to market, together with the ordinary profits of that capital, can be carried on without a bounty. Such a branch plainly stands on the same footing as every other branch of trade conducted without bounties, and it cannot need one any more than they do. The only trades that need bounties are those in which the merchant must sell his goods at a price that fails to replace his capital along with the ordinary profit, or in which he must sell them for less than it actually cost him to bring them to market. The bounty is given to make up this loss, and to encourage him to continue a trade, or perhaps to begin one, whose expenses are supposed to exceed its returns: a trade in which every transaction eats away part of the capital employed, and which is of such a nature that if all other trades resembled it, there would soon be no capital left in the country.

It should be observed that trades supported by bounties are the only ones that can be carried on between two nations for any considerable length of time in such a way that one of them always and regularly loses, selling its goods for less than it really cost to send them to market. If the bounty did not repay the merchant what he would otherwise lose on the price of his goods, his own interest would soon compel him to employ his capital some other way, or to find a trade in which the price of the goods would replace, with the ordinary profit, the capital he spent in sending them to market. The effect of bounties, like that of every other expedient of the mercantile system, can only be to force a country's trade into a channel far less advantageous than the one in which it would naturally run of its own accord.

The ingenious and well-informed author of the *Tracts upon the Corn Trade* has shown very clearly that since the bounty on the export of corn (by which is meant grain, chiefly wheat) was first established, the value of the corn exported, estimated moderately enough, has exceeded the value of the corn imported, estimated very high, by a sum much greater than the total of all the bounties paid during that period. On the true principles of the mercantile system, he supposes, this is clear proof that the forced corn trade benefits the nation, since the value of exports has exceeded that of imports by a far greater sum than the whole extraordinary expense the public has incurred to get the corn exported. What he fails to consider is that this extraordinary expense, the bounty itself, is the smallest part of what the export of corn actually costs society. The capital the farmer spent in growing the corn must also be taken into account. Unless the price the corn fetches in foreign markets replaces not only the bounty but also this capital, together with its ordinary profits, society loses by the difference, and the national stock is diminished by that amount. Yet the very reason a bounty was thought necessary in the first place is the supposed inability of the price to do this.

It has been said that the average price of corn has fallen considerably since the bounty was established. I have already tried to show that the average price of corn began to fall somewhat toward the end of the last century and has continued to fall through the first sixty-four years of the present one. But this development, assuming it to be real, as I believe it is, must have happened in spite of the bounty, and cannot possibly have happened because of it. It has occurred in France as well as in England, even though France had no bounty at all and, until 1764, subjected the export of corn to a general prohibition. This gradual fall in the average price of grain is therefore probably due, in the end, neither to the one regulation nor to the other, but to that gradual and imperceptible rise in the real value of silver which, as I tried to show in the first book of this inquiry, has taken place in the general market of Europe over the course of the present century. It seems altogether impossible that the bounty could ever have helped to lower the price of grain.

In years of plenty, as I have already observed, the bounty causes an extraordinary volume of exports and therefore necessarily keeps the price of corn in the home market above the level to which it would naturally fall. To do so was the avowed purpose of the measure. In years of scarcity the bounty is frequently suspended; yet the large exports it produces in years of plenty must often prevent, to a greater or lesser degree, the abundance of one year from relieving the scarcity of another. In years of plenty and scarcity alike, therefore, the bounty necessarily tends to raise the money price of corn in the home market somewhat higher than it would otherwise be.

No reasonable person, I think, will dispute that, given the existing state of tillage, the bounty must have this tendency. But many people have believed that it encourages tillage, and in two distinct ways. First, by opening a wider foreign market to the farmer's corn, it tends, they imagine, to increase the demand for that commodity and consequently its production. Second, by securing him a better price than he could otherwise expect in the existing state of tillage, it tends, they suppose, to encourage tillage. Over a long period of years, they imagine, this double encouragement must bring about such an increase in the production of corn as may lower its price in the home market by far more than the bounty can raise it, whatever state tillage happens to be in at the end of that period.

My answer is that whatever extension of the foreign market the bounty may produce must, in every particular year, come entirely at the expense of the home market. Every bushel of corn exported by means of the bounty, which would not have been exported without it, would otherwise have stayed in the home market, increasing consumption and lowering the price. It should be observed that the corn bounty, like every other export bounty, imposes two separate taxes on the people. The first is the tax they must contribute to pay for the bounty. The second is the tax that arises from the higher price of the commodity in the home market, and since the whole body of the people buy corn, this second tax must, in the case of this particular commodity, be paid by the whole body of the people. For corn, therefore, the second tax is by far the heavier of the two. Suppose that, taking one year with another, the bounty of five shillings on every quarter of wheat exported raises the home price of wheat by only sixpence a bushel, or four shillings a quarter (a quarter being eight bushels), above what it would otherwise have been given the actual size of the crop. Even on this very moderate assumption, the great body of the people, besides contributing the tax that pays the five-shilling bounty on every quarter exported, must pay a further four shillings on every quarter they themselves consume. Yet according to the very well-informed author of the *Tracts upon the Corn Trade*, the average proportion of corn exported to corn consumed at home is no more than one to thirty-one. For every five shillings the people contribute toward the first tax, then, they must contribute six pounds four shillings toward the second. So heavy a tax on the first necessity of life must either reduce the subsistence of the laboring poor, or else bring about some increase in their money wages proportionate to the increase in the money price of their subsistence. Insofar as it works in the first way, it must reduce the ability of the laboring poor to raise and educate their children, and must to that extent tend to restrain the population of the country. Insofar as it works in the second, it must reduce the ability of those who employ the poor to employ as many as they otherwise might, and must to that extent tend to restrain the industry of the country. The extraordinary export of corn caused by the bounty, therefore, not only shrinks the home market in every particular year by exactly as much as it enlarges the foreign market and foreign consumption. By restraining the population and industry of the country, its ultimate tendency is also to stunt and hold back the gradual growth of the home market, and so, in the long run, to diminish rather than enlarge the total market for and consumption of corn.

It has been thought, however, that this increase in the money price of corn, by making the crop more profitable to the farmer, must necessarily encourage its production.

My answer is that this might be so if the bounty raised the real price of corn: that is, if it enabled the farmer, with the same quantity of corn, to maintain a larger number of laborers, in whatever manner, generous, moderate, or meager, laborers are commonly maintained in his neighborhood. But it is evident that neither the bounty nor any other human institution can have any such effect. The bounty can affect, to any considerable degree, only the nominal price of corn, not its real price. And though the tax this measure imposes on the whole body of the people may be very burdensome to those who pay it, it is of very little advantage to those who receive it.

The real effect of the bounty is not so much to raise the real value of corn as to lower the real value of silver: to make a given quantity of silver exchange for a smaller quantity not only of corn but of every other domestically produced commodity. For the money price of corn governs the money price of all other domestic commodities.

It governs the money price of labor, which must always be high enough to let the laborer buy enough corn to maintain himself and his family in the generous, moderate, or meager manner in which the advancing, stationary, or declining condition of society obliges his employers to maintain him.

It governs the money price of every other part of the raw produce of land, which at every stage of a country's development must bear a certain proportion to the price of corn, though that proportion differs from one stage to another. It governs, for example, the money price of grass and hay, of butcher's meat, of horses and their upkeep, and therefore of land carriage, which is to say of the greater part of the country's inland commerce.

By governing the money price of all the other raw produce of land, it governs the price of the materials of nearly every manufacture. By governing the money price of labor, it governs the price of manufacturing skill and industry. And by governing both, it governs the price of the finished manufacture. The money price of labor, and of everything produced by land or by labor, must necessarily rise or fall in proportion to the money price of corn.

Suppose, then, that because of the bounty the farmer can sell his corn for four shillings a bushel instead of three shillings and sixpence, and can pay his landlord a money rent proportionate to this rise in the money price of his produce. If, as a result of this rise in the price of corn, four shillings will buy no more domestic goods of any other kind than three shillings and sixpence would have bought before, then neither the farmer's circumstances nor the landlord's will be much improved by the change. The farmer will not be able to cultivate much better, and the landlord will not be able to live much better. In buying foreign commodities, the higher price of corn may give them some slight advantage; in buying domestic commodities, it can give them none at all. And almost the whole of the farmer's spending, and by far the greater part even of the landlord's, goes on domestic commodities.

A fall in the value of silver that results from the abundance of the mines, and that operates equally, or very nearly equally, across most of the commercial world, matters very little to any particular country. The resulting rise in all money prices does not make those who receive them really richer, but neither does it make them really poorer. A set of silver tableware becomes genuinely cheaper, and everything else keeps exactly the same real value as before.

But a fall in the value of silver that results from the peculiar situation or the political institutions of a particular country, and that occurs in that country alone, is a matter of very great consequence. Far from tending to make anyone really richer, it tends to make everyone really poorer. The rise in the money price of all commodities, being in this case confined to that one country, tends to discourage, more or less, every kind of industry carried on within it. It enables foreign nations, by supplying almost every sort of goods for a smaller quantity of silver than the country's own workers can afford to accept, to undersell them not only in foreign markets but even in their home market.

Spain and Portugal, as the owners of the mines, are peculiarly placed to be the distributors of gold and silver to all the other countries of Europe. Those metals ought naturally, therefore, to be somewhat cheaper in Spain and Portugal than anywhere else in Europe. The difference, however, should amount to no more than the cost of freight and insurance. Because these metals are so valuable in proportion to their bulk, the freight on them is trivial, and their insurance costs the same as that of any other goods of equal value. Spain and Portugal, therefore, would suffer very little from their peculiar situation if they did not aggravate its disadvantages through their political institutions.

Spain, by taxing the export of gold and silver, and Portugal, by prohibiting it, burden that export with the cost of smuggling, and so raise the value of those metals in other countries above their value at home by the full amount of that cost. When you dam a stream, as soon as the reservoir behind the dam is full, just as much water must run over the top as if there were no dam at all. In the same way, a ban on export cannot keep in Spain and Portugal any more gold and silver than they can put to use: than the annual produce of their land and labor allows them to employ in coin, plate, gilding, and other ornaments of gold and silver. Once they have that quantity, the reservoir is full, and the whole stream that flows in afterward must run over. By all accounts, accordingly, the annual export of gold and silver from Spain and Portugal is, despite these restraints, very nearly equal to the whole annual import. Yet just as the water must always stand deeper behind the dam than in front of it, so the quantity of gold and silver that these restraints hold back in Spain and Portugal must be greater, in proportion to the annual produce of their land and labor, than what is found in other countries. The higher and stronger the dam, the greater the difference between the depth of water behind it and in front of it. Likewise, the higher the tax, the heavier the penalties guarding the prohibition, and the more vigilant and severe the officers who enforce the law, the greater must be the difference between the proportion of gold and silver to annual produce in Spain and Portugal and the same proportion in other countries. That difference is said, accordingly, to be very considerable: one frequently finds there an abundance of silver plate in houses that contain nothing else which, in other countries, would be thought suitable to or in keeping with that kind of magnificence. The cheapness of gold and silver, or, what amounts to the same thing, the dearness of all commodities, which necessarily follows from this excess of the precious metals, discourages both the agriculture and the manufactures of Spain and Portugal. It enables foreign nations to supply them with many kinds of raw produce, and with almost every kind of manufactured goods, for a smaller quantity of gold and silver than it would cost them to grow or make those goods at home. The tax and the prohibition work in two ways. They not only lower the value of the precious metals considerably in Spain and Portugal; by holding back there a certain quantity of metal that would otherwise flow out to other countries, they also keep its value in those other countries somewhat higher than it would otherwise be, and so give those countries a double advantage in their trade with Spain and Portugal. Open the floodgates, and there will soon be less water above the dam and more below it, until the two levels quickly meet. Remove the tax and the prohibition, and as the quantity of gold and silver falls considerably in Spain and Portugal, it will rise somewhat in other countries; the value of those metals, their proportion to the annual produce of land and labor, will soon come to a level, or very nearly so, everywhere. The loss Spain and Portugal might suffer from this export of their gold and silver would be entirely nominal and imaginary. The nominal value of their goods, and of the annual produce of their land and labor, would fall, and would be expressed by a smaller quantity of silver than before; but its real value would be the same as before, and would suffice to maintain, command, and employ the same quantity of labor. As the nominal value of their goods fell, the real value of the gold and silver they kept would rise, and a smaller quantity of those metals would serve all the purposes of commerce and circulation that a larger quantity had served before. The gold and silver that went abroad would not go for nothing; it would bring back an equal value of goods of one kind or another. Nor would those goods all be mere luxuries and extravagances, to be consumed by idle people who produce nothing in return for what they consume. Since this extraordinary export of gold and silver would not increase the real wealth and income of idle people, neither would it much increase their consumption. The greater part of those goods probably, and some part of them certainly, would consist of materials, tools, and provisions for employing and maintaining industrious people, who would reproduce, with a profit, the full value of what they consumed. Part of the society's dead stock would thus be converted into active stock, setting in motion a greater quantity of industry than had been employed before. The annual produce of their land and labor would immediately increase a little, and within a few years would probably increase a great deal, their industry having been relieved of one of the most oppressive burdens it now labors under.

The bounty on the export of corn necessarily works in exactly the same way as this absurd policy of Spain and Portugal. Whatever the existing state of tillage, it makes our corn somewhat dearer in the home market than it would otherwise be in that state, and somewhat cheaper in foreign markets. And since the average money price of corn governs, more or less, the price of every other commodity, the bounty lowers the value of silver considerably at home and tends to raise it slightly abroad. It enables foreigners, the Dutch in particular, not only to eat our corn more cheaply than they otherwise could, but sometimes to eat it more cheaply than even our own people can at the same time, as we are assured by an excellent authority, Sir Matthew Decker. It prevents our own workers from supplying their goods for as small a quantity of silver as they otherwise might, and enables the Dutch to supply theirs for a smaller quantity still. It tends to make our manufactures somewhat dearer, and theirs somewhat cheaper, in every market than they would otherwise be, and so to give their industry a double advantage over ours.

Because the bounty raises in the home market not so much the real as the nominal price of our corn, increasing not the quantity of labor a given quantity of corn can maintain and employ but only the quantity of silver it will exchange for, it discourages our manufactures without doing any considerable service either to our farmers or to our country gentlemen. It does, admittedly, put a little more money into the pockets of both, and it may be somewhat difficult to persuade most of them that this is not a very considerable service. But if this money loses as much in value, in the quantity of labor, provisions, and domestic goods of every kind it can buy, as it gains in quantity, the service will be little more than nominal and imaginary.

There is perhaps only one class of men in the entire commonwealth to whom the bounty either was or could be of real service: the corn merchants, the exporters and importers of corn. In years of plenty, the bounty necessarily caused greater exports than would otherwise have taken place; and by preventing the abundance of one year from relieving the scarcity of another, it caused greater imports in years of scarcity than would otherwise have been needed. It increased the corn merchant's business in both kinds of year. In years of scarcity, it enabled him not only to import a greater quantity but to sell it at a better price, and so at a greater profit, than he could otherwise have made had the abundance of one year not been more or less prevented from relieving the scarcity of another. It is among this class of men, accordingly, that I have observed the greatest zeal for continuing or renewing the bounty.

Our country gentlemen, when they imposed high duties on the import of foreign corn, duties that in years of moderate plenty amount to a prohibition, and when they established the bounty, appear to have been imitating the conduct of our manufacturers. Through the first of these measures they secured for themselves a monopoly of the home market, and through the second they tried to ensure that this market would never be glutted with their commodity. By both together they sought to raise its real value, in the same way that our manufacturers, through similar measures, had raised the real value of many different kinds of manufactured goods. What they perhaps failed to notice was the great and essential difference that nature has established between grain and almost every other kind of goods.

When, either by granting a monopoly of the home market or by paying a bounty on exports, you enable our wool or linen manufacturers to sell their goods for a somewhat better price than they could otherwise obtain, you raise not only the nominal price of those goods but their real price. You make them exchangeable for a greater quantity of labor and of the necessities of life. You increase not only the nominal but the real profit of those manufacturers, their real wealth and income, and you enable them either to live better themselves or to employ more labor in those particular branches of manufacture. You genuinely encourage those industries, and you direct toward them a larger share of the country's labor than would naturally flow to them of its own accord. But when, by the same kinds of measures, you raise the nominal or money price of grain, you do not raise its real value. You do not increase the real wealth or the real income of either our farmers or our landowners. Nor do you encourage the growing of grain, because you do not enable them to maintain and employ more laborers in raising it. The nature of things has stamped upon grain a real value that cannot be altered merely by altering its money price. No export bounty and no monopoly of the home market can raise that value, and the freest competition cannot lower it. Throughout the world at large, that value equals the quantity of labor that the grain can maintain; and in any particular place, it equals the quantity of labor it can maintain in whatever manner, whether generous, moderate, or meager, labor is commonly maintained there. Wool and linen cloth are not the standard commodities by which the real value of all other commodities must ultimately be measured and determined; grain is. The real value of every other commodity is ultimately measured and determined by the ratio between its average money price and the average money price of grain. The real value of grain does not change with the shifts in its average money price that sometimes occur from one century to the next. What changes with those shifts is the real value of silver.

Bounties on the export of any domestically produced commodity are open, first, to the general objection that can be raised against every expedient of the mercantile system: they force some part of the country's industry into a channel less advantageous than the one it would follow of its own accord. Second, they are open to the particular objection that they force it not merely into a less advantageous channel but into one that is actually disadvantageous, since a trade that cannot be carried on except by means of a bounty is necessarily a losing trade. The bounty on grain exports is open to a further objection as well: it cannot in any respect promote the production of the very commodity it was designed to encourage.

When our landowners demanded the establishment of the bounty, therefore, they were imitating our merchants and manufacturers, but they did not act with the thorough understanding of their own interest that usually guides the conduct of those two other classes. They burdened the public revenue with a very considerable expense, and they imposed a very heavy tax on the whole body of the people. Yet they did not raise the real value of their own commodity to any perceptible degree. And by somewhat lowering the real value of silver, they discouraged to some extent the general industry of the country. Instead of advancing the improvement of their own lands, which necessarily depends on that general industry, they held it back to a greater or lesser degree.

One would suppose that, if the aim is to encourage the production of a commodity, a bounty on production would work more directly than a bounty on exportation. It would, besides, impose only one tax on the people: the amount they must contribute to pay for the bounty. Rather than raising the price of the commodity in the home market, it would tend to lower it, and so, instead of imposing a second tax on the people, it might at least partly repay them for what they had contributed to the first. Bounties on production, however, have very rarely been granted. The prejudices instilled by the commercial system have taught us to believe that national wealth arises more directly from exportation than from production, and exportation has accordingly been favored as the more immediate means of bringing money into the country. It has also been claimed that experience shows bounties on production to be more vulnerable to fraud than bounties on exportation. How far this is true I do not know. That export bounties have been abused for many fraudulent purposes is very well known. But it is not in the interest of merchants and manufacturers, who invented all these expedients, that the home market should be flooded with their goods, an outcome that a bounty on production might sometimes produce. An export bounty prevents this effectively, by enabling them to send their surplus abroad and keep up the price of what remains at home. Of all the expedients of the mercantile system, it is accordingly the one they like best. I have known the proprietors of certain particular works to agree privately among themselves to pay, out of their own pockets, a bounty on the export of a certain proportion of the goods they dealt in. This arrangement succeeded so well that it more than doubled the price of their goods in the home market, despite a very considerable increase in output. The bounty on grain must have operated in a remarkably different way if it has lowered the money price of that commodity.

Something resembling a bounty on production has, however, been granted on certain particular occasions. The tonnage bounties paid to the white herring and whale fisheries, which are calculated according to the carrying capacity of the vessels, might perhaps be considered of this kind. They tend directly, one may suppose, to make the goods cheaper in the home market than they would otherwise be. In other respects, it must be admitted, their effects are the same as those of export bounties. Through them, a part of the country's capital is employed in bringing goods to market whose price does not cover the cost of producing them together with the ordinary profits of capital.

But even though the tonnage bounties to these fisheries do not add to the wealth of the nation, it might be argued that they contribute to its defense by increasing the number of its sailors and ships. It may be claimed that such bounties can sometimes achieve this at a much smaller expense than maintaining a great standing navy, if I may use that expression, in the same way that one maintains a standing army.

Despite these favorable arguments, the following considerations lead me to believe that in granting at least one of these bounties, the legislature has been very grossly deceived.

First, the bounty on herring busses, the decked fishing vessels used in this trade, seems too large.

From the start of the winter fishing season of 1771 to the end of the winter season of 1781, the tonnage bounty on the herring-buss fishery stood at thirty shillings per ton. During these eleven years, the total number of barrels caught by the Scottish herring-buss fishery came to 378,347. Herrings caught and cured at sea are called "sea-sticks." To make them into what are called merchantable herrings, fit for sale, they must be repacked with additional salt, and in this process it is reckoned that three barrels of sea-sticks usually make two barrels of merchantable herrings. By this reckoning, the number of barrels of merchantable herrings caught during these eleven years comes to only 252,231¼. Over the same eleven years, the tonnage bounties paid amounted to £155,463 and 11 shillings, which works out to 8 shillings and 2¼ pence on every barrel of sea-sticks, and to 12 shillings and 3¾ pence on every barrel of merchantable herrings.

The salt used to cure these herrings is sometimes Scottish and sometimes foreign, and both are delivered to the fish-curers free of all excise duty. The excise duty on Scottish salt is currently 1 shilling and 6 pence per bushel, and on foreign salt 10 shillings per bushel. A barrel of herrings is thought to require about one and a quarter bushels of foreign salt, while two bushels is the supposed average for Scottish salt. If the herrings are declared for export, none of this duty is paid. If they are declared for domestic consumption, only one shilling per barrel is paid, whether they were cured with foreign or Scottish salt. That shilling was the old Scottish duty on a bushel of salt, the quantity that, by a low estimate, had been considered necessary to cure a barrel of herrings. In Scotland, foreign salt is used for very little besides curing fish. Yet from April 5, 1771, to April 5, 1782, the quantity of foreign salt imported amounted to 936,974 bushels, at eighty-four pounds to the bushel, while the quantity of Scottish salt delivered from the saltworks to the fish-curers came to no more than 168,226 bushels, at only fifty-six pounds to the bushel. It would appear, therefore, that the fisheries use mainly foreign salt. On every barrel of herrings exported there is, in addition, a bounty of 2 shillings and 8 pence, and more than two-thirds of the herrings caught by busses are exported. Put all these items together, and you will find that during these eleven years, every barrel of buss-caught herrings cured with Scottish salt cost the government 17 shillings and 11¾ pence when exported, and 14 shillings and 3¾ pence when declared for domestic consumption. Every barrel cured with foreign salt cost the government £1, 7 shillings, and 5¾ pence when exported, and £1, 3 shillings, and 9¾ pence when declared for domestic consumption. The price of a barrel of good merchantable herrings ranges from seventeen or eighteen shillings up to twenty-four or twenty-five, averaging about a guinea, or twenty-one shillings.

Second, the bounty to the white herring fishery is a tonnage bounty. It is proportioned to the carrying capacity of the ship, not to its diligence or success in fishing, and it has, I fear, been all too common for vessels to fit out for the sole purpose of catching not the fish but the bounty. In 1759, when the bounty stood at fifty shillings per ton, the entire buss fishery of Scotland brought in only four barrels of sea-sticks. In that year each barrel of sea-sticks cost the government £113 and 15 shillings in bounties alone, and each barrel of merchantable herrings £159, 7 shillings, and 6 pence.

Third, the method of fishing for which this tonnage bounty has been granted, using busses, or decked vessels of between twenty and eighty tons, seems less suited to the situation of Scotland than to that of Holland, from whose practice it appears to have been borrowed. Holland lies a great distance from the seas where herrings are known chiefly to gather, and so it can carry on this fishery only with decked vessels capable of carrying enough water and provisions for a voyage to distant waters. But the Hebrides, or Western Islands, the Shetland Islands, and the northern and northwestern coasts of Scotland, the regions near which the herring fishery is chiefly conducted, are everywhere cut through by arms of the sea that run a considerable way inland and are known in the local language as sea-lochs. It is to these sea-lochs that the herrings mainly resort during the seasons when they visit these waters, for the visits of this fish, and I am assured of many other kinds of fish, are not altogether regular and constant. A boat fishery therefore seems to be the method best suited to Scotland's particular situation, with the fishermen bringing the herrings ashore as fast as they are caught, either to be cured or to be eaten fresh. But the strong encouragement that a bounty of thirty shillings per ton gives to the buss fishery is necessarily a discouragement to the boat fishery, which receives no such bounty and so cannot bring its cured fish to market on the same terms. Accordingly, the boat fishery, which was very considerable before the buss bounty was established and is said to have employed as many seamen as the buss fishery does today, has now decayed almost entirely. I must admit, however, that I cannot claim to speak with much precision about the former extent of this now ruined and abandoned fishery. Since no bounty was paid on fitting out the boats, the officers of the customs and the salt duties kept no record of it.

Fourth, in many parts of Scotland, during certain seasons of the year, herrings make up no small part of the diet of the common people. A bounty that tended to lower their price in the home market might do a good deal to relieve a great number of our fellow subjects whose circumstances are far from comfortable. But the herring-buss bounty serves no such good purpose. It has ruined the boat fishery, which is by far the best suited to supplying the home market, and the additional export bounty of 2 shillings and 8 pence per barrel sends the greater part, more than two-thirds, of the buss fishery's catch abroad. I have been assured that thirty to forty years ago, before the buss bounty was established, sixteen shillings a barrel was the usual price of white herrings. Ten to fifteen years ago, before the boat fishery was entirely ruined, the price was said to range from seventeen to twenty shillings a barrel. Over the last five years it has averaged twenty-five shillings a barrel. This high price, however, may have been due to a genuine scarcity of herrings off the Scottish coast. I must also note that the cask, or barrel, which is usually sold along with the herrings and whose cost is included in all the prices above, has roughly doubled in price since the beginning of the American war, rising from about three shillings to about six. I should note as well that the accounts I have received of prices in earlier times have been by no means entirely uniform or consistent. An old man of great accuracy and experience has assured me that more than fifty years ago, a guinea was the usual price of a barrel of good merchantable herrings, and this, I believe, may still be regarded as the average price. All accounts agree, however, I think, that the price in the home market has not been lowered as a result of the buss bounty.

When the proprietors of fisheries, after receiving such generous bounties, continue to sell their product at the same price as before, or even higher, one might expect their profits to be very great, and it is not improbable that some individuals have indeed done very well. In general, however, I have every reason to believe that the opposite has been the case. The usual effect of such bounties is to encourage reckless speculators to venture into a business they do not understand, and what they lose through their own negligence and ignorance more than outweighs everything they can gain from the utmost generosity of government. In 1750, by the same act that first granted the bounty of thirty shillings per ton to encourage the white herring fishery, the twenty-fourth chapter of the statutes passed in the twenty-third year of George II's reign, a joint-stock company was created with a capital of £500,000. Its subscribers received, on top of all the other encouragements already mentioned, namely the tonnage bounty, the export bounty of 2 shillings and 8 pence per barrel, and the delivery of both British and foreign salt free of duty, an annual payment of three pounds for every hundred pounds they subscribed and paid into the company's stock. This payment was to continue for fourteen years and to be made by the receiver-general of customs in equal half-yearly installments. Besides this great company, whose governor and directors were to reside in London, the act made it lawful to establish separate fishing chambers in all the various ports of the kingdom outside London, provided that at least £10,000 was subscribed to the capital of each, to be managed at its own risk and for its own profit and loss. These smaller chambers were given the same annual payment and the same encouragements of every kind as the great company. The great company's subscription was soon filled, and several fishing chambers were established in the various outlying ports. Despite all these encouragements, nearly all of these companies, large and small, lost either the whole or the greater part of their capital. Scarcely a trace of any of them now remains, and the white herring fishery is now carried on entirely, or almost entirely, by private individuals at their own risk.

If some particular manufacture were indeed necessary for the defense of society, it might not always be prudent to rely on our neighbors to supply it. And if that manufacture could not otherwise be sustained at home, it might not be unreasonable to tax all other branches of industry in order to support it. The bounties on the export of British-made sailcloth and British-made gunpowder may perhaps both be justified on this principle.

It can very seldom be reasonable to tax the industry of the great mass of the people in order to support that of some particular class of manufacturers. Yet in the carelessness of great prosperity, when the public enjoys more revenue than it knows what to do with, granting such bounties to favored manufactures may be as natural as any other idle expense. In public as in private spending, great wealth may often be accepted as an excuse for great folly. But there must surely be something more than ordinary absurdity in continuing such extravagance in times of general hardship and distress.

What is called a bounty is sometimes nothing more than a drawback, a refund of duties previously paid, and is therefore not open to the same objections as a true bounty. The bounty on exported refined sugar, for example, may be regarded as a drawback of the duties on the brown and Muscovado sugars, the raw, unrefined sugars from which it is made. The bounty on exported finished silk may be regarded as a drawback of the duties on imported raw silk and thrown silk, which has already been twisted into thread. The bounty on exported gunpowder may be regarded as a drawback of the duties on imported brimstone, or sulfur, and saltpeter. In the language of the customs service, only allowances given on goods exported in the same form in which they were imported are called drawbacks. When manufacturing of any kind has altered that form so much that the goods come under a new name, the allowances are called bounties.

Prizes awarded by the public to craftsmen and manufacturers who excel in their particular occupations are not open to the same objections as bounties. By encouraging extraordinary skill and ingenuity, they keep alive the spirit of rivalry among the workers already employed in those occupations, and they are not large enough to divert toward any one of them a greater share of the country's capital than would go to it naturally. Their tendency is not to upset the natural balance among different employments but to make the work done in each as perfect and complete as possible. The expense of prizes, moreover, is very small, while that of bounties is very great. The bounty on grain alone has sometimes cost the public more than £300,000 in a single year.

Bounties are sometimes called prizes, just as drawbacks are sometimes called bounties. But in every case we must pay attention to the nature of the thing itself, without regard to the word.

#### Digression Concerning the Corn Trade and the Corn Laws

I cannot conclude this chapter on bounties without observing that the praise bestowed on the law establishing the bounty on grain exports, and on the system of regulations connected with it, is entirely undeserved. A close examination of the nature of the grain trade and of the principal British laws relating to it will sufficiently demonstrate the truth of this claim. The great importance of the subject must justify the length of the digression.

The trade of the grain merchant consists of four branches. Although the same person may sometimes carry on all four, they are by their nature four separate and distinct trades. They are, first, the trade of the inland dealer; second, that of the merchant who imports grain for domestic consumption; third, that of the merchant who exports domestic produce for foreign consumption; and fourth, that of the merchant-carrier, who imports grain in order to export it again.

I. The interest of the inland dealer and that of the great body of the people, however opposed they may at first appear, are exactly the same, even in years of the greatest scarcity. It is in his interest to raise the price of his grain as high as the real scarcity of the season requires, and it can never be in his interest to raise it any higher. By raising the price, he discourages consumption and leads everyone, but particularly the poorer classes, toward thrift and careful management. If he raises it too high, he discourages consumption so much that the season's supply is likely to exceed the season's consumption and to last for some time after the next harvest begins to come in. He then runs the risk not only of losing a considerable part of his grain to natural causes such as spoilage, but of being forced to sell what remains for much less than he could have gotten for it several months earlier. If he does not raise the price high enough, he discourages consumption so little that the season's supply is likely to fall short of the season's consumption. He then not only loses part of the profit he might otherwise have made, but exposes the people, before the season is out, to the dreadful horrors of famine rather than the mere hardships of a shortage. It is in the people's interest that their daily, weekly, and monthly consumption should be matched as exactly as possible to the season's supply. The interest of the inland grain dealer is the same. By supplying them, as nearly as he can judge, in this proportion, he is likely to sell all his grain at the highest price and with the greatest profit, and his knowledge of the state of the harvest and of his own daily, weekly, and monthly sales enables him to judge, with more or less accuracy, how far they are in fact being supplied in this way. Without intending the people's interest, he is necessarily led, by a regard for his own interest, to treat them, even in years of scarcity, much as the prudent captain of a ship is sometimes obliged to treat his crew. When he foresees that provisions are likely to run short, he puts them on reduced rations. Even if, from excess of caution, he sometimes does this without any real need, all the hardship his crew can suffer as a result is trivial compared with the danger, misery, and ruin to which a less provident course might sometimes expose them. In the same way, even if the inland grain merchant, from excess of greed, should sometimes raise his price somewhat higher than the scarcity of the season requires, all the hardship the people can suffer from this conduct, which effectively secures them against famine at the end of the season, is trivial compared with what they might have faced had he dealt more generously at the beginning of it. The grain merchant himself is likely to suffer most from this excess of greed. He suffers not only from the anger it generally provokes against him but also, even if he escapes the effects of that anger, from the quantity of grain it inevitably leaves on his hands at the end of the season. If the next season happens to be favorable, he must always sell that surplus for a much lower price than he might otherwise have obtained.

If it were possible for one great company of merchants to take possession of the entire harvest of a large country, it might perhaps be in their interest to deal with it as the Dutch are said to deal with the spices of the Moluccas, destroying or throwing away a considerable part of it in order to keep up the price of the rest. But it is scarcely possible, even by the force of law, to establish so extensive a monopoly over grain. Wherever the law leaves the trade free, grain is of all commodities the least liable to be cornered or monopolized by a few large fortunes buying up the greater part of it. Its total value far exceeds what the capital of a few private individuals could purchase, and even if they could afford it, the way grain is produced makes such a purchase altogether impracticable. In every civilized country it is the commodity consumed in the greatest quantity each year, and so more labor is employed annually in producing grain than in producing anything else. When it first comes out of the ground, it is necessarily divided among a greater number of owners than any other commodity, and these owners can never be gathered into one place, as a group of independent manufacturers might be, but are necessarily scattered across every corner of the country. These first owners either supply the consumers in their own neighborhood directly, or they supply other inland dealers who in turn supply those consumers. The inland dealers in grain, therefore, including both the farmer and the baker, are necessarily more numerous than the dealers in any other commodity, and their dispersal makes it altogether impossible for them to enter into any general combination. If, in a year of scarcity, any one of them found that he had a good deal more grain on hand than he could hope to sell at the current price before the end of the season, he would never think of holding up that price to his own loss and to the sole benefit of his rivals and competitors. He would lower it at once, in order to get rid of his grain before the new harvest began to come in. The same motives and the same interests that would govern the conduct of any one dealer would govern that of every other, and would oblige them all, in general, to sell their grain at whatever price, in their best judgment, best suited the scarcity or plenty of the season.

Anyone who examines carefully the history of the dearths and famines that have afflicted any part of Europe during the present century or the two before it, several of which we have fairly exact accounts of, will find, I believe, that a dearth has never arisen from any combination among the inland grain dealers, nor from any cause other than a real scarcity. That scarcity has sometimes, perhaps, and in certain places, been brought about by the devastation of war, but in by far the greatest number of cases by bad weather. And he will find that a famine has never arisen from any cause other than the violence of government attempting, by improper means, to remedy the hardships of a dearth.

In a large grain-growing country, where there is free trade and communication among all its different parts, the scarcity produced by even the most unfavorable seasons can never be so great as to cause a famine. The scantiest harvest, if managed with thrift and economy, will feed through the year the same number of people who are ordinarily fed more abundantly by a harvest of moderate plenty. The seasons most harmful to the crop are those of excessive drought or excessive rain. But because grain grows on high ground and low ground alike, on land inclined to be too wet and on land inclined to be too dry, the drought or the rain that harms one part of the country benefits another.
