And although the harvest, in both a wet season and a dry one, is considerably smaller than in a more temperate year, in both cases what is lost in one part of the country is to some degree made up by what is gained in another. In rice-growing countries, where the crop requires not only very moist soil but must, at a certain stage of its growth, be laid under water, the effects of a drought are far more grim. Even in such countries, however, a drought is perhaps scarcely ever so universal as to make a famine inevitable, if the government would allow free trade. The drought in Bengal a few years ago would probably have produced a very severe dearth. Certain improper regulations, certain ill-judged restrictions imposed on the rice trade by the employees of the East India Company, may well have helped to turn that dearth into a famine.

When a government, in order to remedy the hardships of a dearth, orders all dealers to sell their grain at what it considers a reasonable price, one of two things follows. Either it prevents them from bringing their grain to market, which may sometimes produce a famine even at the beginning of the season; or, if they do bring it, it enables the people, and thereby encourages them, to consume it so fast that a famine must necessarily follow before the season is out. The unlimited, unrestrained freedom of the grain trade, being the only effective preventive of the miseries of famine, is also the best means of easing the hardships of a dearth, for the hardships of a real scarcity cannot be remedied; they can only be eased. No trade deserves the full protection of the law more than this one, and no trade needs it so badly, because no trade is so exposed to popular hatred.

In years of scarcity, the lower classes blame their distress on the greed of the grain merchant, who becomes the object of their hatred and fury. Instead of making a profit at such times, he is often in danger of being utterly ruined and of having his warehouses plundered and destroyed by their violence. Yet it is precisely in years of scarcity, when prices are high, that the grain merchant expects to make his principal profit. He is generally under contract with certain farmers to supply him, for a fixed number of years, with a fixed quantity of grain at a fixed price. This contract price is settled according to what is taken to be the moderate and reasonable price, that is, the ordinary or average price, which before the recent years of scarcity was commonly about twenty-eight shillings for a quarter of wheat (a quarter being a measure of eight bushels), and proportionately for other grains. In years of scarcity, therefore, the grain merchant buys a large part of his grain at the ordinary price and sells it at a much higher one. That this extraordinary profit is no more than enough to put his trade on a fair footing with other trades, and to compensate for the many losses he sustains on other occasions, both from the perishable nature of the commodity and from the frequent and unforeseen swings in its price, seems evident enough from one circumstance alone: great fortunes are made as rarely in this trade as in any other. The popular hatred that attends it in years of scarcity, the only years in which it can be highly profitable, makes people of good reputation and substantial means unwilling to enter it. It is left to an inferior class of dealers, so that millers, bakers, mealmen, and meal-factors, together with a number of wretched peddlers, are almost the only middlemen who, in the domestic market, stand between the grower and the consumer.

The traditional policy of Europe, instead of discouraging this popular hatred of a trade so beneficial to the public, seems on the contrary to have sanctioned and encouraged it.

Under chapter 14 of the statute passed in the fifth and sixth years of Edward VI, it was enacted that anyone who bought grain of any kind with the intention of selling it again should be deemed an unlawful engrosser, that is, one who buys up goods in bulk to resell them. For a first offense he was to suffer two months' imprisonment and forfeit the value of the grain; for a second, six months' imprisonment and forfeiture of double the value; and for a third, he was to be set in the pillory, imprisoned for as long as the king pleased, and stripped of all his goods and possessions. The traditional policy of most other parts of Europe was no better than that of England.

Our ancestors seem to have imagined that the people would buy their grain more cheaply from the farmer than from the grain merchant, who, they feared, would demand an exorbitant profit for himself on top of the price he had paid the farmer. They therefore tried to wipe out his trade altogether. They even tried, as far as possible, to prevent any middleman of any kind from coming between the grower and the consumer. This was the purpose of the many restrictions they placed on the trade of those they called kidders, or carriers of grain, a trade no one was allowed to practice without a license certifying his qualifications as a man of honesty and fair dealing. Under the statute of Edward VI, the authority of three justices of the peace was required to grant this license. But even this restriction was later thought insufficient, and a statute of Elizabeth confined the power of granting it to the quarter sessions, the courts that sat four times a year in each county.

In this way the traditional policy of Europe tried to regulate agriculture, the great trade of the countryside, by principles quite different from those it laid down for manufacturing, the great trade of the towns. By leaving the farmer no customers other than the consumers themselves or their immediate agents, the kidders and carriers of grain, it tried to force him to practice the trade not only of a farmer but also of a grain merchant or grain retailer. The manufacturer, on the contrary, was in many cases forbidden to practice the trade of a shopkeeper or to sell his own goods at retail. By the first law, the state meant to promote the general interest of the country, that is, to make grain cheap, though perhaps without any clear understanding of how this was to be done. By the second, it meant to promote the interest of a particular class of men, the shopkeepers, who, it was supposed, would be so badly undersold by the manufacturer that their trade would be ruined if he were allowed to retail at all.

The manufacturer, however, even if he had been allowed to keep a shop and sell his own goods at retail, could not have undersold the ordinary shopkeeper. Whatever part of his capital he placed in his shop, he must have withdrawn from his manufacturing. To carry on his business on equal terms with other people, he would have needed the profit of a manufacturer on the one side and that of a shopkeeper on the other. Suppose, for example, that in the town where he lived ten percent was the ordinary profit on capital employed both in manufacturing and in shopkeeping. In that case he would have had to charge a profit of twenty percent on every piece of his own goods that he sold in his shop. When he moved them from his workshop to his shop, he would have had to value them at the price for which he could have sold them wholesale to a dealer or shopkeeper. Had he valued them lower, he would have lost part of the profit on his manufacturing capital. When he then sold them from his shop, unless he got the same price a shopkeeper would have charged, he lost part of the profit on his shopkeeping capital. So although he might appear to make a double profit on the same piece of goods, those goods had formed part of two distinct capitals in succession, and he made only a single profit on the whole capital employed in handling them. If he made less than that profit, he was a loser, and was not employing his whole capital as advantageously as most of his neighbors.

What the manufacturer was forbidden to do, the farmer was to some degree required to do: to divide his capital between two different employments, keeping one part of it in his granaries and stackyard to meet the occasional demands of the market, and using the other in cultivating his land. But just as he could not afford to employ the second part for less than the ordinary profits of farming capital, so he could no more afford to employ the first for less than the ordinary profits of mercantile capital. Whether the capital that actually carried on the business of a grain merchant belonged to the person called a farmer or to the person called a grain merchant, an equal profit was required in either case to compensate its owner for using it in this way, to put his business on a level with other trades, and to keep him from having an interest in switching to some other line as soon as possible. The farmer who was thus forced to act as a grain merchant could not, therefore, afford to sell his grain any cheaper than any other grain merchant would have been obliged to sell it under free competition.

The dealer who can employ his entire capital in a single branch of business has an advantage of the same kind as the worker who can devote all his labor to a single operation. Just as the worker acquires a dexterity that enables him, with the same two hands, to do a much greater quantity of work, so the dealer acquires so easy and ready a method of conducting his business, of buying and selling his goods, that with the same capital he can handle a much greater volume of trade. And just as the worker can commonly offer his labor a good deal more cheaply, so the dealer can commonly offer his goods somewhat more cheaply than if his capital and attention were spread across a greater variety of objects. Most manufacturers could not afford to retail their own goods as cheaply as a vigilant and active shopkeeper whose sole business was to buy them wholesale and sell them again at retail. Most farmers could still less afford to retail their own grain, supplying the inhabitants of a town perhaps four or five miles away from most of them, as cheaply as a vigilant and active grain merchant whose sole business was to buy grain wholesale, collect it in a large warehouse, and sell it again at retail.

The law that forbade the manufacturer to act as a shopkeeper tried to force this division in the employment of capital to proceed faster than it otherwise would have. The law that obliged the farmer to act as a grain merchant tried to keep it from proceeding so fast. Both laws were plain violations of natural liberty, and therefore unjust; and both were as unwise as they were unjust. It is in the interest of every society that things of this kind should never be either forced or obstructed. A man who employs his labor or his capital in a greater variety of ways than his situation requires can never harm his neighbor by underselling him. He may harm himself, and he generally does. "Jack-of-all-trades will never be rich," as the proverb says. But the law ought always to trust people with the care of their own interests, since in their local circumstances they must generally be better able to judge them than the legislature can. Of the two, however, the law that obliged the farmer to act as a grain merchant was by far the more harmful.

It obstructed not only that division in the employment of capital which is so advantageous to every society, but also the improvement and cultivation of the land. By obliging the farmer to carry on two trades instead of one, it forced him to divide his capital into two parts, only one of which could be employed in cultivation. Had he been free to sell his whole crop to a grain merchant as fast as he could thresh it, his entire capital could have returned at once to the land, to be spent on buying more livestock and hiring more laborers in order to improve and cultivate it better. But because he was obliged to sell his grain at retail, he had to keep a large part of his capital tied up in his granaries and stackyard throughout the year, and so could not farm as well as he otherwise might have with the same capital. This law, therefore, necessarily obstructed the improvement of the land, and instead of tending to make grain cheaper, it must have tended to make it scarcer, and therefore dearer, than it would otherwise have been.

After the business of the farmer, the business of the grain merchant is in fact the trade that, if properly protected and encouraged, would contribute most to the growing of grain. It would support the farmer's trade in the same way that the wholesale dealer's trade supports the manufacturer's. The wholesale dealer offers the manufacturer a ready market, takes his goods off his hands as fast as he can make them, and sometimes even advances him their price before they are made. In doing so, he enables the manufacturer to keep his entire capital, and sometimes more than his entire capital, constantly employed in manufacturing, and therefore to produce a far greater quantity of goods than if he had to sell them himself to the final consumers, or even to retailers. Since the wholesale merchant's capital is generally large enough to replace that of many manufacturers, this relationship between him and them gives the owner of one large capital an interest in supporting the owners of a great many small ones, and in helping them through the losses and misfortunes that might otherwise ruin them.

A relationship of the same kind, established universally between farmers and grain merchants, would have effects equally beneficial to the farmers. They would be able to keep their entire capital, and even more than their entire capital, constantly employed in cultivation. In the event of any of those accidents to which no trade is more liable than theirs, they would find in their regular customer, the wealthy grain merchant, someone with both an interest in supporting them and the means to do so, and they would not be wholly dependent, as they are now, on the forbearance of their landlord or the mercy of his steward. Suppose it were possible, as perhaps it is not, to establish this relationship universally and all at once. Suppose it were possible to turn the whole farming capital of the kingdom, all at once, to its proper business, the cultivation of land, withdrawing it from every other employment into which any part of it may now be diverted. And suppose it were possible, in order to support and assist the operations of this great capital when needed, to provide all at once another capital almost equally great. It is perhaps not easy to imagine how great, how widespread, and how sudden an improvement this change of circumstances alone would produce across the whole face of the country.

The statute of Edward VI, then, by preventing as far as possible any middleman from coming between the grower and the consumer, tried to wipe out a trade whose free exercise is not only the best means of easing the hardships of a dearth but also the best preventive of that calamity, since after the farmer's trade, no trade contributes so much to the growing of grain as the grain merchant's.

The severity of this law was later softened by several subsequent statutes, which in turn permitted the engrossing of grain so long as the price of wheat did not exceed twenty shillings, then twenty-four, thirty-two, and forty shillings a quarter. Finally, chapter 7 of the statute passed in the fifteenth year of Charles II declared it lawful for all persons to engross grain, that is, to buy it in order to sell it again, so long as the price of wheat did not exceed forty-eight shillings a quarter, and that of other grains in proportion, provided they were not forestallers, meaning that they did not resell in the same market within three months. All the freedom the trade of the inland grain dealer has ever yet enjoyed was granted to it by this statute. The statute passed in the twelfth year of the present king's reign, which repeals almost all the other old laws against engrossers and forestallers, does not repeal the restrictions of this particular statute, and they therefore remain in force.

This statute, however, to some extent lends its authority to two very absurd popular prejudices.

First, it assumes that when the price of wheat has risen as high as forty-eight shillings a quarter, and that of other grains in proportion, grain is likely to be engrossed in a way that harms the people. But from what has already been said, it seems evident enough that grain can at no price be engrossed by the inland dealers in a way that harms the people. Besides, although forty-eight shillings a quarter may be considered a very high price, in years of scarcity it is a price that often prevails immediately after the harvest, when scarcely any of the new crop can yet have been sold, and when it is impossible even for ignorance to suppose that any part of it could have been engrossed so as to harm the people.

Second, it assumes that there is a certain price at which grain is likely to be forestalled, that is, bought up in order to be sold again soon afterward in the same market, in a way that harms the people. But if a merchant ever buys up grain, whether on its way to a particular market or in that market itself, in order to sell it again soon afterward in the same market, it must be because he judges that the market cannot be as generously supplied throughout the season as it is on that particular occasion, and that the price must therefore soon rise. If he judges wrongly, and the price does not rise, he loses not only the whole profit on the capital he employs in this way but part of the capital itself, through the expense and waste that inevitably accompany the storing and keeping of grain. He therefore harms himself far more seriously than he can harm even the particular people whom he may prevent from supplying themselves on that particular market day, since they can buy just as cheaply on any other market day afterward. If he judges correctly, then far from harming the great body of the people, he does them a most important service. By making them feel the hardships of a shortage somewhat earlier than they otherwise would, he spares them from feeling those hardships later with the severity that would certainly follow if low prices encouraged them to consume faster than the real scarcity of the season allowed. When a scarcity is real, the best thing that can be done for the people is to spread its burden as evenly as possible across all the months, weeks, and days of the year. The corn merchant's own interest leads him to study how to do this as exactly as he can. Since no one else has the same interest, the same knowledge, or the same ability to do it so precisely, this most important operation of commerce ought to be entrusted entirely to him. The corn trade, at least so far as it concerns the supply of the home market, ought to be left perfectly free.

The popular fear of engrossing and forestalling, that is, of buying up stocks of grain to hold them back from sale, or of intercepting supplies before they reach the market, may be compared to the popular terror and suspicion of witchcraft. The unfortunate wretches accused of witchcraft were no more innocent of the misfortunes blamed on them than those accused of engrossing and forestalling. The law that ended all prosecutions for witchcraft, and so took away any man's power to gratify his malice by accusing his neighbor of that imaginary crime, seems to have effectively ended those fears and suspicions, because it removed the chief thing that encouraged and sustained them. A law restoring complete freedom to the inland corn trade would probably prove just as effective in ending the popular fears of engrossing and forestalling.

For all its imperfections, the statute of the fifteenth year of Charles II, chapter 7, has perhaps done more than any other law on the statute book both to keep the home market plentifully supplied and to increase tillage. It is from this law that the inland corn trade has derived all the liberty and protection it has ever yet enjoyed. And the inland trade promotes both the supply of the home market and the interest of tillage far more effectively than either the import trade or the export trade.

The author of the *Tracts upon the Corn Trade* has calculated that the average quantity of all sorts of grain imported into Great Britain amounts to no more than one part in five hundred and seventy of all the grain consumed. For supplying the home market, then, the inland trade must be five hundred and seventy times as important as the import trade.

According to the same author, the average quantity of all sorts of grain exported from Great Britain does not exceed one thirty-first part of the annual produce. For encouraging tillage by providing a market for home produce, then, the inland trade must be thirty times as important as the export trade.

I have no great faith in political arithmetic, the practice of estimating national quantities by calculation, and I do not mean to vouch for the exactness of either figure. I mention them only to show how much less weight the most judicious and experienced observers give to the foreign corn trade than to the home trade. The great cheapness of corn in the years immediately before the bounty was established may perhaps, with reason, be attributed in some measure to the working of this statute of Charles II, which had been enacted about twenty-five years earlier and had therefore had ample time to take effect.

A very few words will explain all I have to say about the other three branches of the corn trade.

II. The trade of the merchant who imports foreign corn for home consumption plainly contributes to the immediate supply of the home market, and to that extent must be of immediate benefit to the great body of the people. It does tend to lower the average money price of corn somewhat, but not to reduce its real value, meaning the quantity of labor it can maintain. If importation were always free, our farmers and country gentlemen would probably, taking one year with another, receive less money for their corn than they do now, when importation is in effect prohibited most of the time. But the money they received would be worth more: it would buy more goods of every other kind and employ more labor. Their real wealth and real revenue would therefore be the same as at present, though expressed in a smaller quantity of silver, and they would be neither unable nor discouraged to grow as much corn as they do now. On the contrary, because the rise in the real value of silver that follows from a lower money price of corn also lowers somewhat the money price of all other commodities, it gives the industry of the country where it occurs some advantage in all foreign markets, and so tends to encourage and enlarge that industry. Yet the extent of the home market for corn must be proportioned to the general industry of the country that grows it, that is, to the number of people who produce something else and therefore have something else, or the price of something else, to give in exchange for corn. In every country, the home market, being the nearest and most convenient, is also the largest and most important market for corn. The rise in the real value of silver that results from lowering the average money price of corn therefore tends to enlarge the largest and most important market for corn, and so to encourage its growth rather than discourage it.

Under the statute of the twenty-second year of Charles II, chapter 13, imported wheat was charged a duty of 16 shillings a quarter whenever the price in the home market did not exceed 53 shillings and 4 pence, and a duty of 8 shillings whenever the price did not exceed £4. For more than a century, the first of these prices has been reached only in times of very great scarcity, and the second, so far as I know, has never been reached at all. Yet until wheat rose above the second price, this statute subjected it to a very high duty, and until it rose above the first, to a duty amounting to an outright prohibition. The importation of other kinds of grain was restricted by price thresholds and duties nearly as high in proportion to their value. Before the statute of the thirteenth year of the present king, the duties payable on imported grain were as follows:

| Grain | Price per quarter | Duty per quarter |
|---|---|---|
| Beans | up to 28s. | 19s. 10d. |
| | above that, up to 40s. | 16s. 8d. |
| | above 40s. | 12d. |
| Barley | up to 28s. | 19s. 10d. |
| | above that, up to 32s. | 16s. |
| | above 32s. | 12d. |
| Malt | — | prohibited by the annual malt-tax bill |
| Oats | up to 16s. | 5s. 10d. |
| | above 16s. | 9½d. |
| Pease | up to 40s. | 16s. 0d. |
| | above 40s. | 9¾d. |
| Rye | up to 36s. | 19s. 10d. |
| | above that, up to 40s. | 16s. 8d. |
| | above 40s. | 12d. |
| Wheat | up to 44s. | 21s. 9d. |
| | above that, up to 53s. 4d. | 17s. |
| | above that, up to £4 | 8s. |
| | above £4 | about 1s. 4d. |
| Buckwheat | up to 32s. | 16s. |

These duties were imposed partly by the twenty-second year of Charles II in place of the old subsidy, and partly by the new subsidy, by the one-third and two-thirds subsidies, and by the subsidy of 1747. Later laws raised them still further.

Had these laws been strictly enforced in years of scarcity, the distress they brought on the people would probably have been very great. On such occasions, however, their enforcement was generally suspended by temporary statutes that allowed foreign corn to be imported for a limited time. The need for these temporary statutes is proof enough that the general law was unsound.

These restraints on importation, though they came before the bounty, were dictated by the same spirit and the same principles that later produced it. However harmful in themselves, these or similar restraints became necessary once the bounty existed. If foreign corn could have been imported duty-free, or for only a small duty, when wheat was below 48 shillings a quarter or not much above it, it could have been exported again to collect the bounty. The public revenue would have suffered a great loss, and the institution would have been entirely perverted, since its purpose was to widen the market for home-grown corn, not for the produce of foreign countries.

III. The trade of the merchant who exports corn for foreign consumption certainly does not contribute directly to the plentiful supply of the home market. It does so indirectly, however. Whatever the usual source of that supply, whether home growth or foreign imports, the home market can never be very plentifully supplied unless more corn is usually grown in the country, or usually imported into it, than is usually consumed there. And unless the surplus can be exported in all ordinary cases, growers will take care never to grow more, and importers never to import more, than the bare consumption of the home market requires. That market will very seldom be overstocked but will generally be understocked, because those whose business it is to supply it will generally fear being left with unsold goods. Prohibiting exportation limits the improvement and cultivation of a country to what its own inhabitants require. Freedom of exportation allows it to extend cultivation to supply foreign nations.

Under the statute of the twelfth year of Charles II, chapter 4, corn could be exported whenever the price of wheat did not exceed 40 shillings a quarter, with other grains in proportion. The fifteenth year of the same king extended this liberty until wheat exceeded 48 shillings a quarter, and the twenty-second year extended it to all higher prices. A poundage, a duty charged according to value, did have to be paid to the king on such exports. But all grain was valued so low in the book of rates, the official schedule used to assess customs, that this poundage came to only 1 shilling a quarter on wheat, 4 pence on oats, and 6 pence on all other grain. The statute of the first year of William and Mary, which established the bounty, in effect removed this small duty whenever wheat did not exceed 48 shillings a quarter, and the statute of the eleventh and twelfth years of William III, chapter 20, expressly removed it at all higher prices.

In this way the merchant-exporter's trade was not only encouraged by a bounty but made far freer than that of the inland dealer. Under the last of these statutes, corn could be engrossed for export at any price, but it could not be engrossed for inland sale unless the price did not exceed 48 shillings a quarter. Yet, as has already been shown, the interest of the inland dealer can never be opposed to that of the great body of the people. The interest of the merchant-exporter can be, and sometimes in fact is. If a neighboring country were struck by famine while his own country was suffering a shortage, it might pay him to carry corn to that neighbor in quantities that would greatly worsen the hardships at home. The plentiful supply of the home market was not the direct aim of those statutes. Their aim, under the pretense of encouraging agriculture, was to raise the money price of corn as high as possible, and thereby to keep the home market, as far as possible, in a state of constant dearth. By discouraging importation, they confined the supply of that market, even in times of great scarcity, to home growth; and by encouraging exportation when the price stood as high as 48 shillings a quarter, they denied that market the whole of the home crop, even in times of considerable scarcity. The temporary laws that prohibited the export of corn for a limited time, and lifted the duties on its import for a limited time, were expedients to which Great Britain was so often forced to resort that they are proof enough of the unsoundness of her general system. Had the system been good, she would not so often have been driven to depart from it.

If all nations followed the liberal system of free exportation and free importation, the separate states into which a great continent is divided would to that extent resemble the separate provinces of a great empire. Among the provinces of a great empire, reason and experience both show that freedom of inland trade is not only the best remedy for a dearth but the most effective safeguard against famine. Freedom of the export and import trade would serve the same purpose among the states of a great continent. The larger the continent, and the easier the communication among all its parts by land and water, the less any single part of it would be exposed to either calamity, since a scarcity in one country would more likely be relieved by plenty in another. But very few countries have fully adopted this liberal system. Almost everywhere the corn trade is restrained to some degree, and in many countries it is bound by regulations so absurd that they frequently turn the unavoidable misfortune of a dearth into the dreadful calamity of a famine. The demand of such countries for corn may often become so great and so urgent that a small neighboring state, itself suffering some degree of dearth at the same time, could not risk supplying them without exposing itself to the same dreadful calamity. The very bad policy of one country may thus make it, to some extent, dangerous and imprudent for another to adopt what would otherwise be the best policy. Unlimited freedom of exportation, however, would be far less dangerous in large states, where the harvest is so much greater that the supply could seldom be much affected by any quantity of corn likely to be exported. In a Swiss canton, or in some of the small states of Italy, it may perhaps sometimes be necessary to restrict the export of corn. In great countries such as France or England, it can hardly ever be necessary. Besides, to prevent the farmer from sending his goods to the best market at all times is plainly to sacrifice the ordinary rules of justice to an idea of public utility, to a kind of reason of state. Such an exercise of legislative authority ought to be used, and can be forgiven, only in cases of the most urgent necessity. If the export of corn is ever to be prohibited, the price at which the prohibition takes effect ought always to be a very high one.

The laws concerning corn may everywhere be compared to the laws concerning religion. People feel so deeply concerned with whatever touches their subsistence in this life or their happiness in the life to come that government must yield to their prejudices and, to preserve public peace, establish whatever system they approve. This is perhaps why we so seldom find a reasonable system established for either of those two great objects.

IV. The trade of the merchant-carrier, who imports foreign corn in order to export it again, contributes to the plentiful supply of the home market. Selling his corn there is not, indeed, the direct purpose of his trade, but he will generally be willing to do so, and even for a good deal less money than he might expect abroad, because he saves the costs of loading and unloading, freight, and insurance. The inhabitants of a country that, through the carrying trade, becomes the warehouse and storehouse supplying other countries can very seldom be in want themselves. Although the carrying trade must in this way lower the average money price of corn in the home market, it would not lower corn's real value; it would only raise the real value of silver somewhat.

In Great Britain the carrying trade was in effect prohibited on all ordinary occasions by the high duties on imported foreign corn, most of which carried no drawback, that is, no refund when the corn was re-exported. On extraordinary occasions, when a scarcity made it necessary to suspend those duties by temporary statutes, exportation was always prohibited. Under this system of laws, therefore, the carrying trade was in effect prohibited altogether.

The system of laws connected with the establishment of the bounty seems, then, to deserve none of the praise that has been bestowed on it. The improvement and prosperity of Great Britain, so often credited to those laws, can very easily be explained by other causes. The security that the laws of Great Britain give every man that he shall enjoy the fruits of his own labor is by itself enough to make any country flourish, despite these and twenty other absurd regulations of commerce; and this security was perfected by the Revolution, at about the same time the bounty was established. The natural effort of every individual to better his own condition, when allowed to exert itself in freedom and security, is so powerful a principle that, alone and without any help, it can not only carry a society to wealth and prosperity but also overcome a hundred needless obstructions with which the folly of human laws too often encumbers it, though the effect of those obstructions is always, to a greater or lesser degree, either to encroach on its freedom or to diminish its security. In Great Britain industry is perfectly secure; and although it is far from perfectly free, it is as free as, or freer than, in any other part of Europe.

Although Great Britain's period of greatest prosperity and improvement came after the system of laws connected with the bounty, we must not on that account attribute it to those laws. It also came after the national debt, and the national debt has most assuredly not been its cause.

The system of laws connected with the bounty has exactly the same tendency as the practice of Spain and Portugal: to lower somewhat the value of the precious metals in the country where it operates. Yet Great Britain is certainly one of the richest countries in Europe, while Spain and Portugal are perhaps among the most impoverished. This difference can easily be explained by two causes. First, the tax in Spain and the prohibition in Portugal on exporting gold and silver, together with the vigilant policing that enforces those laws, must act far more directly and far more forcefully to reduce the value of those metals in two very poor countries, which between them import more than six million pounds sterling a year, than the corn laws can act in Great Britain. Second, in those countries this bad policy is not offset by the general liberty and security of the people. There, industry is neither free nor secure, and the civil and ecclesiastical governments of both Spain and Portugal are such as would by themselves be enough to perpetuate their present poverty, even if their regulations of commerce were as wise as most of them are absurd and foolish.

The statute of the thirteenth year of the present king, chapter 43, seems to have established a new system of corn laws, better than the old one in many respects but perhaps not quite as good in one or two.

Under this statute, the high duties on grain imported for home consumption are removed as soon as the price of middling wheat, that is, wheat of middle quality, rises to 48 shillings a quarter; of middling rye, pease, or beans, to 32 shillings; of barley, to 24 shillings; and of oats, to 16 shillings. In their place a small duty is imposed of only 6 pence on the quarter of wheat, with other grains in proportion. For all these kinds of grain, but particularly for wheat, the home market is thus opened to foreign supplies at considerably lower prices than before.

Under the same statute, the old bounty of 5 shillings on exported wheat ends as soon as the price rises to 44 shillings a quarter, instead of 48 shillings as before. The bounty of 2 shillings and 6 pence on exported barley ends as soon as the price rises to 22 shillings, instead of 24 shillings as before. The bounty of 2 shillings and 6 pence on exported oatmeal ends as soon as the price rises to 14 shillings, instead of 15 shillings as before. The bounty on rye is reduced from 3 shillings and 6 pence to 3 shillings, and it ends as soon as the price rises to 28 shillings, instead of 32 shillings as before. If bounties are as unsound as I have tried to prove, the sooner they end and the lower they are, the better.

The same statute permits corn to be imported duty-free at the lowest prices for re-export, provided that in the meantime it is kept in a warehouse under the joint locks of the king and the importer. This liberty extends to only twenty-five of the ports of Great Britain. They are, however, the principal ones, and most of the others may not have warehouses suitable for the purpose.

To this extent the law seems clearly an improvement on the old system.

But the same law grants a bounty of 2 shillings a quarter on the export of oats whenever the price does not exceed 14 shillings. No bounty had ever before been given on the export of this grain, any more than on pease or beans.

The same law also prohibits the export of wheat as soon as the price rises to 44 shillings a quarter; of rye, as soon as it rises to 28 shillings; of barley, as soon as it rises to 22 shillings; and of oats, as soon as they rise to 14 shillings. All of these prices seem a good deal too low. There also seems to be something improper in prohibiting exportation altogether at exactly the prices at which the bounty, which was given to force exportation, is withdrawn. Either the bounty should have been withdrawn at a much lower price, or exportation should have been allowed up to a much higher one.

To this extent, then, the law seems inferior to the old system. Yet for all its imperfections, we may perhaps say of it what was said of the laws of Solon: that although it is not the best in itself, it is the best that the interests, prejudices, and temper of the times would allow. In due course it may perhaps prepare the way for a better one.

### CHAPTER VI: OF TREATIES OF COMMERCE

When a nation binds itself by treaty either to admit certain goods from one foreign country while prohibiting them from all others, or to exempt one country's goods from duties that it imposes on everyone else's, the favored country, or at least its merchants and manufacturers, must necessarily gain a great deal from the arrangement. Those merchants and manufacturers enjoy a kind of monopoly in the country that is so indulgent to them. That country becomes a market for their goods that is both larger and more profitable. It is larger because, with the goods of other nations either excluded or burdened with heavier duties, it takes a greater quantity of theirs. It is more profitable because the merchants of the favored country, holding a kind of monopoly there, will often sell their goods at a better price than they could if exposed to free competition from every other nation.

Such treaties, however, though they may benefit the merchants and manufacturers of the favored country, necessarily harm those of the country that grants the favor. A monopoly is granted against them to a foreign nation, and they must often pay more for the foreign goods they need than they would if other nations were free to compete. The portion of its own produce with which such a nation buys foreign goods must therefore be sold more cheaply, because when two things are exchanged for each other, the cheapness of the one is the necessary consequence of the dearness of the other; indeed, it is the same thing. The exchangeable value of the nation's annual produce is therefore likely to be reduced by every treaty of this kind. This reduction, however, can hardly amount to a positive loss. It is only a lessening of the gain the nation might otherwise have made. Though it sells its goods more cheaply than it otherwise might, it will probably not sell them for less than they cost. Nor will it sell them, as happens with goods sold under bounties, at a price that fails to replace the capital employed in bringing them to market together with the ordinary profits of that capital. The trade could not continue for long if it did. Even the country granting the favor, then, may still gain by the trade, though less than it would under free competition.

Some commercial treaties, however, have been thought advantageous on entirely different grounds. A trading country has sometimes granted a monopoly of this kind, against its own interest, to certain goods of a foreign nation because it expected that, across the whole of the commerce between them, it would sell more each year than it bought, and that the balance would be paid to it every year in gold and silver. It is on this principle that the commercial treaty between England and Portugal, concluded in 1703 by Mr. Methuen, has been so widely praised. What follows is a literal translation of that treaty, which consists of only three articles.

ART. I. His sacred royal majesty of Portugal promises, in his own name and in that of his successors, to admit into Portugal forever hereafter the woolen cloths and the other woolen manufactures of the British, as was customary until they were prohibited by law, but on the following condition:

ART. II. Namely, that her sacred royal majesty of Great Britain shall be obliged, in her own name and in that of her successors, forever hereafter to admit the wines grown in Portugal into Britain, so that at no time, whether Britain and France are at peace or at war, shall anything more be demanded for these wines, by the name of customs or duty or under any other title, directly or indirectly, whether they are imported into Great Britain in pipes, hogsheads, or other casks, than what is demanded for the same quantity or measure of French wine, minus one-third of that customs duty. But if at any time this deduction or reduction of customs, which is to be made as stated above, is in any way tampered with or impaired, it shall be just and lawful for his sacred royal majesty of Portugal to prohibit once again the woolen cloths and the other British woolen manufactures.

ART. III. The most excellent lords plenipotentiary promise and undertake that their masters named above shall ratify this treaty, and that the ratifications shall be exchanged within two months.

By this treaty, the crown of Portugal is bound to admit English woolens on the same footing as before the prohibition; that is, it may not raise the duties above what was paid before that time. But it is not bound to admit them on better terms than those granted to any other nation, France or Holland, for example. The crown of Great Britain, by contrast, is bound to admit the wines of Portugal on payment of only two-thirds of the duty charged on the wines of France, which are the wines most likely to compete with them. To this extent, then, the treaty is plainly advantageous to Portugal and disadvantageous to Great Britain.

It has nevertheless been celebrated as a masterpiece of English commercial policy. Every year Portugal receives from Brazil more gold than it can use in its domestic commerce, whether as coin or as plate. This surplus is too valuable to be left lying idle and locked away in chests, and since it can find no profitable market at home, it must, despite any prohibition, be sent abroad and exchanged for something that does command a better market at home. A large share of it comes to England every year, in return either for English goods or for the goods of other European nations that receive their payments by way of England. Mr. Barretti was told that the weekly packet boat from Lisbon brings to England, taking one week with another, more than £50,000 in gold. The figure was probably exaggerated. It would amount to more than £2,600,000 a year, which is more than Brazil is thought to produce.

Some years ago our merchants were displeased with the crown of Portugal. Certain privileges had been granted to them, not by treaty but by the free goodwill of that crown, though probably at the request of the crown of Great Britain and in return for much greater favors from it, namely defense and protection. These privileges had been either infringed or revoked. The very people who usually took the greatest interest in praising the Portugal trade were therefore inclined, at that time, to present it as less advantageous than had generally been supposed. The far greater part of this annual import of gold, they claimed, indeed almost all of it, was received not on Great Britain's account but on that of other European nations, since the fruits and wines of Portugal imported into Great Britain each year very nearly matched the value of the British goods sent there.

Let us suppose, however, that the whole of it was on Great Britain's account, and that it came to an even larger sum than Mr. Barretti seems to believe. The trade would not, for that reason, be any more advantageous than any other trade in which, for the same value sent out, we received an equal value of consumable goods in return.

Only a very small part of this import can be supposed to go each year toward increasing the kingdom's plate or its coin. All the rest must be sent abroad again and exchanged for consumable goods of one kind or another. But if those consumable goods were bought directly with the produce of English industry, England would gain more than by first buying Portuguese gold with that produce and then buying the consumable goods with the gold. A direct foreign trade for consumption is always more advantageous than a roundabout one, and bringing the same value of foreign goods to the home market requires a much smaller capital by the direct route than by the indirect one. It would therefore have been more to England's advantage if a smaller share of its industry had been devoted to producing goods suited to the Portuguese market, and a larger share to producing goods suited to the other markets where the consumable goods demanded in Great Britain are to be found. Obtaining both the gold it needs for its own use and the consumable goods would, in this way, employ a much smaller capital than at present. A surplus of capital would therefore be left over for other purposes: setting in motion an additional quantity of industry and raising a greater annual produce.

Even if Britain were shut out of the Portugal trade entirely, it would have very little difficulty obtaining all the gold it needs each year, whether for plate, for coin, or for foreign trade. Gold, like every other commodity, can always be had somewhere for its value by anyone who has that value to give for it. Portugal's annual surplus of gold, moreover, would still be sent abroad, and if Great Britain did not carry it away, some other nation would, and that nation would be glad to sell it again at its price, just as Great Britain does now. It is true that in buying gold from Portugal we buy it at first hand, whereas in buying it from any other nation except Spain we would buy it at second hand and might pay somewhat more. This difference, however, would surely be too small to deserve public attention.

Almost all our gold, it is said, comes from Portugal, while with other nations the balance of trade is either against us or not much in our favor. But we should remember that the more gold we import from one country, the less we must necessarily import from all the others. The effective demand for gold, like the demand for every other commodity, is limited in every country to a certain quantity. If nine-tenths of that quantity is imported from one country, only one-tenth remains to be imported from all the rest. Furthermore, the more gold that is imported each year from certain particular countries, beyond what is needed for plate and coin, the more must necessarily be exported to certain others. And the more that most trivial object of modern policy, the balance of trade, appears to be in our favor with some particular countries, the more it must necessarily appear to be against us with many others.

It was on the strength of this foolish notion that England could not survive without the Portugal trade, however, that France and Spain, toward the end of the recent war, without claiming any offense or provocation, demanded that the king of Portugal close his ports to all British ships and, to guarantee that exclusion, admit French or Spanish garrisons into them. Had the king of Portugal accepted the humiliating terms that his brother-in-law the king of Spain proposed to him, Britain would have been relieved of a far greater burden than the loss of the Portugal trade: the burden of supporting a very weak ally, so wholly unprepared for his own defense that the entire power of England, had it been directed to that single purpose, could hardly, perhaps, have defended him for another campaign. The loss of the Portugal trade would no doubt have caused considerable difficulty for the merchants then engaged in it, who might not, for a year or two, have found any other equally profitable way of employing their capital. That, in all likelihood, would have been the whole of the harm England could have suffered from this celebrated piece of commercial policy.

The great annual import of gold and silver is intended neither for plate nor for coin but for foreign trade. A roundabout foreign trade for consumption can be carried on more advantageously with these metals than with almost any other goods. Because they are the universal instruments of commerce, they are more readily accepted in exchange for every commodity than any other goods. And because of their small bulk and great value, they cost less to carry back and forth from one place to another than almost any other kind of merchandise, and they lose less of their value in transit. Of all the commodities bought in one foreign country for no other purpose than to be sold or exchanged again for other goods in another, none are as convenient as gold and silver. The principal advantage of the Portugal trade lies in making easier all the various roundabout foreign trades for consumption carried on in Great Britain. Though it is not an advantage of the first importance, it is undoubtedly a considerable one.

It seems evident enough that whatever annual addition can reasonably be supposed to be made to the kingdom's plate or coin could require only a very small annual import of gold and silver, and that even if we had no direct trade with Portugal, this small quantity could always be obtained very easily somewhere or other.

Although the goldsmiths' trade is very considerable in Great Britain, by far the greater part of the new plate they sell each year is made from old plate melted down. The addition made each year to the kingdom's total stock of plate therefore cannot be very large, and it could require only a very small annual import.

The same is true of the coin. Nobody imagines, I believe, that even the greater part of the annual coinage, which for ten years running, before the recent reform of the gold coin, amounted to more than £800,000 a year in gold, was an annual addition to the money already circulating in the kingdom. In a country where the government pays the cost of coinage, the value of coin, even when it contains its full standard weight of gold and silver, can never be much greater than that of an equal quantity of the same metals uncoined. All it takes to obtain an equal quantity of coin for any quantity of uncoined gold or silver is the trouble of going to the mint and perhaps a delay of a few weeks. But in every country, most of the coin in circulation is almost always worn to some degree, or has otherwise fallen below its standard. In Great Britain, before the recent reform, it had fallen a good deal: the gold was more than 2 percent, and the silver more than 8 percent, below its standard weight. Now, if forty-four and a half guineas at their full standard weight, which together make a pound weight of gold, could buy very little more than a pound weight of uncoined gold, then forty-four and a half guineas that had lost part of their weight could not buy a full pound, and something had to be added to make up the shortfall. The current market price of gold bullion, therefore, instead of matching the mint price of £46 14s. 6d., was then about £47 14s., and sometimes about £48. Yet while most of the coin was in this degraded state, forty-four and a half guineas fresh from the mint would buy no more goods in the market than any other ordinary guineas. Once they came into a merchant's strongbox and were mixed with other money, they could not afterward be told apart without more trouble than the difference was worth. Like other guineas, they were worth no more than £46 14s. 6d. If thrown into the melting pot, however, they yielded, with no noticeable loss, a pound weight of standard gold, which could be sold at any time for between £47 14s. and £48, paid in gold or silver coin that served every purpose of money as well as the coin that had been melted down. There was an obvious profit, therefore, in melting down newly minted money, and it was done so promptly that no precaution the government could take was able to prevent it. For this reason the work of the mint resembled the weaving of Penelope, the wife of Ulysses in Homer's *Odyssey*, who wove a shroud by day and secretly unraveled it by night: what was done in the day was undone in the night. The mint was occupied not so much in making daily additions to the coin as in replacing the very best part of it, which was melted down every day.

If the private individuals who bring their gold and silver to the mint had to pay for the coinage themselves, it would add to the value of those metals in the same way that the craftsmanship, or "fashion," adds to the value of plate. Coined gold and silver would be worth more than uncoined. The seigniorage, the charge levied for minting, provided it was not exorbitant, would add to the bullion the full value of the duty. Because the government everywhere holds the exclusive privilege of coining money, no coin can reach the market more cheaply than the government chooses to supply it. If the duty were exorbitant, however, rising far above the real value of the labor and expense that coinage requires, the wide gap between the value of bullion and the value of coin might tempt counterfeiters, both at home and abroad, to pour in so much false money that the value of the government's currency would fall. Yet in France, where the seignorage is eight percent, no noticeable inconvenience of this kind arises. The dangers a counterfeiter faces everywhere, if he lives in the country whose coin he imitates, and the dangers his agents or correspondents face, if he lives abroad, are far too great to be worth running for a profit of six or seven percent.

The seignorage in France raises the value of the coin above what the quantity of pure gold it contains would justify. By the edict of January 1726, the mint price of fine gold of twenty-four carats was fixed at 740 livres, 9 sous, and 1 1/11 deniers for the mark of eight Paris ounces. The French gold coin, once allowance is made for the "remedy" of the mint, the small tolerance permitted below the official standard, contains twenty-one and three-quarter carats of fine gold and two and a quarter carats of alloy. A mark of standard gold is therefore worth no more than about 671 livres and 10 deniers. But in France this mark of standard gold is coined into thirty louis d'or of twenty-four livres each, or 720 livres. Coinage therefore raises the value of a mark of standard gold bullion by the difference between 671 livres 10 deniers and 720 livres, which comes to 48 livres, 19 sous, and 2 deniers.

A seignorage will in many cases remove altogether, and will in every case reduce, the profit to be made from melting down new coin. That profit always arises from the difference between the quantity of bullion the common currency ought to contain and the quantity it actually contains. If this difference is smaller than the seignorage, melting brings a loss rather than a profit. If the two are equal, there is neither profit nor loss. If the difference is greater than the seignorage, there will be some profit, but less than there would be without any seignorage at all. Before the recent reform of the gold coin, for example, had there been a seignorage of five percent on coinage, melting down the gold coin would have produced a loss of three percent. With a seignorage of two percent, there would have been neither profit nor loss. With a seignorage of one percent, there would have been a profit of only one percent instead of two. Wherever money is received by tale, that is, counted by the piece rather than weighed, a seignorage is therefore the most effective means of preventing the melting down of the coin, and for the same reason, of preventing its export. The best and heaviest pieces are the ones most commonly melted or exported, because they yield the largest profits.

The law encouraging coinage by making it duty-free was first enacted under Charles II for a limited period, then extended by successive renewals until 1769, when it was made permanent. The Bank of England, to replenish its reserves of money, frequently has to carry bullion to the mint, and its directors probably imagined that it served their interest to have the coinage paid for by the government rather than by themselves. The government most likely agreed to make the law permanent out of deference to this great company. Should the custom of weighing gold fall out of use, however, as its inconvenience makes quite likely, and should the English gold coin come to be received by tale, as it was before the recent recoinage, this great company may find that here, as on some other occasions, it has seriously misjudged its own interest.

Before the recent recoinage, the gold currency of England was two percent below its standard weight, and since there was no seignorage, it was worth two percent less than the quantity of standard gold bullion it ought to have contained. When the Bank bought gold bullion to have it coined, it therefore had to pay two percent more for it than the bullion was worth once coined. But had there been a seignorage of two percent on coinage, the ordinary gold currency, though still two percent below its standard weight, would nonetheless have been equal in value to the quantity of standard gold it ought to have contained, because the value added by the coinage, like the value that workmanship adds to silver plate, would have made up for the deficiency in weight. The Bank would, of course, have had to pay the seignorage, and since that was two percent, its loss on the whole transaction would have been two percent: exactly the same as it actually was, and no greater.

Had the seignorage been five percent while the gold currency was only two percent below its standard weight, the Bank would have gained three percent on the price of the bullion; but since it would have had to pay a seignorage of five percent on the coinage, its loss on the whole transaction would, in the same way, have been exactly two percent.

Had the seignorage been only one percent, with the gold currency two percent below its standard weight, the Bank would have lost only one percent on the price of the bullion; but since it would also have had to pay a seignorage of one percent, its loss on the whole transaction would again have been exactly two percent, just as in every other case.

If there were a reasonable seignorage while the coin also contained its full standard weight, as it has very nearly done since the recent recoinage, whatever the Bank might lose by the seignorage it would gain on the price of the bullion, and whatever it might gain on the price of the bullion it would lose by the seignorage. It would therefore neither lose nor gain on the whole transaction, and in this case, as in all the cases above, it would stand in exactly the same position as if there were no seignorage at all.

When the tax on a commodity is moderate enough not to encourage smuggling, the merchant who deals in that commodity advances the tax but does not, strictly speaking, pay it, since he recovers it in the price of the goods. The tax is ultimately paid by the final purchaser or consumer. But money is a commodity in which every person is a merchant. No one buys it except in order to sell it again, and in ordinary circumstances there is no final purchaser or consumer of it. When the tax on coinage is moderate enough not to encourage counterfeiting, therefore, everyone advances the tax, yet no one finally pays it, because everyone recovers it in the increased value of the coin.

A moderate seignorage, then, would in no case increase the expense of the Bank, or of any other private parties who bring their bullion to the mint for coining, and the absence of a moderate seignorage in no case reduces that expense. Whether or not there is a seignorage, if the currency contains its full standard weight, coinage costs nobody anything; and if the currency falls short of that weight, coinage must always cost the difference between the quantity of bullion the coin ought to contain and the quantity it actually contains.

When the government pays the expense of coinage, therefore, it not only incurs a small cost but also forgoes a small revenue it might collect through a proper duty, and neither the Bank nor any other private party gains the slightest benefit from this useless piece of public generosity.

The directors of the Bank, however, would probably be reluctant to accept a seignorage on the strength of a theory that promises them no gain and claims only to protect them from loss. In the present condition of the gold coin, and so long as it continues to be received by weight, they would certainly gain nothing from such a change. But if the custom of weighing the gold coin should ever lapse, as it very likely will, and if the gold coin should ever sink back into the debased condition it was in before the recent recoinage, the Bank's gain from a seignorage, or more properly its savings, would probably be very considerable. The Bank of England is the only company that sends any substantial quantity of bullion to the mint, and the burden of the annual coinage falls entirely, or almost entirely, on it. If the annual coinage had only to make good the unavoidable losses and ordinary wear of the coin, it could seldom exceed fifty thousand pounds, or a hundred thousand at most. But when the coin is debased below its standard weight, the annual coinage must, in addition, fill the large gaps that export and the melting pot are constantly opening in the circulating currency. For this reason, during the ten or twelve years immediately before the recent reform of the gold coin, the annual coinage averaged more than £850,000. Yet a seignorage of four or five percent on the gold coin would probably, even in the conditions that then prevailed, have put an effective stop to the business of both export and the melting pot. Instead of losing roughly two and a half percent every year on the bullion coined into more than £850,000, an annual loss of more than £21,250, the Bank would probably not have lost a tenth of that sum.

The revenue Parliament sets aside to cover the expense of coinage is only fourteen thousand pounds a year, and the real cost to the government, meaning the fees of the officers of the mint, does not ordinarily exceed half that sum, so I am assured. Saving so small an amount, or even gaining another that could hardly be much larger, may seem too trivial a matter to deserve the serious attention of government. But saving eighteen or twenty thousand pounds a year, in the event of something that is not improbable, that has often happened before, and that is very likely to happen again, is surely a matter that deserves the serious attention even of so great a company as the Bank of England.

Some of the preceding reasoning and observations might perhaps have been better placed in the chapters of the first book that treat the origin and use of money and the difference between the real and nominal price of commodities. But since the law encouraging coinage springs from the popular prejudices that the mercantile system introduced, I judged it more fitting to reserve them for this chapter. Nothing could suit the spirit of that system better than a kind of bounty on the production of money, the very thing which, on its assumptions, constitutes the wealth of every nation. It is one of its many admirable expedients for enriching the country.

### CHAPTER VII: OF COLONIES

#### Part I: Of the Motives for Establishing New Colonies

The interest that led to the first settlement of the various European colonies in America and the West Indies was not nearly as plain and distinct as the interest that guided the founding of the colonies of ancient Greece and Rome.

Each of the states of ancient Greece possessed only a very small territory. When the population of any one of them grew beyond what that territory could comfortably support, part of the people was sent out to find a new home in some remote and distant part of the world, since the warlike neighbors surrounding each state on every side made it difficult for any of them to enlarge its territory much at home. The colonies of the Dorians went chiefly to Italy and Sicily, which, in the period before the founding of Rome, were inhabited by barbarous and uncivilized peoples. The colonies of the Ionians and Aeolians, the two other great tribes of the Greeks, went to Asia Minor and the islands of the Aegean Sea, whose inhabitants at that time seem to have been in much the same condition as those of Sicily and Italy. The mother city regarded the colony as a child, always entitled to great favor and assistance and owing in return much gratitude and respect. But she regarded it as an emancipated child, over whom she claimed no direct authority or jurisdiction. The colony settled its own form of government, enacted its own laws, elected its own magistrates, and made peace or war with its neighbors as an independent state, with no need to wait for the approval or consent of the mother city. Nothing could be plainer or more distinct than the interest that directed every such undertaking.

Rome, like most of the other ancient republics, was originally founded on an agrarian law, which divided the public territory in fixed proportions among the citizens who made up the state. The ordinary course of human affairs, through marriage, inheritance, and sale, inevitably disrupted this original division, and frequently brought lands that had been allotted to support many different families into the possession of a single person. To remedy this disorder, for so it was regarded, a law was passed limiting the amount of land any citizen could own to five hundred iugera, or about 350 English acres. Although we read that this law was enforced on one or two occasions, it was otherwise either neglected or evaded, and the inequality of fortunes kept growing. Most citizens had no land, and without it the manners and customs of the time made it difficult for a free man to maintain his independence. In our own day, a poor man who owns no land but has a little capital can either farm another man's land or carry on some small retail trade; and if he has no capital at all, he can find work as a farm laborer or as a craftsman. Among the ancient Romans, however, the lands of the rich were all cultivated by slaves, who worked under an overseer who was himself a slave, so that a poor free man had little chance of being employed either as a farmer or as a laborer. All trades and manufactures, even the retail trade, were likewise carried on by the slaves of the rich for their masters' benefit, and the wealth, authority, and protection of those masters made it difficult for a poor free man to compete against them. The citizens who had no land therefore had scarcely any means of subsistence except the handouts distributed by candidates at the annual elections. Whenever the tribunes wanted to stir up the people against the rich and the powerful, they reminded them of the ancient division of lands and described the law restricting this kind of private property as the fundamental law of the republic. The people grew clamorous for land, and the rich and powerful, we may be sure, were entirely determined not to give up any part of theirs. To satisfy the people in some measure, they frequently proposed sending out a new colony. But even on such occasions, conquering Rome had no need to turn her citizens out to seek their fortune, so to speak, across the wide world without knowing where they would settle. She generally assigned them lands in the conquered provinces of Italy, where, being within the republic's dominions, they could never form an independent state. At most they were a kind of corporation, which could enact bylaws for its own government but remained at all times subject to the correction, jurisdiction, and legislative authority of the mother city. Sending out a colony of this kind not only gave the people some satisfaction but often established a sort of garrison in a newly conquered province whose obedience might otherwise have been doubtful. A Roman colony, then, whether we consider the nature of the establishment itself or the motives behind it, was altogether different from a Greek one. Accordingly, the words that denote these two kinds of establishment in the original languages have very different meanings. The Latin word *colonia* means simply a plantation, a place where settlers are planted. The Greek word *apoikia*, by contrast, means a separation of dwelling, a departure from home, a going out of the house. Yet although the Roman colonies differed from the Greek ones in many respects, the interest that prompted their founding was equally plain and distinct. Both institutions arose either from irresistible necessity or from clear and evident utility.

The founding of the European colonies in America and the West Indies arose from no necessity. And although the benefits that have resulted from them have been very great, those benefits are not nearly so clear and evident. They were not understood when the colonies were first established; they were not the motive either for that establishment or for the discoveries that made it possible; and the nature, extent, and limits of those benefits are perhaps not well understood even today.

During the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, the Venetians carried on a very profitable trade in spices and other East Indian goods, which they distributed among the other nations of Europe. They bought these goods chiefly in Egypt, which was then ruled by the Mamelukes. The Mamelukes were enemies of the Turks, as were the Venetians, and this common interest, assisted by Venetian money, produced a connection that gave the Venetians something close to a monopoly of the trade.

The great profits of the Venetians aroused the greed of the Portuguese. Throughout the fifteenth century, the Portuguese had been trying to find a sea route to the countries from which the Moors brought them ivory and gold dust across the desert. They discovered Madeira, the Canaries, the Azores, the Cape Verde Islands, the coast of Guinea, the coasts of Loango, Congo, Angola, and Benguela, and finally the Cape of Good Hope. They had long wished to share in the profitable trade of the Venetians, and this last discovery opened a likely prospect of doing so. In 1497, Vasco da Gama sailed from the port of Lisbon with a fleet of four ships and, after a voyage of eleven months, arrived on the coast of Hindustan. This completed a course of discoveries that had been pursued with great steadiness, and with very little interruption, for nearly a century.

Some years earlier, while Europe waited in suspense to see whether the Portuguese projects, whose success still appeared doubtful, would succeed, a Genoese pilot conceived the even more daring plan of reaching the East Indies by sailing west. The location of those countries was at that time very imperfectly known in Europe. The few European travelers who had been there had exaggerated the distance, perhaps out of simplicity and ignorance, since what was in reality very great seemed almost infinite to those who had no means of measuring it, or perhaps in order to heighten the marvels of their own adventures in visiting regions so immensely remote from Europe. The longer the route was by the east, Columbus quite reasonably concluded, the shorter it would be by the west. He therefore proposed to take that route as both the shortest and the surest, and he had the good fortune to persuade Isabella of Castile that his plan was feasible. He sailed from the port of Palos in August 1492, nearly five years before Vasco da Gama's expedition left Portugal, and after a voyage of between two and three months he discovered first some of the small Bahama, or Lucayan, islands, and afterward the great island of Santo Domingo.

But the countries Columbus discovered, on this or any of his later voyages, bore no resemblance to those he had gone in search of. Instead of the wealth, cultivation, and dense population of China and Hindustan, he found in Santo Domingo, and in every other part of the New World he ever visited, nothing but a land entirely covered with forest, uncultivated, and inhabited only by a few tribes of naked and miserable savages. He was very reluctant, however, to believe that these were not the same as some of the countries described by Marco Polo, the first European who had visited China or the East Indies, or at least the first to leave behind a description of them. A very slight resemblance, such as the one he found between Cibao, the name of a mountain in Santo Domingo, and Cipangu, the name Marco Polo gave to Japan, was often enough to bring him back to this cherished belief, even against the clearest evidence. In his letters to Ferdinand and Isabella, he called the lands he had discovered the Indies. He had no doubt that they were the outer edge of the countries Marco Polo had described, and that they lay not far from the Ganges or from the lands conquered by Alexander the Great. Even when he was at last convinced that they were different, he still assured himself that those rich countries could not be far off, and on a later voyage he accordingly went looking for them along the coast of the mainland of South America, known as Tierra Firme, and toward the Isthmus of Darien.

Because of this mistake by Columbus, the name of the Indies has clung to those unfortunate lands ever since. When it was finally established beyond doubt that the new Indies were altogether different from the old, the new were called the West Indies, to distinguish them from the old, which were called the East Indies.

It mattered a great deal to Columbus, however, that the lands he had discovered, whatever they were, should be presented to the Spanish court as being of very great importance. Yet in what constitutes the real wealth of every country, the animal and vegetable products of the soil, there was nothing at that time that could justify such a description.

The cori, an animal somewhere between a rat and a rabbit, which the naturalist Buffon supposed to be the same as the aperea of Brazil, was the largest four-footed animal bearing live young on Santo Domingo. This species seems never to have been very numerous, and the dogs and cats brought by the Spaniards are said to have long since almost entirely exterminated it, along with some other species still smaller. These animals, however, together with a fairly large lizard called the iguana, made up the principal part of the animal food the land provided.

The vegetable food of the inhabitants, though not very abundant because of their lack of industry, was not quite so scanty. It consisted of maize, yams, potatoes, bananas, and similar plants, all of which were then entirely unknown in Europe. They have never since been much valued there, nor thought to provide nourishment equal to that drawn from the common kinds of grain and legumes cultivated in this part of the world since time immemorial.

The cotton plant, it is true, supplied the raw material for a very important manufacture, and was at that time undoubtedly the most valuable of all the vegetable products of those islands in European eyes. But although the muslins and other cotton goods of the East Indies were highly prized throughout Europe at the end of the fifteenth century, the cotton manufacture itself was not carried on anywhere in Europe. Even this product, therefore, could not then appear to Europeans to be of very great importance.

Finding nothing in either the animals or the plants of the newly discovered lands that could justify a highly favorable account of them, Columbus turned his attention to their minerals. In the richness of this third kingdom of nature, he persuaded himself, he had found full compensation for the insignificance of the other two. The little pieces of gold with which the inhabitants decorated their clothing, and which, he was told, they often found in the streams and torrents running down from the mountains, were enough to convince him that those mountains were full of the richest gold mines. Santo Domingo was therefore described as a land abounding in gold, and for that reason, according to the prejudices not only of our own time but of that time as well, as an inexhaustible source of real wealth to the crown and kingdom of Spain.
