When Columbus returned from his first voyage and was presented, with something like the honors of a triumph, to the sovereigns of Castile and Aragon, the principal products of the lands he had discovered were carried before him in solemn procession. The only valuable part of them consisted of some small headbands, bracelets, and other ornaments of gold, and some bales of cotton. The rest were mere objects of popular wonder and curiosity: some reeds of extraordinary size, some birds of very beautiful plumage, and some stuffed skins of the huge alligator and the manatee. All of these were preceded by six or seven of the wretched natives, whose unusual color and appearance added greatly to the novelty of the spectacle.

On the strength of Columbus's reports, the Council of Castile resolved to take possession of lands whose inhabitants were plainly incapable of defending themselves. The pious aim of converting them to Christianity sanctified the injustice of the undertaking. But the hope of finding treasures of gold there was the sole motive that prompted it, and to give this motive greater weight, Columbus proposed that half of all the gold and silver found there should belong to the crown. The council approved the proposal.

As long as all or most of the gold the first adventurers brought back to Europe was obtained by so easy a method as plundering the defenseless natives, it was perhaps not very difficult to pay even this heavy tax. But once the natives had been entirely stripped of everything they had, which in Santo Domingo and in all the other lands discovered by Columbus was accomplished within six or eight years, and once it had become necessary to dig in the mines to find more, there was no longer any possibility of paying it. The strict enforcement of the tax is said to have caused the complete abandonment of the mines of Santo Domingo, which have never been worked since. The tax was therefore soon reduced to a third, then to a fifth, later to a tenth, and finally to a twentieth of the gross output of the gold mines. The tax on silver long remained at a fifth of the gross output and was lowered to a tenth only in the course of the present century. But the first adventurers do not seem to have cared much about silver. Nothing less precious than gold seemed worth their attention.

All the other Spanish enterprises in the New World that followed those of Columbus seem to have been driven by the same motive. It was the sacred thirst for gold that carried Ojeda, Nicuesa, and Vasco Núñez de Balboa to the Isthmus of Darien, that carried Cortés to Mexico, and Almagro and Pizarro to Chile and Peru. Whenever these adventurers arrived on an unknown coast, their first question was always whether there was any gold to be found there, and according to the answer they received on this point, they decided either to leave the country or to settle in it.

Of all the costly and uncertain projects that bring bankruptcy on most of the people who engage in them, there is perhaps none more thoroughly ruinous than the search for new silver and gold mines. It is perhaps the most disadvantageous lottery in the world, the one in which the gains of those who draw the prizes bear the smallest proportion to the losses of those who draw blanks; for though the prizes are few and the blanks many, the usual price of a ticket is the entire fortune of a very rich man. Mining projects, instead of returning the capital invested in them along with the ordinary profits of capital, commonly swallow up both capital and profit. They are therefore, of all projects, the ones to which a prudent lawmaker who wished to increase his nation's capital would least wish to give any extraordinary encouragement, or toward which he would least wish to direct a larger share of that capital than would flow to them of its own accord. In fact, such is the absurd confidence nearly all men have in their own good luck that wherever there is the slightest chance of success, too great a share of capital tends to flow to these projects of its own accord.

But although the verdict of sober reason and experience on such projects has always been extremely unfavorable, the verdict of human greed has generally been quite the opposite. The same passion that suggested to so many people the absurd idea of the philosopher's stone, the substance the alchemists believed could turn base metals into gold, has suggested to others the equally absurd idea of immensely rich mines of gold and silver. These people did not consider that the value of those metals has, in every age and nation, arisen chiefly from their scarcity. Nor did they consider that this scarcity arises from the very small quantities nature has deposited in any one place, from the hard and stubborn materials with which she has almost everywhere surrounded those small quantities, and consequently from the labor and expense required everywhere to break through to them. They imagined that veins of these metals might be found in many places as large and abundant as the veins commonly found of lead, copper, tin, or iron. Sir Walter Raleigh's dream of the golden city and country of El Dorado is enough to show us that even wise men are not always free from such strange delusions. More than a hundred years after that great man's death, the Jesuit Gumilla was still convinced that this wonderful country was real, and he declared with great warmth, and, I have no doubt, with great sincerity, how happy he would be to carry the light of the gospel to a people who could reward the pious labors of their missionary so handsomely.

In the lands the Spaniards first discovered, no gold or silver mines are known at present that are thought to be worth working. The quantities of those metals the first adventurers are said to have found there were probably greatly exaggerated, as was the richness of the mines worked immediately after the discovery. What those adventurers were reported to have found, however, was enough to inflame the greed of all their countrymen. Every Spaniard who sailed to America expected to find an El Dorado. Fortune, too, did on this occasion what she has done on very few others. She fulfilled, to some degree, the extravagant hopes of her devotees, and in the discovery and conquest of Mexico and Peru, the first of which took place about thirty years and the second about forty years after Columbus's first expedition, she presented them with something not very unlike the abundance of precious metals they had been seeking.

A project of trade with the East Indies, then, led to the first discovery of the West. A project of conquest led to all the Spanish settlements in those newly discovered lands. The motive that spurred them to this conquest was a project of gold and silver mines; and a series of accidents that no human wisdom could have foreseen made this project far more successful than its undertakers had any reasonable grounds to expect.

The first adventurers of all the other European nations that attempted to establish settlements in America were driven by the same fantastic hopes, but they were not equally successful. It was more than a hundred years after the first settlement of Brazil before any silver, gold, or diamond mines were discovered there. In the English, French, Dutch, and Danish colonies, none has ever yet been discovered, or at least none that is currently thought worth working. The first English settlers in North America nevertheless offered the king a fifth of all the gold and silver that might be found there, as an inducement for granting them their charters. In the charters granted to Sir Walter Raleigh, to the London and Plymouth companies, to the Council of Plymouth, and others, this fifth was accordingly reserved to the crown. To the expectation of finding gold and silver mines, those first settlers also added the hope of discovering a northwest passage to the East Indies. They have so far been disappointed in both.

#### Part II: Causes of the Prosperity of New Colonies

The colony of a civilized nation that takes possession of an empty country, or of one so thinly inhabited that the natives readily make way for the new settlers, advances more rapidly to wealth and greatness than any other human society.

The colonists bring with them a knowledge of agriculture and other useful arts superior to anything that could develop on its own, over the course of many centuries, among savage and barbarous peoples. They also bring the habit of subordination, some notion of the regular government that prevails in their own country, of the system of laws that supports it, and of a regular administration of justice, and they naturally establish something similar in the new settlement. Among savage and barbarous peoples, however, the natural progress of law and government is even slower than the natural progress of the arts, once law and government have been established far enough to protect those arts. Every colonist gets more land than he can possibly cultivate. He pays no rent and scarcely any taxes. No landlord shares in its produce, and the sovereign's share is usually a trifle. He has every motive to make as large as possible a produce that will be almost entirely his own. But his land is generally so extensive that, with all his own labor and all the labor of whatever other people he can manage to employ, he can seldom make it yield a tenth of what it is capable of producing. He is therefore eager to gather laborers from every quarter and to reward them with the most generous wages. But those generous wages, together with the abundance and cheapness of land, soon make those laborers leave him to become landowners themselves, and they in turn pay equally generous wages to other laborers, who soon leave them for the same reason they left their first master. Generous pay for labor encourages marriage. Children are well fed and properly cared for through the vulnerable years of infancy, and once they are grown, the value of their labor far exceeds the cost of their upkeep. When they reach maturity, the high price of labor and the low price of land allow them to establish themselves just as their fathers did before them.

In other countries, rent and profit consume wages, and the two upper classes, those who live by rent and those who live by profit, oppress the lower class, who live by wages. In new colonies, however, the self-interest of the two upper classes compels them to treat the lower one with greater generosity and humanity, at least where that class is not enslaved. Uncultivated land of the greatest natural fertility can be had for next to nothing. The proprietor, who in such places is always also the one who undertakes and directs the work, expects his revenue to grow as the land is improved, and that increase is his profit, which under these circumstances is usually very large. But he cannot earn this large profit without employing other people to clear and cultivate the land, and the imbalance between the vast extent of land and the small population, which is typical of new colonies, makes such labor hard to find. He therefore does not haggle over wages; he is willing to hire labor at any price. High wages encourage population growth. The abundance and cheapness of good land encourage improvement and enable the proprietor to pay those high wages. Those wages make up almost the entire price of the land, and although they are high when considered as the wages of labor, they are low when considered as the price of something so valuable. Whatever promotes the growth of population and improvement also promotes the growth of real wealth and greatness.

The ancient Greek colonies accordingly seem to have advanced toward wealth and greatness very rapidly. Within a century or two, several of them appear to have rivaled and even surpassed their mother cities. Syracuse and Agrigentum in Sicily, Tarentum and Locri in Italy, and Ephesus and Miletus in Asia Minor were, by all accounts, at least the equal of any city in ancient Greece. Although they were founded later, they seem to have cultivated all the refined arts, including philosophy, poetry, and eloquence, as early as any part of the mother country, and to have carried them to as high a level. It is remarkable that the schools of the two oldest Greek philosophers, Thales and Pythagoras, were founded not in Greece proper but in its colonies, the first in Asia and the second in Italy. All these colonies had settled in lands inhabited by savage and barbarous peoples who readily gave way to the newcomers. They had plenty of good land, and because they were entirely independent of the mother city, they were free to manage their own affairs in whatever way they judged best suited to their own interest.

The history of the Roman colonies is far less distinguished. Some of them, such as Florence, did grow over many centuries into considerable states, after the fall of Rome itself. But none of them seems ever to have advanced very rapidly. They were all planted in conquered provinces, which in most cases had already been fully inhabited. The amount of land assigned to each colonist was seldom large, and because the colony was not independent, the colonists were not always free to manage their own affairs in the way they judged best suited to their own interest.

In the abundance of good land, the European colonies established in America and the West Indies resemble those of ancient Greece and even far surpass them. In their dependence on the mother country, they resemble those of ancient Rome, but their great distance from Europe has, in every case, softened the effects of that dependence to some degree. Their position has kept them farther from the mother country's sight and farther from its reach. When they have pursued their own interest in their own way, their conduct has often been overlooked, either because it was not known in Europe or because it was not understood there; and on some occasions it has simply been tolerated and accepted, because their distance made it hard to restrain. Even the violent and arbitrary government of Spain has often been forced to withdraw or soften orders it had issued for governing its colonies, for fear of a general uprising. The progress of all the European colonies in wealth, population, and improvement has accordingly been very great.

From the moment its colonies were first established, the Spanish crown drew some revenue from them through its share of the gold and silver they produced. This was, moreover, a kind of revenue well suited to rouse in human greed the wildest hopes of still greater riches. From the very beginning, therefore, the Spanish colonies drew a great deal of attention from their mother country, while those of the other European nations were for a long time largely neglected. The Spanish colonies did not perhaps flourish any better for this attention, nor did the others flourish any worse for this neglect. In proportion to the extent of territory they nominally possess, the Spanish colonies are considered less populous and less prosperous than those of almost any other European nation. Even so, their progress in population and improvement has certainly been very rapid and very great. The city of Lima, founded after the conquest, is described by Ulloa as having had fifty thousand inhabitants nearly thirty years ago. Quito, which had been nothing but a wretched Indian hamlet, is described by the same author as equally populous in his day. Gemelli Carreri, who is said to have been a traveler only in pretense but who seems everywhere to have written from excellent information, reports that Mexico City contained a hundred thousand inhabitants. Despite all the exaggerations of the Spanish writers, that figure is probably more than five times what the city held in the time of Montezuma. These numbers far exceed those of Boston, New York, and Philadelphia, the three largest cities of the English colonies. Before the Spanish conquest, there were no animals strong enough to pull a plow or cart in either Mexico or Peru. The llama was their only beast of burden, and its strength seems to have been considerably less than that of an ordinary donkey. The plow was unknown to them. They did not know how to use iron. They had no coined money and no established medium of exchange of any kind; their commerce was conducted by barter. A kind of wooden spade was their chief agricultural tool. Sharp stones served them as knives and hatchets for cutting; fish bones and the tough sinews of certain animals gave them needles for sewing; and these seem to have been the principal tools of their crafts. Under such conditions, it seems impossible that either of those empires could have been as improved or as well cultivated as it is today, now that both are amply supplied with every kind of European livestock, and the use of iron, the plow, and many European arts has been introduced among them. Yet the population of every country must correspond to its degree of improvement and cultivation. In spite of the cruel destruction of the native inhabitants that followed the conquest, these two great empires are probably more populous now than they have ever been, and the people are surely very different; for we must acknowledge, I think, that the Spanish creoles, the descendants of Spaniards born in America, are in many respects superior to the ancient Indians.

After the Spanish settlements, the Portuguese settlement in Brazil is the oldest of any European nation in America. For a long time after its discovery, however, no gold or silver mines were found there, and because it therefore yielded little or no revenue to the crown, it was largely neglected for many years. It was during this period of neglect that it grew into a great and powerful colony. While Portugal was under Spanish rule, Brazil was attacked by the Dutch, who took possession of seven of the fourteen provinces into which it is divided. They expected to conquer the other seven soon, but Portugal then regained its independence when the House of Braganza was raised to the throne. The Dutch, as enemies of Spain, now became friends of the Portuguese, who were likewise Spain's enemies. They therefore agreed to leave to the king of Portugal the part of Brazil they had not conquered, and he agreed to leave to them the part they had, since the matter did not seem worth quarreling over with such valuable allies. But the Dutch government soon began to oppress the Portuguese colonists, who, rather than wasting their time on complaints, took up arms against their new masters. By their own courage and determination, with the tacit approval of the mother country but without any open assistance from it, they drove the Dutch out of Brazil. Finding it impossible to keep any part of the country for themselves, the Dutch consented to its complete restoration to the Portuguese crown. This colony is said to contain more than six hundred thousand people who are either Portuguese or of Portuguese descent: creoles, mulattoes, and people of mixed Portuguese and native Brazilian ancestry. No other colony in America is believed to contain so many people of European extraction.

Toward the end of the fifteenth century and through most of the sixteenth, Spain and Portugal were the two great naval powers on the ocean; for although the commerce of Venice reached every part of Europe, its fleet had scarcely ever sailed beyond the Mediterranean. By right of first discovery, the Spanish claimed all of America as their own. Though they could not prevent a naval power as great as Portugal from settling in Brazil, the terror of their name was such at that time that most other European nations were afraid to establish themselves anywhere else on that great continent. The French who tried to settle in Florida were all murdered by the Spanish. But the decline of Spanish naval power, which followed the defeat or failure of what they called their Invincible Armada near the end of the sixteenth century, left them unable to obstruct the settlements of other European nations any longer. In the course of the seventeenth century, therefore, the English, French, Dutch, Danes, and Swedes, all the great nations with ports on the ocean, attempted to establish settlements in the New World.

The Swedes established themselves in New Jersey, and the number of Swedish families still found there is sufficient proof that this colony would very likely have prospered if the mother country had protected it. But Sweden neglected it, and it was soon absorbed by the Dutch colony of New York, which in turn passed under English rule in 1674.

The small islands of St. Thomas and Santa Cruz are the only territories in the New World the Danes have ever possessed. These little settlements were also placed under the government of an exclusive company, which held the sole right both to buy the colonies' surplus produce and to supply them with whatever foreign goods they needed. In both its buying and its selling, therefore, the company had not only the power to oppress them but the strongest temptation to do so. Government by an exclusive company of merchants is perhaps the worst of all possible governments for any country. It could not, however, halt the progress of these colonies altogether, though it made that progress slower and more sluggish. The late king of Denmark dissolved this company, and since then the colonies have prospered greatly.

The Dutch settlements in the West Indies, like those in the East Indies, were originally placed under the government of an exclusive company. The progress of some of them, therefore, though considerable compared with almost any long-settled and established country, has been sluggish and slow compared with that of most new colonies. The colony of Surinam, though quite substantial, still falls short of most of the sugar colonies of the other European nations. The colony of New Netherland, now divided into the two provinces of New York and New Jersey, would probably have soon become substantial as well, even had it remained under Dutch rule. The abundance and cheapness of good land are such powerful causes of prosperity that even the very worst government can hardly check their effect entirely. The colonists' great distance from the mother country would also have allowed them to evade, to some degree, the company's monopoly over them by smuggling. At present, the company permits any Dutch ship to trade with Surinam on payment of a license fee of two and a half percent of the value of its cargo, and reserves to itself exclusively only the direct trade from Africa to America, which consists almost entirely of the slave trade. This relaxation of the company's exclusive privileges is probably the chief cause of the degree of prosperity the colony now enjoys. Curaçao and St. Eustatius, the two principal islands belonging to the Dutch, are free ports, open to the ships of all nations. That freedom, amid better-endowed colonies whose ports are open to the ships of only one nation, has been the great cause of the prosperity of these two barren islands.

The French colony of Canada was, for most of the last century and part of this one, governed by an exclusive company. Under so unfavorable an administration, its progress was necessarily very slow compared with that of other new colonies; but it became much more rapid once the company was dissolved after the collapse of the speculative venture known as the Mississippi Scheme. When the English took possession of the country, they found nearly twice the number of inhabitants that Father Charlevoix had attributed to it twenty or thirty years earlier. That Jesuit had traveled over the whole country and had no inclination to make it appear less significant than it really was.

The French colony of Saint-Domingue was established by pirates and freebooters, who for a long time neither needed the protection of France nor acknowledged its authority. When that band of outlaws had become sufficiently settled citizens to acknowledge this authority, it still had to be exercised for a long time with great gentleness. During this period, the colony's population and improvement increased very quickly. Even the oppression of the exclusive company to which it was subjected for a time, along with all the other French colonies, though it undoubtedly held the colony back, could not stop its progress altogether. Its prosperity resumed as soon as it was relieved of that oppression. It is now the most important of the sugar colonies in the West Indies, and its output is said to exceed that of all the English sugar colonies combined. The other French sugar colonies are, in general, all thriving.

But no colonies have advanced more rapidly than those of the English in North America.

Plenty of good land, and the freedom to manage their own affairs in their own way, appear to be the two great causes of the prosperity of all new colonies.

In the abundance of good land, the English colonies of North America, though certainly very well supplied, are nonetheless inferior to those of the Spanish and Portuguese, and no better off than some of the colonies the French held before the recent war. But the political institutions of the English colonies have been more favorable to the improvement and cultivation of this land than those of the other three nations.

First, the accumulation of uncultivated land in a few hands, though by no means prevented altogether, has been more restrained in the English colonies than in any others. Colonial law obliges every proprietor to improve and cultivate a certain proportion of his land within a fixed period and declares that, if he fails to do so, the neglected land may be granted to someone else. This law has perhaps not been very strictly enforced, but it has had some effect.

Second, Pennsylvania has no right of primogeniture, the rule by which the eldest son inherits the whole estate; land, like movable property, is divided equally among all the children of the family. In three of the provinces of New England, the eldest son receives only a double share, as under the law of Moses. In those provinces, therefore, even if a single individual should sometimes accumulate too much land, it is likely to be adequately divided again within a generation or two. In the other English colonies, it is true, primogeniture applies, as it does under English law. But in all the English colonies, land is held by free socage, a form of tenure carrying fixed, non-military obligations, which makes land easy to sell or transfer. The recipient of a large grant generally finds it in his interest to sell off most of it as quickly as he can, reserving for himself only a small fixed annual payment known as a quit-rent. In the Spanish and Portuguese colonies, by contrast, the succession of every great estate that carries a title of honor is governed by what is called the right of majorazzo. Such estates pass entirely to a single heir and are in effect entailed, meaning they are legally barred from being sold or divided. The French colonies, admittedly, are subject to the Custom of Paris, the body of customary law that, in the inheritance of land, is far more favorable to younger children than English law. But in the French colonies, if any part of an estate held by the noble tenure of chivalry and homage is sold, it remains subject for a limited time to a right of redemption, by which either the heir of the overlord or the heir of the family may buy it back. And since all the largest estates in the country are held by such noble tenures, their sale is necessarily hampered. Yet in a new colony, a great uncultivated estate is likely to be broken up far more quickly by sale than by inheritance. The abundance and cheapness of good land, as has already been observed, are the principal causes of the rapid prosperity of new colonies. The concentration of land in a few hands effectively destroys that abundance and cheapness. The concentration of uncultivated land is, moreover, the greatest obstacle to its improvement, and the labor employed in improving and cultivating land yields the largest and most valuable produce to society. In this case, the produce of labor pays not only its own wages and the profit of the capital that employs it, but also the rent of the land on which it is employed. The labor of the English colonies, being more fully devoted to the improvement and cultivation of land, is therefore likely to yield a larger and more valuable produce than that of any of the other three nations, where the concentration of landholding diverts labor, to a greater or lesser degree, into other occupations.

Third, the labor of the English colonists is not only likely to yield a larger and more valuable produce; because their taxes are moderate, a larger share of that produce also belongs to them, and they can save it and use it to set a still greater quantity of labor in motion. The English colonists have never yet contributed anything toward the defense of the mother country or the support of its civil government. On the contrary, they themselves have so far been defended almost entirely at the mother country's expense, and the cost of fleets and armies is out of all proportion greater than the necessary cost of civil government. The cost of their own civil government has always been very modest. It has generally been limited to what was needed to pay adequate salaries to the governor, the judges, and a few other officers of public administration, and to maintain a handful of the most useful public works. Before the beginning of the present disturbances, the civil establishment of Massachusetts Bay cost only about £18,000 a year; those of New Hampshire and Rhode Island, £3,500 each; that of Connecticut, £4,000; those of New York and Pennsylvania, £4,500 each; that of New Jersey, £1,200; and those of Virginia and South Carolina, £8,000 each. The civil establishments of Nova Scotia and Georgia are partly supported by an annual grant from Parliament, but Nova Scotia also pays about £7,000 a year toward the public expenses of the colony, and Georgia about £2,500. In short, all the various civil establishments in North America, excluding those of Maryland and North Carolina, for which no exact figures have been obtained, cost their inhabitants no more than £64,700 a year before the present disturbances began. This is a memorable example of how little it can cost for three million people to be not only governed but well governed. The most important part of the expense of government, that of defense and protection, has, it is true, always fallen on the mother country. The ceremonies of civil government in the colonies, such as the reception of a new governor or the opening of a new assembly, are dignified enough but are not accompanied by any costly pomp or parade. Their church government is run on an equally frugal plan. Tithes are unknown among them, and their clergy, who are far from numerous, are supported either by modest salaries or by the voluntary contributions of the people. The power of Spain and Portugal, by contrast, draws some support from the taxes levied on their colonies. France, it is true, has never drawn any significant revenue from its colonies, since the taxes it levies on them are generally spent within them. But the colonial governments of all three nations operate on a much more elaborate scale and are accompanied by far more expensive ceremony. The sums spent on receiving a new viceroy of Peru, for example, have often been enormous. Such ceremonies are not only real taxes paid by the wealthy colonists on those particular occasions; they also cultivate among them habits of vanity and extravagance on every other occasion. They are not only very burdensome occasional taxes but also help to establish permanent taxes of the same kind that are more burdensome still: the ruinous taxes of private luxury and extravagance. In the colonies of all three nations, moreover, church government is extremely oppressive. Tithes are imposed in all of them and are collected with the utmost rigor in those of Spain and Portugal. All of them are also burdened with a multitude of mendicant friars, whose begging, not merely licensed but consecrated by religion, is a most grievous tax on the poor, who are carefully taught that giving is a duty and that refusing the friars their charity is a very great sin. On top of all this, the clergy in every one of these colonies are the largest accumulators of land.

Fourth, in disposing of their surplus produce, meaning whatever they grow beyond their own consumption, the English colonies have been more favored than those of any other European nation, and have been allowed a wider market. Every European nation has tried, to a greater or lesser degree, to monopolize the commerce of its colonies. For that reason each has barred foreign ships from trading with them and has forbidden the colonies to import European goods from any foreign nation. But the manner in which this monopoly has been exercised has differed greatly from one nation to another.

Some nations have handed the entire commerce of their colonies to an exclusive company. The colonists were obliged to buy from that company all the European goods they needed and to sell it the whole of their surplus produce. It was therefore in the company's interest not only to sell the former as dearly and buy the latter as cheaply as possible, but also to buy no more of the colonial produce, even at that low price, than it could resell at a very high price in Europe. Its interest lay not only in depressing the value of the colony's surplus produce in every case, but in many cases in discouraging and holding down the natural growth of its quantity. Of all the devices that could be contrived to stunt the natural growth of a new colony, an exclusive company is without doubt the most effective. This, however, has been the policy of Holland, although in the course of the present century the Dutch company has in many respects ceased to exercise its exclusive privilege. It was also the policy of Denmark until the reign of the late king. France has adopted it at various times. And recently, since 1755, after every other nation had abandoned it as absurd, it has become the policy of Portugal, at least with respect to two of the principal provinces of Brazil, Pernambuco and Maranhão.

Other nations, without setting up an exclusive company, have confined the whole commerce of their colonies to a single port of the mother country. No ship was allowed to sail from that port except in a convoy fleet at a fixed season or, if alone, under a special license, which in most cases had to be paid for handsomely. This policy did open colonial trade to every native of the mother country, provided he traded from the proper port, at the proper season, and in the proper vessels. But since all the merchants who pooled their capital to fit out these licensed vessels would find it in their interest to act together, the trade conducted in this way was bound to run on very nearly the same principles as that of an exclusive company. The merchants' profits would be almost as exorbitant and oppressive. The colonies would be poorly supplied, and would be forced both to buy very dear and to sell very cheap. Until a few years ago, however, this had always been the policy of Spain, and the price of all European goods in the Spanish West Indies is accordingly said to have been enormous. At Quito, according to the Spanish naval officer and traveler Antonio de Ulloa, a pound of iron sold for about four shillings and sixpence sterling, and a pound of steel for about six shillings and ninepence. Yet the colonies part with their own produce chiefly in order to buy European goods. The more they pay for the one, therefore, the less they really receive for the other, and the dearness of the European goods amounts to the same thing as the cheapness of the colonial produce. In this respect Portugal follows the old policy of Spain with regard to all her colonies except Pernambuco and Maranhão, and for those two she has recently adopted a still worse one.

Still other nations leave the trade of their colonies open to all their subjects, who may carry it on from any port of the mother country and need no license beyond the ordinary clearance papers of the customhouse. In this case the sheer number and dispersal of the traders makes it impossible for them to form any general combination, and their competition is enough to prevent them from making very exorbitant profits. Under so liberal a policy, the colonies can both sell their own produce and buy the goods of Europe at a reasonable price. Since the dissolution of the Plymouth Company, when our colonies were still in their infancy, this has always been the policy of England. It has generally been the policy of France as well, and consistently so since the dissolution of what is commonly called in England their Mississippi Company. The profits of the trade that France and England carry on with their colonies are therefore no doubt somewhat higher than they would be if competition were open to all other nations, but they are by no means exorbitant. Accordingly, the price of European goods is not extravagantly high in most of the colonies of either nation.

In exporting their own surplus produce, too, the colonies of Great Britain are confined to the market of the mother country only for certain commodities. Because these commodities were specifically listed in the Navigation Act and in several later acts, they have come to be called enumerated commodities. All the rest are called non-enumerated, and may be exported directly to other countries, provided they travel in British or colonial ships whose owners and at least three-quarters of whose crews are British subjects.

Among the non-enumerated commodities are some of the most important products of America and the West Indies: grain of all kinds, lumber, salted provisions, fish, sugar, and rum.

Grain is naturally the first and chief crop of every new colony. By granting the colonies a very wide market for it, the law encourages them to extend its cultivation far beyond what a thinly settled country can consume, and so to lay up in advance an ample subsistence for a steadily growing population.

In a country entirely covered with forest, where timber is consequently worth little or nothing, the cost of clearing the ground is the main obstacle to improvement. By granting the colonies a very wide market for their lumber, the law tries to make improvement easier by raising the price of a commodity that would otherwise have little value, enabling the settlers to make some profit from what would otherwise be pure expense.

In a country neither half populated nor half cultivated, cattle naturally multiply beyond what the inhabitants can consume, and for that reason are often worth little or nothing. But as has already been shown, the price of cattle must stand in a certain proportion to the price of grain before most of the land in any country can be improved. By granting American cattle in every form, dead and alive, a very wide market, the law tries to raise the value of a commodity whose high price is essential to improvement. The good effects of this freedom must, however, be somewhat reduced by the statute passed in the fourth year of George III, chapter 15, which places hides and skins among the enumerated commodities and so tends to lower the value of American cattle.

Increasing the shipping and naval power of Great Britain by expanding the fisheries of our colonies is an aim the legislature seems to have kept almost constantly in view. For this reason the colonial fisheries have received all the encouragement that freedom can give, and they have flourished accordingly. The New England fishery in particular was, before the recent disturbances, perhaps one of the most important in the world. The whale fishery in Great Britain, despite an extravagant bounty, is carried on to so little purpose that many people believe, though I do not claim to vouch for it, that its entire produce is worth hardly more than the bounties paid out for it each year. In New England the same fishery is carried on without any bounty and on a very large scale. Fish is one of the principal goods the North Americans trade to Spain, Portugal, and the Mediterranean.

Sugar was originally an enumerated commodity that could be exported only to Great Britain. In 1751, however, at the petition of the sugar planters, its export was permitted to every part of the world. The restrictions attached to this freedom, together with the high price of sugar in Great Britain, have largely nullified it. Great Britain and her colonies still remain almost the only market for the sugar grown on British plantations. Their consumption is rising so quickly that, although imports of sugar have increased very greatly over the past twenty years with the continued development of Jamaica and of the islands France ceded to Britain, exports to foreign countries are said to be little greater than before.

Rum is a very important article in the trade the Americans carry on with the coast of Africa, from which they bring back enslaved Africans in exchange.

If the entire American surplus of grain of all kinds, salted provisions, and fish had been placed on the list and thereby forced into the British market, it would have competed too heavily with the produce of our own people's labor. It was probably less out of any concern for America's interest than out of jealousy of this competition that these important commodities were not only kept off the list, but that the import into Great Britain of all grain except rice, and of all salted provisions, has under the ordinary state of the law been forbidden.

The non-enumerated commodities could originally be exported to any part of the world. Lumber and rice, having once been placed on the list and later removed from it, were afterward restricted, as far as the European market was concerned, to the countries lying south of Cape Finisterre, the headland in the northwest of Spain. By the statute of the sixth year of George III, chapter 52, all non-enumerated commodities were made subject to the same restriction. The parts of Europe south of Cape Finisterre are not manufacturing countries, and so we are less anxious that colonial ships returning from them might bring back manufactured goods that could compete with our own.

The enumerated commodities fall into two classes. The first consists of goods that are either peculiar to America or cannot be produced, or at any rate are not produced, in the mother country. Of this kind are molasses, coffee, cocoa beans, tobacco, pimento, ginger, whalebone, raw silk, cotton, wool, beaver and other American furs, indigo, fustic and other dyewoods. The second class consists of goods that are not peculiar to America and that are, or can be, produced in the mother country, though not in quantities large enough to meet most of her demand, which is supplied mainly from abroad. Of this kind are all naval stores, including masts, yards, and bowsprits, tar, pitch, and turpentine; pig and bar iron; copper ore; hides and skins; and pot and pearl ashes, the crude and refined forms of potash used in making soap and glass.

The largest imports of goods in the first class could neither discourage the growth nor interfere with the sale of any part of the mother country's produce. By confining them to the home market, it was expected that our merchants would not only be able to buy them more cheaply in the plantations, and so to sell them at home at a better profit, but would also establish a profitable carrying trade between the plantations and foreign countries, a trade of which Great Britain, as the European country into which these goods first had to be imported, would necessarily be the center or entrepôt. It was supposed that imports of the second class, too, could be managed so as to compete not with goods of the same kind produced at home but with those imported from abroad. By means of suitable duties, the colonial goods could be kept always somewhat dearer than the domestic ones and yet a good deal cheaper than the foreign ones. By confining such commodities to the home market, therefore, the intention was to discourage the produce not of Great Britain but of certain foreign countries with which the balance of trade was believed to run against her.

The ban on exporting masts, yards, bowsprits, tar, pitch, and turpentine from the colonies to any country other than Great Britain naturally tended to lower the price of timber in the colonies, and therefore to raise the cost of clearing their land, which was the chief obstacle to their improvement. But around the beginning of the present century, in 1703, the pitch and tar company of Sweden tried to raise the price of its goods to Great Britain by forbidding their export except in its own ships, at its own price, and in whatever quantities it saw fit. To counter this remarkable piece of mercantile policy, and to make herself as independent as possible not only of Sweden but of all the other northern powers, Great Britain granted a bounty on the import of naval stores from America. The effect of this bounty was to raise the price of timber in America far more than confinement to the home market could lower it. Since both regulations were enacted at the same time, their combined effect was to encourage rather than discourage the clearing of land in America.

Pig and bar iron, too, have been placed among the enumerated commodities. But because, when imported from America, they are exempt from substantial duties that apply when they come from any other country, one part of the regulation does more to encourage the building of furnaces in America than the other does to discourage it. No manufacture consumes as much wood as an ironworks furnace, and none can do as much to clear a country overgrown with forest.

The tendency of some of these regulations to raise the value of timber in America, and thereby to make it easier to clear the land, was perhaps neither intended nor understood by the legislature. But although their beneficial effects in this respect were accidental, they were no less real for that.

Trade between the British colonies of America and the West Indies is entirely free, in both enumerated and non-enumerated commodities. These colonies have now grown so populous and prosperous that each finds in some of the others a large and extensive market for every part of its produce. Taken together, they form a great internal market for one another's goods.

England's liberality toward the trade of her colonies, however, has been confined mainly to the market for their produce, either in its raw state or at what might be called the very first stage of manufacture. The more advanced or refined manufactures, even of colonial produce, the merchants and manufacturers of Great Britain prefer to keep for themselves. They have persuaded the legislature to prevent such manufactures from being established in the colonies, sometimes through high duties and sometimes through outright prohibitions. For example, muscovado sugar, the raw brown sugar of the plantations, pays on import only six shillings and fourpence per hundredweight; white sugar pays one pound, one shilling, and a penny; and refined sugar, whether double or single refined, in loaves, pays four pounds, two shillings, and five and eight-twentieths pence. When these high duties were imposed, Great Britain was the only market to which the sugar of the British colonies could be exported, and she remains the principal one. The duties therefore amounted to a prohibition: at first on claying or refining sugar for any foreign market, and now on claying or refining it for the market that takes perhaps more than nine-tenths of the entire crop. Claying was a method of whitening sugar by letting moisture from wet clay drain through it. Accordingly, the business of claying or refining sugar, although it has flourished in every sugar colony of France, has been little pursued in any colony of England except for the colonial market itself. While Grenada was in French hands, there was a refinery for claying sugar on nearly every plantation. Since the island passed to the English, almost all such works have been abandoned, and at present, in October 1773, I am assured that no more than two or three remain there. Now, however, through an indulgence of the customhouse, clayed or refined sugar is commonly imported as muscovado if it has been ground from loaves into powder.

While Great Britain encourages the making of pig and bar iron in America by exempting it from duties that apply to the same goods from any other country, she absolutely forbids the building of steel furnaces and slitting mills, which cut bar iron into rods, in any of her American plantations. She will not allow her colonies to work at these more refined manufactures even for their own use, but insists that they buy every such article they need from her merchants and manufacturers.

She forbids the shipment by water from one province to another, and even the carriage by land on horseback or by cart, of hats, wool, and woolen goods produced in America. This regulation effectively prevents any manufacture of such goods for distant sale from being established, and confines the colonists' industry in this line to the coarse household manufactures that a private family commonly makes for its own use, or for that of a few neighbors in the same province.

To forbid a great people from making all they can of every part of their own produce, or from employing their capital and labor in whatever way they judge most advantageous to themselves, is a plain violation of the most sacred rights of mankind. Unjust as such prohibitions may be, however, they have not so far been very harmful to the colonies. Land there is still so cheap, and labor consequently so dear, that the colonists can import almost all the more refined or advanced manufactures from the mother country more cheaply than they could make them themselves. Even if they had not been forbidden to establish such manufactures, then, regard for their own interest would probably have kept them from doing so at their present stage of development. At that stage, these prohibitions perhaps neither cramp their industry nor hold it back from any employment it would have taken up of its own accord. They are merely needless badges of slavery, imposed without sufficient reason by the groundless jealousy of the merchants and manufacturers of the mother country. In a more advanced state, they might become truly oppressive and unbearable.

Just as Great Britain confines some of the most important colonial products to her own market, so in compensation she gives some of them an advantage in that market. She does this sometimes by imposing higher duties on the same products when they come from other countries, and sometimes by paying bounties on their import from the colonies. In the first way she favors, in the home market, the sugar, tobacco, and iron of her own colonies; in the second, their raw silk, hemp and flax, indigo, naval stores, and building timber. This second method of encouraging colonial produce, through bounties on import, is, as far as I have been able to learn, peculiar to Great Britain. The first is not. Portugal is not satisfied with imposing higher duties on tobacco imported from any other country, but forbids it under the severest penalties.

In the import of goods from Europe, England has likewise treated her colonies more liberally than any other nation has.

Great Britain allows a part of the duty paid on imported foreign goods, almost always half, generally more, and sometimes the whole, to be refunded when those goods are exported again to any foreign country. Such refunds are called drawbacks. It was easy to foresee that no independent foreign country would accept these goods if they arrived burdened with the heavy duties imposed on nearly all foreign goods entering Great Britain. Unless some part of those duties was refunded on export, therefore, the carrying trade would come to an end, and the carrying trade is one the mercantile system particularly favors.

Our colonies, however, are by no means independent foreign countries. Having claimed for herself the exclusive right of supplying them with all European goods, Great Britain could have forced them, as other countries have forced their colonies, to receive those goods loaded with the full duties paid in the mother country. On the contrary, until 1763 the same drawbacks were paid on the export of most foreign goods to our colonies as to any independent foreign country. In 1763, it is true, the statute of the fourth year of George III, chapter 15, considerably curtailed this indulgence, enacting "that no part of the duty called the old subsidy should be drawn back for any goods of the growth, production, or manufacture of Europe or the East Indies, which should be exported from this kingdom to any British colony or plantation in America; wines, white calicoes, and muslins excepted." Before this law, many kinds of foreign goods could be bought more cheaply in the plantations than in the mother country, and some still can.

It should be observed that the merchants who carry on the colonial trade have been the chief advisers behind most of the regulations governing it. We should not be surprised, then, if in many of these regulations their interest has been given more weight than that of either the colonies or the mother country. In granting those merchants the exclusive privilege of supplying the colonies with all the goods they wanted from Europe, and of buying whatever part of the colonial surplus would not compete with any trade they themselves carried on at home, the interest of the colonies was sacrificed to the interest of the merchants. In allowing the same drawbacks on the re-export of most European and East Indian goods to the colonies as on their re-export to any independent country, the interest of the mother country was sacrificed to them as well, even by the mercantile system's own understanding of that interest. It was in the merchants' interest to pay as little as possible for the foreign goods they sent to the colonies, and therefore to recover as much as possible of the duties they had paid in advance on importing them into Great Britain. They could then sell in the colonies either the same quantity of goods at a greater profit or a greater quantity at the same profit, and so gain something one way or the other. It was likewise in the interest of the colonies to obtain all such goods as cheaply and in as great abundance as possible. But this might not always serve the interest of the mother country. She could often suffer on two fronts: in her revenue, by refunding a large part of the duties that had been paid when such goods were first imported; and in her manufactures, by being undersold in the colonial market, since these refunds, known as drawbacks, allowed foreign manufactures to be shipped there on very easy terms. The growth of Britain's linen industry, it is commonly said, has been considerably held back by the drawbacks granted on German linen re-exported to the American colonies.

Yet although Britain's policy toward the trade of her colonies has been shaped by the same mercantile spirit as that of other nations, it has on the whole been less narrow and oppressive than that of any of them.

In everything except their foreign trade, the English colonists have complete liberty to manage their own affairs in their own way. That liberty is in every respect equal to the liberty of their fellow citizens at home, and it is secured in the same manner: by an assembly of the people's representatives, which claims the sole right of imposing taxes to support the colonial government. The authority of this assembly holds the executive power in check, and no colonist, however humble or however unpopular, has anything to fear from the resentment of the governor or of any other civil or military officer in the province, so long as he obeys the law. Like the House of Commons in England, the colonial assemblies do not always represent the people very equally, but they come closer to doing so. And because the executive either lacks the means to corrupt them or, supported as it is by the mother country, has no need to, they are perhaps generally more responsive to the wishes of their constituents. The councils that form the upper chamber of the colonial legislatures, corresponding to the House of Lords in Britain, are not made up of a hereditary nobility. In some colonies, as in three of the governments of New England, these councils are not appointed by the king but chosen by the people's representatives. None of the English colonies has any hereditary nobility at all. In every one of them, as in every other free country, the descendant of an old colonial family is more respected than a newcomer of equal merit and fortune; but he is only more respected, and he holds no privileges that would let him make trouble for his neighbors. Before the present disturbances began, the colonial assemblies held not only the legislative power but a share of the executive as well. In Connecticut and Rhode Island, they elected the governor. In the other colonies, they appointed the revenue officers who collected the taxes those assemblies imposed, and these officers answered directly to them. There is therefore more equality among the English colonists than among the inhabitants of the mother country. Their manners are more republican, and their governments, particularly those of three of the New England provinces, have so far been more republican too.

The absolute governments of Spain, Portugal, and France, by contrast, extend to their colonies, and the discretionary powers that such governments commonly delegate to all their subordinate officers are naturally exercised there, because of the great distance, with more than ordinary violence. Under every absolute government there is more liberty in the capital than in any other part of the country. The sovereign himself can never have either the interest or the inclination to pervert the course of justice or to oppress the great body of the people. In the capital his presence restrains, to a greater or lesser degree, all his subordinate officers; but in the remote provinces, from which the people's complaints are less likely to reach him, those officers can practice their tyranny with far more safety. And the European colonies in America are more remote than the most distant provinces of the greatest empires ever known before. The government of the English colonies is perhaps the only one since the world began that could give perfect security to the inhabitants of so distant a province. The administration of the French colonies, however, has always been conducted with much more gentleness and moderation than that of the Spanish and Portuguese. This superior conduct suits both the character of the French nation and the thing that shapes the character of every nation, namely the nature of its government. The French government, though arbitrary and violent compared with that of Great Britain, is lawful and free compared with those of Spain and Portugal.

It is in the progress of the North American colonies, however, that the superiority of English policy chiefly appears. The progress of France's sugar colonies has been at least equal, and perhaps superior, to that of most of England's; and yet England's sugar colonies enjoy a free government of nearly the same kind as her colonies in North America. But the French sugar colonies are not discouraged, as the English ones are, from refining their own sugar; and, what matters still more, the character of their government naturally leads to better management of their enslaved Africans.

In all the European colonies, sugarcane is cultivated by enslaved Africans. It is supposed that people born in the temperate climate of Europe could not endure the labor of digging the ground under the burning sun of the West Indies. Sugarcane cultivation, as currently practiced, is entirely hand labor, although many believe the drill plough, a horse-drawn implement that sows seed in regular rows, could be introduced into it with great advantage. Now, just as the profit and success of farming carried on with cattle depend heavily on the good management of those cattle, so the profit and success of farming carried on with slaves must depend equally on the good management of those slaves; and in this respect the French planters, I think it is generally agreed, are superior to the English. The law, insofar as it gives the slave some weak protection against his master's violence, is likely to be better enforced in a colony whose government is largely arbitrary than in one whose government is entirely free. In every country where the unfortunate law of slavery is established, a magistrate who protects a slave is to some degree interfering in the master's management of his private property. In a free country, where the master may be a member of the colonial assembly or a voter for one, the magistrate dares do this only with the greatest caution and circumspection. The deference he is obliged to show the master makes it harder for him to protect the slave. But in a country where the government is largely arbitrary, where the magistrate routinely interferes even in how individuals manage their private property, and may send them a *lettre de cachet*, a royal order for imprisonment without trial, if they fail to manage it to his liking, it is much easier for him to give the slave some protection; and common humanity naturally inclines him to do so. The magistrate's protection makes the slave less contemptible in his master's eyes, and the master is thereby led to regard him with more consideration and treat him more gently. Gentle treatment makes the slave not only more faithful but more intelligent, and therefore more useful on both counts. He comes closer to the condition of a free servant and may develop some degree of integrity and attachment to his master's interest. These are virtues that often belong to free servants, but they can never belong to a slave treated as slaves commonly are in countries where the master is perfectly free and secure.

That a slave's condition is better under an arbitrary government than under a free one is, I believe, borne out by the history of every age and nation. In Roman history, the first time we read of a magistrate intervening to protect a slave from his master's violence is under the emperors. When Vedius Pollio, in the presence of Augustus, ordered one of his slaves, who had committed some slight fault, to be cut into pieces and thrown into his fishpond to feed his fish, the emperor indignantly commanded him to free at once not only that slave but every other slave he owned. Under the Republic, no magistrate could have had enough authority to protect the slave, much less to punish the master.

It should be observed that the capital that has developed France's sugar colonies, particularly the great colony of Saint-Domingue, has been raised almost entirely from the gradual improvement and cultivation of those colonies themselves. It has been almost wholly the produce of the colonists' soil and labor, or, what amounts to the same thing, the price of that produce, gradually accumulated through good management and reinvested to raise a still greater produce. But a great part of the capital that has developed and cultivated England's sugar colonies was sent out from England, and by no means all of it was the produce of the colonists' own soil and labor. The prosperity of the English sugar colonies has been owed in large measure to England's great wealth, part of which has overflowed, so to speak, onto these colonies. The prosperity of the French sugar colonies, however, has been owed entirely to the good conduct of the colonists, which must therefore have been in some respects superior to that of the English; and this superiority has been noted in nothing so much as in the management of their slaves.

Such have been the general outlines of the policy of the different European nations toward their colonies.

European policy, then, has very little to boast of, either in the original founding of the American colonies or, as far as their internal government is concerned, in their subsequent prosperity.

Folly and injustice seem to have been the principles that presided over and directed the first scheme of founding those colonies: the folly of hunting for gold and silver mines, and the injustice of coveting a country whose peaceable native peoples, far from ever having harmed the people of Europe, had received the first adventurers with every mark of kindness and hospitality.

The adventurers who founded some of the later settlements did, it is true, combine the fanciful scheme of finding gold and silver mines with other, more reasonable and more praiseworthy motives; but even these motives do very little credit to the policy of Europe.

The English Puritans, restricted at home, fled to America for freedom and established there the four governments of New England. The English Catholics, treated with far greater injustice, established Maryland; the Quakers, Pennsylvania. The Portuguese Jews, persecuted by the Inquisition, stripped of their fortunes, and banished to Brazil, introduced by their example some degree of order and industry among the transported convicts and prostitutes who had originally populated that colony, and they taught them to cultivate sugarcane. On every one of these occasions, it was not the wisdom and policy of European governments but their disorder and injustice that peopled and cultivated America.

In carrying out some of the most important of these settlements, the various governments of Europe deserved as little credit as they did in conceiving them. The conquest of Mexico was the project not of the Spanish royal council but of a governor of Cuba, and it was accomplished through the spirit of the bold adventurer to whom it was entrusted, despite everything that governor, who soon regretted having trusted such a man, could do to obstruct it. The conquerors of Chile and Peru, and of nearly all the other Spanish settlements on the American mainland, took with them no public encouragement beyond a general permission to make settlements and conquests in the name of the king of Spain. These ventures were all undertaken at the private risk and expense of the adventurers themselves. The Spanish government contributed scarcely anything to any of them. The English government contributed just as little toward founding some of its most important colonies in North America.

Once these settlements had been established and had grown important enough to attract the mother country's attention, her first regulations concerning them were always aimed at securing for herself the monopoly of their trade: confining their market and enlarging her own at their expense, and so dampening and discouraging the course of their prosperity rather than quickening and advancing it. The different ways in which this monopoly has been exercised constitute one of the most essential differences among the policies of the various European nations toward their colonies. The best of them all, England's, is merely somewhat less narrow and oppressive than any of the others.

In what way, then, has European policy contributed either to the first establishment or to the present greatness of the American colonies? In one way, and one way only, it has contributed a great deal. *Magna virum mater!* Great mother of men! It bred and formed the men who were capable of achieving such great deeds and of laying the foundation of so great an empire; and no other part of the world has a political order capable of forming such men, or has ever in fact formed them. The colonies owe to European policy the education and the large ambitions of their active and enterprising founders; and some of the greatest and most important of them, so far as their internal government is concerned, owe it scarcely anything else.

#### Part III: Of the Advantages Which Europe Has Derived from the Discovery of America, and from That of a Passage to the East Indies by the Cape of Good Hope

Such are the advantages the American colonies have derived from the policy of Europe.

What advantages has Europe derived from the discovery and colonization of America?

These advantages can be divided into two kinds: first, the general advantages that Europe, considered as one great country, has derived from those great events; and second, the particular advantages that each colonizing country has derived from the colonies belonging specifically to it, by virtue of the authority or dominion it exercises over them.

The general advantages that Europe, considered as one great country, has derived from the discovery and colonization of America consist, first, in an increase in its enjoyments and, second, in a growth of its industry.

The surplus produce of America imported into Europe supplies the inhabitants of this great continent with a variety of goods they could not otherwise have had, some for convenience and use, some for pleasure, and some for ornament, and so adds to their enjoyments.

It will readily be granted that the discovery and colonization of America have increased the industry, first, of all the countries that trade with it directly, such as Spain, Portugal, France, and England; and second, of all those that, without trading with it directly, send goods of their own production there through other countries. Examples of the latter are Austrian Flanders and some provinces of Germany, which ship a considerable quantity of linen and other goods to America through the countries just mentioned. All such countries have plainly gained a wider market for their surplus produce and must consequently have been encouraged to increase it.

It is perhaps less evident that these great events should also have encouraged the industry of countries such as Hungary and Poland, which may never have sent a single article of their own produce to America. That they have done so, however, cannot be doubted. Some part of America's produce is consumed in Hungary and Poland, where there is some demand for the sugar, chocolate, and tobacco of that new quarter of the world. But these goods must be bought either with something produced by the industry of Hungary and Poland or with something that was itself bought with part of that produce. These American goods are new values, new equivalents, introduced into Hungary and Poland to be exchanged there for those countries' surplus produce. By being brought there, they create a new and wider market for that surplus. They raise its value and so encourage its increase. Even if none of that surplus is ever carried to America, it may be carried to other countries that buy it with part of their share of America's surplus produce; and it may find a market through the circulation of a trade that America's surplus produce originally set in motion.

These great events may even have increased the enjoyments and expanded the industry of countries that never sent any goods to America and never received any from it. Even such countries may have received a greater abundance of other goods from countries whose surplus produce had grown through the American trade. Just as this greater abundance must have increased their enjoyments, so it must also have expanded their industry. A greater number of new equivalents, of one kind or another, must have been offered to them in exchange for the surplus produce of that industry. A wider market must have been created for that surplus, raising its value and so encouraging its increase. The mass of goods thrown each year into the great circle of European commerce, and distributed each year through its various turns among all the nations within it, must have been enlarged by the whole surplus produce of America. Each of those nations is therefore likely to have received a larger share of this larger mass, which will have increased their enjoyments and expanded their industry.

The exclusive trade of the mother countries tends to reduce, or at least to hold below the level they would otherwise reach, both the enjoyments and the industry of all these nations in general, and of the American colonies in particular. It is a dead weight on one of the great springs that drive a large part of humanity's business. By making colonial produce more expensive in every other country, it reduces the consumption of that produce. It thereby cramps the industry of the colonies, along with both the enjoyments and the industry of all other countries, which enjoy less when they pay more for what they enjoy and produce less when they get less for what they produce. By making the produce of every other country more expensive in the colonies, it cramps in the same way the industry of all other countries, along with both the enjoyments and the industry of the colonies. It is like a clog, the heavy block fastened to an animal's leg to hamper its movement: for the supposed benefit of certain particular countries, it hinders the pleasures and burdens the industry of every other country, but of the colonies more than any. It not only shuts all other countries out of one particular market as far as possible, but also confines the colonies as far as possible to one particular market; and there is a very great difference between being shut out of one market while all others are open and being confined to one market while all others are closed. Yet the surplus produce of the colonies is the original source of all the increase in enjoyments and industry that Europe derives from the discovery and colonization of America, and the exclusive trade of the mother countries tends to make this source far less abundant than it would otherwise be.

The particular advantages that each colonizing country derives from the colonies belonging specifically to it are of two kinds: first, the common advantages that every empire derives from the provinces under its rule; and second, the peculiar advantages that are supposed to arise from provinces of so peculiar a nature as the European colonies in America.

The common advantages that every empire derives from the provinces under its rule consist, first, in the military force they furnish for its defense and, second, in the revenue they furnish for the support of its civil government. The Roman colonies furnished both from time to time. The Greek colonies sometimes furnished a military force but seldom any revenue. They seldom acknowledged themselves subject to the rule of the mother city. They were generally her allies in war but very rarely her subjects in peace.

The European colonies in America have never yet furnished any military force for the defense of the mother country. Their military force has never even been sufficient for their own defense, and in the various wars the mother countries have fought, defending their colonies has generally drawn off a very considerable share of those countries' military strength. In this respect, therefore, every European colony without exception has been a source of weakness rather than of strength to its mother country.

Only the colonies of Spain and Portugal have contributed any revenue toward the defense of the mother country or the support of her civil government. The taxes levied on the colonies of other European nations, and on those of England in particular, have seldom equaled the expense laid out on them in peacetime and have never been enough to cover what they cost in wartime. Such colonies, therefore, have been a source of expense, not of revenue, to their mother countries.

The advantages of such colonies to their mother countries consist entirely in the peculiar advantages supposed to arise from provinces of so peculiar a nature as the European colonies in America; and the exclusive trade, it is acknowledged, is the sole source of all those peculiar advantages.

As a result of this exclusive trade, the entire portion of the surplus produce of the English colonies, for example, that consists of what are called enumerated commodities, the goods listed by law as permitted to be shipped only to England, can be sent to no country but England. Other countries must then buy it from her. It must therefore be cheaper in England than in any other country, and must add more to England's enjoyments than to those of any other country. It must likewise do more to encourage her industry. For whatever portions of her own surplus produce England exchanges for these enumerated commodities, she must get a better price than other countries can get for comparable portions of theirs when they exchange them for the same commodities. The manufactures of England, for example, will purchase a greater quantity of the sugar and tobacco of her own colonies than the comparable manufactures of other countries can buy. Insofar as English manufactures and those of other countries are both exchanged for the sugar and tobacco of the English colonies, this superior price gives English industry an encouragement that foreign industry cannot enjoy under the same circumstances. The exclusive trade of the colonies, therefore, diminishes the enjoyments and the industry of the countries that do not possess it, or at least holds them below the level they would otherwise reach, and to that extent it gives a clear advantage to the countries that do possess it.

This advantage, however, may prove to be relative rather than absolute. It gives superiority to the country that enjoys it not by raising that country's industry and produce above the level they would naturally reach under free trade, but by depressing the industry and produce of other countries.

Consider the tobacco of Maryland and Virginia. Because of the monopoly England holds over it, that tobacco certainly reaches England more cheaply than it reaches France, to which England commonly sells a considerable share of it. But had France and every other European country always been allowed to trade freely with Maryland and Virginia, the tobacco of those colonies might by now be cheaper than it actually is, not only for all those other countries but for England as well. With a market so much larger than any it has yet enjoyed, tobacco production might, and probably would, by now have grown enough to bring the profits of a tobacco plantation down to their natural level with those of a grain plantation, which they are thought to exceed somewhat even now. The price of tobacco might, and probably would, have fallen somewhat below its present level. A given quantity of goods, whether from England or from those other countries, might then have bought more tobacco in Maryland and Virginia than it does at present, and so would have fetched a correspondingly better price there. To whatever extent that weed, through its cheapness and abundance, can increase the enjoyments or expand the industry of England or of any other country, it would probably have produced both effects to a somewhat greater degree under free trade than it can now.
