England, admittedly, would then have held no advantage over other countries. She might have bought her colonies' tobacco somewhat more cheaply, and therefore sold some of her own goods somewhat more dearly, than she actually does; but she could not have bought the one more cheaply, or sold the other more dearly, than any other country. She might perhaps have gained an absolute advantage, but she would certainly have lost a relative one.

Yet to secure this relative advantage in the colony trade, and to carry out the spiteful and malicious project of excluding other nations from any share in it as far as possible, England has very probably done more than sacrifice part of the absolute advantage that she, like every other nation, might have drawn from that trade. There is good reason to believe she has also subjected herself to both an absolute and a relative disadvantage in almost every other branch of trade.

When England claimed the monopoly of the colony trade through the Navigation Act, the foreign capital previously employed in that trade was necessarily withdrawn from it. English capital, which had formerly carried on only part of the trade, now had to carry on the whole of it. The capital that had once supplied the colonies with only part of the goods they needed from Europe was now the only capital available to supply all of them. But it could not supply all of them, and the goods it did supply were necessarily sold at very high prices. Likewise, the capital that had once bought only part of the colonies' surplus produce was now the only capital available to buy the whole. But it could not buy the whole at anything near the old price, and so whatever it did buy, it necessarily bought very cheaply. In a line of business where the merchant sold very dear and bought very cheap, profits must have been very high, far above the ordinary level in other branches of trade. This superior profit in the colony trade was bound to pull away from other branches some of the capital previously employed in them. As this outflow of capital gradually increased competition among capitals in the colony trade, it gradually reduced competition in all the other branches; as it gradually lowered profits in the one, it gradually raised them in the others, until profits everywhere settled at a new level, different from and somewhat higher than the one that had prevailed before.

This double effect, drawing capital away from all other trades and raising the rate of profit in every trade somewhat above what it would otherwise have been, was not produced only when the monopoly was first established. It has continued ever since.

First, the monopoly has continually drawn capital away from all other trades and into the colony trade.

Although the wealth of Great Britain has grown enormously since the Navigation Act was passed, it has certainly not grown in the same proportion as that of the colonies. Yet the foreign trade of every country naturally grows in proportion to its wealth, just as its surplus produce grows in proportion to its total produce. Since Great Britain had monopolized almost the whole of what might be called the colonies' foreign trade, and since her capital had not grown in step with the expansion of that trade, she could carry it on only by continually withdrawing from other branches some of the capital previously employed there, and by withholding from them a great deal more that would otherwise have flowed to them. Accordingly, ever since the Navigation Act, the colony trade has steadily expanded while many other branches of foreign trade, especially trade with other parts of Europe, have steadily declined. Our manufactures for export, which before the Act were suited to the nearby European market or to the more distant market of the countries around the Mediterranean, have for the most part been adapted to the still more distant market of the colonies, a market where they hold a monopoly rather than one where they face many competitors. Sir Matthew Decker and other writers have attributed the decline of other branches of foreign trade to excessive and badly designed taxation, to the high price of labor, to the growth of luxury, and so on. The true cause may lie entirely in the overgrowth of the colony trade. The mercantile capital of Great Britain, though very large, is not infinite; and though it has increased greatly since the Navigation Act, it has not increased in the same proportion as the colony trade. That trade, therefore, could not possibly have been carried on without withdrawing some part of this capital from other branches, and consequently without some decline in those branches.

It should be remembered that England was already a great trading nation, with a very large mercantile capital that was growing larger every day, not only before the Navigation Act established the monopoly of the colony trade, but before that trade amounted to much at all. In the Dutch war under Cromwell's government, her navy was superior to Holland's; and in the war that broke out at the beginning of Charles II's reign, it was at least equal, and perhaps superior, to the combined navies of France and Holland. Its superiority would scarcely appear greater today, at least if the Dutch navy now bore the same proportion to Dutch commerce that it did then. But this great naval power cannot have been the product of the Navigation Act in either war. During the first, the plan of the Act had only just been drawn up; and although it had been fully enacted into law before the second broke out, no part of it could yet have had any significant effect, least of all the part that established exclusive trade with the colonies. Both the colonies and their trade were insignificant then compared with what they are now. Jamaica was an unhealthy wilderness, thinly inhabited and even more thinly cultivated. New York and New Jersey belonged to the Dutch, and half of St. Christopher's to the French. Antigua, the two Carolinas, Pennsylvania, Georgia, and Nova Scotia had not yet been settled. Virginia, Maryland, and New England had been settled, and they were thriving colonies; yet there was perhaps not a single person at that time, in Europe or America, who foresaw or even suspected the rapid progress they have since made in wealth, population, and improvement. Barbados, in short, was the only British colony of any consequence whose condition then bore any resemblance to its condition today. The colony trade, of which England enjoyed only a part even for some time after the Navigation Act (since the Act was not strictly enforced until several years after it was passed), could not then have been the cause of England's great commerce, or of the great naval power that commerce sustained. The trade that sustained that naval power was the trade of Europe and of the countries around the Mediterranean. But Great Britain's present share of that trade could not support any such naval power. Had the growing colony trade been left open to all nations, whatever share of it fell to Great Britain, and she would probably have won a very considerable share, would have been entirely an addition to the great trade she already possessed. Because of the monopoly, the growth of the colony trade has not so much added to the trade Great Britain already had as wholly changed its direction.

Second, the monopoly has necessarily helped to keep the rate of profit in every branch of British trade higher than it would naturally have been had all nations been allowed to trade freely with the British colonies.

By drawing into the colony trade a greater share of Great Britain's capital than would have gone there of its own accord, and by expelling all foreign capital, the monopoly necessarily reduced the total amount of capital employed in that trade below what it would have been under free trade. By lessening the competition of capitals in that branch, it necessarily raised the rate of profit there. And by lessening the competition of British capitals in all other branches, it necessarily raised the rate of British profit in all of them as well. Whatever the condition or size of Great Britain's mercantile capital at any given moment since the Navigation Act, the monopoly of the colony trade must, for as long as that condition lasted, have raised the ordinary rate of British profit above what it would otherwise have been, both in the colony trade and in every other branch of British trade. If the ordinary rate of British profit has fallen considerably since the Act was passed, as it certainly has, it would have fallen lower still had the monopoly not helped to hold it up.

But anything that raises a country's ordinary rate of profit above what it would otherwise be necessarily subjects that country to both an absolute and a relative disadvantage in every branch of trade in which she does not hold a monopoly.

It imposes an absolute disadvantage because, in those branches, her merchants cannot obtain this higher profit without charging more than they otherwise would, both for the foreign goods they import into their own country and for the domestic goods they export abroad. Their country must then both buy dearer and sell dearer; it must buy less and sell less; it must enjoy less and produce less than it otherwise would.

It imposes a relative disadvantage because, in those same branches, it places other countries, which are not subject to the same absolute disadvantage, either further above her or less far below her than they would otherwise be. It allows them to enjoy more and produce more in proportion to what she enjoys and produces. It makes their superiority greater, or their inferiority smaller, than it would otherwise be. By raising the price of her produce above its natural level, it enables the merchants of other countries to undersell her in foreign markets, and so to push her out of almost every branch of trade in which she does not hold a monopoly.

Our merchants often complain that the high wages of British labor are the reason their manufactures are undersold in foreign markets, but they say nothing about the high profits of capital. They complain of other people's extravagant gains, and are silent about their own. Yet the high profits of British capital may contribute as much to raising the price of British manufactures as the high wages of British labor do in many cases, and in some cases perhaps more.

In this way, one may fairly say, the capital of Great Britain has been partly drawn and partly driven out of most of the branches of trade in which she holds no monopoly, especially the trade of Europe and of the countries around the Mediterranean.

It has been partly drawn away from those branches by the attraction of higher profits in the colony trade, which arose from that trade's continual growth and from the continual inability of the capital that carried it on one year to carry it on the next.

It has been partly driven away from them by the advantage that Britain's high rate of profit gives to other countries in every branch of trade in which Great Britain holds no monopoly.

Just as the monopoly of the colony trade has drawn out of those other branches some of the British capital that would otherwise have been employed in them, so it has forced into them a great deal of foreign capital that would never have gone there had it not been expelled from the colony trade. In those other branches, it has reduced the competition of British capitals and so raised the rate of British profit above what it would otherwise have been. At the same time, it has increased the competition of foreign capitals and so lowered the rate of foreign profit below what it would otherwise have been. In both ways, it must clearly have placed Great Britain at a relative disadvantage in all those other branches of trade.

It may be objected, however, that the colony trade is more advantageous to Great Britain than any other, and that the monopoly, by forcing into it a larger share of British capital than would otherwise have gone there, has directed that capital into the employment most beneficial to the country.

The most advantageous employment of any capital, for the country to which it belongs, is the one that maintains the greatest quantity of productive labor at home and does the most to increase the annual produce of that country's land and labor. But as the second book of this work has shown, the quantity of productive labor that any capital can maintain in the foreign trade of consumption, the trade that buys foreign goods for use at home, is exactly proportional to the frequency of its returns. A capital of a thousand pounds, for instance, employed in a foreign trade of consumption whose returns come in regularly once a year, can keep in constant employment, in its home country, as much productive labor as a thousand pounds can maintain there for a year. If the returns come in two or three times a year, it can keep in constant employment as much productive labor as two or three thousand pounds can maintain there for a year. For this reason, a foreign trade of consumption carried on with a neighboring country is generally more advantageous than one carried on with a distant country; and for the same reason, as the second book also showed, a direct foreign trade of consumption is generally more advantageous than a roundabout one, in which home goods are first exchanged for foreign goods that must then be traded again before the desired imports are obtained.

Yet wherever the monopoly of the colony trade has affected the employment of British capital, it has in every case forced some part of it out of a foreign trade of consumption with a neighboring country and into one with a more distant country, and in many cases out of a direct foreign trade of consumption and into a roundabout one.

First, the monopoly of the colony trade has in every case forced some part of Great Britain's capital out of a foreign trade of consumption with a neighboring country and into one with a more distant country.

In every case it has forced some of that capital out of the trade with Europe and the countries around the Mediterranean and into the trade with the more distant regions of America and the West Indies, where returns are necessarily less frequent, not only because of the greater distance but because of the particular circumstances of those countries. New colonies, as has already been observed, are always short of capital. They always have far less of it than they could employ, with great profit and advantage, in improving and cultivating their land. They therefore constantly demand more capital than they possess, and to make up the shortfall they try to borrow as much as they can from the mother country, to which they are consequently always in debt. The most common way the colonies incur this debt is not by borrowing on formal bonds from wealthy people in the mother country, though they sometimes do that as well, but by running as far into arrears with their correspondents, the merchants who supply them with goods from Europe, as those correspondents will allow. Their annual payments often amount to no more than a third of what they owe, and sometimes to less. The whole capital their correspondents advance to them is therefore seldom returned to Britain in less than three years, and sometimes not in less than four or five. But a British capital of a thousand pounds that returns to Great Britain only once every five years can keep in constant employment only one-fifth of the British industry it could maintain if the whole were returned once a year. Instead of the quantity of industry a thousand pounds could maintain for a year, it can keep in constant employment only the quantity that two hundred pounds can maintain for a year. The planter, no doubt, makes up, and probably more than makes up, any loss his correspondent might suffer from this delay, through the high price he pays for European goods, through the interest on the bills of exchange he issues payable at distant dates, and through the commission charged for renewing those he issues payable at near dates. But though he may make good his correspondent's loss, he cannot make good Great Britain's. In a trade whose returns are very slow, the merchant's profit may be as great as, or greater than, in a trade whose returns are frequent and quick; but the advantage to the country where he lives, meaning the quantity of productive labor constantly maintained there and the annual produce of its land and labor, must always be much smaller. Anyone with experience of these different branches of trade will readily grant, I imagine, that returns from the trade to America, and still more from the trade to the West Indies, are generally not only slower but also more irregular and more uncertain than returns from the trade to any part of Europe, or even to the countries around the Mediterranean.

Second, the monopoly of the colony trade has in many cases forced some part of Great Britain's capital out of a direct foreign trade of consumption and into a roundabout one.

Among the enumerated commodities, the goods that may be shipped to no market but Great Britain, there are several whose quantity greatly exceeds British consumption, so that part of them must be exported to other countries. This cannot be done without forcing some of Great Britain's capital into a roundabout foreign trade of consumption. Maryland and Virginia, for example, send Great Britain more than ninety-six thousand hogsheads, or large casks, of tobacco every year, while British consumption is said not to exceed fourteen thousand. More than eighty-two thousand hogsheads, therefore, must be exported to other countries: to France, to Holland, and to the countries around the Baltic and Mediterranean seas. The portion of British capital that brings those eighty-two thousand hogsheads to Great Britain, re-exports them to those other countries, and brings back goods or money from those countries in return is employed in a roundabout foreign trade of consumption, and it is necessarily forced into that employment in order to dispose of this great surplus. To estimate how many years it will take for the whole of this capital to return to Great Britain, we must add the time required for returns from those other countries to the time required for returns from America. If the whole capital employed in our direct foreign trade of consumption with America often does not come back in less than three or four years, the whole capital employed in this roundabout trade is unlikely to come back in less than four or five. If the first can keep in constant employment only a third or a fourth of the domestic industry that a capital returned once a year could maintain, the second can keep in constant employment only a fourth or a fifth. At some of the outports, the provincial ports outside London, credit is commonly extended to the foreign correspondents to whom the tobacco is exported. At the port of London, it is true, tobacco is commonly sold for cash; the rule there is "Weigh and pay," meaning the buyer pays as soon as the goods are weighed. At the port of London, therefore, the final returns of the whole roundabout trade take longer than the returns from America only by the time the goods may lie unsold in the warehouse, where, however, they may sometimes lie for quite a long time. Yet had the colonies not been confined to the British market for the sale of their tobacco, very little more of it would probably have come to us than our own consumption required. The goods that Great Britain now buys for her own use with the great surplus of tobacco she exports to other countries, she would in that case probably have bought with the direct produce of her own industry, or with some portion of her own manufactures. That produce and those manufactures, instead of being shaped almost entirely for one great market, as they are now, would probably have been adapted to a great number of smaller ones. In place of one great roundabout foreign trade of consumption, Great Britain would probably have carried on a great many small direct trades of the same kind. Because returns come back so much more often in direct trades, a part of the capital that now carries on the great roundabout trade, probably only a small part and perhaps no more than a third or a quarter of it, might have been enough to carry on all the small direct ones. That smaller capital might have kept an equal quantity of British industry in constant employment and given equal support to the annual produce of Britain's land and labour. With every purpose of this trade answered by a much smaller capital, a large surplus of capital would have been left free for other uses: to improve the land, to expand manufactures, and to extend British commerce. It would have entered into competition, at the very least, with the other British capitals employed in all those different ways. It would have lowered the rate of profit in all of them, and thereby given Great Britain, in every one of them, an advantage over other countries even greater than the one she now enjoys.

The monopoly of the colony trade has also forced some part of Britain's capital out of every kind of foreign trade of consumption, in which British goods are exchanged for foreign goods to be used at home, and into a carrying trade, which merely transports goods between other countries. It has therefore turned that capital away from supporting, to a greater or lesser degree, the industry of Great Britain, and set it to supporting entirely the industry of others: partly that of the colonies and partly that of certain foreign countries.

Consider the eighty-two thousand hogsheads, or great casks, of tobacco re-exported from Great Britain every year as surplus. The goods bought with them are not all consumed in Great Britain. Some of them, such as linen from Germany and Holland, are sent back to the colonies for their own particular use. But the portion of British capital that buys the tobacco with which this linen is afterward bought is necessarily withdrawn from supporting the industry of Great Britain. It is employed entirely in supporting the industry partly of the colonies and partly of the particular countries that pay for the tobacco with the produce of their own labour.

By drawing into the colony trade a far greater proportion of British capital than would naturally have gone to it, the monopoly seems, moreover, to have entirely broken the natural balance that would otherwise have existed among all the different branches of British industry. Instead of being adapted to a great number of small markets, the industry of Great Britain has been fitted mainly to one great market. Instead of running through a great many small channels, her commerce has been trained to run mainly through one great channel. As a result, the whole system of her industry and commerce has been made less secure, and the whole condition of her body politic less healthy than it would otherwise have been. In her present state, Great Britain resembles one of those unhealthy bodies in which some of the vital organs have grown too large, and which are therefore prone to many dangerous disorders that rarely afflict a body whose parts are properly proportioned. A small blockage in that great blood vessel, which has been artificially swollen beyond its natural size and through which an unnatural share of the country's industry and commerce has been forced to circulate, is very likely to bring the most dangerous disorders upon the whole body politic. Accordingly, the prospect of a rupture with the colonies has filled the people of Great Britain with more terror than they ever felt at the approach of a Spanish armada or the threat of a French invasion. It was this terror, whether well or ill founded, that made the repeal of the Stamp Act a popular measure, among the merchants at least. Faced with total exclusion from the colony market, even if it lasted only a few years, most of our merchants imagined that they foresaw a complete halt to their trade, most of our master manufacturers the utter ruin of their businesses, and most of our workmen the end of their employment. A rupture with any of our neighbours on the Continent would also be likely to cause some halt or interruption in the work of some people in each of these classes, yet it is anticipated without any such general alarm. When the circulation of blood is stopped in some of the smaller vessels, the blood easily empties itself into the larger ones without causing any dangerous disorder. But when it is stopped in one of the larger vessels, convulsions, apoplexy, or death follow immediately and unavoidably. If even one of those overgrown manufactures that have been artificially raised to an unnatural height, whether by bounties or by the monopoly of the home and colony markets, meets with some small halt or interruption in its business, the result is often a riot and disorder that alarms the government and troubles even the deliberations of Parliament. How great, then, it was thought, must be the disorder and confusion caused by a sudden and complete halt in the employment of so large a proportion of our principal manufacturers?

The only expedient that seems able to deliver Great Britain from this danger in all future times is some moderate and gradual relaxation of the laws that give her the exclusive trade with the colonies, until that trade has been made largely free. Such a relaxation would enable her, or even force her, to withdraw some part of her capital from this overgrown employment and to turn it, though at lower profit, toward other employments. By gradually shrinking one branch of her industry and gradually enlarging all the rest, it could little by little restore all the branches to the natural, healthy, and proper proportion that perfect liberty necessarily establishes and that perfect liberty alone can preserve. To open the colony trade to all nations at once might cause not only some temporary inconvenience but a great and permanent loss to most of those whose labour or capital is currently engaged in it. The sudden loss of employment for the ships alone that import the eighty-two thousand hogsheads of tobacco beyond Britain's own consumption might be felt very sharply. Such are the unfortunate effects of all the regulations of the mercantile system. They not only introduce very dangerous disorders into the body politic, but disorders that are often difficult to cure without causing, for a time at least, still greater ones. How, then, the colony trade ought gradually to be opened; which restraints ought to be removed first and which last; and how the natural system of perfect liberty and justice ought gradually to be restored: these questions we must leave to the wisdom of future statesmen and legislators.

Five separate events, unforeseen and unimagined, have very fortunately combined to keep Great Britain from feeling as sharply as was generally expected the total exclusion, now in force for more than a year (since the first of December 1774), from a very important branch of the colony trade: that of the twelve associated provinces of North America. First, while preparing for their non-importation agreement, those colonies drained Great Britain completely of every commodity suited to their market. Second, the extraordinary demand of the Spanish flota, the great convoy that sails from Spain to her American possessions, has this year drained Germany and the North of many commodities, linen in particular, that used to compete with British manufactures even in the British market. Third, the peace between Russia and Turkey has created an extraordinary demand from the Turkish market, which had been very poorly supplied while the country was in distress and a Russian fleet was cruising among the islands of the Aegean. Fourth, the demand of northern Europe for British manufactures has been growing year after year for some time past. Fifth, the recent partition of Poland, and the peace that followed from it, has opened the market of that great country and so added an extraordinary demand from that quarter to the growing demand of the North. All of these events except the fourth are by nature temporary and accidental, and if exclusion from so important a branch of the colony trade should unfortunately continue much longer, it may still cause some degree of distress. Because this distress will come on gradually, however, it will be felt far less severely than if it had come all at once; and in the meantime the industry and capital of the country may find new employment and a new direction, so that the distress never rises to any considerable height.

So far, then, as the monopoly of the colony trade has drawn into that trade a greater proportion of British capital than would otherwise have gone to it, it has in every case turned that capital from a foreign trade of consumption with a neighbouring country into one with a more distant country. In many cases it has turned it from a direct foreign trade of consumption into a roundabout one, and in some cases from every kind of foreign trade of consumption into a carrying trade. In every case, therefore, it has turned capital from a direction in which it would have maintained a greater quantity of productive labour into one in which it can maintain a much smaller quantity. Furthermore, by fitting so great a part of Britain's industry and commerce to a single particular market, it has made the whole state of that industry and commerce more precarious and less secure than if their produce had been adapted to a wider variety of markets.

We must carefully distinguish between the effects of the colony trade and the effects of the monopoly of that trade. The first are always and necessarily beneficial; the second always and necessarily harmful. But the first are so beneficial that the colony trade, though subject to a monopoly and despite that monopoly's harmful effects, is still on the whole beneficial, and greatly so, though considerably less so than it would otherwise be.

In its natural and free state, the colony trade opens a great though distant market for whatever part of the produce of British industry may exceed the demand of the markets nearer home: those of Europe and of the countries surrounding the Mediterranean. In its natural and free state, the colony trade draws away none of the produce that had ever been sent to those markets, yet encourages Great Britain to increase her surplus continually by continually offering new equivalents in exchange for it. In its natural and free state, the colony trade tends to increase the quantity of productive labour in Great Britain without in any way altering the direction of the labour already employed there. In the natural and free state of the colony trade, the competition of all other nations would prevent the rate of profit from rising above the common level, either in the new market or in the new employment. The new market, drawing nothing from the old one, would create, so to speak, a new produce for its own supply; and that new produce would form a new capital for carrying on the new employment, which in the same way would draw nothing from the old one.

The monopoly of the colony trade, by contrast, excludes the competition of other nations and so raises the rate of profit in both the new market and the new employment, thereby drawing produce from the old market and capital from the old employment. To increase our share of the colony trade beyond what it would otherwise be is the declared purpose of the monopoly. If our share of that trade were to be no greater with the monopoly than without it, there would have been no reason to establish the monopoly at all. But whatever forces into a branch of trade whose returns are slower and more distant than those of most other trades a greater proportion of a country's capital than would go there of its own accord necessarily makes the whole quantity of productive labour maintained there each year, and the whole annual produce of that country's land and labour, smaller than they would otherwise be. It holds the revenue of the country's inhabitants below the level it would naturally reach, and so reduces their power to accumulate. It not only prevents their capital, at every moment, from maintaining as great a quantity of productive labour as it otherwise would, but also prevents it from growing as fast as it otherwise would, and consequently from maintaining a still greater quantity of productive labour.

For Great Britain, however, the natural good effects of the colony trade more than outweigh the bad effects of the monopoly, so that, monopoly and all, the trade even as it is now conducted is not merely advantageous but greatly advantageous. The new market and the new employment opened by the colony trade are far larger than the portion of the old market and the old employment lost through the monopoly. The new produce and the new capital created, so to speak, by the colony trade maintain in Great Britain a greater quantity of productive labour than can have been thrown out of work by the diversion of capital from other trades with more frequent returns. If the colony trade, even as now conducted, is advantageous to Great Britain, however, it is so not because of the monopoly but in spite of it.

The colony trade opens a new market chiefly for the manufactured produce of Europe rather than for its raw produce. Agriculture is the proper business of every new colony, a business that the cheapness of land makes more profitable than any other. New colonies therefore abound in the raw produce of the land, and instead of importing it from other countries, they generally have a large surplus to export. In new colonies, agriculture either draws workers away from every other occupation or keeps them from entering any other. There are few hands to spare for the necessary manufactures and none for the ornamental ones. The colonists find it cheaper to buy most manufactures of both kinds from other countries than to make them themselves. It is chiefly by encouraging the manufactures of Europe that the colony trade indirectly encourages European agriculture. The manufacturers to whom that trade gives employment constitute a new market for the produce of the land, and the most advantageous market of all. In this way the home market for the corn and cattle of Europe, for its bread and butcher's meat, is greatly enlarged by the trade with America.

That the monopoly of trade with populous and thriving colonies is not enough by itself to establish, or even to maintain, manufactures in any country is amply shown by the examples of Spain and Portugal. Both were manufacturing countries before they had any colonies of consequence. Since acquiring the richest and most fertile colonies in the world, both have ceased to be so.

In Spain and Portugal, the bad effects of the monopoly, aggravated by other causes, have perhaps nearly outweighed the natural good effects of the colony trade. These other causes appear to be monopolies of various other kinds; the debasement of the value of gold and silver below its level in most other countries; exclusion from foreign markets through ill-judged taxes on exports; and the narrowing of the home market through still more ill-judged taxes on carrying goods from one part of the country to another. Above all, there is that irregular and partial administration of justice which often shields the rich and powerful debtor from the pursuit of the creditor he has wronged. It makes the industrious part of the nation afraid to produce goods for the use of those haughty and powerful men, to whom they dare not refuse credit and from whom they can never be sure of being repaid.

In England, on the contrary, the natural good effects of the colony trade, aided by other causes, have largely overcome the bad effects of the monopoly. These causes appear to be the general freedom of trade, which, despite some restraints, is at least equal and perhaps superior to that of any other country; the freedom to export, duty-free, nearly every kind of domestic produce to nearly any foreign country; and, perhaps more important still, the unlimited freedom to carry goods from one part of our own country to any other without having to report to any public office and without being subject to questioning or inspection of any kind. Above all, there is that equal and impartial administration of justice which makes the rights of the humblest British subject respected by the greatest, and which, by securing to every man the fruits of his own labour, gives the greatest and most effective encouragement to every kind of industry.

If the manufactures of Great Britain have been advanced by the colony trade, however, as they certainly have, it has not been by means of the monopoly of that trade but in spite of it. The effect of the monopoly has been not to increase the quantity of a part of Britain's manufactures but to alter its quality and form, adapting to a market whose returns are slow and distant goods that would otherwise have been adapted to one whose returns are frequent and near. Its effect, consequently, has been to turn a part of Britain's capital from an employment in which it would have maintained a greater quantity of manufacturing industry to one in which it maintains a much smaller quantity, and thus to diminish rather than increase the total amount of manufacturing industry maintained in Great Britain.

The monopoly of the colony trade, then, like all the other petty and malicious devices of the mercantile system, depresses the industry of every other country, and chiefly that of the colonies, without in the least increasing the industry of the country in whose favour it was established, and in fact diminishing it.

Whatever the size of that country's capital at any given moment, the monopoly prevents it from maintaining as great a quantity of productive labour as it otherwise would, and from yielding as great a revenue to the country's industrious inhabitants as it otherwise would. But since capital can be increased only by savings out of revenue, the monopoly, by preventing capital from yielding as great a revenue as it otherwise would, necessarily prevents it from growing as fast as it otherwise would. It therefore prevents it from maintaining a still greater quantity of productive labour and from yielding a still greater revenue to the country's industrious inhabitants. The monopoly must therefore have made one great original source of revenue, the wages of labour, less abundant at all times than it would otherwise have been.

By raising the rate of mercantile profit, the monopoly discourages the improvement of land. The profit of improvement depends on the difference between what the land actually produces and what it can be made to produce through the application of a certain amount of capital. If that difference yields a greater profit than an equal capital could earn in any mercantile employment, the improvement of land will draw capital away from all mercantile employments. If it yields less, mercantile employments will draw capital away from the improvement of land. Whatever raises the rate of mercantile profit, therefore, either reduces the advantage or increases the disadvantage of the profit of improvement. In the first case it keeps capital from going to improvement; in the second it draws capital away from it. And by discouraging improvement, the monopoly necessarily slows the natural growth of another great original source of revenue, the rent of land. By raising the rate of profit, the monopoly also necessarily keeps the market rate of interest higher than it would otherwise be. But the price of land relative to the rent it yields, which is expressed as the number of years' rent a buyer commonly pays to purchase it, necessarily falls as the rate of interest rises and rises as the rate of interest falls. The monopoly therefore injures the landlord in two different ways: by slowing the natural growth, first, of his rent, and second, of the price he could obtain for his land in proportion to the rent it yields.

The monopoly does, it is true, raise the rate of mercantile profit and so somewhat increases the gains of our merchants. But because it obstructs the natural growth of capital, it tends to reduce rather than increase the total revenue that the country's inhabitants draw from the profits of capital, since a small profit on a large capital generally yields a greater revenue than a large profit on a small one. The monopoly raises the rate of profit, but it prevents the total sum of profit from rising as high as it otherwise would.

The monopoly makes all the original sources of revenue, the wages of labour, the rent of land, and the profits of capital, much less abundant than they would otherwise be. To promote the petty interest of one small class of men in one country, it injures the interest of every other class of men in that country and of all men in every other country.

It is solely by raising the ordinary rate of profit that the monopoly has proved, or could prove, advantageous to any particular class of men. But besides all the harmful effects on the country at large already described as necessarily resulting from a higher rate of profit, there is one more, perhaps more fatal than all the others combined, which, if experience is any guide, is inseparable from it. A high rate of profit seems everywhere to destroy the thrift that would otherwise be natural to the merchant's character. When profits are high, that sober virtue seems unnecessary, and costly luxury seems better suited to the affluence of his position. But the owners of the great mercantile capitals are necessarily the leaders and directors of all the industry of every nation, and their example shapes the habits of its whole working population far more than the example of any other class. If an employer is attentive and thrifty, his workman is very likely to be the same; but if the master is dissolute and disorderly, the servant, who shapes his work to the pattern his master prescribes, will shape his life to the example his master sets. Accumulation is thus prevented in the hands of exactly those people who are naturally most inclined to accumulate, and the funds set aside for maintaining productive labor receive no addition from the incomes of those who ought, in the natural course of things, to add to them most. Instead of growing, the nation's capital gradually dwindles away, and the amount of productive labor it supports shrinks from one day to the next. Have the exorbitant profits of the merchants of Cadiz and Lisbon increased the capital of Spain and Portugal? Have they relieved the poverty, or encouraged the industry, of those two beggared countries? So lavish has been the style of mercantile spending in those two trading cities that their exorbitant profits, far from enlarging the general capital of the country, seem barely to have sufficed to maintain the capitals on which they were earned. Foreign capitals are every day intruding themselves, so to speak, further and further into the trade of Cadiz and Lisbon. It is to drive those foreign capitals out of a trade that their own capital grows daily less able to carry on that the Spanish and Portuguese keep tightening, day after day, the galling restraints of their absurd monopoly. Compare the commercial habits of Cadiz and Lisbon with those of Amsterdam, and you will see how differently the conduct and character of merchants are shaped by high profits and by low ones. The merchants of London, it is true, have not yet generally become such magnificent lords as those of Cadiz and Lisbon; but neither are they, as a rule, such attentive and thrifty burghers as those of Amsterdam. Many of them are thought to be a good deal richer than most merchants of Cadiz and Lisbon, though not quite so rich as many in Amsterdam; yet their rate of profit is commonly much lower than that of the first group and a good deal higher than that of the second. "Light come, light go," says the proverb, and the ordinary level of spending everywhere seems to be governed less by a person's real capacity to spend than by the supposed ease of getting money to spend.

In this way the single advantage that the monopoly secures for a single class of men harms the general interest of the country in many different ways.

To found a great empire for the sole purpose of raising up a people of customers may at first sight seem a project fit only for a nation of shopkeepers. It is, however, a project entirely unfit for a nation of shopkeepers, and extremely fit for a nation whose government is influenced by shopkeepers. Such statesmen, and only such statesmen, are capable of imagining that they will gain some advantage by spending the blood and treasure of their fellow citizens to found and maintain an empire of this kind. Say to a shopkeeper, "Buy me a good estate, and I will always buy my clothes at your shop, even if I pay somewhat more than I would elsewhere," and you will not find him eager to accept your offer. But if someone else were to buy you such an estate, the shopkeeper would be very grateful to your benefactor if he required you to buy all your clothes at his shop. England purchased for certain of her subjects, who felt uneasy at home, a great estate in a distant country. The price, admittedly, was very small. Land nowadays ordinarily sells for "thirty years' purchase," that is, for a sum equal to thirty years of its rent; this estate cost little more than the expense of fitting out the various expeditions that made the first discovery, surveyed the coast, and took a fictitious possession of the country. The land was good and of great extent, and the cultivators, having plenty of good ground to work and being for some time free to sell their produce wherever they pleased, became within little more than thirty or forty years, between 1620 and 1660, so numerous and prosperous a people that the shopkeepers and other traders of England wished to secure the monopoly of their custom for themselves. Without claiming to have paid any part either of the original purchase money or of the later costs of improvement, they petitioned Parliament that the cultivators of America should in future be confined to their shop: first, for buying all the goods they needed from Europe, and second, for selling whatever parts of their own produce those traders found it convenient to buy. For the traders did not find it convenient to buy all of it. Certain colonial products, if imported into England, might have competed with trades the merchants themselves carried on at home. Those particular products, therefore, they were willing to let the colonists sell wherever they could, and the farther away the better; for that reason they proposed that the colonists' market for such goods be confined to the countries south of Cape Finisterre, on the northwestern tip of Spain. A clause in the famous Navigation Act turned this thoroughly shopkeeperly proposal into law.

The maintenance of this monopoly has so far been the principal, or more properly perhaps the sole, end and purpose of the dominion that Great Britain claims over her colonies. The great advantage of provinces that have never yet supplied either revenue or military force for the support of the civil government or the defense of the mother country is supposed to lie in this exclusive trade. The monopoly is the principal badge of their dependency, and it is the only fruit that has yet been gathered from that dependency. Whatever Great Britain has so far spent on maintaining this dependency has really been spent to support this monopoly. Before the present disturbances began, the cost of the ordinary peacetime establishment of the colonies amounted to the pay of twenty regiments of infantry; the cost of the artillery, stores, and extraordinary provisions with which they had to be supplied; and the cost of a very considerable naval force, kept up continually to guard the immense coast of North America, and that of our West Indian islands, against the smuggling vessels of other nations. The whole expense of this peacetime establishment was charged to the revenue of Great Britain, and yet it was the smallest part of what dominion over the colonies has cost the mother country. To know the full amount, we must add to the annual cost of this peacetime establishment the interest on the sums that Great Britain has spent on their defense at various times, because she regarded her colonies as provinces subject to her rule. We must add, in particular, the whole expense of the recent war and a great part of the expense of the war before it. The recent war was entirely a colonial quarrel, and its whole cost, wherever in the world it was spent, whether in Germany or the East Indies, ought in justice to be charged to the account of the colonies. It came to more than ninety million pounds sterling, counting not only the new debt that was contracted but also the additional land tax of two shillings in the pound, an extra tenth levied on the assessed annual value, or rent, of land, and the sums borrowed every year from the sinking fund, the money set aside for paying down the national debt. The Spanish war that began in 1739 was chiefly a colonial quarrel. Its main object was to prevent the searching of colonial ships that carried on a contraband trade with the Spanish Main, the Spanish-held mainland coast of the Caribbean. This whole expense is, in reality, a bounty paid to support a monopoly. Its professed purpose was to encourage the manufactures and increase the commerce of Great Britain. Its real effect has been to raise the rate of mercantile profit, and to induce our merchants to put a larger share of their capital than they otherwise would have into a branch of trade whose returns come more slowly and from farther away than those of most other trades. If a bounty could have prevented those two outcomes, it might well have been worth paying one.

Under the present system of management, then, Great Britain derives nothing but loss from the dominion she claims over her colonies.

To propose that Great Britain should voluntarily give up all authority over her colonies, leaving them to elect their own magistrates, enact their own laws, and make peace and war as they saw fit, would be to propose a measure that no nation in the world has ever adopted or ever will. No nation ever voluntarily gave up its dominion over any province, however troublesome it was to govern and however small its revenue relative to the expense it caused. Such sacrifices, though they might often serve a nation's interest, always wound its pride. And, what perhaps matters even more, they always run against the private interest of its governing class, who would thereby lose the disposal of many positions of trust and profit, and many opportunities of acquiring wealth and distinction, which possession of even the most turbulent province, and the most unprofitable to the great body of the people, seldom fails to provide. The most visionary enthusiasts would hardly be capable of proposing such a measure, at least with any serious hope of its being adopted. Yet if it were adopted, Great Britain would not only be freed at once from the whole annual expense of the colonies' peacetime establishment, but could also conclude with them a commercial treaty that would effectively secure her a free trade, more advantageous to the great body of the people, though less so to the merchants, than the monopoly she now enjoys. By parting as good friends, the natural affection of the colonies for the mother country, which our recent quarrels have perhaps nearly extinguished, would quickly revive. It might dispose them not only to honor, for whole centuries, the commercial treaty concluded with us at parting, but to favor us in war as well as in trade, and to become, instead of turbulent and factious subjects, our most faithful, affectionate, and generous allies. The same kind of parental affection on the one side and filial respect on the other might then revive between Great Britain and her colonies as used to exist between the colonies of ancient Greece and the mother cities from which they descended.

To make any province advantageous to the empire it belongs to, it ought to provide the public, in peacetime, with a revenue sufficient not only to cover the whole cost of its own peacetime establishment but also to contribute its proportionate share to supporting the general government of the empire. Every province necessarily adds, to a greater or lesser degree, to the expense of that general government. If a particular province does not contribute its share toward that expense, then an unequal burden must fall on some other part of the empire. By the same reasoning, the extraordinary revenue each province provides in wartime ought to bear the same proportion to the extraordinary revenue of the whole empire as its ordinary revenue does in peacetime. It will readily be granted that neither the ordinary nor the extraordinary revenue Great Britain draws from her colonies bears this proportion to the whole revenue of the British Empire. It has indeed been supposed that the monopoly makes up for the shortfall in the colonies' public revenue by increasing the private income of the people of Great Britain and thereby enabling them to pay higher taxes. But I have tried to show that this monopoly, though a very grievous tax on the colonies, and though it may increase the income of one particular class in Great Britain, reduces rather than increases the income of the great body of the people, and so reduces rather than increases their ability to pay taxes. Moreover, the men whose income the monopoly does increase form a particular class that is both absolutely impossible to tax beyond the proportion of other classes and extremely unwise even to attempt to tax beyond it, as I shall try to show in the following book. No special resource, therefore, can be drawn from this particular class.

The colonies may be taxed either by their own assemblies or by the Parliament of Great Britain.

It seems hardly probable that the colonial assemblies could ever be managed so as to levy on their constituents a public revenue large enough not only to maintain their own civil and military establishments at all times, but also to pay their proper share of the expense of the general government of the British Empire. It took a long time before even the Parliament of England, though placed directly under the eye of the sovereign, could be brought under such a system of management, or made generous enough in its grants to support the civil and military establishments of its own country. Such a system could be established, even with regard to the Parliament of England, only by distributing among individual members of Parliament a great part of the offices arising from that civil and military establishment, or of the power to dispose of those offices. But the colonial assemblies' distance from the eye of the sovereign, their number, their scattered locations, and their various constitutions would make it very difficult to manage them in the same way, even if the sovereign had the same means of doing so; and those means are lacking. It would be absolutely impossible to distribute among all the leading members of all the colonial assemblies enough of the offices of the general government of the British Empire, or enough power over their disposal, to persuade them to sacrifice their popularity at home and tax their constituents to support a general government whose rewards would be divided almost entirely among people who were strangers to them. Besides this, the administration's unavoidable ignorance of the relative importance of the various members of those various assemblies, the offense that would frequently be given, and the blunders that would constantly be made in trying to manage them in this way, seem to make such a system wholly impracticable with regard to them.

Furthermore, the colonial assemblies cannot be supposed to be proper judges of what is needed for the defense and support of the whole empire. That responsibility is not entrusted to them. It is not their business, and they have no regular means of being informed about it. The assembly of a province, like the vestry of a parish, the local body that managed a parish's own affairs, may judge very soundly about the business of its own district, but it has no proper means of judging the affairs of the whole empire. It cannot even judge properly what proportion its own province bears to the whole empire, or how its wealth and importance compare with those of the other provinces, because those other provinces are not under its inspection and supervision. What is necessary for the defense and support of the whole empire, and in what proportion each part ought to contribute, can be judged only by the assembly that inspects and supervises the affairs of the whole empire.

It has accordingly been proposed that the colonies should be taxed by requisition: the Parliament of Great Britain would determine the sum each colony ought to pay, and the provincial assembly would assess and levy it in whatever way best suited the circumstances of the province. In this way, what concerned the whole empire would be decided by the assembly that inspects and supervises the affairs of the whole empire, while the provincial affairs of each colony could still be regulated by its own assembly. Although under this arrangement the colonies would have no representatives in the British Parliament, there is no likelihood, if we may judge by experience, that the parliamentary requisition would be unreasonable. The Parliament of England has never shown the slightest inclination to overburden those parts of the empire that are not represented in it. The islands of Guernsey and Jersey, which have no means of resisting the authority of Parliament, are more lightly taxed than any part of Great Britain. In attempting to exercise its supposed right, whether well or ill founded, of taxing the colonies, Parliament has never yet demanded of them anything even approaching a fair proportion of what their fellow subjects at home pay. Besides, if the colonies' contribution were made to rise or fall in proportion to the rise or fall of the land tax, Parliament could not tax them without at the same time taxing its own constituents, and in that case the colonies might be considered virtually represented in Parliament.

There is no lack of examples of empires in which the various provinces are not taxed, if I may use the expression, in one mass, but in which the sovereign fixes the sum each province ought to pay, and in some provinces assesses and levies it as he sees fit, while in others he leaves it to be assessed and levied as the provincial estates, the representative assemblies of each province, decide. In some provinces of France, the king not only imposes whatever taxes he sees fit but also assesses and collects them in whatever way he sees fit. From others he demands a certain sum but leaves it to the estates of each province to assess and collect that sum as they think best. Under the scheme of taxing by requisition, the Parliament of Great Britain would stand in nearly the same relation to the colonial assemblies as the king of France does to the estates of those provinces that still enjoy the privilege of having estates of their own, which are thought to be the best governed provinces of France.

But although under this scheme the colonies would have no just reason to fear that their share of the public burden would ever exceed its proper proportion to that of their fellow citizens at home, Great Britain would have just reason to fear that it would never reach that proper proportion. For some time now, the Parliament of Great Britain has not had the same established authority in the colonies that the French king has in those provinces of France that still keep their own estates. Unless the colonial assemblies were very favorably disposed—and unless they are managed more skillfully than they ever have been, they are not likely to be—they could still find many pretexts for evading or rejecting even the most reasonable requisitions of Parliament. Suppose a war with France breaks out, and ten million pounds must be raised at once to defend the seat of the empire. This sum must be borrowed on the credit of some parliamentary fund pledged to pay the interest. Parliament proposes to raise part of this fund by a tax levied in Great Britain, and part by a requisition on all the various colonial assemblies of America and the West Indies. Would people readily lend their money on the credit of a fund that depended partly on the goodwill of all those assemblies, far from the seat of the war, and perhaps sometimes believing themselves little concerned in its outcome? On such a fund, probably no more money would be lent than the tax levied in Great Britain could be expected to cover. The whole burden of the debt incurred for the war would thus fall, as it always has so far, on Great Britain: on one part of the empire, and not on the whole. Great Britain is perhaps the only state since the world began that, as it extended its empire, has only increased its expenses without once adding to its resources. Other states have generally shifted the greater part of the cost of defending the empire onto their subject and subordinate provinces. Great Britain has so far allowed her subject and subordinate provinces to shift almost the whole of that cost onto her. To put Great Britain on a footing of equality with her own colonies, which the law has so far presumed to be subject and subordinate, it seems necessary, under the scheme of taxing them by parliamentary requisition, that Parliament have some means of making its requisitions immediately effective in case the colonial assemblies try to evade or reject them. What those means might be is not easy to imagine, and no one has yet explained them.

At the same time, should the Parliament of Great Britain ever be fully established in the right to tax the colonies independently of the consent of their own assemblies, the importance of those assemblies would come to an end from that moment, and with it the importance of all the leading men of British America. Men want a share in the management of public affairs chiefly for the importance it gives them. The stability and endurance of every system of free government depend on the power that most of the leading men, the natural aristocracy of every country, have to preserve or defend their respective importance. The whole play of domestic faction and ambition consists in the attacks these leading men continually make on one another's importance and in the defense of their own. The leading men of America, like those of every other country, want to preserve their own importance. They feel, or imagine, that if their assemblies, which they like to call parliaments and to regard as equal in authority to the Parliament of Great Britain, were degraded into the humble ministers and executive officers of that Parliament, most of their own importance would be gone. They have therefore rejected the proposal of being taxed by parliamentary requisition, and, like other ambitious and high-spirited men, have chosen instead to draw the sword in defense of their own importance.

As the Roman republic declined, the allies of Rome, who had borne the main burden of defending the state and extending its empire, demanded to be admitted to all the privileges of Roman citizens. When they were refused, the Social War, the war of the allies, broke out. During that war Rome granted those privileges to most of them, one by one, and in proportion as they detached themselves from the general confederacy. The Parliament of Great Britain insists on taxing the colonies, and the colonies refuse to be taxed by a parliament in which they are not represented. Suppose Great Britain were to offer each colony that broke away from the general confederacy a number of representatives in proportion to what it contributed to the public revenue of the empire. In return, the colony would be subject to the same taxes as the home country, and it would be admitted to the same freedom of trade with its fellow subjects in Britain. Its number of representatives would grow as its share of the contribution grew. Such an arrangement would offer the leading men of each colony a new way of gaining importance, and a new and more dazzling object of ambition. Instead of haggling over the small prizes to be won in what might be called the paltry raffle of colonial faction, they could hope, with the confidence that people naturally have in their own ability and luck, to draw some of the great prizes that occasionally come off the wheel of the great state lottery of British politics.

Unless this method or some other is found for preserving the importance and satisfying the ambition of America's leading men, and no method seems more obvious than this one, it is unlikely that they will ever submit to us voluntarily. We ought to remember that every drop of blood shed in forcing them to submit is the blood either of those who are our fellow citizens or of those whom we wish to have as our fellow citizens. Anyone who imagines that, in the present state of affairs, our colonies can easily be conquered by force alone is deceiving himself. The men who now direct the resolutions of what they call their Continental Congress feel, at this moment, a sense of their own importance that perhaps the greatest subjects in Europe hardly feel. Once shopkeepers, tradesmen, and attorneys, they have become statesmen and legislators. They are busy devising a new form of government for an extensive empire, one which they believe will become, and which does indeed seem very likely to become, one of the greatest and most formidable the world has ever seen. Perhaps five hundred different people act in various capacities directly under the Continental Congress, and perhaps five hundred thousand act under those five hundred, and all of them feel, in the same way, a corresponding rise in their own importance. Almost every member of the governing party in America now occupies, in his own imagination, a position higher not only than any he has held before but than any he ever expected to hold. Unless some new object of ambition is offered either to him or to his leaders, he will, if he has the ordinary spirit of a man, die in defense of that position.

President Hénault, the French historian, once remarked that we now read with pleasure accounts of many minor episodes from the time of the Catholic League, events which, when they happened, were probably not regarded as particularly important news. But in those days, he observes, every man imagined himself to be of some consequence, and most of the countless memoirs that have come down to us from that period were written by people who enjoyed recording and magnifying events in which they flattered themselves they had played a significant part. It is well known how stubbornly the city of Paris defended itself on that occasion, and what a terrible famine it endured rather than submit to Henry IV, the best and afterward the most beloved of all the French kings. Most of the citizens, or those who governed most of them, were fighting to defend their own importance, which they foresaw would come to an end as soon as the old government was restored. Unless our colonies can be persuaded to consent to a union, they are very likely to defend themselves against the best of all mother countries as stubbornly as the city of Paris defended itself against one of the best of kings.

The idea of representation was unknown in the ancient world. When the people of one state were granted citizenship in another, the only way they could exercise that right was to come in a body and vote and deliberate alongside the people of the other state. Admitting the greater part of Italy's inhabitants to the privileges of Roman citizenship completely ruined the Roman republic. It became impossible to tell who was a Roman citizen and who was not. No tribe, the voting division into which Roman citizens were organized, could recognize its own members. A mob of any description could be brought into the popular assemblies, drive out the genuine citizens, and decide the affairs of the republic as though they themselves were citizens. But if America were to send fifty or sixty new representatives to Parliament, the doorkeeper of the House of Commons would have no great difficulty telling who was a member and who was not. So although the Roman constitution was inevitably ruined by Rome's union with its Italian allies, there is not the slightest likelihood that the British constitution would be harmed by Great Britain's union with its colonies. On the contrary, such a union would complete the British constitution, which seems imperfect without it. An assembly that deliberates and decides on the affairs of every part of the empire ought, if it is to be properly informed, to include representatives from every part of it. I do not claim that this union could be easily accomplished, or that difficulties, and serious ones, would not arise in carrying it out. Yet I have heard of none that seem insurmountable. The main difficulties perhaps arise not from the nature of things but from the prejudices and opinions of the people on both sides of the Atlantic.

We on this side of the ocean fear that a multitude of American representatives might upset the balance of the constitution, increasing too much either the influence of the Crown on one side or the power of the democracy on the other. But if the number of American representatives were proportioned to the revenue raised by American taxation, the number of people to be managed would increase in exact proportion to the means of managing them, and the means of managing them would increase in exact proportion to the number of people to be managed. After the union, the monarchical and democratic elements of the constitution would stand in exactly the same relative strength to one another as they had before.

The people on the other side of the ocean fear that their distance from the seat of government might expose them to many kinds of oppression. But their representatives in Parliament, who ought from the very beginning to be numerous, could easily protect them from all oppression. Distance would not greatly weaken the representative's dependence on his constituents. He would still feel that he owed his seat in Parliament, and all the standing that came with it, to their goodwill. It would therefore be in his interest to cultivate that goodwill by protesting, with all the authority of a member of the legislature, against every abuse committed by any civil or military officer in those remote parts of the empire. Moreover, the people of America might tell themselves, and with some show of reason, that their distance from the seat of government would not last very long. That country has so far advanced so rapidly in wealth, population, and development that in little more than a century, perhaps, the revenue from American taxation might exceed that from British taxation. The seat of the empire would then naturally move to whichever part of the empire contributed most to the general defense and support of the whole.

The discovery of America and the discovery of a passage to the East Indies by way of the Cape of Good Hope are the two greatest and most important events recorded in the history of mankind. Their consequences have already been great, but in the short span of two to three centuries since these discoveries were made, the full extent of those consequences cannot possibly have been seen. No human wisdom can foresee what benefits or what misfortunes may yet come to mankind from these great events. By joining together, to some degree, the most distant parts of the world, by enabling them to relieve one another's wants, increase one another's comforts, and encourage one another's industry, their general tendency would seem to be beneficial. For the native peoples of both the East and West Indies, however, whatever commercial benefits these events may have produced have been swallowed up and lost in the terrible misfortunes they brought about. Yet these misfortunes seem to have arisen from accident rather than from anything inherent in the events themselves. At the particular moment when these discoveries were made, the Europeans happened to enjoy so great a superiority of force that they could commit every kind of injustice in those remote countries without fear of consequence. In the future, perhaps, the natives of those countries may grow stronger, or the peoples of Europe may grow weaker, and the inhabitants of every quarter of the world may arrive at that equality of courage and force which, by inspiring mutual fear, is the only thing that can intimidate independent nations into some degree of respect for one another's rights. And nothing seems more likely to establish this equality of force than the mutual exchange of knowledge and of every kind of improvement that an extensive commerce among all countries naturally, or rather necessarily, brings with it.

Meanwhile, one of the chief effects of these discoveries has been to raise the mercantile system to a degree of splendor and glory it could never otherwise have reached. The aim of that system is to enrich a great nation through trade and manufacturing rather than through the improvement and cultivation of land, through the industry of the towns rather than that of the countryside. As a result of these discoveries, the commercial towns of Europe, which had once manufactured and carried goods for only a very small part of the world, namely the parts of Europe bordering the Atlantic Ocean and the countries surrounding the Baltic and Mediterranean seas, have now become manufacturers for the numerous and prosperous farmers of America, and the carriers, and in some respects the manufacturers as well, for almost every nation of Asia, Africa, and America. Two new worlds have been opened to their industry, each of them far greater and more extensive than the old one, and the market of one of them is growing larger every day.

The countries that possess colonies in America and trade directly with the East Indies do indeed enjoy all the show and splendor of this great commerce. Yet other countries, despite all the spiteful restrictions designed to shut them out, often enjoy a larger share of its real benefit. The colonies of Spain and Portugal, for example, do more to encourage the industry of other countries than that of Spain and Portugal themselves. In linen alone, the consumption of those colonies is said to exceed three million pounds sterling a year, though I cannot vouch for the figure. This vast consumption is supplied almost entirely by France, Flanders, Holland, and Germany, with Spain and Portugal furnishing only a small part of it. The capital that supplies the colonies with this great quantity of linen is distributed every year among the inhabitants of those other countries and provides them with an income. Only the profits on it are spent in Spain and Portugal, where they help sustain the lavish extravagance of the merchants of Cádiz and Lisbon.

Even the regulations by which each nation tries to secure for itself the exclusive trade of its own colonies often do more harm to the countries they are meant to favor than to the countries they are aimed against. The unjust suppression of other countries' industry falls back, so to speak, on the heads of the oppressors, and crushes their own industry more than it does that of the others. Under these regulations, for example, a Hamburg merchant must send the linen he intends for the American market by way of London, and he must bring back from London the tobacco he intends for the German market, because he can neither send the linen directly to America nor bring the tobacco directly from there. This restriction probably forces him to sell the linen somewhat more cheaply, and to buy the tobacco somewhat more dearly, than he otherwise might, and his profits are probably reduced somewhat as a result. In the trade between Hamburg and London, however, he certainly gets the returns on his capital far more quickly than he could possibly have done in a direct trade with America, even if we were to assume, which is by no means the case, that American payments were as punctual as those of London. In the trade to which these regulations confine the Hamburg merchant, therefore, his capital can keep a much greater quantity of German labor in constant employment than it could have done in the trade from which he is excluded. So although the one employment may perhaps be less profitable to him than the other, it cannot be less advantageous to his country. The case is entirely different for the employment into which the monopoly naturally draws, so to speak, the capital of the London merchant. That employment may perhaps be more profitable to him than most others, but because its returns are so slow, it cannot be more advantageous to his country.

After all the unjust attempts of every country in Europe to monopolize the full advantage of its colonies' trade, then, no country has yet managed to monopolize anything except the expense of maintaining in peacetime, and defending in wartime, the oppressive authority it claims over them. The inconveniences arising from the possession of its colonies, each country has kept entirely to itself. The advantages arising from their trade, it has been forced to share with many other countries.

At first glance, no doubt, a monopoly of the great commerce of America naturally appears to be an acquisition of the highest value. To the undiscerning eye of giddy ambition, amid the confused scramble of politics and war, it naturally presents itself as a dazzling prize worth fighting for. Yet the very quality that makes the prize so dazzling, the immense size of the commerce, is precisely what makes the monopoly of it harmful. It causes an employment that is by its nature less advantageous to the country than most others to absorb a far greater share of the country's capital than would otherwise have gone to it.

As was shown in the second book, the mercantile capital of every country naturally seeks out, so to speak, the employment most advantageous to that country. If it is employed in the carrying trade, the business of transporting goods between foreign countries, the country to which it belongs becomes the warehouse for the goods of all the countries whose trade that capital carries on. But the owner of that capital naturally wishes to sell as large a share of those goods as he can at home. By doing so he spares himself the trouble, risk, and expense of exporting them, and for that reason he will gladly sell them at home not only for a much lower price but for a somewhat smaller profit than he might expect to make by sending them abroad. He therefore naturally tries, as far as he can, to turn his carrying trade into a foreign trade of consumption, the business of importing foreign goods for use at home.
