If his capital is employed in a foreign trade of consumption, he will for the same reason gladly sell at home as large a share as he can of the domestic goods he gathers for export to some foreign market, and so he will try, as far as he can, to turn his foreign trade of consumption into a home trade. In this way the mercantile capital of every country naturally seeks the near employment and avoids the distant one. It naturally seeks the employment in which returns are frequent and avoids the one in which they are remote and slow. It naturally seeks the employment in which it can support the greatest quantity of productive labor in the country to which it belongs, or in which its owner lives, and avoids the one in which it can support the smallest. It naturally seeks the employment that is, in ordinary circumstances, most advantageous to that country, and avoids the one that is, in ordinary circumstances, least advantageous.

But suppose that in one of these distant employments, which are ordinarily less advantageous to the country, profits happen to rise somewhat higher than is needed to offset the natural preference for nearer employments. This higher profit will then draw capital away from the nearer employments until the profits in all of them return to their proper level. Such a higher profit, however, is evidence that, in the society's actual circumstances, these distant employments are somewhat undersupplied with capital relative to other employments, and that the society's capital is not distributed in the most suitable way among all the different employments carried on within it. It is evidence that something is being bought more cheaply or sold more dearly than it ought to be, and that some particular class of citizens is to some degree oppressed, either by paying more or by receiving less than is consistent with the equality that ought to prevail, and naturally does prevail, among all the different classes. Although the same capital will never support as much productive labor in a distant employment as in a near one, a distant employment may be just as necessary to the welfare of society as a near one, since the goods it deals in may be needed to carry on many of the nearer employments. But if the profits of those who deal in such goods rise above their proper level, those goods will be sold more dearly than they should be, somewhat above their natural price, and everyone engaged in the nearer employments will be to some degree oppressed by that high price. In this case, then, their own interest requires that some capital be withdrawn from the nearer employments and directed toward the distant one, so as to bring its profits down to their proper level and the price of its goods down to their natural price. In this exceptional case, the public interest requires that some capital be withdrawn from employments that are ordinarily more advantageous and directed toward one that is ordinarily less advantageous to the public. And in this exceptional case, people's natural interests and inclinations coincide with the public interest just as exactly as they do in all ordinary cases, leading them to withdraw capital from the near employments and turn it toward the distant ones.

In this way, the private interests and passions of individuals naturally lead them to direct their capital toward the employments that are, in ordinary circumstances, most advantageous to society. And if their natural preference should lead them to direct too much capital toward those employments, the resulting fall of profit there, and its rise everywhere else, immediately prompts them to correct this faulty distribution. Without any intervention of law, therefore, the private interests and passions of men naturally lead them to divide and distribute the capital of every society among all the different employments carried on in it, as nearly as possible in the proportion most agreeable to the interest of the whole society.

All the various regulations of the mercantile system necessarily disturb, to a greater or lesser degree, this natural and most advantageous distribution of capital. But those concerning the trade to America and the East Indies disturb it perhaps more than any others, because the trade to those two great continents absorbs more capital than any other two branches of trade. The regulations by which this disturbance is brought about in those two branches, however, are not entirely the same. Monopoly is the great engine of both, but it is a different kind of monopoly in each. Indeed, monopoly of one kind or another seems to be the sole engine of the mercantile system.

In the trade to America, every nation tries to secure as fully as possible the entire market of its own colonies by openly excluding all other nations from any direct trade with them. For most of the sixteenth century, the Portuguese tried to manage the trade to the East Indies in the same way, claiming the sole right to sail the Indian seas on the grounds that they had been the first to discover the route. The Dutch still exclude every other European nation from any direct trade with their Spice Islands. Monopolies of this kind are plainly established against all other European nations, who are thereby not only shut out of a trade into which it might suit them to put some of their capital, but forced to pay somewhat more for the goods that trade deals in than they would if they could import those goods directly from the countries that produced them.

Since the decline of Portuguese power, however, no European nation has claimed the exclusive right to sail the Indian seas, whose principal ports are now open to the ships of every European nation. Yet except in Portugal, and in France within the last few years, the trade to the East Indies has in every European country been placed under an exclusive company. Monopolies of this kind are, strictly speaking, established against the very nation that creates them. Most of that nation's people are thereby not only shut out of a trade into which it might suit them to put some of their capital, but forced to pay somewhat more for the goods that trade deals in than they would if it were open and free to all their countrymen. Since the founding of the English East India Company, for example, the rest of the inhabitants of England, in addition to being excluded from the trade, must have paid, in the price of the East India goods they consumed, not only for all the extraordinary profits the company may have made on those goods by virtue of its monopoly, but also for all the extraordinary waste necessarily caused by the fraud and abuse that are inseparable from managing the affairs of so large a company. The absurdity of this second kind of monopoly is therefore far more obvious than that of the first.

Both kinds of monopoly disturb, to a greater or lesser degree, the natural distribution of a society's capital, but they do not always disturb it in the same way.

Monopolies of the first kind always draw into the particular trade where they are established a larger share of the nation's capital than would flow into that trade of its own accord.

Monopolies of the second kind may sometimes draw capital toward the trade in which they are established and sometimes drive it away, depending on circumstances. In poor countries, they naturally draw more capital into that trade than would otherwise go there. In rich countries, they naturally drive away a good deal of capital that would otherwise enter it.

Poor countries such as Sweden and Denmark, for example, would probably never have sent a single ship to the East Indies had the trade not been placed in the hands of an exclusive company. The founding of such a company inevitably encourages people to venture into the trade. Their monopoly protects them from every competitor in the home market, while in foreign markets they have the same chance as the traders of any other nation. The monopoly holds out to them the certainty of a large profit on a considerable quantity of goods, and the chance of a considerable profit on a large quantity. Without such extraordinary encouragement, the poor traders of such poor countries would probably never have thought of risking their small capitals in so distant and uncertain a venture as the East India trade must naturally have seemed to them.

A rich country like Holland, on the contrary, would probably send far more ships to the East Indies under free trade than it actually does. The limited capital of the Dutch East India Company probably keeps out of that trade many great mercantile fortunes that would otherwise enter it. The mercantile capital of Holland is so large that it is, as it were, constantly overflowing: sometimes into the public debts of foreign governments, sometimes into loans to private traders and speculators abroad, sometimes into the most roundabout forms of foreign trade, in which goods for home consumption are bought with other foreign goods rather than with the country's own produce, and sometimes into the carrying trade, the business of shipping goods between one foreign country and another. Since every nearby employment is completely filled, and all the capital that can be placed there at any tolerable profit has already been placed, the capital of Holland necessarily flows toward the most distant employments. If the East India trade were entirely free, it would probably absorb the greater part of this surplus capital. The East Indies offer a market, both for the manufactures of Europe and for the gold, silver, and various other products of America, larger and more extensive than Europe and America combined.

Every disturbance of the natural distribution of capital necessarily harms the society in which it occurs, whether it drives away from a particular trade the capital that would otherwise go to it, or draws into a particular trade capital that would not otherwise come. If Holland's trade to the East Indies would be greater without an exclusive company than it actually is, that country must suffer a considerable loss, because part of its capital is shut out of the employment best suited to it. In the same way, if the trade of Sweden and Denmark to the East Indies would be smaller without an exclusive company, or, as is perhaps more likely, would not exist at all, those two countries must also suffer a considerable loss, because part of their capital is drawn into an employment more or less unsuited to their present circumstances. It would perhaps be better for them, as things now stand, to buy East India goods from other nations, even at a somewhat higher price, than to divert so large a part of their small capital into so distant a trade. In that trade the returns come in very slowly, and the capital can support only a small quantity of productive labor at home, in countries where productive labor is badly needed, where so little has been done, and where so much remains to be done.

Even if a particular country could not carry on any direct trade with the East Indies without an exclusive company, it would not follow that such a company ought to be established there. It would follow only that, in those circumstances, the country ought not to trade directly with the East Indies. The experience of the Portuguese sufficiently demonstrates that such companies are not generally necessary for carrying on the East India trade: they enjoyed almost the whole of it for more than a century without any exclusive company.

It has been argued that no private merchant could easily have enough capital to maintain factors and agents in the various ports of the East Indies, whose job would be to gather goods for the ships he might send out from time to time. Yet unless he could do this, the difficulty of finding a cargo might often cause his ships to miss the season for the return voyage, and the expense of so long a delay would not only consume the entire profit of the venture but would frequently produce a very considerable loss. This argument, however, if it proved anything at all, would prove that no great branch of trade could be carried on without an exclusive company, which contradicts the experience of every nation. In no great branch of trade is the capital of any single private merchant enough to carry on all the subordinate branches that must be maintained in order to sustain the principal one. But when a nation is ripe for some great branch of trade, some merchants naturally turn their capital toward the principal branch and others toward its subordinate branches. In this way all the different branches are carried on, though it very seldom happens that they are all carried on with the capital of one private merchant. If a nation is ripe for the East India trade, then, a certain portion of its capital will naturally divide itself among all the different branches of that trade. Some of its merchants will find it in their interest to live in the East Indies and to use their capital there in gathering goods for the ships sent out by other merchants who live in Europe. The settlements that the various European nations have acquired in the East Indies, if they were taken away from the exclusive companies that now own them and placed under the direct protection of the sovereign, would make such residence both safe and easy, at least for merchants of the nations to which those settlements belong. If, at any particular time, the portion of a country's capital that of its own accord tended and inclined, so to speak, toward the East India trade was not sufficient to carry on all its different branches, this would prove that the country was not, at that time, ripe for the trade. It would do better to buy the East India goods it needed from other European nations for a while, even at a higher price, than to import them directly from the East Indies itself. Whatever it lost through the high price of those goods could seldom equal the loss it would suffer by diverting a large part of its capital from other employments more necessary, more useful, or better suited to its circumstances and situation than a direct trade with the East Indies.

Although Europeans possess many considerable settlements on the coast of Africa and in the East Indies, they have not yet established in either region colonies as numerous and thriving as those on the islands and mainland of America. Africa, like several of the countries grouped under the general name of the East Indies, is inhabited by peoples at a rude and early stage of society. But those peoples were by no means as weak and defenseless as the wretched and helpless natives of America, and in proportion to the natural fertility of the lands they inhabited, they were also far more numerous. The most primitive nations of Africa or the East Indies were herders; even the Khoikhoi of southern Africa, whom Europeans called Hottentots, kept flocks. The natives of every part of America except Mexico and Peru, however, were only hunters, and the same extent of equally fertile land can support a far greater number of herders than of hunters. In Africa and the East Indies, therefore, it was more difficult to displace the natives and to spread European plantations over most of the lands of the original inhabitants. Moreover, as has already been observed, the character of exclusive companies is unfavorable to the growth of new colonies, and this has probably been the main reason for the little progress colonies have made in the East Indies. The Portuguese carried on their trade with both Africa and the East Indies without any exclusive companies, and their settlements at Congo, Angola, and Benguela on the African coast, and at Goa in the East Indies, though greatly held back by superstition and every kind of bad government, still bear some resemblance to the colonies of America and are partly inhabited by Portuguese families who have lived there for several generations. The Dutch settlements at the Cape of Good Hope and at Batavia are at present the most considerable colonies Europeans have established in either Africa or the East Indies, and both are especially fortunate in their location. The Cape of Good Hope was inhabited by a people almost as primitive as the natives of America, and quite as incapable of defending themselves. It is, besides, a kind of halfway house between Europe and the East Indies, where almost every European ship stops for a time on both the outward and the homeward voyage. Supplying those ships with every sort of fresh provision, with fruit, and sometimes with wine, provides by itself a very large market for the colony's surplus produce. What the Cape of Good Hope is between Europe and every part of the East Indies, Batavia is among the principal countries of the East Indies themselves. It lies on the busiest route from Hindustan to China and Japan, at roughly the midpoint of that route. Almost all the ships sailing between Europe and China also call at Batavia. On top of all this, it is the center and chief market of what is called the country trade of the East Indies, the trade carried on among the Asian ports themselves, not only the part of that trade conducted by Europeans but also the part conducted by the native peoples, and vessels crewed by the inhabitants of China and Japan, of Tonkin, Malacca, Cochin-China, and the island of Celebes are often to be seen in its harbor. Such advantageous locations have allowed these two colonies to overcome every obstacle that the oppressive character of an exclusive company may from time to time have placed in the way of their growth. They have even allowed Batavia to overcome the further disadvantage of what is perhaps the most unhealthy climate in the world.

The English and Dutch companies, though they have founded no considerable colonies apart from the two just mentioned, have both made considerable conquests in the East Indies. But in the way they both govern their new subjects, the natural character of an exclusive company has shown itself most plainly. In the Spice Islands, the Dutch are said to burn whatever spices a fertile season produces beyond the amount they expect to sell in Europe at what they consider a sufficient profit. On the islands where they have no settlements, they pay a bounty to anyone who gathers the young blossoms and green leaves of the clove and nutmeg trees that grow wild there, and this savage policy has now, it is said, almost entirely wiped those trees out. Even on the islands where they do have settlements, they have, it is said, greatly reduced the number of such trees. If the produce even of their own islands were much greater than their market required, the natives, they suspect, might find ways to smuggle some of it to other nations, and the best way to secure their own monopoly, they imagine, is to make sure that no more grows than they themselves bring to market. By various forms of oppression, they have reduced the population of several of the Moluccas to roughly the number needed to supply fresh provisions and other necessities to their own insignificant garrisons and to whatever ships occasionally arrive for a cargo of spices. Yet even under the government of the Portuguese, those islands are said to have been reasonably well populated. The English company has not yet had time to establish so thoroughly destructive a system in Bengal, but the plan of its government has had exactly the same tendency. It has not been uncommon, I am reliably assured, for the chief of a factory, that is, the senior clerk of one of the company's trading posts, to order a peasant to plow up a rich field of poppies and sow it with rice or some other grain. The pretext was to prevent a shortage of food; the real reason was to let the chief sell, at a better price, a large quantity of opium he happened to have on hand. On other occasions the order has been reversed, and a rich field of rice or other grain has been plowed up to make room for a poppy plantation when the chief foresaw that an extraordinary profit was likely to be made from opium. The company's servants have, on several occasions, tried to establish for their own benefit a monopoly over some of the most important branches not only of the country's foreign trade but of its internal trade as well. Had they been allowed to go on, they would inevitably, at some point, have tried to restrict the production of the goods they had thus monopolized, limiting it not merely to the quantity they themselves could buy, but to the quantity they could expect to sell at what they considered a sufficient profit. Within a century or two, the policy of the English company would probably have proved, in this way, just as completely destructive as that of the Dutch.

Nothing, however, could be more directly contrary to the real interest of these companies, considered as the sovereigns of the countries they have conquered, than this destructive plan. In almost every country, the sovereign's revenue is drawn from that of the people. The greater the people's revenue, and so the greater the annual produce of their land and labor, the more they can afford to pay the sovereign. It is therefore in his interest to increase that annual produce as much as possible. But if this is the interest of every sovereign, it is especially so of one whose revenue, like that of the sovereign of Bengal, comes chiefly from a rent on land. That rent must necessarily be proportional to the quantity and value of the produce, and both of these must depend on the extent of the market. The quantity produced will always be adjusted, more or less exactly, to the consumption of those who can afford to pay for it, and the price they pay will always be proportional to the intensity of their competition. It is in the interest of such a sovereign, therefore, to open the widest possible market for his country's produce and to allow the most complete freedom of commerce, so as to increase the number and competition of buyers as much as possible. For the same reason, he should abolish not only all monopolies but all restraints on carrying domestic produce from one part of the country to another, on exporting it to foreign countries, or on importing goods of any kind for which it can be exchanged. In this way he is most likely to increase both the quantity and the value of that produce, and consequently his own share of it, which is his revenue.

But a company of merchants, it seems, is incapable of thinking of itself as a sovereign, even after it has become one. Trade, buying in order to sell again, its members still consider their principal business, and by a strange absurdity they regard the role of sovereign as a mere appendix to that of merchant: something to be subordinated to trade, or a means by which they can buy more cheaply in India and so sell at a better profit in Europe. To this end they try to keep every competitor out of the markets of the countries under their rule, and consequently to reduce at least some part of the surplus produce of those countries to what barely meets their own demand, or to what they can expect to sell in Europe at a profit they think reasonable. Their mercantile habits thus lead them, almost inevitably and perhaps without their noticing, to prefer on all ordinary occasions the small and passing profit of the monopolist to the great and lasting revenue of the sovereign, and would gradually lead them to treat the countries under their rule much as the Dutch treat the Moluccas. It is in the interest of the East India Company, considered as a sovereign, that the European goods carried to its Indian dominions be sold there as cheaply as possible, and that the Indian goods brought from there fetch as good a price, or be sold there as dearly, as possible. But its interest as a merchant is the reverse. As sovereigns, the company's interest is exactly the same as that of the country it governs. As merchants, its interest is directly opposed to that of the country.

If the character of such a government is in this way essentially, and perhaps incurably, flawed even in its direction from Europe, the character of its administration in India is more flawed still. That administration necessarily consists of a council of merchants, a profession no doubt highly respectable, but one that in no country in the world carries the kind of authority that naturally awes the people and commands their willing obedience without force. Such a council can command obedience only through the military force that accompanies it, and its government is therefore necessarily military and despotic. Its proper business, however, is that of merchants: to sell, on their employers' account, the European goods sent out to them, and to buy Indian goods in return for the European market. Its business is to sell the one as dearly and to buy the other as cheaply as possible, and therefore to exclude, as far as possible, all rivals from the particular market where they keep their shop. So far as the company's trade is concerned, then, the character of the administration in India is the same as that of the directors in Europe. It tends to make government serve the interest of monopoly, and consequently to stunt the natural growth of at least some parts of the country's surplus produce, holding them to what barely meets the company's demand.

All the members of the administration, moreover, trade to some degree on their own account, and it is useless to forbid them. Nothing could be more foolish than to expect that the clerks of a great trading house ten thousand miles away, and therefore almost entirely out of sight, would, on a simple order from their employers, immediately stop doing any business on their own account; give up forever all hope of making a fortune when they have the means to do so in their own hands; and content themselves with the modest salaries their employers allow them, salaries which, modest as they are, can seldom be raised, since they are usually as large as the real profits of the company's trade can afford. Under such circumstances, forbidding the company's servants to trade on their own account can have scarcely any effect except to enable its senior servants, under the pretext of carrying out their employers' orders, to oppress any junior servants who have had the misfortune to fall out of favor with them. The servants naturally try to establish the same monopoly for their private trade as for the company's public trade. If they are allowed to act as they wish, they will establish this monopoly openly and directly, simply by forbidding everyone else to trade in the goods they choose to deal in, and this is perhaps the best and least oppressive way of establishing it. But if an order from Europe forbids them to do this, they will nonetheless try to establish a monopoly of the same kind secretly and indirectly, in a way far more destructive to the country. They will use the full authority of government, and corrupt the administration of justice, to harass and ruin anyone who interferes with them in any branch of commerce they may choose to carry on through agents who are concealed, or at least not publicly acknowledged. And the private trade of the servants will naturally extend to a much greater variety of goods than the public trade of the company. The company's public trade goes no further than the trade with Europe, and covers only part of the country's foreign trade. The private trade of the servants, however, may extend to every branch of its internal and foreign trade alike. The company's monopoly can tend to stunt only the natural growth of that part of the surplus produce which, under free trade, would be exported to Europe. The servants' monopoly tends to stunt the natural growth of every kind of produce they choose to deal in, whether intended for home consumption or for export, and consequently to degrade the cultivation of the entire country and reduce the number of its inhabitants. Whenever the servants choose to deal in any sort of produce, even the necessities of life, their monopoly tends to reduce its quantity to what they can both afford to buy and expect to sell at a profit that satisfies them.

By the very nature of their position, the servants must also be more inclined than their employers to pursue their own interest with rigorous severity against that of the country they govern. The country belongs to their employers, who cannot help having some regard for the interest of what belongs to them; but it does not belong to the servants. The real interest of the employers, if they were capable of understanding it, is the same as that of the country. This is true of the company considered as a whole, though the interest of each individual holder of India stock is by no means the same as that of the country in whose government his vote gives him some influence. It is chiefly from ignorance, and from the narrowness of mercantile prejudice, that the employers ever oppress it. But the real interest of the servants is by no means the same as that of the country, and even the most complete information would not necessarily put an end to their oppressions. Accordingly, the regulations sent out from Europe, though often weak, have for the most part been well meaning. More intelligence, and perhaps less good intention, has sometimes appeared in the regulations established by the servants in India. It is a very strange government in which every member of the administration wants to leave the country, and so to be finished with the government, as soon as he can. The day after he has left, taking his whole fortune with him, it is a matter of perfect indifference to his interests if the entire country were swallowed by an earthquake.

Nothing I have said here, however, is meant to cast any shameful charge on the general character of the East India Company's servants, still less on that of any particular person. It is the system of government, the situation in which they are placed, that I mean to condemn, not the character of the men who have acted within it. They behaved as their situation naturally led them to behave, and those who have protested most loudly against them would probably have done no better in their place. In war and in negotiation, the councils of Madras and Calcutta have on several occasions acted with a resolve and a decisive wisdom that would have honored the Roman Senate in the finest days of the Republic. Yet the members of those councils had been trained for professions far removed from war and politics. Their situation alone, without education, experience, or even example to guide them, seems to have produced in them, all at once, the great qualities it demanded, inspiring them with abilities and virtues they could hardly have known they possessed. If their situation has sometimes moved them to acts of magnanimity that no one could reasonably have expected of them, we should not be surprised that it has at other times prompted them to deeds of a rather different kind.

Exclusive companies of this sort, therefore, are harmful in every respect. They are always more or less burdensome to the countries in which they are established, and ruinous to those that have the misfortune to fall under their government.

### CHAPTER VIII: CONCLUSION OF THE MERCANTILE SYSTEM

Encouraging exports and discouraging imports are the two great engines by which the mercantile system proposes to enrich every country. With certain commodities, however, it seems to follow the opposite plan, discouraging their export and encouraging their import. Its ultimate object, it claims, is always the same: to enrich the country by securing a favorable balance of trade. It discourages the export of the materials of manufacture and of the tools of trade in order to give our own workmen an advantage and enable them to undersell the workmen of other nations in every foreign market. By restraining the export of a few commodities of no great price, it expects to bring about a much larger and more valuable export of others. It encourages the import of the materials of manufacture so that our own people can work them up more cheaply, and so prevent a larger and more valuable import of finished goods. I do not find, at least in our statute book, any encouragement given to the import of the tools of trade. Once manufacturing has grown to a certain scale, the making of those tools becomes itself the business of a great many very important manufactures, and any special encouragement to import them would interfere too much with the interests of those manufactures. Such imports, therefore, far from being encouraged, have frequently been prohibited. Wool cards, for example, the hand tools set with wire teeth that were used to comb out wool before spinning, were barred from import by a statute of the third year of Edward IV, except when they came from Ireland or arrived as goods salvaged from shipwrecks or captured from enemy vessels. That prohibition was renewed in the thirty-ninth year of Elizabeth and has been continued and made perpetual by later laws.

The import of the materials of manufacture has sometimes been encouraged by exempting them from the duties paid on other goods, and sometimes by bounties.

Sheep's wool from several countries, cotton wool from every country, undressed flax, most dyeing drugs, most undressed hides from Ireland or the British colonies, seal skins from the British Greenland fishery, and pig and bar iron from the British colonies, along with several other materials of manufacture, have all been encouraged by exemption from every duty, provided they are properly entered at the customhouse. The private interest of our merchants and manufacturers may perhaps have extracted these exemptions from the legislature, as it extracted most of our other commercial regulations. The exemptions are nonetheless perfectly just and reasonable, and if they could be extended to all the other materials of manufacture without harm to the necessities of the state, the public would certainly gain.

The greed of our great manufacturers, however, has in some cases pushed these exemptions well beyond anything that can fairly be called the raw materials of their work. An act of the twenty-fourth year of George II, chapter 46, imposed a small duty of only one penny a pound on imported foreign brown linen yarn, in place of the much higher duties it had paid before: sixpence a pound on sail yarn, a shilling a pound on all French and Dutch yarn, and £2 13s. 4d. per hundredweight on all Prussian or Muscovy yarn. Our manufacturers were not satisfied with this reduction for long. In the twenty-ninth year of the same king, chapter 15, the very law that granted a bounty on the export of British and Irish linen priced at no more than eighteen pence a yard also abolished even this small duty on imported brown linen yarn. Yet the various operations needed to prepare linen yarn employ a good deal more labor than the later operation of weaving linen cloth from that yarn. Leaving aside the work of the flax growers and flax dressers, at least three or four spinners are needed to keep a single weaver in constant employment, and more than four-fifths of all the labor that goes into linen cloth is spent on making the yarn. But our spinners are poor people, mostly women, scattered across every part of the country without support or protection. Our great master manufacturers make their profits not by selling the spinners' work but by selling the finished work of the weavers. Just as it is in their interest to sell the finished product as dear as possible, so it is in their interest to buy the materials as cheap as possible. By extracting from the legislature bounties on the export of their own linen, high duties on the import of all foreign linen, and an outright ban on the domestic consumption of certain kinds of French linen, they try to sell their own goods as dear as they can. By encouraging the import of foreign linen yarn, and so setting it in competition with the yarn our own people make, they try to buy the work of the poor spinners as cheap as they can. They are as determined to keep down the wages of their own weavers as the earnings of the poor spinners, and it is in no way for the benefit of the workers that they strive either to raise the price of the finished product or to lower the price of the raw materials. The industry that our mercantile system chiefly encourages is the industry carried on for the benefit of the rich and powerful. The industry carried on for the benefit of the poor and needy is too often either neglected or oppressed.

Both the bounty on the export of linen and the exemption from duty on imported foreign yarn were granted for only fifteen years, but they have been extended twice, and they will now expire at the end of the parliamentary session immediately following June 24, 1786.

Encouragement by bounty to the import of the materials of manufacture has been confined mainly to goods brought in from our American plantations.

The first bounties of this kind were granted around the beginning of the present century, on the import of naval stores from America. The term covered timber suitable for masts, yards, and bowsprits, the great spars of a sailing ship, together with hemp, tar, pitch, and turpentine. The bounty of £1 a ton on masting timber and the bounty of £6 a ton on hemp were, however, also extended to supplies brought into England from Scotland. Both bounties continued at the same rate, without any change, until each was allowed to lapse: the bounty on hemp on January 1, 1741, and the bounty on masting timber at the end of the parliamentary session immediately following June 24, 1781.

The bounties on imported tar, pitch, and turpentine went through several changes while they lasted. At first the bounty on tar was £4 a ton, the bounty on pitch the same, and the bounty on turpentine £3 a ton. The £4 bounty on tar was later restricted to tar prepared in a particular way, while the bounty on other good, clean, and merchantable tar was reduced to £2 4s. a ton. The bounty on pitch was likewise cut to £1, and that on turpentine to £1 10s. a ton.

The second bounty on the import of any material of manufacture, in order of time, was granted by an act of the twenty-first year of George II, chapter 30, on indigo from the British plantations. Under this act, plantation indigo worth three-quarters of the price of the best French indigo was entitled to a bounty of sixpence a pound. Like most bounties, it was granted only for a limited period. It was extended several times but reduced to fourpence a pound, and it was allowed to expire at the end of the parliamentary session that followed March 25, 1781.

The third bounty of this kind was granted by an act of the fourth year of George III, chapter 26, on the import of hemp or undressed flax from the British plantations. It came at roughly the time when we were beginning, by turns, to court our American colonies and to quarrel with them. The bounty was granted for twenty-one years, from June 24, 1764, to June 24, 1785. For the first seven years it stood at £8 a ton, for the second seven at £6, and for the third at £4. It was not extended to Scotland, whose climate is poorly suited to the crop, although hemp is sometimes grown there in small quantities and of inferior quality. A bounty on Scottish flax imported into England would have discouraged too heavily the native produce of the southern part of the United Kingdom.

The fourth bounty of this kind was granted by an act of the fifth year of George III, chapter 45, on the import of wood from America. It ran for nine years, from January 1, 1766, to January 1, 1775. During the first three years it paid £1 for every hundred and twenty good deals, which are sawn planks of fir or pine, and 12s. for every load of fifty cubic feet of other squared timber. For the next three years it paid 15s. on deals and 8s. on other squared timber, and for the final three years 10s. on deals and 5s. on other squared timber.

The fifth bounty of this kind was granted by an act of the ninth year of George III, chapter 38, on the import of raw silk from the British plantations. It ran for twenty-one years, from January 1, 1770, to January 1, 1791. For the first seven years it was set at £25 for every £100 of value, for the second seven at £20, and for the third at £15. Raising silkworms and preparing silk demand so much hand labor, and labor is so very dear in America, that even this large bounty, I have been told, was unlikely to have much effect.

The sixth bounty of this kind was granted by an act of the eleventh year of George III, chapter 50, on the import from the British plantations of staves and heading for pipes, hogsheads, and barrels, which is to say the curved side boards and the end boards from which casks of various sizes are built. It ran for nine years, from January 1, 1772, to January 1, 1781. For a certain quantity of each, it was set at £6 for the first three years, £4 for the second three, and £2 for the third.

The seventh and last bounty of this kind was granted by an act of the nineteenth year of George III, chapter 37, on the import of hemp from Ireland. It was granted on the same terms as the bounty on hemp and undressed flax from America, for twenty-one years, from June 24, 1779, to June 24, 1800. The term is likewise divided into three periods of seven years, and in each period the Irish rate matches the American one. Unlike the American bounty, however, it does not extend to undressed flax, which would have discouraged the growing of that plant in Great Britain too heavily. When this last bounty was granted, the British and Irish legislatures were on scarcely better terms with each other than the British and American legislatures had been earlier. One may hope that this favor to Ireland has been granted under happier circumstances than all those granted to America. The same commodities on which we paid bounties when they came from America were subjected to considerable duties when they came from any other country. The interest of our American colonies was regarded as identical with that of the mother country. Their wealth was considered our wealth. Whatever money was sent out to them, it was said, all came back to us through the balance of trade, and no expense we could lay out on them could ever make us a farthing poorer. They were ours in every respect, and money spent on them was money spent on improving our own property and on the profitable employment of our own people. There is no need at present, I think, to say anything more to expose the folly of a system that bitter experience has now exposed well enough. Had our American colonies truly been part of Great Britain, these bounties might have been regarded as bounties on production. They would then still have been open to every objection that applies to such bounties, but to no others.

The export of the materials of manufacture is sometimes discouraged by outright prohibition and sometimes by high duties.

Our woollen manufacturers have been more successful than any other class of workmen in persuading the legislature that the prosperity of the nation depends on the success and growth of their particular business. They have obtained a monopoly against consumers through an absolute ban on importing woollen cloth from any foreign country, and they have also obtained a second monopoly, this time against sheep farmers and wool growers, through a similar ban on exporting live sheep and wool. Many of the laws passed to protect the public revenue are rightly criticized for their severity, since they impose heavy penalties on acts that had always been considered innocent until statutes declared them crimes. But I will venture to say that the cruellest of our revenue laws are mild and gentle compared with some of those that the clamor of our merchants and manufacturers has extracted from the legislature to prop up their own absurd and oppressive monopolies. Like the code of Draco, the ancient Athenian lawgiver whose laws were said to prescribe death for nearly every offense, and so to have been written in blood rather than ink, these laws may be said to be written entirely in blood.

Under a statute of the eighth year of Elizabeth, chapter 3, anyone who exported sheep, lambs, or rams was, for a first offense, to forfeit all his goods permanently, to serve a year in prison, and then to have his left hand cut off in a market town on market day and nailed up there. For a second offense, he was to be judged a felon and put to death. The aim of this law seems to have been to prevent our breeds of sheep from being propagated in foreign countries. Under a statute of the thirteenth and fourteenth years of Charles II, chapter 18, the export of wool was made a felony, and the exporter was subjected to the same penalties and forfeitures as any felon.

For the honor of our national humanity, one must hope that neither of these statutes was ever enforced. The first, however, has never been directly repealed so far as I know, and Serjeant Hawkins, the author of a standard treatise on the criminal law, appears to regard it as still in force. It may nonetheless be considered effectively repealed by a statute of the twelfth year of Charles II, chapter 32, section 3. Without expressly removing the penalties imposed by earlier statutes, that act imposes a new one: a fine of 20s. for every sheep exported or attempted to be exported, together with the forfeiture of the sheep and of the owner's share in the ship. The second statute was expressly repealed by an act of the seventh and eighth years of William III, chapter 28, section 4, which declares: "Whereas the statute of the thirteenth and fourteenth years of King Charles II, made against the export of wool, among other things mentioned in that act, enacts that this offense shall be deemed a felony; and whereas the severity of that penalty has prevented offenders from being effectively prosecuted; be it therefore enacted, by the authority aforesaid, that the part of the said act which makes this offense a felony be repealed and made void."

Yet the penalties that remain, whether imposed by this milder statute or imposed by earlier statutes and left unrepealed by it, are still severe enough. Besides forfeiting the goods, the exporter incurs a fine of 3s. for every pound weight of wool exported or attempted to be exported, which is four or five times its value. Any merchant or other person convicted of this offense is barred from recovering any debt or account owed to him by an agent or anyone else. Whatever his fortune, and whether or not he can pay these heavy penalties, the law means to ruin him completely. But because the morals of the great body of the people are not yet as corrupt as those of the men who devised this statute, I have never heard of anyone taking advantage of this clause. If the person convicted cannot pay the penalties within three months of judgment, he is to be transported to the colonies for seven years, and if he returns before his term has expired, he is liable to the penalties of felony without benefit of clergy, the old legal privilege that spared certain first offenders from the gallows, so that he faces death. A shipowner who knows of the offense forfeits his whole interest in the ship and its fittings. The master and crew, if they know of the offense, forfeit all their goods and possessions and serve three months in prison. A later statute raised the master's imprisonment to six months.

To prevent exports, the entire inland trade in wool has been placed under very burdensome and oppressive restrictions. Wool may not be packed in any box, barrel, cask, case, chest, or other container, but only in packs of leather or pack-cloth, marked on the outside with the word WOOL or YARN in large letters at least three inches tall. The penalty is forfeiture of the wool and its package, plus 8s. for every pound weight, payable by the owner or packer. Wool may not be loaded onto any horse or cart, or carried by land within five miles of the coast, except between sunrise and sunset, on pain of forfeiting the wool, the horses, and the carts. The hundred, the subdivision of a county lying next to the coast, from which or through which the wool is carried or exported, forfeits £20 if the wool is worth less than £10, and if it is worth more, three times its value together with triple costs, provided suit is brought within the year. The penalty is to be levied on any two of the inhabitants, whom the county sessions must then reimburse through a rate charged on the other inhabitants, as in cases of robbery. Anyone who settles privately with the hundred for less than this penalty is to be imprisoned for five years, and any other person may bring the prosecution. These regulations apply throughout the whole kingdom.

In the particular counties of Kent and Sussex, however, the restrictions are even more troublesome. Every owner of wool within ten miles of the coast must give a written account to the nearest customs officer, within three days of shearing, stating the number of his fleeces and the places where they are stored. Before he moves any part of them, he must give similar notice of the number and weight of the fleeces, the name and residence of the buyer, and the place to which the wool is to be carried. No one within fifteen miles of the sea in those counties may buy any wool until he has entered into a bond to the king guaranteeing that he will not resell any of it to anyone else within fifteen miles of the sea. If wool is found being carried toward the coast in those counties without having been entered and secured in this way, it is forfeited, and the offender also forfeits three shillings for every pound of weight. If anyone stores unentered wool within fifteen miles of the sea, it must be seized and forfeited; and if, after the seizure, anyone claims it, he must give security to the Exchequer that, should he lose at trial, he will pay triple costs on top of all the other penalties.

When such restrictions are imposed on the inland trade, we may assume that the coasting trade cannot be left very free. Every owner of wool who carries, or has carried, any wool to a port or place on the coast, intending to ship it from there by sea to another place or port on the coast, must first have an entry made at the port of departure recording the weight, marks, and number of the packages. He must do this before he brings the wool within five miles of that port. Otherwise he forfeits the wool, along with the horses, carts, and other vehicles, and he also suffers the penalties and forfeitures imposed by the other laws against the export of wool. This law, the 1st of William III, chapter 32, is nevertheless indulgent enough to declare that it shall not prevent anyone from carrying his wool home from the place of shearing, even if that place lies within five miles of the sea. He must, however, within ten days of shearing and before he moves the wool, certify in his own hand to the nearest customs officer the true number of fleeces and where they are stored, and he must not move them without first certifying to that officer, again in his own hand, his intention to do so three days in advance. A bond must also be given that wool shipped along the coast will be landed at the specific port named in its outward entry. If any part of it is landed without an officer present, the wool is forfeited, as other goods would be, and the usual additional penalty of three shillings per pound is incurred as well.

To justify their demand for such extraordinary restrictions and regulations, our woollen manufacturers confidently asserted that English wool was of a peculiar quality, superior to that of any other country. The wool of other countries, they claimed, could not be worked into any tolerable product without some admixture of English wool, and fine cloth could not be made without it. If the export of English wool could be stopped entirely, England could therefore monopolize almost the whole woollen trade of the world; and having no rivals, she could sell at whatever price she pleased and soon acquire an almost incredible degree of wealth through the most favorable balance of trade. Like most doctrines confidently asserted by any considerable number of people, this one was, and still is, implicitly believed by a much greater number: by almost everyone unacquainted with the woollen trade or who has not looked into the matter closely. Yet it is entirely false. So far from English wool being in any respect necessary for making fine cloth, it is wholly unfit for the purpose. Fine cloth is made entirely of Spanish wool. English wool cannot even be mixed with Spanish wool without spoiling and degrading, to some degree, the fabric of the cloth.

It was shown in an earlier part of this work that the effect of these regulations has been to depress the price of English wool, not only below what it would naturally be at present, but far below what it actually was in the time of Edward III. When Scottish wool became subject to the same regulations as a result of the Union, its price is said to have fallen by about half. The very accurate and intelligent author of the *Memoirs of Wool*, the Reverend John Smith, observes that the price of the best English wool in England is generally lower than what wool of much inferior quality ordinarily fetches in the Amsterdam market. Depressing the price of this commodity below what might be called its natural and proper price was the declared purpose of these regulations, and there seems no doubt that they have produced the effect expected of them.

It might be thought that this reduction in price, by discouraging the raising of wool, must have greatly reduced the annual output of the commodity. The output may not have fallen below what it once was, but it would presumably have fallen below what it would otherwise be under present conditions, had an open and free market allowed the price to rise to its natural and proper level. I am inclined to believe, however, that the quantity produced each year cannot have been much affected by these regulations, though it may perhaps have been affected a little. Raising wool is not the chief purpose for which the sheep farmer employs his labor and capital. He expects his profit less from the price of the fleece than from the price of the carcass, and the average or ordinary price of the carcass must in many cases make up to him for whatever shortfall there may be in the average or ordinary price of the fleece. As was observed in an earlier part of this work, "whatever regulations tend to sink the price, either of wool or of raw hides, below what it naturally would be, must, in an improved and cultivated country, have some tendency to raise the price of butcher's meat. The price, both of the great and small cattle which are fed on improved and cultivated land, must be sufficient to pay the rent which the landlord, and the profit which the farmer, has reason to expect from improved and cultivated land. If it is not, they will soon cease to feed them. Whatever part of this price, therefore, is not paid by the wool and the hide, must be paid by the carcase. The less there is paid for the one, the more must be paid for the other. In what manner this price is to be divided upon the different parts of the beast, is indifferent to the landlords and farmers, provided it is all paid to them. In an improved and cultivated country, therefore, their interest as landlords and farmers cannot be much affected by such regulations, though their interest as consumers may, by the rise in the price of provisions." By this reasoning, the lowered price of wool is unlikely, in an improved and cultivated country, to cause any reduction in the annual output of the commodity, except insofar as a higher price for mutton may somewhat reduce the demand for, and therefore the production of, that particular kind of meat. Even this effect is probably not very considerable.

But although the effect on the quantity of the annual output may not have been large, it might be thought that the effect on its quality must necessarily have been very great. One might suppose that the decline in the quality of English wool, if not below its former standard then below what it would naturally have reached at the present stage of improvement and cultivation, must have been very nearly proportional to the decline in price. Quality depends on the breed, on the pasture, and on the management and cleanliness of the sheep throughout the whole period in which the fleece grows; and it is natural enough to imagine that attention to these things can never exceed what the price of the fleece is likely to repay for the labor and expense that such attention requires. It happens, however, that the quality of the fleece depends largely on the health, growth, and size of the animal, so that the same care needed to improve the carcass is, to some extent, sufficient to improve the fleece as well. Despite the lowered price, English wool is said to have improved considerably even in the course of the present century. The improvement might perhaps have been greater had the price been better; but the low price, though it may have hindered that improvement, has certainly not prevented it altogether.

The severity of these regulations, therefore, seems to have affected neither the quantity nor the quality of the annual output of wool as much as might have been expected, though I think it probable that it has affected quality a good deal more than quantity. And the interest of the wool growers, though it must have suffered to some degree, seems on the whole to have suffered much less than one might readily have imagined.

These considerations will not, however, justify an absolute prohibition on the export of wool. They will fully justify a considerable tax on that export.

To injure the interest of any one class of citizens, to any degree, for no other purpose than to promote the interest of another, is plainly contrary to the justice and equal treatment that the sovereign owes to all the different classes of his subjects. Yet the prohibition certainly injures the interest of the wool growers to some degree, and for no other purpose than to promote that of the manufacturers.

Every class of citizens is bound to contribute to the support of the sovereign or the commonwealth. A tax of five or even ten shillings on every tod of wool exported (the tod being a traditional measure of wool, usually twenty-eight pounds) would yield a very considerable revenue to the sovereign. It would injure the growers somewhat less than the prohibition does, since it probably would not lower the price of wool quite so much. And it would give the manufacturer a sufficient advantage: though he might not buy his wool quite as cheaply as under the prohibition, he would still buy it at least five or ten shillings cheaper than any foreign manufacturer could, and he would also save the freight and insurance that the foreigner would have to pay. It is hardly possible to devise a tax that could raise a considerable revenue for the sovereign while causing so little inconvenience to anyone.

The prohibition, despite all the penalties that guard it, does not prevent the export of wool. It is well known that wool is exported in great quantities. The large gap between the home price and the foreign price creates such a temptation to smuggle that all the rigor of the law cannot stop it. This illegal export benefits no one but the smuggler. A legal export, subject to a tax, would provide the sovereign with revenue and so spare the public some other tax that might be more burdensome and inconvenient; it might therefore prove beneficial to every class of subjects in the state.

The export of fuller's earth, or fuller's clay, a substance thought to be necessary for preparing and cleaning woollen goods, has been subjected to nearly the same penalties as the export of wool. Even tobacco-pipe clay, though admitted to be different from fuller's clay, has been placed under the same prohibitions and penalties, because the two resemble each other and fuller's clay might sometimes be exported under the name of pipe clay.

The 13th and 14th of Charles II, chapter 7, prohibited the export not only of raw hides but of tanned leather, except in the form of boots, shoes, or slippers. The law thereby gave our bootmakers and shoemakers a monopoly against both our graziers and our tanners. Under later statutes, our tanners have obtained an exemption from this monopoly in return for paying a small tax of just one shilling on the hundredweight of tanned leather, a hundredweight being one hundred and twelve pounds. They have also obtained a drawback, or refund, of two-thirds of the excise duties imposed on their product, even when it is exported without further manufacture. All manufactured leather goods may be exported duty-free, and the exporter is in addition entitled to a refund of the entire excise. Our graziers remain subject to the old monopoly. Graziers live apart from one another, scattered through every corner of the country, and cannot without great difficulty combine either to impose monopolies on their fellow citizens or to free themselves from those that others have imposed on them. Manufacturers of every kind, gathered together in large numbers in all the great cities, can do so easily. Even the export of cattle horns is prohibited, so that the two insignificant trades of the horner and the comb-maker enjoy, in this respect, a monopoly against the graziers.

Restraints, whether by prohibition or by taxation, on the export of goods that are partly but not completely manufactured are not peculiar to the leather trade. As long as anything remains to be done to fit a commodity for immediate use and consumption, our manufacturers believe that they ought to be the ones to do it. Woollen yarn and worsted are prohibited from export under the same penalties as wool. Even white cloths, that is, undyed cloths, are subject to an export duty, and our dyers have to that extent obtained a monopoly against our clothiers. The clothiers would probably have been able to defend themselves against it, but it happens that most of our principal clothiers are also dyers themselves. The export of watch cases, clock cases, and dial plates for clocks and watches has been prohibited. Our clockmakers and watchmakers, it seems, do not want the price of this kind of workmanship raised on them by foreign competition.

Several old statutes of Edward III, Henry VIII, and Edward VI prohibited the export of all metals. Only lead and tin were excepted, probably because of the great abundance of those metals, whose export made up a considerable part of the kingdom's trade in those days. To encourage the mining industry, the 5th of William and Mary, chapter 17, exempted from this prohibition iron, copper, and mundic metal made from British ore. The export of all kinds of copper bars, foreign as well as British, was later permitted by the 9th and 10th of William III, chapter 26. The export of unmanufactured brass, including what are called gun-metal, bell-metal, and shroff metal, is still prohibited. Brass manufactures of all kinds may be exported duty-free.

Where the export of the materials of manufacture is not prohibited altogether, it is in many cases subject to considerable duties.

The 8th of George I, chapter 15, made duty-free the export of all goods produced or manufactured in Great Britain on which duties had been imposed by earlier statutes. The following goods, however, were excepted: alum, lead, lead ore, tin, tanned leather, copperas, coal, wool, cards for carding wool, white woollen cloths, lapis calaminaris (calamine), skins of all kinds, glue, coney hair or wool (that is, rabbit fur), hare's wool, hair of all kinds, horses, and litharge of lead. Except for horses, every item on this list is either a material of manufacture, an unfinished manufacture (which may be regarded as material for further manufacture), or an instrument of trade. The statute leaves all of them subject to every old duty ever imposed on them, including the old subsidy and the duty of one percent on exports.

The same statute exempted a large number of foreign dyeing drugs from all import duties. Each of them, however, was then made subject to a certain export duty, though not a very heavy one. Our dyers, it seems, while they judged it in their interest to encourage the import of these drugs by exempting them from all duties, also judged it in their interest to place some small discouragement on their export. The greed that prompted this notable piece of mercantile ingenuity, however, most probably defeated its own purpose. It inevitably taught importers to be more careful than they otherwise would have been not to bring in more than the home market required. The home market was therefore always likely to be more scantily supplied, and the commodities always likely to be somewhat dearer there, than if their export had been made as free as their import.

Under the statute just mentioned, gum senega, or gum arabic, being among the listed dyeing drugs, could be imported duty-free. On re-export, it was subject to a small poundage duty of only threepence per hundredweight. At that time France held an exclusive trade with the country most productive of these drugs, the region around the Senegal River, and the British market could not easily be supplied by importing them directly from where they grew. The 25th of George II therefore allowed gum senega to be imported from any part of Europe, contrary to the general provisions of the Navigation Act. Since the law did not intend to encourage this kind of trade, so contrary to the general principles of England's mercantile policy, it imposed a duty of ten shillings per hundredweight on such imports, and no part of this duty was to be refunded on re-export. The successful war that began in 1755 gave Great Britain the same exclusive trade with those countries that France had previously enjoyed. As soon as peace was made, our manufacturers sought to take advantage of this position and to establish a monopoly in their own favor against both the growers and the importers of this commodity. Accordingly, by the statute of the fifth year of George III, chapter 37, the export of gum senega from His Majesty's dominions in Africa was confined to Great Britain and subjected to all the same restrictions, regulations, forfeitures, and penalties that governed the enumerated commodities of the British colonies in America and the West Indies, those goods which the colonists were permitted to ship to no market but Britain's. Its importation, it is true, carried only a small duty of sixpence per hundredweight, but its re-exportation was charged the enormous duty of one pound ten shillings per hundredweight. Our manufacturers intended that the whole produce of those countries should be brought into Great Britain. So that they themselves could buy it at a price of their own choosing, they also intended that none of it should leave again except at a cost high enough to discourage the attempt. On this occasion, however, as on many others, their greed defeated its own purpose. So steep a duty presented such a temptation to smuggling that great quantities of the gum were exported in secret, probably to every manufacturing country in Europe but especially to Holland, and not only from Great Britain but directly from Africa. For this reason, by the statute of 14 George III, chapter 10, the export duty was reduced to five shillings per hundredweight.

In the book of rates, the official schedule of values on which the old subsidy (an ancient customs duty) was assessed, beaver skins were valued at six shillings and eightpence apiece. The various subsidies and imposts laid on their importation before 1722 amounted to one-fifth of that valuation, or sixteen pence a skin. All of this was refunded as a "drawback" when the skins were exported again, except for half the old subsidy, which came to only twopence. This import duty on so important a raw material of manufacture had been thought too high, and in 1722 the valuation was lowered to two shillings and sixpence. That change reduced the import duty to sixpence, of which only half was to be refunded on export. The same successful war then brought the country most productive of beaver under British rule, and because beaver skins were among the enumerated commodities, their export from America was confined to the British market. Our manufacturers soon perceived the advantage they might draw from this circumstance. In 1764 the import duty on beaver skins was cut to one penny, while the export duty was raised to sevenpence a skin, with no refund of the import duty. The same law imposed a duty of eighteen pence a pound on the export of beaver wool, or "woumbs," the fine underfur of the animal, without altering the duty on importing that commodity. When it was brought in by British merchants in British ships, that import duty amounted at the time to between fourpence and fivepence apiece.

Coal may be regarded both as a raw material of manufacture and as an instrument of trade. Heavy duties have accordingly been laid on its export, amounting at present, in 1783, to more than five shillings a ton, or more than fifteen shillings a chaldron by Newcastle measure, the customary unit in which coal was shipped. In most cases this is more than the original value of the coal at the pit, or even at the port from which it is shipped abroad.

The export of instruments of trade in the strict sense, however, is generally restrained not by high duties but by outright prohibition. Thus, by the statute of 7 and 8 William III, chapter 20, section 8, the export of frames or machines for knitting gloves or stockings is forbidden. The penalty is not only the forfeiture of any such frames or machines that are exported or that someone attempts to export, but also a fine of forty pounds, half going to the king and the other half to whoever informs on the offender or brings suit against him. In the same way, by the statute of 14 George III, chapter 71, the export to foreign countries of any tools used in the cotton, linen, woolen, and silk manufactures is forbidden. The penalty is the forfeiture of the tools, together with a fine of two hundred pounds to be paid by the offender, and a further fine of two hundred pounds to be paid by any ship's master who knowingly allows such tools to be loaded aboard his vessel.

When such heavy penalties were laid on the export of the dead instruments of trade, it could hardly be expected that the living instrument, the skilled craftsman himself, would be left free. Accordingly, under the statute of 5 George I, chapter 27, anyone convicted of enticing a craftsman in any of the manufactures of Great Britain to go abroad to practice or teach his trade is liable, for a first offense, to a fine of up to one hundred pounds and to three months' imprisonment, continuing until the fine is paid. For a second offense he is liable to a fine of any amount the court sees fit, and to twelve months' imprisonment, again continuing until the fine is paid. The statute of 23 George II, chapter 13, raised these penalties. For a first offense the fine became five hundred pounds for every craftsman so enticed, with twelve months' imprisonment until the fine is paid. For a second offense it became one thousand pounds, with two years' imprisonment until the fine is paid.

Under the first of these two statutes, once it is proved that anyone has been enticing a craftsman, or that a craftsman has promised or contracted to go abroad for these purposes, the court may at its discretion require the craftsman to give security that he will not go overseas, and may commit him to prison until he does so.

If a craftsman has already gone overseas and is practicing or teaching his trade in a foreign country, he may be warned by one of His Majesty's ministers or consuls abroad, or by one of His Majesty's secretaries of state then in office. If within six months of that warning he does not return to this realm and thereafter live in it permanently, he is declared incapable of receiving any legacy left to him within the kingdom, of serving as executor or administrator for anyone, and of acquiring any land within the kingdom by inheritance, bequest, or purchase. He also forfeits to the king all his lands, goods, and personal property, is declared an alien in every respect, and is placed outside the king's protection.

There is no need, I imagine, to point out how contrary such regulations are to that much-vaunted liberty of the subject which we profess to guard so jealously, but which in this case is so plainly sacrificed to the paltry interests of our merchants and manufacturers.

The laudable motive behind all these regulations is to extend our own manufactures, not by improving them, but by holding back those of all our neighbors, and by putting an end, as far as possible, to the troublesome competition of such hateful and disagreeable rivals. Our master manufacturers think it reasonable that they alone should hold a monopoly over the ingenuity of all their countrymen. In some trades they restrict the number of apprentices that may be employed at one time, and in all trades they impose the requirement of a long apprenticeship, and by these means each of them tries to confine the knowledge of his particular occupation to as few people as possible. Yet they are unwilling that any member of even this small number should go abroad to instruct foreigners.

Consumption is the sole end and purpose of all production, and the interest of the producer ought to be attended to only so far as may be necessary to promote the interest of the consumer.

This maxim is so perfectly self-evident that it would be absurd to try to prove it. Yet under the mercantile system the interest of the consumer is almost constantly sacrificed to that of the producer, and the system seems to treat production, not consumption, as the ultimate end and object of all industry and commerce.

In the restraints on importing every foreign commodity that might compete with goods of our own growth or manufacture, the interest of the consumer at home is plainly sacrificed to that of the producer. It is entirely for the producer's benefit that the consumer is made to pay the higher price which this monopoly almost always brings about.

It is entirely for the producer's benefit that bounties are granted on the export of some of his products. The consumer at home is obliged to pay, first, the tax needed to fund the bounty, and second, the still heavier tax that inevitably arises from the higher price of the commodity in the home market.

Under the famous commercial treaty with Portugal, duties prevent the consumer from buying from a neighboring country a commodity that our own climate cannot produce, and oblige him instead to buy it from a distant country, even though the commodity of the distant country is admitted to be of worse quality than that of the near one. The consumer at home must put up with this inconvenience so that the producer may send some of his own products into the distant country on better terms than he would otherwise have been allowed. The consumer must also pay whatever rise in the home price of those very products this forced exportation may cause.

But it is in the system of laws established for managing our American and West Indian colonies that the interest of the consumer at home has been sacrificed to that of the producer with a more extravagant prodigality than in all our other commercial regulations. A great empire has been founded for the sole purpose of raising up a nation of customers, who would be obliged to buy from the shops of our various producers every article those producers could supply. For the sake of the slight rise in price that this monopoly might give our producers, consumers at home have been burdened with the entire expense of maintaining and defending that empire. For this purpose, and for this purpose alone, more than two hundred million pounds have been spent in the last two wars, and a new debt of more than one hundred and seventy million has been incurred, over and above everything spent for the same purpose in earlier wars. The interest on this debt alone exceeds not only the whole extraordinary profit that could ever have been claimed from the monopoly of the colony trade, but the entire value of that trade, or the entire value of the goods exported to the colonies in an average year.

It cannot be very difficult to determine who devised this whole mercantile system. It was not, we may be sure, the consumers, whose interest has been entirely neglected, but the producers, whose interest has been so carefully looked after; and among the producers, our merchants and manufacturers have been by far the chief architects. In the mercantile regulations examined in this chapter, the interest of our manufacturers has received the most particular attention, and the interest sacrificed to it has been not so much that of the consumers as that of certain other groups of producers.

### CHAPTER IX: OF THE AGRICULTURAL SYSTEMS, OR OF THOSE SYSTEMS OF POLITICAL ECONOMY WHICH REPRESENT THE PRODUCE OF LAND, AS EITHER THE SOLE OR THE PRINCIPAL SOURCE OF THE REVENUE AND WEALTH OF EVERY COUNTRY

The agricultural systems of political economy will not require as long an explanation as the one I thought it necessary to give the mercantile, or commercial, system.

The system that treats the produce of land as the *sole* source of every country's revenue and wealth has never, so far as I know, been adopted by any nation. At present it exists only in the speculations of a few highly learned and ingenious men in France. It would hardly be worth examining at great length the errors of a system that has never done any harm anywhere in the world, and probably never will. I shall nevertheless try to explain, as distinctly as I can, the broad outlines of this very ingenious system.

Monsieur Colbert, the famous minister of Louis XIV, was a man of integrity, great diligence, and thorough command of detail. He had long experience and sharp judgment in examining public accounts, and he possessed, in short, every ability suited to bringing method and good order to the collection and spending of the public revenue. Unfortunately, he had embraced all the prejudices of the mercantile system. That system is by its very nature a system of restraint and regulation, and it could scarcely fail to appeal to a hardworking, methodical man of business who was used to regulating the various departments of public offices and to setting up the checks and controls that kept each one within its proper sphere. Colbert tried to regulate the industry and commerce of a great country on the same model as the departments of a government office. Instead of allowing every person to pursue his own interest in his own way, on the liberal plan of equality, liberty, and justice, he granted extraordinary privileges to certain branches of industry and placed equally extraordinary restraints on others. Like other European ministers, he was inclined to favor the industry of the towns over that of the countryside; but he went further, and was willing to depress and hold down rural industry in order to support the industry of the towns.
