To make food cheap for town dwellers, and so to encourage manufacturing and foreign commerce, he banned the export of grain altogether, thereby shutting the country people out of every foreign market for by far the most important part of what they produced. This prohibition, combined with the restrictions that France's old provincial laws placed on moving grain from one province to another, and with the arbitrary and degrading taxes levied on farmers in almost every province, discouraged French agriculture and held it far below the level it would naturally have reached on such fertile soil and in so favorable a climate.

This depression was felt to some degree in every part of the country, and many inquiries were launched into its causes. One of those causes appeared to be the preference that Colbert's institutions gave to the industry of the towns over that of the countryside.

There is a proverb that if a rod is bent too far one way, you must bend it just as far the other way to straighten it. The French philosophers who proposed the system that treats agriculture as the sole source of every country's revenue and wealth seem to have adopted this maxim. Just as Colbert's plan certainly overvalued the industry of the towns relative to that of the countryside, their system seems just as certainly to undervalue it.

They divide all the groups of people who have ever been thought to contribute in any way to the annual produce of a country's land and labor into three classes. The first is the class of landowners. The second is the class of cultivators, meaning farmers and rural laborers, whom they honor with the special title of the *productive* class. The third is the class of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants, whom they try to belittle with the humiliating title of the *barren*, or *unproductive*, class.

The landowners contribute to the annual produce through whatever they may spend from time to time on improving their land: on buildings, drainage, enclosures, and other improvements that they either make or maintain. These improvements allow the cultivators to raise a larger crop with the same capital, and therefore to pay a higher rent. The increase in rent may be regarded as the interest or profit owed to the landowner on the money, or capital, he has spent improving his land. In this system such outlays are called *ground expenses* (*dépenses foncières*).

The cultivators, or farmers, contribute to the annual produce through what this system calls their *original* and *annual expenses* (*dépenses primitives* and *dépenses annuelles*), which they spend on working the land. The original expenses consist of the farm implements, the livestock, the seed, and the upkeep of the farmer's family, hired hands, and animals for at least a large part of the first year of his tenancy, or until the land begins to return something to him. The annual expenses consist of the seed, the wear and tear on farm implements, and the yearly upkeep of the farmer's hired hands and livestock, together with that of his family insofar as any of them can be counted as laborers working the land. The portion of the produce that remains to the farmer after he pays the rent ought to be enough, first, to repay him within a reasonable time, or at least within the term of his lease, for the whole of his original expenses together with the ordinary profits of capital; and second, to repay him each year for the whole of his annual expenses, again together with the ordinary profits of capital. These two kinds of expenses are two separate capitals that the farmer puts into cultivation. Unless they are regularly restored to him along with a reasonable profit, he cannot keep his occupation on an equal footing with other occupations, and his own interest will compel him to abandon it as soon as possible and look for another. That portion of the produce needed to keep the farmer in business ought to be regarded as a fund set apart for cultivation, sacred and untouchable. A landlord who encroaches on it necessarily reduces the yield of his own land, and within a few years leaves the farmer unable to pay not only this excessive, rack-rented sum but even the reasonable rent the land could otherwise have fetched. The rent that properly belongs to the landlord is nothing more than the *net produce* left over after all the necessary expenses of raising the gross, or total, produce have been paid in full. It is because the cultivators' labor, beyond fully covering all those necessary expenses, yields a net produce of this kind that this system singles them out with the honorable title of the productive class. For the same reason, the system calls their original and annual expenses *productive expenses*, since beyond replacing their own value they bring about the annual reproduction of this net produce.

The so-called ground expenses, the money the landlord spends improving his land, are likewise honored in this system with the title of productive expenses. Until the whole of those expenses, together with the ordinary profits of capital, has been fully repaid to him through the increased rent his land brings in, that increase ought to be regarded as sacred and inviolable by both church and king, and subject neither to tithe nor to taxation. If it is treated otherwise, then by discouraging the improvement of land the church discourages the future growth of its own tithes, and the king the future growth of his own taxes. Because in a well-ordered state of affairs these ground expenses, beyond reproducing their own value in full, also generate a net produce after a certain time, the system counts them as productive expenses.

The landlord's ground expenses, along with the farmer's original and annual expenses, are, however, the only three kinds of expenditure this system considers productive. Every other kind of expenditure, and every other group of people, including those whom most people regard as the most productive of all, is represented in this account as wholly barren and unproductive.

Artisans and manufacturers in particular, whose work in the common view adds so much to the value of the raw produce of land, are represented in this system as a wholly barren and unproductive class. Their labor, it is argued, merely replaces the capital that employs them, together with its ordinary profits. That capital consists of the materials, tools, and wages advanced to them by their employer, and it is the fund set aside for their employment and upkeep. Its profits are the fund set aside for the upkeep of the employer himself. Just as the employer advances to his workers the materials, tools, and wages their work requires, so he advances to himself what he needs to live on, and he generally scales this allowance to the profit he expects to make from the price of their work. Unless that price repays him both for the living he advances to himself and for the materials, tools, and wages he advances to his workers, it plainly does not repay him for the whole expense he has laid out. The profits of manufacturing capital, therefore, are not like the rent of land, a net produce remaining after the whole expense needed to obtain them has been fully repaid. The farmer's capital yields him a profit just as the master manufacturer's does; but it also yields a rent to a second person, which the master manufacturer's capital does not. The money spent employing and maintaining artisans and manufacturers therefore does no more than keep its own value in existence, so to speak, without producing any new value, and it is consequently a wholly barren and unproductive expense. The money spent employing farmers and rural laborers, by contrast, not only keeps its own value in existence but also produces a new value, the landlord's rent. It is therefore a productive expense.

Mercantile capital is just as barren and unproductive as manufacturing capital. It merely keeps its own value in existence without producing any new value. Its profits are only the repayment of the living that its owner advances to himself while he has the capital employed, or until he receives the returns on it. They are only the repayment of part of the expense that employing it requires.

The labor of artisans and manufacturers, on this view, never adds anything to the value of the entire annual quantity of the raw produce of land. It does indeed add greatly to the value of certain particular parts of it. But the consumption of other parts that it causes in the meantime is exactly equal to the value it adds, so that the value of the whole is never increased in the slightest at any moment. A lacemaker working the lace for a pair of fine ruffles, for example, may sometimes raise the value of perhaps a pennyworth of flax to thirty pounds sterling. At first sight he appears to have multiplied the value of that bit of raw produce some seven thousand two hundred times, yet in reality he adds nothing to the value of the entire annual quantity of raw produce. Working that lace costs him perhaps two years of labor. The thirty pounds he receives for the finished piece is no more than the repayment of the subsistence he advanced to himself during the two years he spent on it. The value he adds to the flax by each day's, month's, or year's work does no more than replace the value of what he consumes during that day, month, or year. At no moment, therefore, does he add anything to the value of the entire annual quantity of the raw produce of land, since the portion of it he is continually consuming always equals the value he is continually producing. The extreme poverty of most of the people employed in this costly though trivial manufacture is enough to convince us that the price of their work does not ordinarily exceed the value of their subsistence. The work of farmers and rural laborers is different. In ordinary circumstances it continually produces a value, the landlord's rent, over and above fully replacing the entire consumption, the entire expense laid out on the employment and upkeep of both the workers and their employer.

According to this system, artisans, manufacturers, and merchants can increase the revenue and wealth of their society only through thrift, or, in the system's own term, through *privation*: that is, by depriving themselves of part of the funds intended for their own subsistence. Those funds are all they reproduce each year. Unless they save some part of them annually, unless they deny themselves the enjoyment of some portion each year, their industry can never increase the revenue and wealth of their society in the smallest degree. Farmers and rural laborers, by contrast, may enjoy the whole of the funds intended for their own subsistence and still increase the revenue and wealth of their society at the same time. Beyond what goes to their own subsistence, their industry yields a net produce every year, and any growth in that net produce necessarily increases the society's revenue and wealth. Nations such as France or England, which consist largely of landowners and cultivators, can therefore grow rich through industry and enjoyment. Nations such as Holland and Hamburg, which are made up chiefly of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers, can grow rich only through thrift and privation. Since the interests of nations in such different circumstances differ so greatly, so too does the general character of their peoples. In nations of the first kind, generosity, openness, and good fellowship naturally form part of the common character; in those of the second, narrowness, meanness, and a selfish temper averse to all social pleasure and enjoyment.

The unproductive class of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers is maintained and employed entirely at the expense of the other two classes, the landowners and the cultivators. These two classes supply it both with the materials for its work and with its means of subsistence, the grain and livestock it consumes while doing that work. The landowners and cultivators ultimately pay both the wages of every worker in the unproductive class and the profits of all their employers. Those workers and their employers are, properly speaking, the servants of the landowners and cultivators. They are simply servants who work outside the house, as domestic servants work within it. Both kinds are maintained at the expense of the same masters, and the labor of both is equally unproductive. It adds nothing to the value of the total raw produce of the land. Far from increasing the value of that total, it is a charge and an expense that must be paid out of it.

The unproductive class is nevertheless not only useful but highly useful to the other two. Thanks to the industry of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers, landowners and cultivators can buy the foreign goods and domestic manufactures they need with the produce of far less of their own labor than they would have to spend if they tried, clumsily and without skill, to import the one or make the other for themselves. The unproductive class also relieves the cultivators of many cares that would otherwise distract them from working the land. The larger crop they are able to raise as a result of this undivided attention is fully sufficient to pay the whole cost that maintaining and employing the unproductive class imposes on either the landowners or themselves. In this way the industry of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers, though wholly unproductive in its own nature, indirectly helps to increase the produce of the land. It increases the productive power of productive labor by leaving it free to confine itself to its proper business, the cultivation of land; and the plough often goes more easily and more effectively because of the labor of the man whose occupation is furthest removed from it.

It can never be in the interest of the landowners and cultivators to restrain or discourage the industry of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers in any way. The more freedom this unproductive class enjoys, the greater the competition among all the trades that compose it, and the more cheaply the other two classes will be supplied with both foreign goods and the manufactures of their own country.

Nor can it ever be in the interest of the unproductive class to oppress the other two. What maintains and employs the unproductive class is the surplus produce of the land, whatever remains after deducting the upkeep first of the cultivators and then of the landowners. The larger this surplus, the greater the maintenance and employment of that class must be. The establishment of perfect justice, perfect liberty, and perfect equality is the very simple secret that most effectively secures the highest degree of prosperity for all three classes.

The merchants, artisans, and manufacturers of mercantile states such as Holland and Hamburg, which consist chiefly of this unproductive class, are likewise maintained and employed entirely at the expense of the owners and cultivators of land. The only difference is that most of those landowners and cultivators live at a highly inconvenient distance from the merchants, artisans, and manufacturers whom they supply with materials and subsistence. They are inhabitants of other countries and subjects of other governments. Such mercantile states, however, are not only useful but highly useful to the inhabitants of those other countries. They fill, to some extent, a very important gap, standing in for the merchants, artisans, and manufacturers whom those countries ought to find at home but, through some defect in their policy, do not.

It can never be in the interest of these landed nations, if I may call them that, to discourage or harass the industry of such mercantile states by imposing high duties on their trade or on the goods they supply. By making those goods dearer, such duties could only lower the real value of the surplus produce of the landed nations' own land, which is what, directly or through its price, pays for those goods. Such duties could only discourage the growth of that surplus, and with it the improvement and cultivation of their own land. The most effective way, on the contrary, to raise the value of that surplus, to encourage its growth, and so to promote the improvement and cultivation of their own land, would be to allow complete freedom to the trade of all such mercantile nations.

This complete freedom of trade would even be the most effective means of supplying the landed nations, in due course, with all the artisans, manufacturers, and merchants they lacked at home, and of filling that very important gap in the most proper and advantageous way.

The steady growth of the surplus produce of their land would in time create more capital than could be employed at the ordinary rate of profit in improving and cultivating the land, and the excess would naturally turn to employing artisans and manufacturers at home. Because these domestic artisans and manufacturers would find both their materials and their subsistence close at hand, they might be able, even with far less art and skill, to work as cheaply right away as the artisans and manufacturers of the mercantile states, who had to bring both from a greater distance. Even if their lack of art and skill kept them for a time from working as cheaply, they would still have a market at home, and might be able to sell their work there as cheaply as the goods of the mercantile states, which could reach that market only from so great a distance. As their art and skill improved, they would soon be able to sell more cheaply still. The artisans and manufacturers of the mercantile states would therefore immediately face rivals in the market of the landed nations, and would soon afterward be undersold and pushed out of it altogether. In time, the cheapness of the landed nations' manufactures, brought about by gradual improvements in art and skill, would carry their sales beyond the home market into many foreign markets, from which they would gradually push out many of the manufacturers of the mercantile nations in the same way.

This continual growth in both the raw and the manufactured produce of the landed nations would in time create more capital than could be employed at the ordinary rate of profit in either agriculture or manufacturing. The excess capital would naturally turn to foreign trade, and would be used to export to other countries whatever part of the raw and manufactured produce of its own country exceeded the demand of the home market. In exporting their own country's produce, the merchants of a landed nation would enjoy the same kind of advantage over those of the mercantile nations that its artisans and manufacturers held over the artisans and manufacturers of those nations: the advantage of finding at home the cargo, stores, and provisions that the others had to seek at a distance. With inferior art and skill in navigation, they would therefore be able to sell that cargo in foreign markets as cheaply as the merchants of the mercantile nations; and with equal art and skill they would be able to sell it more cheaply. They would soon become rivals of those mercantile nations in this branch of foreign trade, and in time would push them out of it altogether.

According to this liberal and generous system, then, the most advantageous way for a landed nation to raise up artisans, manufacturers, and merchants of its own is to grant the most complete freedom of trade to the artisans, manufacturers, and merchants of every other nation. By doing so it raises the value of the surplus produce of its own land, and the continual growth of that surplus gradually builds up a fund which, in due course, will necessarily call into being all the artisans, manufacturers, and merchants the nation requires.

When a landed nation does the opposite, and burdens the trade of foreign nations with high duties or outright prohibitions, it necessarily harms its own interest in two distinct ways. First, by raising the price of all foreign goods and all kinds of manufactures, it necessarily lowers the real value of the surplus produce of its own land, since it is with that produce, or what amounts to the same thing, with the price of that produce, that it buys those foreign goods and manufactures. Second, by handing its own merchants, artisans, and manufacturers a kind of monopoly over the home market, it raises the rate of profit in commerce and manufacturing relative to the rate of profit in agriculture. As a result, it either draws away from agriculture some of the capital previously employed there, or prevents some of the capital that would otherwise have gone into agriculture from going there at all. This policy therefore discourages agriculture in two ways: first, by lowering the real value of what agriculture produces, and with it the rate of agricultural profit; and second, by raising the rate of profit in every other employment. Agriculture becomes less advantageous, and trade and manufacturing more advantageous, than they would otherwise be, and every man is drawn by his own interest to shift as much of his capital and labor as he can from the first to the second.

Suppose that by this oppressive policy a landed nation could raise up its own artisans, manufacturers, and merchants somewhat sooner than it could through free trade, a claim that is itself far from certain. It would still be raising them up prematurely, so to speak, before it was fully ready for them. By forcing one kind of industry too quickly, it would depress another kind of greater value. By hastily promoting a kind of industry that merely replaces the capital employing it, together with the ordinary profit, it would depress a kind of industry that, beyond replacing its capital and profit, also yields a net product: a clear rent to the landlord. It would depress productive labor by prematurely encouraging labor that is entirely barren and unproductive.

The founder of this system, the very ingenious and profound Monsieur Quesnay, set out in a series of arithmetical formulas how, according to the system, the total annual produce of the land is distributed among the three classes already described, and how the labor of the unproductive class does no more than replace the value of its own consumption without adding anything to that total. The first of these formulas, which he singles out for special distinction under the name of the Economic Table, shows how he supposes this distribution takes place under conditions of the most complete liberty, and therefore of the greatest prosperity: a state in which the annual produce yields the largest possible net product, and in which each class receives its proper share of the whole. Several later formulas show how he supposes the distribution works under various conditions of restraint and regulation, in which either the class of proprietors or the barren and unproductive class is favored over the class of cultivators, and in which one or the other encroaches, to a greater or lesser degree, on the share that properly belongs to this productive class. According to the system, every such encroachment, every violation of the natural distribution that complete liberty would establish, must necessarily lower, more or less, from one year to the next, the value and total amount of the annual produce, and must bring about a gradual decline in the real wealth and revenue of the society. The pace of this decline will be faster or slower depending on the degree of the encroachment, that is, on how far the natural distribution established by complete liberty has been violated. The later formulas represent the different degrees of decline which, according to the system, correspond to the different degrees to which this natural order is violated.

Certain theorizing physicians seem to have imagined that the health of the human body could be preserved only by one precise regimen of diet and exercise, so that every departure from it, however slight, would necessarily produce some degree of illness or disorder in proportion to the departure. Experience, however, appears to show that the human body often maintains, at least to all appearances, the most perfect health under an enormous variety of regimens, including some generally believed to be far from wholesome. The healthy body, it seems, contains within itself some unknown principle of preservation, able in many respects to prevent or correct the ill effects of even a very faulty regimen. Quesnay, who was himself a physician, and a highly theoretical one, appears to have held a similar notion about the body politic, imagining that it could thrive and prosper only under one precise regimen: the exact regimen of perfect liberty and perfect justice. He seems not to have considered that in the body politic, the natural effort every man continually makes to better his own condition is itself a principle of preservation, capable in many respects of preventing and correcting the ill effects of a political economy that is to some degree both partial and oppressive. Such a political economy no doubt slows, to a greater or lesser extent, a nation's natural progress toward wealth and prosperity, but it cannot always halt that progress altogether, and still less can it drive the nation backward. If no nation could prosper without perfect liberty and perfect justice, then no nation in the world could ever have prospered. In the body politic, however, the wisdom of nature has fortunately made ample provision for remedying many of the ill effects of human folly and injustice, just as it has in the physical body for remedying the effects of human sloth and intemperance.

The chief error of this system, however, appears to lie in its treatment of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants as an entirely barren and unproductive class. The following observations may show why that description is mistaken.

First, it is acknowledged that this class reproduces each year the value of its own annual consumption, and at the very least keeps in existence the stock or capital that maintains and employs it. On this ground alone, the labels "barren" and "unproductive" seem badly misapplied. We would not call a marriage barren or unproductive because it produced only a son and a daughter to replace the father and mother, and so did not increase the number of human beings but merely maintained it. Farmers and farm laborers, it is true, reproduce each year not only the stock that maintains and employs them but also a net product, a clear rent to the landlord. Just as a marriage that yields three children is certainly more productive than one that yields only two, so the labor of farmers and farm laborers is certainly more productive than that of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers. Yet the greater output of the one class does not make the other barren or unproductive.

Second, it seems entirely wrong, on this account, to regard artisans, manufacturers, and merchants in the same light as domestic servants. The labor of domestic servants does not keep in existence the fund that maintains and employs them. Their upkeep and employment are borne wholly by their masters, and the work they perform is not of a kind that repays that expense. It consists of services that generally vanish at the very moment they are performed, and it does not fix or embody itself in any saleable commodity that could replace the value of their wages and upkeep. The labor of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants, by contrast, naturally does fix and embody itself in such a commodity. It is for this reason that, in the chapter where I treat productive and unproductive labor, I classed artisans, manufacturers, and merchants among the productive laborers, and domestic servants among the barren or unproductive.

Third, it seems wrong on any assumption to say that the labor of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants does not increase the real revenue of the society. Suppose, as this system seems to suppose, that the value of this class's daily, monthly, and yearly consumption exactly equals the value of its daily, monthly, and yearly production. It still would not follow that its labor adds nothing to the real revenue, to the real value of the annual produce of the society's land and labor. Consider an artisan who, in the first six months after the harvest, produces ten pounds' worth of work, while consuming during the same period ten pounds' worth of grain and other necessities. He nonetheless adds ten pounds in value to the annual produce of the society's land and labor. While he has been consuming a half-year's revenue of ten pounds' worth of grain and other necessities, he has produced an equal value of work, which can purchase an equal half-year's revenue either for himself or for someone else. The value of what has been consumed and produced over these six months is therefore not ten pounds but twenty. It is possible that no more than ten pounds' worth of this value ever existed at any single moment. But had the ten pounds' worth of grain and other necessities consumed by the artisan been consumed instead by a soldier or a domestic servant, the value of the portion of the annual produce still in existence at the end of the six months would have been ten pounds less than it actually is because of the artisan's labor. So even if the value of what the artisan produces is never, at any single moment, greater than the value of what he consumes, the value of goods actually present in the market is, at every moment, greater than it would otherwise be because of what he produces.

When the advocates of this system claim that the consumption of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants equals the value of what they produce, they probably mean only that their revenue, the fund set aside for their consumption, equals that value. Had they put it more precisely, and claimed only that the revenue of this class equaled the value of what it produced, the reader might readily have reflected that whatever was naturally saved out of that revenue must necessarily add, more or less, to the real wealth of the society. To construct something resembling an argument, then, they had to express themselves as they did; and even granting that things are as the argument seems to assume, it proves to be a very inconclusive one.

Fourth, farmers and farm laborers can no more increase the real revenue, the annual produce of the land and labor of their society, without frugality than artisans, manufacturers, and merchants can. The annual produce of the land and labor of any society can be increased in only two ways: first, by some improvement in the productive powers of the useful labor actually maintained within it; or second, by some increase in the quantity of that labor.

The improvement in the productive powers of useful labor depends, first, on improvement in the skill of the worker, and second, on improvement in the machinery he works with. But because the labor of artisans and manufacturers can be subdivided further than that of farmers and farm laborers, with each worker's task reduced to a simpler operation, it is also capable of both kinds of improvement to a much greater degree. In this respect, therefore, the class of cultivators can have no advantage whatever over that of artisans and manufacturers.

The increase in the quantity of useful labor actually employed within any society must depend entirely on the increase of the capital that employs it; and the increase of that capital must in turn be exactly equal to the amount saved out of revenue, either by the particular people who manage and direct its employment or by others who lend it to them. If merchants, artisans, and manufacturers are, as this system seems to suppose, naturally more inclined to thrift and saving than proprietors and cultivators, then to that extent they are more likely to increase the quantity of useful labor employed in their society, and therefore to increase its real revenue, the annual produce of its land and labor.

Fifth and finally, even if we suppose, as this system appears to, that the revenue of a country's inhabitants consists entirely in the quantity of subsistence their industry can obtain for them, the revenue of a trading and manufacturing country must still, other things being equal, always be much greater than that of a country without trade or manufactures. Through trade and manufactures, a country can import each year a greater quantity of subsistence than its own lands, as presently cultivated, could supply. The inhabitants of a town, though they often own no land of their own, draw to themselves through their industry so large a quantity of the raw produce of other people's land that it furnishes them not only with the materials of their work but with their means of subsistence. What a town always is in relation to the surrounding countryside, one independent state may often be in relation to others. In this way Holland draws a great part of its subsistence from other countries: live cattle from Holstein and Jutland, and grain from nearly every country in Europe. A small quantity of manufactured produce buys a great quantity of raw produce. A trading and manufacturing country therefore naturally buys, with a small part of its manufactured produce, a great part of the raw produce of other countries; whereas a country without trade and manufactures is generally obliged to spend a great part of its raw produce to buy a very small part of the manufactured produce of others. The first exports what can sustain and provide for only a very few, and imports the subsistence and comforts of a great many. The second exports the subsistence and comforts of a great many, and imports those of only a very few. The inhabitants of the first must always enjoy a far greater quantity of subsistence than their own lands, as presently cultivated, could supply. The inhabitants of the second must always enjoy a far smaller quantity.

Yet for all its imperfections, this system is perhaps the closest approach to the truth that has so far been published on the subject of political economy, and for that reason it well deserves the attention of anyone who wishes to study the principles of that very important science carefully. In treating labor employed on land as the only productive labor, the views it teaches may be too narrow and confined. But in holding that the wealth of nations consists not in the unconsumable riches of money but in the consumable goods reproduced each year by the labor of society, and in holding that complete liberty is the only effective means of making this annual reproduction as great as possible, its doctrine appears in every respect as sound as it is generous and liberal. Its followers are very numerous. And since people are fond of paradoxes, and of seeming to understand what lies beyond the grasp of ordinary minds, the paradox it maintains about the unproductive nature of manufacturing labor has perhaps done not a little to swell the number of its admirers. For some years now they have formed a fairly considerable sect, known in the French republic of letters as the Economists. Their works have certainly been of some service to their country, not only by bringing into general discussion many subjects never properly examined before, but also by influencing public administration, to some extent, in favor of agriculture. It is in consequence of their arguments that French agriculture has been freed from several of the burdens it formerly suffered under. The term for which a lease can be granted that remains binding on every future purchaser or owner of the land has been extended from nine years to twenty-seven. The old provincial restrictions on moving grain from one province of the kingdom to another have been entirely abolished, and the freedom to export it to all foreign countries has been established as the common law of the kingdom in all ordinary circumstances.

The members of this sect, in their very numerous works, which deal not only with what is properly called political economy, the nature and causes of the wealth of nations, but with every other branch of civil government, all follow the doctrine of Quesnay implicitly and without any noticeable variation. For this reason there is little variety in most of their writings. The clearest and most coherent account of the doctrine is found in a short book by Monsieur Mercier de la Rivière, for a time intendant of Martinique, entitled *The Natural and Essential Order of Political Societies*. The admiration of the whole sect for their master, who was himself a man of the greatest modesty and simplicity, is no less than that of any of the ancient philosophers for the founders of their schools. "Since the world began," writes a very diligent and respected author, the Marquis de Mirabeau, "there have been three great inventions that have chiefly given stability to political societies, apart from the many other inventions that have enriched and adorned them. The first is the invention of writing, which alone gives humankind the power to pass on, unaltered, its laws, its contracts, its histories, and its discoveries. The second is the invention of money, which binds together all the relations among civilized societies. The third is the Economic Table, the product of the other two, which completes them both by perfecting their purpose: the great discovery of our age, whose benefits our descendants will reap."

Just as the political economy of the nations of modern Europe has favored manufactures and foreign trade, the industry of the towns, over agriculture, the industry of the countryside, so the political economy of other nations has followed a different plan and favored agriculture over manufactures and foreign trade.

The policy of China favors agriculture above every other occupation. In China, the condition of a farm laborer is said to be as much superior to that of an artisan as, in most parts of Europe, the condition of an artisan is to that of a laborer. In China, every man's great ambition is to obtain a small piece of land, whether as owner or tenant; and leases there are said to be granted on very moderate terms and to give tenants adequate security. The Chinese hold foreign trade in little esteem. "Your beggarly commerce!" was how the mandarins of Peking used to speak of it to Monsieur de Lange, the Russian envoy. Apart from their trade with Japan, the Chinese carry on little or no foreign trade themselves in their own ships, and they admit the ships of foreign nations into only one or two ports of their kingdom. In China, therefore, foreign trade is confined on every side within a much narrower circle than it would naturally occupy if it were allowed more freedom, whether in Chinese ships or in those of foreign nations.

Because manufactured goods often contain great value in a small bulk, and can therefore be carried from one country to another at less expense than most kinds of raw produce, they are in nearly every country the principal support of foreign trade. In countries that are smaller than China, and less favorably placed for internal commerce, manufactures also generally depend on the support of foreign trade. Without an extensive foreign market they could hardly flourish, either in countries of such moderate size that they offer only a narrow home market, or in countries where communication between one province and another is so difficult that the goods of any particular place cannot reach the whole of the home market the country might otherwise provide. The perfection of manufacturing industry, it must be remembered, depends entirely on the division of labor, and the extent to which the division of labor can be introduced into any manufacture is necessarily governed, as has already been shown, by the extent of the market. But the great size of the Chinese empire, the vast number of its inhabitants, the variety of its climates, and therefore of the products of its different provinces, together with the easy communication by water between most of them, make the home market of that country so large that it alone is enough to support very great manufactures and to allow very considerable subdivisions of labor. The home market of China is perhaps not much smaller than the market of all the different countries of Europe combined. A more extensive foreign trade, however, which added to this great home market the foreign market of all the rest of the world, especially if a considerable part of that trade were carried on in Chinese ships, could hardly fail to greatly increase the manufactures of

China, and to raise considerably the productive powers of its manufacturing industry. Through wider navigation, the Chinese would naturally learn to use and build for themselves all the machines employed in other countries, along with the other advances in art and industry practiced in every part of the world. Under their present policy, they have little opportunity to improve themselves by the example of any other nation except the Japanese.

The policy of ancient Egypt, and that of the Hindu (or "Gentoo") government of Hindustan, also seems to have favored agriculture above all other occupations. In both ancient Egypt and Hindustan, the whole population was divided into castes or tribes, each of which was confined, from father to son, to a particular occupation or class of occupations. The son of a priest was necessarily a priest; the son of a soldier, a soldier; the son of a laborer, a laborer; the son of a weaver, a weaver; the son of a tailor, a tailor; and so on. In both countries the caste of priests held the highest rank and the caste of soldiers the next, and in both the caste of farmers and laborers ranked above the castes of merchants and manufacturers.

The governments of both countries paid particular attention to the interests of agriculture. The works that the ancient sovereigns of Egypt built to distribute the waters of the Nile were famous in antiquity, and the ruins of some of them still astonish travelers. Similar works built by the ancient sovereigns of Hindustan to distribute the waters of the Ganges and many other rivers, though less celebrated, seem to have been just as great. Both countries, accordingly, though occasionally subject to famine, were renowned for their fertility. Although both were extremely populous, in years of moderate plenty each could export large quantities of grain to its neighbors.

The ancient Egyptians had a superstitious aversion to the sea, and because the Hindu religion does not allow its followers to light a fire, and therefore to cook any food, on the water, it effectively forbids them all long sea voyages. Both Egyptians and Indians must therefore have depended almost entirely on the shipping of other nations to export their surplus produce. This dependence, by confining the market, must have discouraged any increase in that surplus. It must also have discouraged the growth of manufactured goods more than that of raw produce, because manufactures require a far larger market than the most important kinds of raw produce from the land. A single shoemaker will make more than 300 pairs of shoes in a year, while his own family will perhaps not wear out six. Unless he has the custom of at least fifty families like his own, then, he cannot sell the whole product of his labor. In a large country, the most numerous class of craftsmen will seldom amount to more than one in fifty, or one in a hundred, of all the families it contains. In large countries such as France and England, however, the number of people employed in agriculture has been estimated by some writers at a half, by others at a third, and by no writer I know of at less than a fifth of the whole population. Since by far the greater part of the agricultural produce of both France and England is consumed at home, each person employed in farming must, by these estimates, need little more than the custom of one, two, or at most four families like his own in order to sell the whole produce of his labor. Agriculture can therefore sustain itself under the handicap of a confined market much better than manufacturing can. In both ancient Egypt and Hindustan, it is true, the narrowness of the foreign market was partly offset by the convenience of many inland waterways, which opened the entire home market, on the most favorable terms, to every kind of produce from every district of those countries. The great size of Hindustan also made its home market very large, large enough to support a wide variety of manufactures. But ancient Egypt, which was never as large as England, must always have had a home market too narrow to support any great variety of manufactures. Accordingly, Bengal, the province of Hindustan that usually exports the most rice, has always been more notable for exporting a wide variety of manufactured goods than for exporting grain. Ancient Egypt, by contrast, though it exported some manufactures, fine linen in particular, along with certain other goods, was always chiefly distinguished for its great exports of grain. It was long the granary of the Roman Empire.

The sovereigns of China, of ancient Egypt, and of the various kingdoms into which Hindustan has at different times been divided, have always drawn the whole, or by far the greater part, of their revenue from some form of land tax or land rent. This tax or rent, like the tithe in Europe, consisted of a fixed share of the produce of the land (a fifth, it is said), delivered either in kind or in money according to a set valuation, and it therefore rose and fell from year to year with every change in the harvest. It was only natural, then, that the sovereigns of those countries should pay particular attention to the interests of agriculture, since the yearly growth or shrinkage of their own revenue depended directly on its prosperity or decline.

The policy of the ancient republics of Greece, and that of Rome, though it honored agriculture above manufacturing or foreign trade, seems rather to have discouraged those latter occupations than to have given any direct or deliberate encouragement to farming. In several of the ancient Greek states, foreign trade was prohibited altogether. In several others, the work of craftsmen and manufacturers was regarded as harmful to the strength and agility of the human body, since it rendered the body incapable of the habits that military and gymnastic training sought to instill, and so made it more or less unfit to endure the fatigues and face the dangers of war. Such occupations were considered fit only for slaves, and free citizens were forbidden to practice them. Even in states where no such prohibition existed, as in Rome and Athens, the great mass of the people was effectively shut out of all the trades now commonly carried on by the poorer inhabitants of towns. At Athens and Rome these trades were entirely in the hands of the slaves of the rich, who worked at them for their masters' benefit. The wealth, power, and protection of those masters made it almost impossible for a poor freeman to find a market for his work when it had to compete with the work of rich men's slaves.

Slaves, however, are very seldom inventive, and all the most important improvements that ease and shorten labor, whether in machinery or in the organization and division of work, have been the discoveries of free men. If a slave proposed an improvement of this kind, his master would be very likely to regard the proposal as the suggestion of laziness, a wish to save the slave's own labor at the master's expense. Instead of a reward, the poor slave would probably meet with much abuse, and perhaps some punishment. In manufactures carried on by slaves, therefore, more labor must generally have been needed to produce the same quantity of work than in those carried on by free men, and for that reason the work of slaves must generally have been more expensive than that of free men. Montesquieu remarks that the Hungarian mines, though no richer than the Turkish mines nearby, have always been worked at lower cost and therefore at greater profit. The Turkish mines are worked by slaves, and the arms of those slaves are the only machines the Turks have ever thought of using. The Hungarian mines are worked by free men, who use a great deal of machinery to ease and shorten their own labor.

From the very little that is known about the price of manufactured goods in the time of the Greeks and Romans, it appears that those of the finer sort were extremely expensive. Silk sold for its weight in gold. Silk, admittedly, was not then made in Europe; it was all brought from the East Indies, and the distance it had to be carried may partly explain its high price. Yet the price a lady would sometimes pay, it is said, for a piece of very fine linen seems to have been just as extravagant, and since linen was always made in Europe or, at the farthest, in Egypt, its high price can be explained only by the great cost of the labor spent on it. The cost of that labor, in turn, could only have arisen from the clumsiness of the machinery employed. The price of fine woolens, though not quite so extravagant, also seems to have been far above that of our own times. Pliny tells us that some cloths, dyed in a particular way, cost a hundred denarii, or three pounds six shillings and eightpence, per pound weight. Others, dyed in another way, cost a thousand denarii per pound weight, or thirty-three pounds six shillings and eightpence. It must be remembered that the Roman pound contained only twelve of our avoirdupois ounces. This high price, admittedly, seems to have been owing chiefly to the dye. But if the cloths themselves had not been far more expensive than any made today, so costly a dye would probably not have been spent on them; the value of the addition would have been too far out of proportion to the value of the thing itself. The price that the same author gives for certain *triclinaria*, a kind of woolen pillow or cushion used to lean on while reclining on couches at table, passes all belief: some are said to have cost more than £30,000, and others more than £300,000. This high price, moreover, is not said to have come from the dye.

Dr. Arbuthnot observes that the dress of fashionable people of both sexes seems to have shown much less variety in ancient than in modern times, and the very slight variety we find in the dress of ancient statues confirms his observation. From this he infers that their clothing must, on the whole, have been cheaper than ours. But the conclusion does not seem to follow. When fashionable dress is very expensive, its variety must be very small. When improvements in the productive powers of manufacturing make any single garment quite moderate in cost, its variety will naturally become very great. The rich, no longer able to distinguish themselves by the expense of any one garment, will naturally try to do so through the number and variety of their garments.

The largest and most important branch of every nation's commerce, as has already been observed, is the trade between the inhabitants of the town and those of the country. Town dwellers draw from the country the raw produce that supplies both the materials of their work and the means of their subsistence, and they pay for it by sending back to the country a certain portion of that produce, manufactured and made ready for immediate use. The trade between these two groups of people consists, in the end, of a certain quantity of raw produce exchanged for a certain quantity of manufactured produce. The dearer the manufactured goods, therefore, the cheaper the raw produce; and whatever tends to raise the price of manufactured goods in any country tends to lower the price of the raw produce of the land, and so to discourage agriculture. The smaller the quantity of manufactured goods that a given quantity of raw produce can buy (or, what comes to the same thing, that the price of a given quantity of raw produce can buy), the smaller the exchangeable value of that raw produce, and the smaller the incentive for the landlord to increase its quantity by improving the land, or for the farmer to do so by cultivating it. Furthermore, whatever tends to reduce the number of craftsmen and manufacturers in any country tends to shrink the home market, the most important of all markets for the raw produce of the land, and so to discourage agriculture still further.

Those systems, therefore, which prefer agriculture to all other occupations and, in order to promote it, impose restraints on manufacturing and foreign trade, work against the very end they propose, and indirectly discourage the very kind of industry they mean to promote. In this respect they are perhaps even more self-contradictory than the mercantile system. That system, by encouraging manufacturing and foreign trade more than agriculture, diverts a portion of society's capital from a more advantageous kind of industry to a less advantageous one. But it still genuinely, and in the end, encourages the kind of industry it means to promote. The agricultural systems, on the contrary, genuinely, and in the end, discourage their own favored kind of industry.

In this way, every system that tries either to draw toward a particular kind of industry, by extraordinary encouragements, a larger share of society's capital than would naturally go to it, or to force away from a particular kind of industry, by extraordinary restraints, some share of the capital that would otherwise be employed in it, in reality undermines the great purpose it means to advance. It slows, rather than speeds, society's progress toward real wealth and greatness, and it reduces, rather than increases, the real value of the annual produce of its land and labor.

Once all systems of preference or restraint are thus completely removed, the obvious and simple system of natural liberty establishes itself of its own accord. Every man, so long as he does not violate the laws of justice, is left perfectly free to pursue his own interest in his own way, and to bring both his labor and his capital into competition with those of any other man or class of men. The sovereign is entirely released from a duty which, in attempting to perform it, he must always be exposed to countless delusions, and which no human wisdom or knowledge could ever be sufficient to perform properly: the duty of supervising the industry of private people and directing it toward the employments best suited to the interests of society. Under the system of natural liberty, the sovereign has only three duties to attend to: three duties of great importance, certainly, but plain and intelligible to ordinary understanding. The first is the duty of protecting society from the violence and invasion of other independent societies. The second is the duty of protecting, as far as possible, every member of society from the injustice or oppression of every other member, which is to say the duty of establishing an exact administration of justice. The third is the duty of building and maintaining certain public works and certain public institutions that it can never be in the interest of any individual, or any small number of individuals, to build and maintain, because the profit could never repay the expense to an individual or a small group, though it may often do much more than repay it to a great society.

The proper performance of these several duties necessarily involves a certain expense, and this expense in turn necessarily requires a certain revenue to support it. In the following book, therefore, I shall try to explain, first, what the necessary expenses of the sovereign or commonwealth are; which of those expenses ought to be paid by the general contribution of the whole society, and which by that of some particular part or particular members of it only. Second, I shall explain the different methods by which the whole society may be made to contribute toward the expenses that fall on the whole society, and what the principal advantages and disadvantages of each method are. Third, I shall explain the reasons and causes that have led almost all modern governments to mortgage some part of this revenue, or to contract debts, and what effects those debts have had on the real wealth of society, the annual produce of its land and labor. The following book will therefore naturally divide into three chapters.

### APPENDIX TO BOOK FOUR

The two following accounts are added to illustrate and confirm what was said in the fifth chapter of the fourth book concerning the tonnage bounty paid to the white-herring fishery. The reader may, I believe, rely on the accuracy of both.

The first is an account of the busses (the decked fishing vessels used in the herring fishery) fitted out in Scotland over eleven years, with the number of empty barrels they carried out and the number of barrels of herring they caught. It also shows the average bounty on each barrel of "sea-sticks" (herring salted and packed loosely at sea, before being repacked on shore) and on each barrel when fully packed.

| Year | Number of busses | Empty barrels carried out | Barrels of herring caught | Bounty paid on the busses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1771 | 29 | 5,948 | 2,832 | £2,885 0s. 0d. |
| 1772 | 168 | 41,316 | 22,237 | £11,055 7s. 6d. |
| 1773 | 190 | 42,333 | 42,055 | £12,510 8s. 6d. |
| 1774 | 240 | 59,303 | 56,365 | £26,932 2s. 6d. |
| 1775 | 275 | 69,144 | 52,879 | £19,315 15s. 0d. |
| 1776 | 294 | 76,329 | 51,863 | £21,290 7s. 6d. |
| 1777 | 240 | 62,679 | 43,313 | £17,592 2s. 6d. |
| 1778 | 220 | 56,390 | 40,958 | £16,316 2s. 6d. |
| 1779 | 206 | 55,194 | 29,367 | £15,287 0s. 0d. |
| 1780 | 181 | 48,315 | 19,885 | £13,445 12s. 6d. |
| 1781 | 135 | 33,992 | 16,593 | £9,613 15s. 6d. |
| **Totals** | **2,186** | **550,943** | **378,347** | **£165,463 14s. 0d.** |

The total catch amounted to 378,347 barrels of sea-sticks, and the average bounty on each barrel of sea-sticks was therefore 8s. 2¼d. But a barrel of sea-sticks is reckoned at only two-thirds of a fully packed barrel, so one-third, or 126,115 barrels, must be deducted, leaving 252,231 fully packed barrels. This raises the bounty on each fully packed barrel to 12s. 3¾d.

If the herring are exported, a further premium is paid:

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Bounty on each fully packed barrel | £0 12s. 3¾d. |
| Export premium | £0 2s. 8d. |
| **Money bounty paid by government on each barrel** | **£0 14s. 11¾d.** |
| Add the duty on the salt usually credited as used in curing each barrel, on average 1¼ bushels of foreign salt at 10s. a bushel | £0 12s. 6d. |
| **Total bounty on each barrel** | **£1 7s. 5¾d.** |

If the herring are cured with British salt, the account stands as follows:

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Bounty, as before | £0 14s. 11¾d. |
| Add the duty on two bushels of Scotch salt at 1s. 6d. a bushel, taken to be the average quantity used in curing each barrel | £0 3s. 0d. |
| **Total bounty on each barrel** | **£0 17s. 11¾d.** |

When buss herring are entered for home consumption in Scotland and pay the duty of a shilling a barrel, the bounty stands thus:

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Bounty, as before | £0 12s. 3¾d. |
| Deduct the duty of a shilling a barrel | £0 1s. 0d. |
| Remainder | £0 11s. 3¾d. |
| Add again the duty on the foreign salt used in curing a barrel of herring | £0 12s. 6d. |
| **Premium allowed on each barrel entered for home consumption** | **£1 3s. 9¾d.** |

If the herring are cured with British salt, the account is as follows:

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Bounty on each barrel brought in by the busses, as above | £0 12s. 3¾d. |
| Deduct the shilling a barrel paid when they are entered for home consumption | £0 1s. 0d. |
| Remainder | £0 11s. 3¾d. |
| Add the duty on two bushels of Scotch salt at 1s. 6d. a bushel, taken to be the average quantity used in curing each barrel | £0 3s. 0d. |
| **Premium on each barrel entered for home consumption** | **£0 14s. 3¾d.** |

Although the duties forgone on exported herring cannot perhaps properly be regarded as a bounty, those forgone on herring entered for home consumption certainly can.

The second is an account of the quantity of foreign salt imported into Scotland, and of Scotch salt delivered duty-free from the Scottish saltworks, for the use of the fishery, from April 5, 1771, to April 5, 1782, together with the yearly average of each.

| Period | Foreign salt imported (bushels) | Scotch salt delivered from the works (bushels) |
|---|---|---|

It should be noted that a bushel of foreign salt weighs 48 pounds, while a bushel of British salt weighs only 56 pounds.

## BOOK FIVE

**Of the Revenue of the Sovereign or Commonwealth**

### CHAPTER I: OF THE EXPENSES OF THE SOVEREIGN OR COMMONWEALTH

#### Part I: Of the Expense of Defence

The first duty of the sovereign is to protect society from the violence and invasion of other independent societies, and this can be done only by means of a military force. But the cost of preparing that force in peacetime, and of employing it in war, varies greatly from one state of society to another, and from one stage of development to the next.

Among nations of hunters, the lowest and most primitive state of society, such as we find among the native tribes of North America, every man is a warrior as well as a hunter. When he goes to war, whether to defend his society or to avenge injuries done to it by other societies, he supports himself by his own labor, just as he does at home. His society, for in this condition there is properly neither sovereign nor commonwealth, bears no expense of any kind, either in preparing him for the field or in maintaining him while he is there.

Among nations of shepherds, a more advanced state of society, such as we find among the Tartars and the Arabs, every man is likewise a warrior. Such nations usually have no fixed home. They live either in tents or in a kind of covered wagon that is easily moved from place to place. The whole tribe or nation changes its location with the seasons of the year and in response to other circumstances. When its herds and flocks have exhausted the pasture of one district, it moves to another, and from there to a third. In the dry season it comes down to the riverbanks; in the wet season it withdraws to the higher country. When such a nation goes to war, the warriors will not entrust their herds and flocks to the feeble protection of their old men, women, and children, and the old men, women, and children will not consent to be left behind without defense and without the means of living. Moreover, since the whole nation is accustomed to a wandering life even in peacetime, it takes the field easily in time of war. Whether it marches as an army or moves about as a company of herdsmen, its way of life is nearly the same, even though the purpose is very different. They all go to war together, therefore, and each does the best he can. Among the Tartars, even the women have often been known to fight in battle. If they win, everything that belonged to the enemy tribe is the reward of victory. But if they are defeated, all is lost: not only their herds and flocks, but their women and children become the spoils of the conqueror. Even most of those who survive the battle are forced to submit to him simply in order to eat. The rest are usually scattered and dispersed across the desert.

The ordinary life and ordinary exercise of a Tartar or an Arab prepare him well enough for war. Running, wrestling, fighting with cudgels, throwing the javelin, drawing the bow, and similar activities are the common pastimes of people who live in the open air, and every one of them is an image of war. When a Tartar or Arab actually goes to war, he is supported by the herds and flocks he brings with him, exactly as in peacetime. His chief or sovereign, for all such nations have chiefs or sovereigns, bears no expense in preparing him for the field, and once he is in it, the prospect of plunder is the only pay he either expects or demands.

An army of hunters can seldom exceed two or three hundred men, because the uncertain living that hunting provides rarely allows a larger number to stay together for any length of time. An army of shepherds, by contrast, may sometimes number two or three hundred thousand. As long as nothing halts their advance, as long as they can move on from a district whose pasture they have consumed to another still untouched, there seems to be almost no limit to the number who can march together. A nation of hunters can never be a serious threat to the civilized nations around it; a nation of shepherds can. Nothing could be less formidable than a war with the native tribes of North America; nothing, on the other hand, could be more dreadful than a Tartar invasion has often proved to be in Asia. Thucydides judged that neither Europe nor Asia could withstand the Scythians if they were united, and the experience of every age has confirmed that judgment. The inhabitants of the vast but defenseless plains of Scythia, or Tartary, have frequently been brought together under the rule of the chief of some conquering horde or clan, and every such union has been marked by the havoc and devastation of Asia. The inhabitants of the inhospitable deserts of Arabia, the other great nation of shepherds, have been united only once, under Muhammad and his immediate successors. Their union, which arose more from religious zeal than from conquest, was marked in the same way. If the hunting nations of America should ever become shepherds, they would be far more dangerous neighbors to the European colonies than they are at present.

In a still more advanced state of society, among nations of farmers who have little foreign trade and no manufactures beyond the coarse household goods that nearly every family makes for its own use, every man is likewise either a warrior or easily becomes one. People who live by agriculture generally spend the whole day outdoors, exposed to every kind of harsh weather. The hardiness of their ordinary life prepares them for the fatigues of war, and some of their necessary tasks closely resemble those of a soldier. A ditch-digger's daily work prepares him to dig trenches and fortify a camp as well as to enclose a field. The ordinary pastimes of such farmers are the same as those of shepherds and are, in the same way, images of war. But because farmers have less leisure than shepherds, they engage in these pastimes less often. They are soldiers, but soldiers not quite so practiced in their drill. Such as they are, however, it rarely costs the sovereign or the commonwealth anything to prepare them for the field.

Agriculture, even in its crudest and most primitive form, implies a settlement, some kind of fixed home that cannot be abandoned without heavy loss. When a nation made up purely of farmers goes to war, therefore, the whole people cannot take the field together. At the very least, the old men, the women, and the children must stay behind to look after the homestead. All the men of military age, however, may take the field, and in small nations of this kind they often have. In every nation, the men of military age are reckoned to make up roughly a fourth or a fifth of the entire population. If the campaign begins after sowing and ends before harvest, the farmer and his principal laborers can be spared from the farm without much loss. He trusts that the work which must be done in the meantime can be managed well enough by the old men, the women, and the children. He is therefore quite willing to serve without pay during a short campaign, and it often costs the sovereign or commonwealth as little to maintain him in the field as to prepare him for it. The citizens of all the various states of ancient Greece seem to have served in this way until after the second Persian war, and the people of the Peloponnese until after the Peloponnesian War. The Peloponnesians, Thucydides observes, generally left the field in summer and went home to bring in the harvest. The Roman people served in the same way under their kings and during the early ages of the republic. Not until the siege of Veii did those who stayed at home begin to contribute something toward the support of those who went to war. In the European monarchies founded on the ruins of the Roman Empire, both before and for some time after the establishment of what is properly called feudal law, the great lords and all their immediate dependents used to serve the crown at their own expense. In the field, as at home, they lived on their own income, not on any stipend or pay received from the king for that particular occasion.

In a more advanced state of society, two separate causes make it altogether impossible for those who take the field to support themselves at their own expense. These two causes are the progress of manufactures and the improvement in the art of war.

If a farmer is called away on an expedition that begins after sowing and ends before harvest, the interruption of his business will not always cause any considerable reduction in his income. Without any labor on his part, Nature herself does most of the work that remains to be done. But the moment an artisan, such as a smith, a carpenter, or a weaver, leaves his workshop, the sole source of his income dries up completely. Nature does nothing for him; he does everything for himself. When he takes the field in defense of the public, therefore, he has no income to live on and must necessarily be supported by the public. And in a country where a large part of the inhabitants are artisans and manufacturers, a large part of those who go to war must be drawn from these classes and must therefore be supported by the public for as long as they remain in its service.

Then, too, the art of war gradually develops into a highly intricate and complicated science. The outcome of a war ceases to be decided, as in the earliest ages of society, by a single irregular skirmish or battle; instead, the contest is generally drawn out over several campaigns, each lasting the greater part of the year. When this happens, it becomes universally necessary for the public to support those who serve it in war, at least while they are engaged in that service. Whatever their ordinary occupation in peacetime, so long and costly a service would otherwise be far too heavy a burden for them to bear. Accordingly, after the second Persian war, the armies of Athens seem to have consisted mostly of mercenary troops, made up partly of citizens and partly of foreigners, but all of them alike hired and paid at the expense of the state. From the time of the siege of Veii onward, the armies of Rome received pay for as long as they remained in the field. Under the feudal governments, the military service owed by the great lords and their immediate dependents was, after a certain period, everywhere commuted into a payment of money, which was used to support those who served in their place.

The number of people who can go to war, relative to the whole population, is necessarily much smaller in a civilized society than in a primitive one. In a civilized society, since soldiers are supported entirely by the labor of those who are not soldiers, their number can never exceed what the non-soldiers can support, over and above supporting themselves, in a manner suited to their respective stations, and the other officers of government and law whom they are also obliged to maintain. In the small agricultural states of ancient Greece, a fourth or a fifth of the whole population regarded themselves as soldiers and would sometimes, it is said, take the field. Among the civilized nations of modern Europe, it is commonly estimated that no more than one percent of the inhabitants of any country can be employed as soldiers without ruining the country that pays for their service.

The cost of preparing an army for the field does not seem to have become significant in any nation until long after the cost of maintaining it in the field had passed entirely to the sovereign or commonwealth. In all the republics of ancient Greece, learning military exercises was a required part of the education the state imposed on every free citizen. Every city seems to have had a public field where, under the protection of the civil magistrate, young people were taught their various exercises by various masters. This very simple institution made up the entire expense that any Greek state appears ever to have incurred in preparing its citizens for war. In ancient Rome, the exercises held on the Campus Martius, the Field of Mars, served the same purpose as those of the gymnasium in ancient Greece. Under the feudal governments, the many public ordinances requiring the citizens of every district to practice archery and several other military exercises were meant to achieve the same end, but they do not seem to have achieved it as well. Whether because the officials charged with enforcing these ordinances had no interest in doing so, or for some other reason, they appear to have been neglected everywhere, and as all those governments developed, military exercises seem to have gradually fallen out of use among the great mass of the people.

In the republics of ancient Greece and Rome, throughout their entire existence, and under the feudal governments for a considerable time after they were first established, soldiering was not a separate and distinct trade forming the sole or principal occupation of a particular class of citizens. Every subject of the state, whatever trade or occupation he ordinarily followed to earn his living, considered himself fit to practice the trade of a soldier on all ordinary occasions as well, and on many extraordinary occasions felt bound to practice it.

The art of war, however, just as it is certainly the noblest of all arts, necessarily becomes one of the most complicated of them as society advances. The state of the mechanical arts, and of certain other arts with which war is necessarily connected, sets the limit of perfection to which it can be brought at any given time. But to bring it to that limit, it must become the sole or principal occupation of a particular class of citizens, and the division of labor is as necessary for the improvement of this art as of any other. In other arts, the division of labor arises naturally from the prudence of individuals, who find that they serve their private interest better by confining themselves to one particular trade than by practicing many. But only the wisdom of the state can make soldiering a particular trade, separate and distinct from all others. A private citizen who, in a time of deep peace and without any special encouragement from the public, spent most of his time in military exercises might no doubt improve himself greatly in them and amuse himself very well, but he certainly would not advance his own interest. Only the wisdom of the state can make it worth his while to devote most of his time to this peculiar occupation, and states have not always possessed that wisdom, even when their circumstances had reached the point where their very survival required it.

A shepherd has a great deal of leisure; a farmer, in the primitive stage of agriculture, has some; an artisan or manufacturer has none at all. The first can devote much of his time to martial exercises without any loss; the second can devote some part of it; but the third cannot spend a single hour on them without some loss, and attention to his own interest naturally leads him to neglect them entirely. The improvements in agriculture that the progress of arts and manufactures inevitably brings about also leave the farmer as little leisure as the artisan. Military exercises come to be neglected as much by the people of the countryside as by those of the town, and the great mass of the population becomes thoroughly unwarlike. At the same time, the wealth that always follows improvements in agriculture and manufacturing, and which is really nothing more than the accumulated product of those improvements, invites invasion by all its neighbors. An industrious nation, and therefore a wealthy one, is of all nations the most likely to be attacked, and unless the state takes some new measure for the public defense, the natural habits of the people leave them wholly incapable of defending themselves.

Under these circumstances, there seem to be only two ways in which the state can make any reasonable provision for the public defense.

First, it may use a very strict system of regulation, working against the entire bent of the people's interests, temperament, and inclinations, to enforce the practice of military exercises, and to compel either all citizens of military age or a certain number of them to combine, to some extent, the trade of a soldier with whatever other trade or profession they happen to follow.

Or second, by maintaining and employing a certain number of citizens in the constant practice of military exercises, it may make soldiering a particular trade, separate and distinct from all others.

If the state adopts the first of these two expedients, its military force is said to consist of a militia; if the second, of a standing army. The practice of military exercises is the sole or principal occupation of the soldiers of a standing army, and the maintenance or pay the state provides them is their principal and ordinary means of support. The practice of military exercises is only an occasional occupation for the soldiers of a militia, who derive their principal and ordinary means of support from some other occupation. In a militia, the character of the laborer, artisan, or tradesman predominates over that of the soldier; in a standing army, the character of the soldier predominates over every other. This distinction seems to constitute the essential difference between the two kinds of military force.

Militias have taken several different forms. In some countries, the citizens assigned to defend the state seem to have been drilled only, without being, if I may put it so, regimented: that is, without being divided into separate and distinct bodies of troops, each performing its exercises under its own proper and permanent officers. In the republics of ancient Greece and Rome, each citizen, as long as he remained at home, seems to have practiced his exercises either on his own or with whichever of his equals he liked best, and not to have been attached to any particular body of troops until he was actually called to take the field. In other countries, the militia has been not only drilled but regimented. In England, in Switzerland, and, I believe, in every other country of modern Europe where any imperfect military force of this kind has been established, every militiaman is attached, even in peacetime, to a particular body of troops that performs its exercises under its own proper and permanent officers.

Before the invention of firearms, the superior army was the one whose soldiers each possessed the greatest individual skill and dexterity in the use of their weapons. Strength and agility of body were of the highest importance and commonly decided the outcome of battles.
