But this skill and dexterity could be acquired only in the way fencing is learned today: by practicing not in large bodies but each man separately, at a particular school, under a particular master, or with his own particular equals and companions. Since the invention of firearms, strength and agility of body, and even extraordinary skill and dexterity with weapons, though far from unimportant, matter less than they did. The nature of the weapon, while it by no means puts the clumsy on a level with the skillful, brings them closer to it than ever before. All the skill and dexterity needed to use it can, it is supposed, be acquired well enough by practicing in large bodies.

In modern armies, regularity, order, and prompt obedience to command count for more in deciding the outcome of battles than the soldiers' skill and dexterity with their weapons. Yet the noise of firearms, the smoke, and the invisible death to which every man feels himself exposed at every moment, as soon as he comes within range of cannon, and often long before the battle can properly be said to have begun, must make it very difficult to maintain any considerable degree of this regularity, order, and prompt obedience, even at the opening of a modern battle. In an ancient battle there was no noise except that of the human voice; there was no smoke, and no invisible cause of wounds or death. Until some deadly weapon actually came near him, every man could see clearly that none was near. Under those conditions, and among troops who had some confidence in their own skill and dexterity with their weapons, it must have been considerably less difficult to preserve some degree of regularity and order, not only at the start but throughout the whole course of an ancient battle, until one of the two armies was decisively beaten. But the habits of regularity, order, and prompt obedience to command can be acquired only by troops that are drilled in large bodies.

A militia, however it may be disciplined or drilled, must always be greatly inferior to a well-disciplined and well-drilled standing army.

Soldiers who are drilled only once a week or once a month can never be as expert in the use of their weapons as those who are drilled every day or every other day. And although this matters less in modern times than it did in ancient ones, the acknowledged superiority of the Prussian troops, which is said to owe a great deal to their superior proficiency in drill, should convince us that it is still, even today, of very considerable importance.

Soldiers who are bound to obey their officer only once a week or once a month, and who at all other times are free to manage their own affairs in their own way without being answerable to him in any respect, can never stand in the same awe of him, nor have the same disposition toward ready obedience, as those whose whole life and conduct he directs every day, who even rise and go to bed, or at least retire to their quarters, according to his orders. In what is called discipline, the habit of ready obedience, a militia must always be even more inferior to a standing army than it may sometimes be in what is called the manual exercise, the handling and use of its weapons. And in modern war, the habit of ready and instant obedience matters far more than a considerable superiority in the handling of arms.

Those militias which, like the Tartar or Arab militia, go to war under the same chieftains they are accustomed to obey in peace, are by far the best. In their respect for their officers and their habit of ready obedience, they come nearest to standing armies. The Highland militia, when it served under its own chieftains, had some advantage of the same kind. The Highlanders, however, were not wandering shepherds but settled ones. Each had a fixed home, and in peaceful times they were not used to following their chieftain from place to place. In wartime, therefore, they were less willing to follow him any great distance or to stay long in the field. Once they had taken some plunder, they were eager to return home, and his authority was seldom enough to keep them. In obedience they always fell well short of what is reported of the Tartars and Arabs. And because their settled life led them to spend less time in the open air, the Highlanders were also less practiced in military exercises, and less skilled with their weapons, than the Tartars and Arabs are said to be.

It should be noted, however, that a militia of any kind that has served for several successive campaigns in the field becomes in every respect a standing army. The soldiers practice with their weapons every day, and, being constantly under the command of their officers, they grow used to the same prompt obedience found in standing armies. What they were before they took the field matters little. After a few campaigns, they necessarily become a standing army in every respect. Should the war in America drag on through another campaign, the American militia may become a full match for that standing army whose valor, in the last war at least, appeared no less than that of the hardiest veterans of France and Spain.

Once this distinction is properly understood, the history of every age will be found to bear witness to the irresistible superiority of a well-regulated standing army over a militia.

One of the first standing armies of which any well-authenticated history gives a clear account is that of Philip of Macedon. His frequent wars with the Thracians, the Illyrians, the Thessalians, and some of the Greek cities near Macedon gradually shaped his troops, which were probably a militia at the outset, to the exact discipline of a standing army. When he was at peace, which was seldom and never for long, he took care not to disband that army. After a long and violent struggle, it defeated and subdued the brave and well-drilled militias of the leading republics of ancient Greece. Afterward, with very little struggle, it overcame the soft and poorly drilled militia of the great Persian Empire. The fall of the Greek republics and of the Persian Empire was the effect of the irresistible superiority that a standing army holds over every other kind of militia. It is the first great revolution in human affairs of which history has preserved any clear and detailed account.

The fall of Carthage, and the consequent rise of Rome, is the second. All the reversals of fortune between those two famous republics can be well explained by the same cause.

From the end of the First Carthaginian War to the beginning of the Second, the armies of Carthage were continually in the field, under three great generals who succeeded one another in command: Hamilcar, his son-in-law Hasdrubal, and his son Hannibal. These armies were employed first in punishing Carthage's own rebellious slaves, then in subduing the revolted nations of Africa, and finally in conquering the great kingdom of Spain. Over the course of those different wars, the army that Hannibal led from Spain into Italy must necessarily have been shaped, little by little, to the exact discipline of a standing army. The Romans, meanwhile, though not altogether at peace, had not been engaged during this period in any war of great consequence, and their military discipline, it is generally said, had grown considerably lax. The Roman armies that Hannibal met at the Trebia, at Lake Trasimene, and at Cannae were militias facing a standing army. This circumstance probably did more than any other to decide the outcome of those battles.

The standing army that Hannibal left behind in Spain had the same superiority over the militia the Romans sent against it. Within a few years, under the command of his brother, the younger Hasdrubal, it drove them almost entirely out of that country.

Hannibal was poorly supplied from home. The Roman militia, continually in the field, became over the course of the war a well-disciplined and well-drilled standing army, and Hannibal's advantage shrank day by day. Hasdrubal judged it necessary to lead all, or nearly all, of the standing army he commanded in Spain to his brother's aid in Italy. On this march he is said to have been misled by his guides. In country he did not know, he was surprised and attacked by another standing army, equal or superior to his own in every respect, and was completely defeated.

Once Hasdrubal had left Spain, the great Scipio found nothing to oppose him but a militia inferior to his own. He conquered and subdued that militia, and in the course of the war his own militia necessarily became a well-disciplined and well-drilled standing army. That standing army was later carried to Africa, where it again met nothing but a militia. To defend Carthage, it became necessary to recall Hannibal's standing army. The disheartened and often-defeated African militia joined it, and at the battle of Zama made up the greater part of Hannibal's troops. The outcome of that day decided the fate of the two rival republics.

From the end of the Second Carthaginian War until the fall of the Roman Republic, the armies of Rome were standing armies in every respect. The standing army of Macedon offered them some resistance. Even at the height of Rome's greatness, it took two great wars and three great battles to subdue that small kingdom, and the conquest would probably have been harder still if its last king had not been a coward. The militias of all the civilized nations of the ancient world, those of Greece, Syria, and Egypt, put up only a feeble resistance to Rome's standing armies. The militias of certain barbarous nations defended themselves far better. The Scythian or Tartar militia that Mithridates drew from the lands north of the Euxine, as the Black Sea was then called, and north of the Caspian Sea, were the most formidable enemies the Romans faced after the Second Carthaginian War. The Parthian and German militias also always commanded respect, and on several occasions they won considerable advantages over Roman armies. In general, though, and when they were well commanded, the Roman armies appear to have been greatly superior. If the Romans never pursued the final conquest of either Parthia or Germany, it was probably because they judged it not worth adding those two barbarous countries to an empire that was already too large. The ancient Parthians appear to have been a nation of Scythian or Tartar origin, and to have kept a good deal of their ancestors' manners. The ancient Germans, like the Scythians or Tartars, were a nation of wandering shepherds who went to war under the same chiefs they were accustomed to follow in peace. Their militia was of exactly the same kind as that of the Scythians or Tartars, from whom they were probably descended as well.

Many different causes contributed to the decline of discipline in the Roman armies. Its extreme severity was perhaps one of them. In the days of Rome's greatness, when no enemy seemed capable of opposing them, the soldiers laid aside their heavy armor as needlessly burdensome and neglected their laborious exercises as needlessly toilsome. Under the emperors, moreover, the standing armies of Rome became a danger to their own masters, especially those guarding the German and Pannonian frontiers, which frequently set up their own generals against the emperors. To make these armies less formidable, Diocletian, according to some authors, or Constantine, according to others, first withdrew them from the frontier. Until then they had always been encamped there in large bodies, generally of two or three legions each. Now they were scattered in small detachments through the various provincial towns, from which they were scarcely ever moved except to repel an invasion. Small bodies of soldiers, quartered in trading and manufacturing towns and seldom moved from those quarters, became tradesmen, craftsmen, and manufacturers themselves. The civilian character came to outweigh the military one, and the standing armies of Rome gradually degenerated into a corrupt, neglected, and undisciplined militia. That militia proved unable to withstand the German and Scythian militias that soon afterward invaded the Western Empire. Only by hiring the militias of some of those nations to set against those of others were the emperors able, for a time, to defend themselves. The fall of the Western Empire is the third great revolution in human affairs of which ancient history has preserved any clear or detailed account. It was brought about by the irresistible superiority that the militia of a barbarous nation holds over that of a civilized one, and that the militia of a nation of shepherds holds over that of a nation of farmers, craftsmen, and manufacturers. The victories won by militias have generally been won not over standing armies but over other militias inferior to themselves in drill and discipline. Such were the victories of the Greek militia over that of the Persian Empire. In later times, the victories of the Swiss militia over the Austrians and Burgundians were of the same kind.

The military force of the German and Scythian nations who settled on the ruins of the Western Empire remained, for some time, the same in their new homes as it had been in their original country. It was a militia of shepherds and farmers that, in wartime, took the field under the same chieftains it was accustomed to obey in peace. It was therefore reasonably well drilled and reasonably well disciplined. As the arts and industry advanced, however, the authority of the chieftains gradually decayed, and the great body of the people had less time to spare for military exercises. Both the discipline and the drill of the feudal militia therefore fell gradually into ruin, and standing armies were gradually introduced to take its place. Moreover, once one civilized nation had adopted the expedient of a standing army, all its neighbors were obliged to follow the example. They soon found that their safety depended on doing so, and that their own militia was wholly incapable of resisting the attack of such an army.

The soldiers of a standing army, even if they have never seen an enemy, have often shown all the courage of veteran troops. From the very moment they took the field, they have seemed fit to face the hardiest and most experienced veterans. In 1756, when the Russian army marched into Poland, the valor of the Russian soldiers appeared no less than that of the Prussians, who were then considered the hardiest and most experienced veterans in Europe. Yet the Russian Empire had enjoyed profound peace for nearly twenty years beforehand, and could have had very few soldiers who had ever seen an enemy. When the Spanish war broke out in 1739, England had enjoyed profound peace for about twenty-eight years. Yet far from being corrupted by that long peace, the valor of her soldiers was never more distinguished than in the attempt on Cartagena, the first unfortunate exploit of that unfortunate war. In a long peace the generals may perhaps sometimes forget their skill. Where a well-regulated standing army has been maintained, however, the soldiers never seem to forget their valor.

When a civilized nation depends on a militia for its defense, it is at all times liable to be conquered by any barbarous nation that happens to be its neighbor. The frequent conquests of all the civilized countries of Asia by the Tartars amply demonstrate the natural superiority of a barbarous nation's militia over that of a civilized one. A well-regulated standing army is superior to every militia. Such an army can best be maintained by a wealthy and civilized nation, and it alone can defend such a nation against invasion by a poor and barbarous neighbor. It is therefore only by means of a standing army that the civilization of any country can be perpetuated, or even preserved, for any considerable time.

Just as a civilized country can be defended only by a well-regulated standing army, so a barbarous country can be rapidly and reasonably civilized only by the same means. A standing army imposes the sovereign's law with irresistible force throughout the most distant provinces of the empire, and it maintains some degree of regular government in countries that could not otherwise sustain any. Anyone who closely examines the improvements Peter the Great introduced into the Russian Empire will find that nearly all of them come down to the establishment of a well-regulated standing army. That army is the instrument that carries out and upholds all his other measures. Whatever degree of order and internal peace the empire has enjoyed ever since is owed entirely to its influence.

Men of republican principles have regarded a standing army with suspicion, as a danger to liberty. It certainly is one wherever the interests of the general and the principal officers are not necessarily bound up with upholding the constitution of the state. Caesar's standing army destroyed the Roman Republic. Cromwell's standing army turned the Long Parliament out of doors. But consider a state where the sovereign is himself the general, and where the leading nobility and gentry of the country are the chief officers of the army. There, military force is placed under the command of those with the greatest interest in supporting the civil authority, because they themselves hold the largest share of that authority. In such a state, a standing army can never be dangerous to liberty. On the contrary, it may in some cases favor liberty. The security it gives the sovereign makes unnecessary that troublesome suspicion which, in some modern republics, seems to watch over the smallest actions and to stand ready at all times to disturb the peace of every citizen. Where the magistrate's security, even with the support of the leading people of the country, is endangered by every popular discontent, and where a small disturbance can bring about a great revolution within a few hours, the whole authority of government must be used to suppress and punish every murmur and complaint against it. By contrast, a sovereign who feels himself supported not only by the natural aristocracy of the country but also by a well-regulated standing army can be little troubled by even the crudest, most groundless, and most unbridled protests. He can safely pardon or ignore them, and his awareness of his own superiority naturally inclines him to do so. A degree of liberty that verges on license can be tolerated only in countries where the sovereign is secured by a well-regulated standing army. Only in such countries does public safety not require that the sovereign be trusted with discretionary power to suppress even the impertinent excesses of this licentious liberty.

The first duty of the sovereign, then, is to defend the society from the violence and injustice of other independent societies, and this duty grows steadily more expensive as the society advances in civilization. The military force of the society originally cost the sovereign nothing, in peace or in war. As improvement progresses, however, he must first maintain it in time of war, and later even in time of peace.

The great change that the invention of firearms brought to the art of war has raised still further two costs: that of drilling and disciplining any given number of soldiers in peacetime, and that of employing them in war. Their weapons and their ammunition have both grown more expensive. A musket is a costlier machine than a javelin or a bow and arrows. A cannon or a mortar is costlier than a ballista or a catapult, the great siege engines of antiquity that hurled bolts and stones by the force of twisted cords. The powder spent in a modern review, the formal drill and inspection of troops, is lost beyond recovery and represents a considerable expense. The javelins and arrows thrown or shot in an ancient review could easily be picked up again, and they were of very little value besides. Cannon and mortars are not only far more expensive than ballistas or catapults but also far heavier, and they require greater expense both to prepare them for the field and to transport them there. Modern artillery is also greatly superior to that of the ancients. As a result, it has become much more difficult, and therefore much more expensive, to fortify a town so that it can resist the attack of that superior artillery for even a few weeks. In modern times, many different causes combine to make the defense of society more expensive. The unavoidable effects of the natural progress of improvement have, in this respect, been considerably increased by a great revolution in the art of war, and a mere accident, the invention of gunpowder, seems to have given rise to that revolution.

In modern war, the great expense of firearms gives a clear advantage to the nation that can best afford it, and consequently to a wealthy and civilized nation over a poor and barbarous one. In ancient times, the wealthy and civilized found it difficult to defend themselves against poor and barbarous nations. In modern times, the poor and barbarous find it difficult to defend themselves against the wealthy and civilized. The invention of firearms seems at first sight so destructive, yet it is certainly favorable both to the permanence and to the spread of civilization.

#### Part II: Of the Expense of Justice

The second duty of the sovereign is to protect every member of the society, as far as possible, from the injustice or oppression of every other member. This duty of establishing an exact administration of justice requires two very different levels of expense in the different periods of society.

Among nations of hunters, there is scarcely any property, or at least none worth more than two or three days' labor, and so there is seldom any established magistrate or any regular administration of justice. Men who have no property can injure one another only in their persons or their reputations. But when one man kills, wounds, beats, or defames another, the injured party suffers, yet the one who does the injury gains nothing. Injuries to property are different. The benefit to the person who does the injury is often equal to the loss of the one who suffers it. Envy, malice, or resentment are the only passions that can prompt one man to injure another in his person or reputation. Most men are not very often under the influence of those passions, and even the very worst men are so only occasionally. And however agreeable it may be to certain characters to gratify these passions, the gratification brings no real or lasting advantage, so in most men it is commonly held in check by considerations of prudence. Men may therefore live together in society with a tolerable degree of security even when there is no civil magistrate to protect them from the injustice of those passions.

Avarice and ambition in the rich, and in the poor the hatred of labor and the love of present ease and enjoyment, are different. These are the passions that prompt men to invade property, and they are far steadier in their operation and far more universal in their influence. Wherever there is great property, there is great inequality. For every very rich man, there must be at least five hundred poor, and the wealth of the few presupposes the poverty of the many. The wealth of the rich arouses the indignation of the poor, who are often both driven by want and prompted by envy to seize his possessions. Only under the shelter of the civil magistrate can the owner of valuable property, acquired by the labor of many years, or perhaps of many successive generations, sleep a single night in safety. He is at all times surrounded by unknown enemies whom he never provoked yet can never appease. Only the powerful arm of the civil magistrate, continually raised to punish their injustice, can protect him from them. The acquisition of valuable and extensive property therefore necessarily requires the establishment of civil government. Where there is no property, or at least none worth more than two or three days' labor, civil government is not so necessary.

Civil government presupposes a certain subordination. But just as the need for civil government gradually grows with the acquisition of valuable property, so the principal causes that naturally introduce subordination gradually grow along with that valuable property.

The causes or circumstances that naturally introduce subordination seem to be four in number. These are the things that, naturally and prior to any civil institution, give some men a degree of superiority over the greater part of their fellows.

The first of these causes or circumstances is superiority of personal qualities. These include strength, beauty, and agility of body, as well as wisdom and virtue, and prudence, justice, fortitude, and moderation of mind. Qualities of the body, unless supported by those of the mind, can give little authority in any period of society. A man must be very strong indeed to force two weak ones to obey him by mere bodily strength. Qualities of the mind alone can give very great authority. They are, however, invisible qualities, always open to dispute and generally disputed. No society, whether barbarous or civilized, has ever found it convenient to settle the rules of rank, precedence, and subordination according to those invisible qualities. Every society has settled them instead according to something plainer and more palpable.

The second of these causes or circumstances is superiority of age. An old man, provided his age is not so far advanced as to raise suspicion of senility, is everywhere more respected than a young man of equal rank, fortune, and abilities. Among nations of hunters, such as the native tribes of North America, age is the sole foundation of rank and precedence. Among them, "father" is the term for a superior, "brother" for an equal, and "son" for an inferior. In the wealthiest and most civilized nations, age regulates rank among those who are equal in every other respect, and among whom, therefore, there is nothing else to regulate it. Among brothers and among sisters, the eldest always takes precedence. When a father's estate passes to the next generation, anything that cannot be divided and must go whole to a single heir, such as a title of honor, is in most cases given to the eldest. Age is a plain and visible quality, and it admits no dispute.

The third of these causes or circumstances is superiority of fortune. The authority of wealth is great at every stage of society, but it is perhaps greatest in the crudest stage that still permits any considerable inequality of fortune. Consider a Tartar chief whose flocks and herds increase each year by enough to feed a thousand men. He has hardly any way to use that increase except to feed a thousand men. His society is too primitive to offer him manufactured goods, trinkets, or baubles of any kind for which he might exchange the portion of his raw produce that exceeds his own consumption. The thousand men he supports depend on him entirely for their subsistence, so they must obey his orders in war and submit to his jurisdiction in peace. He is necessarily both their general and their judge, and his chieftainship follows inevitably from the superiority of his fortune. In a wealthy and civilized society, a man may possess a far greater fortune and still be unable to command a dozen people. The produce of his estate may be enough to support more than a thousand people, and perhaps it actually does. But those people pay for everything they get from him, and he gives almost nothing to anyone except in exchange for an equivalent. Hardly anyone therefore considers himself entirely dependent on him, and his authority reaches no further than a few household servants. Even so, the authority of fortune remains very great in a wealthy and civilized society. Every period that has admitted any considerable inequality of fortune has complained that wealth commands far more authority than either age or personal qualities. The first stage of society, that of hunters, admits no such inequality. Universal poverty establishes universal equality, and superiority of age or of personal qualities is the feeble but only foundation of authority and subordination. In this stage, therefore, there is little or no authority or subordination. The second stage, that of shepherds, admits very great inequalities of fortune, and in no other stage does superior fortune give so much authority to those who possess it. Accordingly, in no other stage are authority and subordination more completely established. The authority of an Arabian sharif is very great; that of a Tartar khan is wholly despotic.

The fourth of these causes or circumstances is superiority of birth. Superior birth presupposes an ancient superiority of fortune in the family of the person who claims it. All families are equally old. A prince's ancestors may be better known, but they can hardly be more numerous than a beggar's. Antiquity of family therefore means, everywhere, the antiquity either of wealth or of the kind of greatness that is usually founded on wealth or accompanied by it. Newly acquired greatness is less respected everywhere than ancient greatness. The hatred people feel for usurpers, and their love for the family of an ancient monarch, rest largely on the contempt men naturally feel for the first and the veneration they feel for the second. A military officer submits without reluctance to a superior who has always commanded him, but he cannot bear to see his own inferior promoted over his head. In the same way, men readily submit to a family to whom they and their ancestors have always submitted, but they are fired with indignation when another family, whose superiority they have never acknowledged, assumes dominion over them.

Because distinction of birth arises only after inequality of fortune, it can have no place among nations of hunters. All their members are equal in fortune, so they must also be very nearly equal in birth. Even among them, it is true, the son of a wise and brave man may be somewhat more respected than a man of equal merit who has the misfortune to be the son of a fool or a coward. The difference, however, will not be very great, and I do not believe there was ever a great family in the world whose luster came entirely from an inheritance of wisdom and virtue.

Among nations of shepherds, distinction of birth not only may arise but always does. Such nations know nothing of luxury in any form, so great wealth can scarcely ever be squandered among them through reckless extravagance. Accordingly, no nations abound more in families revered and honored for their descent from a long line of great and illustrious ancestors, because among no other nations is wealth likely to remain so long in the same families.

Birth and fortune are plainly the two circumstances that chiefly set one man above another. They are the two great sources of personal distinction, and they are therefore the principal causes that naturally establish authority and subordination among men. Among nations of shepherds, both causes operate with their full force. The great shepherd or herdsman is respected for his great wealth and for the many people who depend on him for their subsistence. He is revered for the nobility of his birth and for the immemorial antiquity of his illustrious family. He thus has a natural authority over all the lesser shepherds and herdsmen of his horde or clan. He can command the combined strength of more people than any of them can, so his military power is greater than that of any of them. In time of war, they are all naturally inclined to gather under his banner rather than anyone else's, and in this way his birth and fortune naturally secure him a kind of executive power. Because he commands the combined strength of more people than any of them, he is also best able to compel any one of them who has injured another to make amends for the wrong. He is therefore the person to whom all who are too weak to defend themselves naturally look for protection. It is to him that they naturally bring their complaints about the injuries they believe have been done to them, and his intervention in such cases is more readily accepted, even by the person accused, than anyone else's would be. In this way his birth and fortune naturally secure him a kind of judicial authority.

Inequality of fortune first appears in the age of shepherds, the second stage of society, and it introduces among men a degree of authority and subordination that could not possibly have existed before. It thereby introduces some measure of the civil government that is indispensable for its own preservation, and it seems to do so naturally, even without anyone considering that necessity. That consideration comes afterward, no doubt, and does much to maintain and secure this authority and subordination. The rich in particular have a necessary interest in supporting the order of things that alone can secure them in the possession of their advantages. Men of lesser wealth combine to defend men of greater wealth in the possession of their property, so that men of greater wealth will combine to defend them in the possession of theirs. All the lesser shepherds and herdsmen feel that the security of their own herds and flocks depends on the security of the great shepherd's or herdsman's herds and flocks. They feel that their lesser authority rests on his greater authority, and that his power to keep their own inferiors in subordination to them depends on their subordination to him. They form a kind of minor nobility, which has an interest in defending the property and upholding the authority of its own petty sovereign, so that he in turn can defend their property and uphold their authority. Civil government, so far as it is instituted for the security of property, is in reality instituted for the defense of the rich against the poor, or of those who have some property against those who have none at all.

The judicial authority of such a sovereign, however, was for a long time a source of revenue to him rather than a cause of expense. Those who came to him for justice were always willing to pay for it, and a petition never failed to arrive with a present. Once the sovereign's authority was firmly established, the person found guilty had to pay a fine to the sovereign, known as an amercement, in addition to the compensation he owed the injured party. He had caused trouble, he had created a disturbance, he had broken the peace of his lord the king, and for those offenses a fine was thought due. In the Tartar governments of Asia, and in the governments of Europe founded by the Germanic and Scythian peoples who overthrew the Roman Empire, the administration of justice was a considerable source of revenue. It enriched the sovereign and also every lesser chief or lord who exercised any particular jurisdiction under him, whether over a particular tribe or clan or over a particular territory or district. Originally, both the sovereign and the lesser chiefs exercised this jurisdiction in person. Later, all of them found it convenient to delegate it to a substitute, a bailiff, or a judge. This deputy, however, still had to account to the lord who appointed him for the profits of the jurisdiction. Anyone who reads the instructions given to the circuit judges in the reign of Henry II, which are preserved in Tyrrell's *History of England*, will see clearly that those judges were a kind of traveling agent, sent around the country to collect certain branches of the king's revenue. In those days, the administration of justice not only yielded a certain revenue to the sovereign. Obtaining that revenue seems to have been one of the chief advantages he expected to gain from administering justice at all.

This scheme of making the administration of justice serve the purposes of revenue could hardly fail to produce several very gross abuses. A person who came seeking justice with a large present in hand was likely to get something more than justice, while one who came with a small present was likely to get something less. Justice might also be delayed often, so that the present would be repeated. The prospect of fining the accused party, moreover, might often supply a very strong reason for finding him in the wrong even when he was not. The ancient history of every country in Europe bears witness that such abuses were far from uncommon.

When the sovereign or chief exercised his judicial authority in person, it must have been almost impossible to obtain redress, however much he abused that authority, because there could seldom be anyone powerful enough to call him to account. When he exercised it through a bailiff, redress might sometimes be had. If the bailiff had committed an injustice solely for his own benefit, the sovereign himself might not always be unwilling to punish him or to make him repair the wrong. But if he had committed some act of oppression for the sovereign's benefit, to win the favor of the man who had appointed him and who might promote him, then redress would on most occasions be as impossible as if the sovereign had committed the act himself. Accordingly, in all barbarous governments, and particularly in those ancient governments of Europe founded on the ruins of the Roman Empire, the administration of justice appears for a long time to have been extremely corrupt. Even under the best monarchs it was far from equal and impartial, and under the worst it was wholly depraved.

Among nations of shepherds, the sovereign or chief is only the greatest shepherd or herdsman of the horde or clan, and he is supported in the same way as any of his vassals or subjects, by the increase of his own herds or flocks. The same holds among nations of farmers who have only just emerged from the shepherd state and have not advanced much beyond it. The Greek tribes appear to have been in this condition around the time of the Trojan War, as were our Germanic and Scythian ancestors when they first settled on the ruins of the western empire. Among such peoples, the sovereign or chief is only the greatest landlord in the country. He is supported in the same way as any other landlord, by revenue drawn from his own private estate, or from what modern Europe called the demesne of the crown: the lands held directly by the monarch. On ordinary occasions his subjects contribute nothing to his support, except when they need his authority to protect them from the oppression of some of their fellow subjects. The presents they give him on those occasions make up his whole ordinary revenue. Apart from some very extraordinary emergencies, perhaps, they are the whole of the income he derives from his dominion over them. When Agamemnon, in Homer, offers Achilles the sovereignty of seven Greek cities in exchange for his friendship, the only advantage he mentions is that the people would honor him with presents. As long as such presents, the profits of justice, or what may be called the fees of court, made up the whole ordinary revenue the sovereign drew from his sovereignty, it could hardly be expected, or even decently proposed, that he give them up entirely. It could be proposed, and often was, that he regulate them and fix them at definite amounts. But once they had been regulated and fixed, it remained very difficult, if not impossible, to stop an all-powerful person from extending them beyond those limits. So long as this state of things continued, therefore, the corruption of justice that naturally arose from the arbitrary and uncertain nature of these presents admitted of scarcely any effective remedy.

Over time, however, the sovereign's private estate became wholly insufficient to pay the costs of sovereignty. There were several causes, chiefly the continually rising expense of defending the nation against invasion by other nations. It then became necessary for the people, for their own security, to contribute toward this expense through taxes of various kinds. At that point it seems to have been very commonly stipulated that no present for the administration of justice should be accepted under any pretext, either by the sovereign or by his bailiffs and deputies, the judges. It seems to have been assumed that these presents could more easily be abolished altogether than effectively regulated and fixed. Judges were assigned fixed salaries, which were supposed to compensate them for the loss of whatever share they might have had in the ancient profits of justice, just as the taxes more than compensated the sovereign for the loss of his. Justice was then said to be administered free of charge.

In reality, justice has never been administered free of charge in any country. Lawyers and attorneys, at least, must always be paid by the parties, and if they were not, they would perform their duties even worse than they do. The fees paid to lawyers and attorneys each year amount, in every court, to a much larger sum than the judges' salaries. The fact that the crown pays those salaries cannot anywhere do much to reduce the necessary cost of a lawsuit. But judges were forbidden to receive any present or fee from the parties not so much to reduce that cost as to prevent the corruption of justice.

The office of judge is in itself so honorable that men are willing to accept it even with very small rewards. The lesser office of justice of the peace involves a good deal of trouble and, in most cases, no pay at all, yet most of our country gentlemen aspire to it. In any civilized country, the salaries of all the judges, high and low, together with the whole cost of administering and enforcing justice, make up only a very small part of the total expense of government, even where that business is not managed with great economy.

The whole expense of justice, moreover, could easily be paid by the fees of court. The public revenue could thus be freed entirely from a definite, though perhaps small, burden without exposing the administration of justice to any real risk of corruption. Fees of court are difficult to regulate effectively when a person as powerful as the sovereign is to share in them and to draw any considerable part of his revenue from them. They are very easy to regulate when the judge is the chief person who can profit from them. The law can easily compel a judge to respect a regulation, though it may not always be able to make the sovereign respect it. Suppose the fees of court were precisely regulated and fixed, and suppose they were paid all at once, at a set point in every case, to a cashier or receiver. He would then distribute them in known proportions among the various judges after the case was decided, and not before. Under such an arrangement there seems to be no more danger of corruption than when fees are prohibited altogether. Without adding much to the cost of a lawsuit, these fees could be made fully sufficient to pay the whole expense of justice. And since they would not be paid to the judges until the case was decided, they might give the court some incentive to examine and decide it diligently. In courts made up of a considerable number of judges, each judge's share could be proportioned to the hours and days he had spent examining the case, either in court or in a committee appointed by the court. In this way the fees might encourage the diligence of each individual judge. Public services are never better performed than when the reward comes only as a consequence of their being performed and is proportioned to the diligence employed in performing them. In the various parlements of France, the high courts of the kingdom, the fees of court make up by far the greater part of the judges' income. These fees are known as *épices* and *vacations*: the first name recalls the gifts of spices once presented to judges, and the second refers to payments for time spent on a case. After all deductions, the net salary the crown pays to a counselor or judge of the parlement of Toulouse, which ranks second in the kingdom in dignity, amounts to only 150 livres a year, about six pounds eleven shillings sterling. About seven years ago, that sum was the ordinary yearly wage of a common footman in the same city. The *épices* are also distributed according to the judges' diligence. A diligent judge earns a comfortable, though moderate, income from his office, while an idle one receives little more than his salary. These parlements are perhaps not very convenient courts of justice in many respects, but they have never been accused of corruption, and they seem never even to have been suspected of it.

Fees of court seem originally to have been the chief support of the various courts of justice in England. Each court tried to draw as much business to itself as it could, and for that reason it was willing to hear many suits that were never meant to fall within its jurisdiction. The Court of King's Bench, established only for the trial of criminal cases, began hearing civil suits, with the plaintiff claiming that the defendant, by failing to do him justice, had committed some trespass or misdemeanor. The Court of Exchequer, established to collect the king's revenue and to enforce payment only of debts owed to the king, began hearing all other debts arising from contracts, with the plaintiff alleging that he could not pay the king because the defendant would not pay him. Through such legal fictions, it often came to depend entirely on the parties which court they chose to try their case, and each court tried to attract as many cases as it could by offering greater speed and impartiality. The present admirable structure of the English courts of justice was perhaps formed in large part by this rivalry among their respective judges in earlier times. Each judge tried to provide, in his own court, the speediest and most effective remedy the law would allow for every kind of injustice. Originally, the courts of common law awarded only damages for breach of contract. The Court of Chancery, acting as a court of conscience, was the first to enforce specific performance, compelling a party actually to carry out the terms of an agreement. When the breach of contract consisted in failing to pay money, the injury could be compensated only by ordering payment, which amounted to specific performance of the agreement. In such cases, therefore, the remedy offered by the courts of law was sufficient. In other cases it was not. When a tenant sued his lord for wrongfully ousting him from his lease, the damages he recovered were in no way equivalent to possession of the land. For some time, therefore, all such cases went to the Court of Chancery, to the considerable loss of the courts of law. It was to win these cases back that the courts of law are said to have invented the artificial and fictitious writ of ejectment, which became the most effective remedy for wrongful ousting or dispossession from land.

A stamp duty on the legal proceedings of each court, collected by that court and applied to the support of its judges and other officers, might likewise provide enough revenue to pay the expense of administering justice without placing any burden on the general revenue of the society. In that case, admittedly, the judges might be tempted to multiply the proceedings in every case unnecessarily, in order to raise as much as possible from the duty. In modern Europe it has been the custom, on most occasions, to pay attorneys and court clerks according to the number of pages they had to write, though the court required each page to contain a set number of lines and each line a set number of words. To increase their pay, attorneys and clerks have contrived to multiply words far beyond any need, and in this way they have corrupted the legal language of, I believe, every court of justice in Europe. A similar temptation might perhaps produce a similar corruption in the forms of legal proceedings.

But whether the administration of justice is arranged so as to pay its own expenses, or whether the judges are maintained by fixed salaries paid to them from some other fund, there seems no need for the person or persons who hold executive power to manage that fund or to pay those salaries. The fund might come from the rent of landed estates, with each estate managed by the particular court it was meant to support. It might even come from the interest on a sum of money, which that court could likewise be entrusted to lend out. Part of the salary of the judges of the Court of Session in Scotland, though only a small part, does in fact come from the interest on such a sum. Yet the inherent instability of a fund of this kind seems to make it unsuitable for supporting an institution that ought to last forever.

The separation of judicial from executive power seems to have arisen originally from the growing business of society as it advanced in improvement. The administration of justice became so laborious and so complicated a duty that it demanded the undivided attention of whoever was charged with it. Because the person holding executive power lacked the leisure to decide private lawsuits himself, a deputy was appointed to decide them in his place. As Rome grew in power, the consul became too occupied with the political affairs of the state to attend to the administration of justice, so a praetor was appointed to administer it in his stead. As the European monarchies founded on the ruins of the Roman Empire developed, sovereigns and great lords everywhere came to regard the administration of justice as an office both too laborious and too lowly to perform in person. Everywhere, therefore, they relieved themselves of it by appointing a deputy, a bailiff, or a judge.

When judicial power is united with executive power, it is scarcely possible that justice will not often be sacrificed to what is commonly called politics. Those entrusted with the great interests of the state may sometimes, even without any corrupt motive, believe it necessary to sacrifice a private person's rights to those interests. Yet the liberty of every individual, his very sense of his own security, depends on the impartial administration of justice. If every individual is to feel perfectly secure in possessing every right that belongs to him, the judicial power must not only be separated from the executive power but made as independent of it as possible. The judge should not be removable from office at the whim of that power. Nor should the regular payment of his salary depend on that power's goodwill, or even on its careful management of its own finances.

#### Part III: On the Expense of Public Works and Public Institutions

The third and last duty of the sovereign or commonwealth is to erect and maintain those public institutions and public works which, though they may be of the greatest advantage to a large society, are nonetheless of such a nature that the profit could never repay the expense to any individual or small group of individuals, and which, therefore, no individual or small group can be expected to erect or maintain. The performance of this duty, too, requires very different levels of expense at different stages of society.

Beyond the public institutions and works needed for the defense of society and for the administration of justice, both of which have already been discussed, the remaining works and institutions of this kind are chiefly those that facilitate the society's commerce and those that promote the instruction of the people. Institutions for instruction are of two kinds: those for educating the young and those for instructing people of all ages. An examination of how the expense of these different kinds of public works and institutions may most properly be met will divide this third part of the present chapter into three articles.

##### Article I: On the Public Works and Institutions for Facilitating the Commerce of Society

*First, those necessary for facilitating commerce in general.*

That the building and maintenance of the public works that facilitate a country's commerce, such as good roads, bridges, navigable canals, and harbors, must require very different levels of expense at different stages of society is evident without proof. The cost of making and maintaining a country's public roads must plainly rise with the annual produce of its land and labor, which is to say with the quantity and weight of the goods that must be hauled along those roads. The strength of a bridge must be suited to the number and weight of the carriages likely to cross it. The depth and water supply of a navigable canal must be proportioned to the number and tonnage of the lighters, the flat-bottomed barges, likely to carry goods on it; and the size of a harbor must be proportioned to the amount of shipping likely to take shelter there.

There seems no necessity for the cost of these public works to be met from what is commonly called the public revenue, whose collection and spending are in most countries assigned to the executive power. Most such works can easily be managed so as to yield a particular revenue of their own, sufficient to cover their expense without placing any burden on the general revenue of the society.

A highway, a bridge, or a navigable canal, for example, can in most cases be both built and maintained by a small toll on the vehicles that use it; a harbor can be maintained by a moderate port duty on the tonnage of the ships that load or unload there. The coinage, another institution for facilitating commerce, not only pays its own way in many countries but also yields the sovereign a small revenue known as seignorage, a charge levied on the minting of coin. The post office, another institution with the same purpose, not only covers its own costs but in almost every country yields the sovereign a very considerable revenue besides.

When the carriages crossing a highway or a bridge, and the lighters sailing on a navigable canal, pay tolls in proportion to their weight or tonnage, they pay for the upkeep of those works exactly in proportion to the wear and tear they cause. It is hard to devise a fairer way of maintaining such works. This tax or toll, moreover, though it is advanced by the carrier, is ultimately paid by the consumer, to whom it is always charged in the price of the goods. But because such public works greatly reduce the cost of carriage, the goods reach the consumer more cheaply, toll and all, than they otherwise could; the toll raises their price by less than the cheapness of carriage lowers it. The person who ultimately pays the tax therefore gains more from the use to which it is put than he loses by paying it. His payment is exactly proportioned to his gain. It is, in reality, nothing more than a portion of that gain which he must give up in order to secure the rest. It seems impossible to imagine a fairer method of raising a tax. When the toll on carriages of luxury, such as coaches and post-chaises (hired traveling carriages), is set somewhat higher relative to their weight than the toll on vehicles of necessary use, such as carts and wagons, the idleness and vanity of the rich are made to contribute, quite effortlessly, to the relief of the poor, by making it cheaper to transport heavy goods to every part of the country.

When highways, bridges, canals, and the like are built and supported in this way by the commerce they carry, they can be built only where that commerce requires them, and therefore only where it is proper to build them. Their expense, and their grandeur and magnificence, must likewise be suited to what that commerce can afford to pay. They must, consequently, be built as it is proper to build them. A magnificent highway cannot be laid through an empty, uninhabited country with little or no commerce, merely because it happens to lead to the country villa of the intendant, the royal official who governs the province, or to that of some great lord whose favor the intendant finds it convenient to court. A great bridge cannot be thrown across a river at a spot where no one crosses, merely to improve the view from the windows of a neighboring palace. Such things sometimes happen in countries where works of this kind are financed by any revenue other than the one they themselves are capable of producing.

In several parts of Europe, the toll or lock duty on a canal is the property of private persons, whose private interest compels them to keep the canal in repair. If it is not kept in tolerable order, navigation necessarily stops altogether, and with it all the profit they can draw from the tolls. If those tolls were placed under the management of commissioners who had no interest in them, the commissioners might pay less attention to maintaining the works that produced them. The Canal of Languedoc cost the king of France and the province more than thirteen million livres, which, at twenty-eight livres to the mark of silver (the mark being a standard weight of silver, and this being the value of French money at the end of the seventeenth century), came to more than nine hundred thousand pounds sterling. When that great work was finished, the surest way of keeping it in constant repair was found to be to make a gift of the tolls to Riquet, the engineer who had planned and directed the work. Those tolls now constitute a very large estate for the various branches of that gentleman's family, who therefore have a strong interest in keeping the work in constant repair. Had the tolls been placed under commissioners with no such interest, they might perhaps have been squandered on ornamental and unnecessary expenses while the most essential parts of the works were left to fall into ruin.

The tolls for maintaining a highway cannot safely be made the property of private persons. A highway, even when entirely neglected, does not become wholly impassable, as a canal does. The owners of the tolls on a highway might therefore neglect its repair altogether and still go on collecting very nearly the same tolls. It is proper, then, that the tolls for maintaining such a work be placed under the management of commissioners or trustees.

In Great Britain, the abuses committed by trustees in managing these tolls have in many cases been very justly complained of. At many turnpikes, the toll gates on the main roads, the money collected is said to be more than double what would be needed to do the work in the most thorough manner, while the work itself is often done very sloppily and sometimes not done at all. This system of repairing highways by tolls, it should be observed, is not of long standing. We should not be surprised, therefore, if it has not yet reached the degree of perfection of which it seems capable. If men of low standing and unfit character are frequently appointed as trustees, and if proper courts of inspection and account have not yet been established to control their conduct and to reduce the tolls to what is barely sufficient for the work they are meant to pay for, the newness of the institution both explains and excuses these defects, most of which may in due time be gradually remedied by the wisdom of Parliament.

The money collected at the various turnpikes in Great Britain is supposed to exceed what is needed to repair the roads by so much that the savings which careful management might produce have been regarded, even by some ministers, as a very great resource that could at some point be applied to the needs of the state. Government, it has been argued, could take the management of the turnpikes into its own hands and employ soldiers, who would work for a very small addition to their pay, and so keep the roads in good order at much less expense than the trustees can, since the trustees have no workmen to employ except those who depend for their whole subsistence on their wages. A great revenue, perhaps half a million pounds, might be gained in this way, it has been claimed, without laying any new burden on the people, and the turnpike roads might be made to contribute to the general expense of the state, just as the post office does at present. (Since publishing the first two editions of this book, I have found good reason to believe that all the turnpike tolls levied in Great Britain do not produce a net revenue amounting to half a million, a sum that, under the management of government, would not be enough to keep five of the principal roads in the kingdom in repair.)

That a considerable revenue might be gained in this way I do not doubt, though probably nowhere near as much as the authors of this scheme have supposed. The plan itself, however, appears open to several very important objections.

First, if the turnpike tolls were ever regarded as one of the resources for meeting the needs of the state, they would certainly be raised whenever those needs were thought to require it. Given the policy of Great Britain, they would probably be raised very quickly. The ease with which a great revenue could be drawn from them would likely encourage the administration to resort to this resource very often. Though it may be more than doubtful whether half a million could be saved from the present tolls by any economy, there can be little doubt that a million might be saved from them if they were doubled, and perhaps two million if they were tripled. (I now have good reason to believe that all these conjectural sums are much too large.) This great revenue, moreover, could be raised without appointing a single new officer to collect and receive it. But turnpike tolls raised continually in this way, instead of facilitating the inland commerce of the country as they do now, would soon become a heavy encumbrance upon it. The cost of transporting all heavy goods from one part of the country to another would soon rise so much, and the market for such goods would consequently shrink so much, that their production would be largely discouraged, and the most important branches of the country's domestic industry would be wiped out altogether.

Second, a tax on carriages in proportion to their weight, though a very fair tax when applied solely to repairing the roads, is a very unfair one when applied to any other purpose, or to meeting the general needs of the state. When it is applied solely to road repair, each carriage is supposed to pay exactly for the wear and tear it causes. But when it is applied to any other purpose, each carriage pays for more than that wear and tear and contributes to some other need of the state. And because the turnpike toll raises the price of goods in proportion to their weight rather than their value, it falls chiefly on the consumers of coarse and bulky commodities, not on those of precious and light ones. Whatever need of the state this tax might be intended to supply would therefore be supplied chiefly at the expense of the poor rather than the rich, at the expense of those least able to supply it rather than those most able.

Third, if the government should at any time neglect the repair of the highways, it would be even harder than it is now to compel the proper use of any part of the turnpike tolls. A large revenue might thus be levied on the people without any of it being applied to the only purpose for which a revenue raised in this way should ever be used. If the low standing and poverty of the turnpike trustees sometimes make it difficult today to force them to repair their wrongs, the wealth and greatness of the government would make it ten times harder in the case supposed here.

In France, the funds set aside for repairing the highways are under the direct control of the executive power. They consist partly of a certain number of days' labor that country people in most parts of Europe are obliged to give to the repair of the highways, and partly of whatever portion of the general revenue of the state the king chooses to spare from his other expenses.

Under the ancient law of France, as under that of most other parts of Europe, the labor of the country people was directed by a local or provincial magistracy that had no direct dependence on the king's council. Under present practice, however, both that labor and any other fund the king may choose to assign for repairing the highways in a particular province or generality, the administrative district under an intendant, are entirely under the intendant's management. The intendant is an officer appointed and removed by the king's council; he receives his orders from it and is in constant correspondence with it. As despotism advances, the authority of the executive power gradually absorbs that of every other power in the state and takes over the management of every branch of revenue destined for any public purpose. In France, nevertheless, the great post roads, the roads that link the principal towns of the kingdom, are generally kept in good order, and in some provinces they are considerably better than most of the turnpike roads of England. But what we call the cross roads, which make up by far the greater part of the roads in the country, are entirely neglected and in many places are utterly impassable for any heavy carriage. In some places it is even dangerous to travel on horseback, and mules are the only conveyance that can safely be trusted. The proud minister of an ostentatious court may often take pleasure in carrying out a work of splendor and magnificence, such as a great highway, which is frequently seen by the leading nobility, whose applause not only flatters his vanity but even helps to support his interest at court. But to carry out a great number of small works, in which nothing that can be done will make any great show or excite the slightest admiration in any traveler, and which, in short, have nothing to recommend them but their extreme usefulness, is a task that appears in every respect too petty and trivial to deserve the attention of so great a magistrate. Under such an administration, therefore, such works are almost always entirely neglected.

In China and in several other governments of Asia, the executive power takes charge both of repairing the highways and of maintaining the navigable canals. These matters, it is said, are constantly urged upon the governor of each province in the instructions he receives, and the court's judgment of his conduct depends heavily on the attention he appears to have paid to this part of his instructions. This branch of public administration is accordingly said to receive great attention in all those countries, but particularly in China, where the highways, and still more the navigable canals, are claimed to far surpass anything of the kind known in Europe. The accounts of these works that have reached Europe, however, have generally been written by credulous and easily dazzled travelers, and often by stupid and lying missionaries. Had the works been examined by more intelligent eyes, and reported by more faithful witnesses, they might not seem so wonderful. The account that the French traveler Bernier gives of some works of this kind in Hindustan falls far short of what had been reported of them by other travelers more inclined to the marvelous than he was. It may also be that in those countries, as in France, the great roads and main lines of communication, which are likely to be talked about at court and in the capital, receive attention while all the rest are neglected. In China, moreover, as in Hindustan and several other governments of Asia, the sovereign's revenue comes almost entirely from a land tax or land rent, which rises and falls with the annual produce of the land. In such countries, therefore, the sovereign's great interest, his revenue, is necessarily and directly tied to the cultivation of the land, to the size of its produce, and to the value of that produce. But to make that produce as large and as valuable as possible, it must be given the widest possible market, and this requires establishing the freest, easiest, and cheapest communication among all the different parts of the country, which can be done only by means of the best roads and the best navigable canals. In no part of Europe, however, does the sovereign's revenue arise chiefly from a land tax or land rent. In all the great kingdoms of Europe, the greater part of it may perhaps ultimately depend on the produce of the land, but that dependence is neither so direct nor so evident. In Europe, therefore, the sovereign does not feel himself so directly called upon to promote the growth of the land's produce in both quantity and value, or to secure the widest market for that produce by maintaining good roads and canals. So even if it were true, which I suspect is more than a little doubtful, that in some parts of Asia this department of public administration is very properly managed by the executive power, there is not the slightest likelihood that, as things now stand, it could be managed even tolerably by that power anywhere in Europe.

Even public works that by their nature cannot yield any revenue to maintain themselves, but whose benefit is largely confined to some particular place or district, are always better maintained by a local or provincial revenue under a local and provincial administration than by the general revenue of the state, which the executive power must always manage. If the streets of London were lit and paved at the expense of the Treasury, is there any likelihood that they would be as well lit and paved as they are now, or even at so small an expense? The expense, moreover, instead of being raised by a local tax on the inhabitants of each particular street, parish, or district of London, would in that case be paid out of the general revenue of the state, and would consequently be raised by a tax on all the inhabitants of the kingdom, most of whom derive no benefit of any kind from the lighting and paving of the streets of London.

However enormous they may appear, the abuses that sometimes creep into the local and provincial administration of a local and provincial revenue are in reality almost always trifling compared with those that commonly occur in the administration and spending of the revenue of a great empire. They are also far more easily corrected. In Great Britain, under the local or provincial administration of the justices of the peace, the six days' labor that country people are obliged to contribute to repairing the highways may not always be applied very judiciously, but it is scarcely ever exacted with cruelty or oppression. In France, under the administration of the intendants, the crown's provincial administrators, the labor is applied no more judiciously, and it is frequently exacted in the most cruel and oppressive manner. These *corvées*, as such compulsory labor duties are called, are one of the principal instruments of tyranny by which those officials punish any parish or commune that has had the misfortune to fall under their displeasure.

###### Of the Public Works and Institutions Necessary for Facilitating Particular Branches of Commerce

The public works and institutions described above are intended to facilitate commerce in general. But to facilitate certain particular branches of commerce, particular institutions are needed, and these in turn require a particular and extraordinary expense.

Some branches of commerce carried on with barbarous and uncivilized nations require extraordinary protection. An ordinary warehouse or trading office would give little security to the goods of merchants trading to the western coast of Africa. To defend those goods from the hostile natives, the place where they are stored must be fortified to some degree. The disorders in the government of Hindustan have been thought to make a similar precaution necessary even among that mild and gentle people. It was on the pretext of protecting their persons and property from violence that both the English and the French East India companies were first permitted to build forts in that country. Among other nations, whose strong governments will not allow foreigners to hold any fortified place within their territory, it may be necessary to maintain an ambassador, minister, or consul. Such an official can settle disputes among his own countrymen according to their own customs, and in their disputes with the natives he can, by virtue of his public office, intervene with greater authority and give them more powerful protection than any private individual could. The interests of commerce have often made it necessary to keep ministers in foreign countries where neither war nor alliance would have required them. The commerce of the Turkey Company first led to the establishment of a regular ambassador at Constantinople, and the first English embassies to Russia arose entirely from commercial interests. The constant friction between those interests, which inevitably arose among the subjects of the different states of Europe, probably introduced the custom of keeping ambassadors or ministers permanently resident in all neighboring countries, even in peacetime. This custom was unknown in the ancient world and appears to be no older than the end of the fifteenth century or the beginning of the sixteenth. That is, it dates from the period when commerce first began to extend to most of the nations of Europe, and when those nations first began to pay attention to its interests.

It does not seem unreasonable that the extraordinary expense of protecting any particular branch of commerce should be paid for by a moderate tax on that branch. This might take the form of a moderate fee paid by traders when they first enter the trade, or, more equitably, a specific duty of a certain percentage on the goods they import from, or export to, the particular countries with which that trade is carried on. The protection of trade in general from pirates and plunderers is said to have prompted the first institution of customs duties. And if it was thought reasonable to impose a general tax on trade to pay for protecting trade in general, it seems equally reasonable to impose a particular tax on a particular branch of trade to pay for the extraordinary expense of protecting that branch.

The protection of trade in general has always been considered essential to the defense of the commonwealth, and for that reason a necessary part of the duty of the executive power. The collection and spending of the general customs duties have therefore always been left to that power. But the protection of any particular branch of trade is itself part of the general protection of trade, and therefore part of that same duty. If nations always acted consistently, the particular duties levied for such particular protection would always have been left to the executive power's disposal as well. In this respect, however, as in many others, nations have not always acted consistently. In most of the commercial states of Europe, particular companies of merchants have had the skill to persuade the legislature to entrust them with this part of the sovereign's duty, together with all the powers necessarily connected with it.

These companies may perhaps have been useful in first introducing certain branches of commerce, by making at their own expense an experiment that the state might not have thought it prudent to make. In the long run, however, they have proved universally either burdensome or useless, and they have either mismanaged the trade or confined it.

When such companies do not trade on a joint stock, but are obliged to admit any properly qualified person who pays a certain fee and agrees to submit to the company's regulations, with each member trading on his own capital and at his own risk, they are called regulated companies. When they trade on a joint stock, with each member sharing in the common profit or loss in proportion to his share of that stock, they are called joint-stock companies. Companies of either kind sometimes have exclusive privileges and sometimes do not.

Regulated companies resemble in every respect the trade guilds so common in the cities and towns of every country in Europe, and they are a kind of enlarged monopoly of the same sort. Just as no inhabitant of a town may practice an incorporated trade without first being admitted to the freedom of its guild, so in most cases no subject of the state may lawfully carry on any branch of foreign trade for which a regulated company has been established without first becoming a member of that company. The monopoly is more or less strict according to how difficult the terms of admission are, and according to how much authority the company's directors have, or how far they are able to manage things so as to keep most of the trade in the hands of themselves and their particular friends. In the oldest regulated companies, the privileges of apprenticeship were the same as in other guilds: a person who had served his apprenticeship under a member of the company was entitled to become a member himself, either without paying any fee or by paying a much smaller one than was demanded of others. The usual guild spirit, wherever the law does not restrain it, prevails in every regulated company. When these companies have been allowed to act according to their natural inclination, they have always tried to subject the trade to many burdensome regulations, so as to confine competition to as few people as possible. When the law has prevented them from doing this, they have become entirely useless and insignificant.

The regulated companies for foreign commerce that still exist in Great Britain are the ancient Company of Merchant Adventurers, now commonly called the Hamburg Company, the Russia Company, the Eastland Company, the Turkey Company, and the African Company.

The terms of admission to the Hamburg Company are now said to be quite easy, and its directors either lack the power to subject the trade to any troublesome restrictions or regulations or, at least, have not lately exercised it. This has not always been so. Around the middle of the seventeenth century, the admission fee was fifty pounds, and at one time a hundred pounds, and the company's conduct was said to be extremely oppressive. In 1643, in 1645, and in 1661, the clothiers and independent traders of the west of England complained to Parliament that the company members were monopolists who restricted the trade and oppressed the country's manufactures. Although those complaints produced no act of Parliament, they had probably intimidated the company enough to force it to reform its conduct. Since then, at least, there have been no complaints against it. An act passed in the tenth and eleventh years of William III's reign (chapter 6) reduced the admission fee for the Russia Company to five pounds, and an act of the twenty-fifth year of Charles II's reign (chapter 7) reduced the fee for the Eastland Company to forty shillings, while at the same time exempting Sweden, Denmark, and Norway, all the countries on the northern side of the Baltic, from that company's exclusive charter. The conduct of those companies had probably prompted these two acts of Parliament. Before then, Sir Josiah Child had described both these companies and the Hamburg Company as extremely oppressive, and had blamed their bad management for the low state of the trade that England then carried on with the countries covered by their charters. But though such companies may not be very oppressive at present, they are certainly entirely useless.
