To be merely useless is perhaps the highest praise that can ever justly be given to a regulated company, and all three of the companies just mentioned seem, in their present state, to deserve it.

The admission fee for the Turkey Company was formerly twenty-five pounds for anyone under twenty-six years of age and fifty pounds for anyone older. Only merchants in the strict sense could be admitted, a restriction that excluded all shopkeepers and retailers. Under one bylaw, no British manufactures could be exported to Turkey except in the company's general ships, and since those ships always sailed from the port of London, this restriction confined the trade to that expensive port and the traders to those who lived in or near London. Under another bylaw, no one living within twenty miles of London who was not a freeman of the City could be admitted as a member. Combined with the previous rule, this necessarily excluded everyone but the freemen of London. Because the timing of the loading and sailing of the general ships depended entirely on the directors, they could easily fill the ships with their own goods and those of their particular friends, shutting out others on the pretext that they had submitted their requests too late. In this state of affairs, the company was in every respect a strict and oppressive monopoly. These abuses led to an act of the twenty-sixth year of George II's reign (chapter 18), which reduced the admission fee to twenty pounds for everyone, without any distinction of age and without any restriction either to merchants in the strict sense or to the freemen of London. The act granted all such persons the liberty of exporting, from any port in Great Britain to any port in Turkey, all British goods whose export was not prohibited, on condition that they paid both the general customs duties and the particular duties assessed to cover the company's necessary expenses, and that they submitted to the lawful authority of the British ambassador and consuls resident in Turkey and to the company's duly enacted bylaws. To guard against oppression through those bylaws, the same act provided that if any seven members of the company considered themselves wronged by a bylaw enacted after the act's passage, they could appeal to the Board of Trade and Plantations, whose authority has since passed to a committee of the Privy Council, provided the appeal was brought within twelve months of the bylaw's enactment. It further provided that if any seven members considered themselves wronged by a bylaw enacted before the act's passage, they could bring a similar appeal, provided it was within twelve months of the day the act took effect. The experience of a single year, however, may not always be enough to reveal to all the members of a large company the harmful tendency of a particular bylaw, and if several of them discover it later, neither the Board of Trade nor the committee of the council can give them any redress. Moreover, the purpose of most of the bylaws of all regulated companies, as of all other guilds, is not so much to oppress those who are already members as to discourage others from becoming members. This can be done not only through a high fee but through many other devices. The constant aim of such companies is always to raise their own rate of profit as high as they can, and to keep the market as understocked as they can, both for the goods they export and for those they import. This can be done only by restraining competition, or by discouraging new adventurers from entering the trade. Furthermore, a fee of even twenty pounds, though perhaps not enough to discourage anyone from entering the Turkey trade with the intention of staying in it, may be enough to discourage a speculative merchant from risking a single venture in it. In every trade, the regular established traders, even when they are not incorporated, naturally combine to raise profits, and nothing is so likely to keep those profits down to their proper level at all times as the occasional competition of speculative adventurers. Although this act of Parliament opened the Turkey trade to some extent, many people still consider it very far from entirely free. The Turkey Company helps to maintain an ambassador and two or three consuls, who, like other public ministers, ought to be maintained entirely by the state, with the trade opened to all of His Majesty's subjects. The various taxes the company levies for this and its other corporate purposes could provide a revenue more than sufficient to allow the state to maintain such ministers.

Sir Josiah Child observed that although regulated companies had often supported public ministers, they had never maintained forts or garrisons in the countries they traded with, whereas joint-stock companies frequently had. And in reality, regulated companies seem much less fit for this kind of service than joint-stock companies. First, the directors of a regulated company have no particular interest in the prosperity of the company's general trade, for whose sake such forts and garrisons are maintained. The decline of that general trade may even often work to the advantage of their own private trade, since by reducing the number of their competitors it may allow them both to buy more cheaply and to sell more dearly. The directors of a joint-stock company, by contrast, have only their share in the profits made on the common stock entrusted to their management. They have no private trade of their own whose interest can be separated from that of the company's general trade. Their private interest is bound up with the prosperity of the company's general trade and with the maintenance of the forts and garrisons necessary for its defense, so they are more likely to give that maintenance the continual and careful attention it necessarily requires. Second, the directors of a joint-stock company always manage a large capital, the company's joint stock, part of which they may often quite properly spend on building, repairing, and maintaining the necessary forts and garrisons. The directors of a regulated company, however, manage no common capital and have no other fund for this purpose than the irregular revenue from admission fees and from the corporate duties imposed on the company's trade. Even if they had the same interest in maintaining such forts and garrisons, therefore, they could seldom have the same means of making that attention effective. The maintenance of a public minister, which requires scarcely any attention and only a moderate and limited expense, is a business far better suited to both the temperament and the capacities of a regulated company.

Long after Sir Josiah Child's time, however, in 1750, a regulated company was established: the present Company of Merchants Trading to Africa. It was at first expressly charged with maintaining all the British forts and garrisons lying between Cape Blanc and the Cape of Good Hope, and afterward with maintaining only those lying between Cape Rouge and the Cape of Good Hope. The act establishing this company, passed in the twenty-third year of George II's reign (chapter 51), seems to have had two distinct aims: first, to restrain effectively the oppressive and monopolizing spirit natural to the directors of a regulated company; and second, to force them, as far as possible, to give a kind of attention that does not come naturally to them, namely to the maintenance of forts and garrisons.

For the first of these purposes, the admission fee is limited to forty shillings. The company is prohibited from trading in its corporate capacity or on a joint stock, from borrowing money under its common seal, and from placing any restrictions on the trade, which may be carried on freely from any place by anyone who is a British subject and has paid the fee. The company is governed by a committee of nine, who meet in London but are elected annually by the freemen of the company at London, Bristol, and Liverpool, three from each city. No committee member may remain in office for more than three consecutive years. Any committee member could be removed by the Board of Trade and Plantations, and now by a committee of the council, after being heard in his own defense. The committee is forbidden to export slaves from Africa or to import any African goods into Great Britain. But because it is charged with maintaining forts and garrisons, it may export goods and stores of various kinds from Great Britain to Africa for that purpose. Out of the money it receives from the company, the committee is allowed a sum not exceeding eight hundred pounds to cover the salaries of its clerks and agents in London, Bristol, and Liverpool, the rent of its offices in London, and all other expenses of management, commission, and agency in England. Whatever remains of this sum after these expenses are paid, the members may divide among themselves as compensation for their trouble, in whatever manner they think fit. Under this constitution, one might have expected the spirit of monopoly to be effectively restrained and the first purpose sufficiently achieved. It seems, however, that it was not. Although an act of the fourth year of George III's reign (chapter 20) had placed the fort of Senegal and all its dependencies under the Company of Merchants Trading to Africa, an act passed the following year (the fifth of George III, chapter 44) removed from the company's jurisdiction not only Senegal and its dependencies but the whole coast from the port of Salé, in southern Barbary, to Cape Rouge. That territory was vested in the Crown, and its trade was declared open to all His Majesty's subjects. The company had been suspected of restraining the trade and establishing some kind of improper monopoly. It is not easy, however, to see how it could have done so under the regulations of the act of the twenty-third year of George II. Yet I observe that in the printed debates of the House of Commons, which are not always the most reliable records of the truth, the company has been accused of exactly this. Since the members of the committee of nine were all merchants, and the governors and agents at the various forts and settlements all depended on them, it is not unlikely that those officials gave special attention to the consignments and commissions of the committee members, which would have established a real monopoly.

For the second purpose, the maintenance of the forts and garrisons, Parliament has allotted the company an annual sum, generally about £13,000. The committee is obliged to account each year for the proper use of this sum to the cursitor baron of the Exchequer, a minor judge of that court whose duties were chiefly administrative, and his account is afterward to be laid before Parliament. But Parliament, which pays so little attention to how millions are spent, is unlikely to pay much to the spending of £13,000 a year. And the cursitor baron of the Exchequer, given his profession and training, is unlikely to be deeply versed in what forts and garrisons ought properly to cost. Captains of His Majesty's navy, it is true, or any other commissioned officers appointed by the Board of Admiralty, may inquire into the condition of the forts and garrisons and report their findings to that board. But the board appears to have no direct jurisdiction over the committee, nor any authority to correct those whose conduct it may investigate in this way. Nor, besides, are naval captains supposed always to be deeply learned in the science of fortification. Removal from an office that can be held for only three years, and whose lawful income even during that term is very small, seems to be the most severe punishment to which any committee member is liable for any fault short of outright malfeasance or embezzlement, whether of public money or of the company's. The fear of that punishment can never be a strong enough motive to compel continual and careful attention to a business in which he has no other interest. The committee has been accused of sending bricks and stones out from England to repair Cape Coast Castle on the coast of Guinea, a task for which Parliament had several times granted an extraordinary sum of money. These bricks and stones, after so long a voyage, were moreover said to be of such poor quality that the walls repaired with them had to be rebuilt from the foundations. The forts and garrisons north of Cape Rouge are not only maintained at the expense of the state but are under the direct government of the executive power. Why those south of that cape, which are also maintained at least partly at the state's expense, should be under a different government, it is hard even to imagine a good reason. The protection of the Mediterranean trade was the original purpose, or pretext, for the garrisons at Gibraltar and Minorca, and the maintenance and government of those garrisons have always been, very properly, entrusted not to the Turkey Company but to the executive power. The pride and dignity of that power rest largely on the extent of its dominions, and it is unlikely to neglect anything necessary for their defense. The garrisons at Gibraltar and Minorca have, accordingly, never been neglected. Although Minorca has been captured twice, and is now probably lost for good, that disaster has never been blamed on any negligence by the executive. I would not, however, wish to be understood as suggesting that either of those expensive garrisons was ever, even in the slightest degree, necessary for the purpose for which they were originally torn away from the Spanish monarchy. That dismemberment may never have accomplished anything of real consequence except to estrange England from her natural ally, the king of Spain, and to bind the two principal branches of the House of Bourbon in a far closer and more lasting alliance than the ties of blood could ever have produced.

Joint-stock companies, whether established by royal charter or by act of Parliament, differ in several respects not only from regulated companies but also from private partnerships.

First, in a private partnership, no partner can transfer his share to another person or bring a new member into the firm without the consent of the partnership. Each member may, however, after giving proper notice, withdraw from the partnership and demand payment of his share of the common capital. In a joint-stock company, by contrast, no member can demand that the company pay out his share, but each member can, without the company's consent, transfer his share to another person and thereby bring in a new member. The value of a share in a joint stock is always the price it will fetch in the market, and this may be greater or less, in any proportion, than the sum for which its owner is credited in the company's capital.

Second, in a private partnership, each partner is liable for the debts contracted by the firm to the full extent of his fortune. In a joint-stock company, each partner is liable only to the extent of his share.

The trade of a joint-stock company is always managed by a court of directors. This court is often subject, in many respects, to the oversight of a general court of proprietors, the assembled body of shareholders. But most of these proprietors seldom claim to understand anything about the company's business, and unless factional strife happens to take hold among them, they give themselves no trouble over it and contentedly accept whatever half-yearly or yearly dividend the directors see fit to pay them. This complete freedom from trouble, and from any risk beyond a fixed sum, encourages many people to venture their money in joint-stock companies who would on no account risk their fortunes in a private partnership. Such companies therefore commonly attract far larger capitals than any private partnership can boast. The trading capital of the South Sea Company at one time amounted to more than £33,800,000. The divided capital of the Bank of England currently stands at £10,780,000. The directors of such companies, however, being managers of other people's money rather than their own, cannot reasonably be expected to watch over it with the same anxious vigilance with which partners in a private firm often watch over their own. Like the stewards of a rich man, they are inclined to regard attention to small matters as beneath their master's dignity, and they very readily excuse themselves from it. Negligence and extravagance must therefore always prevail, to a greater or lesser degree, in the management of such a company's affairs. This is why joint-stock companies engaged in foreign trade have seldom been able to hold their own in competition with private traders. They have very rarely succeeded without an exclusive privilege, and often have not succeeded even with one. Without an exclusive privilege, they have generally mismanaged the trade; with one, they have both mismanaged it and confined it.

The Royal African Company, predecessor of the present African Company, held an exclusive privilege by royal charter. But because that charter had never been confirmed by act of Parliament, the trade was, as a consequence of the Declaration of Rights, thrown open to all His Majesty's subjects soon after the Revolution of 1688. The Hudson's Bay Company stands in the same legal position as the Royal African Company did: its exclusive charter has never been confirmed by act of Parliament. The South Sea Company, for as long as it remained a trading company, held an exclusive privilege confirmed by act of Parliament, as does the present United Company of Merchants Trading to the East Indies.

The Royal African Company soon found that it could not withstand the competition of private traders, whom, despite the Declaration of Rights, it continued for some time to call "interlopers" and to prosecute as such. In 1698, however, the private traders were made subject to a duty of ten percent on nearly every branch of their trade, the proceeds to be used by the company for the upkeep of its forts and garrisons. Yet even with this heavy tax on its rivals, the company still could not hold its own. Its capital and credit steadily declined. By 1712 its debts had grown so large that a special act of Parliament was thought necessary, both for the company's protection and for that of its creditors. The act provided that a resolution supported by two-thirds of these creditors, measured both by number and by the value of their claims, should bind all the rest, both as to the time the company would be allowed for paying its debts and as to any other arrangement that might be thought fit concerning them. By 1730 its affairs were in such disorder that it was wholly unable to maintain its forts and garrisons, which had been the sole purpose and pretext of its founding. From that year until the company's final dissolution, Parliament judged it necessary to grant an annual sum of £10,000 for their upkeep. In 1732, after many years of losses in the trade of carrying enslaved Africans to the West Indies, the company at last resolved to abandon it altogether: it would sell the slaves it purchased on the African coast to private traders bound for America, and would employ its own agents in a trade with the interior of Africa for gold dust, elephant ivory, dyestuffs, and similar goods. But it fared no better in this narrower trade than it had in its former, broader one. Its affairs continued their gradual decline until at last, bankrupt in every respect, the company was dissolved by act of Parliament, and its forts and garrisons were transferred to the present regulated company of merchants trading to Africa. Before the Royal African Company was founded, three other joint-stock companies had been established in succession for the African trade. All were equally unsuccessful. Each of them, however, held an exclusive charter, which, though never confirmed by act of Parliament, was in those days believed to confer a genuine exclusive privilege.

The Hudson's Bay Company, before its misfortunes in the recent war, had been far more fortunate than the Royal African Company. Its necessary expenses are much smaller. The entire number of people it maintains in its various settlements and outposts, which it has honored with the name of "forts," is said not to exceed one hundred and twenty. This number is nonetheless enough to prepare in advance the cargo of furs and other goods needed to load the company's ships, which, because of the ice, can seldom remain more than six or eight weeks in those waters. Private traders could not, for several years at least, acquire this advantage of having a cargo ready and waiting, and without it there seems to be no possibility of trading to Hudson's Bay at all. The company's moderate capital, which is said not to exceed £110,000, may moreover be sufficient to let it buy up the whole, or nearly the whole, of the trade and surplus produce of the vast but impoverished country covered by its charter. Accordingly, no private traders have ever attempted to trade to that country in competition with it. The company has therefore always enjoyed an exclusive trade in fact, though it may have no right to one in law. Beyond all this, the company's moderate capital is said to be divided among a very small number of proprietors. A joint-stock company with few proprietors and a moderate capital comes very close in nature to a private partnership, and may be capable of nearly the same degree of vigilance and attention. It is no wonder, then, that thanks to these several advantages the Hudson's Bay Company was able, before the recent war, to carry on its trade with a considerable degree of success. It seems unlikely, however, that its profits ever came near what the late Mr. Dobbs imagined them to be. A far more sober and judicious writer, Mr. Anderson, author of the *Historical and Chronological Deduction of the Origin of Commerce*, rightly observes that when one examines the accounts Mr. Dobbs himself gave of the company's exports and imports over several consecutive years, and makes proper allowance for its extraordinary risks and expenses, its profits do not appear to be worth envying, nor do they seem to exceed the ordinary profits of trade by much, if at all.

The South Sea Company never had any forts or garrisons to maintain, and so was entirely spared one great expense to which other joint-stock companies in foreign trade are subject. But it had an immense capital divided among an immense number of proprietors. Folly, negligence, and extravagance were therefore naturally to be expected throughout the management of its affairs. The fraud and recklessness of its speculative share-dealing schemes are well enough known, and an account of them would be beside the present subject. Its commercial ventures were not much better conducted. The first trade it undertook was that of supplying the Spanish West Indies with enslaved Africans, a trade in which it held the exclusive privilege under what was called the Asiento Contract, granted to it by the Treaty of Utrecht. Since little profit was expected from this trade, both the Portuguese and the French companies that had held it on the same terms before having been ruined by it, the company was allowed, by way of compensation, to send one ship of a fixed tonnage each year to trade directly with the Spanish West Indies. Of the ten voyages this annual ship was permitted to make, the company is said to have made a considerable gain on one, that of the *Royal Caroline* in 1731, and to have lost money, to a greater or lesser extent, on nearly all the rest. Its factors and agents blamed this poor performance on the extortion and oppression of the Spanish government, but it was perhaps chiefly due to the extravagance and plundering of those very factors and agents, some of whom are said to have made great fortunes in a single year. In 1734 the company petitioned the king for permission to dispose of the trade and tonnage of its annual ship, on account of the meager profit it yielded, and to accept whatever equivalent it could obtain from the king of Spain.

In 1724 the company had taken up the whale fishery. It held no monopoly in this trade, but as long as it carried it on, no other British subjects seem to have engaged in it. Of the eight voyages its ships made to Greenland, it gained on one and lost on all the rest. After the eighth and final voyage, when it had sold off its ships, stores, and equipment, the company found that its total loss on this branch of business, capital and interest included, came to more than £237,000.

In 1722 the company petitioned Parliament for permission to divide its immense capital of more than £33,800,000, the whole of which had been lent to the government, into two equal parts. One half, amounting to more than £16,900,000, was to be placed on the same footing as other government annuities and shielded from the debts contracted and losses incurred by the directors in pursuing their commercial ventures; the other half was to remain, as before, a trading capital, exposed to those debts and losses. The request was too reasonable to be refused. In 1733 the company petitioned Parliament again, asking that three-quarters of its trading capital be converted into annuity stock, leaving only one-quarter as trading capital, exposed to the hazards of its directors' mismanagement. By this time both its annuity stock and its trading capital had each been reduced by more than two million pounds through various repayments from the government, so that this remaining quarter amounted to only £3,662,784, 8 shillings, and 6 pence. In 1748, by the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, all the company's claims against the king of Spain arising from the Asiento Contract were surrendered in exchange for what was supposed to be an equivalent. Its trade with the Spanish West Indies came to an end, the remainder of its trading capital was converted into annuity stock, and the company ceased in every respect to be a trading company.

It should be noted that in the trade the South Sea Company conducted through its annual ship, the only trade from which it was ever expected to make any considerable profit, it was not without competitors in either the foreign or the home market. At Cartagena, Portobelo, and Veracruz it faced the competition of Spanish merchants, who brought European goods from Cadiz to those markets of the same kind as the outbound cargo of the company's ship; and in England it faced the competition of English merchants, who imported from Cadiz goods from the Spanish West Indies of the same kind as the ship's return cargo. The goods of both the Spanish and the English merchants were, it is true, perhaps subject to higher duties. But the losses caused by the negligence, extravagance, and corruption of the company's employees had probably amounted to a tax far heavier than all those duties combined. That a joint-stock company should be able to carry on any branch of foreign trade successfully, when private traders can enter into any kind of open and fair competition with it, seems contrary to all experience.

The old English East India Company was established in 1600 by a charter from Queen Elizabeth. In the first twelve voyages it fitted out for India, it appears to have traded as a regulated company, with separate capitals for each venture, though only in the company's general ships. In 1612 its members combined into a joint stock. The charter was exclusive, and although it was never confirmed by act of Parliament, it was in those days believed to confer a genuine exclusive privilege. For many years, therefore, the company was not much troubled by interlopers. Its capital, which never exceeded £744,000, in shares of £50 each, was neither so enormous nor its dealings so extensive as to furnish either an excuse for gross negligence and extravagance or a cover for gross corruption. Despite some extraordinary losses, caused partly by the malice of the Dutch East India Company and partly by other misfortunes, it carried on a successful trade for many years. But in the course of time, as the principles of liberty came to be better understood, it grew ever more doubtful how far a royal charter not confirmed by act of Parliament could confer an exclusive privilege. On this question the decisions of the courts were not consistent, but shifted with the authority of the government and the temper of the times. Interlopers multiplied, and toward the end of the reign of Charles II, throughout that of James II, and during part of that of William III, they reduced the company to great distress. In 1698 a proposal was put before Parliament to lend the government two million pounds at eight percent, on condition that the subscribers be incorporated as a new East India Company with exclusive privileges. The old East India Company offered £700,000, nearly the whole of its capital, at four percent on the same terms. But such was the state of public credit at the time that it suited the government better to borrow two million pounds at eight percent than £700,000 at four. The new subscribers' proposal was accepted, and a new East India Company was established accordingly. The old company, however, retained the right to continue its trade until 1701. It had, moreover, very shrewdly subscribed £315,000 into the stock of the new company in the name of its treasurer. Because of careless wording in the act of Parliament that vested the East India trade in the subscribers to this two-million-pound loan, it was not clear that they were all obliged to combine into a joint stock. A few private traders, whose subscriptions came to only £7,200, insisted on their right to trade separately on their own capital and at their own risk. The old East India Company had the right to a separate trade on its own capital until 1701, and it also had the right, both before and after that date, like any other private trader, to a separate trade on the £315,000 it had subscribed into the new company's stock. The competition of the two companies with the private traders, and with each other, is said to have very nearly ruined them both. On a later occasion, in 1750, when a proposal was put before Parliament to place the trade under the management of a regulated company and so open it up to some degree, the East India Company, in opposing the proposal, described in very strong terms what it considered the miserable effects of this earlier competition. In India, the company said, it had driven the price of goods so high that they were not worth buying, and in England, by glutting the market, it had driven their price so low that no profit could be made on them. That a more plentiful supply must have greatly lowered the price of Indian goods in the English market, to the great advantage and convenience of the public, can hardly be doubted. But that it should have greatly raised their price in the Indian market seems quite improbable, since all the additional demand that competition could have created must have been no more than a drop of water in the immense ocean of Indian commerce. Besides, an increase in demand, though it may at first sometimes raise the price of goods, never fails to lower it in the long run. It encourages production and thereby increases competition among producers, who, in order to undersell one another, resort to new divisions of labor and new improvements in technique that might otherwise never have been thought of. The miserable effects the company complained of were cheaper consumption and encouragement to production, precisely the two effects that it is the great business of political economy to promote. The competition of which the company gave so doleful an account, however, had not been allowed to last long. In 1702 the two companies were partly united by a three-party agreement, to which the queen was the third party, and in 1708 they were fully consolidated by act of Parliament into a single company under their present name, the United Company of Merchants Trading to the East Indies. It was thought worthwhile to insert a clause in this act allowing the separate traders to continue their trade until Michaelmas, the feast of September 29, 1711, while at the same time empowering the directors, upon three years' notice, to buy out their small capital of £7,200 and so convert the company's entire capital into a joint stock. By the same act, in return for a new loan to the government, the company's capital was increased from two million pounds to £3,200,000. In 1743 the company advanced another million to the government. But because this million was raised not by a call upon the proprietors but by selling annuities and issuing bonds, it did not increase the capital on which the proprietors could claim a dividend. It did, however, increase the company's trading capital, since it was just as liable as the other £3,200,000 for the losses suffered and debts contracted by the company in pursuing its commercial ventures. From 1708, or at least from 1711, the company, freed from all competitors and firmly established in the monopoly of English trade with the East Indies, carried on a successful trade and paid its proprietors a moderate annual dividend out of its profits. During the war with France that began in 1741, the ambition of Monsieur Dupleix, the French governor of Pondicherry, drew the company into the wars of the Carnatic and the politics of the Indian princes. After many notable victories and equally notable defeats, it finally lost Madras, then its principal settlement in India. Madras was restored to it by the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, and at about this time the spirit of war and conquest seems to have taken hold of the company's servants in India, and never to have left them since. During the war with France that began in 1755, the company's forces shared in the general good fortune of British arms. They defended Madras, took Pondicherry, recovered Calcutta, and acquired the revenues of a rich and extensive territory, said at the time to amount to more than three million pounds a year. The company remained in undisturbed possession of this revenue for several years, but in 1767 the government laid claim to its territorial acquisitions, and to the revenue arising from them, as rightfully belonging to the Crown, and the company, in settlement of this claim, agreed to pay the government £400,000 a year. Before this, the company had gradually raised its dividend from about six to ten percent; that is, on its capital of £3,200,000 it had increased the dividend by £128,000, raising it from £192,000 to £320,000 a year. At about this time it was attempting to raise the dividend still further, to twelve and a half percent, which would have made its annual payments to its proprietors equal to what it had agreed to pay the government each year, namely £400,000. But during the two years in which its agreement with the government was to run, it was prevented from any further increase in its dividend by two successive acts of Parliament, the purpose of which was to enable it to make faster progress in paying off its debts, then estimated at more than six or seven million pounds sterling. In

1769, they renewed their agreement with the government for another five years, on the condition that during that period they would be allowed to raise their dividend gradually to twelve and a half percent, though never by more than one percent in any single year. Even at its highest point, therefore, this increase in the dividend could add only £680,000 to the company's combined annual payments to its proprietors and to the government, beyond what those payments had been before its recent territorial acquisitions. The supposed gross revenue of those territories has already been mentioned. According to an account brought home in 1769 by the *Cruttenden*, an East India Company merchant ship, the net revenue, after all deductions and military expenses, was stated at £2,048,747. The company was said at the same time to possess a further revenue of £439,000, drawn partly from land but chiefly from the customs duties established at its various settlements. The profits of its trade, too, amounted at this time to at least £400,000 a year according to the testimony of its chairman before the House of Commons, and to at least £500,000 according to that of its accountant. Even by the lowest estimate, those profits at least equaled the highest dividend that was to be paid to the proprietors. So large a revenue could certainly have supported an increase of £680,000 in the company's annual payments while still leaving a substantial sinking fund, a reserve set aside each year to retire debt, large enough to reduce its obligations rapidly. Yet by 1773 its debts, far from shrinking, had grown. The company had fallen into arrears with the Treasury on the annual payment of £400,000. It owed the customhouse for unpaid duties. It owed the Bank of England a large sum of borrowed money. And it faced a fourth debt of more than £1,200,000 in bills of exchange drawn on it from India and recklessly accepted. The distress caused by these accumulated claims forced the company to cut its dividend at a stroke to six percent and to throw itself on the mercy of the government, begging first to be released from any further payment of the agreed £400,000 a year, and second for a loan of £1,400,000 to save it from immediate bankruptcy. The great increase in the company's fortune had apparently done nothing except give its servants a pretext for greater extravagance, and a cover for greater corruption, out of all proportion even to that increase. The conduct of the company's servants in India, and the general state of its affairs in both India and Europe, became the subject of a parliamentary inquiry, which led to several very important changes in the constitution of its government at home and abroad. In India, its principal settlements of Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta, which until then had been entirely independent of one another, were placed under a governor-general assisted by a council of four members. Parliament reserved to itself the first appointment of this governor and council, who were to reside at Calcutta, since that city had now become what Madras had formerly been: the most important of the English settlements in India. The Mayor's Court of Calcutta, originally created to try commercial cases arising in the city and its neighborhood, had gradually extended its jurisdiction as the empire expanded. It was now cut back and confined to its original purpose, and in its place a new supreme court of justice was established, consisting of a chief justice and three judges appointed by the Crown. In Europe, the holding required to entitle a proprietor to vote in the company's general courts was raised from £500, the original price of a share in the company's stock, to £1,000. To vote on this qualification, moreover, a proprietor who had acquired his stock by purchase rather than inheritance now had to have held it for at least one year, instead of the six months previously required. The court of twenty-four directors had formerly been elected every year; it was now enacted that each director would henceforth be chosen for four years, with six of them leaving office by rotation each year and being ineligible for reelection when the six new directors were chosen for the following year. As a result of these changes, it was expected that both the court of proprietors and the court of directors would act with more dignity and steadiness than they usually had in the past. But it seems impossible, by any changes whatever, to make those courts in any way fit to govern a great empire, or even to share in governing one, because most of their members will always have too small a stake in that empire's prosperity to give serious attention to whatever might promote it. A man of great fortune, and sometimes even a man of small fortune, is often willing to buy a £1,000 share of India stock simply for the influence he expects to gain from a vote in the court of proprietors. That vote gives him a share, if not in the plunder of India, then at least in the appointment of its plunderers. The court of directors makes those appointments, but it is necessarily subject in some degree to the influence of the proprietors, who not only elect the directors but sometimes overrule their appointments of the company's servants in India. Provided he can enjoy this influence for a few years and use it to provide for a certain number of his friends, such a proprietor often cares little about the dividend, or even about the value of the stock on which his vote is based. About the prosperity of the great empire whose government his vote allows him to share, he seldom cares at all. No other sovereigns ever were, or by the nature of things ever could be, so completely indifferent to the happiness or misery of their subjects, the improvement or ruin of their territories, and the glory or disgrace of their administration as the greater part of the proprietors of such a trading company are, and from irresistible moral causes must necessarily be. Some of the new regulations introduced as a result of the parliamentary inquiry were more likely to increase this indifference than to reduce it. A resolution of the House of Commons, for example, declared that once the £1,400,000 lent to the company by the government had been repaid, and its bonded debts reduced to £1,500,000, the company might then, and only then, pay a dividend of eight percent on its capital. Whatever remained of its revenues and net profits at home was to be divided into four parts: three would be paid into the Exchequer for public use, and the fourth would be held in reserve as a fund either for further reducing the bonded debt or for meeting any other unforeseen needs the company might face. But if the company had been poor stewards and poor sovereigns when the whole of its net revenue and profits belonged to itself and was at its own disposal, it was surely not likely to do better once three-quarters of that revenue belonged to other people, and the remaining quarter, though spent for the company's benefit, was to be spent under the supervision and with the approval of others.

The company might well prefer that its own servants and dependents enjoy either the pleasure of squandering, or the profit of embezzling, whatever surplus remained after the proposed eight percent dividend was paid, rather than see that surplus pass into the hands of people with whom these resolutions could hardly fail to put it somewhat at odds. The interest of those servants and dependents might carry so much weight in the court of proprietors as to incline it at times to protect the authors of depredations committed in direct defiance of its own authority. For most proprietors, upholding the authority of their own court might sometimes matter less than protecting the very people who had defied it.

The regulations of 1773, accordingly, did not end the disorder of the company's government in India. During a brief spell of good conduct, the company had at one point gathered more than £3,000,000 sterling into the treasury at Calcutta, and it afterward extended either its rule or its plundering over a vast additional territory that included some of the richest and most fertile regions of India. Despite all this, everything was wasted and destroyed. The company found itself wholly unprepared to halt or resist the invasion of Hyder Ali, and as a result of these disorders it is now, in 1784, in greater distress than ever, and is once again reduced to begging the government's help to stave off immediate bankruptcy. The various parties in Parliament have proposed different plans for the better management of its affairs, and all of those plans seem to agree in assuming what was always abundantly evident: that the company is entirely unfit to govern its territorial possessions. Even the company itself seems convinced of its own incapacity to that extent, and therefore appears willing to surrender those possessions to the government.

The right to make war and peace in distant and uncivilized countries is necessarily bound up with the right to maintain forts and garrisons there. The joint-stock companies that have held the one right have consistently exercised the other, and have often had it expressly granted to them. How unjustly, how capriciously, and how cruelly they have usually exercised it is all too well known from recent experience.

When a company of merchants undertakes, at its own risk and expense, to open a new trade with some remote and uncivilized nation, it may not be unreasonable to incorporate them as a joint-stock company and, if they succeed, to grant them a monopoly of that trade for a fixed number of years. This is the easiest and most natural way for the state to reward them for undertaking a dangerous and expensive experiment whose benefits the public will later enjoy. A temporary monopoly of this kind can be justified on the same principles by which a similar monopoly over a new machine is granted to its inventor, or over a new book to its author. But when the term expires, the monopoly should certainly end. The forts and garrisons, if any were found necessary, should be taken over by the government, with their value paid to the company, and the trade should be thrown open to all the subjects of the state. Under a perpetual monopoly, all the state's other subjects are taxed, quite absurdly, in two different ways: first, through the high price of goods they could buy much more cheaply under free trade; and second, through their complete exclusion from a branch of business that many of them might find both convenient and profitable to pursue. And they are taxed in this way for the most worthless of all purposes, merely to enable the company to sustain the negligence, extravagance, and corruption of its own servants, whose disorderly conduct seldom allows the company's dividend to exceed the ordinary rate of profit in trades that are entirely free, and very often causes it to fall well short of that rate. Experience suggests, however, that without a monopoly a joint-stock company cannot carry on any branch of foreign trade for long. To buy in one market in order to sell at a profit in another, when there are many competitors in both; to watch not only the occasional shifts in demand but the far greater and more frequent shifts in competition, that is, in the supply which that demand is likely to receive from others; and to adjust both the quantity and the quality of each assortment of goods to all these circumstances with skill and judgment: this is a kind of warfare whose operations are constantly changing. It can hardly ever be conducted successfully without a degree of unremitting vigilance and attention that cannot long be expected from the directors of a joint-stock company. When the East India Company's funds are redeemed and its exclusive privilege expires, an act of Parliament gives it the right to continue as a corporation with a joint stock and to trade to the East Indies in its corporate capacity, alongside the rest of its fellow subjects. In that situation, however, the superior vigilance and attention of private traders would in all likelihood soon make the company weary of the trade.

A distinguished French writer with great knowledge of political economy, the Abbé Morellet, lists fifty-five joint-stock companies for foreign trade established in various parts of Europe since 1600, all of which, according to him, failed through mismanagement despite their exclusive privileges. He has been misinformed about the history of two or three of them, which were not joint-stock companies and did not fail. To balance this, however, several joint-stock companies that did fail are missing from his list.

The only trades a joint-stock company seems able to carry on successfully without an exclusive privilege are those whose operations can all be reduced to what is called a routine, that is, to a uniform method admitting little or no variation. There are four trades of this kind: first, banking; second, insurance against fire, against the risks of the sea, and against capture in time of war; third, building and maintaining a navigable channel or canal; and fourth, the similar business of bringing in water to supply a great city.

Although the principles of banking may seem somewhat obscure, its practice can be reduced to strict rules. To depart from those rules on any occasion, tempted by some alluring prospect of extraordinary gain, is almost always extremely dangerous and is often fatal to the banking company that attempts it. Joint-stock companies, however, are by their constitution generally more attached to established rules than any private partnership, and they therefore seem extremely well suited to this trade. Accordingly, the principal banking companies in Europe are joint-stock companies, and many of them manage their business very successfully without any exclusive privilege. The Bank of England has no exclusive privilege except that no other banking company in England may consist of more than six partners. The two banks of Edinburgh are joint-stock companies without any exclusive privilege at all.

The value of the risk of loss by fire, by sea, or by capture may not be calculable with great precision, but it does allow a rough estimate that makes it reducible, to some degree, to strict rule and method. The insurance trade can therefore be carried on successfully by a joint-stock company without any exclusive privilege, and neither the London Assurance nor the Royal Exchange Assurance company holds one.

Once a navigable channel or canal has been built, managing it becomes quite simple and easy, and can be reduced to strict rule and method. Even its construction can be handled in this way, since it can be contracted out to builders at a fixed price per mile and per lock. The same is true of a canal, an aqueduct, or a great water main for supplying a large city. Such undertakings, therefore, can be managed very successfully by joint-stock companies without any exclusive privilege, and often are.

Still, it would certainly not be reasonable to establish a joint-stock company for an undertaking merely because such a company might manage it successfully, or to exempt a particular group of dealers from general laws that apply to all their neighbors merely because they might prosper with such an exemption. For such an establishment to be entirely reasonable, two further conditions must accompany the undertaking's reducibility to strict rule and method. First, it must be shown by the clearest evidence that the undertaking is of greater and more general usefulness than most ordinary trades; and second, that it requires more capital than can easily be gathered into a private partnership. If a moderate capital were enough, the undertaking's great usefulness would not by itself justify establishing a joint-stock company, because private traders would readily and easily meet the demand for whatever it produced. In the four trades mentioned above, both conditions are met.

The great and general usefulness of banking, when it is prudently managed, has been fully explained in the second book of this inquiry. But a public bank that is to support public credit, and in particular emergencies to advance the government the entire yield of a tax, amounting perhaps to several million pounds, a year or two before that tax is collected, requires more capital than can easily be gathered into any private partnership.

The insurance trade gives great security to private fortunes. By dividing among a great many people a loss that would ruin a single individual, it makes that loss fall lightly and easily on society as a whole. To provide this security, however, insurers must have a very large capital. Before the two joint-stock insurance companies were established in London, a list of one hundred and fifty private insurers who had failed within the space of a few years was reportedly laid before the attorney general.

That navigable channels and canals, and the works sometimes needed to supply a great city with water, are of great and general usefulness, and at the same time often require more expense than suits the fortunes of private individuals, is sufficiently obvious.

Apart from these four trades, I have not been able to think of any other in which all three conditions needed to justify a joint-stock company are met. The English Copper Company of London, the lead-smelting company, and the glass-grinding company cannot even claim any great or unusual usefulness in the object they pursue, nor does pursuing that object appear to require an expense beyond the fortunes of many private individuals. Whether their trade can be reduced to the kind of strict rule and method that would make it suitable for management by a joint-stock company, or whether they have any reason to boast of extraordinary profits, I do not claim to know. The Mine Adventurers' Company went bankrupt long ago. A share in the stock of the British Linen Company of Edinburgh currently sells far below its face value, though less far below it than some years ago. Joint-stock companies established for the public-spirited purpose of promoting some particular manufacture, besides managing their own affairs badly and so diminishing the general stock of society, can hardly fail in other respects to do more harm than good. However upright their intentions, their directors inevitably come to favor particular branches of the manufacture, in which the undertakers mislead and deceive them. This favoritism genuinely discourages the other branches and necessarily disturbs, to some degree, the natural proportion that would otherwise establish itself between sound industry and its profit. That natural proportion is, of all encouragements to the general industry of a country, the greatest and the most effective.

##### Article II: Of the Expense of the Institutions for the Education of Youth

Institutions for the education of the young can, in the same way, generate enough revenue to cover their own expenses. The fee, or honorarium, that the student pays the teacher naturally constitutes a revenue of this kind.

Even where the teacher's pay does not come entirely from this natural source, it still need not be drawn from the general revenue of society, whose collection and spending are in most countries entrusted to the executive power. Throughout most of Europe, accordingly, the endowment of schools and colleges places either no burden on that general revenue or only a very small one. Everywhere it comes chiefly from some local or provincial revenue, from the rent of some landed estate, or from the interest on some sum of money set aside for this specific purpose and placed under the management of trustees, sometimes by the sovereign himself and sometimes by a private donor.

Have these public endowments generally advanced the purpose for which they were established? Have they encouraged the diligence and improved the abilities of the teachers? Have they steered education toward subjects more useful, both to the individual and to the public, than those it would naturally have pursued of its own accord? It should not be very difficult to give at least a probable answer to each of these questions.

In every profession, the effort most of its members put forth is always proportioned to the necessity they are under of making it. That necessity is greatest for those whose professional earnings are the only source from which they expect to make their fortune, or even to earn their ordinary income and living. To acquire that fortune, or merely to secure that living, they must perform in the course of a year a certain amount of work of known value; and where competition is free, the rivalry of competitors, all trying to push one another out of employment, compels every one of them to do his work with a certain degree of precision. The greatness of the rewards to be won by success in certain professions may, no doubt, sometimes spur the efforts of a few people of exceptional spirit and ambition. Great rewards, however, are plainly not necessary to call forth the greatest efforts. Rivalry and emulation make excellence an object of ambition even in humble occupations, and often produce the very greatest exertions. Great rewards on their own, by contrast, unsupported by the necessity of hard work, have seldom been enough to produce any considerable effort. In England, success in the legal profession leads to some very great prizes of ambition; and yet how few men born to comfortable fortunes have ever risen to eminence in that profession in this country?

The endowments of schools and colleges have necessarily reduced, to a greater or lesser degree, the teachers' need to work hard. Their livelihood, insofar as it comes from their salaries, plainly derives from a fund entirely independent of their success and reputation in their profession.

In some universities, the salary makes up only part of a teacher's income, and often only a small part; the greater share comes from the fees his students pay him. In this case the pressure to work hard, though always weakened to some degree, is not removed entirely. His reputation in his profession still matters to him, and he still depends to some extent on the affection, gratitude, and good report of those who have attended his teaching. He is unlikely to win these favorable feelings in any better way than by deserving them, that is, by the ability and diligence with which he carries out every part of his duty.

In other universities, the teacher is forbidden to accept any fee from his students, and his salary makes up the whole of the income his post provides. Here his interest is set as directly against his duty as it is possible to set it. It is in every man's interest to live as comfortably as he can. If his pay will be exactly the same whether or not he performs some very laborious duty, then it is certainly in his interest, at least as interest is commonly understood, either to neglect that duty altogether or, if he answers to some authority that will not allow this, to perform it as carelessly and sloppily as that authority will tolerate. If he is naturally energetic and fond of work, it is in his interest to spend that energy on something that can bring him some advantage, rather than on his duty, which can bring him none.

Suppose the authority he answers to is the corporate body itself: the college or university of which he is a member, and in which most of the other members are, like him, people who either are teachers or ought to be. They are then likely to make common cause, to be very lenient with one another, and each to agree that his neighbor may neglect his duty, provided he himself is allowed to neglect his own. At the University of Oxford, most of the public professors have for many years now given up even the pretense of teaching.

Suppose instead that the authority lies not so much in the corporate body to which he belongs as in some outside party, such as the bishop of the diocese, the governor of the province, or perhaps a minister of state. In that case it is not very likely that he will be allowed to neglect his duty entirely. Yet all that such superiors can force him to do is meet his students for a certain number of hours, which means giving a certain number of lectures each week or each year. What those lectures contain must still depend on the teacher's diligence, and that diligence will likely be in proportion to the motives he has for exerting it. An outside jurisdiction of this kind is, moreover, liable to be exercised both ignorantly and capriciously. By its nature it is arbitrary and discretionary, and the people who wield it neither attend the teacher's lectures themselves nor, perhaps, understand the subjects he is meant to teach, so they are seldom able to wield it with judgment. The arrogance of office also makes them frequently indifferent to how they exercise it, and very apt to reprimand him or strip him of his post wantonly and without just cause. Anyone subject to such a jurisdiction is necessarily degraded by it. Instead of being one of the most respected members of society, he becomes one of the lowest and most contemptible. Only powerful protection can effectively shield him from the mistreatment to which he is constantly exposed, and he is most likely to secure that protection not through ability or diligence in his profession, but through servility to his superiors and a constant readiness to sacrifice to their wishes the rights, the interests, and the honor of the corporate body to which he belongs. Anyone who has watched the administration of a French university for any length of time will have had occasion to notice the effects that naturally follow from an arbitrary outside jurisdiction of this kind.

Whatever compels a certain number of students to attend a particular college or university, regardless of the merit or reputation of its teachers, tends to some degree to reduce the need for that merit or reputation.

When the privileges that come with degrees in arts, law, medicine, and divinity can be obtained only by residing for a fixed number of years at certain universities, those privileges necessarily drive a certain number of students to such universities, regardless of the merit or reputation of the teachers. The privileges of graduates are a kind of apprenticeship statute, comparable to the laws requiring a fixed term of apprenticeship before a man may practice a trade, and they have done exactly as much to improve education as those other statutes have done to improve the arts and manufactures.

Charitable endowments for scholarships, exhibitions, bursaries, and the like necessarily tie a certain number of students to particular colleges, entirely apart from the merit of those colleges. If the students supported by such endowments were left free to choose whichever college they liked best, that freedom might help to stir up some competition among the colleges. A rule that forbade even the independent members of a college, those not supported by any endowment, from leaving it for another without first requesting and obtaining permission from the college they meant to abandon would, on the contrary, go a long way toward extinguishing that competition.

Suppose that in each college, the tutor responsible for instructing a student in all the arts and sciences was not chosen freely by the student but appointed by the head of the college. Suppose, further, that in cases of neglect, incompetence, or mistreatment, the student was not allowed to exchange him for another without first requesting and obtaining permission. Such a rule would not only go a long way toward extinguishing all competition among the tutors of a college; it would also greatly reduce, in every one of them, the need for diligence and attention to their pupils. Such teachers, though very well paid by their students, might be just as inclined to neglect them as teachers who receive nothing from their students and have no reward beyond their salary.

If the teacher happens to be a sensible man, it must be unpleasant for him to be aware, while lecturing, that he is speaking or reading nonsense, or something very little better than nonsense. It must also be unpleasant for him to see most of his students desert his lectures, or perhaps attend them with plain enough signs of neglect, contempt, and ridicule. If he is obliged to give a certain number of lectures, these motives alone, without any other interest, might incline him to take some trouble to make them reasonably good. A number of expedients, however, can be devised that will thoroughly blunt the edge of all these incentives to diligence. Instead of explaining the subject to his students himself, the teacher may read to them from some book on it. If the book is written in a foreign and dead language, he may translate it for them into their own tongue, or, to spare himself still more trouble, have them translate it for him, adding an occasional remark of his own, and he may then flatter himself that he is giving a lecture. The slightest degree of knowledge and effort will allow him to do this without exposing himself to contempt or ridicule by saying anything truly foolish, absurd, or laughable. The discipline of the college, meanwhile, may enable him to compel all his pupils to attend his sham lecture with perfect regularity, and to behave with the utmost decency and respect throughout the whole performance.

The discipline of colleges and universities is generally designed not for the benefit of the students but for the interest, or more precisely the ease, of the masters. Its aim in every case is to uphold the master's authority and, whether he neglects his duty or performs it, to oblige the students to behave toward him as though he performed it with the greatest diligence and ability. It seems to assume perfect wisdom and virtue in the one group, and the greatest weakness and folly in the other. Where the masters actually perform their duty, however, I believe there are no examples of most students neglecting theirs. No discipline is ever needed to compel attendance at lectures that are genuinely worth attending, as is well known wherever such lectures are given. Some degree of force and restraint may no doubt be needed to make children, or very young boys, attend to those parts of education they are thought to require at that early stage of life. But after the age of twelve or thirteen, provided the master does his duty, force or restraint is scarcely ever needed to carry on any part of education. Most young men are so generous that, far from being inclined to neglect or despise their master's instruction, they are generally ready, provided he shows some serious intention of being useful to them, to forgive a great many lapses in the way he performs his duty, and sometimes even to hide a good deal of gross negligence from the public.

It is worth observing that those parts of education for which there are no public institutions are generally the best taught. When a young man goes to a fencing school or a dancing school, he does not always learn to fence or dance very well, but he seldom fails to learn to fence or dance. The good results of the riding school are not usually so evident, and the expense of a riding school is so great that in most places it is a public institution. The three most essential parts of a literary education, reading, writing, and arithmetic, are still more commonly acquired in private schools than in public ones, and it very seldom happens that anyone fails to acquire them to the degree that is necessary.

In England, the public schools are much less corrupt than the universities. In the schools, young people are taught, or at least can be taught, Greek and Latin, which is everything the masters claim to teach or are expected to teach. In the universities, young people are neither taught, nor can always find any proper means of being taught, the sciences that these incorporated bodies exist to teach. The schoolmaster's reward in most cases depends mainly, and in some cases almost entirely, on the fees of his pupils. Schools have no exclusive privileges. To obtain the honors of a degree, a person need not bring a certificate showing that he studied a certain number of years at a public school. If examination shows that he understands what is taught there, no one asks where he learned it.

It may perhaps be said that the subjects commonly taught in universities are not taught very well. But without those institutions, they would not have been commonly taught at all, and both individuals and the public would have suffered a good deal from the lack of those important parts of education.

Most of the present universities of Europe were originally ecclesiastical corporations, established for the education of churchmen. They were founded by the authority of the pope and were so completely under his direct protection that all their members, masters and students alike, enjoyed what was then called the benefit of clergy: they were exempt from the civil courts of the countries where their universities stood, and answerable only to the church's tribunals. What was taught in most of those universities suited the purpose for which they had been founded. It was either theology or something merely preparatory to theology.

When Christianity was first established by law, a debased form of Latin had become the common language of all of western Europe. The church service, and the translation of the Bible read aloud in churches, were accordingly both in that debased Latin, which was simply the ordinary language of the country. After the invasions of the barbarian peoples who overthrew the Roman Empire, Latin gradually ceased to be the spoken language of any part of Europe. But popular reverence naturally preserves the established forms and ceremonies of religion long after the circumstances that first introduced them and made them reasonable have disappeared. So although the great mass of the people no longer understood Latin anywhere, the entire church service continued to be performed in it. Two different languages were thus established in Europe, just as in ancient Egypt: a language of the priests and a language of the people, a sacred and a profane language, a learned and an unlearned one. Since the priests needed to understand something of the sacred and learned language in which they were to conduct services, the study of Latin formed an essential part of university education from the very beginning.

The same was not true of either Greek or Hebrew. The infallible decrees of the church had declared that the Latin translation of the Bible, commonly called the Latin Vulgate, had been dictated by divine inspiration just as the originals had, and therefore carried the same authority as the Greek and Hebrew texts. Since knowledge of those two languages was not indispensable to a churchman, their study did not for a long time form a required part of the ordinary university course. There are some Spanish universities, I am assured, in which Greek has never yet formed any part of that course. The first Protestant reformers found the Greek text of the New Testament, and even the Hebrew text of the Old, more favorable to their views than the Vulgate translation, which, as one might naturally suppose, had gradually been adapted to support the doctrines of the Catholic Church. They therefore set about exposing the many errors in that translation, and the Roman Catholic clergy were obliged in turn to defend or explain them. This could hardly be done without some knowledge of the original languages, and so the study of those languages was gradually introduced into most universities, both those that embraced the doctrines of the Reformation and those that rejected them. Greek was bound up with every part of classical learning, which, though at first cultivated chiefly by Catholics and Italians, happened to come into fashion at about the same time that the doctrines of the Reformation were launched. In most universities, therefore, Greek was taught before the study of philosophy, as soon as the student had made some progress in Latin. Hebrew had no connection with classical learning and, apart from the Holy Scriptures, was not the language of a single book held in any esteem, so its study did not usually begin until after philosophy, when the student had moved on to theology.

Originally, the first elements of both Greek and Latin were taught in the universities, and in some universities they still are. In others, the student is expected to have already acquired at least the rudiments of one or both languages, whose study continues everywhere to make up a very considerable part of university education.

Ancient Greek philosophy was divided into three great branches: physics, or natural philosophy; ethics, or moral philosophy; and logic. This general division seems perfectly suited to the nature of things.

The great phenomena of nature, such as the movements of the heavenly bodies, eclipses, and comets; thunder, lightning, and other extraordinary atmospheric events; and the generation, life, growth, and decay of plants and animals, are things that necessarily excite wonder, and so they naturally prompt human curiosity to inquire into their causes. Superstition first tried to satisfy this curiosity by attributing all these wonderful appearances to the direct action of the gods. Philosophy later tried to explain them through more familiar causes, causes that people understood better than the workings of the gods. Since these great phenomena are the first objects of human curiosity, the science that claims to explain them must naturally have been the first branch of philosophy to be cultivated. Accordingly, the earliest philosophers of whom history has preserved any record appear to have been natural philosophers.

In every age and country, people must have paid attention to one another's characters, intentions, and actions, and many respectable rules and maxims for the conduct of life must have been laid down and approved by common consent. As soon as writing came into use, wise men, or those who imagined themselves wise, would naturally try to add to the stock of these established and respected maxims and to express their own sense of what conduct was proper or improper. Sometimes they did so in the more artful form of moral fables, like those attributed to Aesop, and sometimes in the simpler form of aphorisms or wise sayings, like the proverbs of Solomon, the verses of Theognis and Phocylides, and parts of the works of Hesiod. For a long time they might go on in this way, simply multiplying maxims of prudence and morality, without even trying to arrange them in any distinct or methodical order, much less to connect them through one or more general principles from which they could all be derived, as effects are derived from their natural causes. The beauty of arranging different observations into a system connected by a few common principles was first seen in the crude early attempts of those ancient times at a system of natural philosophy. Something similar was later attempted in morals. The maxims of everyday life were arranged in a methodical order and connected through a few common principles, in the same way that thinkers had tried to arrange and connect the phenomena of nature. The science that claims to investigate and explain those connecting principles is what is properly called moral philosophy.

Different authors put forward different systems of both natural and moral philosophy. But the arguments they used to support those systems, far from always being rigorous demonstrations, were often at best very slender probabilities, and sometimes mere sophistries founded on nothing but the imprecision and ambiguity of ordinary language. In every age, speculative systems have been adopted for reasons too flimsy to sway the judgment of any sensible man in a matter involving the smallest sum of money. Gross sophistry has scarcely ever influenced human opinion except in matters of philosophy and speculation, and there it has often had the greatest influence of all. The champions of each system of natural and moral philosophy naturally tried to expose the weakness of the arguments offered for rival systems. In examining those arguments, they were necessarily led to consider the difference between a probable argument and a demonstrative one, between a fallacious argument and a conclusive one. Logic, the science of the general principles of good and bad reasoning, necessarily grew out of the observations that this kind of scrutiny gave rise to. Although it arose later than both physics and ethics, it was commonly taught before either of them in most, though not all, of the ancient schools of philosophy. The thinking seems to have been that a student ought to understand clearly the difference between good and bad reasoning before being led to reason about subjects of such great importance.

In most of the universities of Europe, this ancient threefold division of philosophy was replaced by a fivefold one.

In ancient philosophy, whatever was taught about the nature of the human mind or of the Deity formed part of the system of physics. Whatever their essence was supposed to be, these beings were parts of the great system of the universe, and parts that produced the most important effects. Whatever human reason could conclude or conjecture about them formed, in effect, two chapters, though certainly two very important ones, of the science that claimed to account for the origin and transformations of that great system. But in the universities of Europe, where philosophy was taught only as a servant of theology, it was natural to dwell longer on these two chapters than on any other part of the science. They were gradually expanded and divided into many subordinate chapters, until at last the doctrine of spirits, about which so little can be known, came to occupy as much room in the system of philosophy as the doctrine of bodies, about which so much can be known. The doctrines on these two subjects came to be regarded as two distinct sciences. What were called metaphysics, or pneumatics (the science of spirits), were set against physics and cultivated not only as the loftier of the two but, for the purposes of a particular profession, as the more useful. The proper subject of experiment and observation, a subject in which careful attention can yield so many useful discoveries, was almost entirely neglected. Meanwhile the subject in which, beyond a very few simple and almost obvious truths, the most careful attention can discover nothing but obscurity and uncertainty, and can therefore produce nothing but subtleties and sophistries, was cultivated intensively.

Once these two sciences had been set against each other, the comparison between them naturally gave birth to a third, called ontology, the science that dealt with the qualities and attributes common to the subjects of both the other two. But if subtleties and sophistries made up most of the metaphysics or pneumatics of the schools, they made up the whole of this cobweb science of ontology, which was also sometimes called metaphysics.

The object that ancient moral philosophy set out to investigate was what constituted the happiness and perfection of a man, considered not only as an individual but as a member of a family, of a state, and of the great society of mankind. In that philosophy, the duties of human life were treated as subordinate to the happiness and perfection of human life. But when moral, as well as natural philosophy, came to be taught only as an aid to theology, the duties of human life were treated chiefly as means to happiness in a life to come. Ancient philosophy had held that perfect virtue necessarily brought its possessor the most perfect happiness in this life. Modern philosophy frequently held that virtue was generally, or indeed almost always, incompatible with any happiness in this life at all. Heaven was to be earned only through penance and self-mortification, through the austerities and self-abasement of a monk, and not through the liberal, generous, and spirited conduct of a man.
