Casuistry, the hair-splitting analysis of particular cases of conscience, together with an ascetic morality, made up the greater part of what the schools taught as moral philosophy in most cases. In this way the most important of all the branches of philosophy became by far the most corrupted.

This, then, was the usual course of philosophical education in most of the universities of Europe. Logic was taught first. Ontology, the abstract study of being as such, came second. Third came pneumatology, the doctrine concerning the nature of the human soul and of God. Fourth followed a debased system of moral philosophy, regarded as directly connected with the doctrines of pneumatology: with the immortality of the soul, and with the rewards and punishments that divine justice would deal out in a life to come. A short and superficial system of physics usually concluded the course.

The changes the European universities made to the ancient course of philosophy were all intended for the education of clergymen, and meant to make that course a more fitting introduction to the study of theology. But the added subtlety and sophistry, the casuistry and ascetic morality that these changes brought with them, certainly did not make it any better suited to the education of gentlemen or men of the world, nor any more likely to improve the understanding or to mend the heart.

This course of philosophy is still taught in most of the universities of Europe, with greater or lesser diligence depending on how far the constitution of each university makes diligence necessary for its teachers. In some of the richest and best-endowed universities, the tutors are content to teach a few disconnected scraps and fragments of this corrupted course, and even these they usually teach carelessly and superficially.

Most of the improvements made in modern times in the various branches of philosophy were not made in universities, though some certainly were. Most universities have not even been quick to adopt those improvements once they were made. Several of these learned bodies chose to remain, for a long time, the sanctuaries where discredited systems and outdated prejudices found shelter and protection after they had been hunted out of every other corner of the world. In general, the richest and best-endowed universities have been the slowest to adopt these improvements and the most reluctant to allow any significant change to the established plan of education. The improvements were more easily introduced into some of the poorer universities, where the teachers depended on their reputations for most of their income and were therefore obliged to pay closer attention to the prevailing opinions of the world.

The public schools and universities of Europe were originally intended only to educate one particular profession, the clergy, and they were not always very diligent in instructing their pupils even in the sciences thought necessary for that profession. Yet they gradually drew to themselves the education of almost everyone else, and particularly of nearly all gentlemen and men of fortune. No better way could apparently be found of spending, with any profit, the long interval between childhood and the age at which men begin to apply themselves in earnest to the real business of the world, the business that will occupy them for the rest of their lives. Most of what is taught in schools and universities, however, does not seem to be the most suitable preparation for that business.

In England it is becoming more customary every day to send young people traveling in foreign countries as soon as they leave school, without sending them to any university. Our young people, it is said, generally come home much improved by their travels. A young man who goes abroad at seventeen or eighteen and returns at twenty-one comes back three or four years older than when he left, and at that age it is very hard not to improve a good deal in three or four years. During his travels he generally picks up some knowledge of one or two foreign languages, though that knowledge is seldom enough to let him speak or write them correctly. In other respects he usually returns more conceited, more unprincipled, more dissipated, and more incapable of any serious application to study or to business than he could easily have become in so short a time had he stayed at home. By traveling so young, and by spending the most precious years of his life in the most frivolous dissipation, far from the supervision and control of his parents and relations, he almost inevitably finds that every useful habit his earlier education may have begun to form in him is weakened or erased instead of being fixed and confirmed. Nothing but the discredit into which the universities are allowing themselves to fall could ever have made so absurd a practice as traveling at this early age respectable. By sending his son abroad, a father relieves himself, at least for a while, of so disagreeable a sight as a son who is idle, neglected, and going to ruin before his eyes.

Such have been the effects of some modern educational institutions.

Other ages and nations appear to have had different plans and different institutions for education.

In the republics of ancient Greece, every free citizen was trained, under the direction of the public magistrate, in gymnastic exercises and in music. Gymnastic exercises were intended to harden his body, sharpen his courage, and prepare him for the fatigues and dangers of war. Since the Greek militia was, by all accounts, one of the best the world has ever seen, this part of their public education must have fully achieved its purpose. The other part, music, was intended, at least according to the philosophers and historians who have described these institutions for us, to humanize the mind, soften the temper, and dispose it to perform all the social and moral duties of public and private life.

In ancient Rome, the exercises of the Campus Martius, the great public field where Roman citizens drilled, served the same purpose as those of the Gymnasium in Greece, and seem to have served it equally well. But the Romans had nothing corresponding to the musical education of the Greeks. Even so, Roman morals, in both private and public life, appear to have been not merely equal but, on the whole, considerably superior to those of the Greeks. For their superiority in private life we have the express testimony of Polybius and of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, two authors well acquainted with both nations, and the whole course of Greek and Roman history bears witness to the superiority of Roman public morals. The good temper and moderation of rival factions seem to be the most essential element in the public morals of a free people. Yet Greek factions were almost always violent and bloody, whereas until the time of the Gracchi no blood had ever been shed in any Roman factional conflict, and from the time of the Gracchi onward the Roman republic may be regarded as having in reality dissolved. Despite, therefore, the highly respectable authority of Plato, Aristotle, and Polybius, and despite the ingenious arguments with which Montesquieu tries to support that authority, it seems probable that the musical education of the Greeks did little to improve their morals, since the Romans, without any such education, had morals that were on the whole superior. Those ancient sages' respect for the institutions of their ancestors probably inclined them to find great political wisdom in what may have been merely an old custom, carried on without interruption from the earliest days of their societies down to times when they had reached a considerable degree of refinement.

Music and dancing are the chief amusements of almost all primitive nations, and the chief accomplishments thought to qualify a man to entertain his company. This is true today among the Black peoples of the African coast. It was true among the ancient Celts and the ancient Scandinavians, and, as we learn from Homer, among the ancient Greeks in the times before the Trojan War. When the Greek tribes organized themselves into small republics, it was natural that the study of these accomplishments should for a long time remain part of the people's public and common education.

The masters who taught the young either music or military exercises do not seem to have been paid, or even appointed, by the state, either in Rome or even in Athens, the Greek republic whose laws and customs we know best. The state required every free citizen to make himself fit to defend it in war, and for that reason to learn his military exercises. But it left him to learn them from whatever masters he could find, and it seems to have provided nothing for this purpose except a public field or exercise ground where he could practice and perform them.

In the early ages of both the Greek and the Roman republics, the rest of education seems to have consisted of learning to read, to write, and to keep accounts according to the arithmetic of the time. Wealthier citizens often seem to have acquired these skills at home with the help of a household tutor, usually a slave or a freedman, while poorer citizens learned them in the schools of masters who made a trade of teaching for pay. These parts of education, however, were left entirely to the care of each child's parents or guardians, and the state does not appear ever to have supervised or directed them. A law of Solon did, it is true, release children from the obligation to support parents who had neglected to train them in some profitable trade or business.

As society grew more refined and philosophy and rhetoric came into fashion, the upper classes would send their children to the schools of philosophers and rhetoricians to be instructed in these fashionable sciences. But those schools received no public support. For a long time they were merely tolerated by the public. For a long time, too, the demand for philosophy and rhetoric was so small that the first professional teachers of either could not find steady work in any single city and had to travel from place to place. This is how Zeno of Elea, Protagoras, Gorgias, Hippias, and many others lived. As demand grew, the schools of philosophy and rhetoric became fixed in one place, first in Athens and later in several other cities. Even then, the state seems never to have encouraged them beyond assigning some of them a particular place to teach, a favor sometimes granted by private donors as well. The state appears to have assigned the Academy to Plato, the Lyceum to Aristotle, and the Portico to Zeno of Citium, the founder of the Stoics. Epicurus, by contrast, bequeathed his own gardens to his school. Until about the time of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, however, no teacher appears to have received any salary from the public, or any income other than the fees paid by his students. The stipend that this philosophical emperor, as we learn from Lucian, granted to one of the teachers of philosophy probably lasted no longer than his own life. There was nothing equivalent to the privileges conferred by a university degree, and attending any of these schools was not a requirement for being allowed to practice any trade or profession. If students could not be drawn by their own belief in the schools' usefulness, the law neither forced anyone to attend nor rewarded anyone for having attended. The teachers had no legal authority over their pupils, and no authority of any kind beyond the natural authority that superior virtue and ability never fail to command from the young toward those entrusted with any part of their education.

At Rome, the study of civil law formed part of the education not of most citizens but of certain particular families. Young people who wished to learn the law had no public school to attend, and no way of studying it except by keeping company with relatives and friends who were thought to understand it. It is perhaps worth noting that although many of the laws of the Twelve Tables, Rome's earliest written code, were copied from those of certain ancient Greek republics, law never seems to have developed into a science in any republic of ancient Greece. In Rome it became a science very early, and it brought considerable distinction to the citizens who were known to understand it. In the republics of ancient Greece, and particularly in Athens, the ordinary courts of justice were made up of large, and therefore disorderly, bodies of people, who often decided cases almost at random, or as clamor, faction, and party spirit happened to dictate. The disgrace of an unjust verdict, when it was shared among five hundred, a thousand, or fifteen hundred people (for some of their courts were that large), could not weigh very heavily on any one individual. At Rome, by contrast, the principal courts consisted either of a single judge or of a small number of judges, whose reputations, especially since they always deliberated in public, could not fail to suffer greatly from any rash or unjust decision. In doubtful cases such courts, anxious to avoid blame, would naturally try to shelter themselves behind the example or precedent of the judges who had sat before them, in the same court or in another. This attention to practice and precedent necessarily shaped Roman law into the regular and orderly system in which it has come down to us, and the same attention has had the same effect on the laws of every other country where it has been practiced. The superiority of Roman character over Greek, so often remarked on by Polybius and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, was probably owed more to the better constitution of the Roman courts than to any of the causes those authors assign to it. The Romans are said to have been particularly distinguished by their greater respect for an oath. But a people accustomed to swearing oaths only before some diligent and well-informed court of justice would naturally pay far closer attention to what they swore than a people accustomed to doing the same before rowdy and disorderly assemblies.

It will readily be granted that the civil and military abilities of the Greeks and Romans were at least equal to those of any modern nation; if anything, our prejudice is to overrate them. Yet apart from military exercises, the state seems to have taken no trouble to cultivate those great abilities, for I cannot bring myself to believe that the musical education of the Greeks had much to do with forming them. Masters had nevertheless been found, it seems, to instruct the upper classes of those nations in every art and science that the circumstances of their society made it necessary or convenient for them to learn. The demand for such instruction produced what it always produces, the talent for supplying it, and the rivalry that unrestrained competition never fails to provoke appears to have brought that talent to a very high degree of perfection. In the attention they commanded, in the sway they gained over the opinions and principles of their listeners, and in their power to give a certain tone and character to the conduct and conversation of those listeners, the ancient philosophers appear to have been far superior to any modern teachers. In modern times, the diligence of public teachers is corrupted in proportion as their circumstances make them independent of their success and reputation in their profession. Their salaries, moreover, place any private teacher who tries to compete with them in the position of a merchant who trades without a bounty, a government subsidy on his goods, against rivals who receive a large one. If he sells his goods at roughly the same price, he cannot make the same profit, and poverty and beggary at the least, if not bankruptcy and ruin, will inevitably be his fate. If he tries to sell them at a much higher price, he is likely to have so few customers that his situation will hardly improve. In many countries, besides, the privileges of a degree are necessary, or at least extremely convenient, for most men in the learned professions, that is, for the great majority of those who need a learned education. But those privileges can be obtained only by attending the lectures of the public teachers. The most careful attendance on the ablest instruction of any private teacher does not always give a man any right to claim them. For all these reasons, the private teacher of any of the sciences commonly taught in universities is generally regarded in modern times as belonging to the very lowest rank of men of letters. A man of real ability could hardly find a more humiliating or less profitable use for it. In this way the endowments of schools and colleges have not only corrupted the diligence of public teachers but have made it almost impossible to find any good private ones.

If there were no public institutions for education, no system and no science would be taught unless there was some demand for it, or unless the circumstances of the times made it necessary, convenient, or at least fashionable to learn. A private teacher could never make a living by teaching either a discredited and outdated system of a science acknowledged to be useful, or a science universally believed to be a useless and pedantic heap of sophistry and nonsense. Such systems and such sciences can survive only in those incorporated educational bodies whose prosperity and revenue are largely independent of their own industry. If there were no public institutions for education, a gentleman who had gone through, with diligence and ability, the most complete course of education the times were thought to offer could not enter the world wholly ignorant of everything that is the common subject of conversation among gentlemen and men of the world.

There are no public institutions for the education of women, and accordingly there is nothing useless, absurd, or fanciful in the ordinary course of their education. They are taught what their parents or guardians judge it necessary or useful for them to learn, and nothing else. Every part of their education plainly tends toward some useful purpose: either to improve the natural attractions of their person, or to form their minds to reserve, modesty, chastity, and thrift, so as to make them likely to become mistresses of a household and to conduct themselves properly once they have. At every stage of her life a woman feels some convenience or advantage from every part of her education. It seldom happens that a man, at any stage of his life, derives any convenience or advantage from some of the most laborious and troublesome parts of his.

Should the public, then, it may be asked, pay no attention to the education of the people? Or if it should pay some, what parts of education ought it to attend to among the different classes of the people, and in what manner?

In some cases, the condition of society necessarily places most individuals in situations that naturally form in them, without any attention from government, almost all the abilities and virtues that such a society requires, or perhaps can accommodate. In other cases, the condition of society does not place most individuals in such situations, and some attention from government is necessary to prevent the almost complete corruption and degeneration of the great body of the people.

As the division of labor advances, the work of the great majority of those who live by their labor, that is, of the great body of the people, comes to be confined to a few very simple operations, often to one or two. But most men's understandings are necessarily formed by their ordinary employments. The man whose whole life is spent performing a few simple operations, whose results are perhaps always the same or very nearly so, has no occasion to exercise his understanding or his inventiveness in devising ways around difficulties that never arise. He naturally loses the habit of such exertion, and generally becomes as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human being to become. The torpor of his mind makes him incapable not only of enjoying or taking part in any rational conversation, but of conceiving any generous, noble, or tender sentiment, and consequently of forming any sound judgment about many even of the ordinary duties of private life. He is wholly incapable of judging the great and far-reaching interests of his country, and unless very particular pains have been taken to make him otherwise, he is equally incapable of defending it in war. The monotony of his settled life naturally corrupts the courage of his mind and makes him regard with horror the irregular, uncertain, and adventurous life of a soldier. It corrupts even the activity of his body, and leaves him unable to exert his strength with vigor and perseverance in any occupation other than the one he was trained for. His skill at his own particular trade thus seems to be acquired at the expense of his intellectual, social, and martial virtues. Yet in every advanced and civilized society, this is the condition into which the laboring poor, that is, the great body of the people, must necessarily fall unless the government takes some pains to prevent it.

It is otherwise in the so-called barbarous societies of hunters, of shepherds, and even of farmers in that primitive stage of agriculture which comes before the improvement of manufactures and the expansion of foreign trade. In such societies, the varied occupations of every man force him to exert his abilities and to invent remedies for the difficulties that are constantly arising. Invention is kept alive, and the mind is not allowed to sink into that drowsy stupidity which, in a civilized society, seems to numb the understanding of almost everyone in the lower ranks.

In these so-called barbarous societies, as has already been observed, every man is a warrior. Every man is also, to some extent, a statesman, able to form a reasonable judgment about the interests of the society and the conduct of those who govern it. How far their chiefs are good judges in peace or good leaders in war is plain to almost every one of them. It is true that in such a society no one can easily acquire the cultivated and refined understanding that a few people sometimes possess in a more civilized state. Although in a primitive society there is a good deal of variety in the occupations of each individual, there is not much variety in the occupations of the society as a whole. Every man does, or is capable of doing, almost everything that any other man does or is capable of doing. Every man has a considerable degree of knowledge, ingenuity, and inventiveness, but hardly anyone has a great degree of them. The degree that is commonly possessed, however, is generally enough to conduct all the simple business of the society. In a civilized state, by contrast, although there is little variety in the occupations of most individuals, there is an almost infinite variety in the occupations of the society as a whole. These many occupations offer an almost infinite range of subjects for the contemplation of those few who, tied to no particular occupation themselves, have the leisure and the inclination to study the occupations of others. Contemplating so great a range of subjects necessarily exercises their minds in endless comparisons and combinations, and makes their understanding both sharp and broad to an extraordinary degree. Yet unless those few happen to be placed in some quite particular positions, their great abilities, however much credit they bring to themselves, may contribute very little to the good government or happiness of their society. Despite the great abilities of those few, all the nobler parts of human character may be largely erased and extinguished in the great body of the people.

In a civilized and commercial society, the education of the common people may require the attention of the public more than the education of people of some rank and fortune. People of some rank and fortune are generally eighteen or nineteen years old before they enter the particular business, profession, or trade by which they intend to make their mark in the world. Before that, they have ample time to acquire every accomplishment that can earn them public esteem or make them worthy of it, or at least to prepare themselves for acquiring those accomplishments later. Their parents or guardians are generally eager enough for them to be so accomplished, and in most cases are willing enough to pay what is necessary for the purpose. When such young people are not properly educated, it is seldom because too little money was spent on their education, but because the money was spent badly. It is seldom for lack of teachers, but because of the negligence and incompetence of the teachers who are available, and because of the difficulty, or rather the impossibility, under present conditions, of finding any better ones. Moreover, the employments in which people of some rank or fortune spend most of their lives are not simple and uniform like those of the common people. Nearly all of them are extremely complicated, and they exercise the head more than the hands. The understanding of those engaged in such work can seldom grow sluggish for want of exercise. Besides, the employments of people of some rank and fortune seldom wear them down from morning to night. They generally have a good deal of leisure, during which they can perfect themselves in any branch of useful or ornamental knowledge whose foundation they laid, or for which they acquired some taste, earlier in life.

It is otherwise with the common people. They have little time to spare for education. Their parents can barely afford to support them even in infancy. As soon as they are able to work, they must take up some trade by which they can earn a living. That trade, too, is generally so simple and uniform that it gives little exercise to the understanding, while their labor is at the same time so constant and so severe that it leaves them little leisure, and less inclination, to apply themselves to anything else, or even to think of it.

But although the common people cannot, in any civilized society, be as well instructed as people of some rank and fortune, the most essential parts of education, namely reading, writing, and arithmetic, can be acquired so early in life that most people, even those destined for the lowest occupations, have time to learn them before they can be put to work. At very small expense, the public can make it easier for almost the whole body of the people to acquire these most essential parts of education, can encourage them to do so, and can even make it compulsory.

The public can make this learning easier by establishing in every parish or district a small school where children may be taught for a fee so modest that even a common laborer can afford it, with the schoolmaster paid partly, but not entirely, by the public. If he were paid entirely, or even mainly, by the public, he would soon learn to neglect his work. In Scotland, the establishment of such parish schools has taught almost all the common people to read, and a very large proportion of them to write and do arithmetic. In England, the establishment of charity schools has had an effect of the same kind, though less universal, because the schools themselves are less universal. If the books used to teach the children in these little schools were somewhat more instructive than they usually are, and if, instead of the smattering of Latin that the children of the common people are sometimes taught there, and which can hardly ever be of any use to them, they were taught the elementary parts of geometry and mechanics, then the education in letters of this class of people would perhaps be as complete as it can be. There is hardly a common trade that does not offer some opportunity to apply the principles of geometry and mechanics, and that would not therefore gradually exercise and improve the common people in those principles, which are the necessary introduction to the most sublime as well as the most useful sciences.

The public can encourage the acquisition of these most essential parts of education by giving small prizes and little badges of distinction to the children of the common people who excel in them.

The public can make it compulsory for almost the whole body of the people to acquire these most essential parts of education by requiring every man to pass an examination or trial in them before he can be admitted as a member of any guild or incorporated trade, or be allowed to set up in any trade, whether in a village or in a chartered town.

It was in just this way, by making it easier to learn military and gymnastic exercises, by encouraging their acquisition, and even by requiring the whole body of the people to learn them, that the Greek and Roman republics maintained the martial spirit of their citizens. They made those exercises easier to learn by designating a particular place for learning and practicing them, and by granting certain masters the privilege of teaching there. Those masters do not appear to have received salaries or exclusive privileges of any kind. Their reward consisted entirely of what they received from their pupils, and a citizen who had learned his exercises in the public gymnasia had no legal advantage whatever over one who had learned them privately, provided the latter had learned them equally well. The republics encouraged the learning of those exercises by awarding small prizes and badges of distinction to those who excelled in them. To win a prize in the Olympic, Isthmian, or Nemean games brought renown not only to the winner but to his whole family and kin. And the obligation of every citizen to serve a certain number of years in the armies of the republic, if called upon, was enough to make it necessary for him to learn those exercises, without which he could not be fit for that service.

The example of modern Europe amply demonstrates that, as a society advances, the practice of military exercises gradually decays unless the government takes proper pains to sustain it, and that the martial spirit of the great body of the people decays along with it. Yet the security of every society must always depend, to a greater or lesser degree, on the martial spirit of the great body of the people. In the present age, it is true, that martial spirit alone, unsupported by a well-disciplined standing army, would probably not be enough for the defense and security of any society. But where every citizen had the spirit of a soldier, a smaller standing army would surely be required. That spirit, moreover, would necessarily do much to reduce the dangers to liberty, whether real or imagined, that are commonly feared from a standing army. Just as it would greatly assist the operations of that army against a foreign invader, so it would obstruct them just as much if they should ever, unfortunately, be turned against the constitution of the state.

The ancient institutions of Greece and Rome seem to have been far more effective at maintaining the martial spirit of the great body of the people than the militias, as they are called, of modern times. They were much simpler. Once established, they ran by themselves, and it took little or no attention from the government to keep them in perfect vigor. Maintaining even tolerable compliance with the complicated regulations of any modern militia, by contrast, demands the continual and laborious attention of the government, without which those regulations are always falling into complete neglect and disuse. The influence of the ancient institutions was also far more universal. Through them, the whole body of the people was thoroughly trained in the use of arms, whereas only a very small part of the people can ever be so trained under the regulations of any modern militia, except perhaps that of Switzerland. Now a coward, a man incapable of either defending or avenging himself, clearly lacks one of the most essential parts of the character of a man. He is as mutilated and deformed in his mind as another man is in his body who has been deprived of some of its most essential limbs, or has lost the use of them. Of the two, the coward is plainly the more wretched and miserable, because happiness and misery, which reside entirely in the mind, must depend more on the healthy or unhealthy, the mutilated or whole condition of the mind than on that of the body. Even if the martial spirit of the people were of no use whatever for the defense of the society, it would still deserve the most serious attention of the government to prevent the kind of mental mutilation, deformity, and wretchedness that cowardice necessarily involves from spreading through the great body of the people. In the same way, it would deserve the government's most serious attention to prevent leprosy, or any other loathsome and repellent disease, from spreading among them, even if the disease were neither fatal nor dangerous, and even if no other public good might come of that attention beyond the prevention of so great a public evil.

The same may be said of the gross ignorance and stupidity that, in a civilized society, so often seem to numb the understanding of all the lower ranks of people. A man without the proper use of the intellectual faculties of a man is, if possible, even more contemptible than a coward, and seems to be mutilated and deformed in a still more essential part of human nature. Even if the state were to gain no advantage from the instruction of the lower ranks of people, it would still deserve the state's attention that they not be left entirely uninstructed. The state, however, gains no small advantage from their instruction. The more instructed they are, the less vulnerable they are to the delusions of religious fanaticism and superstition, which among ignorant nations frequently give rise to the most dreadful disorders. An instructed and intelligent people, moreover, are always more decent and orderly than an ignorant and stupid one. Each of them individually feels more worthy of respect, and more likely to win the respect of their lawful superiors, and they are therefore more inclined to respect those superiors. They are more inclined to examine, and better able to see through, the self-interested complaints of faction and sedition, and for that reason they are less likely to be misled into any reckless or unnecessary opposition to the measures of government. In free countries, where the security of the government depends heavily on the favorable judgment the people form of its conduct, it must surely be of the highest importance that they not be inclined to judge it rashly or capriciously.

##### Article III: On the Expense of the Institutions for the Instruction of People of All Ages

The institutions for the instruction of people of all ages are chiefly those for religious instruction. This is a kind of instruction whose aim is not so much to make people good citizens in this world as to prepare them for another and better world in the life to come. The teachers of the doctrine that contains this instruction, like other teachers, may depend for their living entirely on the voluntary contributions of their hearers, or they may draw it from some other fund to which the law of their country entitles them, such as a landed estate, a tithe or land tax, or a fixed salary or stipend. Their effort, zeal, and diligence are likely to be much greater in the first situation than in the second. In this respect, the teachers of a new religion have always had a considerable advantage in attacking the old, established systems, whose clergy, resting comfortably on their benefices (the church livings that supplied their income), had neglected to keep alive the fervor of faith and devotion in the great body of the people, and, having given themselves over to idleness, had become entirely incapable of any vigorous effort even in defense of their own establishment. The clergy of an established and well-endowed religion often become men of learning and refinement, who possess all the virtues of gentlemen, or all those that can win the esteem of gentlemen. But they tend gradually to lose the qualities, both good and bad, that gave them authority and influence with the lower ranks of people, and that had perhaps been the original causes of their religion's success and establishment. When such a clergy is attacked by a band of popular and bold, though perhaps stupid and ignorant, zealots, they feel themselves as utterly defenseless as the idle, soft, and overfed nations of southern Asia felt when they were invaded by the active, hardy, and hungry Tartars of the north. In such an emergency, a clergy of this kind generally has no other recourse than to call on the civil authorities to persecute, destroy, or expel their adversaries as disturbers of the public peace. It was in this way that the Roman Catholic clergy called on the civil authorities to persecute the Protestants, and the Church of England to persecute the Dissenters; and in general, every religious sect that has once enjoyed the security of a legal establishment for a century or two has found itself incapable of mounting any vigorous defense against a new sect that chose to attack its doctrine or discipline. On such occasions, the advantage in learning and good writing may sometimes lie with the established church. But the arts of popularity, all the arts of winning converts, are always on the side of its adversaries. In England, those arts have long been neglected by the well-endowed clergy of the established church, and they are now cultivated chiefly by the Dissenters and the Methodists. The independent incomes, however, that have in many places been provided for dissenting ministers, by means of voluntary subscriptions, trust arrangements, and other evasions of the law, seem to have greatly dampened the zeal and activity of those ministers. Many of them have become very learned, ingenious, and respectable men, but in general they have ceased to be very popular preachers. The Methodists, with not half the learning of the Dissenters, are far more in fashion.

In the Church of Rome, the diligence and zeal of the lower clergy are kept more alive by the powerful motive of self-interest than perhaps in any established Protestant church. Many of the parish clergy derive a very considerable part of their living from the voluntary offerings of the people, a source of income that confession gives them many opportunities to increase. The mendicant orders, the begging friars, derive their entire living from such offerings. It is with them as with the hussars and light infantry of certain armies, troops who were expected to support themselves from what they could seize: no plunder, no pay. The parish clergy are like those teachers whose reward depends partly on their salary and partly on the fees or honoraria they receive from their pupils, which must always depend, more or less, on their diligence and reputation. The mendicant orders are like those teachers whose living depends entirely on their diligence. They are therefore obliged to use every art that can stir the devotion of the common people. Machiavelli observes that the founding of the two great mendicant orders of St. Dominic and St. Francis revived the flagging faith and devotion of the Catholic Church in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. In Roman Catholic countries, the spirit of devotion is sustained entirely by the monks and the poorer parish clergy. The great dignitaries of the church, with all the accomplishments of gentlemen and men of the world, and sometimes those of men of learning, take care to maintain the necessary discipline over their subordinates, but seldom trouble themselves about the instruction of the people.

"Most of the arts and professions in a state," says by far the most illustrious philosopher and historian of the present age, "are of such a nature that, while they promote the interests of society, they are also useful or agreeable to certain individuals. In that case, the constant rule of the magistrate, except perhaps when an art is first introduced, is to leave the profession to itself and to entrust its encouragement to the individuals who reap its benefits. The craftsmen, finding their profits rise with the favor of their customers, increase their skill and diligence as much as they can; and since matters are not disturbed by any ill-judged interference, the supply of the commodity is always sure to be roughly proportioned to the demand.

"But there are also some callings which, though useful and even necessary in a state, bring no advantage or pleasure to any individual, and the supreme power is obliged to change its conduct toward the members of those professions. It must give them public support for their subsistence, and it must guard against the negligence to which they will naturally be prone, either by attaching particular honors to the profession, by establishing a long hierarchy of ranks and a strict dependence, or by some other means. Those employed in the public finances, the navy, and the magistracy are examples of this class of men.

"It might naturally be thought, at first sight, that the clergy belong to the first class, and that their encouragement, like that of lawyers and physicians, may safely be left to the generosity of individuals who are attached to their doctrines and who find benefit or consolation in their spiritual ministry and help. Their diligence and vigilance will no doubt be sharpened by this additional motive, and their skill in their profession, as well as their dexterity in governing the minds of the people, must grow daily through increasing practice, study, and attention.

"But if we consider the matter more closely, we shall find that this self-interested diligence of the clergy is exactly what every wise legislator will try to prevent. For in every religion except the true one, it is highly harmful, and it even has a natural tendency to corrupt the truth by mixing into it a strong dose of superstition, folly, and delusion. Each spiritual practitioner, in order to make himself more precious and sacred in the eyes of his followers, will inspire them with the most violent hatred of all other sects, and will constantly try, by some novelty, to rouse the flagging devotion of his audience. No regard will be paid to truth, morals, or decency in the doctrines taught. Every tenet will be adopted that best suits the unruly passions of human nature. Customers will be drawn to each meeting-house by fresh diligence and skill in playing on the passions and credulity of the populace. And in the end, the civil magistrate will find that he has paid dearly for his intended thrift in sparing the cost of a fixed establishment for the priests, and that, in reality, the most decent and advantageous bargain he can strike with the spiritual guides is to bribe their idleness by assigning fixed salaries to their profession, making it unnecessary for them to be any more active than is needed merely to keep their flock from straying in search of new pastors. And in this way, ecclesiastical establishments, though they commonly arose at first from religious motives, prove in the end advantageous to the political interests of society."

But whatever the good or bad effects of giving the clergy an independent income may have been, it has perhaps very seldom been granted to them with any view to those effects. Times of violent religious controversy have generally been times of equally violent political faction. On such occasions, each political party has found, or imagined, that it was in its interest to ally itself with one or another of the contending religious sects. But this could be done only by adopting, or at least by favoring, the tenets of that particular sect. The sect that had the good fortune to be allied with the victorious party necessarily shared in the victory of its ally, by whose favor and protection it was soon able, to some degree, to silence and subdue all its adversaries. Those adversaries had generally allied themselves with the enemies of the victorious party, and were therefore that party's enemies as well. Once the clergy of this particular sect had become complete masters of the field, and their influence and authority over the great body of the people stood at its height, they were powerful enough to overawe the chiefs and leaders of their own party and to compel the civil magistrate to respect their opinions and wishes. Their first demand was usually that he silence and subdue all their adversaries; their second, that he grant them an independent income. Since they had generally contributed a good deal to the victory, it seemed not unreasonable that they should have some share of the spoils. They were tired, besides, of humoring the people and of depending on popular whim for their livelihood. In making this demand, then, they looked to their own ease and comfort, without troubling themselves about the effect it might have, in later times, on the influence and authority of their order. The civil magistrate, who could satisfy them only by giving them something he would much rather have taken or kept for himself, was seldom eager to grant it. Necessity, however, always forced him to yield in the end, though often only after many delays, evasions, and pretended excuses.

But suppose politics had never called on religion for help. Suppose the victorious party, once it had won, had never adopted the tenets of one sect in preference to another. It would then probably have dealt equally and impartially with all the different sects, and allowed every man to choose his own priest and his own religion as he saw fit. In that case there would no doubt have been a great multitude of religious sects. Almost every congregation might have formed a little sect of its own, or held some peculiar tenets of its own. Each teacher would no doubt have felt obliged to exert himself to the utmost, and to use every art, both to keep and to increase the number of his disciples. But since every other teacher would have felt the same obligation, no single teacher or group of teachers could have succeeded very greatly. The self-interested and active zeal of religious teachers can be dangerous and troublesome only where a society tolerates a single sect, or where an entire large society is divided into two or three great sects, the teachers of each acting in concert under a regular discipline and chain of command. That zeal must be entirely harmless, however, where the society is divided into two or three hundred, or perhaps as many thousand, small sects, none of them large enough to disturb the public peace. The teachers of each sect, seeing themselves surrounded on all sides by more adversaries than friends, would be forced to learn the candor and moderation so seldom found among the teachers of the great sects. Those great sects have their tenets upheld by the civil magistrate and revered by nearly all the inhabitants of vast kingdoms and empires, and so their teachers see nothing around them but followers, disciples, and humble admirers. The teachers of each little sect, by contrast, finding themselves almost alone, would be obliged to respect the teachers of almost every other sect. The concessions they would find it both convenient and agreeable to make to one another might in time reduce the doctrine of most of them to that pure and rational religion, free of every admixture of absurdity, imposture, or fanaticism, which wise men in every age of the world have wished to see established. Positive law, meaning the law actually enacted by the state, has perhaps never yet established such a religion in any country, and probably never will, because in matters of religion positive law always has been, and probably always will be, more or less swayed by popular superstition and enthusiasm. This plan of church government, or more properly of no church government at all, was what the sect called the Independents (a sect, no doubt, of very wild enthusiasts) proposed to establish in England toward the end of the civil war. Had it been established, then despite its thoroughly unphilosophical origin, it would probably by now have produced the most philosophical good temper and moderation toward every sort of religious principle. It has been established in Pennsylvania, where, although the Quakers happen to be the most numerous, the law in fact favors no sect over any other; and there it is said to have produced exactly this philosophical good temper and moderation.

Yet even if this equal treatment failed to produce such good temper and moderation in all, or even in most, of the religious sects of a given country, the excessive zeal of each for its own tenets could hardly produce any very harmful effects, provided the sects were numerous enough, and each therefore too small to disturb the public peace. On the contrary, that zeal would produce several good ones. And if the government were firmly resolved both to leave them all alone and to make them all leave one another alone, there is little danger that they would fail to subdivide themselves of their own accord, quickly enough to become sufficiently numerous before long.

In every civilized society, in every society where the distinction of ranks has once been fully established, two different schemes or systems of morality have always been current at the same time. One may be called the strict or austere system; the other the liberal or, if you prefer, the loose system. The common people generally admire and revere the first; what are called people of fashion generally esteem and adopt the second. The chief difference between these two opposite systems seems to lie in how severely we ought to condemn the vices of levity, the vices that tend to arise from great prosperity and from an excess of gaiety and high spirits. In the liberal or loose system, luxury, wanton and even disorderly merriment, the pursuit of pleasure to the point of some intemperance, the breach of chastity (at least in one of the two sexes), and the like are generally treated with a good deal of indulgence, and are easily excused or pardoned altogether, provided they are not accompanied by gross indecency and do not lead to falsehood and injustice. In the austere system, by contrast, these excesses are regarded with the utmost abhorrence and detestation. The vices of levity are always ruinous to the common people. A single week of thoughtlessness and dissipation is often enough to undo a poor workman forever, and to drive him, in his despair, to commit the most monstrous crimes. The wiser and better sort among the common people therefore always regard such excesses with the utmost abhorrence and detestation, because their experience tells them that these excesses are immediately fatal to people in their condition. The disorder and extravagance of several years, on the other hand, will not always ruin a man of fashion. People of that rank are very apt to regard the power to indulge in some degree of excess as one of the advantages of their fortune, and the liberty to do so without censure or reproach as one of the privileges of their station. In people of their own station, therefore, they view such excesses with only slight disapproval, and censure them very lightly or not at all.

Almost all religious sects have begun among the common people, from whom they have generally drawn both their earliest and their most numerous converts. Accordingly, these sects have almost always adopted the austere system of morality. There have been a very few exceptions, but only a few. It was the system that best recommended them to the class of people to whom they first proposed their plan for reforming what had previously been established. Many of them, perhaps most, have even tried to win credit by refining on this austere system and carrying it to some degree of folly and extravagance; and this excessive rigor has often done more than anything else to win them the respect and veneration of the common people.

A man of rank and fortune is, by virtue of his station, a conspicuous member of a great society that watches every part of his conduct, and so obliges him to watch every part of it himself. His authority and standing depend very largely on the respect this society holds for him. He dares not do anything that would disgrace or discredit him within it, and he is bound to observe very strictly whatever kind of morality, liberal or austere, the general consent of this society prescribes for persons of his rank and fortune. A man of humble condition, by contrast, is far from being a conspicuous member of any great society. So long as he remains in a country village, his conduct may be watched, and he may be obliged to watch it himself. In this situation, and only in this situation, he may have what is called a reputation to lose. But as soon as he moves to a great city, he sinks into obscurity and darkness. Nobody observes or attends to his conduct, and he is therefore very likely to neglect it himself and abandon himself to every kind of low profligacy and vice. Nothing lifts him out of this obscurity so effectively, and nothing draws the attention of a respectable society to his conduct so strongly, as becoming a member of a small religious sect. From that moment he acquires a degree of standing he never had before. All his fellow members have an interest, for the sake of the sect's reputation, in watching his conduct. If he causes any scandal, or strays very far from the austere morals they almost always demand of one another, they have an interest in punishing him with expulsion or excommunication from the sect, which is always a very severe punishment, even when no further harm follows from it. In little religious sects, accordingly, the morals of the common people have almost always been remarkably regular and orderly, generally far more so than in the established church. The morals of these little sects, indeed, have often been rather disagreeably rigorous and unsociable.

There are, however, two very easy and effective remedies by whose combined operation the state might, without violence, correct whatever was unsociable or disagreeably rigorous in the morals of all the little sects into which the country was divided.

The first of these remedies is the study of science and philosophy, which the state might make nearly universal among all people of middling or more than middling rank and fortune. It would do so not by paying salaries to teachers, which only makes them negligent and idle, but by instituting some form of examination, even in the higher and more difficult sciences, that every person would have to pass before being permitted to practice any learned profession, or before being accepted as a candidate for any honorable office of trust or profit. If the state required this class of people to acquire learning, it would have no need to trouble itself about supplying them with proper teachers. They would soon find better teachers for themselves than any the state could provide. Science is the great antidote to the poison of enthusiasm and superstition; and where all the upper ranks of people were protected from that poison, the lower ranks could not be much exposed to it.

The second of these remedies is the frequency and gaiety of public entertainments. The state could encourage, that is, give complete liberty to, all those who, out of their own interest, would try to amuse and divert the people, without scandal or indecency, through painting, poetry, music, and dancing, and through every kind of dramatic performance and exhibition. By doing so it would easily dispel, in most of the people, that melancholy and gloomy temper which is almost always the nurse of popular superstition and enthusiasm. Public entertainments have always been objects of dread and hatred to all the fanatical promoters of these popular frenzies. The gaiety and good humor such entertainments inspire were entirely at odds with the frame of mind best suited to the fanatics' purpose, the frame of mind they could most easily work upon. Dramatic performances, moreover, often exposed their tricks to public ridicule and sometimes even to public condemnation, and for that reason they were, more than any other entertainment, the special objects of their abhorrence.

In a country where the law favored the teachers of no one religion over those of another, none of them would need to be in any particular or direct dependence on the sovereign or executive power, nor would he need to have anything to do with appointing them to their offices or removing them. In such circumstances he would have no reason to concern himself with them beyond keeping the peace among them, as he does among the rest of his subjects; that is, preventing them from persecuting, abusing, or oppressing one another. But the case is entirely different in countries with an established or governing religion. There the sovereign can never be secure unless he has the means of influencing, to a considerable degree, the greater part of the teachers of that religion.

The clergy of every established church form a great corporation. They can act in concert and pursue their interest on a single plan and in a single spirit, as fully as if they were under the direction of one man; and often they are in fact under such direction. Their interest as a corporate body is never the same as the sovereign's, and is sometimes directly opposed to it. Their great interest is to maintain their authority over the people, and this authority rests on the supposed certainty and importance of the entire doctrine they teach, and on the supposed necessity of accepting every part of it with the most unquestioning faith in order to escape eternal misery. Should the sovereign be so imprudent as to seem to mock, or himself to doubt, even the most trivial part of their doctrine, or should he, out of humanity, try to protect those who did either, the touchy honor of a clergy wholly independent of him is immediately provoked. They denounce him as a profane person and bring all the terrors of religion to bear in order to compel the people to transfer their allegiance to some more orthodox and obedient prince. Should he resist any of their claims or encroachments, the danger is just as great. Princes who have dared to rebel against the church in this way have generally been charged not only with the crime of rebellion but with the further crime of heresy, notwithstanding their solemn professions of faith and their humble submission to every tenet she saw fit to prescribe for them. For the authority of religion is superior to every other authority, and the fears it inspires overcome all other fears. When the authorized teachers of religion spread among the great body of the people doctrines that undermine the sovereign's authority, he can maintain that authority only by violence, or by the force of a standing army. Even a standing army cannot give him lasting security in such a case. If the soldiers are not foreigners, which can seldom be the case, but are drawn from the great body of the people, which must almost always be the case, they are likely to be quickly corrupted by those very doctrines. The revolutions that the turbulence of the Greek clergy continually brought about at Constantinople for as long as the Eastern Empire lasted, and the upheavals that the turbulence of the Roman clergy continually caused in every part of Europe over the course of several centuries, are sufficient proof of how precarious and insecure the position of any sovereign must always be who has no proper means of influencing the clergy of his country's established and governing religion.

It is evident enough that articles of faith, like all other spiritual matters, fall outside the proper province of a temporal sovereign, who, however well qualified he may be to protect the people, is seldom supposed to be qualified to instruct them. In such matters, therefore, his authority can seldom be enough to counterbalance the united authority of the clergy of the established church. Yet the public peace, and his own security, may often depend on the doctrines they choose to spread concerning those matters. Since he can seldom oppose their decisions directly with the proper weight and authority, he must be able to influence them; and he can influence them only through the fears and hopes he can arouse in the greater part of the individuals who belong to the order. Those fears may be the fear of losing their positions or suffering some other punishment; those hopes, the hope of further advancement.

In all Christian churches, the clergy's benefices, the church offices together with the incomes attached to them, are a kind of freehold property, held not at the pleasure of a superior but for life or during good behavior. If they held them on a more precarious tenure, liable to be turned out at every slight offense given to the sovereign or his ministers, it might be impossible for them to keep their authority with the people. The people would then regard them as hired dependents of the court and could no longer have any confidence in the sincerity of their teaching. But if the sovereign tried irregularly and by force to strip any number of clergymen of their freeholds, perhaps for having spread some factious or seditious doctrine with more than ordinary zeal, he would only make both them and their doctrine, through such persecution, ten times more popular, and therefore ten times more troublesome and dangerous, than before. Fear is in almost every case a wretched instrument of government, and it ought never, in particular, to be used against any order of men with the slightest claim to independence. Trying to terrify them only aggravates their ill humor and hardens them in an opposition that gentler treatment might easily have persuaded them to soften or abandon altogether. The French parliaments were sovereign courts of justice, and a royal edict had to be formally entered in their registers before it could take legal effect. The violence that the French government usually employed to force them to register an unpopular edict very seldom succeeded, although the means it commonly used, the imprisonment of every resisting member, would seem forceful enough. The princes of the house of Stuart sometimes used similar means to influence certain members of the English Parliament, and they generally found them just as intractable. The Parliament of England is now managed in another way; and a very small experiment that the Duke of Choiseul made on the parliament of Paris, about twelve years ago, showed clearly enough that all the parliaments of France could have been managed even more easily in the same way. That experiment was not pursued. For although management and persuasion are always the easiest and safest instruments of government, just as force and violence are the worst and most dangerous, such, it seems, is the natural arrogance of man that he almost always scorns the good instrument except when he cannot or dare not use the bad one. The French government could and dared use force, and therefore scorned to use management and persuasion. But there is no order of men, I believe, as the experience of every age shows, against whom the use of force and violence is so dangerous, or rather so utterly ruinous, as the respected clergy of an established church. Even under the most despotic governments, the rights, privileges, and personal liberty of every individual churchman who is on good terms with his own order are more respected than those of any other person of roughly equal rank and fortune. This holds at every degree of despotism, from the gentle and mild government of Paris to the violent and furious government of Constantinople. But although this order of men can hardly ever be forced, they can be managed as easily as any other. The security of the sovereign, as well as the public peace, seems to depend very much on the means he has of managing them; and those means seem to consist entirely in the advancement he has at his disposal to bestow on them.

Under the ancient constitution of the Christian church, the bishop of each diocese was elected by the joint votes of the clergy and the people of the cathedral city. The people did not keep their right of election for long, and while they did keep it, they almost always acted under the influence of the clergy, who in such spiritual matters seemed to be their natural guides. The clergy, however, soon tired of the trouble of managing them and found it easier to elect their bishops themselves. In the same way, the abbot was elected by the monks of the monastery, at least in most abbeys. All the lesser church offices within the diocese were conferred by the bishop, who gave them to whatever churchmen he thought fit. In this way all church appointments lay at the disposal of the church itself. The sovereign might have some indirect influence over these elections, and it was sometimes customary to ask both his consent to hold an election and his approval of its result; yet he had no direct or adequate means of managing the clergy. Every clergyman's ambition naturally led him to court not so much his sovereign as his own order, from which alone he could expect advancement.

Throughout most of Europe, the pope gradually drew into his own hands, first, the right of appointment to almost all bishoprics and abbeys, the so-called consistorial benefices, and afterward, by various schemes and pretexts, to most of the lesser offices within each diocese, leaving the bishop little more than was barely necessary to give him a respectable authority over his own clergy. Under this arrangement the sovereign's position was even worse than it had been before. The clergy of all the different countries of Europe were thus formed into a kind of spiritual army, dispersed in different quarters, it is true, but with all its movements and operations now capable of being directed by one head and carried out on one uniform plan. The clergy of each particular country could be regarded as a particular detachment of that army, whose operations could easily be supported and reinforced by all the other detachments stationed in the surrounding countries. Each detachment was not only independent of the sovereign of the country in which it was quartered and by which it was maintained, but dependent on a foreign sovereign, who could at any moment turn its arms against the ruler of that country and back them with the arms of all the other detachments.

Those arms were the most formidable that can well be imagined. In the early condition of Europe, before arts and manufactures had taken hold, the wealth of the clergy gave them the same kind of influence over the common people that the wealth of the great barons gave those lords over their vassals, tenants, and retainers. On the great landed estates that the misguided piety of princes and private persons alike had bestowed on the church, jurisdictions were established of the same kind as those of the great barons, and for the same reason. On those estates the clergy, or their bailiffs, could easily keep the peace without the support or assistance of the king or anyone else, while neither the king nor anyone else could keep the peace there without the support and assistance of the clergy. The courts the clergy held in their own baronies and manors were therefore just as independent of the king's courts, and just as completely closed to their authority, as those of the great secular lords. The tenants of the clergy, like those of the great barons, were almost all tenants at will, holding their land only for as long as the landlord pleased. They were entirely dependent on their immediate lords and could therefore be called out at any time to fight in whatever quarrel the clergy saw fit to draw them into. Beyond the rents of their own estates, the clergy also collected, through the tithe, the tenth of the produce owed to the church, a very large share of the rents of every other estate in every kingdom of Europe. Most of the revenue from both these sources was paid in kind: in grain, wine, cattle, poultry, and the like. The quantity far exceeded what the clergy could consume themselves, and there were no arts or manufactures whose products they could take in exchange for the surplus. The only way the clergy could draw any benefit from this immense surplus was to use it as the great barons used theirs, in the most lavish hospitality and the most extensive charity. The hospitality and charity of the medieval clergy are accordingly said to have been very great. They supported nearly all the poor of every kingdom, and many knights and gentlemen often had no other means of living than to travel from monastery to monastery, ostensibly out of devotion but in reality to enjoy the hospitality of the clergy. The retainers of certain prelates were often as numerous as those of the greatest lay lords, and the retainers of the clergy taken as a whole were perhaps more numerous than those of all the lay lords combined. There was also always far more unity among the clergy than among the lay lords. The clergy were held under a regular discipline and subordination to papal authority. The lay lords were under no regular discipline or subordination of any kind, and were almost always as jealous of one another as they were of the king. So even if the tenants and retainers of the clergy, taken together, had been fewer than those of the great lay lords, and their tenants probably were far fewer, their unity alone would have made them more formidable.

The hospitality and charity of the clergy did more than give them command of a great temporal force; they also greatly increased the weight of their spiritual weapons. Those virtues earned them the deepest respect and veneration among all the lower ranks of people, many of whom were fed by the clergy constantly, and nearly all of whom were fed by them at one time or another. Everything that belonged or related to so popular an order, its possessions, its privileges, and its doctrines, inevitably appeared sacred in the eyes of the common people, and every violation of them, whether real or merely alleged, appeared the very height of sacrilegious wickedness and profanity. Under such conditions, if the sovereign often found it hard to resist a combination of a few great nobles, it is no wonder he found it harder still to resist the united force of the clergy of his own realm, backed by the clergy of every neighboring realm. In such circumstances the wonder is not that he was sometimes forced to yield, but that he was ever able to resist at all.

The privileges the clergy enjoyed in those times, which seem to us today the most absurd of all, such as their complete exemption from secular jurisdiction, or what in England was called "benefit of clergy," the right of a clergyman accused of a crime to be tried in the church's courts rather than the king's, were the natural, or rather the necessary, consequences of this state of affairs. How dangerous it must have been for a sovereign to try to punish a clergyman for any crime whatever, if the clerical order was inclined to protect him, and to declare either that the evidence was insufficient to convict so holy a man, or that the punishment was too severe to inflict on one whose person religion had made sacred. In such circumstances the sovereign could do no better than leave him to be tried by the ecclesiastical courts. Those courts, for the sake of their own order's reputation, had every interest in restraining its members as far as possible from committing serious crimes, or even from causing the kind of gross scandal that might turn the minds of the people against them.

Given the state of things across most of Europe during the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth centuries, and for some time before and after, the constitution of the Church of Rome may be regarded as the most formidable alliance ever formed against the authority and security of civil government, and against the liberty, reason, and happiness of humankind, which can flourish only where civil government is strong enough to protect them. Within that constitution, the grossest delusions of superstition were so firmly propped up by the private interests of so many people that they were placed beyond the reach of any assault by human reason. Reason might perhaps have succeeded in exposing some of those delusions, even to the eyes of the common people, but it could never have dissolved the bonds of private interest. Had this constitution faced no enemy but the feeble efforts of human reason, it would have lasted forever. Yet that vast and solidly built structure, which all the wisdom and virtue of man could never have shaken, much less overthrown, was first weakened and then partly destroyed by the natural course of events, and it now seems likely, perhaps within a few more centuries, to crumble into ruins altogether.

The gradual progress of arts, manufactures, and commerce, the same forces that destroyed the power of the great barons, destroyed in the same way, across most of Europe, the entire temporal power of the clergy. In the products of arts, manufactures, and commerce, the clergy, like the great barons, found something for which they could exchange their raw produce, and so discovered the means of spending their whole revenues on themselves without giving any significant share to anyone else. Their charity gradually became less extensive and their hospitality less generous, or less lavish. Their retainers consequently grew fewer, and by degrees disappeared entirely. The clergy, too, like the great barons, wanted higher rents from their landed estates so that they could spend them in the same way, on the gratification of their own private vanity and folly. But higher rents could be obtained only by granting leases to their tenants, who thereby became largely independent of them. In this manner the ties of interest that had bound the lower ranks of people to the clergy were gradually broken and dissolved. They were broken even sooner than the ties that bound the same people to the great barons, because most church benefices, the offices that carried a fixed income from church property, were much smaller than the estates of the great barons, and so the holder of each benefice was much sooner able to spend its whole revenue on himself. Through most of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, the power of the great barons remained, across most of Europe, in full vigor. But the temporal power of the clergy, the absolute command they had once held over the great body of the people, had by then decayed considerably. Across most of Europe, the power of the church had by that time been reduced almost entirely to what arose from its spiritual authority, and even that spiritual authority was much weakened once it was no longer sustained by the charity and hospitality of the clergy. The lower ranks of people no longer regarded the clergy as they once had, as the comforters of their distress and the relievers of their poverty. On the contrary, they were provoked and disgusted by the vanity, luxury, and extravagance of the richer clergy, who seemed to spend on their own pleasures what had always been regarded as the inheritance of the poor.

In this situation, the sovereigns of the various states of Europe tried to recover the influence they had once had over the filling of the great church offices. They did so by restoring to the deans and chapters of each diocese their ancient right of electing the bishop, and to the monks of each abbey their right of electing the abbot. Re-establishing this ancient order was the aim of several statutes passed in England during the fourteenth century, particularly the one known as the Statute of Provisors, and of the Pragmatic Sanction established in France in the fifteenth century. For an election to be valid, the sovereign had both to consent to it beforehand and to approve the person elected afterward; and although the election was still nominally free, he retained every indirect means of influencing the clergy of his realm that his position naturally afforded. Other regulations with a similar purpose were established elsewhere in Europe. But before the Reformation, the pope's power of collation, his right to appoint holders to the great church benefices, seems nowhere to have been so effectively or so thoroughly restrained as in France and England. Later, in the sixteenth century, the Concordat gave the kings of France the absolute right of nomination to all the great benefices of the French church, those known as consistorial benefices because they were confirmed by the pope in his consistory, or council of cardinals.

Since the establishment of the Pragmatic Sanction and the Concordat, the clergy of France have generally shown less deference to the decrees of the papal court than the clergy of any other Catholic country. In every dispute their sovereign has had with the pope, they have almost always sided with the king. This independence of the French clergy from the court of Rome seems to rest chiefly on the Pragmatic Sanction and the Concordat. In the earlier periods of the monarchy, the clergy of France appear to have been as devoted to the pope as those of any other country. When Robert, the second king of the Capetian line, was most unjustly excommunicated by the court of Rome, his own servants, it is said, threw the food from his table to the dogs and refused to taste anything that had been polluted by contact with a man in his condition. It may safely be assumed that they were taught to do so by the clergy of his own kingdom.

The claim to appoint to the great benefices of the church, a claim in whose defense the court of Rome had often shaken, and sometimes overturned, the thrones of some of the greatest sovereigns in Christendom, was thus restrained, modified, or abandoned altogether in many parts of Europe even before the Reformation. As the clergy now had less influence over the people, the state had more influence over the clergy. The clergy therefore had both less power and less inclination to disturb the state.

Such was the declining authority of the Church of Rome when the disputes that gave birth to the Reformation began in Germany and soon spread through every part of Europe. The new doctrines were everywhere received with great popular favor. They were spread with all the enthusiastic zeal that commonly animates the spirit of party when it attacks established authority. The teachers of those doctrines, though perhaps no more learned in other respects than many of the theologians who defended the established church, seem generally to have known ecclesiastical history better, along with the origin and development of the system of beliefs on which the church's authority rested, and this gave them the advantage in almost every dispute. The austerity of their manners gave them authority with the common people, who contrasted the strict regularity of their conduct with the disorderly lives of most of their own clergy. They also possessed, to a far greater degree than their opponents, every art of winning popularity and gaining converts, arts that the lofty and dignified sons of the church had long neglected as largely useless to them.
