The reasonableness of the new doctrines recommended them to some, their novelty to many, and hatred and contempt for the established clergy to a still greater number. But what recommended them to by far the greatest number was the zealous, passionate, and fanatical eloquence, often coarse and rustic, with which they were preached almost everywhere.

The success of the new doctrines was so great almost everywhere that princes who happened at the time to be on bad terms with the court of Rome could easily use them to overthrow the church in their own dominions; for the church, having lost the respect and veneration of the lower ranks of people, could put up scarcely any resistance. The court of Rome had offended some of the smaller princes in the northern parts of Germany, whom it had probably regarded as too insignificant to be worth managing. All of them, accordingly, established the Reformation in their own territories. The tyranny of Christian II and of Trolle, archbishop of Uppsala, enabled Gustavus Vasa to drive them both out of Sweden. The pope favored the tyrant and the archbishop, and Gustavus Vasa found no difficulty in establishing the Reformation in Sweden. Christian II was later deposed from the throne of Denmark, where his conduct had made him as hated as in Sweden. The pope, however, was still inclined to favor him, and Frederick of Holstein, who had taken the throne in his place, took his revenge by following the example of Gustavus Vasa. The magistrates of Bern and Zurich, who had no particular quarrel with the pope, established the Reformation with great ease in their respective cantons, where shortly before some of the clergy had, by a fraud rather grosser than usual, made the whole order both hateful and contemptible.

In this critical state of its affairs, the papal court took considerable pains to cultivate the friendship of the powerful sovereigns of France and Spain, the latter of whom was at that time also emperor of Germany. With their help it managed, though not without great difficulty and much bloodshed, either to suppress the Reformation entirely in their dominions or greatly to obstruct its progress. It was also quite willing to accommodate the king of England. But given the circumstances of the time, it could not do so without offending a still greater sovereign, Charles V, king of Spain and emperor of Germany. Henry VIII, accordingly, though he did not himself embrace most of the doctrines of the Reformation, was able, because of their general prevalence, to suppress all the monasteries and abolish the authority of the Church of Rome in his dominions. That he went so far, though he went no further, gave some satisfaction to the supporters of the Reformation, who, having gained control of the government in the reign of his son and successor, completed without any difficulty the work Henry VIII had begun.

In some countries, such as Scotland, where the government was weak, unpopular, and not very firmly established, the Reformation was strong enough to overthrow not only the church but the state as well, for having tried to support the church.

Among the followers of the Reformation, scattered through all the different countries of Europe, there was no general tribunal, like the court of Rome or an ecumenical council, that could settle all disputes among them and, with irresistible authority, prescribe to all of them the exact limits of orthodoxy. When the reformers of one country happened to differ from their fellow believers in another, they had no common judge to appeal to, and the dispute could never be resolved; and many such disputes arose among them. Those concerning the government of the church and the right of conferring church benefices were perhaps the most consequential for the peace and welfare of civil society. They accordingly gave rise to the two principal parties or sects among the followers of the Reformation, the Lutheran and the Calvinist, the only ones whose doctrine and discipline have yet been established by law anywhere in Europe.

The followers of Luther, together with what is called the Church of England, preserved more or less of government by bishops. They established a hierarchy among the clergy, gave the sovereign the disposal of all the bishoprics and other consistorial benefices in his realm, and thereby made him the real head of the church. Without depriving the bishop of the right to appoint to the smaller benefices in his diocese, they not only admitted but encouraged, even for those benefices, the right of presentation, the right of a patron to nominate a clergyman to a vacant living, whether that patron was the sovereign or any other layman. This system of church government was from the beginning favorable to peace and good order and to submission to the civil sovereign. Accordingly, it has never caused a riot or civil disturbance in any country where it has once been established. The Church of England in particular has always prided herself, with good reason, on the unimpeachable loyalty of her principles. Under such a government, the clergy naturally try to recommend themselves to the sovereign, to the court, and to the nobility and gentry of the country, through whose influence they chiefly expect to win promotion. They court these patrons sometimes, no doubt, with the basest flattery and servile agreement; but often, too, by cultivating all the qualities that most deserve, and are therefore most likely to win, the esteem of people of rank and fortune: by their knowledge of every branch of useful and ornamental learning, by the decent liberality of their manners, by the social good humor of their conversation, and by their open contempt for those absurd and hypocritical austerities that fanatics preach and pretend to practice. The fanatics do this in order to draw veneration upon themselves, and to draw upon most men of rank and fortune, who admit that they do not practice such austerities, the loathing of the common people. Such a clergy, however, while courting the upper ranks in this way, are very apt to neglect entirely the means of maintaining their influence and authority with the lower. They are heard, esteemed, and respected by their superiors; but before their inferiors they are often unable to defend their own sober and moderate doctrines effectively, and to the satisfaction of such listeners, against the most ignorant enthusiast who chooses to attack them.

The followers of Zwingli, or more properly of Calvin, on the other hand, gave the people of each parish the right to elect their own pastor whenever the church fell vacant, and at the same time established the most complete equality among the clergy. The first part of this arrangement, for as long as it remained in force, seems to have produced nothing but disorder and confusion, and to have tended equally to corrupt the morals of both clergy and people. The second part seems never to have had any but entirely agreeable effects.

As long as the people of each parish kept the right to elect their own pastors, they acted almost always under the influence of the clergy, and generally of the most factious and fanatical among them. To preserve their influence in these popular elections, many of the clergy became fanatics themselves, or pretended to, encouraged fanaticism among the people, and almost always favored the most fanatical candidate. A matter as small as the appointment of a parish minister nearly always gave rise to a violent contest, not only in that parish but in all the neighboring parishes, which seldom failed to join the quarrel. When the parish lay in a large city, it split the whole population into two parties; and when that city either constituted a small republic in itself or was the head and capital of one, as was the case with many of the principal cities of Switzerland and Holland, every petty dispute of this kind not only inflamed the hostility of all their other factions but threatened to leave behind it both a new schism in the church and a new faction in the state. In those small republics, therefore, the magistrate soon found it necessary, for the sake of the public peace, to take into his own hands the right of presentation to all vacant benefices. In Scotland, the largest country in which this Presbyterian form of church government has ever been established, the rights of patronage were in effect abolished by the act that established Presbyterianism at the beginning of the reign of William III. That act, at any rate, enabled certain classes of people in each parish to buy, for a very small price, the right of electing their own pastor. The constitution this act established was allowed to stand for about twenty-two years, but it was abolished by the statute passed in the tenth year of Queen Anne's reign, chapter 12, because of the confusion and disorder that this more popular method of election had caused almost everywhere. In a country as large as Scotland, however, a disturbance in a remote parish was less likely to trouble the government than in a smaller state. The statute of Queen Anne restored the rights of patronage. Yet although Scottish law gives the benefice, without exception, to the person presented by the patron, the church sometimes requires (for she has not been very consistent in her decisions on this point) a certain degree of consent from the people before she will confer on the presentee what is called the cure of souls, the spiritual charge and ecclesiastical jurisdiction of the parish. At times, at least, out of an affected concern for the peace of the parish, postpones the settlement until that consent can be obtained. The neighboring clergy often meddle privately in these affairs, sometimes to secure the people's consent but more often to block it, and they cultivate popular arts so that they can meddle more effectively when such occasions arise. These practices are perhaps the main causes that keep alive whatever remains of the old fanatical spirit, whether among the clergy or the people of Scotland.

The equality that the Presbyterian form of church government establishes among the clergy has two parts: first, equality of authority, or ecclesiastical jurisdiction; and second, equality of benefice, meaning the income attached to each clerical post. In every Presbyterian church the equality of authority is complete, but the equality of benefice is not. The difference between one benefice and another, however, is seldom large enough to tempt even the holder of a small one to court his patron with flattery and servile agreement in hopes of a better post. In all the Presbyterian churches where the rights of patronage are firmly established, the clergy generally try to win the favor of their superiors by nobler and better means: by their learning, by the blameless regularity of their lives, and by the faithful and diligent performance of their duties. Their patrons often complain of the independence of their spirit, which they tend to read as ingratitude for past favors. At worst, though, this independence is seldom anything more than the indifference that naturally arises when a man knows he can expect no further favors of that kind. There is perhaps nowhere in Europe a more learned, decent, independent, and respectable body of men than the greater part of the Presbyterian clergy of Holland, Geneva, Switzerland, and Scotland.

Where church benefices are all nearly equal, none of them can be very large. This modesty of income can no doubt be carried too far, but it has some very agreeable effects. Nothing but exemplary morals can give dignity to a man of small fortune. Frivolity and vanity inevitably make him ridiculous, and they are also almost as ruinous to him as they are to the common people. In his own conduct, therefore, he is obliged to follow the moral code that the common people respect most. He wins their esteem and affection by the very way of life that his own interest and circumstances would lead him to adopt. The common people regard him with the kindness we naturally feel toward someone whose condition comes somewhat close to our own, but who, we believe, ought to stand higher. Their kindness naturally draws out his. He takes care to instruct them and is attentive in helping and relieving them. He does not even scorn the prejudices of people so well disposed toward him, and he never treats them with the contemptuous and arrogant manner we so often meet in the proud dignitaries of rich and well-endowed churches. The Presbyterian clergy, accordingly, have more influence over the minds of the common people than perhaps the clergy of any other established church. And it is only in Presbyterian countries that we ever find the common people converted to the established church completely, almost to a man, and without persecution.

In countries where most church benefices are quite modest, a university chair is generally a better position than a church living. In that case the universities can pick and choose their members from all the churchmen of the country, who in every country make up by far the largest class of learned men. Where many church benefices are very valuable, on the other hand, the church naturally draws away from the universities most of their eminent scholars, who generally find some patron willing to do himself credit by securing them church preferment. In the first situation we are likely to find the universities filled with the most eminent scholars the country has to offer. In the second we are likely to find few eminent men among them, and those few among the youngest members of the faculty, who are themselves likely to be drained away before they have gained enough experience and knowledge to be of much use. Voltaire observed that Father Porée, a Jesuit of no great standing in the republic of letters, was the only professor France had ever had whose works were worth reading. In a country that has produced so many eminent writers and scholars, it must seem rather strange that hardly one of them should have been a university professor. The famous Gassendi was, early in his life, a professor at the University of Aix. When his genius first began to show itself, it was pointed out to him that by entering the church he could easily find a far quieter and more comfortable living, as well as a better position for pursuing his studies, and he promptly took the advice. Voltaire's observation may be applied, I believe, not only to France but to every other Roman Catholic country. We very rarely find in any of them an eminent scholar who holds a university professorship, except perhaps in law and medicine, professions from which the church is less likely to draw them away. After the Church of Rome, the Church of England is by far the richest and best-endowed church in Christendom. In England, accordingly, the church is continually draining the universities of their best and ablest members, and an old college tutor known and distinguished throughout Europe as an eminent scholar is as rare there as in any Roman Catholic country. In Geneva, on the contrary, and in the Protestant cantons of Switzerland, the Protestant regions of Germany, Holland, Scotland, Sweden, and Denmark, the most eminent scholars those countries have produced have been, not all of them indeed, but by far the greater part, professors in universities. In those countries the universities are continually draining the church of its most eminent learned men.

It may be worth remarking that, apart from the poets, a few orators, and a few historians, most of the other eminent men of letters in both Greece and Rome appear to have been teachers, whether public or private, and generally of either philosophy or rhetoric. This remark holds true from the days of Lysias and Isocrates, of Plato and Aristotle, down to those of Plutarch and Epictetus, Suetonius and Quintilian. Requiring a man to teach a particular branch of knowledge year after year seems, in fact, to be the most effective way of making him a complete master of it himself. Because he must go over the same ground every year, he will, if he is good for anything, inevitably come to know every part of it well within a few years. And if he forms too hasty an opinion on some point one year, he is very likely to correct it when his lectures bring him back to the same subject the following year. Just as teaching is certainly the natural occupation of a man devoted purely to learning, so it is also, perhaps, the training most likely to make him a man of solid learning and knowledge. Modest church benefices naturally tend to draw most of a country's learned men into the occupation in which they can be most useful to the public, while at the same time giving them perhaps the best education they are capable of receiving. They tend to make that learning both as solid and as useful as possible.

It should be observed that the revenue of every established church, except for whatever portion may come from particular lands or manors, is a branch of the general revenue of the state, diverted to a purpose very different from the state's defense. The tithe, for example, is in effect a land tax, and it leaves landowners less able to contribute toward the defense of the state than they would otherwise be. Yet the rent of land is, according to some, the only fund, and according to others the principal fund, from which the needs of the state must ultimately be supplied in all great monarchies. The more of this fund that goes to the church, the less, clearly, can be spared for the state. It may be laid down as a firm rule that, all other things being equal, the richer the church, the poorer must necessarily be either the sovereign on the one hand or the people on the other, and in every case the less able the state must be to defend itself. In several Protestant countries, and particularly in all the Protestant cantons of Switzerland, the revenue that once belonged to the Roman Catholic Church, namely the tithes and church lands, has proved sufficient not only to pay adequate salaries to the established clergy but also to cover, with little or no addition, all the other expenses of the state. The magistrates of the powerful canton of Bern, in particular, have accumulated from the savings of this fund a very large sum, believed to amount to several million. Part of it is held in a public treasury, and part is invested at interest in the public debt of the various indebted nations of Europe, chiefly that of France and Great Britain. What the entire expense of the church of Bern, or of any other Protestant canton, amounts to for the state, I do not claim to know. According to a very exact account, the whole revenue of the clergy of the Church of Scotland in 1755, including their glebe or church lands and the rental value of their manses, or dwelling houses, reasonably estimated, came to only £68,514, 1 shilling, and 5 and one-twelfth pence. This very moderate revenue provides a decent living for nine hundred and forty-four ministers. The entire expense of the church, including what is spent from time to time on building and repairing churches and ministers' manses, can hardly be supposed to exceed eighty or eighty-five thousand pounds a year. The richest church in Christendom does no better at maintaining uniformity of faith, fervor of devotion, and a spirit of order, regularity, and strict morals among the great body of the people than this very poorly endowed Church of Scotland. Every good effect, civil and religious, that an established church can be expected to produce, it produces as fully as any other. Most of the Protestant churches of Switzerland, which are in general no better endowed than the Church of Scotland, produce those effects to an even higher degree. In most of the Protestant cantons, not a single person can be found who does not profess to belong to the established church. If anyone does profess another faith, the law requires him to leave the canton. But so severe, or rather so oppressive, a law could never have been enforced in such free countries had the diligence of the clergy not already converted the whole body of the people to the established church, with perhaps only a few individual exceptions. In some parts of Switzerland, accordingly, where a Protestant and a Roman Catholic territory have been joined by historical accident and the conversion has been less complete, both religions are not merely tolerated but established by law.

The proper performance of any service seems to require that its pay be proportioned as exactly as possible to the nature of the service. If a service is badly underpaid, it is apt to suffer from the poor quality and incompetence of most of the people employed in it. If it is greatly overpaid, it is apt to suffer perhaps even more from their negligence and idleness. A man with a large income, whatever his profession, thinks he ought to live like other men with large incomes and spend much of his time in festivity, vanity, and dissipation. In a clergyman, however, such a way of life not only consumes the time that should be devoted to the duties of his office but also, in the eyes of the common people, almost entirely destroys the sanctity of character that alone allows him to perform those duties with proper weight and authority.

#### Part IV: Of the Expense of Supporting the Dignity of the Sovereign

Beyond the expenses needed to enable the sovereign to carry out his various duties, a certain expense is required to support his dignity. This expense varies both with the stage of a society's development and with its form of government.

In a wealthy and advanced society, where every rank of people grows more lavish each day in its houses, furniture, table, dress, and carriages, the sovereign can hardly be expected to hold out alone against the fashion. He naturally, or rather necessarily, becomes more lavish in all these things as well. His dignity even seems to require it.

Since a monarch stands further above his subjects in dignity than the chief magistrate of any republic is ever thought to stand above his fellow citizens, a greater expense is needed to support that higher dignity. We naturally expect more splendor in the court of a king than in the residence of a doge or a burgomaster.

#### Conclusion

The expense of defending the society and that of supporting the dignity of the chief magistrate are both incurred for the general benefit of the whole society. It is reasonable, therefore, that both should be paid for by the general contribution of the whole society, with each member contributing as nearly as possible in proportion to his ability.

The expense of administering justice may also, no doubt, be regarded as incurred for the benefit of the whole society, so there is nothing improper in its being paid for by the general contribution of the whole society. The people who give rise to this expense, however, are those who through some form of injustice make it necessary for others to seek redress or protection from the courts. The people who benefit most directly from it, in turn, are those whom the courts either restore to their rights or maintain in them. The expense of administering justice may therefore quite properly be paid by the particular contribution of one or the other of these two groups, or of both, as different occasions require; that is, by court fees. There can be no need to draw on the general contribution of the whole society except to convict criminals who have no estate or fund of their own sufficient to pay those fees.

Local or provincial expenses whose benefit is local or provincial, such as what is spent on policing a particular town or district, ought to be paid for out of a local or provincial revenue and should be no burden on the general revenue of the society. It is unjust for the whole society to contribute toward an expense whose benefit is confined to only a part of it.

The expense of maintaining good roads and means of communication is no doubt beneficial to the whole society, and may therefore be paid for by the general contribution of the whole society without any injustice. This expense, however, benefits most immediately and directly those who travel or carry goods from one place to another, and those who consume such goods. The turnpike tolls in England, and the duties called *péages* in other countries, place the whole of it on these two groups, and in doing so relieve the general revenue of the society of a very considerable burden.

The expense of institutions for education and religious instruction is likewise no doubt beneficial to the whole society, and may therefore be paid for by the general contribution of the whole society without injustice. It might, however, with equal propriety and even with some advantage, be paid entirely by those who receive the immediate benefit of such education and instruction, or by the voluntary contribution of those who believe they need one or the other.

When institutions or public works that benefit the whole society either cannot be, or are not, maintained entirely by the contributions of the particular members who benefit most directly from them, the shortfall must in most cases be made up by the general contribution of the whole society. Beyond covering the expense of defending the society and of supporting the dignity of the chief magistrate, the general revenue of the society must make up the shortfall in many particular branches of revenue. In the following chapter I shall try to explain the sources of this general or public revenue.

### CHAPTER II: OF THE SOURCES OF THE GENERAL OR PUBLIC REVENUE OF THE SOCIETY

The revenue that must pay not only for the defense of society and for upholding the dignity of the chief magistrate, but also for all the other necessary expenses of government for which the constitution of the state has made no particular provision, may be drawn from one of two places. It may come, first, from some fund that belongs specifically to the sovereign or the commonwealth and is independent of the revenue of the people; or, second, from the revenue of the people themselves.

#### Part I: Of the Funds, or Sources, of Revenue That May Belong Specifically to the Sovereign or Commonwealth

The funds or sources of revenue that may belong specifically to the sovereign or commonwealth must consist either of stock, meaning capital, or of land.

The sovereign, like any other owner of capital, may draw a revenue from it either by employing it himself or by lending it out. In the first case his revenue is profit. In the second, it is interest.

The revenue of a Tartar or Arab chief consists of profit. It comes mainly from the milk and the natural increase of his own herds and flocks, whose management he oversees himself as the chief shepherd or herdsman of his own horde or tribe. Yet only in this earliest and crudest stage of civil government has profit ever made up the main part of the public revenue of a monarchy.

Small republics have sometimes drawn a considerable revenue from the profits of commercial ventures. The republic of Hamburg is said to do so from the profits of a public wine cellar and a public apothecary's shop. A state whose sovereign has the leisure to carry on the trade of a wine merchant or a druggist cannot be a very large one. The profit of a public bank has been a source of revenue to more substantial states, not only to Hamburg but also to Venice and Amsterdam. Some people have even thought a revenue of this kind worth the attention of an empire as great as Great Britain. If the ordinary dividend of the Bank of England is reckoned at five and a half percent, and its capital at £10,780,000, then its net annual profit, after the costs of management have been paid, must come, it is said, to £592,900. The government, so the argument runs, could borrow this capital at three percent interest and, by taking the management of the bank into its own hands, could clear a profit of £269,500 a year. Experience suggests that the orderly, watchful, and thrifty administration of aristocracies like those of Venice and Amsterdam is extremely well suited to managing a commercial enterprise of this sort. But whether a government like England's could safely be trusted with such a project is, at the very least, far more doubtful. Whatever its virtues, that government has never been famous for good economy. In time of peace it has generally conducted itself with the slothful and negligent lavishness that is perhaps natural to monarchies, and in time of war it has consistently acted with all the thoughtless extravagance into which democracies are apt to fall.

The post office is properly a commercial enterprise. The government advances the cost of setting up the various offices and of buying or hiring the necessary horses and carriages, and it is repaid, with a large profit, by the charges on what is carried. It is perhaps the only commercial enterprise that has been successfully managed by, I believe, every kind of government. The capital that must be advanced is not very large. There is no mystery to the business. And the returns are not only certain but immediate.

Princes, however, have often engaged in many other commercial ventures, and have been willing, like private individuals, to improve their fortunes by becoming speculators in the ordinary branches of trade. They have hardly ever succeeded. The lavishness with which the affairs of princes are always conducted makes success almost impossible. A prince's agents regard their master's wealth as inexhaustible. They are careless about the price at which they buy, careless about the price at which they sell, and careless about the cost of carrying his goods from one place to another. Those agents often live with the extravagance of princes, and sometimes, despite that extravagance and through a judicious method of keeping their accounts, they acquire the fortunes of princes as well. This, Machiavelli tells us, was how the agents of Lorenzo de' Medici, no prince of meager abilities, carried on his trade. The republic of Florence was obliged several times to pay off the debts into which their extravagance had drawn him. He accordingly found it convenient to give up the business of merchant, the very business to which his family had originally owed its fortune. In the later part of his life he spent both what remained of that fortune and the revenue of the state, which was at his disposal, on projects and expenses more fitting to his station.

No two characters seem more incompatible than those of trader and sovereign. If the trading spirit of the English East India Company makes its directors very bad sovereigns, the spirit of sovereignty seems to have made them equally bad traders. While they were merely traders, they managed their trade successfully and were able to pay a moderate dividend out of their profits to the holders of their stock. Since becoming sovereigns, with a revenue that is said to have been originally more than three million pounds sterling, they have been forced to beg the ordinary assistance of the government to avoid immediate bankruptcy. In their former situation, their servants in India thought of themselves as the clerks of merchants. In their present situation, those servants think of themselves as the ministers of sovereigns.

A state may sometimes draw part of its public revenue from the interest on money as well as from the profits of capital. If it has accumulated a treasure, it may lend part of that treasure either to foreign states or to its own subjects.

The canton of Bern draws a considerable revenue by lending part of its treasure to foreign states, which it does by placing it in the public funds of the various indebted nations of Europe, chiefly France and England. The security of this revenue must depend, first, on the security of the funds in which it is placed, or on the good faith of the government that manages them; and second, on the certainty or likelihood that peace with the debtor nation will continue. In the event of war, the very first act of hostility by the debtor nation might be to confiscate the funds of its creditor. So far as I know, this policy of lending money to foreign states is peculiar to the canton of Bern.

The city of Hamburg has established a kind of public pawnshop, which lends money to the state's subjects against pledged goods at six percent interest. This pawnshop, or "lombard," as it is called, is claimed to yield the state a revenue of 150,000 crowns. At four shillings and sixpence to the crown, that comes to £33,750 sterling.

The government of Pennsylvania, without accumulating any treasure, devised a way of lending to its subjects. What it lent was not money, admittedly, but something equivalent to money. It advanced paper bills of credit to private individuals at interest, secured on land worth twice the amount of the loan. These bills were to be redeemed fifteen years after their date. In the meantime they could be passed from hand to hand like banknotes, and an act of the assembly declared them legal tender for all payments between one inhabitant of the province and another. By this means the government raised a moderate revenue, which went a considerable way toward covering an annual expense of about £4,500, the entire ordinary expense of that frugal and orderly government. The success of such an expedient must have depended on three distinct circumstances. The first was the demand for some instrument of commerce other than gold and silver coin, or else the demand for a quantity of consumable goods that could not be obtained without sending the greater part of the colony's gold and silver abroad to pay for them. The second was the good credit of the government that adopted the expedient. The third was the moderation with which it was used, so that the total value of the paper bills of credit never exceeded the value of the gold and silver coin that would have been needed to carry on the colony's circulation had there been no paper bills at all. Several other American colonies adopted the same expedient on various occasions, but for want of this moderation it produced, in most of them, far more disorder than convenience.

The unstable and perishable nature of capital and credit, however, makes them unfit to be relied on as the principal foundations of that sure, steady, and permanent revenue which alone can give security and dignity to government. No great nation that had advanced beyond the pastoral stage seems ever to have drawn the greater part of its public revenue from such sources.

Land is a fund of a more stable and permanent nature, and the rent of public lands has accordingly been the principal source of public revenue for many great nations far advanced beyond the pastoral stage. For a long time the ancient republics of Greece and Italy drew from the produce or rent of public lands the greater part of the revenue that paid the necessary expenses of the commonwealth. For a long time, too, the rent of the crown lands made up the greater part of the revenue of the ancient sovereigns of Europe.

War and the preparation for war are the two circumstances that, in modern times, account for the greater part of the necessary expense of all great states. But in the ancient republics of Greece and Italy every citizen was a soldier, and he both served and trained himself for service at his own expense. Neither of these circumstances, therefore, could put the state to any very considerable expense, and the rent of a quite moderate landed estate might have been fully sufficient to pay all the other necessary expenses of government.

In the ancient monarchies of Europe, the manners and customs of the age prepared the great body of the people sufficiently for war. When they took the field, the terms of their feudal tenures required that they be maintained either at their own expense or at that of their immediate lords, without placing any new burden on the sovereign. Most of the other expenses of government were very modest. The administration of justice, as has already been shown, was a source of revenue rather than a cause of expense. The labor of the country people for three days before and three days after the harvest was considered a sufficient fund for building and maintaining all the bridges, highways, and other public works that the commerce of the country was thought to require. In those days the sovereign's chief expense seems to have been the upkeep of his own family and household. The officers of his household were accordingly the great officers of state. The Lord Treasurer collected his rents. The Lord Steward and the Lord Chamberlain oversaw the expenses of his family. The care of his stables was entrusted to the Lord Constable and the Lord Marshal. His houses were all built in the form of castles and seem to have been the principal fortresses he possessed. The keepers of those houses or castles might be regarded as a kind of military governor, and they seem to have been the only military officers whom it was necessary to maintain in peacetime. Under these circumstances, the rent of a great landed estate might, on ordinary occasions, very well cover all the necessary expenses of government.

In the present condition of most of the civilized monarchies of Europe, the rent of all the land in the country would hardly amount, perhaps, to the ordinary revenue that these governments levy on the people even in peacetime, if that land were managed as it probably would be were it all owned by a single proprietor. The ordinary revenue of Great Britain, for example, comes to more than ten million pounds a year. This figure includes not only what is needed to pay the current expenses of the year but also what is needed to pay the interest on the public debts and to pay down part of their principal. Yet the land tax, at four shillings in the pound, which is to say at one-fifth, falls short of two million a year. This so-called land tax, moreover, is supposed to be one-fifth not only of the rent of all the land, but also of the rent of all the houses and of the interest on all the capital stock of Great Britain. The only capital excepted is the portion either lent to the public or employed as farming capital in the cultivation of land. A very considerable part of what this tax yields comes from the rent of houses and the interest on capital. The land tax of the City of London, for example, at four shillings in the pound, amounts to £123,399 6s. 7d.; that of the City of Westminster to £63,092 1s. 5d.; and that of the palaces of Whitehall and St. James's to £30,754 6s. 3d. A certain proportion of the land tax is assessed in the same way on all the other cities and incorporated towns in the kingdom, and it comes almost entirely either from the rent of houses or from what is supposed to be the interest on trading and other capital. According to the valuation on which Great Britain is assessed for the land tax, then, the entire mass of revenue arising from the rent of all the lands, the rent of all the houses, and the interest on all the capital, excepting only what is lent to the public or employed in cultivating land, does not exceed ten million pounds sterling a year. That is no more than the ordinary revenue the government levies on the people even in peacetime. Taking the kingdom as a whole, this valuation is no doubt far below the real value, though in several particular counties and districts it is said to come close to it. Many people have estimated the rent of the land alone, excluding the rent of houses and the interest on capital, at twenty million. That estimate was made largely at random, and I suspect it is as likely to be above the truth as below it. But if the lands of Great Britain, in their present state of cultivation, yield a rent of no more than twenty million a year, they could hardly yield half that rent, and most probably not a quarter of it, if they all belonged to a single proprietor and were placed under the negligent, costly, and oppressive management of his factors and agents. The crown lands of Great Britain do not at present yield a quarter of the rent that could probably be drawn from them if they were the property of private persons. If the crown lands were more extensive, they would probably be managed even worse.

The revenue that the great body of the people draws from land is proportioned not to its rent but to its produce. The whole annual produce of every country's land, apart from what is set aside for seed, is either consumed each year by the great body of the people or exchanged for something else that they consume. Whatever holds the produce of the land below the level it would otherwise reach holds down the revenue of the great body of the people even more than it holds down that of the landowners. The rent of land, the portion of the produce that belongs to the owners, is scarcely anywhere in Great Britain supposed to exceed a third of the whole produce. Suppose that land which, under one state of cultivation, yields a rent of ten million pounds a year would, under another, yield a rent of twenty million, and suppose that in both cases the rent is a third of the produce. The owners' revenue would then fall short of what it might be by only ten million a year, but the revenue of the great body of the people would fall short by thirty million a year, after deducting only what is needed for seed. The population of the country would be smaller by the number of people whom thirty million a year, always deducting the seed, could support. That number would depend on the particular manner of living and spending that prevailed among the different ranks of people among whom the remainder was distributed.

No civilized state of any kind in Europe today draws the greater part of its public revenue from the rent of state-owned land. Yet in all the great monarchies of Europe, many large tracts of land still belong to the crown. They are generally forest, and sometimes they are forests where you may travel several miles and scarcely find a single tree, a sheer waste and loss of territory with respect to both produce and population. In every great European monarchy, the sale of the crown lands would raise a very large sum of money, which, if applied to paying off the public debts, would free from mortgage a far greater revenue than those lands have ever yielded to the crown. In countries where highly improved and cultivated land, yielding at the time of sale as high a rent as can easily be got from it, commonly sells at thirty years' purchase, meaning a price equal to thirty years of its rent, the unimproved, uncultivated, and low-rented crown lands might well be expected to sell at forty, fifty, or sixty years' purchase. The crown could immediately enjoy the revenue that this great price would redeem from mortgage. Within a few years it would probably enjoy another revenue as well. Once the crown lands had become private property, they would within a few years be well improved and well cultivated. The increase in their produce would increase the population of the country by enlarging the revenue and consumption of the people. And the revenue the crown draws from customs and excise duties would necessarily grow along with the revenue and consumption of the people.

In any civilized monarchy, the revenue the crown draws from its lands appears to cost individuals nothing, but in reality it costs society more than perhaps any other equal revenue the crown enjoys. It would in every case be in the interest of society to replace this revenue with some other revenue of equal size and to divide the lands among the people, which could perhaps best be done by putting them up for public sale.

Lands kept for pleasure and display, such as parks, gardens, and public walks, are everywhere regarded as sources of expense rather than of revenue. They seem to be the only lands that ought to belong to the crown in a great and civilized monarchy.

Public capital and public land, then, the two sources of revenue that may belong specifically to the sovereign or commonwealth, are both unsuitable and insufficient funds for meeting the necessary expenses of any great and civilized state. It follows that the greater part of this expense must be met by taxes of one kind or another, with the people contributing part of their own private revenue to make up a public revenue for the sovereign or commonwealth.

#### Part II: Of Taxes

The private revenue of individuals, as was shown in the first book of this inquiry, arises ultimately from three different sources: rent, profit, and wages. Every tax must in the end be paid from one or another of these three sources, or from all of them without distinction. I shall try to give the best account I can, first, of the taxes intended to fall on rent; second, of those intended to fall on profit; third, of those intended to fall on wages; and fourth, of those intended to fall indiscriminately on all three sources of private revenue. Considering each of these four kinds of tax in turn will divide the second part of this chapter into four articles, three of which will require further subdivision. Many of these taxes, as the following review will show, are not finally paid out of the fund or source of revenue on which they were intended to fall.

Before I examine particular taxes, I must lay down the following four maxims concerning taxes in general.

1. The subjects of every state ought to contribute toward the support of the government as nearly as possible in proportion to their respective abilities, that is, in proportion to the revenue each of them enjoys under the protection of the state. The expense of government to the individuals of a great nation is like the expense of management to the joint tenants of a great estate, who are all obliged to contribute in proportion to their respective interests in it. The observance or neglect of this maxim constitutes what is called the equality or inequality of taxation. It should be noted, once and for all, that every tax falling finally on only one of the three kinds of revenue mentioned above is necessarily unequal, insofar as it does not touch the other two. In the examination of various taxes that follows, I shall seldom take further notice of this kind of inequality. In most cases I shall confine my remarks to the inequality that arises when a particular tax falls unequally on the particular kind of private revenue it affects.

2. The tax that each individual is bound to pay ought to be certain, not arbitrary. The time of payment, the manner of payment, and the amount to be paid ought all to be clear and plain to the taxpayer and to everyone else. Where this is not the case, every person subject to the tax is placed more or less in the power of the tax collector. The collector can either increase the tax on any taxpayer he dislikes or, through fear of such an increase, extort some gift or perquisite for himself. Uncertainty in taxation encourages the insolence and favors the corruption of a class of men who are naturally unpopular even when they are neither insolent nor corrupt. Certainty about what each individual ought to pay is a matter of such great importance in taxation that a very considerable degree of inequality, as I believe the experience of all nations shows, is not nearly so great an evil as a very small degree of uncertainty.

3. Every tax ought to be levied at the time, or in the manner, most likely to be convenient for the taxpayer. A tax on the rent of land or of houses, payable on the same date on which those rents are customarily paid, is levied at the moment when payment is most convenient, or when the taxpayer is most likely to have the means to pay. Taxes on consumable goods that are luxuries are all ultimately paid by the consumer, and generally in a way that suits him well. He pays them little by little, as he has occasion to buy the goods. And since he is also free to buy or not to buy as he pleases, it must be his own fault if such taxes ever cause him any serious inconvenience.

4. Every tax ought to be designed so that it takes out of the people's pockets, and keeps out of them, as little as possible beyond what it brings into the public treasury. A tax may take or keep from the people a great deal more than it delivers to the treasury in four ways. First, collecting it may require a great number of officials, whose salaries may consume most of what the tax produces, and whose fees and perquisites may impose yet another tax on the people. Second, it may obstruct the industry of the people and discourage them from entering certain branches of business that might give livelihood and employment to great numbers. While compelling the people to pay, it may thus shrink, or even destroy, some of the very funds that would have made payment easier. Third, through the forfeitures and other penalties incurred by those unfortunate individuals who try and fail to evade it, the tax may often ruin them, and so end whatever benefit the community might have drawn from the employment of their capital. A poorly judged tax offers a powerful temptation to smuggling, and the penalties for smuggling must rise in proportion to that temptation. Contrary to all the ordinary principles of justice, the law first creates the temptation and then punishes those who yield to it. It commonly increases the punishment, moreover, in proportion to the very circumstance that ought surely to lessen it: the temptation to commit the offense. Fourth, by subjecting the people to frequent visits and hateful inspections by tax collectors, it may expose them to a great deal of needless trouble, vexation, and oppression. Vexation is not, strictly speaking, an expense, but it is certainly equivalent to whatever sum each person would willingly pay to be spared it. It is in one or another of these four ways that taxes so often burden the people far more than they benefit the sovereign.

The evident justice and usefulness of these maxims have commended them, to a greater or lesser degree, to the attention of every nation. All nations have tried, as best they could judge, to make their taxes as equal as they could devise; as certain; as convenient to the taxpayer in both the time and the manner of payment; and, relative to the revenue they produced for the prince, as light a burden on the people as possible. The brief review that follows, covering some of the principal taxes imposed in different ages and countries, will show that these efforts have not all met with equal success.

##### Article I: Taxes upon Rent: Taxes upon the Rent of Land

A tax on the rent of land may be imposed according to a fixed standard, with each district assessed at a set rent that is never afterward revised. Alternatively, it may be imposed so as to change with every change in the actual rent of the land, rising or falling as its cultivation improves or declines.

A land tax assessed on each district according to a fixed and unchanging standard, as the land tax of Great Britain is, will inevitably become unequal over time, even if it was equal when first established, because different parts of the country will be improved or neglected to different degrees. In England, the valuation by which the various counties and parishes were assessed for the land tax under the statute passed in the fourth year of the reign of William and Mary was highly unequal even at the outset. To that extent, the tax violates the first of the four maxims set out above. It conforms perfectly to the other three. It is perfectly certain. Because the tax falls due on the same date as the rent, the timing is as convenient for the taxpayer as it could be. Although the landlord is in every case the real taxpayer, the tenant usually advances the money, and the landlord is obliged to credit it against the rent. The tax is collected by far fewer officials than any other tax yielding a comparable revenue. Since the tax on each district does not rise when rents rise, the sovereign takes no share in the profits of the landlord's improvements. Those improvements do sometimes help to lighten the burden on the other landlords of the district. But the resulting increase in the tax on any particular estate is always so slight that it can never discourage improvement or hold the produce of the land below the level it would otherwise reach. Since the tax has no tendency to reduce the quantity of that produce, it can have none to raise its price. It does not obstruct the industry of the people, and it imposes no inconvenience on the landlord beyond the unavoidable one of paying it. The advantage the landlord has gained from the permanence of the valuation by which all the land of Great Britain is rated for this tax, however, has been owed chiefly to circumstances that have nothing to do with the nature of the tax itself.

It has been owed in part to the great prosperity of nearly every part of the country. Since the valuation was first established, the rents of almost every estate in Great Britain have risen steadily, and hardly any have fallen. Nearly all landlords have therefore gained the difference between the tax they would pay on the present rent of their estates and the tax they actually pay under the old valuation. Had the condition of the country been different, and had rents been falling gradually as cultivation declined, nearly all landlords would have lost that difference instead. In the circumstances that have happened to prevail since the Revolution of 1688, the fixed valuation has benefited the landlord and harmed the sovereign. In other circumstances, it might have benefited the sovereign and harmed the landlord.

Because the tax is payable in money, the valuation of the land is likewise expressed in money. Since this valuation was established, the value of silver has remained fairly steady, and the standard of the coinage has not been altered in either weight or purity. Had silver risen sharply in value, as it appears to have done during the two centuries before the discovery of the American mines, the fixed valuation might have become very oppressive to the landlord. Had silver fallen sharply in value, as it certainly did for at least a century after those mines were discovered, the same fixed valuation would have greatly reduced this branch of the sovereign's revenue. And had any significant change been made in the standard of the coinage, either by assigning the same quantity of silver a lower face value or by assigning it a higher one, the effect would have been equally serious. Suppose that an ounce of silver, instead of being coined into five shillings and two pence, had been coined into pieces bearing a face value as low as two shillings and seven pence, or as high as ten shillings and four pence. In the one case the change would have hurt the landowner's income; in the other, the sovereign's.

In circumstances somewhat different from those that have actually occurred, then, this fixed valuation might have been a serious inconvenience either to the taxpayers or to the commonwealth. Over the course of ages, such circumstances are bound to arise sooner or later. Empires, like every other work of human hands, have all so far proved mortal, yet every empire aims at immortality. Any constitutional arrangement intended to last as long as the empire itself ought therefore to be convenient not merely in certain circumstances but in all circumstances. It ought to be suited not to conditions that are temporary, occasional, or accidental, but to those that are necessary, and therefore always the same.

A tax on the rent of land that changes with every change in the rent, rising and falling as cultivation improves or is neglected, is recommended as the most equitable of all taxes by that group of French men of letters who call themselves the economists. All taxes, they claim, ultimately fall on the rent of land, and ought therefore to be imposed equally on the fund that must in the end pay them. It is certainly true that all taxes ought to fall as equally as possible on the fund that must finally pay them. But without entering into a tedious discussion of the abstract arguments with which they support their very ingenious theory, the review that follows will make sufficiently clear which taxes fall in the end on the rent of land and which fall on some other fund.

In the Venetian territories, all arable land leased to farmers is taxed at one-tenth of the rent. The leases are entered in a public register kept by the revenue officers of each province or district. When proprietors farm their own land, it is valued by a fair estimate, and they are allowed a reduction of one-fifth of the tax, so that on such land they pay only eight percent of the estimated rent instead of ten.

A land tax of this kind is certainly more equal than the English land tax. It might not be quite as certain, and assessing it might often cause the landlord a good deal more trouble. It might also be considerably more expensive to collect.

It might be possible, however, to devise a system of administration that would largely prevent this uncertainty and keep this expense within bounds.

The landlord and tenant, for example, might be jointly required to enter their lease in a public register. Suitable penalties might be imposed for concealing or misrepresenting any of its terms. If part of those penalties were paid to whichever of the two parties informed against the other and secured a conviction for such concealment or misrepresentation, it would effectively deter them from colluding to defraud the public revenue. Every term of the lease could be adequately known from such a record.

Some landlords, rather than raising the rent, demand a lump-sum payment, known as a fine, for renewing the lease. In most cases this is the expedient of a spendthrift, who sells a future income of much greater value for a sum of ready money. It therefore usually harms the landlord; it often harms the tenant; and it always harms the community. It frequently takes so large a part of the tenant's capital, and so greatly reduces his ability to cultivate the land, that he finds it harder to pay a small rent than he would otherwise have found it to pay a large one. Whatever reduces his ability to cultivate necessarily holds the most important part of the community's revenue below what it would otherwise have been. By taxing such fines considerably more heavily than ordinary rent, this harmful practice might be discouraged, to the considerable advantage of every party concerned: the landlord, the tenant, the sovereign, and the community as a whole.

Some leases require the tenant to follow a particular method of cultivation and a particular rotation of crops for the whole term of the lease. This condition generally stems from the landlord's conceit in his own superior knowledge, a conceit that is in most cases quite unfounded. It ought always to be treated as an additional rent, paid in compliance rather than in money. To discourage the practice, which is generally a foolish one, this kind of rent might be valued rather high and therefore taxed somewhat more heavily than ordinary money rents.

Some landlords require rent in kind, paid in grain, cattle, poultry, wine, oil, and the like, rather than in money; others require rent in labor service. Such rents always harm the tenant more than they benefit the landlord. They take more out of the tenant's pocket, or keep more out of it, than they put into the landlord's. In every country where they are customary, the tenants are poor and destitute in close proportion to how widely the practice prevails. By valuing such rents in the same way, rather high, and taxing them somewhat more heavily than ordinary money rents, a practice harmful to the whole community might perhaps be sufficiently discouraged.

When landlords chose to farm part of their own land themselves, the rent might be valued by a fair arbitration among the neighboring farmers and landlords, and a moderate reduction of the tax might be granted, as in the Venetian territories, provided that the rent of the land they farmed did not exceed a certain amount. It matters that landlords should be encouraged to cultivate part of their own land. Their capital is generally greater than a tenant's, and even with less skill they can often raise a larger crop. A landlord can afford to try experiments and is generally inclined to do so. Failed experiments cost him only a moderate loss; successful ones contribute to the improvement and better cultivation of the whole country. It might be important, however, for the tax reduction to encourage him to farm his own land only up to a certain point. If most landlords were tempted to farm all of their land themselves, the country would be filled, in place of sober and industrious tenants bound by their own interest to cultivate as well as their capital and skill allow, with idle and dissolute estate managers. Their abusive management would soon degrade cultivation and reduce the annual produce of the land, diminishing not only their masters' income but the most important part of the income of the whole society.

Such a system of administration might free a tax of this kind from any degree of uncertainty capable of causing oppression or inconvenience to the taxpayer. At the same time, it might introduce into the ordinary management of land a policy that could contribute a great deal to the general improvement and good cultivation of the country.

Collecting a land tax that changed with every change in rent would no doubt cost somewhat more than collecting one rated permanently on a fixed valuation. Some additional expense would necessarily arise from the register offices it would be appropriate to set up in the various districts of the country, and from the occasional valuations of land that proprietors chose to farm themselves. All of this, however, might cost very little, and far less than is spent collecting many other taxes that yield a trifling revenue compared with what could easily be raised by a tax of this kind.

The most important objection that can be raised against such a variable land tax seems to be the discouragement it might give to the improvement of land. A landlord would certainly be less inclined to make improvements if the sovereign, who contributed nothing to the expense, were to share in the profit. Even this objection might be met, however. Before beginning an improvement, the landlord might be allowed to establish the actual value of his land jointly with the revenue officers, through the fair arbitration of a certain number of neighboring landlords and farmers chosen equally by both sides. He would then be taxed according to that valuation for a number of years fully sufficient to repay him completely. One of the principal advantages claimed for this kind of land tax is that it directs the sovereign's attention to the improvement of the land, out of regard for the growth of his own revenue. The period allowed for repaying the landlord, therefore, ought not to be much longer than necessary for that purpose, lest the remoteness of the sovereign's interest weaken this attention too much. It would be better, however, for the period to be somewhat too long than at all too short. No incentive to the sovereign's attention can ever outweigh the smallest discouragement to the landlord's. The sovereign's attention can at best be a very general and vague consideration of what is likely to improve the cultivation of the greater part of his dominions. The landlord's attention is a particular and minute consideration of how every inch of ground on his estate can be put to its most profitable use. The sovereign's chief concern ought to be to encourage, by every means in his power, the attention of both landlord and farmer. He does this by allowing both to pursue their own interest in their own way and according to their own judgment; by giving both the most complete security that they will enjoy the full reward of their own industry; and by securing for both the widest possible market for everything they produce, which requires establishing the easiest and safest communications by land and by water throughout his own dominions, together with the most unrestricted freedom to export to the dominions of all other princes.

If such a system of administration could manage a tax of this kind so that it gave no discouragement to the improvement of land, and even some encouragement, it seems unlikely to cause the landlord any inconvenience beyond the unavoidable one of having to pay it. Through every change in the condition of society, whether agriculture improved or declined, whatever the changes in the value of silver or in the standard of the coinage, a tax of this kind would adjust itself to the actual state of things, of its own accord and without any attention from government, and it would remain equally just and equitable through all those changes. It would therefore be far better suited to being established as a permanent and unalterable regulation, or what is called a fundamental law of the commonwealth, than any tax levied according to a fixed valuation.

Some states, instead of the simple and obvious expedient of a register of leases, have resorted to the laborious and expensive one of an actual survey and valuation of all the land in the country. They probably suspected that landlord and tenant might collude to conceal the real terms of the lease in order to defraud the public revenue. The Domesday Book, compiled for William the Conqueror, seems to have been the result of a very precise survey of this kind.

In the original dominions of the king of Prussia, the land tax is assessed according to an actual survey and valuation that is reviewed and revised from time to time. Under that valuation, lay proprietors pay from twenty to twenty-five percent of their income, and clergy from forty to forty-five percent. The survey and valuation of Silesia was carried out by order of the present king, reportedly with great precision. Under it, the lands belonging to the bishop of Breslau are taxed at twenty-five percent of their rent; the other revenues of the clergy of both religions, Catholic and Protestant, at fifty percent; the estates of the Teutonic Order and of the Order of Malta at forty percent; lands held by noble tenure at thirty-eight and one-third percent; and lands held by common, or base, tenure at thirty-five and one-third percent.

The survey and valuation of Bohemia is said to have taken more than a hundred years. It was not completed until after the peace of 1748, by order of the present empress-queen. The survey of the duchy of Milan, begun in the reign of Charles VI, was not completed until after 1760, and it is regarded as one of the most precise ever made. The survey of Savoy and Piedmont was carried out by order of the late king of Sardinia.

In the dominions of the king of Prussia, the revenue of the church is taxed much more heavily than that of lay proprietors. Most of the church's revenue is a burden on the rent of land. Rarely is any part of it applied to improving the land, or used in any way that helps to increase the income of the great body of the people. His Prussian Majesty probably thought it reasonable, on that account, that it should contribute a good deal more toward meeting the needs of the state. In some countries, church lands are exempt from all taxes; in others, they are taxed more lightly than other land. In the duchy of Milan, lands the church owned before 1575 are rated for the tax at only one-third of their value.

In Silesia, lands held by noble tenure are taxed three percent more heavily than those held by base tenure. His Prussian Majesty probably supposed that the honors and privileges of various kinds attached to noble tenure would adequately compensate its holders for a slightly heavier tax, while the humiliating inferiority of base tenure would be somewhat eased by a slightly lighter one. In other countries, the tax system aggravates this inequality rather than easing it. In the dominions of the king of Sardinia, and in those provinces of France subject to what is called the real or predial taille, the form of that tax assessed on land itself, the burden falls entirely on lands held by base tenure, while those held by noble tenure are exempt.

A land tax assessed according to a general survey and valuation, however equal it may be at first, must become unequal within a quite moderate period of time. To keep it from becoming so would require the continual and painstaking attention of government to every change in the condition and output of every farm in the country. The governments of Prussia, Bohemia, Sardinia, and the duchy of Milan actually exercise this kind of vigilance. It is so ill-suited to the nature of government, however, that it is unlikely to last long, and if it does continue, it will probably cause the taxpayers far more trouble and vexation in the long run than it could ever bring them relief.

In 1666, the generality of Montauban, one of the administrative districts into which France was divided for purposes of taxation, was assessed for the real or predial taille according to what is said to have been a very exact survey and valuation. By 1727 this assessment had become thoroughly unequal. To remedy the problem, the government found no better expedient than to impose an additional tax of 120,000 livres on the whole generality. This additional tax is apportioned among all the districts subject to the taille according to the old assessment. It is collected, however, only from those districts that the old assessment undertaxes under present conditions, and the proceeds go to relieve those that the same assessment overtaxes. Suppose two districts are each taxed at a thousand livres under the old assessment, although under present conditions one ought to pay nine hundred and the other eleven hundred. The additional tax rates each of them at eleven hundred livres. It is collected only from the undercharged district, however, and the whole of it goes to relieve the overcharged one, which consequently pays only nine hundred livres. The government neither gains nor loses by the additional tax, all of which goes to correct the inequalities of the old assessment. Its application is largely left to the discretion of the intendant, the royal administrator of the generality, and it must therefore be, to a great extent, arbitrary.

###### Taxes Proportioned Not to the Rent, but to the Produce of Land

Taxes on the produce of land are in reality taxes on rent. The farmer may advance them in the first instance, but the landlord ultimately pays them. When a certain portion of the produce must be handed over as a tax, the farmer estimates as best he can what that portion is likely to be worth, averaging good years with bad, and he reduces the rent he agrees to pay the landlord by a corresponding amount. There is no farmer who does not calculate in advance what the church tithe, which is a land tax of exactly this kind, is likely to amount to over an average of years.

The tithe, like every other land tax of this kind, appears perfectly equal but is in fact very unequal, because a fixed portion of the produce amounts, in different situations, to very different portions of the rent. On some very rich lands the produce is so great that half of it is enough to repay the farmer the capital he has spent on cultivation, together with the ordinary profits that farming capital earns in the neighborhood. The other half, or its value, he could afford to pay the landlord as rent if there were no tithe. But if a tenth of the produce is taken from him as tithe, he must demand a reduction of one-fifth of his rent, or he cannot recover his capital with the ordinary profit. In this case the landlord's rent, instead of amounting to half, or five-tenths, of the whole produce, will amount to only four-tenths of it. On poorer lands, by contrast, the produce is sometimes so small and the cost of cultivation so great that four-fifths of the whole produce are needed to repay the farmer his capital with the ordinary profit. Here, even without any tithe, the landlord's rent could amount to no more than one-fifth, or two-tenths, of the whole produce. If the farmer pays one-tenth of the produce as tithe, he must demand an equal reduction in the landlord's rent, which will thus fall to only one-tenth of the whole produce. On the rent of rich lands, then, the tithe may sometimes be a tax of no more than one-fifth, or four shillings in the pound; on the rent of poorer lands it may sometimes be a tax of one-half, or ten shillings in the pound.

The tithe is often a very unequal tax on rent, and it is always a great discouragement both to the landlord's improvements and to the farmer's cultivation. The landlord cannot venture on the most important improvements, which are generally also the most expensive, and the farmer cannot venture to raise the most valuable crops, which are generally also the most expensive to grow, when the church, which bears no part of the cost, is to take so large a share of the profit. For a long time the tithe confined the cultivation of madder, a plant whose root yields a valuable red dye, to the United Provinces of the Netherlands. Being Presbyterian countries, and therefore exempt from this destructive tax, they enjoyed a kind of monopoly of that useful dye against the rest of Europe. The recent attempts to introduce the crop into England have been made only because of the statute providing that five shillings an acre should be accepted in place of every kind of tithe on madder.

Across most of Europe the church is supported chiefly by a land tax proportioned not to the rent but to the produce of the land, and in many countries of Asia the state is supported in the same way. In China, the sovereign's principal revenue consists of a tenth of the produce of all the lands of the empire. This tenth, however, is estimated so moderately that in many provinces it is said not to exceed a thirtieth of the ordinary produce. The land tax, or land rent, formerly paid to the Muslim government of Bengal before that country fell into the hands of the English East India Company is said to have amounted to about a fifth of the produce. The land tax of ancient Egypt is likewise said to have amounted to a fifth.

In Asia this kind of land tax is said to give the sovereign an interest in the improvement and cultivation of the land. The sovereigns of China, those of Bengal under its Muslim government, and those of ancient Egypt are accordingly said to have been extremely attentive to building and maintaining good roads and navigable canals. In this way they sought to increase both the quantity and the value of every part of the produce of the land as far as possible, by opening to every part of it the widest market their own dominions could provide. The church tithe, by contrast, is divided into such small portions that none of its owners can have any interest of this kind. The parson of a parish could never find it worth his while to build a road or canal to a distant part of the country in order to widen the market for the produce of his own particular parish. Such taxes, when they are meant to support the state, have some advantages that may partly offset their drawbacks. When they are meant to support the church, they bring nothing but drawbacks.

Taxes on the produce of land may be levied either in kind or in money according to a set valuation.

The parson of a parish, or a gentleman of small fortune living on his own estate, may sometimes find some advantage in receiving his tithe or his rent in kind. The quantity to be collected, and the district within which it is collected, are so small that each of them can oversee with his own eyes the collection and disposal of every part of what is owed to him. A gentleman of great fortune who lived in the capital would risk heavy losses through the negligence, and heavier losses through the fraud, of his stewards and agents if the rents of an estate in a distant province were paid to him in this way. The sovereign's losses from the abuses and plunder of his tax collectors would necessarily be far greater. The servants of the most careless private person are perhaps more closely watched by their master than are those of the most careful prince. A public revenue paid in kind would suffer so badly from the mismanagement of its collectors that only a very small part of what was levied on the people would ever reach the prince's treasury. Part of the public revenue of China, however, is said to be paid in this way. The mandarins and other tax collectors no doubt find it to their advantage to keep up a form of payment that is so much more open to abuse than any payment in money.

A tax on the produce of land that is levied in money may be levied in either of two ways. It may follow a valuation that changes with every movement of the market price, or it may follow a fixed valuation, under which a bushel of wheat, for example, is always valued at the same money price whatever the state of the market. The yield of a tax levied in the first way will vary only with changes in the actual produce of the land, that is, with the improvement or neglect of cultivation. The yield of a tax levied in the second way will vary not only with changes in the produce of the land but also with changes in the value of the precious metals, and with changes in the quantity of those metals contained at different times in coins of the same denomination. The yield of the first will always bear the same proportion to the value of the actual produce of the land. The yield of the second may, at different times, bear very different proportions to that value.

When a fixed sum of money is paid in full settlement of all tax or tithe, instead of either a share of the produce or the price of a share, the tax becomes exactly the same in nature as the land tax of England. It neither rises nor falls with the rent of the land, and it neither encourages nor discourages improvement. The tithe in most of those parishes that pay what is called a modus, a fixed money payment accepted in place of all other tithe, is a tax of this kind. Under the Muslim government of Bengal, a modus, said to have been a very moderate one, was established in most of the districts, or zemindaries, of the country in place of the payment in kind of a fifth of the produce. Some of the East India Company's servants, on the pretext of restoring the public revenue to its proper value, have in some provinces replaced this modus with a payment in kind. Under their management the change is likely both to discourage cultivation and to create new opportunities for abuse in collecting the public revenue, which has fallen far below what it was said to have been when the Company first took charge of it. The Company's servants may perhaps have profited by the change, but probably at the expense of both their employers and the country.

###### Taxes on the Rent of Houses

The rent of a house may be divided into two parts. One may quite properly be called the building-rent; the other is commonly called the ground-rent.

The building-rent is the interest or profit on the capital spent in building the house.
