To put the builder's trade on a level with other trades, this rent must be enough, first, to pay him the same interest he would have earned had he lent his capital on good security, and second, to keep the house in constant repair, or, what amounts to the same thing, to replace within a certain number of years the capital that was spent on building it. The building-rent, or the ordinary profit of building, is therefore everywhere governed by the ordinary rate of interest. Where the market rate of interest is four percent, a house whose rent, after covering the ground-rent, yields six or six and a half percent on the whole cost of building may perhaps give the builder a sufficient profit. Where the market rate of interest is five percent, it may perhaps need to yield seven or seven and a half percent. If at any time the building trade yields a much greater profit than this in relation to the rate of interest, it will soon draw enough capital away from other trades to bring its profit down to the proper level. If at any time it yields much less, other trades will soon draw enough capital away from it to raise that profit again.

Whatever part of a house's total rent exceeds what is needed to provide this reasonable profit goes naturally to the ground-rent. Where the owner of the ground and the owner of the building are different people, this surplus is in most cases paid entirely to the owner of the ground. It is the price the occupant of the house pays for some real or supposed advantage of location. In country houses far from any large town, where there is plenty of land to choose from, the ground-rent is next to nothing, no more than the land beneath the house would pay if it were farmed. In country villas near a large town it is sometimes considerably higher, and particular convenience or beauty of situation is often well paid for there. Ground-rents are generally highest in the capital, and in those particular parts of it where demand for houses happens to be greatest, whatever the reason for that demand, whether trade and business, pleasure and society, or mere vanity and fashion.

A tax on house-rent, paid by the tenant and proportioned to the whole rent of each house, could not affect the building-rent, at least not for any considerable time. If the builder did not earn his reasonable profit, he would be forced to leave the trade, and the resulting rise in the demand for building would soon restore his profit to its proper level with that of other trades. Nor would such a tax fall entirely on the ground-rent. It would divide itself so as to fall partly on the occupant of the house and partly on the owner of the ground.

Suppose, for example, that a particular person judges he can afford to spend sixty pounds a year on rent, and suppose also that a tax of four shillings in the pound, or one-fifth, payable by the occupant, is laid on house-rent. A house renting at sixty pounds will then cost him seventy-two pounds a year, twelve pounds more than he thinks he can afford. He will therefore settle for a poorer house, one renting at fifty pounds, which together with the additional ten pounds of tax comes to sixty pounds a year, the sum he judges he can afford. To pay the tax, he will give up part of the additional comfort he might have enjoyed in a house renting for ten pounds a year more. He will give up only part of it, for he will seldom be forced to give up the whole; because of the tax, he will get a better house for fifty pounds a year than he could have got without it. This is because a tax of this kind, by removing this particular bidder, must reduce the competition for houses renting at sixty pounds, and in the same way it must reduce the competition for those renting at fifty pounds, and likewise for houses at every other rent except the lowest, for which it would for some time increase the competition. The rents of every class of house for which competition had fallen would necessarily come down to some degree. Since no part of this reduction could affect the building-rent, at least for any considerable time, the whole of it must in the long run fall on the ground-rent. The final payment of the tax would therefore fall partly on the occupant of the house, who would have to give up part of his comfort to pay his share, and partly on the owner of the ground, who would have to give up part of his income to pay his. In what proportion the final payment would be divided between them is perhaps not easy to determine. The division would probably differ widely from one set of circumstances to another, and depending on those circumstances, a tax of this kind might bear very unequally on both the occupant of the house and the owner of the ground.

The inequality with which such a tax might fall on the owners of different ground-rents would arise entirely from the accidental inequality of this division. The inequality with which it might fall on the occupants of different houses would arise not only from this but from a further cause. The share of house-rent in a person's total living expenses differs according to the level of his fortune. It is perhaps highest at the top and diminishes gradually through the lower levels, so that in general it is lowest at the very bottom. The necessities of life make up the chief expense of the poor. They find it hard to get food, and most of their small income goes to getting it. The luxuries and vanities of life make up the chief expense of the rich, and a magnificent house adorns and shows off to best advantage all the other luxuries and vanities they possess. A tax on house-rents would therefore generally fall most heavily on the rich, and there would perhaps be nothing very unreasonable in an inequality of this sort. It is not very unreasonable that the rich should contribute to public expenses not merely in proportion to their income, but somewhat more than in that proportion.

Although the rent of houses resembles the rent of land in some respects, it differs from it in one essential way. The rent of land is paid for the use of something productive: the land that pays it also produces it. The rent of houses is paid for the use of something unproductive. Neither the house nor the ground it stands on produces anything. Whoever pays the rent must therefore draw it from some other source of income, separate from and independent of the house itself. A tax on the rent of houses, insofar as it falls on the occupants, must be drawn from the same source as the rent, and must be paid out of their income, whether that income comes from the wages of labor, the profits of capital, or the rent of land. Insofar as it falls on the occupants, then, it is one of those taxes that fall not on one source of income alone but indifferently on all three, and it is in every respect of the same nature as a tax on any other consumable commodity. There is perhaps no single item of expenditure or consumption by which the generosity or meanness of a person's whole spending can be better judged than his house-rent. A proportional tax on this particular item might perhaps raise a larger revenue than any that has yet been drawn from it anywhere in Europe. If the tax were very high, however, most people would try to avoid as much of it as they could by settling for smaller houses and diverting most of their spending into other channels.

The rent of houses could easily be determined with sufficient accuracy by the same kind of administrative procedure that would be needed to determine the ordinary rent of land. Uninhabited houses ought to pay no tax. A tax on them would fall entirely on the owner, who would then be taxed for property that yielded him neither comfort nor income. Houses occupied by their owners ought to be assessed not according to what they may have cost to build, but according to the rent that a fair arbitrator would judge they were likely to bring if leased to a tenant. If they were assessed according to their building costs, a tax of three or four shillings in the pound, combined with other taxes, would ruin nearly all the rich and great families of this country, and, I believe, of every other civilized country. Anyone who carefully examines the various town and country houses of some of the richest and greatest families in this country will find that, at a rate of only six and a half or seven percent on the original cost of building, their house-rent nearly equals the entire net rent of their estates. These houses represent the accumulated spending of several successive generations on objects of great beauty and magnificence, but of very little exchangeable value in proportion to what they cost. Since this book was first published, a tax built on nearly these principles has been imposed.

Ground-rents are an even more suitable subject of taxation than the rent of houses. A tax on ground-rents would not raise the rent of houses. It would fall entirely on the owner of the ground-rent, who always acts as a monopolist and extracts the highest rent that can be got for the use of his land. How much can be got for it depends on whether the competitors for it happen to be richer or poorer, and on how much they can afford to spend to indulge their fancy for a particular spot of ground. In every country the greatest number of rich competitors is found in the capital, and that is accordingly where the highest ground-rents are always found. Since a tax on ground-rents would in no way increase the wealth of these competitors, they would probably not be inclined to pay more for the use of the ground. It would matter little whether the tax was advanced by the occupant or by the owner of the ground. The more the occupant was obliged to pay in tax, the less he would be willing to pay for the ground, so the final payment of the tax would fall entirely on the owner of the ground-rent. The ground-rents of uninhabited houses ought to pay no tax. Both ground-rents and the ordinary rent of land are a kind of income that the owner in many cases enjoys without any care or effort of his own. If part of this income were taken from him to pay the expenses of the state, no form of industry would be discouraged by it. The annual produce of the land and labor of society, which is the real wealth and income of the great body of the people, might be the same after such a tax as before. Ground-rents and the ordinary rent of land are therefore perhaps the kinds of income best able to bear a special tax.

In this respect ground-rents seem an even more suitable subject for special taxation than the ordinary rent of land. The ordinary rent of land is in many cases owed, at least in part, to the attention and good management of the landlord, and a very heavy tax might discourage that attention and good management too much. Ground-rents, insofar as they exceed the ordinary rent of land, are owed entirely to the good government of the sovereign, which, by protecting the industry either of the whole people or of the inhabitants of some particular place, enables them to pay so much more than its real value for the ground on which they build their houses, or to give its owner so much more than compensation for whatever loss he might suffer by putting it to this use. Nothing could be more reasonable than that a fund which owes its very existence to the good government of the state should be taxed in a special way, or should contribute somewhat more than most other funds toward the support of that government.

Although taxes have been imposed on the rent of houses in many countries of Europe, I know of none in which ground-rent has been treated as a separate object of taxation. Those who design taxes have probably found it difficult to determine what part of a house's rent should be regarded as ground-rent and what part as building-rent. Yet it should not be very hard to distinguish the two.

In Great Britain, the rent of houses is supposed to be taxed at the same proportion as the rent of land, through what is called the annual land tax. The valuation on which each parish and district is assessed for this tax never changes. It was extremely unequal from the start, and it remains so. Throughout most of the kingdom, the tax falls even more lightly on the rent of houses than on the rent of land. Only in a few districts, which were rated high to begin with and in which house rents have since fallen considerably, is the land tax of three or four shillings in the pound said to amount to the same proportion of the real rent of houses. Empty houses, though subject to the tax by law, are in most districts exempted from it by the indulgence of the assessors, and this exemption sometimes causes slight variations in the rate paid by particular houses, even though the total charged to the district stays the same. Increases in rent produced by new buildings, repairs, and similar improvements help to discharge the district's fixed quota, which causes still further variations in the rate on individual houses.

In the province of Holland, every house is taxed at two and a half percent of its value, without any regard either to the rent it actually brings in or to whether it is occupied or empty. There seems to be a real hardship in forcing an owner to pay tax on an empty house from which he draws no income, especially a tax so heavy. In Holland, where the market rate of interest does not exceed three percent, a tax of two and a half percent on the entire value of a house must in most cases come to more than a third of the building-rent, and perhaps of the whole rent. It is true that the valuation used to rate houses, though very unequal, is said always to fall below their real value. Whenever a house is rebuilt, improved, or enlarged, it is valued afresh and the tax is adjusted accordingly.

Those who devised the various taxes imposed on houses in England at different times seem to have believed that it was very difficult to determine, with reasonable accuracy, the real rent of each house. They therefore based their taxes on some more visible feature, one they presumably supposed would, in most cases, bear some proportion to the rent.

The first tax of this kind was hearth-money, a tax of two shillings on every hearth. To find out how many hearths a house contained, the tax collector had to enter every room in it. This hated inspection made the tax hated in turn, and soon after the Revolution it was abolished as a badge of slavery.

The next tax of this kind was a charge of two shillings on every inhabited dwelling-house. A house with ten windows paid four shillings more, and a house with twenty windows or more paid eight shillings. The tax was later altered so that houses with at least twenty but fewer than thirty windows paid ten shillings, and those with thirty or more paid twenty shillings. Windows can in most cases be counted from outside, and in every case without entering each room. The collector's visit under this tax was therefore less offensive than under the hearth-money.

This tax was later repealed and replaced by the window tax, which has since been altered and increased twice. As it stands at present, in January 1775, the window tax imposes, in addition to a duty of three shillings on every house in England and one shilling on every house in Scotland, a duty on each window. In England this duty rises by degrees from twopence, the lowest rate, on houses with no more than seven windows, to two shillings, the highest rate, on houses with twenty-five windows or more.

The chief objection to all such taxes is their inequality, and it is inequality of the worst kind, since they must often fall much more heavily on the poor than on the rich. A house renting for ten pounds in a country town may sometimes have more windows than a house renting for five hundred pounds in London. Although the occupant of the first is likely to be a far poorer man than the occupant of the second, he must, so far as the window tax determines his contribution, pay more toward the support of the state. Such taxes therefore run directly contrary to the first of the four maxims of taxation laid down earlier, which holds that subjects ought to contribute in proportion to their respective abilities. They do not seem to offend much against any of the other three.

The natural tendency of the window tax, as of every other tax on houses, is to lower rents, since the more a man pays in tax, the less he can obviously afford to pay in rent. Yet since the window tax was imposed, house rents have, on the whole, risen to some degree in almost every town and village in Great Britain that I know. Almost everywhere, the demand for houses has grown so much that it has pushed rents up further than the window tax could push them down. This is one of the many proofs of the country's great prosperity and of the rising income of its inhabitants. Without the tax, rents would probably have risen higher still.

##### Article II: Taxes on Profit, or on the Revenue Arising from Stock

The revenue or profit arising from stock, that is, from capital, naturally divides into two parts: the part that pays the interest and belongs to the owner of the capital, and the surplus that remains after the interest has been paid.

This second part of profit is plainly not something that can be taxed directly. It is the compensation, and in most cases no more than a very moderate compensation, for the risk and trouble of employing the capital. The person who employs it must receive this compensation, or he cannot, consistently with his own interest, continue to employ it. If he were taxed directly in proportion to his whole profit, he would therefore be forced either to raise his rate of profit or to charge the tax against the interest on the money, which is to say, to pay less interest. If he raised his rate of profit in proportion to the tax, then the whole tax, although he might advance it himself, would ultimately be paid by one of two different groups of people, depending on how he employed the capital under his management. If he employed it as farming capital in the cultivation of land, he could raise his rate of profit only by keeping a larger share of the produce of the land, or, what comes to the same thing, the price of a larger share. Since this could be done only by reducing the rent, the final burden of the tax would fall on the landlord. If he employed it as mercantile or manufacturing capital, he could raise his rate of profit only by raising the price of his goods, and in that case the final burden would fall entirely on the consumers of those goods. If he did not raise his rate of profit, he would be forced to charge the whole tax against the portion of profit set aside to pay interest. He could then afford to pay less interest on whatever capital he borrowed, and the full weight of the tax would ultimately fall on the interest of money. To whatever extent he could not relieve himself of the tax in one way, he would be compelled to do so in the other.

At first glance, the interest of money seems as suitable a subject for direct taxation as the rent of land. Like the rent of land, it is a net product that remains after the whole risk and trouble of employing the capital has been fully compensated. A tax on the rent of land cannot raise rents, because the net product that remains after replacing the farmer's capital, together with his reasonable profit, can be no greater after the tax than before it. For the same reason, a tax on the interest of money could not raise the rate of interest, provided the quantity of capital or money in the country, like the quantity of land, is assumed to remain the same after the tax as before. As was shown in the first book of this inquiry, the ordinary rate of profit is everywhere governed by the quantity of capital to be employed, relative to the quantity of employment, or of business, it must carry out. But a tax on the interest of money could neither increase nor diminish the quantity of employment, or of business to be done by capital. If the quantity of capital to be employed was neither increased nor diminished by such a tax, then the ordinary rate of profit would necessarily remain unchanged. The portion of this profit needed to compensate the risk and trouble of the employer would likewise stay the same, since that risk and trouble would not be altered in any respect. The remainder, the portion that belongs to the owner of the capital and pays the interest on money, would therefore necessarily stay the same as well. At first glance, then, the interest of money appears to be as fit a subject for direct taxation as the rent of land.

There are, however, two circumstances that make the interest of money a much less suitable object of direct taxation than the rent of land.

First, the quantity and value of the land any man owns can never be a secret, and can always be determined with great precision. But the total amount of capital he owns is almost always a secret and can hardly ever be determined with any reasonable accuracy. It is, moreover, subject to almost constant change. A year seldom passes, often not a month, and sometimes scarcely a single day, in which it does not rise or fall to some degree. An inquisition into every man's private affairs, and one that, in order to fit the tax to them, kept watch over every fluctuation in his fortune, would be a source of such continual and endless vexation that no one could bear it.

Second, land cannot be moved, whereas capital easily can. The owner of land is necessarily a citizen of the particular country in which his estate lies. The owner of capital is properly a citizen of the world and is not necessarily attached to any particular country. He would be inclined to leave a country in which he was exposed to a vexatious inquisition for the purpose of assessing him for a burdensome tax, and would move his capital to some other country where he could either carry on his business or enjoy his fortune with greater ease. By removing his capital, he would put an end to all the industry it had supported in the country he left. Capital cultivates land; capital employs labor. A tax that tended to drive capital out of a country would to that extent tend to dry up every source of revenue, both for the sovereign and for the society. Its removal would inevitably diminish, to a greater or lesser degree, not only the profits of capital but also the rent of land and the wages of labor.

Accordingly, nations that have tried to tax the revenue arising from capital have had to settle, in place of any severe inquisition of this kind, for some very loose and therefore more or less arbitrary estimate. The extreme inequality and uncertainty of a tax assessed in this manner can be offset only by its extreme moderation. As a result, every man finds himself rated so far below his real income that he is little troubled even if his neighbor should be rated somewhat lower still.

Under what is called the land tax in England, the intention was that capital should be taxed in the same proportion as land. When the tax on land stood at four shillings in the pound, or one-fifth of the presumed rent, capital was meant to be taxed at one-fifth of the presumed interest. When the present annual land tax was first imposed, the legal rate of interest was six percent. Every hundred pounds of capital was accordingly supposed to be taxed at twenty-four shillings, one-fifth of six pounds. Since the legal rate of interest was reduced to five percent, every hundred pounds of capital is supposed to be taxed at only twenty shillings. The sum to be raised by the land tax was divided between the countryside and the principal towns. Most of it was laid on the countryside, and of the share laid on the towns, most was assessed on houses. What remained to be assessed on the capital or trade of the towns (the capital employed on the land was not meant to be taxed) fell far below the real value of that capital or trade. Whatever inequalities there may have been in the original assessment, therefore, caused little disturbance. Every parish and district is still rated for its land, its houses, and its capital according to that original assessment, and the nearly universal prosperity of the country, which in most places has greatly raised the value of all three, has made those inequalities of even less consequence now. Because the rate charged to each district always remains the same, the uncertainty of this tax, insofar as it might be assessed on the capital of any individual, has also been greatly reduced and made of much less importance. If most of the land in England is not rated for the land tax at half its actual value, most of the capital in England is perhaps rated at scarcely a fiftieth of its actual value. In some towns, such as Westminster, the entire land tax is assessed on houses, and capital and trade go untaxed. In London it is otherwise.

In every country, a severe inquisition into the circumstances of private persons has been carefully avoided.

In Hamburg, every inhabitant is obliged to pay the state one-quarter of one percent of everything he owns, and since the wealth of the people of Hamburg consists mainly of capital, this tax may be regarded as a tax on capital. Every man assesses himself. Each year, in the presence of the magistrate, he deposits in the public treasury a sum of money that he declares on oath to be one-quarter of one percent of all he possesses, without stating what that amount is and without being subject to any examination on the matter. This tax is generally believed to be paid with great honesty. In a small republic, where the people have complete confidence in their magistrates, are convinced that the tax is necessary for the support of the state, and believe it will be faithfully applied to that purpose, such conscientious and voluntary payment may sometimes be expected. Nor is it peculiar to the people of Hamburg.

The canton of Unterwalden, in Switzerland, is frequently ravaged by storms and floods, which expose it to extraordinary expenses. On such occasions the people assemble, and everyone is said to declare with the greatest frankness what he is worth, so that he may be taxed accordingly. In Zurich, the law requires that in times of necessity everyone be taxed in proportion to his income, the amount of which he must declare on oath. They have no suspicion, it is said, that any of their fellow citizens will deceive them. In Basel, the state's chief revenue comes from a small duty on exported goods. All citizens swear an oath that they will pay, every three months, all the taxes the law imposes. All merchants, and even all innkeepers, are trusted to keep their own accounts of the goods they sell, whether inside or outside the territory. At the end of every three months they send this account to the treasurer, with the amount of tax calculated at the bottom. No one suspects that the revenue suffers from this trust.

In those Swiss cantons, then, compelling every citizen to declare the amount of his fortune publicly and under oath is apparently not considered a hardship. In Hamburg it would be considered the greatest hardship of all. Merchants engaged in the risky ventures of trade all tremble at the thought of being obliged to expose the true state of their affairs at all times. They foresee that the ruin of their credit and the failure of their ventures would too often follow. A sober and frugal people, who have nothing to do with such ventures, feel no need for any such concealment.

In Holland, soon after the late Prince of Orange was raised to the office of stadtholder, a tax of two percent, known as "the fiftieth penny," was imposed on the entire property of every citizen. Every citizen assessed himself and paid his tax in the same way as in Hamburg, and it was generally believed to have been paid with great honesty. The people at that time felt the warmest attachment to their new government, which they had just established through a general uprising. The tax was to be paid only once, to relieve the state in a particular emergency. It was, in fact, too heavy to be permanent. In a country where the market rate of interest seldom exceeds three percent, a tax of two percent amounts to thirteen shillings and four pence in the pound, or two-thirds, of the highest net revenue commonly drawn from capital. It is a tax that very few people could pay without eating to some extent into their capital. In a particular emergency, a people may, out of great public zeal, make a great effort and give up even part of their capital to relieve the state. But they cannot possibly continue to do so for any considerable time, and if they did, the tax would soon ruin them so completely as to leave them wholly unable to support the state.

The tax on capital imposed by the land tax bill in England, although it is proportioned to the capital, is not meant to diminish or take away any part of that capital. It is meant only as a tax on the interest of money, proportioned to the tax on the rent of land, so that when the latter stands at four shillings in the pound, the former may stand at four shillings in the pound too. The tax at Hamburg, and the still more moderate taxes of Unterwalden and Zurich, are likewise meant to be taxes not on capital but on the interest, or net revenue, of capital. The tax in Holland was meant to be a tax on the capital itself.

###### Taxes on the Profit of Particular Employments

In some countries, special taxes are imposed on the profits of capital, sometimes when it is employed in particular branches of trade and sometimes when it is employed in agriculture.

Taxes of the first kind in England include the tax on hawkers and peddlers, the tax on hackney coaches and sedan chairs available for hire, and the fee that alehouse keepers pay for a license to sell ale and spirits at retail. During the recent war, another tax of the same kind was proposed on shops. Since the war had been undertaken, it was argued, in defense of the country's trade, the merchants who stood to profit from it ought to contribute toward its cost.

A tax on the profits of capital employed in any particular branch of trade, however, can never fall finally on the dealers, who in all ordinary cases must have their reasonable profit and, where competition is free, can seldom have more than that. It always falls on the consumers, who are obliged to pay, in the price of the goods, the tax the dealer has advanced, and generally with some markup added.

When a tax of this kind is proportioned to the dealer's volume of trade, it is ultimately paid by the consumer and imposes no hardship on the dealer. When it is not so proportioned but is the same for all dealers, it is still ultimately paid by the consumer, yet it favors the large dealer and causes some hardship to the small one. The tax of five shillings a week on every hackney coach, and of ten shillings a year on every hackney chair, insofar as it is advanced by the various keepers of such coaches and chairs, is fairly exactly proportioned to the extent of their respective businesses. It neither favors the large dealer nor oppresses the smaller one. But the tax of twenty shillings a year for a license to sell ale, forty shillings for a license to sell spirits, and forty shillings more for a license to sell wine, being the same for all retailers, must necessarily give some advantage to the large dealers and cause some hardship to the small ones. The large dealers will find it easier than the small ones to recover the tax in the price of their goods. The moderate size of the tax, however, makes this inequality of less importance, and many people may think it not improper to discourage, to some degree, the multiplication of little alehouses. The proposed tax on shops was meant to be the same for every shop, and it could hardly have been otherwise. It would have been impossible to proportion the tax on a shop with any reasonable accuracy to the extent of the trade carried on in it without an inquisition that would have been altogether intolerable in a free country. Had the tax been considerable, it would have crushed the small shopkeepers and forced almost the entire retail trade into the hands of the large dealers. With the competition of the small dealers removed, the large ones would have enjoyed a monopoly of the trade, and, like all other monopolists, they would soon have combined to raise their profits far beyond what was needed to pay the tax. The final burden, instead of falling on the shopkeeper, would have fallen on the consumer, along with a considerable surcharge added to the shopkeeper's profit. For these reasons the plan for a tax on shops was dropped, and the subsidy of 1759 was put in its place.

What in France is called the personal *taille* is perhaps the most important tax on the profits of capital employed in agriculture that is levied anywhere in Europe.

In the disorderly condition of Europe while feudal government prevailed, the sovereign had to content himself with taxing those who were too weak to refuse. The great lords, though willing to assist him in particular emergencies, refused to submit to any regular tax, and he was not strong enough to compel them. The occupiers of land throughout Europe were, for the most part, originally bondmen. Through the greater part of Europe, they were gradually emancipated. Some came to own landed estates, which they held by some base or ignoble tenure, sometimes under the king and sometimes under another great lord, much like the old copyholders of England, who held their land by the custom of a manor rather than by free tenure. Others did not acquire ownership but obtained leases, for a term of years, on the lands they occupied under their lord, and so became less dependent on him. The great lords seem to have looked on the prosperity and independence that this lower order of men had come to enjoy with a malignant and contemptuous indignation, and they gladly consented to let the sovereign tax them. In some countries the tax was confined to lands owned under an ignoble tenure, and in that case the taille was called "real," because it attached to the land itself. The land tax established by the late king of Sardinia, and the taille in the provinces of Languedoc, Provence, Dauphiné, and Brittany, in the generality of Montauban, in the elections of Agen and Condom, and in several other districts of France, are taxes on lands owned under an ignoble tenure. In other countries the tax was laid on the supposed profits of everyone who held, on a farm or lease, land belonging to other people, whatever the tenure by which the owner held it, and in that case the taille was called "personal." In most of the French provinces known as the "countries of elections," the taille is of this kind. Because the real taille is imposed on only part of the country's land, it is necessarily unequal. It is not always arbitrary, though on some occasions it is. The personal taille is meant to be proportioned to the profits of a certain class of people, and those profits can only be guessed at, so it is necessarily both arbitrary and unequal.

In France, the personal taille now (1775) imposed each year on the twenty generalities known as the countries of elections amounts to 40,107,239 livres and 16 sous. The share of this sum assessed on each province changes from year to year. It depends on reports made to the king's council about whether the harvests have been good or bad, and about other circumstances that may raise or lower each province's ability to pay. Each generality, a fiscal province under the authority of a royal intendant, is divided into a number of smaller districts called elections. The share of the generality's total that falls on each election likewise changes yearly, according to reports made to the council about their respective abilities. It seems impossible that the council, however good its intentions, could ever match either of these two assessments with tolerable accuracy to the real ability of the province or district on which it is laid. Ignorance and misinformation must always mislead even the most upright council to some degree. The share that each parish must bear of the election's total, and the share that each individual must bear of his parish's assessment, are varied in the same way from year to year as circumstances are thought to require. In the first case these circumstances are judged by the officers of the election, and in the second by the officers of the parish, and both are more or less under the direction and influence of the intendant. Such assessors are said to be frequently misled not only by ignorance and misinformation but by friendship, party animosity, and private resentment. Plainly, no one subject to such a tax can ever know, before he is assessed, what he will have to pay. He cannot be certain even after he is assessed. Someone may be taxed who ought to have been exempt, or taxed beyond his proper share. Both must pay in the meantime, but if they complain and prove their case, the whole parish is reassessed the following year in order to reimburse them. If any taxpayer goes bankrupt or becomes insolvent, the collector must advance that person's tax out of his own pocket, and the whole parish is reassessed the next year to reimburse the collector. If the collector himself goes bankrupt, the parish that elected him must answer for his conduct to the receiver-general of the election. It would be troublesome for the receiver to prosecute an entire parish, so he picks out five or six of the richest taxpayers, as he chooses, and compels them to make good whatever was lost through the collector's insolvency. The parish is then reassessed to reimburse those five or six. Such reassessments always come on top of the taille for the year in which they are imposed.

When a tax is imposed on the profits of capital in a particular branch of trade, the traders all take care to bring no more goods to market than they can sell at a price high enough to reimburse them for advancing the tax. Some withdraw part of their capital from the trade, and the market is more sparingly supplied than before. The price of the goods rises, and the final burden of the tax falls on the consumer. When a tax is imposed on the profits of capital employed in agriculture, however, it is not in the farmers' interest to withdraw any part of their capital from that employment. Each farmer occupies a certain quantity of land, for which he pays rent. Cultivating that land properly requires a certain quantity of capital, and withdrawing any part of it is unlikely to make the farmer better able to pay either the rent or the tax. To pay the tax, it can never be in his interest to reduce his output, and so it can never be in his interest to supply the market more sparingly than before. The tax will therefore never allow him to raise the price of his produce and reimburse himself by shifting the final burden onto the consumer. Yet the farmer, like every other dealer, must earn his reasonable profit, or he must give up the business. Once a tax of this kind has been imposed, he can earn that reasonable profit only by paying less rent to the landlord. The more he is obliged to pay in tax, the less he can afford to pay in rent. A tax of this kind imposed while a lease is still running may well distress or ruin the farmer. When the lease is renewed, it must always fall on the landlord.

In the countries where the personal taille is in force, the farmer is commonly assessed in proportion to the capital he appears to employ in cultivation. For this reason he is often afraid to keep a good team of horses or oxen, and he tries to farm with the poorest and most wretched implements he can. His distrust of his assessors' fairness is so great that he counterfeits poverty and wishes to appear barely able to pay anything at all, for fear of being made to pay too much. By this miserable policy he perhaps does not always serve his own interest in the most effective way, and he probably loses more through the reduction of his output than he saves through the reduction of his tax. The market is no doubt somewhat worse supplied as a result of this wretched cultivation. But the small rise in price this may cause is unlikely even to compensate the farmer for his smaller output, and it is still less likely to enable him to pay more rent to the landlord. The public, the farmer, and the landlord all suffer more or less from this degraded cultivation. I have already observed, in the third book of this Inquiry, that the personal taille tends in many different ways to discourage cultivation, and so to dry up the principal source of the wealth of every great country.

The so-called poll taxes in the southern provinces of North America and in the West India islands are annual taxes of so much a head on every enslaved Black laborer. Properly speaking, they are taxes on the profits of a certain kind of capital employed in agriculture. Since most of the planters are both farmers and landlords, the final burden of the tax falls on them in their capacity as landlords, and they have no means of recovering it from anyone else.

Taxes of so much a head on the bondmen employed in cultivation seem in former times to have been common all over Europe. A tax of this kind still exists in the Russian empire. This is probably why poll taxes of every kind have often been described as badges of slavery. Yet every tax is, to the person who pays it, a badge not of slavery but of liberty. It shows that he is indeed subject to government, but also that, since he has some property, he cannot himself be the property of a master. A poll tax on slaves is entirely different from a poll tax on free men. The latter is paid by the persons on whom it is imposed; the former is paid by a different set of persons. The latter is either wholly arbitrary or wholly unequal, and in most cases it is both. The former is unequal in some respects, since different slaves are of different values, but it is in no respect arbitrary. Every master who knows how many slaves he owns knows exactly what he has to pay. Because these different taxes are called by the same name, however, they have been regarded as being of the same nature.

The taxes imposed in Holland on male and female servants fall not on capital but on expenditure, and to that extent they resemble taxes on consumable goods. The tax of a guinea a head on every male servant, recently imposed in Great Britain, is of the same kind. It falls most heavily on the middle ranks. A man with two hundred pounds a year may keep one male servant, while a man with ten thousand pounds a year will not keep fifty. It does not touch the poor.

Taxes on the profits of capital in particular employments can never affect the rate of interest. No one will lend his money at lower interest to people engaged in the taxed employments than to people engaged in the untaxed ones. But taxes on the revenue from capital in all employments, where the government tries to levy them with any degree of exactness, will in many cases fall on the interest of money. The vingtième, or "twentieth penny," in France is a tax of the same kind as what is called the land tax in England, and it is assessed in the same way on the revenue from land, houses, and capital. Insofar as it affects capital, it is assessed, though not with great rigor, at least with far more exactness than the part of the English land tax that is imposed on the same fund. In many cases it falls entirely on the interest of money. In France, money is frequently invested in what are called contracts for the constitution of a rent. These are perpetual annuities that the debtor may redeem at any time by repaying the sum originally advanced, but whose redemption the creditor cannot demand except in particular cases. The vingtième seems not to have raised the rate paid on these annuities, even though it is levied exactly on every one of them.

##### Appendix to Articles I and II: Taxes upon the Capital Value of Lands, Houses, and Stock

While property remains in the hands of the same person, whatever permanent taxes have been imposed on it have never been intended to reduce or take away any part of its capital value, but only part of the revenue arising from it. When property changes hands, however, whether it passes from the dead to the living or from one living person to another, it has often been subjected to taxes that necessarily take away some part of its capital value.

The transfer of every kind of property from the dead to the living, and the transfer of immovable property in land and houses from one living person to another, are by nature either public and widely known or impossible to conceal for long. Such transactions can therefore be taxed directly. The transfer of capital or movable property between living persons through the lending of money is often a secret transaction, and it can always be made one. It cannot easily be taxed directly, and so it has been taxed indirectly in two ways. The first is to require that the deed containing the obligation to repay be written on paper or parchment that has paid a certain stamp duty, and to make it invalid otherwise. The second is to require, under the same penalty of invalidity, that the deed be recorded in either a public or a secret register, and to impose certain duties on that registration. Stamp duties and registration duties have often been imposed as well on deeds transferring property of every kind from the dead to the living, and on deeds transferring immovable property between living persons, although these transactions could easily have been taxed directly.

The vicesima hereditatum, or twentieth penny on inheritances, which Augustus imposed on the ancient Romans, was a tax on the transfer of property from the dead to the living. Dio Cassius, the author who writes about it least obscurely, says that it was imposed on all successions, legacies, and gifts made in the event of death, except those to the nearest relatives and to the poor.

The Dutch tax on successions is of the same kind. Collateral successions, in which property passes to relatives outside the direct line, are taxed according to the degree of kinship, at rates from five to thirty percent of the whole value of the inheritance. Legacies left by will to collateral relatives are subject to the same duties. Legacies from husband to wife, or from wife to husband, pay the fiftieth penny, or one-fiftieth of their value. The luctuosa hereditas, the "mournful succession," in which parents or grandparents inherit from their children, pays only the twentieth penny. Direct successions, in which children inherit from their parents, pay no tax at all. To those of his children who live in the same house with him, a father's death seldom brings any increase of income, and often brings a considerable loss of it, through the loss of his labor, of his office, or of some estate he held for life. A tax that aggravated their loss by taking any part of his estate from them would be cruel and oppressive. It may sometimes be otherwise, however, with children who, in the language of Roman law, are said to be "emancipated," or in the language of Scots law, "forisfamiliated": children who have received their portion, have families of their own, and are supported by funds separate from and independent of their father's. Whatever part of his estate came to such children would be a real addition to their fortune, and it might therefore perhaps be made liable to some tax without more inconvenience than attends all duties of this kind.

The casualties of feudal law, the incidental dues that arose on particular occasions, were taxes on the transfer of land both from the dead to the living and between living persons. In ancient times they formed, in every part of Europe, one of the principal branches of the crown's revenue.

The heir of every vassal who held directly from the crown paid a certain duty, generally a year's rent, on being formally invested with the estate. If the heir was a minor, the entire rents of the estate went to the superior lord for as long as the minority lasted, with no charge on them except the minor's maintenance and the payment of the widow's dower, if there happened to be a widow with a claim on the land. When the minor came of age, yet another tax, called relief, was owed to the superior, and it generally amounted to a further year's rent. In the present age a long minority very often frees a great estate of all its debts and restores the family to its former splendor. In those times it could have no such effect. The usual result of a long minority was not the clearing of the estate but its waste.

Under feudal law the vassal could not sell or otherwise alienate his land without the consent of his superior, who generally extorted a fine or payment for granting it. This fine was at first arbitrary, but in many countries it came to be fixed at a certain proportion of the price of the land. In some countries where most of the other feudal customs have fallen into disuse, this tax on the alienation of land still forms a very considerable branch of the sovereign's revenue. In the canton of Bern it is as high as one-sixth of the price of all noble fiefs and one-tenth of the price of all ignoble ones. In the canton of Lucerne the tax on the sale of land is not universal and applies only in certain districts. But anyone who sells his land in order to leave the territory pays ten percent of the whole sale price. Taxes of the same kind, on the sale either of all lands or of lands held by certain tenures, exist in many other countries and form a more or less considerable branch of the sovereign's revenue.

Such transactions may be taxed indirectly, by means of either stamp duties or registration duties, and these duties may or may not be proportioned to the value of the thing transferred.

In Great Britain, stamp duties are higher or lower not so much according to the value of the property transferred as according to the nature of the deed. An eighteen-penny stamp or a half-crown stamp is enough for a bond securing the largest sum of money. The highest duties do not exceed six pounds for each sheet of paper or skin of parchment, and these high duties fall chiefly on grants from the crown and on certain legal proceedings, without any regard to the value of the thing concerned. In Great Britain there are no duties on the registration of deeds or other writings, apart from the fees of the officers who keep the register, and these are seldom more than a reasonable payment for their labor. The crown derives no revenue from them.

In Holland there are both stamp duties and registration duties, which in some cases are proportioned to the value of the property transferred and in others are not. All wills must be written on stamped paper whose price is proportioned to the property being disposed of, so that there are stamps costing anywhere from three pence, or three stivers, a sheet up to three hundred florins, equal to about twenty-seven pounds ten shillings in English money. If the testator uses a stamp of a lower price than he should have, his estate is confiscated. This comes on top of all their other taxes on successions. Apart from bills of exchange and certain other commercial bills, all other deeds, bonds, and contracts are subject to a stamp duty, though this duty does not rise in proportion to the value of the thing concerned. All sales of land and houses, and all mortgages on either, must be registered, and on registration they pay the state a duty of two and a half percent of the price or of the sum mortgaged. This duty extends to the sale of all ships and vessels of more than two tons' burden, whether decked or undecked; these, it seems, are regarded as a kind of house on the water. The sale of movable goods, when ordered by a court of justice, is subject to the same duty of two and a half percent.

In France there are both stamp duties and registration duties. The stamp duties are treated as a branch of the aides, the excise duties, and in the provinces where those duties are in force they are collected by the excise officers. The registration duties are treated as a branch of the crown's domain and are collected by a different set of officers.

These methods of taxation, by stamp duties and registration duties, are a very recent invention. Yet in little more than a century stamp duties have become almost universal in Europe, and registration duties extremely common. There is no art that one government learns more quickly from another than that of draining money from the pockets of the people.

Taxes on the transfer of property from the dead to the living fall, finally as well as immediately, on the persons to whom the property passes. Taxes on the sale of land fall entirely on the seller. The seller is almost always under some necessity to sell, and must therefore accept whatever price he can get. The buyer is hardly ever under any necessity to buy, and will therefore give only the price he chooses. He considers what the land will cost him in tax and price together, and the more he must pay in tax, the less he will be willing to give in price. Such taxes therefore almost always fall on someone in need, and so they must often be very cruel and oppressive. Taxes on the sale of newly built houses, where the building is sold without the ground, generally fall on the buyer, because the builder must generally make his profit or else give up the trade. If he advances the tax, the buyer must generally repay it to him. Taxes on the sale of old houses, for the same reason as those on the sale of land, generally fall on the seller, who in most cases is driven to sell by either convenience or necessity. The number of newly built houses brought to market each year is more or less governed by demand. Unless demand is great enough to give the builder his profit after all expenses are paid, he will build no more houses. The number of old houses that happen to come to market at any moment is governed by accidents, most of which have no connection with demand. Two or three large bankruptcies in a commercial town will bring many houses up for sale, and they must be sold for whatever they will fetch. Taxes on the sale of ground rents fall entirely on the seller, for the same reason as those on the sale of land. Stamp duties and registration duties on bonds and contracts for borrowed money fall entirely on the borrower, and in practice they are always paid by him. Duties of the same kind on legal proceedings fall on the parties to the suit. For both parties, they reduce the capital value of the property in dispute. The more it costs to acquire any property, the lower its net value must be once it has been acquired.

All taxes on the transfer of property of every kind, insofar as they reduce the capital value of that property, tend to reduce the funds set aside for the maintenance of productive labor. They are all more or less unthrifty taxes. They increase the revenue of the sovereign, which seldom maintains any but unproductive laborers, at the expense of the capital of the people, which maintains none but productive ones.

Even when such taxes are proportioned to the value of the property transferred, they are still unequal, because property of equal value does not always change hands with equal frequency. When they are not proportioned to that value, as is the case with most stamp duties and registration duties, they are more unequal still. They are in no respect arbitrary, however, but are, or can be, perfectly clear and certain in every case. Though they sometimes fall on someone who is not well able to pay, the timing of the payment is, in most cases, convenient enough for him. When the payment falls due, he will usually have more than usual on hand with which to make it. These taxes are collected at very little expense, and they generally impose no hardship on the people who pay them beyond the one that can never be avoided, which is the payment itself. In France, the stamp duties draw few complaints. The registration duties, which the French call the *contrôle*, draw many. They are said to give rise to a great deal of extortion by the agents of the farmers-general, the private financiers who purchase from the Crown the right to collect the tax, because the tax is in large part arbitrary and uncertain. In most of the pamphlets that have been written attacking the present system of French finance, the abuses of the *contrôle* figure as a principal charge. Uncertainty, however, does not seem to be necessarily inherent in the nature of such taxes. If the popular complaints are justified, the abuse must arise less from the nature of the tax itself than from the lack of precision and clarity in the wording of the edicts or laws that impose it.

The registration of mortgages, and in general of all claims on real property, is extremely advantageous to the public, because it gives great security to creditors and purchasers alike. The registration of most other kinds of deeds, by contrast, is often inconvenient and even dangerous to individuals, while bringing no advantage to the public. Any register that is admitted to require secrecy ought never to exist at all. A person's credit should never depend on so slender a safeguard as the honesty and conscience of the lower officers of the revenue. Yet wherever registration fees have been turned into a source of revenue for the sovereign, registry offices have usually multiplied without limit, covering deeds that ought to be registered and deeds that ought not. France has several different kinds of secret registers. This abuse may not be a necessary consequence of such taxes, but it must be acknowledged to be a very natural one.

Stamp duties such as those in England on playing cards and dice, and on newspapers and periodical pamphlets, are properly taxes on consumption, since the final payment falls on the people who use or consume these goods. Stamp duties such as those on licences to sell ale, wine, and spirits at retail, though perhaps intended to fall on the profits of the retailers, are likewise paid in the end by the people who drink those liquors. These taxes bear the same name as the stamp duties on the transfer of property already discussed, and they are collected by the same officers and in the same manner. They are nonetheless of an entirely different nature, and they fall on entirely different funds.

##### Article III: Taxes on the Wages of Labour

I have tried to show in the first book that the wages of ordinary workmen are everywhere necessarily governed by two separate circumstances: the demand for labour, and the ordinary or average price of provisions. The demand for labour, according to whether it is increasing, stationary, or declining, and so calls for an increasing, stationary, or declining population, governs the labourer's standard of subsistence and determines whether it will be generous, moderate, or meagre. The ordinary average price of provisions then determines how much money must be paid to the workman so that, taking one year with another, he can buy that generous, moderate, or meagre subsistence. So long as the demand for labour and the price of provisions stay the same, therefore, a direct tax on the wages of labour can have no other effect than to raise those wages by somewhat more than the tax.

Suppose, for example, that in a particular place the demand for labour and the price of provisions were such that ten shillings a week was the ordinary wage, and that a tax of one-fifth was laid on wages, which is to say four shillings in every pound of twenty shillings. If the demand for labour and the price of provisions stayed the same, the labourer in that place would still need to earn a subsistence that could be bought only for ten shillings a week, so that after paying the tax he would be left with ten shillings a week in free wages. But to leave him that much after paying such a tax, the price of labour in that place would soon have to rise, not merely to twelve shillings a week, but to twelve shillings and sixpence. To enable him to pay a tax of one-fifth, that is, his wages must soon rise not by one-fifth but by one-fourth. Whatever the rate of the tax, wages must in every case rise not only in that proportion but in a higher one. If the tax were one-tenth, for instance, wages would soon have to rise not by one-tenth but by one-eighth.

A direct tax on the wages of labour, therefore, even if the labourer might hand over the money himself, could not properly be said to be even advanced by him, at least if the demand for labour and the average price of provisions remained the same after the tax as before. In every such case, not only the tax but something more than the tax would in reality be advanced by his immediate employer. Who bore the final payment would differ from case to case. The rise that such a tax produced in the wages of manufacturing labour would be advanced by the master manufacturer, who would be both entitled and obliged to add it, together with a profit, to the price of his goods. The final payment of this rise in wages, along with the manufacturer's additional profit, would therefore fall on the consumer. The rise that such a tax produced in the wages of agricultural labour would be advanced by the farmer, who would need a larger capital in order to keep the same number of labourers as before. To recover this larger capital together with the ordinary profits of stock, he would have to keep back a larger share of the produce of the land, or, what comes to the same thing, the price of a larger share, and he would consequently pay less rent to the landlord. In this case, then, the final payment of the rise in wages, along with the additional profit of the farmer who advanced it, would fall on the landlord. In every case, a direct tax on the wages of labour must in the long run cause both a greater reduction in the rent of land and a greater rise in the price of manufactured goods than would have followed if a sum equal to the yield of the tax had been properly assessed partly on the rent of land and partly on consumable goods.

If direct taxes on wages have not always produced a proportional rise in those wages, the reason is that they have generally produced a considerable fall in the demand for labour. The decline of industry, the shrinking of employment for the poor, and the reduction of the annual produce of the country's land and labour have generally been the effects of such taxes. Even so, because of them, the price of labour must always be higher than it would otherwise have been under the actual state of demand, and this increase in price, together with the profit of those who advance it, must always be paid in the end by landlords and consumers.

A tax on the wages of agricultural labour does not raise the price of the raw produce of the land in proportion to the tax, for the same reason that a tax on the farmer's profit does not raise that price in that proportion.

Absurd and destructive as such taxes are, they exist in many countries. In France, the portion of the *taille*, the principal direct tax levied on commoners, that is charged on the earnings of workmen and day labourers in country villages is properly a tax of this kind. Their wages are calculated according to the common rate in the district where they live, and so that they will be as little exposed as possible to overcharging, their yearly earnings are reckoned on no more than two hundred working days a year. Each person's tax varies from year to year according to various circumstances, and the judges of those circumstances are the collector or the commissioner whom the intendant, the royal administrator of the province, appoints to assist him. In Bohemia, as a result of the reform of the financial system begun in 1748, a very heavy tax is imposed on the earnings of artisans. They are divided into four classes. The highest class pays a hundred florins a year, which, at twenty-two and a half pence to the florin, comes to nine pounds, seven shillings, and sixpence. The second class is taxed at seventy florins, the third at fifty, and the fourth, which includes village artisans and the lowest class of those in towns, at twenty-five.

I have tried to show in the first book that the earnings of skilled artists and of men in the liberal professions necessarily keep a certain proportion to the earnings of the humbler trades. A tax on these earnings, therefore, could have no other effect than to raise them by somewhat more than the tax. If they did not rise in this way, the skilled arts and the liberal professions, no longer being on a level with other occupations, would be abandoned by so many people that they would soon return to that level.

The earnings of public offices are not, like those of trades and professions, governed by free competition in the market, and they therefore do not always bear a fair proportion to what the nature of the work requires. In most countries they are probably higher than it requires, since the people who run the government are generally inclined to look after themselves and their immediate dependants rather more than enough. In most cases, therefore, the earnings of offices can very well bear to be taxed. Moreover, the holders of public offices, especially the more lucrative ones, are objects of general envy in every country, and a tax on their earnings, even one somewhat higher than the tax on any other kind of income, is always very popular. In England, for example, at a time when the land tax was supposed to assess every other kind of income at four shillings in the pound, it was very popular to impose an actual tax of five shillings and sixpence in the pound on the salaries of offices worth more than a hundred pounds a year. The exceptions were the pensions of the younger members of the royal family, the pay of army and navy officers, and a few other incomes less exposed to envy. England has no other direct taxes on the wages of labour.

##### Article IV: Taxes Intended to Fall Indiscriminately on Every Kind of Revenue

The taxes intended to fall indiscriminately on every kind of revenue are capitation taxes and taxes on consumable goods. These must be paid out of whatever revenue the taxpayers happen to have, whether the rent of their land, the profits of their stock, or the wages of their labour.

###### Capitation Taxes

Capitation taxes, which are taxes levied on each person as an individual, become wholly arbitrary if one tries to proportion them to the fortune or income of each taxpayer. The state of a man's fortune changes from day to day, and without an inquisition more intolerable than any tax, renewed at least once a year, it can only be guessed at. In most cases, therefore, his assessment must depend on the good or bad temper of his assessors, and so must be wholly arbitrary and uncertain.

If capitation taxes are proportioned not to each taxpayer's supposed fortune but to his rank, they become wholly unequal, since people of the same rank frequently have very unequal fortunes.

If one tries to make such taxes equal, then, they become wholly arbitrary and uncertain, and if one tries to make them certain and not arbitrary, they become wholly unequal. Whether the tax is light or heavy, uncertainty is always a great grievance. With a light tax, a considerable degree of inequality can be tolerated; with a heavy one, it is altogether intolerable.

In the various poll taxes levied in England during the reign of William III, most taxpayers were assessed according to their rank: dukes, marquises, earls, viscounts, barons, esquires, gentlemen, the eldest and younger sons of peers, and so on. All shopkeepers and tradesmen worth more than three hundred pounds, which is to say the more prosperous among them, were subject to the same assessment, however great the differences in their fortunes. Their rank counted for more than their wealth. Several groups who had been rated according to their supposed fortune in the first poll tax were afterwards rated according to their rank. Serjeants-at-law, who were the senior barristers, along with attorneys and proctors, the latter of whom practised in the ecclesiastical and admiralty courts, had been assessed in the first poll tax at three shillings in the pound on their supposed income, and were afterwards assessed simply as gentlemen. In assessing a tax that was not very heavy, a considerable degree of inequality had been found less unbearable than any degree of uncertainty.

In the capitation that has been levied in France without interruption since the beginning of the present century, the highest orders of people are rated according to their rank by a fixed schedule, while the lower orders are rated according to their supposed fortune by an assessment that changes from year to year. The officers of the king's court, the judges and other officers of the superior courts of justice, the officers of the army, and others are assessed in the first way. The lower ranks of people in the provinces are assessed in the second. In France, the great readily accept a considerable degree of inequality in a tax that, so far as it touches them, is not very heavy, but they would not tolerate the arbitrary assessment of an intendant.

The lower ranks of people in that country must patiently endure whatever treatment their superiors see fit to give them.

In England, the various poll taxes never yielded the sum expected of them, or the sum it was supposed they might have yielded had they been strictly collected. In France, the capitation always yields the sum expected. When the mild government of England assessed the different ranks of people for the poll tax, it was content with whatever that assessment happened to produce. It demanded no compensation for the loss the state might suffer from those who could not pay, or from those who would not pay, of whom there were many, and who, under the lenient enforcement of the law, were not compelled to. The harsher government of France assigns a fixed sum to each *généralité*, a fiscal district under an intendant's authority, and the intendant must raise it however he can. If a province complains of being assessed too highly, it may obtain, in the following year's assessment, a reduction proportioned to the previous year's overcharge, but it must pay in the meantime. To be certain of raising the sum assigned to his district, the intendant was empowered to assess it at a larger figure, so that the default or inability of some taxpayers could be made up by overcharging the rest, and until 1765 the size of this surplus assessment was left entirely to his discretion. In that year, it is true, the royal council took this power for itself. The thoroughly well-informed author of the *Memoirs upon the Impositions in France* observes that in the provincial capitation, the share falling on the nobility and on those whose privileges exempt them from the *taille* is the smallest. The largest share falls on those subject to the *taille*, who are assessed for the capitation at so much in the pound of what they pay toward that other tax. Capitation taxes, insofar as they are levied on the lower ranks of people, are direct taxes on the wages of labour, and they carry all the disadvantages of such taxes.

Capitation taxes are collected at little expense, and where they are rigorously enforced, they provide the state with a very dependable revenue. That is why they are very common in countries where little attention is paid to the ease, comfort, and security of the lower ranks of people. In general, however, only a small part of the public revenue of a great empire has ever been drawn from such taxes, and the largest sum they have ever produced could always have been raised in some other way far more convenient to the people.

###### Taxes on Consumable Goods

The impossibility of taxing people in proportion to their income by means of any capitation seems to have led to the invention of taxes on consumable goods. Not knowing how to tax its subjects' income directly and proportionally, the state tries to tax it indirectly by taxing their spending, which is presumed in most cases to be roughly proportional to their income. Their spending is taxed by taxing the consumable goods on which it is laid out.

Consumable goods are either necessaries or luxuries.

By necessaries I mean not only the goods that are indispensable for sustaining life, but whatever the custom of the country makes it improper for respectable people, even of the lowest order, to be without. A linen shirt, for example, is not, strictly speaking, a necessity of life. The Greeks and Romans, I suppose, lived very comfortably without linen. But at present, throughout most of Europe, a respectable day labourer would be ashamed to appear in public without a linen shirt, since the lack of one would be taken to signify that disgraceful degree of poverty into which, it is presumed, no one can fall except through extremely bad conduct. Custom has in the same way made leather shoes a necessity of life in England. The poorest respectable person of either sex would be ashamed to appear in public without them. In Scotland, custom has made them a necessity for the lowest order of men, but not for women of the same order, who may walk about barefoot without any discredit. In France they are a necessity for neither men nor women, since the lowest rank of both sexes appear in public there without any discredit, sometimes in wooden shoes and sometimes barefoot. Under necessaries, therefore, I include not only the things that nature has made necessary to the lowest rank of people, but also those that the established rules of decency have made so. Everything else I call luxuries, without intending by that name to cast the slightest reproach on their moderate use. Beer and ale in Great Britain, for example, and wine even in the wine-producing countries, I call luxuries. A man of any rank may abstain entirely from such drinks without any reproach. Nature does not make them necessary for sustaining life, and custom nowhere makes it improper to live without them.

Since the wages of labour are everywhere governed partly by the demand for labour and partly by the average price of the necessary articles of subsistence, whatever raises this average price must necessarily raise wages, so that the labourer can still buy the quantity of those necessary articles that the state of the demand for labour, whether increasing, stationary, or declining, requires him to have. A tax on those articles necessarily raises their price by somewhat more than the amount of the tax, because the dealer who advances the tax must generally recover it with a profit. Such a tax must therefore cause a rise in wages proportional to this rise in price.

In this way a tax on the necessaries of life operates in exactly the same manner as a direct tax on the wages of labour. The labourer, though he may hand over the money himself, cannot properly be said, at least for any considerable length of time, even to advance it. In the long run it must always be advanced to him by his immediate employer in the form of higher wages. If his employer is a manufacturer, he will add the rise in wages, together with a profit, to the price of his goods, so that the final payment of the tax, along with this surcharge, will fall on the consumer. If his employer is a farmer, the final payment, along with a similar surcharge, will fall on the landlord's rent.

The case is different with taxes on what I call luxuries, even the luxuries of the poor. A rise in the price of the taxed goods will not necessarily cause any rise in wages. A tax on tobacco, for example, though it is a luxury of the poor as well as of the rich, will not raise wages. Tobacco is taxed in England at three times its original price and in France at fifteen times, yet these high duties appear to have no effect on wages. The same may be said of the taxes on tea and sugar, which in England and Holland have become luxuries of the lowest ranks of people, and of those on chocolate, which is said to have become such a luxury in Spain.

The various taxes imposed on spirits in Great Britain over the course of the present century are not thought to have had any effect on wages. The rise in the price of porter, a strong dark beer, caused by an additional tax of three shillings on the barrel of strong beer, has not raised the wages of common labour in London. These were about eighteen or twenty pence a day before the tax, and they are no higher now.

The high price of such goods does not necessarily reduce the ability of the lower ranks of people to raise families. On the sober and industrious poor, taxes on such goods act as sumptuary laws, the old statutes that restricted spending on luxuries, and they incline these people either to moderate or to give up entirely the use of superfluities they can no longer easily afford. As a result of this enforced thrift, their ability to raise families is often, perhaps, increased by the tax rather than diminished. It is the sober and industrious poor who generally raise the largest families and who chiefly supply the demand for useful labour. Not all the poor, it is true, are sober and industrious, and the dissolute and disorderly might go on indulging in such goods after the rise in price just as before, without regard for the hardship this indulgence might bring on their families. Such disorderly people, however, seldom raise large families, since their children generally perish from neglect, mismanagement, and food that is scanty or unwholesome. If the children survive, through the strength of their constitutions, the hardships to which their parents' bad conduct exposes them, the example of that conduct usually corrupts their morals, so that instead of being useful to society through their industry, they become public nuisances through their vices and disorders. Although the higher price of the luxuries of the poor might therefore somewhat increase the distress of such disorderly families, and so somewhat reduce their ability to raise children, it would probably not much reduce the useful population of the country.

Any rise in the average price of necessities, unless it is offset by a proportional rise in wages, must to some degree reduce the ability of the poor to raise large families, and therefore their ability to supply the demand for useful labor. This holds whatever the state of that demand may be: whether it is growing, stationary, or declining, and whether it calls for a growing, stationary, or declining population.

Taxes on luxuries do not tend to raise the price of any commodity except the one taxed. Taxes on necessities, by raising the wages of labor, inevitably tend to raise the price of all manufactured goods, and so to shrink their sale and consumption. Taxes on luxuries are ultimately paid by the consumers of the taxed goods, who receive no compensation for them. They fall without distinction on every kind of income: the wages of labor, the profits of capital, and the rent of land. Taxes on necessities, insofar as they affect the laboring poor, are ultimately paid partly by landlords, through lower rents on their land, and partly by wealthy consumers, whether landlords or others, through higher prices for manufactured goods.
