In both cases the burden comes with a considerable surcharge. When the price of manufactured goods that are true necessities of life and are made for the poor rises, as with coarse woolens, the poor must be compensated by a further increase in their wages. If the middle and upper classes understood their own interest, they would always oppose every tax on the necessities of life and every tax on the wages of labor. The final payment of both falls entirely on themselves, and always with a considerable surcharge. These taxes fall most heavily on landlords, who always pay twice: as landlords, through reduced rents, and as wealthy consumers, through higher expenses. Sir Matthew Decker observed that certain taxes are sometimes repeated and compounded four or five times over in the price of certain goods, and with respect to taxes on the necessities of life the observation is entirely correct. In the price of leather, for example, you must pay not only the tax on the leather of your own shoes but also part of the tax on the shoes of the shoemaker and the tanner. You must also pay for the tax on the salt, the soap, and the candles that those workmen use while they are working for you, and for the tax on the leather that the salt-maker, the soap-maker, and the candle-maker use while they are working for them.

In Great Britain, the main taxes on the necessities of life are those on the four commodities just mentioned: salt, leather, soap, and candles.

Salt is a very old and very widespread object of taxation. The Romans taxed it, and it is taxed today, I believe, in every part of Europe. Because the quantity any individual consumes in a year is so small, and can be bought so gradually, it seems to have been assumed that nobody would feel even a fairly heavy tax on it very sharply. In England it is taxed at three shillings and fourpence a bushel, about three times the original price of the commodity. In some other countries the tax is higher still. Leather is a true necessity of life. The use of linen makes soap one as well, since linen must be washed. In countries where the winter nights are long, candles are an indispensable tool of work. In Great Britain, leather and soap are taxed at three halfpence a pound and candles at a penny. On the original price of leather, these taxes may amount to about eight or ten percent; on soap, to about twenty or twenty-five percent; and on candles, to about fourteen or fifteen percent. Though lighter than the tax on salt, they are still very heavy. Since all four of these commodities are true necessities of life, such heavy taxes on them must somewhat increase the expenses of the sober and hardworking poor, and must therefore raise the wages of their labor to a greater or lesser degree.

In a country with winters as cold as those of Great Britain, fuel during that season is, in the strictest sense, a necessity of life. It is needed not only for cooking food but for the reasonable comfort of the many kinds of workmen who labor indoors, and coal is the cheapest of all fuels. The price of fuel has so great an influence on the price of labor that, throughout Great Britain, manufacturing has concentrated mainly in the coal-producing counties; other parts of the country, because of the high price of this essential article, cannot produce as cheaply. In some manufactures, moreover, coal is a necessary tool of the trade, as in glassmaking, ironworking, and the working of all other metals. If a bounty, or government subsidy, could ever be justified, it might perhaps be justified for transporting coal from the regions where it is plentiful to those where it is needed. Instead of a bounty, however, the legislature has imposed a tax of three shillings and threepence a ton on coal shipped along the coast by sea, which on most kinds of coal comes to more than sixty percent of its original price at the pit. Coal carried overland or by inland waterways pays no duty. So where coal is naturally cheap, it is consumed duty-free; where it is naturally expensive, it is burdened with a heavy duty.

Such taxes, though they raise the cost of subsistence and therefore the wages of labor, nonetheless provide the government with a considerable revenue that might not be easy to raise any other way. There may therefore be good reasons for keeping them. The bounty on the export of grain, insofar as it tends, given the present state of agriculture, to raise the price of that essential article, produces all the same harmful effects, and far from yielding any revenue, it frequently costs the government a great deal. The high duties on imported foreign grain, which in years of moderate abundance amount to an outright ban, and the absolute ban on importing live cattle or salted provisions, which is in force under ordinary law and which, because of the present scarcity, has been suspended for a limited time with respect to Ireland and the British colonies, have all had the harmful effects of taxes on the necessities of life while producing no revenue for the government. Nothing more seems necessary to repeal such regulations than to convince the public of the futility of the system that gave rise to them.

Taxes on the necessities of life are much higher in many other countries than in Great Britain. Many countries impose duties on flour and meal when they are ground at the mill and on bread when it is baked in the oven. In Holland the money price of the bread consumed in towns is thought to be doubled by such taxes. In place of part of these taxes, people living in the countryside pay a fixed annual sum per person according to the kind of bread they are presumed to eat. Those who eat wheat bread pay three guilders and fifteen stivers, about six shillings and ninepence halfpenny. These and other taxes of the same kind, by raising the price of labor, are said to have ruined most of the manufactures of Holland. Similar taxes, though not quite as heavy, are levied in the Milanese territory, in the states of Genoa, in the duchy of Modena, in the duchies of Parma, Piacenza, and Guastalla, and in the Papal States. A French author of some reputation, in a work titled *Le Réformateur*, has proposed reforming his country's finances by replacing most other taxes with this most ruinous of all taxes. As Cicero said, there is nothing so absurd that some philosopher has not at some time asserted it.

Taxes on butcher's meat are even more common than taxes on bread. It may well be doubted whether butcher's meat is a necessity of life anywhere. Experience shows that grain and other vegetables, together with milk, cheese, and butter, or oil where butter cannot be had, can provide, without any butcher's meat at all, the most plentiful, wholesome, nourishing, and invigorating diet. Decency nowhere requires a man to eat butcher's meat, as in most places it requires him to wear a linen shirt or a pair of leather shoes.

Consumable goods, whether necessities or luxuries, can be taxed in two different ways. Either the consumer pays an annual sum for the right to use or consume goods of a certain kind, or the goods are taxed while they are still in the hands of the dealer, before they are delivered to the consumer. Goods that last a considerable time before they are entirely used up are best taxed in the first way; those consumed immediately or quickly, in the second. The coach tax and the plate tax, which is levied on household silverware, are examples of the first method; most of the other excise and customs duties are examples of the second.

With good care, a coach may last ten or twelve years. It could be taxed once and for all before it leaves the coach-maker's hands. But it is certainly more convenient for the buyer to pay four pounds a year for the privilege of keeping a coach than to pay forty or forty-eight pounds extra to the coach-maker all at once, or a sum equal to what the tax is likely to cost him over the whole time he uses that coach. In the same way, a service of silver plate may last more than a century. It is certainly easier for the owner to pay five shillings a year for every hundred ounces of plate, nearly one percent of its value, than to buy out this long-running annual charge in a single payment worth twenty-five or thirty years of it, which would raise the price by at least twenty-five or thirty percent. Likewise, the various taxes that fall on houses are certainly more convenient to pay in moderate annual installments than as a single heavy tax of equal value levied when the house is first built or sold.

Sir Matthew Decker made a well-known proposal that all commodities, even those consumed immediately or quickly, should be taxed in this way: the dealer would advance nothing, and the consumer would pay a fixed annual sum for a license to consume certain goods. The aim of his scheme was to promote every branch of foreign trade, particularly the carrying trade, in which merchants ship goods between foreign countries, by abolishing all duties on imports and exports. This would allow merchants to devote their entire capital and credit to buying goods and paying freight, without diverting any part of either to advancing taxes. The plan of taxing goods of immediate or rapid consumption in this way, however, seems open to four very serious objections. First, the tax would be more unequal, or less well proportioned to the spending and consumption of the various taxpayers, than it is under the usual method. The taxes on ale, wine, and spirits, which the dealers advance, are ultimately paid by the various consumers in exact proportion to what each consumes. But if the tax were paid by buying a license to drink those liquors, the sober drinker would be taxed far more heavily, relative to his consumption, than the drunkard. A family that entertained generously would be taxed far more lightly than one that had fewer guests. Second, paying for an annual, half-yearly, or quarterly license to consume certain goods would largely destroy one of the chief conveniences of taxes on goods of rapid consumption, which is that they are paid piecemeal. Of the threepence halfpenny now paid for a pot of porter, a dark beer popular among working people, the various taxes on malt, hops, and beer, together with the extra profit the brewer charges for having advanced them, may come to about three halfpence. If a workman can comfortably spare those three halfpence, he buys a pot of porter. If he cannot, he settles for a pint, and since a penny saved is a penny earned, he gains a farthing, a quarter of a penny, by his moderation. He pays the tax a little at a time, as he can afford it and when he can afford it, and every act of payment is entirely voluntary, something he can avoid if he chooses. Third, such taxes would work less effectively as sumptuary laws, the laws meant to restrain excessive consumption. Once the license had been bought, the tax would be the same whether the buyer drank much or little. Fourth, if a workman had to pay all at once, in yearly, half-yearly, or quarterly installments, a tax equal to what he now pays with little or no inconvenience on all the pots and pints of porter he drinks over such a period, the sum might often cause him great hardship. It therefore seems evident that this method of taxation could never, without the most grievous oppression, yield a revenue anywhere near what the present method yields without any oppression at all. Nevertheless, in several countries, goods of immediate or very rapid consumption are taxed in this way. In Holland, people pay a fixed sum per person for a license to drink tea. I have already mentioned a tax on bread which, as far as bread eaten in farmhouses and country villages is concerned, is levied there in the same manner.

Excise duties are imposed mainly on domestically produced goods intended for domestic consumption. They are levied on only a few kinds of goods in the most general use. There can never be any doubt about which goods are subject to these duties, or about the particular duty each kind of good must pay. They fall almost entirely on what I call luxuries, always excepting the four duties already mentioned on salt, soap, leather, and candles, and perhaps the duty on green glass.

Customs duties are much older than excise duties. They seem to have been called customs because they were customary payments, in use since time immemorial. They appear originally to have been regarded as taxes on the profits of merchants. In the barbarous era of feudal anarchy, merchants, like all the other inhabitants of chartered towns, were regarded as little better than freed serfs, whose persons were despised and whose gains were envied. The great nobles, who had agreed that the king might impose tallage, an arbitrary levy, on the profits of their own tenants, were quite willing for him to levy it also on a class of men whom they had far less interest in protecting. In those ignorant times it was not understood that the profits of merchants cannot be taxed directly, or that the final payment of all such taxes must fall, with a considerable surcharge, on consumers.

The gains of foreign merchants were viewed even less favorably than those of English merchants, and it was natural that the former should be taxed more heavily than the latter. This distinction between the duties on foreigners and those on English merchants began in ignorance but has been continued out of the spirit of monopoly, to give our own merchants an advantage in both the home market and foreign markets. Apart from this distinction, the old customs duties were imposed equally on all kinds of goods, necessities as well as luxuries, exports as well as imports. Why, it seems to have been reasoned, should dealers in one kind of goods be favored over those in another? Or why should the exporting merchant be favored over the importing merchant?

The old customs were divided into three branches. The first, and perhaps the oldest of all these duties, was the duty on wool and leather. It seems to have been mainly or entirely an export duty. When the woolen manufacture became established in England, a similar duty was imposed on woolen cloth, so that the king would not lose any of his customs revenue on wool through the export of cloth made from it. The other two branches were a duty on wine, which was levied at so much per ton and was therefore called tonnage, and a duty on all other goods, which was levied at so much per pound of their estimated value and was therefore called poundage. In the forty-seventh year of Edward III's reign, a duty of sixpence in the pound was imposed on all goods exported and imported, except wool, sheepskins with the wool still on them, leather, and wine, which were subject to their own particular duties. In the fourteenth year of Richard II, this duty was raised to one shilling in the pound, but three years later it was reduced again to sixpence. It was raised to eightpence in the second year of Henry IV, and to one shilling in his fourth year. From then until the ninth year of William III, the duty remained at one shilling in the pound. The duties of tonnage and poundage were usually granted to the king by a single act of Parliament and were called the subsidy of tonnage and poundage. Because the subsidy of poundage had remained for so long at one shilling in the pound, or five percent, the word "subsidy" came, in the language of the customs, to mean a general duty of this kind at five percent. This subsidy, now called the old subsidy, is still levied according to the book of rates, an official schedule of the values assigned to goods, established by the statute of the twelfth year of Charles II. The practice of fixing the value of goods subject to this duty by means of such a book of rates is said to date from before the time of James I. The new subsidy, imposed by the statute of the ninth and tenth years of William III, added another five percent on most goods. The one-third subsidy and the two-thirds subsidy together made up a further five percent, of which they were the respective portions. The subsidy of 1747 added a fourth five percent on most goods, and that of 1759 a fifth on certain particular goods. Besides these five subsidies, a great variety of other duties have been imposed from time to time on particular kinds of goods, sometimes to meet the pressing needs of the state, and sometimes to regulate the country's trade according to the principles of the mercantile system.

That system has steadily come more and more into fashion. The old subsidy was levied without distinction on exports and imports alike. The four later subsidies, along with the other duties since imposed from time to time on particular goods, have, with a few exceptions, been laid entirely on imports. Most of the old duties on the export of domestically produced and manufactured goods have either been reduced or abolished altogether, and in most cases abolished. Bounties have even been paid on the export of some of these goods. Drawbacks, which are refunds of duties already paid, have also been granted when foreign goods are re-exported, sometimes for the whole of the import duty and in most cases for part of it. Only half of the import duties imposed by the old subsidy are refunded on re-export, but the whole of those imposed by the later subsidies and other duties are refunded in the same way on most goods. This growing favor toward exports and discouragement of imports has admitted only a few exceptions, which mainly concern the raw materials of certain manufactures. Our merchants and manufacturers want these materials to come as cheaply as possible to themselves and as dearly as possible to their rivals and competitors in other countries. For this reason, foreign materials are sometimes allowed to be imported duty-free, as with Spanish wool, flax, and raw linen yarn. The export of raw materials produced at home, and of those that are the particular products of our colonies, has sometimes been prohibited and sometimes subjected to higher duties. The export of English wool has been prohibited. The export of beaver skins, beaver wool, and gum senega, a gum harvested in Senegal, has been subjected to higher duties, since Great Britain, through its conquest of Canada and Senegal, acquired almost a monopoly of those commodities.

I have tried to show in the fourth book of this Inquiry that the mercantile system has not been very favorable to the income of the great body of the people, that is, to the annual produce of the land and labor of the country. It seems to have been no more favorable to the income of the sovereign, at least insofar as that income depends on customs duties.

As a result of that system, the import of several kinds of goods has been prohibited altogether. In some cases this prohibition has entirely prevented the import of those goods, and in others has greatly reduced it by forcing importers to resort to smuggling. It has entirely prevented the import of foreign woolens, and it has greatly reduced that of foreign silks and velvets. In both cases it has completely wiped out the customs revenue that might have been collected on those imports.

The high duties imposed on many kinds of foreign goods to discourage their consumption in Great Britain have in many cases done nothing but encourage smuggling, and in every case they have reduced customs revenue below what more moderate duties would have produced. Dr. Swift remarked that in the arithmetic of the customs, two and two sometimes make only one instead of four. The saying holds entirely true of such heavy duties, which could never have been imposed had the mercantile system not taught us, in many cases, to use taxation as an instrument not of revenue but of monopoly.

The bounties sometimes paid on the export of domestic produce and manufactures, and the drawbacks paid on the re-export of most foreign goods, have given rise to a great deal of fraud and to a kind of smuggling more destructive to the public revenue than any other. It is well known that, in order to obtain the bounty or drawback, goods are sometimes loaded onto ships and sent out to sea, only to be secretly landed again soon afterward in some other part of the country. The loss of customs revenue caused by bounties and drawbacks, a large share of which are obtained fraudulently, is very great. In the year ending on the 5th of January 1755, the gross revenue of the customs amounted to £5,068,000. The bounties paid out of this revenue, even though there was no bounty on grain that year, came to £167,806. The drawbacks paid on debentures and certificates, the official documents entitling exporters to their refunds, came to £2,156,800. Bounties and drawbacks together amounted to £2,324,600. After these deductions, the customs revenue came to only £2,743,400. Deducting a further £287,900 for the costs of administration, in salaries and other expenses, the net customs revenue for that year comes to £2,455,500. The cost of administration thus amounts to between five and six percent of the gross customs revenue, and to somewhat more than ten percent of what remains of that revenue after bounties and drawbacks have been paid out.

Because heavy duties are imposed on almost all imported goods, our merchant importers smuggle as much as they can and declare as little as they can at the custom-house. Our merchant exporters, by contrast, declare more than they actually export. Sometimes they do so out of vanity, wishing to pass for great dealers in goods that pay no duty; sometimes they do so to claim a bounty or a drawback. As a result of these opposite frauds, our exports appear in the custom-house books to outweigh our imports by a wide margin, to the unspeakable comfort of those politicians who measure national prosperity by what they call the balance of trade.

All imported goods, unless specifically exempted, are liable to some customs duty, and such exemptions are few. If goods are imported that are not listed in the book of rates, the official schedule of customs duties, they are taxed at 4s. 9¾d. for every twenty shillings of value, as sworn by the importer. This is nearly five "subsidies," or five poundage duties of a shilling in the pound. The book of rates is extremely comprehensive and lists a great variety of articles, many of them little used and therefore not well known. For this reason it is often uncertain under which heading a particular kind of goods ought to be classed, and consequently what duty it ought to pay. Mistakes on this point sometimes ruin the custom-house officer, and they frequently cause the importer a great deal of trouble, expense, and vexation. In clarity, precision, and distinctness, therefore, customs duties are much inferior to excise duties.

For most members of a society to contribute to the public revenue in proportion to their respective spending, it does not seem necessary to tax every single article of that spending. The revenue raised by excise duties is supposed to fall as equally on those who pay it as the revenue raised by customs duties, and yet excise duties are imposed on only a few articles of the most general use and consumption. Many people have held that, with proper management, customs duties might likewise be confined to a few articles, without any loss to the public revenue and with great advantage to foreign trade.

The foreign articles of most general use and consumption in Great Britain currently seem to consist chiefly of foreign wines and brandies; of certain products of America and the West Indies, such as sugar, rum, tobacco, and cocoa; and of certain products of the East Indies, such as tea, coffee, china-ware, spices of every kind, and several sorts of piece-goods, or woven cloth sold by the length. These articles perhaps supply, at present, the greater part of the revenue drawn from customs duties. The taxes that now exist on foreign manufactures, apart from those on the few items in this list, have for the most part been imposed not for the sake of revenue but for the sake of monopoly, to give our own merchants an advantage in the home market. If every prohibition were removed, and all foreign manufactures were subjected to moderate taxes set at whatever rate experience showed would yield the greatest revenue on each article, our own workmen would still enjoy a considerable advantage in the home market. Meanwhile many articles that now yield the government no revenue at all, or only a trifling one, might yield a very large one.

High taxes frequently produce a smaller revenue for the government than more moderate taxes would, sometimes by reducing the consumption of the taxed goods and sometimes by encouraging smuggling.

When the loss of revenue results from reduced consumption, there is only one remedy, and that is to lower the tax. When the loss results from the encouragement given to smuggling, it may perhaps be remedied in two ways: by reducing the temptation to smuggle, or by increasing the difficulty of smuggling. The temptation can be reduced only by lowering the tax, and the difficulty can be increased only by establishing the system of administration best suited to preventing it.

Experience appears to show, I believe, that the excise laws obstruct and hamper the smuggler far more effectively than the customs laws do. If the customs adopted a system of administration as close to that of the excise as the nature of the different duties allows, smuggling might be made very much more difficult. Many people have supposed that this change could be made quite easily.

It has been proposed that an importer of goods liable to customs duties should be allowed to choose between two options. He might take the goods to his own private warehouse, or he might lodge them in a warehouse provided either at his own expense or at the public's, but kept under the lock of the custom-house officer and never opened except in his presence. If the merchant took the goods to his own private warehouse, the duties would be paid immediately and never afterwards refunded, and the warehouse would be open at all times to inspection by the custom-house officer, so that he could verify how far the quantity it contained matched the quantity on which duty had been paid. If the merchant took the goods to the public warehouse, no duty would be paid until they were removed for home consumption. If they were removed for export, they would go duty-free, provided proper security was always given that they would in fact be exported. Dealers in those particular goods, whether wholesale or retail, would be subject at all times to inspection by the custom-house officer, and would be obliged to prove, by proper certificates, that duty had been paid on the entire quantity in their shops or warehouses. What are called the excise duties on imported rum are already collected in this way, and the same system might perhaps be extended to all duties on imported goods, provided always that those duties, like the excise duties, were confined to a few kinds of goods of the most general use and consumption. If they extended to nearly every kind of goods, as they do at present, public warehouses large enough could not easily be provided, and goods of a very delicate nature, or goods whose preservation required much care and attention, could not safely be entrusted by the merchant to any warehouse but his own.

Suppose that such a system of administration could prevent smuggling on any considerable scale, even under fairly high duties. Suppose further that each duty were raised or lowered from time to time, in whichever direction seemed most likely to yield the greatest revenue to the state, so that taxation was always used as an instrument of revenue and never as an instrument of monopoly. It then seems not improbable that a revenue at least equal to the present net revenue of the customs could be drawn from duties on the import of only a few kinds of goods of the most general use and consumption, and that customs duties could thus be brought to the same degree of simplicity, certainty, and precision as excise duties. What the revenue now loses through drawbacks, the refunds of duty paid on foreign goods that are re-exported but afterwards smuggled back ashore and consumed at home, would under this system be saved entirely. If to this saving, which would by itself be very considerable, were added the abolition of all bounties on the export of home produce, except where those bounties were really drawbacks of excise duties already paid, there can be little doubt that the net revenue of the customs would, after such a change, be fully equal to what it had ever been.

If such a change of system caused the public revenue no loss, the trade and manufactures of the country would certainly gain a very considerable advantage. Trade in the untaxed commodities, which would be by far the greater number, would be perfectly free and could be carried on to and from every part of the world with every possible advantage. Among those commodities would be all the necessaries of life and all the raw materials of manufacture. To the extent that the free import of the necessaries of life lowered their average money price in the home market, it would lower the money price of labour, without in any way reducing its real reward. The value of money is proportional to the quantity of the necessaries of life it will buy, while the value of the necessaries of life is entirely independent of the quantity of money that can be had for them. The fall in the money price of labour would necessarily bring a proportional fall in the price of all home manufactures, which would thereby gain some advantage in every foreign market. The price of certain manufactures would fall in a still greater proportion through the free import of their raw materials. If raw silk could be imported duty-free from China and Hindustan, the silk manufacturers of England could greatly undersell those of both France and Italy. There would be no need to prohibit the import of foreign silks and velvets. The cheapness of their goods would secure to our own workmen not only the home market but a very large command of the foreign market as well.

Even the trade in the taxed commodities would be carried on with much more advantage than at present. If those goods were released from the public warehouse for export, they would be exempt from all taxes, and the trade in them would be perfectly free. Under this system the carrying trade, the business of shipping goods between foreign countries, would enjoy every possible advantage in all kinds of goods. If the goods were released for home consumption, the importer would not have to pay the tax in advance until he had a chance to sell them, whether to a dealer or to a consumer, and so he could always afford to sell them more cheaply than if he had been obliged to pay it at the moment of import. In this way, under the same taxes, the foreign trade that supplies home consumption, even in the taxed goods, could be carried on with much more advantage than it is now.

The aim of Sir Robert Walpole's famous excise scheme was to establish, for wine and tobacco, a system not very different from the one proposed here. Although the bill then brought before Parliament covered only those two commodities, it was generally believed to be intended as the first step toward a broader scheme of the same kind. Party faction, combined with the interests of smuggling merchants, raised so violent and so unjust an outcry against the bill that the minister thought it wise to drop it, and for fear of provoking a similar outcry, none of his successors has dared to revive the project.

The duties on foreign luxuries imported for home consumption, though they sometimes fall on the poor, fall chiefly on people of middling or more than middling fortune. Such are, for example, the duties on foreign wines, coffee, chocolate, tea, sugar, and the like.

The duties on the cheaper luxuries produced at home for home consumption fall fairly equally on people of every rank, in proportion to their respective spending. The poor pay the duties on malt, hops, beer, and ale on their own consumption; the rich pay them both on their own consumption and on that of their servants.

It must be observed that the total consumption of the lower ranks of people, those below the middling rank, is in every country much greater, not only in quantity but in value, than that of the middling rank and those above it. The total spending of the lower ranks is much greater than that of the upper. In the first place, almost the entire capital of every country is distributed each year among the lower ranks as the wages of productive labour. Second, a large part of the revenue arising from both the rent of land and the profits of capital is distributed each year among the same rank, as the wages and maintenance of household servants and other unproductive labourers. Third, some part of the profits of capital belongs to the same rank, as income from the employment of their small capitals. The profits made each year by small shopkeepers, tradesmen, and retailers of every kind are everywhere very considerable and make up a very considerable portion of the annual produce. Fourth and last, some part even of the rent of land belongs to the same rank: a considerable part to those somewhat below the middling rank, and a small part even to the lowest rank, since common labourers sometimes own an acre or two of land. Although the spending of these lower ranks is very small when taken individually, the whole mass of it, taken collectively, always amounts to by far the largest portion of the society's total spending. What remains of the annual produce of the land and labour of the country for the consumption of the upper ranks is always much less, in value as well as in quantity. Taxes on spending that fall chiefly on the upper ranks, and so on the smaller portion of the annual produce, are therefore likely to be much less productive than taxes that fall indiscriminately on the spending of all ranks, or even than those that fall chiefly on the spending of the lower ranks; that is, less productive than taxes that fall indiscriminately on the whole annual produce, or chiefly on the larger portion of it. Accordingly, of all the different taxes on spending, the excise on the materials and manufacture of home-made fermented and distilled liquors is by far the most productive, and this branch of the excise falls very largely, perhaps principally, on the spending of the common people. In the year ending on the 5th of July 1775, the gross yield of this branch of the excise amounted to £3,341,837 9s. 9d.

It must always be remembered, however, that it is the luxuries of the lower ranks, and never their necessary spending, that ought to be taxed. The final burden of any tax on their necessary spending would fall entirely on the upper ranks, on the smaller portion of the annual produce rather than the larger. Such a tax must in every case either raise the wages of labour or reduce the demand for it. It could not raise wages without throwing the final burden of the tax onto the upper ranks. It could not reduce the demand for labour without reducing the annual produce of the land and labour of the country, which is the fund from which all taxes must ultimately be paid. Whatever level of demand for labour such a tax brought about, it must always raise wages higher than they would otherwise be at that level, and the final cost of that increase in wages must in every case fall on the upper ranks.

In Great Britain, fermented liquors brewed and spirits distilled not for sale but for private use are not liable to any excise duty. The purpose of this exemption is to spare private families the odious visits and inspections of the tax-gatherer, but its effect is that the burden of these duties often falls much more lightly on the rich than on the poor. Distilling for private use is not very common, though it is sometimes done. But in the country, many middling families and almost all rich and great ones brew their own beer. Their strong beer therefore costs them eight shillings a barrel less than it costs the common brewer, who must make his profit on the tax as well as on all the other expenses he advances. Such families must therefore drink their beer at least nine or ten shillings a barrel more cheaply than the common people can drink liquor of the same quality, since the common people everywhere find it more convenient to buy their beer a little at a time from the brewery or the alehouse. In the same way, malt made for the use of a private family is not subject to the visits or inspections of the tax-gatherer, but in this case the family must pay a fixed composition, a set sum in lieu of the tax, of seven shillings and sixpence a head. Seven shillings and sixpence equals the excise on ten bushels of malt, a quantity fully equal to what all the members of any sober family, men, women, and children, are likely to consume on average. But in rich and great families, where country hospitality is widely practised, the malt liquor drunk by members of the family makes up only a small part of the household's consumption. Whether because of this composition or for other reasons, malting for private use is not nearly so common as brewing for private use. It is difficult to imagine any fair reason why those who brew or distil for private use should not be subject to a composition of the same kind.

It has often been said that a larger revenue than is now drawn from all the heavy taxes on malt, beer, and ale could be raised by a much lighter tax on malt alone. The opportunities for defrauding the revenue are much greater in a brewery than in a malt-house, and those who brew for private use are exempt from all duties or compositions, which is not the case with those who malt for private use.

In the London porter breweries, a quarter of malt, a measure of eight bushels, is commonly brewed into more than two and a half barrels of porter, and sometimes into three. The various taxes on malt amount to six shillings a quarter, and those on strong ale and beer to eight shillings a barrel. In the porter brewery, therefore, the combined taxes on malt, beer, and ale come to between twenty-six and thirty shillings on the produce of a quarter of malt. In the country brewery, which brews for ordinary country sale, a quarter of malt is seldom brewed into less than two barrels of strong beer and one barrel of small, or weak, beer, and frequently into two and a half barrels of strong beer. The various taxes on small beer amount to one shilling and fourpence a barrel. In the country brewery, therefore, the combined taxes on malt, beer, and ale seldom come to less than twenty-three shillings and fourpence, and frequently to twenty-six shillings, on the produce of a quarter of malt. Taking the whole kingdom on average, then, the total duties on malt, beer, and ale cannot be estimated at less than twenty-four or twenty-five shillings on the produce of a quarter of malt. But it is said that if all the various duties on beer and ale were removed and the malt tax were tripled, raised from six to eighteen shillings a quarter, this single tax would raise a greater revenue than is now drawn from all those heavier taxes together.

In 1772 the old malt tax produced £722,023 11s. 11d., and the additional malt tax £356,776 7s. 9¾d. In 1773 the old tax produced £561,627 3s. 7½d., and the additional tax £278,650 15s. 3¾d. In 1774 the old tax produced £624,614 17s. 5¾d., and the additional tax £310,745 2s. 8½d. In 1775 the old tax produced £657,357 0s. 8¼d., and the additional tax £323,785 12s. 6¼d. These sums total £3,835,580 12s. 0¾d., which, divided by four, gives an average for those four years of £958,895 3s. 0d.

In 1772 the country excise produced £1,243,120 5s. 3d., and the London brewery £408,260 7s. 2¾d. In 1773 the country excise produced £1,245,808 3s. 3d., and the London brewery £405,406 17s. 10½d. In 1774 the country excise produced £1,246,373 14s. 5½d., and the London brewery £320,601 18s. 0¼d. In 1775 the country excise produced £1,214,583 6s. 1¼d., and the London brewery £463,670 7s. 0¼d. These sums total £6,547,832 19s. 2¼d., which, divided by four, gives an average for those four years of £1,636,958 4s. 9½d. Adding to this the average malt tax of £958,895 3s. 0¼d., the whole amount of these various taxes comes to £2,595,835 7s. 10d. But by tripling the malt tax, raising it from six to eighteen shillings on the quarter of malt, that single tax would produce £2,876,685 9s. 0d., a sum exceeding the foregoing by £280,832 1s. 3d.

It is true that the old malt tax also includes a tax of four shillings on the hogshead of cider and another of ten shillings on the barrel of mum, a strong, heavy beer brewed chiefly from wheat malt. In 1774 the tax on cider produced only £3,083 6s. 8d. It probably fell somewhat short of its usual amount, since all the various taxes on cider produced less than usual that year. The tax on mum, though much heavier, is even less productive, because so much less of that liquor is drunk. But to balance whatever the ordinary yield of those two taxes may be, the so-called country excise includes, first, the old excise of six shillings and eightpence on the hogshead of cider; second, a similar tax of six shillings and eightpence on the hogshead of verjuice, the sour juice of unripe grapes or crab-apples; third, another of eight shillings and ninepence on the hogshead of vinegar; and finally, a fourth tax of elevenpence on the gallon of mead or metheglin, a spiced variety of mead. The yield of these various taxes will probably far more than offset that of the duties imposed on cider and mum under what is called the annual malt tax.

Malt is consumed not only in brewing beer and ale but also in making low wines, the weak first product of distillation, and spirits. If the malt tax were raised to eighteen shillings a quarter, it might be necessary to make some reduction in the various excises imposed on those kinds of low wines and spirits in which malt forms any part of the ingredients. In what are called malt spirits, malt commonly makes up only a third of the ingredients, the other two-thirds being either raw barley, or one-third barley and one-third wheat. In the distilling of malt spirits, both the opportunity and the temptation to smuggle are much greater than in a brewery or a malt-house: the opportunity because the product is smaller in bulk and greater in value, and the temptation because the duties are higher, amounting to 3s. 10⅔d. on the gallon of spirits. The duties levied directly on proof spirits come to only 2s. 6d. a gallon, but when these are added to the duties on the low wines from which the spirits are distilled, the total comes to 3s. 10⅔d. To prevent fraud, both low wines and proof spirits are now rated according to what they measure in the wash, the fermented liquid from which they are distilled.

By raising the duties on malt and reducing those on distilling, both the opportunities and the temptation to smuggle would be lessened, which might bring a still further increase in revenue.

For some time now it has been the policy of Great Britain to discourage the drinking of spirits, on account of their supposed tendency to ruin the health and corrupt the morals of the common people. In keeping with this policy, the reduction of the taxes on distilling ought not to be so great as to lower the price of spirits in any way. Spirits could remain as expensive as ever, while the wholesome and invigorating drinks of beer and ale could be made considerably cheaper. The people might thus be partly relieved of one of the burdens they currently complain of most, while the revenue might at the same time be considerably increased.

The objections that Dr. Davenant raised against this change in the present system of excise duties appear to be groundless. His objections are that the tax, instead of being divided fairly evenly among the profits of the maltster, the brewer, and the retailer, as it is now, would fall entirely on the maltster insofar as it touched profit at all; that the maltster could not recover the tax through a higher price for his malt as easily as the brewer and the retailer now recover it through a higher price for their drink; and that so heavy a tax on malt might lower the rent and profit of land used for growing barley.

No tax can lower the rate of profit in any particular trade for any considerable length of time, because that rate must always stay level with the profits of other trades in the same neighbourhood. The present duties on malt, beer, and ale do not reduce the profits of those who deal in these goods. Each of them recovers the tax, together with an additional profit on it, through the higher price of what he sells. A tax may, it is true, make the goods it falls on so expensive that people buy less of them. But malt is consumed in the form of malt liquors, and a tax of eighteen shillings on a quarter of malt (a measure of eight bushels) could hardly make those liquors dearer than the various taxes now do, which together amount to twenty-four or twenty-five shillings. The liquors would more probably become cheaper, and their consumption would be more likely to rise than to fall.

It is hard to see why the maltster should find it more difficult to recover eighteen shillings through a higher price for his malt than the brewer now finds it to recover twenty-four or twenty-five, and sometimes thirty, shillings through the price of his beer. The maltster, admittedly, would have to pay in advance a tax of eighteen shillings on every quarter of malt instead of the present six. But the brewer must now advance a tax of twenty-four or twenty-five, and sometimes thirty, shillings on every quarter of malt he brews. Advancing a lighter tax could be no more inconvenient for the maltster than advancing a heavier one now is for the brewer. Nor does the maltster always keep a stock of malt in his granaries that takes longer to sell than the stock of beer and ale the brewer often keeps in his cellars, so the maltster may often see the return on his money as quickly as the brewer does. And whatever inconvenience the maltster might suffer from having to advance a heavier tax could easily be remedied by allowing him a few months' more credit than the brewer is now commonly given.

Nothing could lower the rent and profit of barley land unless it lowered the demand for barley. A change of system that cut the duties on a quarter of malt brewed into beer and ale from twenty-four or twenty-five shillings to eighteen would be more likely to raise that demand than to reduce it. Besides, the rent and profit of barley land must always remain roughly equal to those of other land of equal fertility and equally good cultivation. If they fell below that level, some barley land would soon be turned to other uses; if they rose above it, more land would soon be turned over to barley. When the ordinary price of some particular product of the land stands at what may be called a monopoly price, a tax on it necessarily reduces the rent and profit of the land that grows it. Consider a tax on the produce of those rare and prized vineyards whose wine falls so far short of the effective demand that its price always stands above its natural proportion to the price of produce from other land of equal fertility and equally good cultivation. Such a tax would necessarily reduce the rent and profit of those vineyards. The price of the wine is already the highest that can be obtained for the quantity usually brought to market, so it could not be raised further without reducing that quantity. And the quantity could not be reduced without a still greater loss, because the land could not be turned to any other crop of equal value. The whole weight of the tax would therefore fall on rent and profit, and more precisely on the rent of the vineyard. Whenever a new tax on sugar has been proposed, our sugar planters have often complained that its whole weight fell not on the consumer but on the producer, since they had never been able to raise the price of their sugar after such a tax above what it had been before. It seems that their price had been a monopoly price before the tax. In that case, the arguments they offered to show that sugar was an improper object of taxation perhaps proved that it was a proper one, because the gains of monopolists, wherever they can be reached, are certainly the most proper of all objects of taxation. But the ordinary price of barley has never been a monopoly price, and the rent and profit of barley land have never risen above their natural proportion to those of other land of equal fertility and equally good cultivation. The various taxes imposed on malt, beer, and ale have never lowered the price of barley, and they have never reduced the rent and profit of barley land. The price of malt to the brewer has consistently risen in proportion to the taxes laid on it. Those taxes, together with the various duties on beer and ale, have consistently either raised the price of these drinks to the consumer or lowered their quality, which amounts to the same thing. The final burden of those taxes has always fallen on the consumer and not on the producer.

The only people likely to lose by the change proposed here are those who brew for their own private use. But this wealthier class now enjoys an exemption from very heavy taxes that the poor labourer and craftsman must pay. That exemption is surely most unjust and unequal, and it ought to be abolished even if the proposed change were never made. It has probably been the interest of this upper class, however, that has so far blocked a change of system that could hardly fail both to increase the revenue and to relieve the people.

Besides the customs and excise duties described above, there are several others that affect the price of goods more unequally and more indirectly. Among these are the duties the French call *péages*, which in old Saxon times were called duties of passage. They seem to have been established originally for the same purpose as the tolls on our turnpike roads, or the tolls on our canals and navigable rivers: to pay for the upkeep of the road or the waterway. When applied to such purposes, these duties are most properly charged according to the bulk or weight of the goods. They were originally local and provincial duties, meant for local and provincial purposes, so their administration was in most cases entrusted to the particular town, parish, or lordship in which they were collected. Such communities were supposed to be answerable in one way or another for how the money was spent. In many countries the sovereign, who answers to no one, has taken the administration of these duties into his own hands. In most cases he has raised the duty considerably, and in many he has entirely neglected the purpose it was meant to serve. Should the turnpike tolls of Great Britain ever become a source of government revenue, the example of many other nations shows what the likely consequence would be. Such tolls are no doubt paid in the end by the consumer. But the consumer is not taxed in proportion to his spending when he pays according to the bulk or weight of what he consumes rather than its value. When such duties are charged not by bulk or weight but by the supposed value of the goods, they become in effect a kind of inland customs or excise. They then greatly obstruct the most important of all branches of commerce, which is the internal commerce of the country.

In some small states, duties similar to these passage duties are charged on goods carried across their territory, by land or by water, from one foreign country to another. In some countries these are called transit duties. Several of the small Italian states along the Po and the rivers that flow into it draw some revenue from duties of this kind. These duties are paid entirely by foreigners. They are perhaps the only duties one state can impose on the subjects of another without obstructing its own industry or commerce in any respect. The most important transit duty in the world is the one the king of Denmark levies on every merchant ship that passes through the Sound, the narrow strait between Denmark and Sweden that forms the main passage into the Baltic.

Taxes on luxuries, such as most customs and excise duties, fall without distinction on every kind of revenue. They are paid in the end, without any reimbursement, by whoever consumes the commodities on which they are laid. Yet they do not always fall equally or proportionally on each individual's revenue. Each man's inclinations govern how much he consumes, so each contributes according to his inclinations rather than in proportion to his revenue: the extravagant contribute more than their proper share, and the thrifty contribute less. While a man of great fortune is still a minor, he usually contributes very little through his consumption to the support of the state whose protection secures his large revenue. Those who live abroad contribute nothing through their consumption to the support of the government of the country in which the source of their revenue lies. Suppose that country has no land tax and no significant duty on the transfer of either movable or immovable property, as is the case in Ireland. Then such absentees may draw a great revenue under the protection of a government to whose support they do not contribute a single shilling. This inequality is likely to be greatest in a country whose government is in some respects subordinate to, and dependent on, the government of another. The people who own the most extensive property in the dependent country will then generally choose to live in the governing one. Ireland is in precisely this situation, and it is no surprise that the proposal of a tax on absentees should be so very popular there. It might perhaps be somewhat difficult to determine what kind or degree of absence should make a man liable to be taxed as an absentee, or exactly when the tax should begin or end. Setting aside this very peculiar situation, however, any inequality in individual contributions arising from such taxes is more than compensated by the very circumstance that causes it. Each man's contribution is entirely voluntary, since it lies wholly in his power to consume the taxed commodity or not. Where such taxes are properly assessed and laid on proper commodities, they are therefore paid with less grumbling than any other kind. When the merchant or manufacturer advances them, the consumer who finally pays them soon comes to confuse them with the price of the goods and almost forgets that he pays any tax at all.

Such taxes are, or can be made, perfectly certain. They can be assessed so as to leave no doubt about what ought to be paid or when it ought to be paid, either as to the amount or as to the time of payment. Customs duties in Great Britain, and other duties of the same kind in other countries, are sometimes uncertain. That uncertainty cannot arise from the nature of the duties themselves. It arises from the inaccurate or unskilful wording of the laws that impose them.

Taxes on luxuries generally are paid piecemeal, and they always can be. They are paid in proportion as the contributors have occasion to buy the goods on which they are laid. In the time and manner of payment, they are, or can be, the most convenient of all taxes. On the whole, therefore, such taxes perhaps conform as well as any others to the first three of the four general maxims of taxation set out earlier, which concern equality, certainty, and convenience of payment. They violate the fourth, economy in collection, in every respect.

In proportion to what they bring into the public treasury, such taxes always take out of the people's pockets, or keep out of them, more than almost any other kind of tax. They seem to do this in all four of the ways in which it is possible to do so.

First, levying such taxes requires a great number of customs and excise officers, even when the taxes are imposed in the most judicious manner. The salaries and perquisites of these officers are a real tax on the people, and they bring nothing into the treasury of the state. It must be acknowledged, however, that this expense is more moderate in Great Britain than in most other countries. In the year ending 5 July 1775, the gross yield of the various duties managed by the commissioners of excise in England came to £5,507,308, 18 shillings, and 8¼ pence. It was collected at a cost of little more than five and a half per cent. From this gross yield one must deduct what was paid out in bounties and drawbacks, which are subsidies and refunds of duty on the export of excisable goods. That deduction brings the net yield below five million. The net yield for that year, after all expenses and allowances were deducted, came to £4,975,652, 19 shillings, and 6 pence. The levying of the salt duty, which is an excise duty but under separate management, is much more expensive. The net revenue of the customs does not reach two and a half million, and it is collected at a cost of more than ten per cent in officers' salaries and other incidental charges. But customs officers also collect perquisites, meaning fees and allowances beyond their pay. These are everywhere much larger than their salaries, and at some ports they are two or three times as large. If salaries and incidental charges alone amount to more than ten per cent of the net revenue of the customs, the whole cost of collecting that revenue, salaries and perquisites together, may come to more than twenty or thirty per cent. Excise officers receive few or no perquisites. The excise is also a more recently established branch of the revenue, so its administration is in general less corrupt than that of the customs, where time has introduced and sanctioned many abuses. It is supposed that a saving of more than £50,000 a year could be made in the cost of the excise by charging on malt alone the whole revenue now raised by the various duties on malt and malt liquors. A much greater saving could probably be made in the annual cost of the customs by confining customs duties to a few kinds of goods and collecting them under the excise laws.

Second, such taxes necessarily obstruct or discourage certain branches of industry. They always raise the price of the commodity taxed, and to that extent they discourage its consumption and therefore its production. If it is a commodity grown or manufactured at home, less labour comes to be employed in raising and producing it. If the tax raises the price of a foreign commodity, goods of the same kind made at home may indeed gain some advantage in the home market, and more domestic industry may be turned toward producing them. But although this rise in the price of a foreign commodity may encourage domestic industry in one particular branch, it necessarily discourages that industry in almost every other. The more the Birmingham manufacturer pays for his foreign wine, the less he necessarily gets for the part of his hardware with which he buys it, or, what amounts to the same thing, with whose price he buys it. That part of his hardware therefore becomes less valuable to him, and he has less incentive to work at producing it. The more the consumers of one country pay for the surplus produce of another, the less they necessarily get for the part of their own surplus produce with which they buy it, or with whose price they buy it. That part of their own surplus produce becomes less valuable to them, and they have less incentive to increase it. All taxes on consumable commodities therefore tend to reduce the quantity of productive labour below what it would otherwise be. If the commodities taxed are domestic, the reduction falls on the labour that produces them. If they are foreign, it falls on the labour that produces the goods used to buy them. Such taxes also always alter, to a greater or lesser degree, the natural direction of the nation's industry. They divert it into a channel that is always different from the one it would have followed of its own accord, and generally less advantageous.

Third, the hope of evading such taxes by smuggling frequently leads to forfeitures and other penalties that utterly ruin the smuggler. The smuggler is no doubt highly blameworthy for breaking the laws of his country. Yet he is often incapable of breaking the laws of natural justice, and he would have been an excellent citizen in every respect if the laws of his country had not made a crime of something nature never meant to be one. Under corrupt governments, where there is at least a general suspicion of much needless expense and serious misuse of public revenue, the laws that protect that revenue command little respect. Few people have scruples about smuggling when they can find an easy and safe opportunity to do it without committing perjury. To profess any scruple about buying smuggled goods would, in most countries, be regarded as a piece of pedantic hypocrisy, even though such buying plainly encourages the breaking of the revenue laws and the perjury that almost always goes with it. Far from earning anyone's respect, such a profession would only expose the person who made it to the suspicion of being a greater rogue than most of his neighbours. The public's tolerance often encourages the smuggler to carry on a trade he has thus been taught to regard as more or less innocent. When the full severity of the revenue laws is about to fall on him, he is often inclined to defend by force what he has grown used to considering his rightful property. At first he was perhaps more imprudent than criminal, but in the end he too often becomes one of the most hardened and determined violators of the laws of society. When the smuggler is ruined, his capital had until then been employed in maintaining productive labour. It is now absorbed into the revenue of the state or into the income of the revenue officer, and there it is used to maintain unproductive labour. The result is a reduction in the general capital of society and in the useful industry that capital might otherwise have supported.

Fourth, such taxes subject at least the dealers in the taxed commodities to frequent visits and hateful inspections by the tax collectors. This sometimes exposes them to a degree of oppression, and it always exposes them to a great deal of trouble and harassment. Harassment, as has already been said, is not strictly an expense. It is nonetheless equivalent to whatever expense a man would willingly pay to be free of it. The excise laws are more effective than the customs laws for the purpose they were designed to serve, but in this respect they are more vexatious. When a merchant has imported goods subject to certain customs duties, paid those duties, and stored the goods in his warehouse, he is in most cases free of any further trouble or harassment from the customs officer. It is otherwise with goods subject to excise duties. The dealers in such goods have no relief from the constant visits and inspections of the excise officers. For this reason excise duties are more unpopular than customs duties, and the officers who collect them are more unpopular as well. It is claimed that these officers generally do their duty perhaps fully as well as customs officers do. Yet because that duty obliges them to be frequently very troublesome to some of their neighbours, they are said to acquire a certain hardness of character that customs officers often lack. This observation, however, may very probably be nothing more than an insinuation spread by dishonest dealers whose smuggling the officers' diligence either prevents or exposes.

The inconveniences that are perhaps to some degree inseparable from taxes on consumable commodities fall as lightly on the people of Great Britain as on the people of any other country whose government is nearly as expensive. Our state is not perfect and could be improved, but it is as good as that of most of our neighbours, or better.

In some countries, people held the notion that duties on consumable goods were taxes on the profits of merchants. As a result, those duties have been charged again on every successive sale of the goods. If the profits of the importing merchant or the manufacturing merchant were taxed, equality seemed to require that the profits of all the intermediate buyers standing between them and the consumer should be taxed as well. The famous *alcavala* of Spain, a general tax on sales, seems to have been established on this principle. It was at first a tax of ten per cent, later fourteen per cent, and it is now only six per cent on the sale of every kind of property, whether movable or immovable. It is charged again every time the property is sold. Collecting this tax requires a multitude of revenue officers, enough to watch the movement of goods not only from one province to another but from one shop to another. It subjects not merely the dealers in certain kinds of goods but the dealers in all kinds, every farmer, manufacturer, merchant, and shopkeeper, to the constant visits and inspections of the tax collectors. Throughout most of a country where a tax of this kind is established, nothing can be produced for sale at a distance. The output of every district must be limited to what its own neighbourhood consumes. It is to the alcavala, accordingly, that the Spanish economist Ustaritz attributes the ruin of Spain's manufactures. He might also have attributed to it the decline of Spanish agriculture, since the tax is imposed not only on manufactures but on the raw produce of the land.

In the kingdom of Naples there is a similar tax of three per cent on the value of all contracts, and consequently on the value of all contracts of sale. It is lighter than the Spanish tax, and most towns and parishes are allowed to pay a fixed lump sum in its place. They raise this sum in whatever way they please, generally in a way that does not interrupt local trade. The Neapolitan tax is therefore nowhere near as ruinous as the Spanish one.

The uniform system of taxation prevails, with a few exceptions of little consequence, in all the different parts of the United Kingdom of Great Britain. It leaves the internal commerce of the country, both the inland trade and the coasting trade, almost entirely free. The inland trade is almost perfectly free. Most goods may be carried from one end of the kingdom to the other without any permit or pass, and without being subject to questioning, visits, or inspection by the revenue officers. There are a few exceptions, but they are of a kind that can cause no interruption to any important branch of the country's inland commerce. Goods shipped along the coast do require certificates, known as coast-cockets, which document their passage from one British port to another. With the exception of coal, however, nearly all of them are duty-free. This freedom of internal commerce, which is the result of a uniform system of taxation, is perhaps one of the principal causes of Great Britain's prosperity, since every large country is necessarily the best and most extensive market for most of what its own industry produces. If the same freedom, arising from the same uniformity, could be extended to Ireland and the colonial plantations, both the greatness of the state and the prosperity of every part of the empire would probably be even greater than they are now.

In France, the revenue laws differ from province to province, and this requires a multitude of revenue officers to guard not only the frontiers of the kingdom but those of nearly every individual province, either to block the entry of certain goods or to make them pay certain duties. The internal commerce of the country is interrupted to no small degree as a result. Some provinces are permitted to compound for the *gabelle*, or salt tax, paying a fixed sum in place of it; others are exempt from it entirely. Some provinces are exempt from the exclusive sale of tobacco, a monopoly that the farmers-general, the syndicate of private financiers who collect the king's revenues, hold throughout most of the kingdom. The *aides*, which correspond to the excise in England, vary greatly from province to province. Some provinces are exempt from them and pay a composition, or equivalent sum, instead. In those where the *aides* are levied and collected by farm, there are many local duties that apply only within a particular town or district. The *traites*, which correspond to our customs, divide the kingdom into three great parts. First come the provinces subject to the tariff of 1664, which are called the provinces of the five great farms; these include Picardy, Normandy, and most of the interior provinces of the kingdom. Second come the provinces subject to the tariff of 1667, which are called the provinces reckoned foreign; these include most of the frontier provinces. Third come the provinces said to be treated as foreign. Because these are allowed to trade freely with foreign countries, they are subjected, in their trade with the rest of France, to the same duties as any foreign country. They are Alsace, the three bishoprics of Metz, Toul, and Verdun, and the three cities of Dunkirk, Bayonne, and Marseilles. The provinces of the five great farms take their name from an ancient division of the customs duties into five great branches, each of which was originally leased out as a separate farm, though they have since all been united into one. Both in these provinces and in those reckoned foreign, there are many local duties that apply only within a particular town or district. There are some even in the provinces treated as foreign, particularly in the city of Marseilles. There is no need to point out how greatly the restraints on the country's internal commerce, and the number of revenue officers, must be multiplied in order to guard the borders of all these provinces and districts, each subject to its own system of taxation.

Beyond the general restraints that arise from this complicated system of revenue laws, the trade in wine, which is perhaps the most important product of France after grain, is subject in most provinces to particular restraints of its own. These arise from the favor that has been shown to the vineyards of certain provinces and districts over those of others. The provinces most famous for their wines will, I believe, be found to be those in which the wine trade is subject to the fewest restraints of this kind. The extensive market these provinces enjoy encourages good management, both in the cultivation of their vineyards and in the subsequent preparation of their wines.

Such varied and complicated revenue laws are not peculiar to France. The little duchy of Milan is divided into six provinces, each with a different system of taxation for several kinds of consumable goods. The still smaller territories of the Duke of Parma are divided into three or four, each of which likewise has a system of its own. Under such absurd management, nothing but the great fertility of the soil and the favorable climate could keep these countries from quickly sinking back into the lowest state of poverty and barbarism.

Taxes on consumable goods may be collected in one of two ways. They may be levied by an administration whose officers are appointed by the government and answer directly to it, in which case the revenue will vary from year to year with the fluctuations in what the tax produces. Or they may be farmed out: leased to a private contractor for a fixed rent, with the farmer allowed to appoint his own officers, who must collect the tax in the manner the law prescribes but who work under his direct supervision and answer directly to him. Farming can never be the best or most economical way of collecting a tax. Over and above what he needs to pay the agreed rent, the officers' salaries, and the entire cost of administration, the farmer must always draw a certain profit from the proceeds of the tax. That profit must be proportioned at least to the money he advances, the risk he runs, the trouble he takes, and the knowledge and skill required to manage so very complicated an enterprise. By setting up an administration of the same kind under its own direct supervision, the government could at least save this profit, which is almost always exorbitant. To farm any considerable branch of the public revenue requires either great capital or great credit, and this alone confines the competition for such an undertaking to a very small number of people. Of the few who have the capital or credit, still fewer have the necessary knowledge or experience, which narrows the competition further. The very few who are in a position to compete find it more in their interest to combine, to become partners rather than rivals, and, when the farm is put up for auction, to bid no rent but one far below its real value. In countries where the public revenues are farmed, the farmers are generally the richest people in the land. Their wealth alone would provoke public resentment, and the vanity that almost always accompanies such newly made fortunes, together with the foolish ostentation with which they usually display them, provokes that resentment still more.

The farmers of the public revenue never find the laws that punish attempts to evade a tax too severe. They have no compassion for the taxpayers, who are not their subjects, and whose universal bankruptcy, should it occur the day after the farm expired, would scarcely affect their interests. In the state's greatest emergencies, when the sovereign is necessarily most anxious that his revenue be paid in full, the farmers seldom fail to complain that unless the laws are made more rigorous than they currently are, they will be unable to pay even the usual rent. In such moments of public distress, their demands cannot be refused. The revenue laws therefore grow gradually more and more severe. The most bloodthirsty are always found in countries where most of the public revenue is farmed, and the mildest in countries where it is collected under the direct supervision of the sovereign. Even a bad sovereign feels more compassion for his people than can ever be expected of the farmers of his revenue. He knows that the lasting greatness of his family depends on the prosperity of his people, and he will never knowingly ruin that prosperity for the sake of some passing interest of his own. It is otherwise with the farmers of his revenue, whose greatness may often be the product of the ruin of his people rather than of their prosperity.

Sometimes a tax is not only farmed for a fixed rent, but the farmer is also granted a monopoly of the commodity being taxed. In France, the duties on tobacco and salt are collected in this way. In such cases, the farmer extracts not one but two exorbitant profits from the people: the profit of the farmer, and the still more exorbitant profit of the monopolist. Since tobacco is a luxury, every man is free to buy it or not as he chooses. But since salt is a necessity, every man is obliged to buy a certain quantity of it from the farmer, on the presumption that if he did not buy that quantity from the farmer, he would buy it from some smuggler. The taxes on both commodities are exorbitant. The temptation to smuggle is consequently irresistible to many people, while the rigor of the law and the vigilance of the farmer's officers make yielding to that temptation almost certainly ruinous. Every year, the smuggling of salt and tobacco sends several hundred people to the galleys, where convicts were condemned to serve as oarsmen, and sends a very considerable number to the gallows. Taxes collected in this manner yield the government a very considerable revenue. In 1767, the tobacco farm was leased for 22,541,278 livres a year, and the salt farm for 36,492,404 livres. In both cases the lease was to begin in 1768 and to run for six years. Those who count the blood of the people as nothing compared with the revenue of the prince may perhaps approve of this method of levying taxes. Similar taxes and monopolies on salt and tobacco have been established in many other countries, particularly in the Austrian and Prussian dominions and in most of the states of Italy.

In France, most of the crown's actual revenue comes from eight sources: the *taille*, the capitation, the two *vingtièmes*, the *gabelles*, the *aides*, the *traites*, the *domaine*, and the tobacco farm. The last five are farmed in most of the provinces. The first three are everywhere collected by an administration under the direct supervision and direction of the government, and it is universally acknowledged that, in proportion to what they take out of the people's pockets, they bring more into the prince's treasury than the other five, whose administration is far more wasteful and expensive.

In their present state, the finances of France seem to admit of three very obvious reforms. First, the *taille* and the capitation could be abolished and the number of *vingtièmes* increased enough to produce an additional revenue equal to what those two taxes now yield. In this way the crown's revenue would be preserved, the cost of collection greatly reduced, the harassment that the *taille* and capitation inflict on the lower ranks of people entirely prevented, and the upper ranks not burdened any more heavily than most of them are now. The *vingtième*, as I have already observed, is a tax very much like what is called the land tax in England. It is acknowledged that the burden of the *taille* falls ultimately on the owners of land. And since most of the capitation is assessed on those who pay the *taille*, at a fixed rate per pound of that other tax, most of the capitation must ultimately fall on the same class of people. Even if the number of *vingtièmes* were increased enough to replace both taxes, therefore, the upper ranks as a whole might be no more burdened than they are at present. Many individuals, no doubt, would be, because of the great inequalities with which the *taille* is commonly assessed on the estates and tenants of different people. The interests and opposition of these favored subjects are the obstacles most likely to prevent this or any similar reform. Second, by making the *gabelle*, the *aides*, the *traites*, the tobacco taxes, and all the various customs and excise duties uniform throughout every part of the kingdom, these taxes could be collected at far less expense, and the internal commerce of the kingdom could be made as free as that of England. Third and last, by placing all these taxes under an administration directly supervised and directed by the government, the exorbitant profits of the farmers-general could be added to the revenue of the state. The opposition arising from the private interests of individuals is likely to be as effective in blocking the last two reforms as the first.

The French system of taxation seems inferior to the British in every respect. In Great Britain, ten million pounds sterling are levied each year on fewer than eight million people, and it cannot be said that any particular class is oppressed.
