From the collections of the Abbé Expilly and the observations of the author of the *Essay on the Legislation and Commerce of Grain*, it appears probable that France, including the provinces of Lorraine and Bar, contains about twenty-three or twenty-four million people, perhaps three times the population of Great Britain. The soil and climate of France are better than those of Great Britain. The country has been improved and cultivated for much longer, and is therefore better supplied with all those things that take a long time to build up and accumulate, such as great towns and convenient, well-built houses in both town and country. With these advantages, one might expect that France could raise a revenue of thirty million pounds for the support of the state with as little inconvenience as Great Britain raises ten million. In 1765 and 1766, according to the best accounts I could obtain, which I acknowledge to be very imperfect, the entire revenue paid into the French treasury usually ran between 308 and 325 million livres. That is, it did not amount to fifteen million pounds sterling, not half of what might have been expected had the French contributed in the same proportion to their numbers as the British. Yet it is generally acknowledged that the people of France are far more oppressed by taxes than the people of Great Britain. And France is certainly the great empire in Europe that, after Great Britain, enjoys the mildest and most lenient government.

In Holland, the heavy taxes on the necessities of life are said to have ruined the country's principal manufactures, and they are likely to discourage, by degrees, even its fisheries and its shipbuilding trade. In Great Britain, the taxes on necessities are slight, and no manufacture has yet been ruined by them. The British taxes that bear hardest on manufactures are certain duties on the import of raw materials, particularly raw silk. The combined revenue of the States-General and of the various cities of Holland, however, is said to exceed five million two hundred and fifty thousand pounds sterling. Since the inhabitants of the United Provinces can hardly be supposed to number more than a third of those of Great Britain, they must be far more heavily taxed in proportion to their numbers.

Once all the proper objects of taxation have been exhausted, if the needs of the state still demand new taxes, those taxes must be imposed on improper objects. The taxes on the necessities of life, therefore, may be no reflection on the wisdom of that republic, which, in order to win and keep its independence, has been drawn, despite its great frugality, into such expensive wars that it has been obliged to contract great debts. The singular provinces of Holland and Zeeland, moreover, require considerable expense merely to preserve their existence and keep from being swallowed by the sea, and this must have added considerably to the load of taxes in those two provinces. The republican form of government appears to be the principal support of Holland's present greatness. The owners of great capitals, the great merchant families, generally have either some direct share in the administration of that government or some indirect influence over it. For the sake of the respect and authority they derive from this position, they are willing to live in a country where their capital, if they employ it themselves, will bring them less profit, and if they lend it to others, less interest; and where the very moderate income they can draw from it will buy fewer of the necessities and comforts of life than anywhere else in Europe. The residence of such wealthy people necessarily keeps a certain degree of industry alive in the country, despite all its disadvantages. Any public calamity that destroyed the republican form of government, that threw the entire administration into the hands of nobles and soldiers, and that wiped out altogether the importance of these wealthy merchants would soon make it disagreeable for them to live in a country where they could no longer expect much respect. They would move both their residence and their capital to some other country, and the industry and commerce of Holland would soon follow the capital that sustained them.

### CHAPTER III: OF PUBLIC DEBTS

In the rude state of society that precedes the spread of commerce and the improvement of manufactures, when the expensive luxuries that only commerce and manufacturing can introduce are entirely unknown, a person with a large revenue has no way to spend or enjoy it except by maintaining nearly as many people as it can support. I tried to show this in the third book of this Inquiry. A large revenue may at any time be said to consist in command over a large quantity of the necessaries of life. In that rude condition, it is usually paid in those necessaries themselves: in the materials of plain food and coarse clothing, in grain and cattle, in wool and raw hides. When neither commerce nor manufacturing offers anything for which the owner can exchange the bulk of what exceeds his own consumption, he can do nothing with the surplus except feed and clothe as many people as it will feed and clothe. Under such conditions, the principal expenses of the rich and the great are a hospitality without luxury and a generosity without ostentation. But these, as I also tried to show in that same book, are not expenses by which people readily ruin themselves. There is perhaps no selfish pleasure so frivolous that its pursuit has not sometimes ruined even sensible men, and a passion for cockfighting has ruined many. Yet I believe there are not many cases of people ruined by hospitality or generosity of this plain kind, though the hospitality of luxury and the generosity of display have ruined a great many. Among our feudal ancestors, the long periods during which estates remained in the same family are proof enough of a general disposition to live within one's income. The rustic hospitality that the great landholders constantly practiced may not seem to us, in the present age, consistent with the orderliness we tend to regard as inseparable from good management. Yet we must at least grant that they were frugal enough not, as a rule, to spend their entire income. They generally had the opportunity to sell part of their wool and raw hides for money. Some of that money they perhaps spent on the few objects of vanity and luxury that the circumstances of the age could provide, but some of it they seem usually to have hoarded. Indeed, there was little else they could do with whatever money they saved. To engage in trade was disgraceful for a gentleman, and to lend money at interest, which was then considered usury and was prohibited by law, would have been more disgraceful still. In those times of violence and disorder, moreover, it was convenient to keep a store of money at hand, so that if they were driven from their homes they would have something of known value to carry with them to a place of safety. The same violence that made hoarding convenient made it equally convenient to hide the hoard. The frequency of treasure-trove, meaning treasure found with no known owner, is sufficient proof of how common it was in those times both to hoard money and to conceal it. Treasure-trove was then regarded as an important branch of the sovereign's revenue. Today, all the treasure-trove in the kingdom would scarcely make an important part of the income of a private gentleman with a good estate.

The same disposition to save and to hoard prevailed in the sovereign as much as in his subjects. Among nations where commerce and manufacturing are little known, the sovereign, as has already been observed in the fourth book, is placed in a situation that naturally inclines him to the thrift that accumulation requires. In that situation, even a sovereign's spending cannot be directed by the vanity that delights in the gaudy finery of a court, because the ignorance of the age supplies few of the trinkets of which such finery consists. Standing armies are not yet necessary, so the sovereign's expenditure, like that of any other great lord, can be devoted to scarcely anything but generosity to his tenants and hospitality to his retainers. Generosity and hospitality very seldom lead to extravagance, though vanity almost always does. Accordingly, as has already been observed, all the ancient sovereigns of Europe kept treasuries. Every Tartar chief of the present day is said to have one.

In a commercial country abounding in every kind of expensive luxury, the sovereign, like almost all the great proprietors in his dominions, naturally spends a large part of his revenue on those luxuries. His own country and its neighbors supply him abundantly with all the costly trinkets that make up the splendid but insignificant pageantry of a court. For the sake of a lesser pageantry of the same kind, his nobles dismiss their retainers, make their tenants independent, and gradually become as insignificant as most of the wealthy townsmen in his realm. The same frivolous passions that govern their conduct govern his. How can we suppose that he alone, of all the rich men in his dominions, should be indifferent to pleasures of this kind? Even if he does not spend so much of his revenue on them as to weaken seriously the defensive power of the state, which he is quite likely to do, he can hardly be expected not to spend on them everything beyond what is required to maintain that defensive power. His ordinary expenditure comes to equal his ordinary revenue, and it is well if it does not frequently exceed it. The accumulation of treasure can no longer be expected, and when extraordinary emergencies demand extraordinary expenses, he has no choice but to call upon his subjects for extraordinary assistance. The present king of Prussia and his late predecessor are the only great princes of Europe who, since the death of Henry IV of France in 1610, are believed to have amassed any considerable treasure. The thrift that leads to accumulation has become almost as rare in republican governments as in monarchies. The Italian republics and the United Provinces of the Netherlands are all in debt. The canton of Berne is the only republic in Europe that has accumulated any considerable treasure; the other Swiss republics have not. A taste for some form of pageantry, or at least for splendid buildings and other public ornaments, often prevails as strongly in the apparently sober senate-house of a small republic as in the dissolute court of the greatest king.

The want of thrift in time of peace imposes the necessity of borrowing in time of war. When war comes, the treasury holds no more money than is needed to cover the ordinary expenses of the peacetime establishment. In war, an establishment three or four times as costly becomes necessary for the defense of the state, and consequently a revenue three or four times greater than in peace. Suppose the sovereign had what he scarcely ever has: the immediate means of increasing his revenue in proportion to his increased expenses. Even then, the proceeds of the taxes from which this additional revenue must come will not begin to reach the treasury until perhaps ten or twelve months after they are imposed. Yet the moment war begins, or rather the moment it appears likely to begin, the army must be enlarged, the fleet must be fitted out, and the garrison towns must be put into a state of defense; and that army, that fleet, and those garrison towns must be supplied with arms, ammunition, and provisions. A large and immediate expense must be incurred at that moment of immediate danger, and it cannot wait for the gradual and slow returns of new taxes. In this emergency, government has no resource but borrowing.

The same commercial state of society that, through the operation of moral causes, drives government to borrow also gives its subjects both the ability and the inclination to lend. If it commonly brings with it the necessity of borrowing, it also brings the ease of doing so.

A country full of merchants and manufacturers is necessarily full of people through whose hands pass not only their own capital but also the capital of everyone who lends them money or entrusts them with goods. That capital passes through their hands as often as, or more often than, the income of a private man who lives on his revenue without any trade or business passes through his. Such a man's income can pass through his hands regularly only once a year. But the whole of the capital and credit of a merchant engaged in a trade with very quick returns may sometimes pass through his hands two, three, or four times a year. A country full of merchants and manufacturers therefore necessarily contains a class of people who are always in a position to advance a very large sum of money to the government, if they choose to do so. This is the source of the ability of the subjects of a commercial state to lend.

Commerce and manufacturing can seldom flourish for long in any state that lacks a regular administration of justice: where the people do not feel secure in the possession of their property, where the faithful performance of contracts is not upheld by law, and where the authority of the state is not understood to be regularly used to compel payment of debts from all who are able to pay. In short, commerce and manufacturing can seldom flourish in any state where there is not a certain degree of confidence in the justice of government. The same confidence that inclines great merchants and manufacturers, in ordinary times, to entrust their property to the protection of a particular government inclines them, in extraordinary times, to entrust that government with the use of their property. By lending money to the government, they do not reduce their ability to carry on their trade and manufactures even for a moment; on the contrary, they usually increase it. The needs of the state make the government willing, on most occasions, to borrow on terms extremely favorable to the lender. The security it gives to the original creditor can be transferred to any other creditor, and because of the universal confidence in the justice of the state, it generally sells on the market for more than was originally paid for it. The merchant or moneyed man profits by lending to the government, and rather than reducing his trading capital, he increases it. He therefore generally considers it a favor when the administration admits him to a share in the first subscription for a new loan. This is the source of the inclination, or willingness, of the subjects of a commercial state to lend.

The government of such a state is very apt to rely on this ability and willingness of its subjects to lend it their money in extraordinary circumstances. It foresees how easy borrowing will be, and so excuses itself from the duty of saving.

In a rude state of society, there are no large mercantile or manufacturing capitals. Individuals who hoard whatever money they can save, and who hide their hoard, do so out of distrust of the justice of government, from fear that if it were known that they had a hoard and where it could be found, they would quickly be plundered. In such conditions, few people would be able, and nobody would be willing, to lend their money to the government in an emergency. The sovereign senses that he must provide for such emergencies by saving, because he foresees that borrowing will be utterly impossible. This foresight strengthens still further his natural disposition to save.

The growth of the enormous debts that now oppress all the great nations of Europe, and that will probably ruin them in the long run, has followed a fairly uniform course. Nations, like private individuals, have generally begun by borrowing on what may be called personal credit, without assigning or mortgaging any particular fund for repayment. When this resource has failed them, they have gone on to borrow on the assignment or mortgage of particular funds.

What is called the unfunded debt of Great Britain is contracted in the first of these two ways. It consists partly of debt that bears, or is supposed to bear, no interest, resembling the debts a private person runs up on account, and partly of debt that bears interest, resembling what a private person contracts by a bill or promissory note. Debts owed for extraordinary services, or for services that were either not provided for or not paid for at the time they were performed, usually make up debt of the first kind. These include part of the extraordinary expenses of the army, the navy, and the ordnance, arrears of subsidies owed to foreign princes, arrears of seamen's wages, and the like. Navy bills and exchequer bills, which are sometimes issued in partial payment of such debts and sometimes for other purposes, make up debt of the second kind. Exchequer bills bear interest from the day they are issued; navy bills, from six months after they are issued. The Bank of England keeps up the value of these bills and eases their circulation, either by voluntarily discounting them at their current value or by agreeing with the government, in return for certain considerations, to circulate exchequer bills, which means receiving them at face value and paying whatever interest happens to be due on them. In this way the Bank often enables the government to contract a very large debt of this kind. In France, where there is no such bank, the state bills, known as *billets d'état*, have sometimes sold at a discount of sixty and seventy percent. During the great recoinage in King William's reign, when the Bank of England saw fit to suspend its usual transactions, exchequer bills and tallies are said to have sold at discounts ranging from twenty-five to sixty percent. This was owing partly, no doubt, to the supposed instability of the new government established by the Revolution, but partly also to the lack of support from the Bank of England.

When this resource is exhausted, and raising money requires assigning or mortgaging some particular branch of the public revenue for the payment of the debt, the government has on different occasions done so in two different ways. Sometimes it has made the assignment or mortgage for a short period only, such as one year or a few years; at other times it has made it in perpetuity. In the first case, the fund was supposed to be sufficient to repay both the principal and the interest of the money borrowed within the limited time. In the second, it was supposed to be sufficient to pay only the interest, or a perpetual annuity equivalent to the interest, with the government free to redeem that annuity at any time by repaying the principal borrowed. Money raised in the first way was said to be raised by anticipation; money raised in the second way, by perpetual funding, or more simply, by funding.

In Great Britain, the annual land and malt taxes are regularly anticipated every year under a borrowing clause routinely inserted into the acts that impose them. The Bank of England generally advances the sums for which those taxes are granted, at a rate of interest that has varied since the Revolution from eight to three percent, and is repaid as their proceeds gradually come in. If there is a shortfall, and there always is, it is made up in the supplies voted for the following year. The only considerable branch of the public revenue that still remains unmortgaged is thus regularly spent before it arrives. Like an improvident spendthrift whose pressing needs will not let him wait for the regular payment of his income, the state is in the constant habit of borrowing from its own agents and paying interest for the use of its own money.

In the reign of King William, and during much of Queen Anne's, before we had grown as familiar as we now are with the practice of perpetual funding, most new taxes were imposed only for a short term of four, five, six, or seven years, and a large part of each year's grants consisted of loans raised in anticipation of the proceeds of those taxes. Since the proceeds were often insufficient to repay the principal and interest within the limited term, deficiencies arose, and to make them good it became necessary to extend the term.

In 1697, by an act of the eighth year of William III, chapter 20, the deficiencies of several taxes were charged on what was then called the first general mortgage or fund. This consisted of an extension, to the first of August 1706, of several different taxes that would otherwise have expired sooner, and whose proceeds were combined into one general fund. The deficiencies charged on this extended term amounted to £5,160,459 14s. 9½d.

In 1701, those duties, together with some others, were extended further for similar purposes, to the first of August 1710, and were called the second general mortgage or fund. The deficiencies charged on it amounted to £2,055,999 7s. 11½d.

In 1707, those duties were extended again, as a fund for new loans, to the first of August 1712, and were called the third general mortgage or fund. The sum borrowed on it was £983,254 11s. 9¼d.

In 1708, those duties were all continued further, as a fund for new loans, to the first of August 1714, and were called the fourth general mortgage or fund. There were two exceptions: the old subsidy of tonnage and poundage, a long-standing customs duty levied on wine by the tun and on other goods by their value in pounds, of which only one half was made part of this fund; and a duty on the importation of Scottish linen, which had been abolished by the articles of union. The sum borrowed on this fund was £925,176 9s. 2¼d.

In 1709, those duties were all continued further for the same purpose, to the first of August 1716, with the exception of the old subsidy of tonnage and poundage, which was now dropped from the fund altogether. They were called the fifth general mortgage or fund. The sum borrowed on it was £922,029 6s.

In 1710, those duties were extended again to the first of August 1720, and were called the sixth general mortgage or fund. The sum borrowed on it was £1,296,552 9s. 11¾d.

In 1711, the same duties, which were by then subject to four separate anticipations, were made perpetual together with several others. They became a fund for paying the interest on the capital of the South Sea Company, which that year had advanced to the government, for paying debts and making good deficiencies, the sum of £9,177,967 15s. 4d. This was the largest loan that had ever been made up to that time.

Before this period, the principal taxes, and so far as I have been able to discover the only ones, imposed in perpetuity to pay the interest on a debt were those for paying the interest on money advanced to the government by the Bank and the East India Company, and on money that a projected land bank was expected to advance but never did. The Bank fund at this time amounted to £3,375,027 17s. 10½d., on which an annuity or interest of £206,501 15s. 5d. was paid. The East India fund amounted to £3,200,000, on which an annuity or interest of £160,000 was paid. The Bank fund bore interest at six percent, and the East India fund at five percent.

In 1715, by an act of the first year of George I, chapter 12, the various taxes that had been mortgaged to pay the Bank annuity, together with several others that this act likewise made perpetual, were combined into one common fund, called the Aggregate Fund. This fund was charged not only with paying the Bank annuity but with several other annuities and obligations of various kinds. It was later enlarged by acts of the third year of George I, chapter 8, and the fifth year of George I, chapter 3, and the various duties then added to it were likewise made perpetual.

In 1717, by an act of the third year of George I, chapter 7, several other taxes were made perpetual and combined into another common fund, called the General Fund, for the payment of certain annuities amounting altogether to £724,849 6s. 10½d.

As a result of these various acts, most of the taxes that had previously been anticipated only for a short term of years were made perpetual, as a fund for paying not the capital but only the interest on the money that had been borrowed against them through successive anticipations.

Had money never been raised except by anticipation, a few years would have freed the public revenue, without any further care on the government's part beyond two precautions: not overloading the fund by charging it with more debt than it could repay within the limited term, and not anticipating it a second time before the first anticipation had expired. But most European governments have proved incapable of these precautions. They have frequently overloaded the fund even on the first anticipation, and when that did not happen, they have generally made sure to overload it by anticipating a second and a third time before the first anticipation had expired. Once the fund had in this way become wholly insufficient to pay both the principal and the interest of the money borrowed on it, it became necessary to charge it with the interest only, or with a perpetual annuity equal to the interest. Such improvident anticipations thus inevitably gave rise to the more ruinous practice of perpetual funding. This practice necessarily postpones the freeing of the public revenue from a fixed date to one so indefinite that it is unlikely ever to arrive. Yet because a larger sum can always be raised by the new practice than by the old one of anticipation, perpetual funding, once people have grown familiar with it, has been universally preferred in the great emergencies of the state. Relieving the present emergency is always the chief concern of those directly responsible for the administration of public affairs. The future liberation of the public revenue they leave to the care of posterity.

During the reign of Queen Anne, the market rate of interest had fallen from six to five percent, and in the twelfth year of her reign, five percent was declared the highest rate that could lawfully be charged on money borrowed on private security. Soon after most of Great Britain's temporary taxes had been made perpetual and distributed among the Aggregate, South Sea, and General Funds, the public's creditors, like those of private persons, were induced to accept five percent interest on their money. This produced a saving of one percent on the capital of most of the debts that had been funded in this way in perpetuity, or one-sixth of most of the annuities paid out of the three great funds just mentioned. This saving left a considerable surplus in the proceeds of the various taxes combined into those funds, over and above what was necessary for paying the annuities now charged upon them, and it laid the foundation of what has since been called the sinking fund. In 1717 this fund amounted to £523,454, 7 shillings, and 7½ pence. In 1727 the interest on most of the public debt was reduced further, to 4 percent, and in 1753 and 1757 to 3½ and then 3 percent. Each of these reductions enlarged the sinking fund still more.

A sinking fund, though established to pay off old debts, makes it much easier to contract new ones. It is a reserve fund, always at hand, which can be mortgaged to support any other doubtful fund on which the state proposes to raise money in an emergency. Whether Britain's sinking fund has more often served the first purpose or the second will become clear soon enough.

Besides these two methods of borrowing, by anticipation and by perpetual funding, there are two others that occupy a kind of middle ground between them: borrowing on annuities for a fixed term of years, and borrowing on annuities for life.

During the reigns of King William and Queen Anne, large sums were frequently borrowed on annuities for terms of years, some longer and some shorter. In 1695 an act was passed to borrow one million pounds on an annuity of 14 percent, or £140,000 a year, for sixteen years. In 1691 an act was passed to borrow a million on life annuities, on terms that would seem very favorable to lenders today, but the subscription was never filled. The following year the shortfall was made good by borrowing on life annuities at 14 percent. This amounted to a little more than seven years' purchase: the lender paid a price equal to slightly more than seven years of annual payments in exchange for an income lasting the rest of his life. In 1695 the purchasers of these annuities were allowed to exchange them for annuities running ninety-six years, on paying into the Exchequer £63 for every £100 they had originally advanced. The difference between 14 percent for life and 14 percent for ninety-six years was thus sold for £63, or four and a half years' purchase. So unstable did the government seem that even on these terms few buyers came forward. In Queen Anne's reign, money was borrowed on various occasions both on life annuities and on annuities for terms of thirty-two, eighty-nine, ninety-eight, and ninety-nine years. In 1719 the holders of the thirty-two-year annuities were persuaded to accept South Sea stock in their place, to the value of eleven and a half years' purchase of the annuities, together with additional stock equal to whatever arrears were then owed on them. In 1720 most of the other term annuities, long and short, were subscribed into the same fund. At that time the long annuities came to £666,821, 8 shillings, and 3½ pence a year. On January 5, 1775, the remainder, the portion not subscribed in 1720, amounted to only £136,453, 12 shillings, and 8 pence.

During the two wars that began in 1739 and 1755, little money was borrowed on either term annuities or life annuities. An annuity for ninety-eight or ninety-nine years, however, is worth nearly as much as a perpetual one, and one might therefore expect it to support nearly as much borrowing. But people who buy into the public stocks in order to make family settlements and provide for the distant future would not want a stock whose value was steadily shrinking, and such people make up a very considerable share of both the holders and the buyers of stock. A long-term annuity, therefore, though its intrinsic value may be very nearly that of a perpetual annuity, will not find nearly as many buyers. Subscribers to a new loan, who generally intend to sell their share as soon as possible, strongly prefer a perpetual annuity that Parliament can redeem to an irredeemable annuity of equal amount running for a long term of years. The value of the former can be assumed to stay always the same, or very nearly so, and it therefore makes a more convenient transferable stock than the latter.

During the two wars just mentioned, annuities for terms of years or for lives were seldom granted except as bonuses to the subscribers of a new loan. These came over and above the redeemable annuity, or interest, on the strength of which the loan was supposedly made. They were granted not as the actual fund on which the money was borrowed but as an extra inducement to the lender.

Life annuities have occasionally been granted in two different ways: on individual lives, or on groups of lives, which in French are called *tontines* after their inventor. When annuities are granted on individual lives, the death of each annuitant relieves the public revenue of whatever his annuity had cost it. When they are granted as tontines, the public revenue begins to be relieved only after every annuitant in a group has died. A group might include twenty or thirty people. The survivors inherit the annuities of those who die before them, and the last survivor inherits the annuities of the entire group. On the same revenue, more money can always be raised by tontines than by annuities on individual lives. An annuity carrying a right of survivorship is genuinely worth more than an equal annuity on a single life. Moreover, every man naturally trusts in his own good fortune, which is the principle behind the success of all lotteries, and so such an annuity generally sells for somewhat more than it is worth. In countries where governments commonly raise money by granting annuities, tontines are for this reason usually preferred to annuities on individual lives. The expedient that will raise the most money is almost always preferred to the one that would free the public revenue most quickly.

In France a much larger share of the public debt consists of life annuities than in England. According to a memorial presented to the king by the *parlement* of Bordeaux in 1764, the entire public debt of France is estimated at 2,400 million livres. Of this, the capital for which life annuities had been granted is supposed to amount to 300 million, an eighth of the whole. The annuities themselves are reckoned at 30 million livres a year, a quarter of the 120 million that is supposed to be the interest on the entire debt. I am well aware that these estimates are not exact. But since so respectable a body has put them forward as approximations to the truth, they may, I believe, be accepted as such. The difference between the two countries' ways of borrowing does not come from any difference in how anxious the French and English governments are to free the public revenue. It arises entirely from the different views and interests of the lenders.

In England the seat of government is the greatest commercial city in the world, and so it is generally merchants who lend money to the government. In doing so they mean not to reduce their trading capital but to increase it, and unless they expected to sell their share of a new loan at some profit, they would never subscribe. If, in return for their money, they received only annuities for lives instead of perpetual annuities, whether on their own lives or on other people's, they would be less likely to sell at a profit. Annuities on their own lives they would always sell at a loss, because no one will pay as much for an annuity on another man's life, when that man is roughly his own age and health, as he would pay for one on his own. An annuity on the life of a third person is, of course, worth the same to buyer and seller. But its real value begins to decline from the moment it is granted, and it keeps declining, ever more steeply, for as long as it lasts. It can never, therefore, make as convenient a transferable stock as a perpetual annuity, whose real value can be assumed to stay always the same, or very nearly so.

In France the seat of government is not a great commercial city, so merchants make up a smaller share of those who lend to the government. Most of the money advanced in every public emergency comes from people engaged in the public finances. These include the farmers-general, who bought from the crown the right to collect certain taxes, along with the receivers of the taxes not farmed out, the court bankers, and others. Such men are commonly of humble birth but great wealth, and often of great pride. They are too proud to marry their equals, and women of rank disdain to marry them. They therefore frequently resolve to remain bachelors. Having no families of their own, and little regard for those of their relatives, whom they are not always eager to acknowledge, they wish only to live in splendor during their own lifetimes and are not unwilling for their fortunes to end with them. Furthermore, France has far more wealthy people than England who either dislike marriage or hold a station in life that makes marriage improper or inconvenient. For such people, who care little or nothing for posterity, nothing could be more convenient than to exchange their capital for an income that will last exactly as long as they want it to, and no longer.

In peacetime, the ordinary expense of most modern governments equals or nearly equals their ordinary revenue. When war comes, therefore, they are both unwilling and unable to raise their revenue in proportion to their rising expense. They are unwilling because they fear offending the people, who would quickly grow disgusted with the war under so great and sudden a rise in taxes. They are unable because they do not know well what taxes would produce the revenue required. The ease of borrowing frees them from the difficulty that this fear and this inability would otherwise cause. By borrowing, they can raise enough money each year to carry on the war with only a very moderate increase in taxes. Through the practice of perpetual funding, they can raise the largest possible sum each year with the smallest possible increase in taxes. In great empires, many of the people who live in the capital, or in provinces far from the fighting, feel scarcely any inconvenience from the war. They enjoy, at their ease, the amusement of reading in the newspapers about the exploits of their own fleets and armies. For them, this amusement makes up for the small difference between the taxes they pay because of the war and those they were used to paying in peacetime. They are generally dissatisfied when peace returns, because it ends their amusement along with a thousand visionary hopes of conquest and national glory from a longer war.

Nor does the return of peace usually relieve them of most of the taxes imposed during the war. These taxes are mortgaged to pay the interest on the debt contracted to carry the war on. After that interest and the ordinary expenses of government are paid, the old revenue together with the new taxes may yield some surplus, and that surplus may perhaps be turned into a sinking fund for paying off the debt. But there are two problems. First, such a sinking fund, even if it were applied to no other purpose, is generally wholly inadequate to pay off the whole wartime debt within any period during which peace can reasonably be expected to last. Second, it is almost always applied to other purposes.

The new taxes were imposed for the sole purpose of paying interest on the money borrowed against them. If they yield more, the excess is generally something no one intended or expected, and it is therefore seldom very large. Sinking funds have generally arisen less from a surplus of the taxes beyond what was needed to pay the interest or annuity originally charged on them than from a later reduction of that interest. The sinking fund of Holland in 1655 and that of the Papal States in 1685 were both formed in this way. This is why such funds are usually inadequate.

Even in the most profound peace, various events occur that require extraordinary spending, and a government always finds it more convenient to cover that spending by misapplying the sinking fund than by imposing a new tax. Every new tax is felt immediately by the people, to a greater or lesser degree. It always provokes some grumbling and meets with some opposition. The more taxes have been multiplied, and the higher they have been raised on every object of taxation, the more loudly the people complain of each new tax. It also becomes harder either to find new things to tax or to raise much higher the taxes already laid on the old ones. A temporary suspension of debt repayment, by contrast, is not immediately felt by the people and provokes neither grumbling nor complaint. Borrowing from the sinking fund is always an obvious and easy way out of the immediate difficulty. The more the public debt has accumulated, the more necessary it becomes to work at reducing it, and the more dangerous and ruinous it is to misapply any part of the sinking fund. Yet under those same conditions, the debt is less likely to be reduced to any significant degree, and it is more likely, indeed more certain, that the sinking fund will be misapplied to cover all the extraordinary expenses that arise in peacetime. When a nation is already overburdened with taxes, only the necessities of a new war can persuade the people to submit with tolerable patience to a new tax, and those necessities must spring either from the passion of national vengeance or from anxiety for national security. This is why the sinking fund is usually misapplied.

In Great Britain, ever since we first resorted to the ruinous expedient of perpetual funding, the reduction of the public debt in peacetime has never borne any proportion to its accumulation in wartime. The foundation of Britain's present enormous debt was first laid in the war that began in 1688 and was concluded by the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697.

On December 31, 1697, the public debts of Great Britain, funded and unfunded, amounted to £21,515,742, 13 shillings, and 8½ pence. A large part of these debts had been contracted on short-term anticipations of revenue, and some on life annuities. As a result, by December 31, 1701, in less than four years, £5,121,041, 12 shillings, and ¾ of a penny had either been paid off or reverted to the public. This was a greater reduction of the public debt than has ever since been achieved in so short a time. The remaining debt therefore came to only £16,394,701, 1 shilling, and 7¼ pence.

In the war that began in 1702 and was concluded by the Treaty of Utrecht, the public debt grew still larger. On December 31, 1714, it amounted to £53,681,076, 5 shillings, and 6½ pence. The subscription of the short and long annuities into the South Sea fund increased the capital of the debt, so that on December 31, 1722, it stood at £55,282,978, 1 shilling, and 3⅚ pence. Reduction of the debt began in 1723 and proceeded so slowly that by December 31, 1739, after seventeen years of profound peace, the total paid off was no more than £8,328,554, 17 shillings, and 11¼ pence. The capital of the public debt at that time stood at £46,954,623, 3 shillings, and 4 7/12 pence.

The Spanish war that began in 1739, and the French war that soon followed it, increased the debt further. On December 31, 1748, after the war had been concluded by the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, the debt amounted to £78,293,313, 1 shilling, and 10¾ pence. The most profound peace, lasting seventeen years, had taken no more than £8,328,354, 17 shillings, and 11¼ pence from it. A war lasting less than nine years had added £31,338,689, 18 shillings, and 6⅙ pence to it. These figures are drawn from James Postlethwaite's *History of the Public Revenue*.

During Mr. Pelham's administration, the interest on the public debt was reduced from 4 to 3 percent, or at least measures were taken to reduce it. The sinking fund was also enlarged, and part of the public debt was paid off. In 1755, before the outbreak of the last war, the funded debt of Great Britain amounted to £72,289,675. On January 5, 1763, when peace was concluded, it amounted to £122,603,336, 8 shillings, and 2¼ pence. The unfunded debt has been put at £13,927,589, 2 shillings, and 2 pence. But the expense of the war did not end with the peace. By January 5, 1764, the funded debt had risen to £129,586,789, 10 shillings, and 1¾ pence, partly through a new loan and partly through the funding of some of the unfunded debt. Even so, according to the very well-informed author of *Considerations on the Trade and Finances of Great Britain*, there still remained an unfunded debt of £9,975,017, 12 shillings, and 2 15/44 pence, which was brought to account in that year and the next. In 1764, therefore, the public debt of Great Britain, funded and unfunded together, amounted according to this author to £139,561,807, 2 shillings, and 4 pence. On top of this, the life annuities granted as bonuses to subscribers to the new loans of 1757 were estimated at fourteen years' purchase and valued at £472,500. The long-term annuities granted as bonuses in 1761 and 1762 were estimated at twenty-seven and a half years' purchase and valued at £6,826,875. During a peace of about seven years, the prudent and truly patriotic administration of Mr. Pelham was unable to pay off an old debt of six million pounds. During a war of nearly the same length, a new debt of more than seventy-five million was contracted.

On January 5, 1775, the funded debt of Great Britain amounted to £124,996,086, 1 shilling, and 6¼ pence. The unfunded debt, not counting a large civil-list debt, came to £4,150,236, 3 shillings, and 11⅞ pence, and the two together to £129,146,322, 5 shillings, and 6 pence. By this account, the total debt paid off during eleven years of profound peace came to only £10,415,476, 16 shillings, and 9⅞ pence. Even this small reduction was not made entirely from savings out of the ordinary revenue of the state. Several outside sums, wholly independent of that revenue, contributed to it. Among these we may count an additional shilling in the pound on the land tax for three years; the two million pounds received from the East India Company as compensation for its territorial acquisitions; and the £110,000 received from the Bank for the renewal of its charter. To these must be added several other sums that arose out of the last war and ought perhaps, for that reason, to be treated as deductions from its expenses. The principal ones are:

- The proceeds of French ships captured as prizes: £690,449, 18 shillings, and 9 pence
- The payment made by France for the maintenance of French prisoners: £670,000
- The sums received from the sale of the ceded islands: £95,500
- Total: £1,455,949, 18 shillings, and 9 pence

To this sum we must add the balance of the accounts of the Earl of Chatham and Mr. Calcraft, other army savings of the same kind, and the sums received from the Bank, the East India Company, and the additional shilling on the land tax. The whole must come to a good deal more than five million pounds. The debt paid off since the peace out of savings from the ordinary revenue has therefore averaged less than half a million a year. The sinking fund has no doubt grown considerably since the peace, through the debt already paid off, the reduction of the redeemable 4 percents to 3 percent, and the life annuities that have expired. If peace were to continue, perhaps a million a year might now be spared from it toward discharging the debt. Another million was in fact paid off in the course of last year. At the same time, however, a large civil-list debt was left unpaid, and we are now engaged in a new war that may prove, as it goes on, as expensive as any of our former wars. As events have since shown, it has proved more expensive than any of them, and it has added more than a hundred million to the debt. During a profound peace of eleven years, little more than ten million was paid off; during a war of seven years, more than a hundred million was contracted. The new debt likely to be contracted before the end of the next campaign may come close to equaling all the old debt paid off from the savings of the ordinary revenue. It would therefore be wholly fanciful to expect the public debt ever to be fully discharged by any savings likely to be made from that ordinary revenue as it now stands.

One writer has portrayed the public funds of the various indebted nations of Europe, and particularly those of England, as a great capital accumulated on top of the country's other capital. By means of this added capital, he claims, the nation's trade is extended, its manufactures are multiplied, and its land is cultivated and improved far beyond what that other capital alone could have achieved. He fails to consider what happened to the capital that the first creditors of the public advanced to the government. From the moment they advanced it, that capital was a portion of the annual produce diverted from serving as capital to serving as revenue. It went from maintaining productive laborers to maintaining unproductive ones, to be spent and wasted, generally within the year, without even the hope of future reproduction. In return for the capital they advanced, the creditors did indeed receive an annuity in the public funds, in most cases of more than equal value. This annuity no doubt replaced their capital and allowed them to carry on their trade and business on the same scale as before, or perhaps a larger one. They could either borrow new capital from others on the credit of this annuity, or sell the annuity and so obtain from others new capital of their own, equal to or greater than what they had advanced to the government. But this new capital, whether they bought it or borrowed it from other people, must already have existed in the country, and it must have been employed, as all capital is, in maintaining productive labor. When it came into the hands of those who had lent to the government, it was in some respects new capital to them, but not to the country. It was merely capital withdrawn from certain employments in order to be turned toward others. Though it replaced for them what they had advanced to the government, it did not replace it for the country. Had they not advanced this capital to the government, the country would have had two capitals, two portions of the annual produce, instead of one, employed in maintaining productive labor.

When the expense of government is met by revenue raised within the year from free or unmortgaged taxes, meaning taxes not already pledged to pay the interest on earlier debts, a portion of private people's income is merely diverted from maintaining one kind of unproductive labor to maintaining another. Some of what they pay in those taxes might, no doubt, have been saved and added to capital, and so employed in maintaining productive labor; but most of it would probably have been spent, and so employed in maintaining unproductive labor. Public expense met in this way certainly hinders, to a greater or lesser degree, the further accumulation of new capital, but it does not necessarily cause the destruction of any capital that already exists.

When the public expense is met by funding, that is, by borrowing against tax revenues mortgaged for the purpose, it is paid for by the annual destruction of capital that previously existed in the country. Part of the annual produce that had been destined to maintain productive labor is diverted toward maintaining unproductive labor. In this case, however, the taxes are lighter than they would have been had enough revenue to cover the same expense been raised within the year. The private income of individuals is therefore less burdened, and their ability to save part of that income and accumulate it into capital is considerably less impaired. If funding destroys more old capital, it also does less to hinder the accumulation or acquisition of new capital than paying for public expense out of revenue raised within the year. Under the system of funding, the thrift and industry of private people can more easily repair the breaches that the waste and extravagance of government may from time to time make in the general capital of society.

This advantage of funding over the other system holds only while a war continues. If the expense of war were always met by revenue raised within the year, the taxes that supplied that extraordinary revenue would last no longer than the war itself. The ability of private people to accumulate, though smaller during the war, would be greater during the peace than it is under the system of funding. War would not necessarily destroy any old capital, and peace would allow much more new capital to accumulate. Wars would generally be concluded more quickly and undertaken less recklessly. Feeling the full burden of a war while it lasted, the people would soon grow weary of it, and the government, in order to accommodate them, would not need to carry it on any longer than necessary. Foreseeing the heavy and unavoidable burdens of war, the people would refrain from recklessly demanding one when there was no real or solid interest to fight for. The periods during which private people's ability to accumulate was somewhat impaired would come less often and last a shorter time, while the periods in which that ability was at its fullest strength would last far longer than they can under the system of funding.

Moreover, once funding has advanced to a certain point, the multiplication of taxes it brings with it can impair private people's ability to accumulate as much in peacetime as the other system would in wartime. The peacetime revenue of Great Britain now amounts to more than ten million pounds a year. If it were free and unmortgaged, it might be enough, with proper management and without borrowing a single shilling more, to carry on the most vigorous war. As things stand, the private income of the inhabitants of Great Britain is as heavily burdened in time of peace, and their ability to accumulate is as much impaired, as it would have been during the most expensive war had the pernicious system of funding never been adopted.

It has been said that in paying the interest on the public debt, the right hand pays the left. The money does not leave the country. Part of the income of one group of inhabitants is simply transferred to another, and the nation is not a farthing poorer. This defense rests entirely on the fallacies of the mercantile system, and after the long examination I have already given that system, there may be no need to say anything further about it. It assumes, besides, that the entire public debt is owed to inhabitants of the country, which happens not to be true, since the Dutch, along with several other foreign nations, hold a very considerable share of our public funds. But even if the whole debt were owed to the country's own inhabitants, it would be no less pernicious on that account.

Land and capital stock are the two original sources of all revenue, private and public alike. Capital stock pays the wages of productive labor, whether that labor is employed in agriculture, manufacturing, or commerce. The management of these two original sources of revenue belongs to two different groups of people: the owners of land, and the owners or employers of capital stock.

For the sake of his own income, the owner of land has an interest in keeping his estate in the best condition he can, by building and repairing his tenants' houses, by making and maintaining the necessary drains and enclosures, and by undertaking all the other expensive improvements that properly fall to the landlord to make and maintain. But various land taxes may so reduce the landlord's income, and various duties on the necessities and comforts of life may make that reduced income worth so little in real terms, that he finds himself entirely unable to make or maintain those costly improvements. Once the landlord stops doing his part, however, it is impossible for the tenant to go on doing his. As the landlord's distress grows, the agriculture of the country must inevitably decline.

When, because of various taxes on the necessities and comforts of life, the owners and employers of capital stock find that whatever income they draw from it will not buy, in their own country, the same quantity of those necessities and comforts that an equal income would buy in almost any other, they will be inclined to move elsewhere. And when, in order to collect those taxes, all or most merchants and manufacturers, that is, all or most of the employers of large capitals, are continually subjected to the humiliating and vexatious visits of the tax collectors, this inclination to move will soon become an actual departure. The industry of the country must fall with the removal of the capital that supported it, and the ruin of trade and manufacturing will follow the decline of agriculture.

The two great sources of revenue, land and capital stock, are managed by the people who have a direct interest in the good condition of each particular piece of land and in the good management of each particular portion of capital. To transfer the greater part of the revenue arising from either source away from these people to another group, the creditors of the public, who have no such particular interest, must in the long run lead both to the neglect of land and to the waste or removal of capital. A public creditor certainly has a general interest in the prosperity of the country's agriculture, manufacturing, and commerce, and therefore in the good condition of its land and the good management of its capital. Should there be any general failure or decline in any of these, the yield of the various taxes might no longer be enough to pay him the annuity or interest he is owed. But a public creditor, considered simply as such, has no interest in the good condition of any particular piece of land or in the good management of any particular portion of capital. As a creditor of the public, he has no knowledge of any such particular portion. He has no oversight of it. He can have no concern for it. Its ruin may in some cases go unnoticed by him, and it cannot affect him directly.

The practice of funding has gradually weakened every state that has adopted it. The Italian republics seem to have begun it. Genoa and Venice, the only two of them that can still claim an independent existence, have both been weakened by it. Spain seems to have learned the practice from the Italian republics, and, its taxes probably being less judicious than theirs, it has been weakened even more in proportion to its natural strength. Spain's debts are of very long standing. It was deeply in debt before the end of the sixteenth century, about a hundred years before England owed a shilling. France, for all its natural resources, languishes under an oppressive load of the same kind. The republic of the United Provinces of the Netherlands is as weakened by its debts as either Genoa or Venice. Is it likely that a practice which has brought either weakness or dissolution to every other country should prove entirely harmless in Great Britain alone?

It may be said that the systems of taxation established in those countries are inferior to England's. I believe they are. But it should be remembered that once even the wisest government has exhausted all the proper objects of taxation, it must, in cases of urgent necessity, resort to improper ones. The wise republic of Holland has on some occasions been forced to resort to taxes as inconvenient as most of those in Spain. Another war, begun before the public revenue had been substantially freed from its burden of debt, and growing as expensive in its course as the last one, may by irresistible necessity make the British system of taxation as oppressive as Holland's, or even Spain's. To the credit of our present system of taxation, it has so far placed so little burden on industry that, even during the most expensive wars, the thrift and good conduct of individuals seem to have been able, through saving and accumulation, to repair all the breaches that the waste and extravagance of government had made in the general capital of society. At the end of the late war, the most expensive Great Britain has ever fought, her agriculture was as flourishing, her manufacturers as numerous and as fully employed, and her commerce as extensive as they had ever been. The capital that supported all these branches of industry must therefore have been as great as it had ever been. Since the peace, agriculture has improved still further. House rents have risen in every town and village in the country, which proves the growing wealth and income of the people. And the annual yield of most of the old taxes, particularly the principal branches of the excise and customs, has risen steadily, an equally clear proof of growing consumption, and therefore of a growing produce, which alone could support that consumption. Great Britain seems to bear with ease a burden that, half a century ago, nobody believed she could bear. We should not, however, rashly conclude from this that she can bear any burden whatever, nor even be too confident that she could bear, without great distress, a burden slightly heavier than the one already laid upon her.

Once national debts have accumulated beyond a certain point, there is scarcely, I believe, a single instance of their having been fairly and completely paid off. Whenever the public revenue has been freed from such debt at all, it has always been through bankruptcy, sometimes an openly declared one, but more often one disguised as a pretended payment.

Raising the denomination of the coin, that is, assigning a higher face value to a coin containing the same amount of metal, has been the most common device for disguising a real public bankruptcy as a pretended payment. Suppose, for example, that a sixpence were raised, by act of Parliament or royal proclamation, to the denomination of a shilling, and twenty sixpences to that of a pound sterling. A person who had borrowed twenty shillings under the old denomination, or nearly four ounces of silver, could then repay the debt under the new one with twenty sixpences, or a little less than two ounces. A national debt of about one hundred and twenty-eight million pounds, close to the principal of the funded and unfunded debt of Great Britain, could in this way be paid with about sixty-four million pounds of our present money. It would, of course, be only a pretended payment, and the public's creditors would in reality be cheated of ten shillings in every pound owed to them, or half of what they were due. The calamity, moreover, would extend far beyond the public's creditors. The creditors of every private person would suffer a proportional loss, and this without any benefit to the public's creditors, and in most cases with a great additional loss to them. If the public's creditors were, as a rule, heavily in debt to others, they might partly make up their loss by paying their own creditors in the same coin in which the public had paid them. But in most countries, the creditors of the public are for the most part wealthy people, who stand toward the rest of their fellow citizens more as creditors than as debtors. A pretended payment of this kind therefore, in most cases, aggravates the loss of the public's creditors rather than relieving it, and, without any benefit to the public, spreads the calamity to a great number of other innocent people. It causes a general and most destructive overturning of private fortunes. In most cases it enriches the idle and extravagant debtor at the expense of the industrious and thrifty creditor, and it transfers a great part of the national capital from the hands likely to increase and improve it to those likely to squander and destroy it. When it becomes necessary for a state to declare itself bankrupt, just as when it becomes necessary for an individual to do so, a fair, open, and declared bankruptcy is always the course least dishonorable to the debtor and least harmful to the creditor. The honor of a state is surely very poorly served when, to cover the disgrace of a real bankruptcy, it resorts to a conjuring trick of this kind, so easily seen through and at the same time so extremely destructive.

Nearly all states, however, ancient as well as modern, have on some occasions played this very trick when reduced to such necessity. At the end of the First Punic War, the Romans reduced the as, the coin or unit by which they reckoned the value of all their other coins, from twelve ounces of copper to only two. They raised two ounces of copper, that is, to a denomination that had always before expressed the value of twelve ounces. In this way the republic was able to pay the great debts it had contracted with one-sixth of what it actually owed. We might suppose today that so sudden and so great a bankruptcy must have provoked a violent public outcry. It does not appear to have provoked any. The law that enacted it was, like all other laws relating to the coinage, introduced and carried through the people's assembly by a tribune, and it was probably a very popular law. In Rome, as in all the other ancient republics, the poor were constantly in debt to the rich and powerful, who, to secure their votes at the annual elections, lent them money at exorbitant interest. Since that interest was never paid, it soon swelled into a sum too great for the debtor to pay, or for anyone else to pay on his behalf. For fear of a very harsh enforcement of the debt, the debtor was obliged, without any further reward, to vote for whichever candidate the creditor recommended. Despite all the laws against bribery and corruption, the largesse of the candidates, together with the occasional distributions of grain ordered by the senate, were the chief sources from which the poorer citizens drew their livelihood during the later period of the Roman republic. To free themselves from this subjection to their creditors, the poorer citizens constantly called either for an outright cancellation of debts or for what they called "new tables," that is, a law entitling them to a full discharge upon paying only a certain fraction of their accumulated debts. The law that reduced the coin of every denomination to one-sixth of its former value, since it allowed them to pay their debts with one-sixth of what they really owed, amounted to the most favorable "new tables" imaginable. To satisfy the people, the rich and powerful were obliged on several occasions to agree to laws both cancelling debts and introducing new tables. They were probably induced to agree to this law partly for the same reason, and partly because, by freeing the public revenue, they could restore strength to a government that they themselves principally directed. An operation of this kind would at a stroke reduce a debt of £128,000,000 to £21,333,333 6s. 8d. During the Second Punic War, the as was reduced still further, first from two ounces of copper to one, and then from one ounce to half an ounce, or one twenty-fourth of its original value. By combining the three Roman operations into one, a debt of one hundred and twenty-eight million pounds of our present money could be reduced all at once to a debt of £5,333,333 6s. 8d. Even the enormous debt of Great Britain could soon be paid in this manner.

By such devices, the coin of every nation, I believe, has been gradually reduced further and further below its original value, and the same nominal sum has gradually come to contain less and less silver.

For the same purpose, nations have sometimes debased the standard of their coin, that is, mixed a greater quantity of base metal into it. Suppose, for example, that a pound weight of our silver coin contained eight ounces of alloy instead of the eighteen pennyweight, a little less than one ounce, permitted by the present standard. A pound sterling, or twenty shillings of such coin, would then be worth little more than six shillings and eightpence of our present money. The quantity of silver contained in six shillings and eightpence of our present money would thus be raised very nearly to the denomination of a pound sterling. Debasing the standard has exactly the same effect as what the French call an *augmentation*, a direct raising of the denomination of the coin.

An augmentation, a direct raising of the coin's denomination, is always, and by its very nature must be, an open and declared operation. Through it, pieces of smaller weight and size are given the same name that was formerly given to pieces of greater weight and size. Debasing the standard, by contrast, has generally been a concealed operation. Through it, the mint issues pieces of the same denomination, and as nearly as could be managed of the same weight, size, and appearance, as pieces that had previously circulated at a much greater value. When King John of France debased his coin to pay his debts, all the officers of his mint were sworn to secrecy. Both operations are unjust. But a simple augmentation is an injustice of open violence, whereas debasement is an injustice of treacherous fraud. The latter, therefore, once discovered, and it could never stay hidden for long, has always provoked far greater indignation than the former. After any considerable augmentation, the coin has very seldom been restored to its former weight; but after even the greatest debasements, it has almost always been restored to its former fineness. Scarcely ever could the fury and indignation of the people be appeased in any other way.

At the end of the reign of Henry VIII and the beginning of that of Edward VI, the English coin was not only raised in its denomination but debased in its standard. The same frauds were practiced in Scotland during the minority of James VI. They have been practiced from time to time in most other countries.

It seems entirely vain to expect that the public revenue of Great Britain can ever be completely freed from debt, or even that any considerable progress can be made toward freeing it, so long as the surplus of that revenue, the amount left over after paying the annual expense of the peacetime establishment, remains so very small. That freeing of the revenue clearly can never be achieved without either a very considerable increase in the public revenue or an equally considerable reduction in public expense.

A more equal land tax, a more equal tax on house rents, and such changes in the present system of customs and excise as were described in the preceding chapter might perhaps produce a considerable increase in revenue without adding to the burden on most of the people, simply by distributing its weight more equally across the whole. Yet even the most optimistic schemer could hardly persuade himself that any increase of this kind would offer reasonable hope of freeing the public revenue altogether, or even of making enough progress toward that end in peacetime to prevent or offset the further accumulation of public debt in the next war.

A much greater increase in revenue might be expected from extending the British system of taxation to all the provinces of the empire inhabited by people of British or European descent. This, however, could hardly be done in keeping with the principles of the British constitution without admitting into the British Parliament, or, if one prefers, into a states-general of the British empire, a fair and equal representation of all those provinces, with each province's representation bearing the same proportion to the yield of its taxes as Great Britain's representation might bear to the yield of the taxes levied on Great Britain. The private interests of many powerful individuals and the entrenched prejudices of great bodies of people do seem, at present, to set such obstacles in the way of so great a change as may be very difficult, perhaps altogether impossible, to overcome. Without presuming to decide whether such a union is practicable or impracticable, it may not be inappropriate, in a speculative work of this kind, to consider how far the British system of taxation might be applied to all the provinces of the empire, what revenue might be expected from it if so applied, and how a general union of this kind might affect the happiness and prosperity of the different provinces it comprised. At worst, such a speculation can be regarded only as a new Utopia, certainly less entertaining than the old one, but no more useless or fanciful.

The four principal branches of British taxation are the land tax, the stamp duties, and the various duties of customs and of excise.

Ireland is certainly as able as Great Britain to pay a land tax, and our American and West Indian plantations are more able. A landlord who is subject to neither the tithe nor the poor rate must certainly be better able to pay such a tax than one who bears both of those other burdens. Where the tithe is levied in kind, as a literal share of the crop, and where no *modus* has been agreed (a fixed money payment accepted in place of that share), it cuts more deeply into what would otherwise be the landlord's rent than a land tax that genuinely amounted to five shillings in the pound, or one quarter of the rent. In most cases such a tithe will be found to exceed a fourth of the real rent of the land, meaning what remains after the farmer's capital has been fully replaced together with his reasonable profit. If every *modus* were abolished, and every impropriation as well (tithes that have passed out of the Church's hands into the possession of laymen), the complete church tithe of Great Britain and Ireland could hardly be estimated at less than six or seven million pounds. If there were no tithe in either country, the landlords could afford to pay six or seven million pounds of additional land tax without being any more burdened than a very large number of them are now. America pays no tithe and could therefore well afford a land tax. It is true that the lands of America and the West Indies are generally neither tenanted nor leased to farmers, and so could not be assessed by any rent roll. But neither were the lands of Great Britain assessed by any rent roll in the fourth year of the reign of William and Mary, when the present land tax was established; they were assessed by a very loose and inaccurate estimate. The lands of America might be assessed in the same way, or else according to a fair valuation based on an accurate survey, like those recently carried out in the Duchy of Milan and in the dominions of Austria, Prussia, and Sardinia.

Stamp duties, plainly, could be levied without any variation in every country where the forms of legal procedure, and the deeds by which both real and personal property are transferred, are the same or nearly the same.

Extending the customs laws of Great Britain to Ireland and the plantations, provided that this was accompanied, as justice requires, by an extension of free trade, would be enormously advantageous to both. All the resented restrictions that now weigh upon the trade of Ireland would come to an end, as would the distinction between the "enumerated" commodities of America, which may be shipped only to Britain, and the "non-enumerated" ones, which may be sent elsewhere. The countries north of Cape Finisterre, on the northwestern tip of Spain, would be as open to every kind of American produce as those south of the cape are now open to certain kinds of it. Because the customs laws would be uniform, trade among all the different parts of the British Empire would be as free as the coastal trade of Great Britain is today. The empire would thus provide, within its own borders, an immense internal market for every kind of produce from every one of its provinces. So great an extension of the market would soon make up to both Ireland and the plantations for everything they might lose through the increase in customs duties.

The excise is the only part of the British tax system that would need to be adjusted at all according to the province to which it was applied. It could be extended to Ireland without any change, since the produce and consumption of that kingdom are exactly the same in kind as those of Great Britain. In applying it to America and the West Indies, whose produce and consumption differ greatly from Britain's, some modification might be needed, just as it has been modified in its application to the cider-making and beer-brewing counties of England.

Consider a fermented drink that Americans call beer, although, being made from molasses, it bears very little resemblance to ours. It makes up a considerable part of the ordinary drink of the American people. Because it keeps for only a few days, it cannot, like our beer, be brewed and stored for sale in large breweries; instead every private family must brew it for its own use, just as it cooks its own food. Yet to subject every private household to the hated visits and inspections of the tax collector, as we subject alehouse keepers and commercial brewers, would be wholly inconsistent with liberty. If, for the sake of equality, it were thought necessary to tax this drink, it could be done by taxing the ingredient from which it is made. That tax might be collected at the place where the molasses is produced, or, if the circumstances of the trade made such an excise unsuitable, by a duty on the molasses when it is imported into the colony where it is to be consumed. Besides the duty of one penny a gallon imposed by the British Parliament on molasses imported into America, there is already a provincial tax of this kind in Massachusetts Bay of eightpence per hogshead on molasses arriving in ships belonging to any other colony, and another in South Carolina of fivepence a gallon on molasses imported from the northern colonies. If neither of these methods proved convenient, each family might instead pay a fixed composition, or lump sum, for its consumption of the drink. This could be set according to the number of people in the household, in the way private families in England compound for the malt tax; or according to the ages and sexes of those people, as several taxes are levied in Holland; or roughly as Sir Matthew Decker proposes that all taxes on consumable goods should be levied in England, by charging the consumer directly for the right to consume them. As has already been observed, this method of taxation is not very convenient when applied to goods that are quickly consumed. It might nonetheless be adopted where nothing better could be done.

Sugar, rum, and tobacco are nowhere necessities of life, yet they have become objects of almost universal consumption, which makes them extremely suitable subjects for taxation. If a union with the colonies were to take place, these goods might be taxed before they left the hands of the manufacturer or grower. Or, if that method did not suit the circumstances of those people, the goods might be deposited in public warehouses, both at the place of manufacture and at every port of the empire to which they might later be shipped. There they would remain, under the joint custody of the owner and the revenue officer, until they were released either to the consumer, to a retailer selling for domestic consumption, or to an exporting merchant, and the tax would not be paid until that release. Goods released for export would go duty-free, on condition that proper security was given that they really would be shipped out of the empire. These are perhaps the principal commodities for which a union with the colonies might require any considerable change in the present British system of taxation.

It must, of course, be quite impossible to determine with any reasonable precision how much revenue this system of taxation would produce if extended to every province of the empire. Under it, more than ten million pounds of revenue are raised each year in Great Britain from fewer than eight million people. Ireland contains more than two million people, and according to the figures laid before the Congress, the twelve associated provinces of America contain more than three million. Those figures, however, may have been exaggerated, perhaps either to encourage their own people or to intimidate ours. Let us suppose, therefore, that our North American and West Indian colonies together contain no more than three million people, so that the whole British Empire in Europe and America contains no more than thirteen million inhabitants. If this system of taxation raises more than ten million pounds sterling from fewer than eight million inhabitants, it ought to raise more than sixteen million two hundred and fifty thousand pounds from thirteen million. From this revenue, supposing the system could produce it, we must subtract the revenue ordinarily raised in Ireland and the plantations to pay for their respective civil governments.
