The cost of the civil and military establishment of Ireland, together with the interest on its public debt, averaged somewhat less than seven hundred and fifty thousand pounds a year over the two years ending in March 1775. According to a very exact account of the revenue of the principal colonies of America and the West Indies, that revenue amounted, before the present disturbances began, to one hundred and forty-one thousand eight hundred pounds. This account, however, leaves out the revenue of Maryland, of North Carolina, and of all our recent acquisitions, both on the continent and among the islands, which may amount to a difference of thirty or forty thousand pounds. For the sake of round numbers, then, let us suppose that the revenue needed to support the civil governments of Ireland and the plantations comes to a million. That would leave fifteen million two hundred and fifty thousand pounds to be applied to the general expenses of the empire and to the payment of the public debt. And if, from the present revenue of Great Britain, a million can be spared in peacetime toward paying that debt, six million two hundred and fifty thousand pounds could easily be spared from this enlarged revenue. This great sinking fund, moreover, could be increased every year by the interest on whatever part of the debt had been paid off the year before. In this way it might grow so rapidly that within a few years it would be enough to discharge the entire debt, and so fully restore the strength of the empire, now weakened and languishing. Meanwhile the people could be relieved of some of the most oppressive taxes, namely those imposed on the necessities of life or on the raw materials of manufacture. The laboring poor would then be able to live better, to work for lower wages, and to bring their goods to market more cheaply. The cheapness of those goods would increase the demand for them, and therefore for the labor of the people who made them. This greater demand for labor would both increase the numbers of the laboring poor and improve their condition. Their consumption would rise, and with it the revenue from every article of their consumption on which taxes were allowed to remain.

The revenue from this system of taxation, however, might not immediately increase in proportion to the number of people brought under it. For some time, considerable leniency would be owed to those provinces of the empire that were being made to bear burdens they had not been accustomed to. And even once the same taxes were being levied everywhere as strictly as possible, they would not everywhere yield a revenue proportional to the population. In a poor country, consumption of the principal goods subject to customs and excise duties is very small, and in a thinly populated country the opportunities for smuggling are very great. Among the lower ranks of people in Scotland, the consumption of malt liquors is very small, and the excise on malt, beer, and ale yields less there than in England relative to the population and to the rates of duty, which in the case of malt differ between the two countries on account of a supposed difference in quality. In these particular branches of the excise, I do not believe there is much more smuggling in one country than in the other. But the duties on distilling, and most of the customs duties, yield less in Scotland than in England relative to population, not only because less of the taxed goods is consumed but also because smuggling is much easier. In Ireland the lower ranks of people are poorer still than in Scotland, and many parts of the country are nearly as thinly populated. In Ireland, therefore, consumption of the taxed goods relative to population might be even smaller than in Scotland, while the ease of smuggling would be about the same. In America and the West Indies, by contrast, white people even of the lowest rank are far better off than people of the same rank in England, and they probably consume much more of all the luxuries in which they commonly indulge. The Black inhabitants, it is true, who make up the greater part of the population both of the southern colonies on the continent and of the West India islands, are held in slavery and are no doubt in a worse condition than the poorest people of Scotland or Ireland. We should not conclude from this, however, that they are worse fed, or that they consume fewer goods that might bear moderate duties than even the lower ranks of people in England. It is in their master's interest that they be well fed and kept in good spirits so that they will work well, in the same way that it is in his interest to keep his working cattle in good condition. Accordingly, nearly everywhere they receive their allowance of rum, and of molasses or spruce beer, just as white servants do, and that allowance would probably not be withdrawn even if those articles were subjected to moderate duties. Consumption of the taxed goods relative to population would therefore probably be as great in America and the West Indies as in any part of the British Empire. The opportunities for smuggling, admittedly, would be much greater, since America, relative to the size of the country, is far more thinly populated than either Scotland or Ireland. Yet if the revenue now raised by the various duties on malt and malt liquors were instead collected through a single duty on malt, the opportunity for smuggling in the most important branch of the excise would be almost entirely removed. And if customs duties, instead of being imposed on nearly every kind of import, were confined to a few articles of the most general use and consumption, and if their collection were placed under the excise laws, the opportunity for smuggling, though not removed so completely, would be greatly reduced. As a result of these two apparently very simple and easy changes, the duties of customs and excise might well produce a revenue as large, relative to consumption in the most thinly populated province, as they now produce relative to consumption in the most populous.

It has been objected that the Americans have no gold or silver money, since the internal commerce of the country is carried on with paper currency, and whatever gold and silver occasionally reach them are all sent to Great Britain in payment for the goods they receive from us. Without gold and silver, the objection continues, there is no way to pay taxes. We already receive all the gold and silver they have. How can we possibly draw from them what they do not have?

The present scarcity of gold and silver money in America is not the result of the country's poverty, nor of the people's inability to buy those metals. In a country where wages are so much higher, and the price of food so much lower, than in England, most people must surely have the means to buy more of them, if doing so were either necessary or convenient. The scarcity of those metals must therefore be a matter of choice, not of necessity.

Gold and silver money is necessary or convenient only for carrying on domestic or foreign business.

As was shown in the second book of this Inquiry, the domestic business of any country can be carried on, at least in peacetime, with paper currency nearly as conveniently as with gold and silver. The Americans could always invest more capital at a profit in improving their land than they can readily obtain, and so it suits them to save as far as possible the expense of so costly an instrument of commerce as gold and silver. They prefer to use the portion of their surplus produce that would be needed to buy those metals in buying instead the tools of their trades, materials for clothing, various kinds of household furniture, and the ironwork needed to build and extend their settlements and plantations: in buying, that is, not dead stock but active and productive stock. The colonial governments find it in their interest to supply the people with enough paper money to carry on their domestic business, and generally more than enough. Some of those governments, Pennsylvania's in particular, earn a revenue by lending this paper money to their citizens at a certain rate of interest. Others, like that of Massachusetts Bay, issue paper money of this kind in emergencies to pay public expenses, and later, when it suits the colony, redeem it at the depreciated value to which it has gradually fallen. In 1747 that colony paid off the greater part of its public debts in this way, with one-tenth of the money for which its bills had been issued. It suits the planters to save the expense of using gold and silver in their domestic dealings, and it suits the colonial governments to provide them with a medium of exchange that, though it carries some very considerable disadvantages, allows them to save that expense. The excess of paper money necessarily drives gold and silver out of the domestic transactions of the colonies, for the same reason that it has driven those metals out of most domestic transactions in Scotland. In both countries the cause of this excess is not poverty but the enterprising, venturesome spirit of the people, and their desire to employ all the capital they can obtain as active and productive stock.

In the external commerce that the various colonies carry on with Great Britain, gold and silver are used more or less exactly in proportion to how necessary they are. Where they are not needed, they seldom appear. Where they are needed, they are generally found.

In the trade between Great Britain and the tobacco colonies, British goods are usually advanced to the colonists on fairly long credit and are later paid for in tobacco, valued at an agreed price. The colonists find it more convenient to pay in tobacco than in gold and silver. Any merchant would find it more convenient to pay for the goods his suppliers had sold him in some other kind of goods that he happened to deal in, rather than in money. Such a merchant would not need to keep any part of his capital idle, in ready cash, to meet occasional demands. He could hold a larger stock of goods in his shop or warehouse at all times, and could trade on a larger scale. But it is seldom convenient for all of a merchant's suppliers to be paid for what they sell him in some other kind of goods that he happens to handle. The British merchants who trade with Virginia and Maryland, however, happen to be a particular group of suppliers who find it more convenient to be paid for the goods they sell to those colonies in tobacco than in gold and silver. They expect to make a profit by selling the tobacco; they could make none by selling gold and silver. Gold and silver, therefore, very rarely appear in the trade between Great Britain and the tobacco colonies. Maryland and Virginia have as little need for those metals in their foreign trade as in their domestic trade. They are accordingly said to have less gold and silver money than any other colonies in America, and yet they are reckoned as thriving, and therefore as rich, as any of their neighbors.

In the northern colonies of Pennsylvania, New York, New Jersey, the four governments of New England, and others, the value of the produce they export to Great Britain does not equal that of the manufactured goods they import, both for their own use and for that of some other colonies for which they act as carriers. A balance must therefore be paid to the mother country in gold and silver, and they generally find the means to pay it.

In the sugar colonies, the value of the produce exported each year to Great Britain is much greater than that of all the goods imported from it. If the sugar and rum sent each year to the mother country were paid for in those colonies, Great Britain would be obliged to send out a very large balance in money every year, and the West Indian trade would be regarded by a certain kind of politician as extremely disadvantageous. But it happens that many of the principal owners of the sugar plantations live in Great Britain. Their rents are sent to them in sugar and rum, the produce of their estates. The sugar and rum that the West India merchants buy in those colonies on their own account are not equal in value to the goods they sell there each year. A balance must therefore be paid to them in gold and silver, and this balance too is generally found.

The difficulty and irregularity of payments from the various colonies to Great Britain have not corresponded at all to the size of the balances each owed. Payments have generally been more regular from the northern colonies than from the tobacco colonies, even though the northern colonies have usually paid a fairly large balance in money, while the tobacco colonies have paid either no balance or a much smaller one. The difficulty of obtaining payment from our various sugar colonies has varied not so much with the size of the balances each owed as with the amount of uncultivated land each contained; that is, with the greater or lesser temptation the planters have been under to overextend themselves, by undertaking to settle and plant more waste land than their capital could support. For this reason, the returns from the great island of Jamaica, where much land remains uncultivated, have generally been more irregular and uncertain than those from the smaller islands of Barbados, Antigua, and St. Christopher's, which have for many years now been completely cultivated, and which have therefore offered the planter less room for speculation. The newly acquired islands of Grenada, Tobago, St. Vincent, and Dominica have opened a fresh field for speculation of this kind, and the returns from those islands have lately been as irregular and uncertain as those from the great island of Jamaica.

It is not, then, the poverty of the colonies that explains the present scarcity of gold and silver coin in most of them. Their heavy demand for active, productive capital makes it convenient for them to keep as little "dead stock" as possible, meaning wealth that lies idle and produces nothing, as coin does while it merely circulates. This inclines them to settle for a cheaper, though less convenient, medium of exchange than gold and silver. They are thereby able to convert the value of that gold and silver into the tools of trade, into materials for clothing, into household furniture, and into the ironwork needed to build and extend their settlements and plantations. In those lines of business that cannot be carried on without gold and silver coin, they always seem able to find the necessary quantity of those metals. When they frequently fail to find it, the failure is generally the result not of any unavoidable poverty but of unnecessary and excessive enterprise. Their payments are irregular and uncertain not because they are poor, but because they are too eager to grow excessively rich. Even if all the colonial tax revenue beyond what was needed to pay for their own civil and military establishments were sent to Great Britain in gold and silver, the colonies would have ample means to buy the required quantity of those metals. In that case they would indeed have to exchange part of the surplus produce with which they now buy active and productive capital for dead stock. In conducting their domestic business, they would have to use a costly instrument of commerce instead of a cheap one, and the expense of acquiring that costly instrument might somewhat dampen the energy and ardor of their excessive enterprise in improving land. It might not, however, be necessary to remit any part of the American revenue in gold and silver at all. It could be sent in the form of bills of exchange drawn upon, and accepted by, particular merchants or companies in Great Britain to whom part of America's surplus produce had been consigned. Having already received the value of that revenue in goods, these merchants would then pay it into the Treasury in money, and the whole transaction might often be completed without a single ounce of gold or silver leaving America.

It is not unjust that both Ireland and America should contribute toward paying off the public debt of Great Britain. That debt was incurred in support of the government established by the Revolution of 1688. To that government the Protestants of Ireland owe not only the whole of the authority they now enjoy in their own country, but every security they possess for their liberty, their property, and their religion. To that same government several of the American colonies owe their present charters, and therefore their present constitutions, and all of the American colonies owe the liberty, security, and property they have enjoyed ever since. The public debt was incurred in the defense not of Great Britain alone but of every province of the empire. The immense debt contracted in the late war in particular, and a large part of the debt contracted in the war before it, were both properly incurred in the defense of America.

By a union with Great Britain, Ireland would gain, in addition to freedom of trade, other advantages far more important, advantages that would much more than compensate for any increase in taxes that might accompany such a union. Through its union with England, the middle and lower ranks of people in Scotland were completely delivered from the power of an aristocracy that had always oppressed them. Through a union with Great Britain, most of the people of every rank in Ireland would gain an equally complete deliverance from a far more oppressive aristocracy. The Irish aristocracy is not founded, like the Scottish one, on the natural and respectable distinctions of birth and fortune, but on the most odious of all distinctions: those of religious and political prejudice. More than any other kind, these distinctions inflame both the insolence of the oppressors and the hatred and indignation of the oppressed, and they commonly make the inhabitants of a single country more hostile to one another than the inhabitants of different countries ever are. Without a union with Great Britain, the people of Ireland are unlikely, for many generations, to regard themselves as one people.

No oppressive aristocracy has ever prevailed in the colonies. Yet even they would gain considerably in happiness and tranquillity from a union with Great Britain. At the very least, it would deliver them from the rancorous and venomous factions that are inseparable from small democracies, factions that have so often divided the loyalties of their people and disturbed the peace of their governments, which are so nearly democratic in form. In the event of a complete separation from Great Britain, which seems very likely to happen unless a union of this kind prevents it, those factions would become ten times more venomous than ever. Before the present disturbances began, the coercive power of the mother country had always been able to keep those factions from breaking out into anything worse than gross brutality and insult. If that coercive power were removed entirely, they would probably soon break out into open violence and bloodshed. In all great countries united under a single, uniform government, the spirit of party commonly runs less strongly in the remote provinces than at the center of the empire. The distance of those provinces from the capital, the principal seat of the great scramble of faction and ambition, makes them less invested in the aims of any of the contending parties, and renders them more indifferent and impartial spectators of the conduct of all. The spirit of party runs less strongly in Scotland than in England. In the event of a union, it would probably run less strongly in Ireland than in Scotland, and the colonies would probably soon enjoy a degree of concord and unanimity at present unknown in any part of the British Empire. It is true that both Ireland and the colonies would be subjected to heavier taxes than any they now pay. But if the public revenue were diligently and faithfully applied to paying off the national debt, most of those taxes might not last long, and the public revenue of Great Britain might soon be reduced to what was needed to maintain a moderate peacetime establishment.

The territorial acquisitions of the East India Company, which belong by undoubted right to the Crown, that is, to the state and people of Great Britain, might be made into yet another source of revenue, perhaps more abundant than all those already mentioned. Those lands are described as more fertile and more extensive than Great Britain, and, in proportion to their size, much richer and more populous. To draw a great revenue from them, it would probably not be necessary to introduce any new system of taxation into countries that are already sufficiently, indeed more than sufficiently, taxed. It might be more proper to lighten rather than increase the burden on those unfortunate countries, and to try to draw a revenue from them not by imposing new taxes but by preventing the embezzlement and misuse of most of the taxes they already pay.

If it should prove impossible for Great Britain to obtain any considerable increase in revenue from any of the sources mentioned above, the only resource left to her is a reduction of her expenses. In the way she collects public revenue and in the way she spends it, Great Britain seems to be at least as economical as any of her neighbors, though in both there may still be room for improvement. The military establishment she maintains for her own defense in peacetime is more moderate than that of any European state that can claim to rival her in wealth or power. None of these items, therefore, seems to allow any considerable reduction in expense. The cost of the colonies' peacetime establishment, however, was very considerable before the present disturbances began, and it is an expense that may, and, if no revenue can be drawn from the colonies, certainly ought to be eliminated altogether. This constant peacetime expense, great as it is, is insignificant compared with what the defense of the colonies has cost us in time of war. The last war, which was undertaken entirely on account of the colonies, cost Great Britain, as already observed, more than ninety million pounds. The Spanish war of 1739 was undertaken principally on their account, and in that war and the French war that followed from it, Great Britain spent more than forty million pounds, a large part of which ought fairly to be charged to the colonies. In those two wars the colonies cost Great Britain much more than double the whole national debt as it stood before the first of them began. Had it not been for those wars, that debt might, and probably would, have been completely paid off by now; and had it not been for the colonies, the first of those wars might not have been undertaken, and the second certainly would not have been. This expense was laid out on the colonies because they were supposed to be provinces of the British Empire. But countries that contribute neither revenue nor military force to the support of the empire cannot be considered provinces. They may perhaps be considered appendages, a sort of splendid and showy equipage of the empire, like the ornate carriage, horses, and liveried servants that a great household keeps for display. But if the empire can no longer afford to keep up this equipage, it ought certainly to give it up; and if it cannot raise its revenue in proportion to its expense, it ought at least to adjust its expense to its revenue. If the colonies, despite their refusal to submit to British taxes, are still to be treated as provinces of the British Empire, their defense in some future war may cost Great Britain as much as it has in any previous war. For more than a century, the rulers of Great Britain have entertained the people with the notion that they possessed a great empire on the western side of the Atlantic. Yet this empire has so far existed only in the imagination. It has been not an empire but the project of an empire; not a gold mine but the project of a gold mine. It is a project that has cost, continues to cost, and, if pursued as it has been until now, is likely to go on costing immense sums without any likelihood of bringing a profit, for the effects of the monopoly of the colony trade, as has been shown, are to the great body of the people a pure loss rather than a profit. Surely it is now time for our rulers either to make real this golden dream, in which they have perhaps indulged themselves as much as the people, or to wake from it themselves and try to wake the people. If the project cannot be completed, it ought to be abandoned. If any of the provinces of the British Empire cannot be made to contribute toward the support of the whole, it is surely time for Great Britain to free herself from the expense of defending those provinces in time of war and of supporting any part of their civil or military establishments in time of peace, and to try to fit her future aims and designs to the real, modest scale of her circumstances.
